papers.node_id: 24geojlegalethics357!!ARTICLE: A Crisis of Confidence and Legal Theory: Why the Economic Downturn Should Help Signal the End of the Doctrine of Efficient Breach
papers.title: ARTICLE: A Crisis of Confidence and Legal Theory: Why the Economic Downturn Should Help Signal the End of the Doctrine of Efficient Breach
papers.abstract:
The doctrine of efficient breach is a common feature of a first-year foundational course in contract law.In what follows, I argue that this familiar doctrine should be condemned, if not discarded.
An efficient breach compels, or at least encourages or invites, a party to intentionally break a contract if he can enter into a second more profitable one and remain better off after compensating the non-breaching party.An efficient breach is said to take place when, for example, A agrees to give B a widget for $ 1, C subsequently offers A $ 3 for the same widget, A breaches his contract with B who suffers $ .50 in damages, and A takes the deal with C--at the end of the day, A will pay B $ 1.50 and keep $ 1.50, thereby increasing his profit ($ 1.50 versus $ 1).The breach is considered "efficient" in these circumstances because the breaching party (A) is in a better economic position; the good, service, or entitlement contracted for (the widget) is put to higher use and resides with theparty that values it more (C), as reflected in the higher purchase price; and the non-breaching party (B) is compensated in lieu of performance.Because of the higher profit resulting from these exchanges, an efficient breach is thought to enhance not only individual pockets but net social wealth as well--"[s]ociety is also better off."
The doctrine of efficient breach is championed by law and economics scholars,who are members of a school of thought that generally believes that the law should be informed by descriptive economic principles and seeks to build a stronger link between the two disciplines as a result.In addition to touting the economic justifications of an efficient breach, these scholars eschew any moralobjections to the doctrine. They emphasize that, as the damages remedy for a breach of contract is compensatory in nature regardless of the breaching party's motive, a party to a contract may breach unilaterally for selfish reasons without incurring any different or additional penalty.As the compensation does not depend on the intent of the breaching party, whether an efficient breach is "right" or "wrong" are, according to economic theorists, moral questions outside of the ambit of--and not a relevant consideration in--contract law.
In 2006, I published an article arguing against the propriety of the doctrine of efficient breach.In particular, I posited that an efficient breach is morally problematic because it degrades contracts as well as the social cooperation and mutual trust that are necessary for individuals to voluntarily commit to do or not do something.Further, an efficient breach, as traditionally defined, is not efficient at a micro level, because a non-breaching party is not fully compensated for his losses, and is not efficient at a macro level, because such a strategic breach leads to a discounting of goods, services, and entitlements in the market due to the possibility that a contracting party may not perform in order to take advantage of a new, "better" deal.In other words, even assuming that morality is immaterial to an assessment of the doctrine, the doctrine is inefficient on its advocates' own economic terms.
The article was written in the era of Enron and similar corporations who had used creative accounting techniques to artificially inflate their respective stock prices and, consequently, their resultant worth and executive officers' pay. The exposure of these accounting irregularities and the attendant exaggerated income statements took down not only these specific companies, but the soundness and stability of the stock market as well. While this fallout was relevant to my discussion of the efficient breach theory, it supplied only the backdrop for the general notion that the short-sighted and selfish economic behavior of a few may have significantly deleterious impacts on practically all others, and at mostprovided thematic support for my substantive attack on the doctrine.
The economic situation since then is as well known as it is bleak. America has experienced the longest and most severe economic turmoil since the Great Depression.To wit, in early 2010 the national unemployment rate was in double digits, 14.8 million Americans were unemployed, and another 9.4 million were "underemployed."On the global scale, the World Bank has predicted the largest decline in global trade in eighty years and projected the likely loss around the world in dollars to exceed $ 50 trillion--more than global gross domestic product.The primary cause for this significant downturn is no secret: the collapse of innovative financial instruments that were backed by subprime mortgages.
While the corporate accounting fiascos of the last decade provided context to my take on efficient breaches, it is my sense that the present economic crisis resulting from reckless subprime lending and related collateralization practices provides evidence that the doctrine of efficient breach should be condemned and discarded. The purpose of this Article is to explore these two related topics: the merits of the doctrine in light of the present economic climate and the commensurate impropriety of its open advancement by law and economics scholars.
To understand subprime behavior and efficient breaches, it is imperative to first examine the necessary social predicate for economic transactions. Accordingly, Part I will offer an overview of society and the market, highlighting the importance of reciprocity and trust to both. Part II will define the economic transactions implicated by this Article: basic contracting, efficient breach of contract, and the subprime behavior of the current economic crisis. The discussion of subprime behavior in this section will include a description not only of its contents but also its consequences on society and the market, including a depletion of the trust and confidence required for a functioning economy and productive society.
Part III will make explicit the nexus between subprime behavior and efficient breaches by explaining that subprime behavior and efficient breaches are linked by shared elements; they are opportunistic in nature, are interested in unilateral gain, involve solely short-term thinking without consideration of long-term effects, completely disregard any widespread third-party or broader social consequences, and entail significant negative externalities. The results of subprime activity suggest that economic behavior possessing these traits diminishes trust in other market participants and in the financial instruments that are designed to facilitate reliable social cooperation. Given these economic and social consequences, I argue that the doctrine of efficient breach should be disapproved as a legal theory, its open promotion discouraged, and at a minimum its discussion tempered by an honest admission of its deficiencies and practical limitations.
My objections to the doctrine stem from the doctrine's essence--an unmitigated selfishness, myopia, and neglect for adverse consequences on others--and a broader economic culture in which individuals believe they are immune from any culpability or social responsibility because their underlying actions are technically legal and perhaps rational on an individual scale. This opportunism, combined with the formal and intellectual cover provided to it, emboldens financial actors to the inevitable detriment of the economy and members of our society. It is the doctrine's contribution to a destructive ethos in which unabashed individual financial enrichment is pursued at the expense of the greater good and at the risk of systemic breakdowns in the economy that is at the heart of my concern.
This Article will be permeated by two considerations. First, that individual and collective psychology, and human nature generally, play a critical role in economic behavior and the fluctuations in the economy. Concepts such as confidence and trust, for example, will help explain the dangers of subprime activity and the doctrine of efficient breach. Second, that as a result, social norms related to proper individual or corporate conduct can direct economic behavior even as we await modified regulatory regimes or stricter formal legal constraints on economic actors.
In arguing against the doctrine, I realize that I am trekking an uphill climb. Law and economics "has become, by almost any measure, the most dominant school of legal thought in the last half a century."The extent to which efficient breach is ingrained in first-year law school curricula demonstrates its prevalencein legal academia.If an idea within the law and economics movement may be significantly detrimental to society either in value-based or economic terms, it becomes necessary to remonstrate with the legal community about this idea precisely because of, not in spite of, the familiarity doctrine or the clout of the movement itself. As no other scholarship has addressed squarely the doctrine of efficient breach as it relates to the current economic decline, and as I have addressed the doctrine in the past, I am inclined to take on this formidable path.
hope the substance of this Article will generate agreement that the doctrine, because of its potential adverse consequences, should be put to rest. If not, this Article hopefully will stimulate a robust conversation on whether we should move in that that direction.

papers.node_id: 116yaleljonline423!!ARTICLE: A Critique of the Efficient Performance Hypothesis
papers.title: ARTICLE: A Critique of the Efficient Performance Hypothesis
papers.abstract:
The classic economic justification of contract law's default remedy of expectation damages is grounded on the efficient breach hypothesis: that promisors should be permitted and encouraged to breach when the net gains from breach exceed the net gains from performance. Expectation damages ensure that all and only efficient breaches will occur because promisors will find breach profitable only if its benefits exceed the value of performance to the promisee. The efficient breach hypothesis, and the defense of expectation damages that rests on it, has long been criticized for being inconsistent with the moral intuition that promisors necessarily forfeit their right to choose not to perform their promise. In his essay,The Efficient Performance Hypothesis,Richard Brooks claims that the theory of financial options can be used to identify a new contract remedy that respects the promisee's moral right to performance without sacrificing the efficiency goal served by expectation damages. In this Response, I argue that options theory is irrelevant to the debate Brooks engages, that the moral objection motivating Brooks's new remedy is itself unmotivated, and that Brooks's remedy is likely to be less efficient than expectation damages.
At bottom, the moral critics of expectation damages reject Holmes's famous claim that a promise imposes an obligation on the promisor to choose whether to perform or pay damages. On Holmes's view, a promise to do X is interpreted, by default, as a promise to do X or pay damages. The moral critics, however, argue that there is a crucial moral difference between a promise to do X and a promise to do X or pay a sum of money. If a promisor makes the first promise, his failure to do X is morally wrong, even if he pays a sum of moneyto the promisee. The payment of money in this case at best constitutes damages for breach of promise. If a promisor makes the second promise, his failure to do X is morally permissible provided he pays the sum of money. Rather than constituting damages for breach, the payment of money in this case constitutes performance.
More than twenty-five years ago, Alan Schwartz presented the first sustained economic argument for an alternative to the expectation default remedy that would grant promisees the right to elect either specific performance or expectation damages.Although Schwartz was principally concerned to demonstrate that such a rule was more efficient than the expectancy default rule, he also noted that the same moral argument made against expectation damages argued in favor of his proposed rule:
[I]f the compensation goal rests on a moral notion that promises should be kept, that contract remedies should effectuate the state of affairs--performance--that the promisor has a duty to bring about and that the promisee has a right to have brought about, then specific performance is a preferable remedy to damages even though it might generate higher costs. These costs would be the price of achieving the moral goal of contract remedies.
In his essay,The Efficient Performance Hypothesis,Richard Brooks expands on Schwartz's insights, arguing that the feature of Schwartz's rule that explains its moral appeal is a formal one that defines an entire class of contract remedies overlooked before Schwartz's article and under-appreciated since. Following a well-developed literature applying finance theory to contract law, Brooks explains that the expectation damages rule can be viewed as giving the promisor a "call option" because it entitles the promisor, rather than the promisee, to decide whether he will perform or breach and pay damages. Brooks argues that the novelty of Schwartz's rule is that, unlike a call option, in the event of breach it entitles the promisee to choose between requiring the promisor to pay damages and forcing the promisor to perform. Brooks then claims that Schwartz's rule can be understood as giving a "put option" to the promisee because it entitles the promisee to compel the promisor to purchase the promisee's right to performance for an amount equal to the promisee's expectancy damages. Brooks's general thesis is that contract remedies that have the form of a put option, unlike those that have the form of a call option, are consistent with the moral intuition that the promisee, and not the promisor, should be entitled to choose whether the promisor will perform his promise.However, Brooks argues that Schwartz's rule violates the ex post efficiency criterion of the efficient breach hypothesis because its damages component, expectation damages, does not force the promisee to internalize the opportunity costs of the promisor. As a result, the promisee might choose specific performance even when it would be more efficient for the promisor to pursue an exclusive alternative to performance.
Brooks claims, however, that the defect in Schwartz's rule is not endemic to the entire class of contract remedies that have the form of a put option. Indeed, Brooks proposes a modification to the damage component (the put option) in Schwartz's rule that he claims makes it just as ex post efficient as the expectation remedy. Instead of measuring damages by the promisee's expectancy, Brook's rule awards an amount equal to the difference between the promisor's expected gains from its best alternative to performance and its expected gains from performance. Brooks calls the damage component of his modified rule a "disgorgement" remedy because it requires the promisor to disgorge any gains from nonperformance. But unlike the traditional disgorgement remedy, Brooks's version does not require that the promisor actually benefit from breach and then disgorge his gains. Instead, it entitles the promisee to the gain the promisor would have realized had he breached and devoted his contractual resources to his best alternative to performance. For clarity, therefore, I will refer to Brooks's proposed damage measure as "hypothetical disgorgement." Since his rule assigns the right to performance to the promisee, Brooks rests its defense on the "efficient performance hypothesis," which claims that, unlike the efficient breach hypothesis, his rule will satisfy the demands of morality as well as ex post efficiency.

questions.question: Whether granting the promisee the unilateral right to demand performance (or to elect an alternative damages measure that captures the promisor's forgone gains) can vindicate moral intuitions about promises while preserving ex post economic efficiency relative to standard monetary damages.

Whether concepts from financial options theory provide a relevant and useful framework for analyzing and designing contract remedies that allocate the decision to perform or breach between promisor and promisee.

Whether the moral claim that a promise to perform is qualitatively different from a promise to perform-or-pay provides a justified basis for preferring performance-favoring remedies even if they may reduce economic efficiency.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 117yaleljpocketpart14!!ARTICLE: What Efficiency Demands: The Efficient Performance Hypothesis Defended
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: What Efficiency Demands: The Efficient Performance Hypothesis Defended

shared_topics.topic: efficient breach versus efficient performance as competing frameworks for contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes Brooks' efficient performance hypothesis and defends the traditional efficient breach justification for expectation damages, while Paper B elaborates and defends the efficient performance hypothesis as an alternative way to reconcile allocative efficiency with different moral conceptions of entitlement.

shared_topics.topic: the comparative roles of expectation damages and specific performance in achieving efficient outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how expectation damages (the default) compare to rules that allow promisees to elect specific performance or damages, arguing expectation damages better secures efficiency; Paper B analyzes how specific performance functions economically under both regimes and argues remedies can be structured to achieve allocative efficiency regardless of which side holds the entitlement.

shared_topics.topic: the use of financial-options analogies (call/put) and the proposal of disgorgement/hypothetical disgorgement as damage measures
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques Brooks' use of call/put option language and his hypothetical disgorgement damage measure as irrelevant or inefficient, whereas Paper B (Brooks) advances and defends the option-theoretic framing and disgorgement-style measures as a way to reassign the choice over performance while preserving efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: who legally/morally holds the entitlement or option to choose performance versus breach (the Holmesian option and its critique)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses moral critics who reject Holmes's claim that promisors implicitly have the option to perform or pay, and challenges Brooks' reallocation of that entitlement; Paper B centers its argument on contrasting moral/entitlement views (promisor versus promisee right to choose nonperformance) and shows how either allocation can be made consistent with efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: ex post allocative efficiency and the empirical indeterminacy of which remedy is optimal
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues Brooks' modified remedy may fail ex post efficiency and critiques its practical effects, while Paper B acknowledges numerous empirical variables and bargaining-cost considerations that make analytical superiority of one remedy over another indeterminate and contingent on context.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 82columlrev1365!!ARTICLE: In Defense of Money Damages for Breach of Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: In Defense of Money Damages for Breach of Contract

shared_topics.topic: moral obligation of promise and its implications for remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both papers interrogate whether promises generate a special moral duty to perform that should influence remedy choice — Paper A critiques attempts (via Brooks and Schwartz) to redesign remedies to honor a promisee's moral right to performance, while Paper B discusses how specific performance strengthens the ethical notion that promisors ought to keep their word and evaluates that moral argument for changing default rules.

shared_topics.topic: comparative economic efficiency of expectation damages versus specific performance
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the economic question of which remedy better promotes efficient outcomes — Paper A contrasts the efficient breach hypothesis with Brooks's 'efficient performance' claim and analyzes ex post efficiency implications of alternative remedies, while Paper B assesses the literature claiming specific performance would be more efficient than money damages and argues for why money damages better serve efficiency in many contexts.

shared_topics.topic: who should have the choice to enforce performance (default rule design)
shared_topics.justification: Both examine whether the default allocation of enforcement choice should favor the promisor (as under expectation damages) or the promisee (as under rules like Schwartz's electable specific performance), with Paper A analyzing option-theory framings (call vs put) and Paper B debating whether promisees should routinely be able to demand specific performance.

shared_topics.topic: how damages should be measured or redesigned to achieve policy goals
shared_topics.justification: Both papers consider alternative damage measures and rule design — Paper A analyzes Brooks's proposed 'hypothetical disgorgement' and how altering the damage metric affects incentives, while Paper B explores modifying money-damages rules to address cases where compensating subjective loss is difficult and to preserve flexibility over an across-the-board shift to specific performance.

shared_topics.topic: trade-offs between moral aims, fairness, and administrative/practical consequences of remedy rules
shared_topics.justification: Both address the tension between satisfying moral intuitions about promise-keeping and the practical risks or costs of changing remedial regimes — Paper A argues the moral critique is unmotivated and that Brooks's remedy may be less efficient, and Paper B emphasizes fairness, error risk, and loss of flexibility if specific performance became the normal remedy.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 73washulq145!!ARTICLE: THE FALLACY OF FULL COMPENSATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE FALLACY OF FULL COMPENSATION

shared_topics.topic: whether specific performance (full compensation) should be the default or more widely available than expectation damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages this by evaluating Schwartz's proposal (and Brooks's variant) to give promisees stronger rights to performance and arguing that expectation damages better preserve ex post efficiency; Paper B addresses the same question by defending the law's reluctance to award full compensation and arguing that prohibitory remedies should be limited for practical and normative reasons.

shared_topics.topic: efficiency, deterrence, and transaction-cost tradeoffs between damages and prohibitory remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on ex post efficiency concerns—arguing that put-style remedies or hypothetical disgorgement can distort promisor opportunity-cost incentives—while Paper B systematically analyzes whether prohibitory remedies actually improve deterrence or social wealth compared with damages and whether transaction-cost explanations suffice.

shared_topics.topic: the conceptual framing of remedies as pricing/call options versus prohibitory/put options and the resulting allocation of choice rights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly applies option theory (call vs put) to show how expectation damages grant the promisor the choice to breach while put-like rules give the promisee choice, and Paper B advances a closely related dichotomy between 'pricing' remedies (damages) and 'prohibitory' remedies (specific performance, injunctions) and examines the consequences of that classification.

shared_topics.topic: normative/moral arguments about the nature of promises and redistributional consequences of awarding performance versus money
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates moral criticisms of expectation damages (the view that promises morally require performance) and whether remedies should respect promisees' moral right to performance, while Paper B questions whether full compensation is normatively desirable given its redistributive effects and social costs.

shared_topics.topic: the proposal that promisees be given an election between specific performance and expectation damages (Schwartz's rule) and its practical implications
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly analyzes and critiques Schwartz's elective rule (and Brooks's modifications), arguing about its moral appeal and efficiency costs; Paper B cites Schwartz's observation as motivation to ask whether the law should commit to full compensation and develops a descriptive and normative account of why the elective/full-compensation approach is not routinely adopted.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 117yaleljpocketpart14!!ARTICLE: What Efficiency Demands: The Efficient Performance Hypothesis Defended
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: What Efficiency Demands: The Efficient Performance Hypothesis Defended

shared_topics.topic: the efficient breach versus efficient performance hypothesis (who holds the entitlement to choose performance or breach)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers centrally debate whether allocative efficiency is best served by a regime that gives the promisor the entitlement to choose nonperformance (the efficient breach framing) or by one that vests that entitlement in the promisee (the efficient performance framing), with Paper A criticizing the latter and Paper B defending it.

shared_topics.topic: the role and justification of expectation damages as the default remedy
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze expectation damages' capacity to produce ex post allocative efficiency and its moral implications, with Paper A defending expectation damages as efficient and morally sufficient and Paper B treating expectation damages as one economically functional remedy that can be reconfigured under different entitlement rules.

shared_topics.topic: specific performance as an economic instrument (not merely a moral remedy)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage the idea that specific performance serves an economic proxy—under one regime signaling the promisor's cost and under the other the promisee's value—and debate whether specific performance is required or merely instrumentally useful for achieving efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: the options/finance analogy for framing remedies (call/put option language and its relevance)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers use and dispute the option-theoretic framing—characterizing expectation damages as a 'call option' for promisors and put-like remedies for promisees—with Paper A challenging the relevance and implications of that analogy and Paper B defending the utility of rights-as-options language for clarifying entitlements.

shared_topics.topic: disgorgement (including Brooks's 'hypothetical disgorgement') as an alternative damages measure
shared_topics.justification: Both papers discuss disgorgement-style damages—Paper B proposing a disgorgement/hypothetical-disgorgement measure to align promisee entitlements with ex post efficiency and Paper A critiquing that measure's relevance to the debate and its likely inefficiency relative to expectation damages.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 57scallrev667!!ARTICLE: A LITTLE ESSAY IN PARTIAL DEFENSE OF THE CONTRACT-MARKET DIFFERENTIAL AS A REMEDY FOR BUYERS.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A LITTLE ESSAY IN PARTIAL DEFENSE OF THE CONTRACT-MARKET DIFFERENTIAL AS A REMEDY FOR BUYERS.

shared_topics.topic: the definition and normative aim of contract damages (what 'compensation' should mean)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly interrogates the meaning of 'compensation' and proposes an alternative definition to justify the contract–market differential as a compensatory remedy; Paper B debates whether expectation damages, disgorgement, or specific performance better realize the normative goals of contract law (compensation, moral rights, or efficiency).

shared_topics.topic: use of market-based benchmarks to measure remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends the contract–market differential by measuring buyer loss against market prices and substitute purchases, while Paper B analyzes damages rules through market-value concepts (promisor gains from alternatives, option-analogies and hypothetical disgorgement) that rely on market valuations to set monetary awards.

shared_topics.topic: theoretical critique and defense of default remedial rules in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A responds to scholarly criticisms and offers rebuttals defending the traditional contract–market differential, and Paper B critiques Richard Brooks' proposed remedy and the broader theoretical justification for expectation/default remedies, engaging in the same genre of doctrinal-theoretical argument.

shared_topics.topic: timing and informational problems in measuring damages (when and how values are fixed)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses problems arising from time lapses between contract breach, market measurement, and resale (and how anomalous markets affect compensation), and Paper B similarly examines ex post versus ex ante informational issues—how expected gains at breach versus later information should affect the appropriate damages measure.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: WILLFULNESS VERSUS EXPECTATION: A PROMISOR-BASED DEFENSE OF WILLFUL BREACH DOCTRINE

shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques challenges to expectation damages (defending them against alternatives like Brooks's put-option-based rule) and interrogates whether expectation damages ensure efficient breaches; Paper B treats expectation damages as the baseline remedy, analyzes occasions when courts exceed expectation (willful breach) and defends doctrines that modify/promote expectation-based outcomes for policy reasons.

shared_topics.topic: the role of moral intuitions about promise-keeping in shaping remedies (performance versus damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly addresses moral objections to expectation damages and proponents' attempts to design remedies (e.g., Schwartz/Brooks) that respect a promisee's moral right to performance; Paper B engages the moral language of 'willful breach' and evaluates whether and how moral blame should affect remedial rules, ultimately offering a non-moral justification for special treatment of certain breaches.

shared_topics.topic: remedies that strip promotors of gains (disgorgement / promisor-centered remedies) and their implications
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes Brooks's proposed 'hypothetical disgorgement' and contrasts it with expectation damages and specific performance; Paper B examines willful-breach doctrines that effectively force promisors to surrender gains (a promisor-centered expectation/disgorgement) and evaluates how such remedies operate to deter opportunistic breaches.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between ex post efficiency and ex ante incentives/commitment (when to allow breach vs deter it)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the efficient breach hypothesis and whether alternative remedies can preserve ex post efficiency while satisfying moral concerns, criticizing rules that fail to internalize promisor opportunity costs; Paper B emphasizes ex ante commitment problems and argues that heightened remedies for willful breaches improve contracting parties' ability to secure credible performance incentives even if they sometimes overcompensate ex post.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Irrevocable Gift Promises and Promises Inducing Reliance: A Mandate for the Return of the Seal in Contract Law

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that formalities (seals, irrevocable trusts, wills, and reliance-related acts) functionally substitute for consideration by providing ritual, evidentiary, and channeling proof that a donor intends to be bound; Paper B treats remedial rules (the default of expectation damages versus rules that grant specific performance or put-like rights) as institutional devices that allocate decision rights over performance and thereby signal which party the law treats as entitled to decide whether a promise will be kept.

shared_topics.topic: reassessment of orthodox contract doctrines and proposals for doctrinal alternatives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the practical role of the consideration doctrine and proposes reviving or expanding the seal and other formal devices as doctrinally coherent substitutes to create enforceable promises; Paper B critiques the efficiency justification for the expectation-damages default and proposes alternative remedial measures (put-type rights, hypothetical disgorgement) as doctrinal adjustments to better align moral intuitions and efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: the normative foundations for enforcing promises—reliance, intent, and moral claims about promise-keeping
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds enforceability in donor intent and the reliance or fiduciary contexts that make enforcement normatively and functionally appropriate, while Paper B engages the moral intuition that a promisor who undertakes an obligation may forfeit the moral right to choose nonperformance and evaluates remedies designed to respect promisee rights and moral claims.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contracting for Cooperation in Recovery

shared_topics.topic: moral versus economic justifications for remedy rules (the promisee's right to performance vs promisor's option)

shared_topics.topic: economic/instrumental analysis of how remedies shape incentives to perform, breach, or cooperate
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses nontechnical economic reasoning to show how different remedial rules (compensatory only versus penalties, termination, adverse inference) affect actors' incentives to disclose nonperformance and to cooperate in enforcement; Paper B uses economic and option-theoretic analysis to evaluate how expectation damages and put-style or disgorgement remedies alter ex post decisionmaking and the incidence of efficient breaches.

shared_topics.topic: the extent to which parties can design contract terms to alter default enforcement and the courts' role in policing those choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines contractual devices (certificates, no-obstruct clauses, liquidated damages) that parties use to secure cooperation and discusses judicial doctrines (economic loss rule, rules against penalties) that block or limit those devices; Paper B analyzes private-law alternatives to the expectation default (party-favored rules like elective specific performance or put-style remedies) and the normative and efficiency constraints on adopting such contractual or default changes.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE FAULT LINES IN CONTRACT DAMAGES

shared_topics.topic: how damage rules create incentives and affect contracting behavior (ex post efficiency and internalization of opportunity costs)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers frame remedies as incentive mechanisms — Paper A develops a fault-based taxonomy showing how different damage measures deter or encourage contracting, breach, and care, while Paper B focuses on whether alternative remedies (put-style rules or disgorgement) properly internalize promisor and promisee opportunity costs to preserve ex post efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: the normative tension between moral intuitions about promise-keeping and economic efficiency in designing contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both works engage the moral objections to expectation damages and assess whether remedies can or should reflect a promisor's moral duty to perform: Paper B directly addresses moral critiques and alternative remedies designed to vindicate a promisee's moral right to performance, and Paper A discusses normative aims of compensation (expectation, reliance, restitution) and justifies a fault-based regime as normatively appropriate because it promotes efficient contracting behavior.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DO THE RIGHT THING: INDIRECT REMEDIES IN PRIVATE LAW

shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats remedies as tools that can leave the choice to the injurer (leading to direct restoration) or induce the victim to trigger compliance, while Paper B frames remedies as conferring option‑like rights (call vs put) that determine whether the promisor or the promisee effectively decides between performance and breach.

shared_topics.topic: the role of economic efficiency (ex post and incentive effects) in choosing remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates expectation damages, Schwartz's election rule, and Brooks's hypothetical disgorgement in terms of ex post efficiency and the efficient breach/efficient performance tradeoffs, and Paper B explicitly critiques current remedies for producing inefficiencies and proposes rules intended to improve economic predictability and reduce undercompensation.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DO THE RIGHT THING: INDIRECT REMEDIES IN PRIVATE LAW

shared_topics.topic: remedies as instruments for shaping parties' incentives and behavior

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DO LIQUIDATED DAMAGES ENCOURAGE BREACH? A PSYCHOLOGICAL EXPERIMENT

papers.title: ARTICLE: A LITTLE ESSAY IN PARTIAL DEFENSE OF THE CONTRACT-MARKET DIFFERENTIAL AS A REMEDY FOR BUYERS.
papers.abstract:
The process of drafting the Article Two remedies provisions of the Uniform Commercial Code focused and intensified the position that the traditional contract-market differential measure of damagesin sale-of-goods cases is inaccurate and inconsistentwith the compensation principleof contract damages.  Theoretical discussions are in unanimous support of this criticism.Notwithstanding these theoretical objections, the courts have rather consistently applied the contract-market differential in sale-of-goods cases.
This Article offers a theoretical defense of the contract-market differential.  My position is that in almost all instances the contract-market differential provides an accurate compensatory remedy.  Quite often the buyer can establish this remedy, without prejudice to the seller, at a lower cost and with less trouble than the cover remedy.  This Article begins by analyzing the normal case in which a dealer-buyer purchases substitute goods at the market price.  In all such cases the contract-market differential provides accurate compensation.  Next, it considers cases in which the dealer-buyer makes no substitute purchase, but the relevant markets behave in a normal manner.  In these cases, too, the contract-market differential is compensatory. Then, it examines anomalous market situations.  While overcompensation is possible in these rare instances, the number of such situations is restricted and they can be further reduced by the dealer-buyer's possibility of low cost resale on the seller's market.  The Article then looks at some remaining variable goods-and-services cases in order to establish the consistency of these aforementioned conclusions.
Part of the difficulty in analyzing the compensatory accuracy of the contract-market differential involves defining "compensation" in contract damages.  In an attempt to resolve this difficulty, this Article sets forth an alternative to the traditional definition of "compensation."
Finally, this Article looks at the specific theoretical criticisms of the contract-market differential and offers some rebuttals.  Professor Peters argues that the contract-market differential is noncompensatory largely due to the time lapse between the time the contract-market differential is measured and either the time of cover or the time at which the dealer-buyer disposes of the goods.Professors Summers and White are less precise regarding the basis of their criticism, but it apparently arises from either the time lapse or the assumption of existing anomalous market conditions.Professors Simon and Novack defendthe contract-market differential remedy, but they overstate the likelihood that overcompensation might occur.  This Article presents rebuttals to all of these positions.
Thus, this Article concludes that the contract-market differential is an accurate compensatory remedy; and, while the theoretical possibility of overcompensation cannot be excluded, its occurrence is unlikely.

questions.question: Whether awarding damages equal to the difference between the contract price and the market price at the relevant time provides accurate compensation to buyers for losses arising from a seller's breach in sale-of-goods transactions.

Under what market conditions (e.g., normal versus anomalous price behavior, timing of measurement, and resale opportunities) does that market-difference damages measure lead to overcompensation or undercompensation of buyers?

Whether buyers can obtain the market-difference damages remedy at lower cost and with less difficulty (and without unfair prejudice to sellers) compared to the alternative of purchasing substitute goods as a remedial strategy.

matched_themes: What counterfactual baseline should courts use to measure plaintiffs' losses for compensation purposes?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?
When is a market-difference (market-price differential) damages measure appropriate for buyers and resellers, and under what market conditions does it overcompensate or undercompensate?
When is an indirect remedy (one that induces self-compliance) preferable to a direct remedy that delivers the outcome?
