papers.title: ARTICLE: A NIHILISTIC VIEW OF THE EFFICIENT BREACH
papers.abstract:
For forty years scholars have debated the concept of the efficient breach of contract.One would think that everything that could be said has been said except to note the futility of the discussion. Yet, recently, the debate has flared up once again.The primary focus of the exchange is whether the expectancy measure of contract damages encourages the efficient breach and the reallocation of resources to those who value them the most.It is the type of issue that legal scholars delight in--all views can be supported or refuted and the likelihood of an empirical answer is remote.ThisArticle argues that there can be no answer, not even a reliable default position.
Although expressed in terms of expectancy, in reality the discussion began when expectancy was effectively "rebranded" in the 1970s as the remedy that leads to the "efficient" breach.Until then, expectancy had been around for more than a century without causing much of a stir.As soon as it was viewed as arguably efficient, the writing began unabated. Robert Birmingham appears to have been the first to note that expectancy could also be squared with efficiency.Richard Posner along with Charles Goetz and Robert Scott echoed the same theme in the same period.In fact, two ideas blossomed from this scholarship. One was that a breach of contract could be "efficient."The other was that expectancy encouraged or allowed the efficient breach.
The rebranding of the 1970s did not please everyone and, by the early 1980s, the battle was joined.It is an odd debate for a number of reasons. Not only had expectancy been around for a very long time before becoming the focus of thousands of pages of writing, the rebranding was only that--nothing substantive changed. In other words, expectancy was and still is just that. Like so much of law and economics, the upshot of many arguments was to provide a new basis for continuing the status quo. Thus, the thousands of pages can only be explained by the discomfort with what expectancy could be viewed as signifying. This leads to the question of what thebrouhaha is about. What is the attraction? One explanation is that the concept is easy to explain and to understand and provides a portal into a host of questions that are asked more generally about the application of economics to law. It is not unique in this respect. Most of law and economics is relatively easy to grasp and raises more general issues.
Commentators fall into three categories. In one category are those who seem comfortable with the idea of an efficient breach but focus on which remedy is consistent with that outcome.Within this category the tension is usually between damages and specific performance or one of its surrogates.There have been defensesand "new defenses"of expectancy and even the possible conversion of one scholar, previously an advocate of specific performance, to a believer in expectancy.Another category is composed of those who believe that contract law has or should have a higher, or at least different, goal. They want to attribute a deontological value to a paid-for promise typically made at arm's length.Typically, they find thatthere is a moral component of promising that a focus on expectancy and efficiency neglects or even discourages.Finally, very recently, the implications of the teachings of behavioral economics and happiness studies have been applied to the issue.The efficient breach, at the very least, seems to require rationality, a concept behaviorists have shown to be rather slippery.Recent studies of happiness have revealed how little we actually understand about what makes people feel better off.This means the concept of efficiency cannot be pinned down with certainty. Even more troubling is the question of how to achieve it.
This Article explains why the illusion of efficiency can be traced to the limited scope of prior analyses. For example, there has not been sufficient focus on the problems of false positives and negatives created by expectancy and specific performance.A false positive is an incorrect belief that a breach is efficient; a false negative is an incorrect belief that a breach would be inefficient. This problem and the ultimate indeterminacy of the efficient breach are linked to two additional failures. First, damages for breach of contract are often seen as existing for the purpose of compensating the non-breaching party.In fact, from an economic perspective, the question is whether the breaching party internalizes the cost of the breach. Perhaps more pressing, the typical analysis does not examine the impact of the payment of damages on firms downstream from the breaching party.In other words, a breach does not affect only those who are parties to the contract. Yet most of the impact of the efficient breach is assessed by a narrow examination of the effects on the parties to the contract. Conventional scholarship about the efficient breach fails to extend the analysis far enough to fully grasp the complexity and likely futility of defining a remedy that is actually consistent with efficiency.
Writings about efficient breach bring to mind a recent article in which Monroe Freeman criticizes "philosophizing about legal ethics."He compares philosophizing about legal ethics to scholars in engineering arguing about the superiority of skyhooks over ordinary cranes or the impact of skyhook cables on air traffic.In short, philosophizing about legal ethics is empty, self-indulgent, and meaningful to only a few. His comparison is equally applicable to discussions of efficient breach. Quite recently, two Yale scholars may have achieved the dubious pinnacle of skyhook philosophizing in the context of the efficient breach.Among other things, they present an argument favoring expectancy over specific performance without linking either to the idea of efficiency. If neither is consistent with efficiency--and they do not demonstrate that they are--then the point is lost.
Part I presents two examples of the efficient breach and explains why expectancy is regarded as efficient. One important aspect of the discussion is the focus on ensuring that a breaching party internalizes--treats as a cost--the harm to the non-breaching party.These examples will be referred back to throughout the Article. Part II discusses the competing definitions of efficiency that complicate the question. It also addresses some of the new teachings from behavioral economics and happiness studies that increase the elusiveness of the already elusive efficient breach. An economic construct--the contract curve--is employed to demonstrate the failings of expectancy. Part III examines specific performance. Specific performance, probably the most favored remedy among those writing in the last forty years, is actually deeply flawed from the perspective of economic efficiency. Part IV considers some more recent defenses of expectancy and shows that they are not new and rely on assumptions that should be discarded, if they have not been already. In particular, the new defense seems to be an attempt to revive the notion of ex ante compensation,a theory that has little merit in theory or practice.In conclusion, this Article notes that no remedy can be favored over any other as an incentive for efficient breach or non-performance.Indeed, perhaps the underlying message of this Articleis that rather than clarifying the law, scholarly efforts have made it cloudier. In fact, to the extent certainty itself is of value, the starts and stops of legal scholarship and its varying recommendations have not been particularly useful. Legal scholarship itself may, at best, have no effect and may add to the uncertainty that makes efficient non-performance less likely.
I. Expectancy and the Efficient Breach: Passing a Rope Through The Eye of the Needle

questions.question: Does awarding monetary damages as the typical remedy cause contracting parties to breach when breach would increase total social welfare (i.e., does monetary compensation encourage the 'efficient' reallocation of resources)?

Can courts or other decisionmakers reliably determine when a breach would increase social welfare-taking into account measurement error, downstream effects on third parties, and behavioral/happiness-based deviations from rational preferences-so that remedy choice can meaningfully promote efficiency?

How often do legal remedies produce false positives (incorrectly treating a breach as welfare-improving) or false negatives (incorrectly treating a breach as welfare-reducing), and how do those errors affect which type of remedy should be preferred?

matched_themes: What counterfactual baseline should courts use to measure plaintiffs' losses for compensation purposes?
When should courts order specific performance (in-kind relief) versus awarding monetary damages?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?
Should the promisor or the promisee have the default right to choose between performance and payment to achieve allocative efficiency?
Does making in-kind performance the legal default (rather than monetary compensation) change parties' enforcement choices, moral judgments, and economic efficiency?
When should courts prefer or enforce in-kind (specific) performance rather than monetary damages for breach of contract?
Should the availability of legal remedies or contractual incompleteness change the moral assessment of a party who breaches under unanticipated circumstances?
How do transaction costs, enforcement frictions, and institutional realities alter the theoretical efficiency of breach-plus-compensation?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
Should contract damages be measured as lost surplus (net benefit) rather than expectancy or market value as a general rule?
How should remedial and enforcement rules be structured to achieve efficient behavior when populations include both internalizers and externalizers?
Can courts reliably determine ex post whether a breach would increase social welfare so that remedy choice can be used to promote efficiency?
To what extent does empirical uncertainty about measuring gains and losses limit courts' ability to design remedies that reflect non-welfare ethical preferences without sacrificing efficiency?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
What are the conceptual and methodological limits of the law-and-economics approach, and has the movement materially changed judicial decision-making?
To what extent should moral blameworthiness and non-economic considerations influence the design and application of contract remedies?
When is an indirect remedy (one that induces self-compliance) preferable to a direct remedy that delivers the outcome?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 97valrev1939!!ARTICLE: THE MYTH OF EFFICIENT BREACH: NEW DEFENSES OF THE EXPECTATION INTEREST
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE MYTH OF EFFICIENT BREACH: NEW DEFENSES OF THE EXPECTATION INTEREST

shared_topics.topic: theoretical soundness of the 'efficient breach' thesis and whether expectation damages promote efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Both papers directly interrogate the theory that expectation damages (the ‘expectancy’ remedy) produce efficient breach outcomes — Paper A argues the concept is indeterminate and that prior analyses are too narrow to support efficiency claims, while Paper B critiques efficient-breach theory as vacuous and develops alternative defenses of expectation damages.

shared_topics.topic: choice between expectation damages (liability rule) and specific performance (property rule)
shared_topics.justification: Both works engage substantively with the comparative normative and doctrinal question of whether contract law should enforce promises by awarding money (liability rule) or by ordering performance (property rule), weighing how each remedy allocates gains from breach and affects incentives.

shared_topics.topic: role of renegotiation, transaction costs, and institutional assumptions in assessing remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how renegotiation and transaction-cost assumptions (including the Coase-theorem environment) affect conclusions about which remedial rule yields efficient or desirable outcomes — Paper B formalizes this with models and the Coase argument, and Paper A criticizes prior work for neglecting wider institutional and downstream effects.

shared_topics.topic: normative/moral claims about promissory obligation and how they interact with economic analysis
shared_topics.justification: Both articles consider the moral dimension of promising (deontological versus instrumental views) and whether economic remedies (damages) disrespect promissory solidarity — Paper A highlights critics who insist on a deontological value to promises, and Paper B develops a moral defense of liability-rule expectation protection (the dual performance hypothesis).

shared_topics.topic: limitations of standard economic assumptions (information, rationality, downstream impacts) for resolving remedy disputes
shared_topics.justification: Both papers emphasize limits of the idealized economic assumptions used in the literature — Paper A invokes behavioral economics, happiness studies, and downstream firm effects to show indeterminacy and false positives/negatives, while Paper B tests the remedies under and beyond idealized assumptions (information, zero transaction costs, no investment) to show when each rule is justified.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 41ambuslj503!!ARTICLE: Formal and Operative Rules in Overliquidation Per Se Cases
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Formal and Operative Rules in Overliquidation Per Se Cases

shared_topics.topic: normative evaluation of contract remedies (damages vs specific performance/liquidated clauses)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when courts enforce or refuse liquidated-damage clauses (especially when no loss occurs) and the normative rationales behind enforcement, while Paper B evaluates whether expectancy damages or specific performance better promote the so‑called "efficient breach," arguing no remedy can be reliably favored as promoting efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: tension between freedom of contract (party autonomy) and compensatory/just‑compensation principles
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames overliquidation per se problems as a clash between party autonomy and just compensation and recommends rules to balance them, and Paper B addresses similar tensions by contrasting deontological defenses of promise‑keeping with law‑and‑economics efficiency arguments that prioritize reallocation and monetary compensation.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal indeterminacy and the insufficiency of formal tests (operative vs formal rules)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how the penalty doctrine and formal labels fail to predict outcomes and proposes identifying operative rules that actually drive judicial decisions, while Paper B likewise argues the efficient‑breach literature and common remedial tests are indeterminate (prone to false positives/negatives) and fail to give reliable guidance.

shared_topics.topic: limits of law‑and‑economics/efficiency reasoning in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A notes economic‑efficiency costs of uncertainty and critiques simplistic invocations of efficiency in enforcing stipulated damages, and Paper B directly critiques the law‑and‑economics treatment of expectancy and efficiency (including behavioral/happiness economics complications) as unable to deliver determinate prescriptions.

shared_topics.topic: the relevance of ex ante versus ex post perspectives in assessing remedy rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A recommends that courts assess enforceability of agreed damages from a prospective (ex ante) viewpoint to respect parties' contractual expectations, and Paper B evaluates/examines ex ante compensation and shows how ex ante versus ex post framing affects claims about whether a remedy promotes efficient breach.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 20hofstralrev933!!SYMPOSIUM: THE FUTURE OF LAW AND ECONOMICS: THE STRANGEST ATTACK YET ON LAW AND ECONOMICS.
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE FUTURE OF LAW AND ECONOMICS: THE STRANGEST ATTACK YET ON LAW AND ECONOMICS.

shared_topics.topic: whether expectancy (damages) encourages an "efficient breach" versus favoring specific performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the debate over expectancy damages being rebranded as the remedy that enables efficient breach and argues indeterminacy in claiming any remedy promotes efficiency; Paper B engages the same efficient‑breach example and debates whether damages or specific performance should be preferred in light of practical complications.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy of damages rules (e.g., Hadley v. Baxendale, liquidated damages) to internalize breach costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that economic analysis should ask whether the breaching party internalizes breach costs and criticizes narrow assessments that ignore mispricing and false positives/negatives; Paper B analyzes the Hadley rule, bargaining around foreseeability, and the use of express or liquidated‑damages clauses to address situations where ordinary damages may fail to compensate losses.

shared_topics.topic: third‑party and downstream externalities from contract breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues conventional efficient‑breach scholarship typically focuses only on contracting parties and neglects spillover effects on downstream firms and others; Paper B similarly catalogs third‑party harms (employees, families, community effects) as complications that may undermine simple efficiency conclusions.

shared_topics.topic: behavioral and psychological critiques of the Law & Economics efficiency model (limits of rationality, retribution, happiness considerations)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A invokes behavioral economics and happiness studies to challenge the rational‑actor bases for efficiency and the attainability of efficiency; Paper B raises psychological factors such as retribution, demoralization, and non‑pecuniary satisfaction as reasons why courts or parties might reject a pure efficiency calculus.

shared_topics.topic: practical limits and indeterminacy of applying economic analysis to contract remedies (transaction costs, bilateral monopoly, judicial supervision)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends that limited scopes of prior analyses create an illusion of efficiency and produce indeterminate guidance about remedies; Paper B likewise highlights transaction costs, bilateral‑monopoly bargaining problems, enforcement and supervision costs, and other practical constraints that complicate using economic theory to prescribe legal rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2013uilllrev151!!ARTICLE: CAN'T BUY ME LOVE: MONETARY VERSUS IN-KIND REMEDIES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CAN'T BUY ME LOVE: MONETARY VERSUS IN-KIND REMEDIES

shared_topics.topic: choice between monetary damages (expectancy) and specific performance/in-kind remedies in contract breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally analyzes the debate over expectancy damages versus specific performance, questioning whether expectancy promotes an 'efficient breach'; Paper B empirically compares monetary and in-kind remedies and argues promisees often prefer in-kind relief, urging more liberal use of specific performance.

shared_topics.topic: economic efficiency as the justificatory metric for remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the law-and-economics framing of remedies and argues that claims of efficiency are indeterminate and limited, while Paper B engages economic welfare analysis by showing that preferences for in-kind remedies can make monetary awards inefficient unless adjusted for lost utility.

shared_topics.topic: limitations and adequacy of monetary compensation to restore losses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights conceptual and practical failures of expectancy damages (false positives/negatives, downstream effects, failure to internalize costs), and Paper B provides experimental evidence that monetary awards often undercompensate relative to in-kind redress and thus may fail to restore injured parties.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal implications for remedial rules and when courts should favor in-kind relief
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions whether any single remedy can be recommended as the default incentive for efficient performance and stresses doctrinal uncertainty, and Paper B draws normative conclusions from its data—arguing courts should consider awarding specific performance more readily and be cautious about relying exclusively on monetary remedies.

shared_topics.topic: role of behavioral and empirical evidence in challenging classical rational-actor assumptions about remedy preferences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A invokes behavioral economics and happiness studies to problematize the rationality assumptions underlying efficiency-based arguments for expectancy, while Paper B supplies experimental data demonstrating lay and business preferences that contradict the standard theoretical presumption of indifference between money and in-kind remedies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 40sandiegolrev1345!!SYMPOSIUM:What to Compensate? Some Surprisingly Unappreciated Reasons Why the Problem Is So Hard
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM:What to Compensate? Some Surprisingly Unappreciated Reasons Why the Problem Is So Hard

shared_topics.topic: determining the appropriate baseline or counterfactual for awarding compensation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is centrally devoted to the problem of selecting the 'but‑for' baseline (the plaintiff's counterfactual welfare) across diverse tort and contract scenarios; Paper B engages the same issue insofar as the expectancy measure and the assessment of efficient breach depend on counterfactual calculations about what parties would have been awarded or lost absent breach.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between compensatory aims and efficiency/incentive goals of remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that what is 'right' to compensate depends on normative choices about welfare and loss, while Paper B critiques the efficient‑breach literature for conflating or failing to reconcile compensatory aims (making the non‑breaching party whole) with efficiency/incentive concerns about resource allocation.

shared_topics.topic: the relevance and limits of non‑pecuniary welfare and behavioral findings for legal remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises cases (e.g., plaintiffs who are better off or psychologically worse off) that show non‑pecuniary changes complicate compensation, and Paper B invokes behavioral economics and happiness studies to argue that welfare/rationality assumptions underlying efficiency and expectancy are unstable.

shared_topics.topic: the choice between damages (expectancy) and specific performance as remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A includes contractual examples about putting promisees in the position they would have been in (a core distinction between expectation damages and specific performance), and Paper B is devoted to evaluating and comparing expectancy damages and specific performance and their respective (in)ability to deliver efficiency or correct compensation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 48dukelj629!!ARTICLE: THE CASE FOR PUNITIVE DAMAGES IN CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE CASE FOR PUNITIVE DAMAGES IN CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: the meaning and coherence of the "efficient breach" doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Both papers centrally engage the efficient-breach concept—Paper A argues the notion is indeterminate and has been overextended by rebranding expectancy damages as "efficient," while Paper B treats the doctrine as the standard justification for denying punitive damages and critiques its scope and application.

shared_topics.topic: which remedies (expectation damages, specific performance, punitive damages) best promote efficient outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how different remedies shape incentives—Paper A critiques expectancy and specific performance as unreliable guides to efficiency, and Paper B compares expectation damages (liability rule) with property-rule remedies (punitive damages, specific performance) arguing punitive damages should be available to induce negotiation and better efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: the role of transaction costs and negotiation versus litigation in designing contract remedies (Calabresi & Melamed framework)
shared_topics.justification: Both works consider transaction costs in assessing remedies—Paper B explicitly adopts Calabresi & Melamed to argue property rules that force negotiation are often more efficient than litigation over damages, while Paper A faults narrow economic analyses that ignore wider transaction-cost implications and the practical limits of remedies in producing efficient reallocations.

shared_topics.topic: the need to distinguish types of breach (opportunistic vs efficient vs involuntary) when setting liability rules
shared_topics.justification: Both papers treat the taxonomy of breaches as normatively important—Paper B draws a sharp distinction among opportunistic, efficient, and involuntary breaches to justify punitive damages for willful/opportunistic conduct, and Paper A emphasizes classification problems (false positives/negatives) and behavioral complexities that make identifying "efficient" breaches unreliable.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 63notredamelrev247!!ARTICLE:A Newly Identified Contract Unconscionability: Unconsionability of Remedy
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:A Newly Identified Contract Unconscionability: Unconsionability of Remedy

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy and fairness of contract damages as the primary remedy for breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates whether expectancy (damages) actually produces efficient outcomes and whether damages properly internalize breach costs, while Paper B examines courts' willingness to limit foreseeable damages as disproportionate and frames such limits as a response to unfair or unconscionable remedies.

shared_topics.topic: tension between economic efficiency (efficient breach) and fairness/deontological concerns in remedy design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally debates the ‘efficient breach’ thesis and its limits, including behavioral and happiness-economics critiques, and Paper B situates judicial and statutory limits on damages as corrective responses motivated by fairness rather than pure efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: use of doctrinal rules (foreseeability, mitigation, specific performance) as instruments to shape remedy outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates the interplay between expectancy damages and specific performance and criticizes narrow doctrinal analyses for producing false positives/negatives about efficiency, whereas Paper B documents how courts historically used foreseeability, certainty, and mitigation doctrines (often covertly) to curtail disproportionate damages and now may do so overtly under section 351(3).

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and ex ante versus ex post incentives in contract formation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes whether breaching parties internalize costs and critiques narrow analyses that ignore downstream firm effects and ex ante incentives, while Paper B focuses on the parties' failure to allocate risk at formation and how courts/statutes should limit remedies to reflect that initial allocation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 33connlrev181!!ARTICLE: The Boundaries of Extracompensatory Relief for Abusive Breach of Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Boundaries of Extracompensatory Relief for Abusive Breach of Contract

shared_topics.topic: how remedial doctrines (expectancy, punitive/extracompensatory damages, specific performance) shape parties' incentives to breach and resource allocation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes whether awarding extracompensatory (punitive) relief for abusive breach can be reconciled with contract law's aim of facilitating exchanges, focusing on how such remedies alter breach incentives; Paper B debates whether the expectancy measure (and alternative remedies like specific performance) encourages the so-called efficient breach and whether any remedy can reliably produce allocative efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between predictability/certainty of contract law and allowing exceptions or harsher sanctions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames severability as necessary to preserve the predictable 'price of breach' while carving out exceptions for abusive conduct; Paper B emphasizes that shifting remedial doctrines (and scholarly vacillation) undermine certainty and thus the very likelihood of efficient non‑performance.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of purely economic accounts for prescribing contract remedies (including behavioral and non‑economic considerations)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that decisions about extracompensatory relief cannot rest solely on economic analysis and must consider social, political, and equitable factors; Paper B critiques the law-and-economics literature on efficient breach, invoking behavioral economics and happiness studies to show that efficiency-based prescriptions are indeterminate.

shared_topics.topic: spillover and boundary problems — how remedial rules create externalities and the importance/challenge of doctrinally defining subcategories
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops 'severability' to prevent collateral risk from leaking into the general pool of transactions when punishing abusive breaches, stressing boundary-drawing; Paper B examines false positives/negatives and downstream effects of breaches, highlighting how narrow party-focused analyses miss important spillovers and make it difficult to classify breaches as truly ‘efficient.’

compared_to.partner_node_id: 52tullrev659!!ARTICLE: Dependent Promises in the History of Leases and Other Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Dependent Promises in the History of Leases and Other Contracts

shared_topics.topic: how remedial doctrines (expectancy damages versus specific performance) shape parties' incentives to perform or breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally debates whether expectancy damages or specific performance better induce 'efficient' performance or breach and concludes no remedy reliably produces efficiency; Paper B's distinction between dependent and independent promises determines whether nonperformance can be withheld or must be remedied (often by damages), thus directly affecting the incentives to perform or to breach.

shared_topics.topic: normative justifications for contract rules (efficiency, fairness, and other policy reasons)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the economic-efficiency justification for allowing or encouraging breach and contrasts it with deontological and behavioral concerns; Paper B analyzes the reasons courts have held promises dependent or independent (e.g., fairness, common sense, property versus contract policy) and treats those policy rationales as central to doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: historical evolution and reinterpretation of contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A recounts the 'rebranding' of expectancy remedies in the 1970s and the ensuing scholarly debate about efficient breach; Paper B rereads the history of dependence/independence of promises (challenging the narrative of a linear shift under Lord Mansfield), so both undertake historical doctrinal analysis to explain current rules.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal rules vary by contract context and the broader effects beyond the contracting parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues many analyses are too narrow because damages and performance rules have effects on downstream firms and broader allocations of resources; Paper B compares leases, property law, and general contract principles to show that contextual differences in contract form and legal domain yield different treatments (dependent vs independent) with distinct systemic consequences.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45flastulrev923!!ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: II. THE BEST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: Hadley v. Baxendale: A Bayesian Analysis of the Hadley Rule
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: II. THE BEST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: Hadley v. Baxendale: A Bayesian Analysis of the Hadley Rule

shared_topics.topic: the normative role of contract remedies (damages vs specific performance) in producing efficient outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the claim that expectancy damages (and specific performance) reliably produce the 'efficient breach' and argues no remedy can be favored as an efficiency incentive, while Paper B evaluates competing liability regimes (no liability, Hadley foreseeability, total liability) to defend a limited-damages rule as the ex ante best choice under Bayesian decisionmaking.

shared_topics.topic: ex ante selection of liability rules and the need for breach costs to be internalized
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that the economic question is whether the breaching party internalizes the cost of breach (and critiques revived ex ante compensation theories), and Paper B models rule choice from behind a veil of ignorance to show which liability rule promisor/promisee pairs would choose ex ante to balance risks and internalization.

shared_topics.topic: the role of information and foreseeability in delimiting recoverable losses
shared_topics.justification: Paper B centers on the Hadley foreseeability limitation as a mechanism for limiting damages based on information available at contracting, while Paper A highlights informational limits (false positives/negatives, downstream effects, and insufficient scope) that make assessments of whether a breach is 'efficient' indeterminate.

shared_topics.topic: the limits and assumptions of economic/decision-theoretic approaches to contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions the reach of law-and-economics explanations (invoking behavioral economics and happiness studies to show rationality and welfare are slippery), and Paper B explicitly relies on Bayesian/Harsanyi decision theory and simplifying assumptions, thereby engaging with the normative and epistemic limits of economic models for remedial design.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 53lalrev1257!!ARTICLE: Comparative Ruminations on the Foreseeability of Damages in Contract Law. Dedicated to Professor Jurgen Basedow, Augsburg University, School of Law.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Comparative Ruminations on the Foreseeability of Damages in Contract Law. Dedicated to Professor Jurgen Basedow, Augsburg University, School of Law.

shared_topics.topic: the proper measure and limits of recoverable contract damages (expectancy vs foreseeability)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the expectancy measure and its claim to produce 'efficient breach' outcomes, showing limits and indeterminacy in using expectancy as the default damages rule; Paper B analyzes the foreseeability (contemplation/Hadley-type) limitation on recoverable contract losses across legal systems, i.e., a different doctrinal constraint on what damages a contracting party may recover.

shared_topics.topic: whether damages should serve compensatory goals or function to allocate risk and create incentives (internalization of breach costs)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly questions whether damages exist to compensate the non-breaching party or to ensure the breaching party internalizes the social cost of breach for efficiency, while Paper B examines doctrinal rules (foreseeability and comparative liability rules) that allocate which losses a defendant must bear, implicating how the law assigns risk and incentive effects.

shared_topics.topic: the normative debate between economic-efficiency justifications and alternative justificatory frameworks for contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages the law-and-economics account of efficient breach versus deontological/promissory views and behavioral critiques; Paper B traces doctrinal choices (contract vs tort distinctions and foreseeability limits) to differing legal justifications and policy rationales underlying compensation rules.

shared_topics.topic: historical and comparative development of contract-remedy doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A recounts the 1970s 'rebranding' and scholarly history of expectancy as tied to efficiency, while Paper B provides a comparative and historical account of the foreseeability/contemplation rule (including Hadley v. Baxendale) and its roots in French law and civil-law traditions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 28gastulrev559!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT BREACHES AND THE CRIMINAL/CIVIL DIVIDE: AN INTER-COMMON LAW ANALYSIS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT BREACHES AND THE CRIMINAL/CIVIL DIVIDE: AN INTER-COMMON LAW ANALYSIS

shared_topics.topic: whether expectancy (monetary) damages promote the 'efficient breach' and resource reallocation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A invokes the economic model (the notion that contract law 'prices' breaches) to explain why contract breaches attract monetary damages rather than criminal punishment, while Paper B is a sustained critique of the efficient-breach thesis and whether expectancy actually induces efficient reallocation of resources.

shared_topics.topic: the moral/deontological value of promises versus economic efficiency in judging breaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts moral-based accounts (moral condemnation of intentional wrongdoing) with economic accounts and develops a voluntary/non‑voluntary obligation distinction to rescue moral theory; Paper B surveys deontological objections—arguing some scholars treat promises as having intrinsic moral weight that expectancy/efficiency neglects.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy of monetary damages as the default remedy for contract breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats monetary damages as the settled civil remedy for contract breaches and asks why monetary sanctions (not imprisonment) suffice, while Paper B interrogates whether expectancy damages (as the default) are appropriate or superior to alternatives like specific performance from an efficiency perspective.

shared_topics.topic: limits of a purely law-and-economics account (indeterminacy and omitted effects)

papers.node_id: 75texlrev293!!ARTICLE: A Primer on Prejudgment Interest
papers.title: ARTICLE: A Primer on Prejudgment Interest
papers.abstract:
If justice were immediate, there would never be an award of prejudgment interest.The injured party would receive an enforceable judgment immediately, with no loss in value from the time value of money. Because justice often takes many years to achieve, interest is added to the original judgment to ensure that compensation is complete.These calculations are ubiquitous, since the laws of most U.S. jurisdictions provide for interest on legal judgments from the time the claim arose until the date of judgment.Such interest is called prejudgment interest.
When the injury occurred long before the judgment, prejudgment interest can equal or even exceed the principal. For example, in 1992 the Seventh Circuit awarded French plaintiffs $ 65 million in damages and $ 148 million in prejudgment interest in a suit arising out of the grounding of thesupertanker, AmocoCadiz, off the coast of Brittany in 1978.Even when the legal resolution occurs quickly, the interest can be large when the judgment is large, especially when interest rates are high. Moreover, because of the effect of compounding, even small differences in interest rates can have large effects on the final award. For example, in AmocoCadiz, a one percent difference in the interest rate (100 basis points) would have changed the final award by $ 20 million.For these reasons, the methods courts use to calculate prejudgment interest are of much practical significance.
The calculation of prejudgment interest is also of theoretical importance. Prejudgment interest plays an important role in promoting fairness and efficiency. Fairness generally requires that the successful plaintiff be fully compensated for its losses and that the defendant pay this amount.Because excess funds can be lent at interest and funds can be borrowed only by paying interest, unless interest is assessed on the original judgment the successful plaintiff is not fully compensatedand the losing defendant is unjustly enriched.The payment of prejudgment interest, therefore, ensures that the plaintiff receives full compensation for its losses and that the defendant pays the full penalty, thereby putting both parties in the same position that they would have been in if the judgment had been paid immediately.
Prejudgment interest also has an efficiency rationale, promoting efficiency in two ways. First, because prejudgment interest is an element of full compensation, it plays a role in ensuring that prospective parties have the appropriate incentives to take precautions when engaging in the same activity that produced the judgment. Efficiency generally requires that victims receive full compensatory damages and that injurers pay this amount.Accordingly, because compensation is incomplete without prejudgment interest, prospective defendants will be underdeterred and will take too few precautions,whereas prospective plaintiffs will be overdeterred and will take excessive precautions. Thus, prejudgment interest helps ensure that prospective parties undertake the efficient levels of precautions.
Second, if there were no provision for prejudgment interest, defendants would have a powerful incentive to stretch out litigation.Delaying judgment would effectively provide the defendant with an interest free loan from the plaintiff until the judgment is rendered. Because the defendant could not otherwise borrow money without paying interest, the defendant would benefit at the plaintiff's expense by stretching out litigation.With interest at a market rate, neither party would benefit from nor be injured by delay in this respect.Thus, awarding prejudgment interest reduces the defendant's incentive to delay judgment.
Nonetheless, the requirement that a losing defendant pay prejudgment interest to a successful plaintiff remains far from universal.Although a growing number of jurisdictions recognize a successful plaintiff's entitlement to prejudgment interest,other jurisdictions expressly bar recovery.Still other courts and statutes leave it to the discretion of the court whether to provide prejudgment interest.Frequently, within a jurisdiction, the availability of prejudgment interest depends on the source of the claim and the nature of the injury. For example, in California a successful plaintiff whose claim is for a certain amount (liquidated) or an amount capable of being made certain by calculation (clearly ascertainable) is entitled to prejudgment interest.In addition, a plaintiff whose damages are neither liquidated nor clearly ascertainable may be awardedinterest.Similarly, under federal law the availability of prejudgment interest appears to depend not only on the relevant statute, but also often on the court in which the claim is filed.
Commentators trace the lingering reluctance of legislatures and courts to provide prevailing plaintiffs with prejudgment interest to an ancient hostility towards interest.Interest was long seen as a means of punishing an egregious defendant rather than compensating a successful plaintiff.That view led to the common-law rule that prejudgment interest was allowed for liquidated claims, but not for unliquidated ones.The logic was that only defendants who could determine exactly what they owed could improperly withhold payment.That distinction between liquidated and unliquidated damages has been widely rejected; prejudgment interest is now widely considered necessary to ensure full compensation to the plaintiff and to prevent unjust enrichment of the defendant.Accordingly, the trend is towards awarding prejudgment interest on all monetary awards.
Nonetheless, there has been little movement to improve how prejudgment interest is calculated.Fairness and efficiency do not merely require that prejudgment interest be assessed;they require that it be assessed correctly.Correctly calculating prejudgment interest requires the proper use of financial principles.
In many jurisdictions, however, the correct calculation of prejudgment interest is prevented by a statute that requires the selection of an improper interest rate or the use of a conceptually wrong computational method.Even when a statute does not require an incorrect calculation, courts often do a poor job of calculating prejudgment interest, thereby undercutting the goals of fairness and efficiency. For example, some jurisdictions have adopted by common law the statutory, fixed postjudgment interest rate as the prejudgment interest rateor award simple interest.
In still other jurisdictions, trial court judges have wide discretion in setting an interest rate and calculating prejudgment interest. Under federal law, for example, courts have significant discretion in determining howprejudgment interest is calculated. That discretion has been broadly exercised, seriously undercutting the law's goals of compensating victims and deterring wrongdoers.
A good example of this phenomenon occurs in successful patent infringement suits. Thanks to a strong statement by the U.S. Supreme Court, awarding prejudgment interest is the rule in patent infringement suits.However, the courts have provided much less guidance on how that interest should be calculated. A recent commentator on the patent decisions of the Federal Circuit, in describing the methods used to calculate prejudgment interest, observed that "the recent cases indicate appellate approval of almost unfettered discretion in the district courts. No reported cases have reversed district judges in their decisions on these points."The range of methodologies approved in patent cases is especially troublingbecause the rationale for unifying patent appeals within the Federal Circuit was to harmonize their treatment.
This wide range of discretion, common with equitable remedies, is unusual with money judgments at law.The usual explanation for the persistence of so much discretion is that courts and legislatures have yet to formulate the proper rules for calculating prejudgment interest.They have not been helped by commentators.In spite of the important role that prejudgment interest plays in the administration of justice, thescholarly literature is limited. What literature there is mostly addresses the implications for litigation and settlement of a rule that awards prejudgment interest compared to one that does not.Discussion of the various methods that could be used to calculate prejudgment interest in the legal literature is nearly absent;that literature consists primarily of contradictory court opinions.Yet most opinions give the issue of prejudgment interest little attention.As the Court of Federal Claims recently stated, "A generally-agreed, standard, objective method of fixing delay damages [prejudgment interest] … is sorely needed."Accordingly, this Article seeks to fill that gap by providing more guidance than is currently available for the calculation of prejudgment interest.
This Article describes how prejudgment interest should be calculated, and if its advice is followed, it will curtail, but not eliminate, discretion. One of the themes that emerges is that there is not likely to be anobservable market interest rate that can be identified in each case as the absolutely correct rate to use. The law will have to be content with proxies and with adjustments that are only approximations. Even so, these proxies and adjustments are constrained by financial principles. Setting out these limits will, I hope, assist not only judgesin assessing prejudgment interest but, in addition, should aid lawyers in framing their arguments and legislators in writing the statutes that provide for interest on judgments.

questions.question: What method should be used to calculate prejudgment interest on monetary awards so that plaintiffs are fully compensated, defendants are not unjustly enriched, and deterrent incentives are preserved?
What interest rate (or market proxy) and compounding convention best approximates the correct time-value-of-money compensation when no single observable market rate exists for the relevant period?
How should courts' discretion be structured or constrained in selecting rates and computational methods for prejudgment interest to produce consistent, fair, and economically efficient outcomes?

papers.node_id: 38ambuslj633!!ARTICLE: A THEORY OF EFFICIENT PENALTY: ELIMINATING THE LAW OF LIQUIDATED DAMAGES
papers.title: ARTICLE: A THEORY OF EFFICIENT PENALTY: ELIMINATING THE LAW OF LIQUIDATED DAMAGES
papers.abstract:
A critique of the law of liquidated damages is important both for reasons of praxis and theory. From a practical perspective, such liquidated damages clausesare commonly found in many types ofcontracts, from employment to construction contracts. A number of reasons exist for the popularity of these clauses. First, because of the fears and costs associated with litigation, parties who draft such clauses do so in the hopes that they will preclude the need for litigation. At the very least, a liquidated damages clause may encourage the parties to settle before the trial phase or to provide some evidentiary value at trial. Parties have also used liquidated damages clauses as a mechanism for retaining monies that have been deposited or paid under the contract.Finally, a party concerned foremost with performance, especially a timely performance, may use such a clause in the hope that it will provide a further inducement for performance.
The second perspective from which to review this area of contract law is the theoretical. The law of liquidated damages is unique within the common law of contracts because it overtly affronts freedom of contract. The freedom of parties to structure their own agreement is universally acknowledged to be at the heart of the common law of contracts.In contrast to this freedom of contract, the limited enforcement of liquidated damages clauses, in which parties have agreed to a specified measure of damages in the event of breach, is along recognized exception. The non-enforcement of liquidated or stipulated damages clauses, those that are classified as excessive penalties, is justified on public policy and fairness grounds.But why are liquidated damages clauses singled-out for specialized scrutiny? This scrutiny is especially questionable in the cases where such clauses are a clear expression of the parties' intentions. The law and economics literature is rich in analysis regarding the efficiency of enforcing or not enforcing liquidated damages clauses. General economic theory suggests that any express agreement between rational contracting parties should be fully enforced. However, an efficient breach argument can be made in favor of the non-enforcement of penalties, namely, that a party may be deterred from an otherwise efficient breach because of the punitive nature of the stipulated damages.
The law of liquidated damages embodies the language of dichotomy. The law is characterized by the great divide between enforceable liquidated damages clauses and unenforceable penalties. Parties may agree to stipulated damages but only at an amount that is considered reasonable. An amount above anticipated or actual compensatory damages is presumed to be a penalty, and the common law abhors penalties.The incongruity between freedom of contract principlesand the non-enforcement of penalty clauses has generatedan extensive body of scholarly commentary.The most recent analysis has evolved from the law and economics school.It is to the law and economics literature that this Article will turn in judging the rationality of the just compensation principle as it relates to the law of liquidated damages.
A theoretical dichotomy has developed among law and economics scholars in the critiquing of the current law of liquidated damages. Arguments have been spun criticizing the non-enforcement of liquidated damages clauses as the inefficient preemption of private bargaining. Professors Goetz and Scott formed their critique in favor of the enforcement of penalty clauses.They used a model of themost efficient insurerto argue that the performing party to the contract is the best insurer. A penalty clause is the insurance policy for which theother party is willing to pay a premium. In the alternative, when a penalty clause is not included, the non-breaching party will be forced to take inefficient precautions (such as third-party insurance) in order to insure against breach. It would be more efficient to enforce the penalty clause than to force the parties to take other precautions or use other remedies. Other scholars have argued that the current law is efficient as currently constituted. In short, they claim that penalties are inefficient because they deter efficient breach. Clarkson, Miller, and Muris have argued that the non-enforcement of penalty clauses is indeed an efficient rule of contract law. Their primary argument is that penalty clauses, if enforced, produce an incentive for the non-performing party to induce a breach by the performing party.In short, the penalty clause provides opportunism for the non-breaching party. However, unlike the opportunism that supports efficient breach theory, non-breaching party opportunism is not conducive to creating additional societal wealth or utility. This Article will argue that the current dichotomies are overly simplistic. It will argue that penalties may be either efficient or inefficient. Therefore, a law that holds all penalties as per se unenforceable is necessarily flawed. Atheory of efficient penaltyrecognizes that the presumption in favor of the enforcement of liquidated damages clauses should be expanded to include liquidated damagesquapenalties. Only liquidated damages clauses that are products of inefficient bargaining should be subject to judicial intervention. The first tool for such intervention should be reformation and not the rescission-only mandate found in the current law of liquidated damages.
Generally, the law of liquidated damages masks an unwarranted judicial intervention into freedom of contract. The courts and legal scholars have failed to adequately rationalize the law's interventionism to void liquidated damages clauses.Professor Hillman hasreferred to this area as the "great paradox in contract law."Ironically, courts have voided liquidated damages clauses under the banner ofintentionality--namely that one of the parties did not intend to liquidate damages despite the existence of an express term stating otherwise. Hence, the law of liquidated damages severely limits the parties' freedom to agree to pre-set damages in most cases. Unless the clause meets necessary requirements, the parties' pre-agreed remedial response to a breach of contract is replaced by one fashioned by the courts ex post.
In order to argue for the elimination of the law of liquidated damages, one must first critique the law as currently constituted. PartII of this Article reviews the philosophical constructs that underlie the law of liquidated damages. The twin pillars of contract remedies, freedom of contract and just compensation, will be analyzed. Freedom of contract is viewed from the perspective of party-constructed justice. This perspective augurs in favor of the enforcement of penalty clauses, especially when they are the products of fair bargaining. In contrast, the just compensation principle sees remedial justice as based upon notions of substantive equality and equity. Thus, the non-breaching party's recovery should be limited to compensatory damages as measured through the expectancy interest. The non-breaching party should not be made better off then it would have been under full performance. An analogy is drawn from the rule against the granting of punitive damages. Part II concludes with a comparative analysis of penalty law in other legal systems. The difference in the approach to penalties in the civil law system demonstrates that the common law of liquidated damages is primarily a historical creation.The non-enforcement of penalties is not the inevitable product of an advanced contract law system.
Part III reviews the chaotic jurisprudence that presently surrounds the law of liquidated damages. This jurisprudence has produced numerous standards for judging the reasonableness of liquidated damages clauses. The one, two, and three-pronged approaches to reasonableness have been used and misused to create numerous other permutations of these standards. The confused jurisprudence includes differences of opinion on the "no actual injury defense" and the burden of proof. Part III concludes with a review of the techniques used to contract around the law of liquidated damages. Most attempts to circumvent the current law have met with failure. In actuality, the courts have expanded the reach of the law by broadening the definition of liquidated damages. The designation of attorney fee clauses as liquidated damages is given as an example of this phenomenon.
Part IV will examine the economic arguments in favor of and against the current non-enforcement of penalty clauses. Efficient breach arguments for not enforcing penalty clauses will be examinedfirst. The most common arguments are that penalty clauses induce inefficient performance and produce negative externalities. This Article rejects these arguments in favor of general economic theory arguments that support enforcement. It is argued that enforcement of penalty clauses will increase efficiency in contracting and dispute resolution. The final section of Part IV asserts that the current dichotomy between liquidated damages and penalties is too simplistic. Instead, a third category of liquidated damages clauses,efficient penalties, should be recognized. Enforcement of such penalty can be justified under both fairness and efficiency grounds. The recognition of efficient penalties requires that the current understanding of a penalty, as an unenforceable inducement to perform, be reformulated.
Part V reviews various provisions of the Uniform Commercial Code that can be used to better understand why the law of liquidated damages is aberrational within the Code's model of contractual exchange. These provisions include Section 2-718 (liquidated damages), 2-719 (limitation of liability), 2-302 (unconscionability), and 2-615 (impracticability). Two recent proposals to revise the law of liquidated damages will also be presented: (1) Revised Article Two of the Uniform Commercial Code and (2) theContract Codewritten under the auspices of the English Law Commission. The English revision effort comes closer to fundamentally changing the law of liquidated damages than the American revision effort. Ultimately, however, both attempts fall short. Part V also suggests that reformation is the best vehicle for reconciling judicial intervention in the area of liquidated damages with freedom of contract.
This Article will conclude that, for reasons of efficiency and fairness, the current tripartite approach provided in section 2-718 of the Uniform Commercial Code should be eliminated. Instead of the parties having to fulfill any such requirements, liquidated damages clauses should be presumed to be enforceable. If it can be shown that a clause was a part of the basis of the bargain, then its full enforcement will be consistent with the intentions of the parties and will diminish the need for lengthy litigation on issues of liability and the amount of damages to be awarded. The elimination of the law of liquidated damages can be justified by a theory of efficient penalty. Such a theory would support the use of the doctrine of unconscionability as the best means for policing liquidated damages clauses. Under the doctrine of unconscionability, clauses that aresubstantively and procedurally unconscionable can be voided or reformed. Finally, reformation should be the preferred response in most cases. Instead of the current mandate to void all unreasonable clauses, the courts should attempt to salvage the parties' contractual intent by reforming such clauses.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A invokes economic and historical arguments about what institutional arrangements produce efficient, impersonal exchange, while Paper B engages law‑and‑economics debates (efficient breach, efficient penalty) to evaluate whether enforcement or non‑enforcement of clauses maximizes welfare.

shared_topics.topic: how enforcement, transaction costs, and incentives affect contractual performance and market behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses coercion, expropriation, and institutional barriers that skew incentives and impede impersonal exchange, and Paper B examines litigation costs, insurance substitutes, and how penalty clauses influence incentives to perform or breach contracts.

shared_topics.topic: comparative and historical analysis of legal regimes that enable market exchange
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses historical examples (e.g., Roman economy, post‑Soviet Russia) to show variation in market institutions, and Paper B compares common law and civil law approaches and the historical development of the liquidated damages doctrine to explain different regulatory effects on contracting.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 103harvlrev687!!ARTICLE: THE DEATH OF THE IRREPARABLE INJURY RULE.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE DEATH OF THE IRREPARABLE INJURY RULE.

shared_topics.topic: economic/law-and-economics analysis of remedial rules and efficiency (including efficient breach and transaction costs)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages the law-and-economics literature on whether enforcing or voiding penalty clauses promotes efficient contracting (efficient breach, insurance/precaution costs), and Paper B evaluates remedial doctrines in terms of transaction costs and the economic consequences of preferring damages over injunctions.

shared_topics.topic: judicial doctrine versus contractual autonomy — when courts should override or respect parties' remedial choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes current doctrines that void penalty clauses as intrusions on freedom of contract and advocates presumptive enforcement or reformation, while Paper B criticizes the rigid irreparable‑injury rhetoric and urges courts to stop hiding substantive decisions behind formal rules, thereby exposing how doctrine affects parties' remedial expectations.

shared_topics.topic: preference for tailored, functional remedies instead of categorical rules (reformation, functional approach to remedies) and the effects on litigation/settlement incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts should reform unreasonable liquidated‑damage clauses rather than void them, preserving parties' bargain and reducing litigation; Paper B urges abandoning blanket 'irreparable injury' rhetoric in favor of functional, case‑specific reasons for granting or denying injunctions, emphasizing how remedy design shapes settlement and procedural outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 48dukelj629!!ARTICLE: THE CASE FOR PUNITIVE DAMAGES IN CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE CASE FOR PUNITIVE DAMAGES IN CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: the normative status of the efficient-breach doctrine as a justification for limiting contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly challenges the use of efficient-breach theory to justify barring punitive damages, arguing it cannot excuse opportunistic breaches and misallocates incentives; Paper B engages the same doctrine in the context of liquidated-damages, considering and rejecting efficiency-based arguments for non-enforcement of penalty clauses and proposing a more nuanced economic account.

shared_topics.topic: whether punitive/penalty or liquidated damages should be enforceable as contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for expanding availability of punitive damages for willful breaches to serve as a property-rule deterrent, while Paper B argues that many liquidated-damage (penalty) clauses are economically efficient and should be presumptively enforceable or reformed rather than voided.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between freedom of contract and judicial intervention (just compensation principle)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze the conflict between party autonomy to set contractual remedies and courts' traditional refusal to enforce punitive/penalty clauses on fairness or compensation grounds—Paper A criticizes the compensatory-only remedial stance, and Paper B critiques judicial override of parties' agreed remedies as an excessive intrusion on freedom of contract.

shared_topics.topic: transaction costs, negotiation vs. litigation, and the property-rule/liability-rule framework for structuring remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly applies Calabresi & Melamed to argue punitive remedies function as property rules that induce pre-breach negotiation and lower transaction (assessment) costs, and Paper B likewise emphasizes that enforcing or reforming agreed penalties can reduce litigation and settlement costs, discussing doctrinal tools (reformation, unconscionability, UCC provisions) to align remedies with transaction-cost considerations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 29yalejonreg1!!ARTICLE: Self-Help and the Rules of Engagement
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Self-Help and the Rules of Engagement

shared_topics.topic: how remedial rules shape parties' incentives to breach, evade enforcement, or act strategically
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how rules permitting or restricting self-help (e.g., breach-of-the-peace vs permissive repossession) change debtor behavior—including strategic obstruction of repossession and use of force—while Paper B analyzes how enforcement or invalidation of liquidated-damages/penalty clauses alters incentives to perform, to breach efficiently, or to opportunistically induce breach.

shared_topics.topic: the tradeoff between private enforcement (self-help or contractual clauses) and state process driven by administrative/litigation costs and delay
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the choice to allow self-help as a balance among the costs of violence, administrative costs of courts, mistakes, and delay; Paper B emphasizes that litigation costs and the desire to avoid trial drive parties to draft liquidated-damages clauses and that enforcement policy should account for these transaction and litigation cost tradeoffs.

shared_topics.topic: the role of uncertainty or clarity of substantive rights in deciding whether to allow private remedies or require judicial verification
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that clear, simple contractual rights (e.g., many personal-property security agreements) justify allowing confrontational self-help, whereas murkier reciprocal rights (e.g., commercial leases) justify funneling disputes to courts; Paper B likewise treats the clarity of the parties' bargain and the basis-of-the-bargain question as central to whether stipulated damages should be enforced, reformed, or voided.

shared_topics.topic: design and choice of doctrinal tools to calibrate remedies (standards, exceptions, reformation, and split functions like verification vs enforcement)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates doctrinal rules governing engagement (breach-of-the-peace standard, claim-of-right, constant pursuit) and proposes hybrid regimes that separate verification from enforcement, while Paper B critiques the binary liquidated-damages/penalty rule and advocates doctrinal alternatives (reformation, unconscionability, UCC provisions) to better align remedy enforcement with efficiency and fairness.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 84nclrev1841!!ARTICLE: A BRIDGE, A TAX REVOLT, AND THE STRUGGLE TO INDUSTRIALIZE: THE STORY AND LEGACY OF ROCKINGHAM COUNTY v. LUTEN BRIDGE CO.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A BRIDGE, A TAX REVOLT, AND THE STRUGGLE TO INDUSTRIALIZE: THE STORY AND LEGACY OF ROCKINGHAM COUNTY v. LUTEN BRIDGE CO.

shared_topics.topic: the design and role of contract damages doctrines (how rules on damages allocate risk and shape parties' behavior)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critically examines the law of liquidated damages—when stipulated penalties should be enforced, how they deter or encourage breach, and how they allocate risk between parties; Paper B revisits Rockingham County v. shared_topics.topic: tension between private contractual autonomy and broader public or policy concerns that justify judicial intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the non‑enforcement of penalties as a clash between freedom of contract and the just‑compensation/public‑policy impulse, arguing for narrower judicial intervention; Paper B shows that the dispute underlying Luten Bridge implicated county governance, taxation, and public policy, illustrating how courts balance private agreements against communal and governmental interests.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 116columlrev2005!!ARTICLE: ECONOMIC ANALYSIS OF CONTRACT LAW FROM THE INTERNAL POINT OF VIEW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ECONOMIC ANALYSIS OF CONTRACT LAW FROM THE INTERNAL POINT OF VIEW

shared_topics.topic: the tension between efficiency (economic incentives) and promissory/moral norms (internal motivations)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the debate over whether contract law should be designed to maximize social welfare through incentives (efficient breach) or to express/promote promissory morality — Paper A models heterogeneous agents (externalizers vs internalizers) and how norms can crowd out moral motivations, while Paper B evaluates the efficient-breach critique of non-enforcement of penalties and weighs efficiency arguments against fairness and opportunism concerns.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules shape contracting behavior and incentives (including deterrence, opportunism, and crowding out)
shared_topics.justification: Both use economic reasoning to assess how doctrines affect behavior: Paper A explores crowding out, willful breach as a deterrence device, and how rules (standards vs bright-line rules) speak to internalizers vs externalizers; Paper B analyzes how penalty clauses, litigation costs, and enforcement doctrines alter parties' incentives to perform, induce breaches, or engage in opportunistic conduct.

shared_topics.topic: freedom of contract versus judicial intervention (when courts should reform or void contractual terms)
shared_topics.justification: Both question the scope of party autonomy in remedies: Paper B centers on the paradox of limiting freedom of contract through the penalty rule and proposes reformation/unconscionability as policing tools, while Paper A considers when normative legal content (rules vs remedial structures) should be crafted to accommodate different motivations and when legal doctrines (e.g., penalty doctrine, standards) should be designed to avoid harmful effects on performance.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 9minnjlscitech861!!SYMPOSIUM: Intentions, Guilt and Social Interactions
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: Intentions, Guilt and Social Interactions

shared_topics.topic: how beliefs about another's motives affect willingness to transact or enforce agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how responders form beliefs about a proposer's social type and sincerity and how those beliefs change acceptance of offers; Paper B discusses how courts and contracting parties act on inferences about parties' motives (and how those inferences influence judicial intervention and contracting practice).

shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies behavioral responses (e.g., rejecting offers, withholding social engagement) when offers are perceived as insincere; Paper B evaluates legal remedies (voiding, reforming, or enforcing clauses, or policing via unconscionability) as institutional responses when contractual terms are judged to reflect unfair or penal motives.

shared_topics.topic: trade-off between efficiency and fairness/trust when motives are suspect
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines whether insincerity aversion prevents mutually beneficial exchanges and implications for trust and social welfare; Paper B evaluates whether enforcing or voiding penalty clauses maximizes contractual efficiency versus fairness and how that balance should guide legal doctrine.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 105michlrev559!!ARTICLE: THE DISGORGEMENT INTEREST IN CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE DISGORGEMENT INTEREST IN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: whether remedies should strip a breacher of gains (disgorgement/penalties) versus merely compensating the promisee
shared_topics.justification: Both pieces confront the question of remedial goals—Paper A debates enforcing liquidated damages or penalties (which may be punitive or gain‑stripping) versus limiting recovery to compensation, and Paper B advocates recognition of a disgorgement interest that requires promissors to surrender gains made possible by breach rather than only compensating the promisee.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68amulrev1751!!ARTICLE: SOMETHING ELSE: SPECIFIC RELIEF FOR BREACH OF HUMAN RIGHTS TERMS IN SUPPLY CHAIN AGREEMENTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SOMETHING ELSE: SPECIFIC RELIEF FOR BREACH OF HUMAN RIGHTS TERMS IN SUPPLY CHAIN AGREEMENTS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how judicial anxieties (indenture and entanglement) and public‑interest concerns can constrain parties' ability to contract for human‑rights outcomes, and Paper B documents how courts' refusal to enforce penalty clauses represents an intervention into parties' bargaining that must be justified or reformed.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A weighs transaction costs and relational benefits from negotiating human‑rights terms and the deterrent/clarifying effect of specific relief, while Paper B uses law‑and‑economics to evaluate whether enforcing or invalidating liquidated/penalty clauses promotes efficient contracting, breach incentives, and reduced litigation costs.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONSEQUENTIAL DAMAGES FOR COMMERCIAL LOSS: AN ALTERNATIVE TO HADLEY v. BAXENDALE

shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates policy grounds for when courts should permit recovery of consequential commercial losses (implicitly weighing parties' expectations against judicial oversight), and Paper B centrally critiques judicial nullification of liquidated/penalty clauses as an intrusion on private ordering, proposing unconscionability/reformation rather than categorical invalidation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83uchilrev759!!Article: Contract as Empowerment
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Contract as Empowerment

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes liquidated damages through economic models and critiques both enforcement and non‑enforcement on efficiency grounds, proposing a theory of 'efficient penalty'; Paper B situates contract doctrine between efficiency and normative concerns, engaging economic accounts (such as efficient breach) and offering an alternative normative framework that seeks to reconcile efficiency with empowerment and fairness.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Economic Theory and the Present Value of Future Lost Earnings: An Integration, Unification, and Simplification of Court Adopted Methodologies

shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents chaotic, multi-pronged judicial tests for when stipulated damages are enforceable and urges doctrinal reform (presumption of enforceability and reformation); Paper B documents divergent court-adopted techniques for present-value calculation and advocates a single, less biased approach (offset) to reduce inequitable variation.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes courts for doctrinally voiding clauses despite parties' expressed intent and for using incoherent standards (e.g., misreading contractual intent and compensatory principles); Paper B demonstrates that courts have incorrectly defined/estimated economic variables (nominal vs. real rates, growth rates), producing biased awards and arguing courts need proper economic definitions.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A NIHILISTIC VIEW OF THE EFFICIENT BREACH

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT DAMAGES IN TENNESSEE

shared_topics.topic: normative law-and-economics questions about efficiency of enforcing agreed remedies / efficient breach
shared_topics.justification: Both works engage the normative question of whether damages rules should promote efficient outcomes: Paper A debates law-and-economics arguments for enforcing or voiding penalty clauses (efficient penalties vs deterrence of efficient breach), and Paper B situates Tennessee damages doctrine in light of the theoretical goal of economically putting the non-breaching party in the position of performance (advocating more liberal awards to approximate that goal).

compared_to.partner_node_id: 36jlegalstud379!!ARTICLE: Sanctions by Social Norms and the Law: Substitutes or Complements?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Sanctions by Social Norms and the Law: Substitutes or Complements?

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes observability, social connectedness, and enforcement costs (informal shame vs costly formal sanctions) as determinants of whether norms suffice, while Paper B highlights litigation costs, monitoring incentives, and the transactional motives for liquidated-damage clauses as central to whether contractual terms should be enforced or judicially altered.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1381!!ARTICLE: IN (PARTIAL) DEFENSE OF STRICT LIABILITY IN CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: IN (PARTIAL) DEFENSE OF STRICT LIABILITY IN CONTRACT
