shared_topics.topic: the appropriate role of judicial intervention versus freedom of contract in policing contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that courts currently overreach by voiding penalty clauses and advocates presumptive enforcement plus use of unconscionability/reformation to limit unwarranted intervention; Paper B defends doctrines (strict liability core) that favor predictable, party-autonomous rules and explains how limiting fault-based inquiries supports contractual autonomy.

shared_topics.topic: how rules about breach and remedies affect parties' incentives to take precautions and allocate risk ex ante
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates whether penalty clauses deter efficient breach or instead function as insurance/inducements affecting parties' precaution and insurance choices; Paper B examines courts' refusal to employ willful-breach or contributory-fault adjustments and argues the strict-liability core shapes promisor and promisee precaution incentives and ex ante risk allocation.

shared_topics.topic: the normative and doctrinal status of the 'efficient breach' idea and fault-based adjustments in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages directly with 'efficient breach' arguments as applied to penalty enforcement and contends some penalties can be efficiency-enhancing; Paper B treats efficient-breach and fault-based justifications for adjusting liability (e.g., willful breach, mitigation) but defends a default no-fault regime despite those efficiency arguments.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 63notredamelrev247!!ARTICLE:A Newly Identified Contract Unconscionability: Unconsionability of Remedy
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:A Newly Identified Contract Unconscionability: Unconsionability of Remedy

shared_topics.topic: limits on enforceability of pre‑agreed contractual remedies (liquidated damages/penalties and disproportionate consequential damages)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers tackle when courts should limit or enforce ex ante remedial clauses—Paper A analyzes courts' power (and Restatement §351(3)) to curtail foreseeable damages that are grossly disproportionate to the contract price, while Paper B critiques the law of liquidated damages and whether penalty clauses should be enforced or invalidated as excessive.

shared_topics.topic: use of the unconscionability doctrine to police remedial terms
shared_topics.justification: Both works examine unconscionability as the doctrinal vehicle for policing unfair remedies—Paper A reframes remedy‑limitation as an 'unconscionability of remedy' parallel to substantive/procedural unconscionability, and Paper B proposes relying on the doctrine of unconscionability (and reformation) to rescue or reform unreasonable liquidated damages clauses.

shared_topics.topic: tension between freedom of contract and just‑compensation/public‑policy limits on remedies
shared_topics.justification: Each article engages the normative conflict between enforcing parties' agreed‑upon remedial allocations and preventing punitive or socially harmful outcomes—Paper B frames this as freedom of contract versus just compensation/penalty concerns, while Paper A shows how courts have historically disguised remedial curtailment to avoid extreme unfairness despite formal party autonomy.

shared_topics.topic: role of statutory and restatement provisions and reform options (UCC, Restatement) in shaping remedy doctrine

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Compensation Myth and U.C.C. Section 2-713

papers.node_id: 89bulrev1397!!ARTICLE: A THEORY OF SELF-HELP REMEDIES IN CONTRACT
papers.title: ARTICLE: A THEORY OF SELF-HELP REMEDIES IN CONTRACT
papers.abstract:
Teaching and scholarship about contract remedies tend to focus on damages and injunctions, the two principal remedies courts provide. Little attention is paid to "self-help remedies," by which I mean actions a party may take to obtain redress for breach of contract without going to court.This isunfortunate. Self-help remedies are of obvious practical significance in their own right. As for theory, the academic obsession with the damage remedy and neglect of self-help has contributed to pervasive under-estimation both of the strength of contract rights in American law and of the weight placed on remedial simplicity. Putting to the side repossession, the principal self-help remedy in contract is the power to withhold performance in response to breach. Often this power is exercised in tandem with the power to refuse non-conforming performance. In addition, a party may threaten to withhold performance in order to extract concessions. The exercise of these powers is regulated after the fact by a dauntingly long list of rules that are scattered across the fields of contract, restitution, and equity.These rules determine when an actor has the power to withhold or refuse performance in response to breach, as well as the power to threaten to do so to extract concessions, and the legal consequences of an actor's decision whether or not to exercise these powers.
This article offers a positive and normative account of this body of law. The positive account centers on two general observations. One observation is that the law permits a party to withhold or refuse performance in response to breach to avoid suffering a loss that damages may not adequately compensate even if the response inflicts a disproportionate loss on the defaulter.When it comes to self-help remedies, there is no "option" to breach a contract even if breach would be efficient.My other observation is that when there is an honest dispute about the performance owed under a contract, and nonperformance will not cause a significant loss, the law prods parties to resolve the dispute without going to court. The law does this by permitting a party who is under a disputed performance obligation to use a threat of nonperformance to extract a settlement and by presuming that whatever performance is rendered and accepted settles any dispute over whether less or more was due. Whennonperformance will cause a significant loss, the law prods parties to perform and accept performance and then resolve their dispute in court.In the law of self-help, uncertain contract rights, unlike indisputable contract rights, sometimes do give way in the interest of efficient performance, but in a way that preserves the power of a party to go to court and have a rights claim resolved.
My normative account of these rules is fairly straightforward as it is fairly easy to show these rules are consistent with norms of both economy and autonomy. I use the normative account of the rules as a springboard to respond to recent economics-minded scholarship that mounts a formidable challenge to the turn against rule formalism in American contract law in the last century. I respond in particular to recent work of Robert Scott.My observation that the law of self-help tolerates a great deal of waste, and even some windfall, to avoid even a modest risk of short-changing contract rights undercuts the theory of efficient breach. This might seem to render economic theories of contract descriptively inaccurate and instead support what I will call autonomy theories.But current economic thinking about contract remedies is dismissive of the possibility and desirability of calibrating damages to ensure efficient decisions in contracting, reliance, and performance. Instead, current thinking favors simple and reliable mechanisms to protect parties from nonperformancewhen the adequacy of performance or damages is difficult to verify.The power to withhold and refuse performance in response to breach in order to avoid the risk of suffering an uncompensated loss is such a mechanism.
part ways with current economic thinking about contract remedies on a different point that is an aspect of the general question of the legal status of informal agreements. Economic and autonomy theories of contract tend to cut in different directions on this question. In a recent article, Professor Scott argues that courts ought to refuse to enforce avoidably indefinite agreements, reasoning that a practice of enforcing indefinite agreements crowds out self-enforcement through reciprocal norms of fairness.While it is difficult to justify the doctrine of indefiniteness in these terms, Scott's larger point may be valid. American contract law is much more open than it used to be to enforcing claims based on uncertain agreements, in particular agreements whose existence or content is uncertain because of the agreement's informality. It is quite plausible that the specter of litigation has made people less willing to use informal agreements to order their affairs. Scott and economic theorists tend to favor blunt rules making some uncertain agreements unenforceable.I argue that the rules that regulate withholding and refusing performance in a case in which there is an honest dispute about rights offer a more attractive solution to the problem of determining when courts should resolve an uncertain rights claim. The rules prod, but do not compel, parties to resolve their disputes outside of court. Their non-compulsory nature makes the rules fairly easy to defend on economic grounds and inoffensive on autonomy grounds.
. The Duty to Mitigate Does Not Require Sacrificing a Right
I show in this Part that the duty to mitigate does not require a party to act in a way that would subject the party to a risk of a loss that may not be adequately compensated in damages even if the action would avoid a significantly greater loss to a defaulter. To make my point, I use a familiar case, Parker v. Twentieth Century-Fox Film Corp.,and a familiar problem that often isillustrated by Rockingham County v. Luten Bridge Co.The mitigation doctrine may seem unrelated to the topic of self-help remedies because the doctrine typically bears on the amount of damages recovered for breach. Parker directly implicates the power to refuse non-conforming performance because the mitigation doctrine was invoked by the defendant in the case to hold the plaintiff at fault for refusing an offer of substitute performance.More generally, both in Parker and in the situation of Luten Bridge, once the mitigation issue is resolved in the plaintiff's favor, the plaintiff is entitled to the contract price.While the remedy is not self-enforcing - the plaintiff may have to sue to collect the money owed - a judgment for the price follows mechanically and a trial to establish the fact and amount of the liability is unnecessary. In both situations, the mitigation doctrine works to simplify or avoid litigation. This also is a key characteristic of the rules we will look at in Parts II and III.
Shirley MacLaine Parker had a contract with Twentieth Century Fox to play the female lead in Bloomer Girl, a musical about gender and racial conflict in the antebellum South with a precociously progressive female lead character.The studio cancelled plans for Bloomer Girl and offered MacLaine as a substitute the female lead in Big Country, Big Man, a dramatic Western, with the same guaranteed compensation of $ 750,000 for fourteen weeks' work.MacLaine turned down the offered role and sued for the guaranteed compensation.In its defense, the studio argued that MacLaine failed to mitigate damages by not taking the offered role.The trial court rejected this defense on a motion for summary judgment.The fighting issue in the case on appeal was whether the question of the comparability of the roles (framed as whether the second role was "different and inferior" to the first) should go to the jury.The California Supreme Court said no, affirming the trial court.
The conduct countenanced in Parker might be quite wasteful. MacLaine did no work for fourteen weeks at a time when she "was one of the biggest female stars in Hollywood."If the studio was serious in its proposal to produce the Western with her as the female lead (which is not clear), then her refusal denied her fans the pleasure of seeing her in the role. Apparently, MacLaine did no other work during the fourteen-week period, for the studio did not seek an offset against damages. While MacLaine's rights were vindicated, it is at best rough justice. MacLaine received fourteen weeks of pay for which she did no work, which is a windfall if MacLaine values leisure more than whatever satisfaction (apart from the fee) she would have derived from performing in the musical.
The interest in remedial simplicity explains why the law tolerates waste and windfall in this situation. There is reason to believe that MacLaine genuinely preferred the role in Bloomer Girl to the role in Big Country, Big Man. To protect MacLaine from a loss in performing the less desired role, while avoiding waste, the law might require her to take the role in the Western while giving her damages for her loss. This the law does not do. Had MacLaine taken the role, she would have been denied damages for her artistic, political, or reputational loss, as any estimate of the loss would be speculative. The only way MacLaine could avoid suffering an uncompensated loss was to do what she did, which was to reject the role in Big Country, Big Man and get a judgment for the contract price.
Parker illustrates several respects in which the duty to mitigate is unlike the duty of care in negligence. First, whether an action is proper is determined by a subjective standard: taking an actor with all of his or her peculiar preferences when an action is of a type that plausibly implicates subjective preferences.Second, when it comes to mitigation, "one is not obligated to exalt the interests of the defaulter to his own probable detriment."The point I just made about Parker is really no more than a gloss on these two familiar propositions. Thus, when a party has subjective preferences in the promised performance that might be harmed by taking a substitute, she may reject the substitute to satisfy those preferences and avoid an uncompensated loss even if that loss might seem a relatively small sacrifice in comparison to the burden imposed on the defaulter. Third, a court will take the question of whether a choice was unreasonable away from the jury if the choice could have been reasonable. Contrast this deferential rule with the rule in negligence under which the issue of whether conduct is unreasonable is taken away from the jury only if no reasonable person could think the conduct unreasonable. Parker is direct authority for precisely this last point, for the fighting issue in the case was whether the question of the comparability of the roles should have gone to the jury.Maxims such as "uncertainty is resolved against a wrongdoer"or a party "should not be faulted for choosing one of several reasonable alternatives"tie all of this together and warn against hindsight judgment.
Rockingham County v. Luten Bridge Co.is often paired with Parker in casebooks.I expect this is done to show the mitigation doctrine has teeth. This is unfortunate, for the case has misled generations of students and even some teachers. The result in Luten Bridge is the exception and not the rule when a plaintiff completes performance after repudiation and sues for the contract price. Usually, when a party completes performance of a contract after repudiation, the party has a reason to do so in addition to collecting the contract price. So long as this reason is non-trivial the party will collect the contract price.
Luten Bridge Company had just begun work on a bridge for Rockingham County when a rump group of Rockingham County commissioners voted to relocate the road and to cancel the bridge contract.Other commissioners who claimed to speak for the county told the company to continue the work.The company completed the bridge.The fighting issues in the case (whichare edited out in most casebooks) are who spoke for the County in the litigation and in the cancellation decision.The court held that the rump group did.The opinion goes on to hold that the company could recover only its costs up to the time of the cancellation plus its lost profits, though it spent much more to finish the bridge.This seems a straightforward application of the mitigation doctrine. Even an inattentive student can see that the company ought to stop because it is wasteful to build a bridge in the middle of nowhere. I expect students are not told that the outcome hinged on the unusual fact that the company did not try to justify its decision to complete the bridge.Had the company given the court a plausible reason why it had to complete the bridge to avoid a loss that damages would not adequately compensate, the case likely would have come out the other way.
Clark v. Marsigliais the leading case requiring a party to stop performance to mitigate damages. The defendant delivered paintings to the plaintiff to clean and repair.After the plaintiff began work, the defendant told him to stop.The plaintiff completed the work and sued for the agreed fee.The plaintiff's theory of the case, which the trial court accepted, was that once the paintings were in his possession, the defendant had no right to take them back and he had the right to complete the work and recover the promised fee.A terse per curiam decision reversing the trial court emphasized the desirability of encouraging a person in the defendant's position to stop work he has ordered when he no longer wants the work done and the unfairness of requiring the defendant to pay for work done after the stop order.This is the mitigation principle pure and simple.
The treatment of Luten Bridge in the casebooks suggests that most teachers do not appreciate that the rule the case stands for is so riddled with exceptionsthat the outcome in the case actually is the exception and not the rule.While Clark was widely embraced in the United States,it is not followed if the plaintiff has an interest in completing performance that damages cannot adequately compensate.Bomberger v. McKelveycanvasses the exceptionsto the rule and notes the common theme.The facts of the case are a striking illustration that a plaintiff may complete performance to avoid a loss that may not be adequately compensated in damages even though completion inflicts a much greater loss on the defaulter. McKelvey bought a lot from Bomberger and agreed to pay Bomberger $ 3500 to demolish a building on the lot, with Bomberger being allowed to salvage what he could from the existing building.The parties understood that Bomberger would contract with the existing tenant to build a replacement building and that the existing tenant would vacate once that building was complete.McKelvey agreed to buy outthe balance of the existing tenant's lease at that time.After the lot was conveyed, McKelvey delayed construction of its planned store because it could not obtain needed materials due to wartime shortages.McKelvey ordered Bomberger not to proceed with the demolition.Bomberger ignored the order and demolished the building, claiming he needed skylights salvaged from the building to complete construction of the replacement building, which was well under way.The case holds Bomberger was entitled to the $ 3500 he was promised for the demolition work plus the $ 2500 he was promised to buy out the existing tenant's lease.The court reached this result despite the facts that the demolished building was worth around $ 26,000, it was generating $ 300 monthly rent, and the materials needed could be replaced at a cost of only $ 540 with approximately a three month delay.
The power to complete performance in response to repudiation and to collect the contract price is not absolute. English law starts from the premise that a party has a right to perform and collect the contract price in response to repudiation. English courts have struggled to define when this right gives way. One judge summed it up this way: "How one defines that point is obviously a matter of some difficulty; for it involves drawing a line between conduct which is merely unreasonable … and conduct which is wholly unreasonable."This delightfully cryptic standard seems to me a fairly apt description of the balance the Court struck in Bomberger. While Bomberger's decision to tear down the building clearly was unreasonable from McKelvey's perspective, and it probably was unreasonable from society's perspective, the decision was reasonable from Bomberger's perspective to avoid a three-month delay in securing payment for work he had already completed on another contract. The result in the case was not foreordained. I expect the California Supreme Court would have affirmed the trial court had it decided the mitigation issue in favor of McKelvey. In this respect, the case is unlike Parker, where a majority of the California Supreme Court held the reasonableness of MacLaine's choice could not be second-guessed. While this is an important qualification on the power recognized in Bomberger, the difference between Parker and Bomberger is one of degree and not of kind. The common theme is that the duty to mitigate does not require a party to respond to breach in a way that willexpose the party to a risk of a loss that may not be adequately compensated in damages even if the response would avoid a much larger loss to the defaulter.
. The Power to Withhold and Refuse Performance when the Rightful Position Is Certain and Damages May Be an Inadequate Remedy to Vindicate the Right
In American law, the doctrine of material breach and the related doctrines of total breach and substantial performance usually define when a party has the power to withhold or refuse performance in response to breach in the absence of an express condition.The mitigation doctrine performs a similar functionwhen called upon, as it was by the studio in Parker, to try to hold a plaintiff at fault for not accepting an offer of substitute performance.My major point in this Part is that the lesson of Parker can be generalized. A party may withhold performance in response to a clear breach, and may refuse non-conforming performance, to avoid suffering a loss that may not be adequately compensated by damages, even if withholding or refusing performance inflicts a disproportionate loss on the defaulter. The power to withhold performance in response to breach and the power to refuse non-conforming performance sometimes are limited to avoid forfeiture and unjust enrichment, but are not limited to avoid what has come to be called economic waste. There is no need to discuss conditions; it is well known that the law may excuse default of a condition to avoid forfeiture but that the law does not excuse default on the ground that fulfilling a condition imposes an unreasonable burden.
The Restatement (Second) of Contracts states five factors that bear on the determination of material breach.They are similar to the five factors thatbear on the determination of "fundamental breach" under the UNIDROIT principles.With no loss of substance, these two lists of five can be reduced to three factors: (1) whether the aggrieved party needs to withhold or refuse performance to avoid suffering a loss that will not be adequately compensated in damages;(2) the burden imposed on the defaulter by withholding or refusing performance;and (3) whether the default was willful or in bad faith.
The Restatement (Second) of Contracts is conspicuously silent about the relative weight assigned to these factors when they cut in different directions.As discussed above, a party may refuse non-conforming performance, or may withhold performance in response to breach, to avoid suffering a loss that may not be adequately compensated by damages, even if the response inflicts a disproportionate loss on the defaulter.The power to revoke acceptance in sales law provides a telling example. The standard for rejection - a buyer may reject a one-off delivery of goods for any imperfection - is famously pro-buyer.Revocation is more troublesome than rejection because the seller is likely to incur a loss when it must recover and resell goods that have been used by the buyer. Under the Uniform Commercial Code, a buyer may revoke acceptance for a hidden defect only if the defect "substantially impairs" the value of the goods to him.Commentators who have looked closely at thecases have found that courts are very protective of buyers' rights in applying this seemingly seller-friendly standard, so long as a buyer revokes promptly upon discovering a defect.
Colonial Dodge, Inc. v Millernicely illustrates this principle. Miller bought a station wagon with special-ordered extra-wide tires.The car was delivered without a spare extra-wide tire. Miller discovered the tire was missing later the same day, but only after he had driven the car four hundred miles. He demanded a spare from the dealer and was told that it could not be supplied because of a strike at the factory. Miller immediately parked the car in front of his house and demanded the dealer retrieve it. Eventually the car was towed from the street by the police, who impounded it for several years as the case passed through the courts. The dealer sued for the price of the car. He won in the trial court, lost on appeal, won on rehearing, and finally lost at the state supreme court by a vote of six to three.The expected loss to Miller from the temporary lack of a spare was small but, perhaps, meaningful to him.Much of the loss would have been psychological in worrying while driving without a spare. There was a small chance that Miller would be stranded without a spare. Miller's worries would never be compensated, and had he been stranded without a spare, few if any, of those losses would be compensated either. Returning the car imposed a large loss on the dealer - for the car could no longer be sold as new. That the case was thought close despite the imbalance between Miller's likely loss if he drove the car for a short period without the spare and the loss to the dealer from returning the car (the thirteen judges who heard the case split seven to six with one switching) is telling evidence of the unwillingness of judges to require buyers to take and pay for clearly defective performance when it might leave them with even a small uncompensated loss though the defaulting seller is subjected to a certain larger loss.
Plante v. Jacobsis a textbook counter example. A builder, Plante, misplaced a living room wall, narrowing the space by one foot.The Jacobses were ordered to pay the balance due on the contract for the work done (around$ 5000) and could not offset the expected cost to move the wall (around $ 4000), because narrowing the room did not lower their home's market value.This is the upshot of two rules that excuse minor defaults in construction contracts. The court applied the rule of substantial performance to give the builder a right to the contract price, and it applied the rule measuring the owner's damages by loss in market value when the remedial cost is much greater to allow the builder to recover most of the balance due.The second rule sometimes is said to be concerned with avoiding the economic waste that would result from repairing a defect when the cost of doing so is much greater than the actual loss from the defect.Others have observed that this misstates the purpose of both rules, which is to avoid forfeiture and unjustenrichment.In Plante, the objective view that the wall was not worth moving and the fact that the Jacobses chose not to move the wall combine to raise a strong inference that allowing the Jacobses to retain the unpaid contract price or to recover the cost of moving the wall would give them a windfall at the builder's expense.
If you remain unconvinced, then an often-overlookedlimitation on the rule might persuade the reader that this body of law is not about avoiding economic waste. If a party completes unfinished work, then courts routinely award the cost of completion without questioning the reasonableness of the decision to complete the work.While there is less authority for the point, the sameseems to be true if a party repairs defective work.The interest in avoiding economic waste cannot explain why, when the cost to complete unfinished work or to repair defective work is significantly greater than the market value of doing the work, an owner is allowed to recover remedial cost if and only if the owner actually does the remedial work.The result is utterly unsurprising once one recalls the lesson of Parker and Bomberger. Parker teaches that a party may refuse nonconforming performance to avoid an uncompensated loss even if the refusal inflicts a disproportionate loss on the defaulter.Bomberger teaches that a party may complete performance in response to repudiation and get a judgment for the contract price to avoid an uncompensated loss even if this inflicts a disproportionate loss on the defaulter.The cases just noted teach that a party may complete unfinished work or repair defective work and recover the cost to avoid an uncompensated loss even if this inflicts a disproportionate loss on the defaulter.
It is tempting to leave this topic with the law tied into this neat little package. But the common law rarely is so neat.In some jurisdictions, the law on remedies for takings, negligence, and nuisance contains a rule that limits damages when property is inadvertently or justifiably taken to the lesser of replacement cost and market value, and that limits damages when property is inadvertently or justifiably harmed to the lesser of repair cost and diminution in market value.In Washington state, this has been called the "lesser than" rule.In New York, this has been called the "lesser of two" rule.This rule does not always give way if a plaintiff replaces or repairs property at a cost significantly greater than market-based damages even though the plaintiff arguably had to act as it did to avoid a loss that might not be adequately compensated in damages. In the federal law of takings, compensation generally is limited to the lesser of market value and replacement cost, without regard to whether the plaintiff replaces the property,with limited exceptions for situations in which market-based damages clearly and predictably undercompensate a plaintiff.There are negligence and nuisance cases thatapply the rule even though a plaintiff replaces or repairs the property at a cost that is significantly greater than market-based damages.
It is hard to know what to make of these cases, particularly the tort cases.I can think of no good reason to have a different and less generous damage rule in the law of negligence and nuisance than in contract law for similar losses. Perhaps we can ignore these cases as relics of a more rule-bound time. Some courts reject the "lesser of two" rule out of hand and take a more flexible approach that permits a fact-finder to award whatever amount of damages fairly compensates a plaintiff.Other courts keep the rule but undercut it with more-or-less open-ended exceptions.Academic commentary is uniformly critical of cases that woodenly apply the rule in circumstances in which the rule's purpose does not justify its application.This purpose is to avoidgiving the plaintiff a windfall when the replacement or repair leaves him with an asset that is newer or better than the asset that was taken or damaged.Still, the contrary cases applying the "lesser of two" rule remind us that it is impossible to give an abstract account of the law that is coherent, consistent, and clear. There will always be odd bits and pieces that do not fit with the general principles that best account for most of the law.
. The Power to Exercise the Nonperformance Option when the Rightful Position Is Uncertain
In the cases that are the focus of Parts I and II, the actor's rightful position under a contract is certain while the magnitude of the actor's loss from breach is uncertain. This Part looks at how the law regulates the exercise of what I will call the "nonperformance option" (meaning the power to withhold or refuse performance, and the power to threaten to do so to extract concessions) when an actor's rightful position is uncertain. In addition to the rules on mitigation and material breach, two new sets of rules are brought to bear to determine the consequences of exercising or not exercising the nonperformance option when an actor's rightful position is uncertain. Which set of rules applies depends on whether nonperformance is likely to have harmful consequences. One set encourages the exercise of the nonperformance option to settle a dispute when nonperformance will not have harmful consequences. The other set, in conjunction with the rules on mitigation and material breach, discourages the exercise of the nonperformance option to settle a dispute when nonperformance will have harmful consequences.
While the general point is novel, the merits of having these two sets of rules are fairly obvious. Picture a contract as two people undertaking to row a boat across a river. On the river, a dispute arises over whether one is pulling his weight. If the river is placid, the day is clear, and there is no need to cross the river quickly, then the law encourages the rowers to resolve the dispute themselves on the river as best they can. The law permits one rower to stop rowing unless the other concedes, and if the rowers manage to make it across the river, the law treats this as the end of the matter and will not allow either rower to seek redress in court unless both rowers clearly agree to stay their dispute for resolution by a court once they get to shore. If the river is dangerous or there is a need to cross quickly, then the law encourages the rowers to put their dispute to the side and row to shore. Once on shore, a court will hear the dispute and try to set matters right. If in dangerous circumstances a rower stops and refuses to row further unless the other pulls his weight, then the rower who stops faces a risk of being held responsible for the resulting losseven if he is in the right in the underlying dispute. The law discourages the rowers from making threats that might lead to disastrous consequences. In sufficiently dangerous circumstances, the rules on duress even permit a rower to deceive the other rower by pretending to submit to a threat to get across the river while planning to assert his rights once safely ashore.
The rules we are about to look at presuppose an honest dispute. Quite different rules come into play if a party makes a dishonest demand for performance or refuses to perform an obligation that he knows is due. A note given to settle a dishonest claim or a release given by a creditor in return for part payment of an undisputed debt may be unenforceable for lack of consideration.Unjustified non-payment of a debt may strip a debtor of contract rights. For example, it may give the creditor the right to accelerate future payments.A knowing breach of an indisputable obligation may result in forfeiture of any right to compensation for work done.Merely asserting a position in bad faith may constitute a material breach, justifying the other party's withdrawal from a contract.And there is the late twentieth centuryinnovation of the tort of bad faith breach of contract. The tort exposes an insurer who unjustifiably denies a claim to liability for emotional distress damages and sometimes to punitive damages.These are dangerous legal shoals, but they do not threaten if a refusal to perform or a demand for performance is honest. Generally, a refusal or demand will be honest if a right is uncertain.
The voluntary payment doctrine is a good place to start. The doctrine prohibits claims to recover overpayment by debtors who pay disputed debts.The doctrine "ensures that those who desire to assert a legal right do so at the first possible opportunity; this way, all interested parties are aware of that position and have the opportunity to tailor their own conduct accordingly."The effect of the doctrine is to encourage a debtor not to pay more than it thinks it owes, for it will have no opportunity to recover an overpayment. The rules on accord and satisfaction empower a debtor to tender part payment, with an implicit threat of non-payment if the creditor rejects part payment, to resolve a dispute on favorable terms.This has been described as "an exquisite form of commercial torture."While torture this may be, a creditor has little hope of avoiding a release on grounds of duress because of the view that it is not improper to exploit another's financial distress by trying to settle a genuinely disputed claim.
The voluntary payment doctrine has the familiar stickiness of an interpretive presumption. Payment is final unless the parties state clearly that final payment was not their intent. The rule is sticky in another more unusual way. Under the traditional rule, a debtor cannot avoid the voluntary payment doctrine by saying that when he pays, he reserves his right to recover the money.The rules on accord and satisfaction (including the unavailability ofrescission on grounds of duress) are similar in that they prevent the creditor from unilaterally reserving the right to sue for the balance if the creditor takes the tendered payment. The upshot of these rules is that avoiding finality of payment requires both parties' expressed assent.
The second set of rules permits, and sometimes even requires, a party to perform a disputed obligation, or to accept performance of disputed sufficiency, and then go to court to vindicate a claim that less was owed or more was due. The unusual facts of Henrici v. South Feather Land & Water Co.serve to illustrate most of these rules. It is a useful case for my purposes because the dispute was over a relatively small sum of money.Due to thisfact, neither party needed to withhold or refuse performance to vindicate its right.
South Feather assumed a long-term contract to supply water to Henrici's farm.It proposed a new pricing scheme that would have slightly increased Henrici's payments.It was not clear South Feather had this right.Henrici refused to take water on the new terms and allowed his farm to go to waste. He had no other source of water for irrigation. The case holds that even though Henrici was in the right in the underlying dispute about price, he could not recover damages for his losses because he should have mitigated damages by taking the water and later suing to recover the overpayment.Crucial to the decision is the court's assumption that Henrici would not have relinquished his right to recover an overpayment had he taken the water and paid what South Feather asked.While the court did not explain, presumably it would have allowed a restitution claim by Henrici to recover the overpayment.
As we shall see, Henrici had another option. He might have tendered the old price pending resolution of the dispute. Had South Feather responded to this tender by cutting off the water supply, then this would be a material breach and it would be responsible for the harm to Henrici's farm. Henrici's tender of the old price would not be a material breach justifying suspension of performance by South Feather because any loss from under-payment is easily compensated should South Feather be in the right.Further, Henrici's tenderof the old price would be in good faith. In sum, Henrici had two choices in the case - he could pay either the new or the old price pending resolution of the dispute - between which the law is indifferent. This is sensible because, putting issues like differences in insolvency risk and collection costs to the side, there is no reason to prefer one party over the other when we ask who should hold money in dispute pending resolution of the dispute.
Changing the facts in Henrici brings into play other rules that encourage performing a disputed obligation, or accepting performance of disputed sufficiency, when nonperformance is harmful. What would happen if South Feather tells Henrici that taking the water constitutes acceptance of the new price and relinquishment of his claim to the old price? This is the accord and satisfaction gambit. It is clear that Henrici may recover his losses if he refuses the water and is in the right on price. His duty to mitigate does not require him to relinquish his claim of a right to pay less.By casting the loss back on South Feather, the law punishes South Feather for unnecessarily escalating the dispute.
Alternatively, in this situation, section 1-308 of the Uniform Commercial Code,gives Henrici the power to take the water and reserve his rights by announcing that he is ignoring South Feather's gambit and reserving his rights.The power to parry South Feather's gambit with a reservation of rights enables Henrici to test South Feather's resolve because South Feather will have to follow through on its threat to stop delivery of water.
The law might even allow Henrici to deceive South Feather to defuse the conflict. Assume South Feather refuses to deliver the water until Henrici pays the total amount it claims is due and signs a release of any claim to a lower price. If Henrici agrees to South Feather's demands to get water he desperately needs, then he might be able to avoid the settlement by claiming duress. South Feather's threat to withhold water is border-line extortion and acore instance of bad faith because the threatened act will inflict a large loss on Henrici while yielding a small benefit to South Feather.The doctrine of duress and U.C.C. section 1-308 in effect allow a party to unilaterally dictate that performance is not final to preserve a claim of right. This is the mirror image of the voluntary payment rule and the rules on accord and satisfaction, which require both parties expressly to assent to preserve a claim.
These rules are reinforced by the doctrine of material breach, which encourages a party to accept a performance of disputed sufficiency or to perform a disputed obligation when this avoids a loss to the other party and is unnecessary to vindicate a claim of right.In particular, when a contract breaks down as a result of escalating hostile conduct, the material breach doctrine casts the loss on whichever party, if either, first acts unjustifiably in further escalating the conflict. To illustrate, consider a scenario in whichSouth Feather demands the higher charge, Henrici pays the lower amount that he thinks is due, and South Feather cuts off the water in response. Cutting off the water will be considered a material breach by South Feather and so the loss will be cast upon it even if it is in the right on price.South Feather does not need to cut off the water to ensure payment of the larger sum, which is penniesmore. Henrici pays the lower sum in good faith. And cutting off the water inflicts a large loss on Henrici. While the break down is a result of both parties obdurate conduct, and Henrici commits the first breach in paying less than he owes, the loss is cast on South Feather because it does not need to cut off the water to vindicate its right to the additional pennies it is owed.
We might extract from the forgoing a simple rule that requires parties to a contract with uncertain performance terms to cooperate when relevant rights are uncertain and the gains from cooperation are large.But this is not the law. As we saw in Parts I and II, a party has the power to withhold or refuse performance in response to breach to avoid a loss that may not be adequately compensated with damages, even if the action inflicts a disproportionate loss on the defaulter. This power does not give way because the right a party seeks to protect by withholding or refusing performance is uncertain. In Parker v. Twentieth Century-Fox,if it had been uncertain whether the studio had the right to substitute Big Man, Big Country for Bloomer Girl, then this uncertainty would not change the result once the court determined the contract did not give the studio this right. This is true even if MacLaine's refusal of the second role had imposed a loss on the studio that was disproportionate to MacLaine's likely loss from taking the second role. Of course, if the studio prevailed on the disputed point, then MacLaine would be liable for the studio's unrecoverable costs and any other losses that can be proven with a reasonable degree of accuracy. This is the familiar result in the situation in which a loss is suffered from a breakdown of a contract when both parties are justifiably obdurate in insisting that performance occur only on their terms on the ground that performance on the other's terms would subject each of them to anuncompensated loss in the event they turn out to be in the right in the underlying dispute. In this situation, the law casts the loss (insofar as it is compensable in damages) on whomever the court finds is in the wrong in the underlying dispute.
Natural features of the situation encourage parties to cooperate if rights are uncertain and if the gains from cooperation are large. The pressure to cooperate is strongest if each party anticipates the entire joint loss will fall on them if they are found to be in the wrong in the underlying dispute. In this situation, a party always may expect to bear his own loss from non-cooperation if he is found to be wrong in the underlying dispute, and he may expect to bear the other party's loss to the extent it is recoverable

questions.question: When and to what extent does contract law permit a party to use self-help (withholding, refusing, or threatening nonperformance) to respond to an alleged breach in order to avoid suffering losses that monetary damages would not adequately compensate?

How does contract law regulate the use of self-help when the parties' contractual rights are uncertain-i.e., does the law push parties toward private settlement or toward performance followed by litigation, and what normative (efficiency and autonomy) reasons justify that allocation?

Does a party's duty to mitigate require accepting substitute or nonconforming performance that would expose the party to a risk of uncompensated loss, or may the party preserve its rights by refusing such performance?

matched_themes: What standard should courts apply to determine whether a party's deviation from contractual obligations is significant enough to excuse the other party's performance?
How should legal doctrine treat contractual waivers (e.g., waivers of fraud claims or other torts)-do courts enforce such waivers or decide cases on alternative grounds?
Should courts allow apportionment of contractual damages when the non-breaching party's reliance or failure to cooperate contributed to the loss?
How should courts choose between cost-to-complete and diminution-in-value remedies in construction disputes, and what objective criteria should guide that choice?
What counterfactual baseline should courts use to measure plaintiffs' losses for compensation purposes?
How should default liability rules interact with parties' freedom to allocate risks by contract and duties of disclosure to achieve efficient and fair risk allocation?
When should courts order specific performance (in-kind relief) versus awarding monetary damages?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?
Should the promisor or the promisee have the default right to choose between performance and payment to achieve allocative efficiency?
How do institutional features-court capacity, procedural devices, and evidentiary rules-affect the substantive development and practical application of contract remedies?
How should courts decide between measuring damages by cost of completion versus diminution in market value when remedial work is breached?
Does making in-kind performance the legal default (rather than monetary compensation) change parties' enforcement choices, moral judgments, and economic efficiency?
When and to what extent should private self-help (withholding performance, repossession, or force) be permitted as a contract-enforcement mechanism?

Should remedies and contract law be structured to preserve conditions necessary for moral agency and promissory responsibility, rather than treating promises solely as instruments of economic cooperation?
How do transaction costs, enforcement frictions, and institutional realities alter the theoretical efficiency of breach-plus-compensation?

Can party-designed enforcement mechanisms (pre-agreed penalties, arbitration, bonding, reputational systems) reliably produce efficient breach outcomes without judicial intervention, and when do they fail?
Should plaintiffs be permitted to recover non-pecuniary harms such as mental distress in breach-of-contract cases?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
Do enforceable contractual damage remedies substitute for or complement informal relational governance in franchise and other repeated relationships?
How should remedial and enforcement rules be structured to achieve efficient behavior when populations include both internalizers and externalizers?
Can courts reliably determine ex post whether a breach would increase social welfare so that remedy choice can be used to promote efficiency?
To what extent does empirical uncertainty about measuring gains and losses limit courts' ability to design remedies that reflect non-welfare ethical preferences without sacrificing efficiency?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
Do limits on recoverable damages (foreseeability, certainty, avoidability) substantially reduce awards below full compensation, and should courts liberalize those limits?
What are the conceptual and methodological limits of the law-and-economics approach, and has the movement materially changed judicial decision-making?
Do courts consider the breaching party's blameworthiness or opportunistic behavior when selecting among compensatory remedies?
To what extent should moral blameworthiness and non-economic considerations influence the design and application of contract remedies?
When is an indirect remedy (one that induces self-compliance) preferable to a direct remedy that delivers the outcome?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 82columlrev1365!!ARTICLE: In Defense of Money Damages for Breach of Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: In Defense of Money Damages for Breach of Contract

shared_topics.topic: when money damages adequately compensate versus when non-monetary relief is needed
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends expectation (money) damages as the normal remedy and analyzes contexts where they may undercompensate (e.g., restoration of leased land), while Paper B repeatedly asks when damages will be inadequate (subjective losses, risk of uncompensated harms) and shows how the law permits self-help or other responses when money relief cannot fully vindicate rights.

shared_topics.topic: the proper role and limits of specific performance and other non-damages remedies (withholding, refusal, completion)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether specific performance should become the paradigmatic remedy instead of damages and argues against routinizing it; Paper B theorizes the law of self-help (withholding performance, refusing nonconforming performance, completing performance) and explains doctrinal limits on those non-damages remedies.

shared_topics.topic: subjective and hard-to-quantify losses as a driver of remedial choice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes difficulty in quantifying promisee's subjective losses (e.g., land restoration, personal value) as a key argument sometimes favoring specific performance but ultimately supports tailored damages rules, while Paper B uses cases like Parker to show courts protect subjective preferences by allowing refusal or recovery even when damages would be speculative.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between economic efficiency and fairness/autonomy in designing remedy rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the recent efficiency-based push for specific performance and defends money damages partly on fairness and flexibility grounds, and Paper B contrasts efficiency-oriented 'efficient breach' theories with autonomy-respecting doctrines that tolerate waste to avoid short-changing rights.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal rules (mitigation, material/substantial breach, voluntary payment/accord and satisfaction) allocate risk and shape parties' self-help options
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for selective modification of damages rules to better meet contract law objectives, and Paper B analyzes how mitigation, material breach, substantial performance, UCC §1-308, and related doctrines govern when parties may withhold, accept, or litigate performance disputes and thereby allocate losses between parties.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE FUTURE OF LAW AND ECONOMICS: THE STRANGEST ATTACK YET ON LAW AND ECONOMICS.

shared_topics.topic: the doctrine of 'efficient breach' and its normative/descriptive validity
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on Jaffee's attack on the concept of efficient breach—questioning whether breaches that raise aggregate welfare should be tolerated—while Paper B shows how doctrines governing self-help and withholding performance (and the law's tolerance for waste to protect rights) empirically and theoretically undermine the simple economics of efficient-breach arguments.

shared_topics.topic: when damages are an adequate remedy versus when courts should enforce specific performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether specific performance should be preferred to damages to prevent opportunistic ‘efficient’ breaches, and Paper B analyzes the conditions under which damages inadequately compensate parties (and so withholding, repudiation, or performance remedies like price recovery or specific relief are justified).

shared_topics.topic: how nonperformance and breach create harms beyond the contracting parties and how law allocates those losses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises third‑party and organizational costs of breach (employees, demoralization, transaction externalities) as critiques of the efficient‑breach model, and Paper B repeatedly frames rules (mitigation, material breach, duress doctrines) around whether nonperformance will cause harmful consequences to others and how losses should be placed.

shared_topics.topic: post‑breach bargaining dynamics, transaction costs, and bilateral‑monopoly problems
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses bilateral monopoly, bargaining holdouts, and transaction costs that complicate post‑breach renegotiation, and Paper B systematically studies threats to withhold performance, threats used to extract concessions, and doctrinal rules (accord and satisfaction, UCC §1‑308, duress) that structure renegotiation incentives and limit opportunism.

shared_topics.topic: the normative tension between efficiency and non‑economic values (autonomy, promise‑keeping, retribution)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights Jaffee's moralist critique—favoring promise‑keeping and critiquing marketizing norms—while Paper B contrasts economic efficiency with autonomy‑based norms and defends remedial rules that protect parties' subjective interests even at the expense of some inefficiency.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2006michstlrev883!!ARTICLE: PENALTIES AS RATIONAL RESPONSE TO BARGAINING IRRATIONALITY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PENALTIES AS RATIONAL RESPONSE TO BARGAINING IRRATIONALITY

shared_topics.topic: adequacy of damages as a substitute for specific performance and its effect on parties' incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that damages often inadequately compensate subjective or hard-to-measure losses, which explains why law tolerates self-help (withholding/refusal) and windfalls to protect performance rights; Paper B likewise treats the under‑compensatory nature of damages as central to why parties use supra‑compensatory penalty clauses and why the indifference principle fails in practice.

shared_topics.topic: limits on freedom of contract versus judicial paternalism in policing remedial terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages the normative dispute between economic (efficiency) and autonomy/formalism approaches in deciding which informal or uncertain agreements courts should enforce and how self‑help should be regulated; Paper B debates whether the special doctrine invalidating penalty clauses is an illegitimate paternalistic intrusion on freedom of contract and argues for relaxing that policing rule.

shared_topics.topic: how bargaining context, consent, and power shape enforcement of disputed contractual rights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how honest disputes, duress, reservation of rights, and unequal costs of nonperformance affect whether parties may withhold performance or must accept and litigate; Paper B empirically examines negotiation settings and bargaining power to argue the law should distinguish negotiated penalty clauses from one‑sided standard form impositions.

shared_topics.topic: use of contractual remedies and clauses as strategic bargaining tools
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies threats to withhold performance, accord and satisfaction, voluntary payment doctrine, and reservation of rights as mechanisms parties use to extract concessions or resolve disputes; Paper B treats liquidated‑damage/penalty clauses as deliberate contractual responses to perceived bargaining/risk preferences and behavioral biases that function as strategic instruments.

shared_topics.topic: the interplay between legal rules and actual contracting behavior (including behavioral considerations)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how remedial rules (material breach, mitigation, UCC §1‑308, duress doctrines) shape parties' real‑world decisions to perform, withhold, or settle; Paper B brings behavioral decision theory evidence that negotiators use heuristics and biases, arguing legal doctrine should respond to such real contracting behavior rather than assume classical rationality.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 98neblrev926!!ARTICLE: Irrevocable Gift Promises and Promises Inducing Reliance: A Mandate for the Return of the Seal in Contract Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Irrevocable Gift Promises and Promises Inducing Reliance: A Mandate for the Return of the Seal in Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: when and how informal or uncertain promises should be enforced (settlement vs judicial resolution)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes rules that govern parties' nonperformance options and how the law prods or discourages self-help (withholding/accepting performance) when contractual rights are uncertain, favoring out-of-court settlements in low-harm disputes; Paper B examines which donative promises outside classic bargain doctrine are nonetheless enforced (trusts, wills, reliance) and asks when courts should treat informal gift promises as legally binding.

shared_topics.topic: the evidentiary/formal mechanisms that substitute for consideration to make promises enforceable
shared_topics.justification: Paper B argues that formalities (seals, trust/will execution) functionally replace consideration by providing ritualized proof and low adjudicative costs for enforcing gift promises; Paper A studies doctrinal devices (accord and satisfaction, UCC §1-308, voluntary payment rule, reservation of rights) that channel evidence and allocate finality so courts can efficiently determine whether disputed performance settled rights.

shared_topics.topic: reliance-based enforcement and the role of promissory estoppel or reliance in protecting non-bargained expectations
shared_topics.justification: Paper B centers reliance promises and promissory estoppel as a route to enforce certain uncompleted or donative promises, articulating the formalities that make reliance enforcement sensible; Paper A engages with related doctrines (restitution, mitigation, voluntary payment) and the allocation of losses when parties act on disputed claims, showing how the law sometimes enforces or protects reliance-like conduct to avoid uncompensated losses.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial design should trade off adjudicative costs, certainty, and substantive justice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A offers a normative account that explains self-help rules as promoting remedial simplicity and lowering litigation costs even at the expense of some waste or windfall; Paper B defends reviving the seal and other formalities to reduce error and adjudicative costs and to give parties a reliable means to make promises enforceable.

shared_topics.topic: the debate between rule/formalism and economic/efficiency approaches to contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques contemporary economic accounts (efficient breach) and defends rule-based doctrines that protect autonomy and rights even when inefficient; Paper B criticizes the indeterminacy of consideration and advocates a formal-rule solution (the seal) grounded in an economic rationale that parties' intended promises should be enforceable, thus engaging the same formalism-versus-efficiency tension.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 57scallrev667!!ARTICLE: A LITTLE ESSAY IN PARTIAL DEFENSE OF THE CONTRACT-MARKET DIFFERENTIAL AS A REMEDY FOR BUYERS.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A LITTLE ESSAY IN PARTIAL DEFENSE OF THE CONTRACT-MARKET DIFFERENTIAL AS A REMEDY FOR BUYERS.

shared_topics.topic: when monetary damages are an adequate (or inadequate) remedy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends the contract–market differential as an accurate compensatory measure in sale-of-goods disputes, arguing it normally makes the buyer whole; Paper B analyzes many doctrines (mitigation, material breach, revocation, completion after repudiation) that arise precisely when courts conclude monetary damages may not adequately vindicate a party's loss and so justify withholding, refusal, or completion remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate metric for measuring compensation (market price vs. replacement/repair cost)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on market-price-based measurement (contract–market differential versus cover) as the proper buyer remedy, while Paper B repeatedly contrasts market-value measures with replacement or repair cost (and the 'lesser of two' rule), exploring when courts award market value or compel/compensate by remedial cost.

shared_topics.topic: remedies under the UCC/Article Two and sale-of-goods law for buyers
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the drafting and application of Article Two remedies and the judicial use of the contract–market differential in sales cases; Paper B engages UCC provisions (e.g., revocation standards, section 1-308) and sales-case examples (rejection, revocation of acceptance, buyer withholding) that govern buyer responses to nonconforming performance.

shared_topics.topic: the temporal dimension of remedy measurement and enforcement (timing of breach, cover/resale, completion, and measurement date)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A confronts critiques that the contract–market differential mismeasures compensation because of time lapses between breach, market measurement, and resale/cover; Paper B treats timing as central to mitigation and remedy outcomes—when parties complete performance after repudiation, when they must tender disputed sums, and how timing affects finality (voluntary payment, accord and satisfaction).

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations of remedial rules: balancing efficiency, simplicity, and autonomy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A offers a theoretical defense of a market-based damages rule grounded in compensatory accuracy and practical simplicity; Paper B provides an explicit normative account arguing remedial simplicity and protection of autonomous contracting choices sometimes justify rules that tolerate waste or windfalls and that push back on simplistic ‘efficient breach’ prescriptions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 24geojlegalethics357!!ARTICLE: A Crisis of Confidence and Legal Theory: Why the Economic Downturn Should Help Signal the End of the Doctrine of Efficient Breach
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Crisis of Confidence and Legal Theory: Why the Economic Downturn Should Help Signal the End of the Doctrine of Efficient Breach

shared_topics.topic: the normative and doctrinal critique of the doctrine of efficient breach

shared_topics.topic: when damages are an inadequate remedial response and justify nonjudicial responses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends that compensatory damages under efficient-breach reasoning leave non-breaching parties undercompensated, and Paper B develops an extended case-law account explaining when courts permit withholding, refusal, or completion of performance because damages would not adequately vindicate the injured party.

shared_topics.topic: the role of social norms, trust, and reciprocity in sustaining contractual exchange and how law shapes them
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers trust and reciprocity as market predicates threatened by doctrines that encourage opportunism, and Paper B analyzes how doctrinal rules (e.g., material breach, mitigation, accord and satisfaction, UCC §1-308) are calibrated to encourage cooperative dispute-resolution and protect informal enforcement norms.

shared_topics.topic: opportunistic short-term behavior, its externalities, and doctrinal limits on exploitative tactics
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links efficient-breach logic to the opportunism that fueled subprime and systemic financial collapse, while Paper B traces doctrines (duress, bad-faith breach, material breach) that limit or penalize exploitative threats and strategically harmful nonperformance.

shared_topics.topic: the contest between law-and-economics efficiency claims and alternative normative frameworks (autonomy, remedial simplicity, rule-formalism)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes law-and-economics scholars for ignoring moral and systemic consequences of efficiency-based rules, and Paper B explicitly responds to economic accounts by defending remedial simplicity, autonomy-protecting rules, and a doctrinal structure that tolerates waste to protect rights.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 75texlrev293!!ARTICLE: A Primer on Prejudgment Interest
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Primer on Prejudgment Interest

shared_topics.topic: when monetary damages are inadequate and the law supplies or calibrates alternative remedies to ensure full compensation

shared_topics.topic: how remedial rules and doctrines should be standardized versus left to judicial discretion
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques wide judicial and statutory variation in how prejudgment interest is calculated and calls for constrained, finance‑based proxies to reduce discretion, and Paper B documents a sprawling, rule‑scattered body of authority governing self‑help and mitigation and evaluates when clearer, principled rules (versus equitable discretion) best serve efficiency and autonomy.

shared_topics.topic: the effects of remedial design on parties' incentives to delay, perform, or settle (strategic behavior)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that prejudgment interest reduces defendants' incentives to delay litigation and aligns incentives for precaution, while Paper B analyzes how powers to withhold performance, threaten nonperformance, or accept disputed performance shape parties' strategic bargaining, settlement choices, and incentives to cooperate or escalate disputes.

shared_topics.topic: using economic and financial reasoning to justify or critique remedial doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds the correct measurement of prejudgment interest in financial principles (time value of money, market rates, compounding), arguing for economically coherent proxies, whereas Paper B deploys economic concepts (efficiency, mitigation costs, uncompensated losses, transaction costs) to explain and normatively defend legal rules on self‑help and mitigation.

shared_topics.topic: the tradeoffs between formal remedial simplicity and tailored equitable responses to avoid windfalls or forfeiture
shared_topics.justification: Paper A warns that incorrect or simplistic interest rules (e.g., fixed statutory rates, simple interest) can produce unjust enrichment or over/undercompensation, while Paper B shows courts tolerate some waste or windfall in favor of remedial simplicity (or to avoid forfeiture) and explores when the law should permit tailored responses (withholding, completion, repairs) instead of blunt monetary adjustments.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: FAULT IN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: how courts allocate losses, burdens of proof, and evidentiary presumptions in breach disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the puzzling allocation of burdens (e.g., contract law often requires the wrongdoer to prove lack of fault), and Paper B analyzes a sprawling set of rules—material breach, mitigation, voluntary payment, accord and satisfaction, UCC §1-308—that assign who bears loss and finality in contested-performance situations.

shared_topics.topic: the normative tension between economic theories of efficient breach and remedial simplicity/autonomy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A assesses whether a fault-based regime would produce more optimal contract enforcement than strict liability, whereas Paper B critiques the efficient-breach logic and defends remedial simplicity and autonomy (including tolerating some waste/windfall) as explanations for self-help and no-option-to-breach rules.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE ROLE OF FAULT IN CONTRACT LAW: UNCONSCIONABILITY, UNEXPECTED CIRCUMSTANCES, INTERPRETATION, MISTAKE, AND NONPERFORMANCE

shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines liability for nonperformance and how fault can excuse or aggravate nonperformance outcomes; Paper B provides a detailed positive and normative account of the law permitting parties to withhold, refuse, or threaten performance and the scattered rules that calibrate those powers and their legal consequences.

shared_topics.topic: the normative tension between economic efficiency (efficient breach) and moral/autonomy or remedial‑simplicity values in remedy design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends contract rules should incorporate moral values (including fault) alongside policy and empirical claims rather than rely on strict‑liability efficiency models; Paper B critiques efficient‑breach reasoning, arguing the law tolerates waste and windfall to protect autonomy and provide simple, reliable remedies that guard against uncompensated losses.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies the 'nonperformance option' — threats to withhold performance, tender-with-reservation-of-rights, and duress/settlement dynamics — and how the law prods settlement or performance depending on harm; Paper B treats the strategic role of remedial rights (penalties, specific performance) as bargaining leverage and analyzes whether promisees would actually demand supracompensatory rights.

shared_topics.topic: the normative tension between efficiency (economic) justifications and autonomy/party-preference in shaping remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques prevailing economic accounts (e.g., efficient breach) and argues remedial simplicity and autonomy explain many doctrines allowing waste to avoid short-changing rights; Paper B directly tests the economic assumption that promisees want supracompensatory remedies and draws implications for default rules and judicial policing of contracts.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: CONTRACTS IN THE REAL WORLD: ESSAY: THE PERSPECTIVE OF LAW ON CONTRACT

shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises how the law’s perspective treats contract as a social practice (and the need to integrate internal/external viewpoints), and Paper B analyzes how self-help, withholding performance, and tolerance of informal agreements shape and are shaped by social practices of self-enforcement and litigation incentives.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Comparative Ruminations on the Foreseeability of Damages in Contract Law. Dedicated to Professor Jurgen Basedow, Augsburg University, School of Law.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: MODERN MARINE INSURANCE: COVERAGES, CURRENT ISSUES, AND CONNECTIONS:Reform of the Insurance Law of England and Wales - Separate Laws for the Different Needs of Businesses and Consumers
