papers.node_id: 2013uilllrev151!!ARTICLE: CAN'T BUY ME LOVE: MONETARY VERSUS IN-KIND REMEDIES
papers.title: ARTICLE: CAN'T BUY ME LOVE: MONETARY VERSUS IN-KIND REMEDIES
papers.abstract:
Most people would agree with Paul McCartney that money cannot buy the experience of love, the delight at hearing a baby coo, or the awe inspired by the sight of a towering mountain. At the same time, there is a common belief that money is an apt substitution for other entitlements in proprietary and commercial contexts. Specifically, legal practitioners, policymakers, and academics often assume that people are basically indifferent between monetary and in-kind remedies of equal pecuniary value. The choice between remedies is a subject of fierce debate in the legal literature, and it is therefore surprising that little research has been directed at determining which type of remedy people prefer. To date, arguments for or against particular remedies rest on theoretical reasoning and intuitions, rather than on experimental or empirical data. A case in point is the debate regarding remedies for breach of contract. Law-and-economics scholars often claim that people ordinarily view a contractual obligation as an option to either perform in-kind or to providemonetary compensation.This claim is based on an untested presumption that promisees would prefer to afford promisors an option to perform or pay in return for a price reduction.Others respond that this is not the case,but they, too, fail to support their claims with hard evidence.
The few existing experimental studies of contract remedies have not resolved this issue. These studies elicited laypersons' opinionsand focused on moral judgments regarding breach.Critics have dismissed such studies for two reasons. First, it was argued that businesspeople plausibly hold different preferences than laypersons and would be more inclined toward maximizing monetary profits.Second, participants in the experiments were told that a breach of contract had occurred, whereas the option-theory posits that promisees allow promisors to substitute money for in-kind performance.Accordingly, voluntary payment of damages constitutes fulfillment of the contractual obligation, not breach. Outside of contract law, there has been no experimental testing of preferences with respect to different types of legal remedies.
This conspicuous absence of data may be due to the widespread belief in the adequacy of monetary remedies. Indeed, monetary compensation is the most common form of redress for rights violations. When the state takes land for public use, when a seller breaches a contract to deliver goods, or when an employer wrongfully discharges an employee, the injured party will ordinarily receive a monetary award.A monetaryremedy has various advantages. It does not interfere excessively with the autonomy of the injuring party. Thus, when a contract for personal services has been breached, the promisor's liberty is curtailed to a lesser extent if she is only obligated to compensate the promisee than if she is required to render the personal services.At the same time, monetary remedies presumably place the right holder in the same position she would have been in had her rights not been infringed upon. For example, it is assumed that takings compensation enables the owner of a vacant parcel to buy a substitute for the expropriated land,and that expectation damages afford the promisee the benefit of the bargain.Moreover, monetary awards allow the recipient greater freedom in pursuing her goals than in-kind awards do. The right holder can use the money to directly remedy her loss or for any other purpose, and thus monetary remedies are closely attuned to individuals' changing preferences. A final advantage monetary remedies afford is that they are comparatively easy to administer. It is far more difficult to supervise the construction of a building than to enforce a monetary judgment on a breaching contractor.Monetary redress seems to be a win-win-win situation for all the parties concerned: plaintiffs, defendants, and the court.
True, the law has always recognized exceptions to the rule of monetary compensation, as in the case of a contract for the sale of unique goods.Since, by definition, there are no satisfactory substitutes for the contracted-for asset, it would be difficult to quantify the losses to the promisee. Therefore, specific performance is granted when the breached contract involves goods like heirlooms and works of art.Another example of in-kind redress is cases of wrongful interference with property. Injunctions are the typical remedy against trespassers to land.
Notwithstanding such examples, there is a widespread, staunch belief that accurate monetary quantification of losses is ordinarily both attainable and advantageous.This can explain the argument, mentioned above, that a promisor who voluntarily makes a payment in lieu of delivering the stipulated goods or services has not breached the contract at all.If there is no difference between performance in-kind and its monetary equivalent, promisees would presumably agree to grant such an option to promisors for a reduction in the price. Indeed, promisors should be encouraged to seek opportunities for more profitable transactions.The crucial question, however, is whether the assumption of indifference between remedies of equal pecuniary value in fact holds true.
This Article sets out to fill the void in the literature by presenting a new experimental study of people's choices between in-kind and monetary redress, examining both ex ante choices among entitlements, such as between two contractual terms, and ex post choices among remedies. In the experiments, laypersons and experienced businesspeople were asked to envision a scenario in which they could choose between an in-kind remedy and a monetary remedy of equal or greater value. The vignettes used in the experiments referred to a wide array of rights from contract, property, torts, and labor law. The results reveal a strong preference for in-kind remedies over monetary ones, even when the right holder is a firm and even when the remedy is related to fungible, easily replaceable assets, whose market value is ascertainable. Importantly, the findings demonstrate that laypersons and experienced businesspeople share a clear preference for in-kind redress. In fact, in the contract vignette, this preference was stronger among businesspeople than among laypersons. Across all the vignettes tested on businesspeople, the more experienced the businesspeople were, the greater their reluctance was to receive a monetary remedy.
People seem to prefer in-kind redress in two situations. When asked to choose between monetary compensation and getting or restoring the very thing that was promised or injured, the participants had a preference for the latter. For example, they elected to receive the sale object rather than either the object or monetary damages, and rejectedcash compensation in favor of compensation in the form of development rights to the remainder of a partially expropriated parcel. Dovetailing with this, when facing a choice between monetary compensation and a substitution in-kind, the respondents again opted for in-kind redress. They preferred to receive an apology rather than additional damages, and to compensate a neighbor for the occasional use of her lawn with similar use rather than with a cash payment. In-kind redress achieves a better "fit" between an obligation and its fulfillment, between a loss and its correction. In-kind remedies seem to achieve "restoration" where monetary remedies can at best offer "consolation."
These findings are highly relevant for legal decision making. Admittedly, the fact that people prefer in-kind remedies over monetary ones does not imply that the law should necessarily award this type of redress. The choice of a remedy reflects several, often conflicting, considerations. Yet, the fact that people may derive greater utility from in-kind remedies is an important consideration and one that must not be overlooked. This is obviously true for economic analysis, whose goal is to maximize the extent to which people's preferences are fulfilled.The identification of remedial preferences, however, is important for any theory that regards the satisfaction of preferences as at least one component of human welfare.
Furthermore, awareness of the preference for in-kind redress is essential even if opposing considerations tilt the scales against it. Non-fulfillment of this preference is a cost that should be part of the calculus. The experimental findings indicate that monetary damages are typically undercompensatory, even in the case of generic goods and commercial stock. Systematic undercompensation is unfair and inefficient.Arguably, damages can provide adequate compensation and ensure optimal deterrence only if they are supplemented by a premium reflecting the loss from the injured party not receiving in-kind redress. The difficulty inquantifying this premium militates against monetary remedies and for in-kind ones.
Part I of this Article presents the experimental study and its findings. Part II discusses various normative implications of the preference for in-kind remedies. It argues, inter alia, that contractual obligations should not generally be understood as granting an option to either perform or pay; that courts should consider awarding specific performance more liberally; and that they should be cautious in invalidating liquidated damages clauses. This Part also argues that we should be wary of expanding liability rules (as opposed to property rules); that injunctions should indeed reign supreme in cases of wrongful interference with property; and that planning authorities should consider additional avenues for non-monetary compensation of landowners. Part III addresses possible critiques of the above arguments. It asks whether people's preference for in-kind redress should be ignored or debiased and examines considerations supporting monetary relief, such as the autonomy of the parties involved and the institutional costs of giving in-kind.

questions.question: Whether people prefer in-kind remedies to monetary compensation when the monetary award equals or exceeds the pecuniary value of the in-kind remedy.
Whether the preference for in-kind over monetary remedies is shared by both laypersons and experienced businesspeople, and how business experience affects that preference.

Whether rights-holders would accept an option allowing counterparties to substitute monetary payment for promised in-kind performance (i.e., whether voluntary monetary substitution is viewed as equivalent to in-kind fulfillment).

matched_themes: How should courts treat pre-agreed breach payments and liquidated damages clauses (enforce, reform, apportion, or void)?

What moral and legal limits should constrain the commodification of promises-i.e., which promises ought not be treated as market commodities and how should the law reflect anti-commodification concerns?
What counterfactual baseline should courts use to measure plaintiffs' losses for compensation purposes?
Does giving the promisee a unilateral right to demand performance or elect a damages measure that captures promisor's forgone gains vindicate moral intuitions while preserving ex post efficiency?
How should default liability rules interact with parties' freedom to allocate risks by contract and duties of disclosure to achieve efficient and fair risk allocation?
Do courts actually prefer monetary damages over specific (in-kind) remedies, or do they grant specific relief except when independent reasons exist to deny it?
When should courts order specific performance (in-kind relief) versus awarding monetary damages?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?

Do contracting parties prefer in-kind remedies or monetary damages, and how do risk preferences, transaction costs, and contracting experience (laypersons versus businesspeople) shape that preference?
Should the promisor or the promisee have the default right to choose between performance and payment to achieve allocative efficiency?
Should parties be presumptively permitted to contractually specify nonstandard damage remedies, or should courts retain authority to impose defaults?
When should courts prefer or enforce in-kind (specific) performance rather than monetary damages for breach of contract?

Should remedies and contract law be structured to preserve conditions necessary for moral agency and promissory responsibility, rather than treating promises solely as instruments of economic cooperation?
How should courts treat and enforce stipulated remedies (liquidated damages clauses) versus substituting judicial remedies?
How do transaction costs, enforcement frictions, and institutional realities alter the theoretical efficiency of breach-plus-compensation?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
Should courts police and limit supracompensatory contractual remedies (penalty-like clauses), or does allowing parties to contract for such terms respect autonomy and promote efficient contracting?
To what extent does empirical uncertainty about measuring gains and losses limit courts' ability to design remedies that reflect non-welfare ethical preferences without sacrificing efficiency?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
Do parties and courts actually choose heterogeneous, context-tailored damage provisions in contracting, and under what conditions would such customization be voluntarily chosen or socially desirable?
To what extent should moral blameworthiness and non-economic considerations influence the design and application of contract remedies?
Do laypersons and experienced businesspeople differ in their preference for in-kind remedies versus money damages, and how does business experience shape these preferences?
When is an indirect remedy (one that induces self-compliance) preferable to a direct remedy that delivers the outcome?
Should courts more readily grant equitable relief to compel performance when monetary damages undercompensate and public interests are implicated?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 117michlrev885!!ARTICLE: Moral Diversity and Efficient Breach
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Moral Diversity and Efficient Breach

shared_topics.topic: contracting parties' preferences and moral beliefs about breach and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both papers present empirical/experimental evidence showing that individuals and firms differ in how they view breaches and remedies: Paper A shows a general preference for in-kind remedies (shared by laypersons and businesspeople), while Paper B documents moral heterogeneity—individuals tend to view breach as morally wrong whereas firms act as Holmesian 'breach-and-pay' actors.

shared_topics.topic: adequacy of monetary (expectation) damages versus in-kind relief
shared_topics.justification: Both engage substantively with whether monetary compensation rightly substitutes for performance: Paper A finds monetary remedies often fail to restore welfare compared with in-kind relief and may be undercompensatory, and Paper B analyzes how the legal reliance on expectation damages interacts with moral commitments and can lead to inefficient or distributionally unfair outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the role and limits of specific performance and other remedy doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Each paper examines specific performance and related remedial doctrines as alternatives to money: Paper A argues courts should more liberally award in-kind relief (specific performance, injunctions), while Paper B evaluates and ultimately rejects simple reliance on specific performance as an effective fix for moral-diversity problems, comparing it to other tools.

shared_topics.topic: how contractual language and default/express terms shape behavior and perceived obligations (liquidated damages, exit clauses)
shared_topics.justification: Both discuss how contract terms alter parties' choices and moral perceptions: Paper A studies ex ante choices among entitlements and the effect of terms on remedy preferences (and cautions re: liquidated-damages clauses), and Paper B shows that express exit clauses or liquidated-damages language change individuals' perceived moral scope and can increase willingness to exercise an option not to perform.

shared_topics.topic: using empirical/experimental methods to inform contract-law policy reforms
shared_topics.justification: Both papers rely on experimental data and translate those findings into normative recommendations for doctrinal or regulatory change—Paper A on awarding remedies and compensatory premiums, and Paper B on choice-architecture reforms like mandatory exit clauses to address moral diversity.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2013michstlrev167!!ARTICLE: A NIHILISTIC VIEW OF THE EFFICIENT BREACH
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A NIHILISTIC VIEW OF THE EFFICIENT BREACH

shared_topics.topic: choice between monetary damages (expectancy) and specific performance/in-kind remedies in contract breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally analyzes the debate over expectancy damages versus specific performance, questioning whether expectancy promotes an 'efficient breach'; Paper B empirically compares monetary and in-kind remedies and argues promisees often prefer in-kind relief, urging more liberal use of specific performance.

shared_topics.topic: economic efficiency as the justificatory metric for remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the law-and-economics framing of remedies and argues that claims of efficiency are indeterminate and limited, while Paper B engages economic welfare analysis by showing that preferences for in-kind remedies can make monetary awards inefficient unless adjusted for lost utility.

shared_topics.topic: limitations and adequacy of monetary compensation to restore losses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights conceptual and practical failures of expectancy damages (false positives/negatives, downstream effects, failure to internalize costs), and Paper B provides experimental evidence that monetary awards often undercompensate relative to in-kind redress and thus may fail to restore injured parties.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal implications for remedial rules and when courts should favor in-kind relief
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions whether any single remedy can be recommended as the default incentive for efficient performance and stresses doctrinal uncertainty, and Paper B draws normative conclusions from its data—arguing courts should consider awarding specific performance more readily and be cautious about relying exclusively on monetary remedies.

shared_topics.topic: role of behavioral and empirical evidence in challenging classical rational-actor assumptions about remedy preferences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A invokes behavioral economics and happiness studies to problematize the rationality assumptions underlying efficiency-based arguments for expectancy, while Paper B supplies experimental data demonstrating lay and business preferences that contradict the standard theoretical presumption of indifference between money and in-kind remedies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2006michstlrev883!!ARTICLE: PENALTIES AS RATIONAL RESPONSE TO BARGAINING IRRATIONALITY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PENALTIES AS RATIONAL RESPONSE TO BARGAINING IRRATIONALITY

shared_topics.topic: whether promisees (and contracting parties) are indifferent between specific performance and money
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reports experimental evidence that laypeople and businesspeople strongly prefer in-kind performance to monetary awards, directly challenging the indifference principle; Paper B marshals behavioral decision theory and survey evidence to argue that parties are not indifferent between performance and damages and that contractual terms (including penalties) reflect this non‑indifference.

shared_topics.topic: the proper treatment and enforceability of liquidated damages / penalty clauses
shared_topics.justification: Paper B is an extended empirical and normative critique of the common‑law rule that invalidates penalty clauses and argues many such clauses should be enforceable; Paper A discusses liquidated damages in its normative Part, warning courts to be cautious about invalidating liquidated damages and suggesting doctrinal implications given observed preferences for in‑kind remedies.

shared_topics.topic: use of behavioral and experimental evidence to inform contract remedial doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Both papers rely on experimental/survey methods and behavioral insights to question classical economic assumptions underlying contract law—Paper A uses experiments on remedial preferences to inform remedies doctrine, while Paper B uses behavioral decision theory surveys to explain bargaining behavior and to argue for changing the law on penalties.

shared_topics.topic: whether monetary damages adequately compensate and the efficiency implications of remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A finds monetary remedies often fail to restore the injured party’s welfare (undercompensatory compared to in‑kind relief) and recommends considering premiums or more in‑kind relief for efficiency; Paper B questions the efficient‑breach justification for limiting penalties, arguing that supra‑compensatory clauses can be Pareto‑efficient responses to bargaining irrationality and thus have different efficiency implications.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between freedom of contract (consent/autonomy) and paternalistic or welfare‑based intervention in remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper B frames liquidated damages law as a clash between freedom of contract and systemic paternalism that prohibits penalties, arguing for greater respect for negotiated consent; Paper A likewise weighs parties' autonomy and institutional costs against the welfare gains from honoring in‑kind preferences and suggests doctrinal adjustments to better respect injured parties' remedial preferences.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 59ohiostlj339!!ARTICLE: Disproportionality and the Law of Consequential Damages: Default Theory and Cognitive Reality
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Disproportionality and the Law of Consequential Damages: Default Theory and Cognitive Reality

shared_topics.topic: adequacy of monetary damages to make injured parties whole versus in-kind relief
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically tests and finds a strong preference for in-kind remedies, arguing monetary awards often fail to restore the claimant's welfare; Paper B interrogates limits on monetary consequential damages (disproportionality), effectively questioning when money is an adequate substitute for losses caused by breach.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal criteria for when courts should require performance or limit monetary recovery (specific performance, Hadley foreseeability, disproportionality, option-theory)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A challenges the option-theory and urges more liberal use of specific performance and injunctions instead of defaulting to money; Paper B analyzes Hadley and the Restatement/UCC disproportionality clause to specify when courts should curtail consequential monetary awards and thereby indirectly when non-monetary expectations ought to be protected.

shared_topics.topic: use of behavioral and experimental evidence to revise law-and-economics assumptions about contracting parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A provides experimental data on laypeople and businesspeople's remedial preferences to challenge orthodox assumptions of indifference between money and in-kind remedies; Paper B draws on cognitive psychology and experimental findings about risk underestimation to justify a doctrinal exception (disproportionality) that standard rational-actor default theory would not support.

shared_topics.topic: implications for default-rule design in contract remedies weighing efficiency against unrecognized preference or behavioral costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues remedy defaults should account for the welfare loss when plaintiffs prefer in-kind relief and suggests premiums or more in-kind awards; Paper B examines default-rule theory and contends that cognitive biases may warrant a limited default (disproportionality) to avoid inefficient allocations of remote risks.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 46hofstralrev827!!ARTICLE: DOES FAILURE TO MITIGATE DAMAGES BAR RECOVERY OF THE COSTS OF MITIGATION?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DOES FAILURE TO MITIGATE DAMAGES BAR RECOVERY OF THE COSTS OF MITIGATION?

shared_topics.topic: adequacy of monetary damages as a substitute for in-kind relief and how courts should measure recovery
shared_topics.justification: Paper A experimentally questions whether money properly substitutes for in-kind performance and finds people often prefer restoration over cash, arguing monetary awards may undercompensate; Paper B addresses whether courts should reduce recovery by the gross avoidable loss or only the net avoidable loss after probable mitigation costs, i.e., how monetary damages should be measured to reflect actual loss.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial rules affect incentives and economic efficiency (e.g., specific performance vs damages, and mitigation incentives)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A weighs efficiency arguments for favoring monetary remedies (less interference, easier to administer) against empirical preference for in-kind relief and recommends doctrinal shifts to better satisfy preferences; Paper B explicitly analyzes how different rules about offsets for mitigation costs change incentives to undertake cost-effective mitigation and the efficiency tradeoffs involved.

shared_topics.topic: the limits and evidentiary difficulties of monetizing harms (uncertainty of valuation and non-pecuniary losses)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes cases (unique goods, emotional or restorative losses) where monetary quantification is inadequate and argues this undermines reliance on damages, while Paper B examines the evidentiary uncertainty of estimating probable mitigation costs that were not actually incurred and the doctrinal discomfort courts may have with awarding such estimated sums.

papers.node_id: 1997detclrev993!!ARTICLE: Capping Market Damages at Lost Profit: An Unwarranted Limitation on a Middleman's Expectancy Interest
papers.title: ARTICLE: Capping Market Damages at Lost Profit: An Unwarranted Limitation on a Middleman's Expectancy Interest
papers.abstract:
An old and cardinal rule of contract damages is to protect the aggrieved party's expectancy interest by placing that party in the same economic position had the contract been fully performed.Upon a seller's nondelivery of a commodity, the courts have traditionally remedied the aggrieved buyer's expectancy interest by awarding damages measured by the difference between the market price and the contract price.Where the buyer has made a forwardcontract to resell the commodity, an award of market damages may greatly exceed the actual profit the buyer would have received had the contract been fully performed. The result is a conflict between the traditional preference for market damages and the normative goal of placing the nonbreaching party in the same position as full performance.
To illustrate this dilemma, assume, for example, a middleman purchases goods from a producer at $ 2 per pound immediately reselling the goods for $ 2.10 per pound to a distributor. After a dramatic rise in the market price of the goods to $ 3 per pound, the producer fails to the deliver the goods and sells the goods at the current market price to another buyer. The middleman, however, does not exercise its right to cover under Uniform Commercial Code ("UCC") section 2-712and instead sues the producer for market damages under UCC section 2-713.Calculating the differential between the market price and contract price leaves the middleman with $ 1 per pound in damages.
The producer counters by claiming that the middleman is not entitled to market damages and should only receive lost profits. In support of its proposition, the producer cites UCC section 1-106 which states that the normative goal of contract remedies is to place the aggrieved party in the same position had the contract been fully performed.Because the middleman would have made only a $ .10 per pound profit had the contract beenperformed, the producer claims that the middleman should be entitled to no more than $ .10 per pound as damages.
When faced with an analogous set of facts, the courts are divided as to which section should control when sections 2-713 and 1-106 give conflicting results.The focus of this Comment is to discuss case lawwhich has directly addressed this issue and the positions taken by the commentators who have remarked upon it. Next, this Comment will determine whether proposed revisions of Article 2 will resolve this issue. Finally, this Comment will analyze the conceptual validity of both respective positions.

questions.question: When a reseller (middleman) is deprived of goods by the seller's breach after the market price rises, should damages be measured by the market-price differential or by the reseller's actual lost profit from the intended resale?

Which remedial principle should control when awarding contract damages that would otherwise overcompensate the nonbreaching party: protecting the full expectancy interest via market-based damages or limiting recovery to actual lost profits to avoid windfalls?
Would changes to the governing commercial remedies rules resolve conflicts between market-based damage measures and limits based on actual lost profits?

matched_themes: Should courts allow apportionment of contractual damages when the non-breaching party's reliance or failure to cooperate contributed to the loss?
What counterfactual baseline should courts use to measure plaintiffs' losses for compensation purposes?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?
Should the promisor or the promisee have the default right to choose between performance and payment to achieve allocative efficiency?
Should parties be presumptively permitted to contractually specify nonstandard damage remedies, or should courts retain authority to impose defaults?
How should damages be measured for illiquid or volatile assets and lost trading opportunities?
Should courts award disgorgement or force surrender of breacher gains in addition to compensation to deter opportunistic breaches?
Should courts limit recoverable consequential damages that are grossly disproportionate to the contract price, and would such limits promote economic efficiency?
Should courts police and limit supracompensatory contractual remedies (penalty-like clauses), or does allowing parties to contract for such terms respect autonomy and promote efficient contracting?
Should contract damages be measured as lost surplus (net benefit) rather than expectancy or market value as a general rule?

How should courts measure damages when a defendant's conduct changes a plaintiff's very existence, preferences, or welfare trajectory (including cases where the plaintiff may be better off than the counterfactual)?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
When is a market-difference (market-price differential) damages measure appropriate for buyers and resellers, and under what market conditions does it overcompensate or undercompensate?
When and under what standards should courts award disgorgement or remedies that strip gains from breaching parties?

shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses the broader debate between awarding expectation damages versus specific performance and whether damages properly reflect the moral and economic loss of the promisee; Paper B squarely examines the concrete conflict between market-damages awards and lost-profit measures for a middleman under the UCC and whether market damages overcompensate the nonbreaching party.

shared_topics.topic: the normative goals of contract remedies (compensation, deterrence, and moral accountability versus party autonomy)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally asks whether contract law enforces moral obligations or instead preserves party autonomy by tolerating efficient breach, while Paper B invokes UCC §1-106 and debates whether remedial rules should put the injured party in the position of full performance or limit recovery in light of normative goals.

shared_topics.topic: the duty to mitigate/cover and allocation of burdens between promisee and promisor
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques mitigation doctrines that shift burdens onto promisees and analyzes how mitigation interacts with moral expectations, and Paper B focuses on a middleman's decision not to exercise UCC cover (§2-712) and how that choice affects available damages under §2-713.

shared_topics.topic: the role and interaction of statutory provisions and case law (UCC, Restatement, precedent) in shaping remedial outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A promises a close legal analysis of Restatement provisions, UCC rules, and cases to rebut Professor Shiffrin, and Paper B analyzes conflicting UCC sections, case law resolving those conflicts, and proposed revisions to Article 2 to determine which remedial rule should control.

shared_topics.topic: the legitimacy of efficient-breach reasoning versus protecting promise-based expectations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly interrogates the efficient-breach doctrine and its compatibility with moral accountability, and Paper B raises the practical implications of efficient breach (seller selling at higher market price) in deciding whether breachers should pay market-based damages or be limited to the middleman's lost profit.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 85geowashlrev1846!!ARTICLE: An Examination of Judicial Reasoning - When a Penalty Is Not a Penalty
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: An Examination of Judicial Reasoning - When a Penalty Is Not a Penalty

shared_topics.topic: whether contract damages should be strictly compensatory or may produce supra‑compensatory outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the common‑law penalty rule that voids supracompensatory liquidated damages as incompatible with compensatory principles, while Paper B analyzes how UCC market‑damage awards can produce windfalls for middlemen that exceed their lost‑profit expectancy.

shared_topics.topic: the proper measure and limits of contractual damages (liquidated damages vs market damages vs lost profits)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on when agreed liquidated sums should be treated as unenforceable penalties, and Paper B confronts the choice between awarding market damages or limiting recovery to lost profits for a middleman—both centrally address which measure of damages is doctrinally and normatively correct.

shared_topics.topic: conflicts between statutory/textual provisions and judicial doctrines and the resulting doctrinal incoherence
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents chaotic and incremental common‑law caselaw (culminating in Cavendish‑ParkingEye) that muddles the penalty rule, and Paper B documents court divisions over how UCC sections 2‑713, 2‑712, and 1‑106 interact, highlighting inconsistent judicial application of damages rules.

shared_topics.topic: proposals for reform and normative guidance on damages doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advocates for clearer reform (potentially repealing the penalty rule) and a principled approach to enforcing agreed damages, while Paper B evaluates proposed revisions to UCC Article 2 and argues for a conceptually coherent rule governing market versus expectancy damages.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 52wmmarylrev1181!!ARTICLE: YOU DO HAVE TO KEEP YOUR PROMISES: A DISGORGEMENT THEORY OF CONTRACT REMEDIES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: YOU DO HAVE TO KEEP YOUR PROMISES: A DISGORGEMENT THEORY OF CONTRACT REMEDIES

shared_topics.topic: competing normative foundations for contract remedies (expectation vs disgorgement/restitution)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A pits the traditional expectancy-interest approach (market damages to put the aggrieved party in the position of full performance) against a lost-profits limitation, while Paper B proposes a disgorgement-based theory that reconceives what contractual remedies should aim to achieve.

shared_topics.topic: how to measure damages for breach (market-price differential vs lost profits vs disgorgement)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the concrete choice between market damages and lost profits—illustrated by a middleman/reseller example—whereas Paper B advances disgorgement as an alternative metric for what a breaching promisor should pay.

shared_topics.topic: tension between statutory/ doctrinal rules and remedial principles/case law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes conflicting UCC provisions and divergent case law governing damage measures and asks which rule should control, and Paper B engages similar doctrinal concerns by interrogating the legal consequences of broken promises and how doctrine should reflect remedial theory.

shared_topics.topic: policy and conceptual questions about the aims of contract remedies (making whole vs preventing unjust enrichment or deterring breach)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions whether awarding market damages overcompensates a middleman and thus conflicts with the goal of placing the nonbreaching party in the position of full performance, while Paper B explores whether remedies should instead focus on disgorging gains or serving other normative goals such as enforcement and deterrence.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 88washlrev1227!!SYMPOSIUM: CONTRACTS IN THE REAL WORLD: ESSAY: THE PERSPECTIVE OF LAW ON CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: CONTRACTS IN THE REAL WORLD: ESSAY: THE PERSPECTIVE OF LAW ON CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: the normative aim of contract remedies (protecting the aggrieved party's expectancy interest) versus doctrinal limits
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly debates whether market damages or lost profits better fulfill the UCC's stated goal of placing the aggrieved party in the position of full performance; Paper B treats how the law's perspective presents normative aims of contract (what contract law is 'for') and urges making such normative commitments explicit in teaching.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal indeterminacy and judicial disagreement in applying contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents and analyzes the split in cases about which UCC provision controls when market-damages and expectancy principles conflict, while Paper B highlights that contract law teaching often understates indeterminacy and disagreement among judges and doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: methods of legal reasoning and interpretation in contract law (inductive case-based vs deductive principle-based analysis)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys case law, commentator positions, and proposed statutory revisions and then subjects those positions to conceptual/normative analysis, exemplifying the tension between case-driven and principle-driven reasoning that Paper B identifies and critiques in contract pedagogy.

shared_topics.topic: the relation between contract doctrine and real-world contracting practices (internal vs external perspectives on how rules affect parties)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the real economic consequences for a market middleman when doctrinal choices award market damages versus lost profits, while Paper B urges integrating internal doctrinal analysis with an external, practice-oriented view of how contract law operates in society and affects contracting behavior.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 31sandiegolrev307!!ARTICLE: Contracts in Wonderland: A Fable Regarding the Administrative Adjudication of Qualifying Facility Contracts in California
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contracts in Wonderland: A Fable Regarding the Administrative Adjudication of Qualifying Facility Contracts in California

shared_topics.topic: normative purpose of contract enforcement (protecting the promisee's expectancy)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the piece around the importance of promises and the legal processes that ensure they are kept, and Paper B directly analyzes the normative goal of contract remedies—placing the aggrieved party in the position of full performance—when choosing between market damages and lost profits.

shared_topics.topic: how adjudicative forum and procedure shape contract outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines administrative adjudication of qualifying-facility contracts in California and its procedural implications for enforcing promises, while Paper B focuses on judicial application of UCC remedial provisions and the courts' role in resolving contract-damage disputes.

shared_topics.topic: legal uncertainty and the breakdown or disregard of settled contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A describes a setting where long-settled rules about making and enforcing promises are being disregarded and have become unclear, and Paper B documents doctrinal division and uncertainty when different UCC sections yield conflicting remedial results.

shared_topics.topic: conflicts between statutory or doctrinal rules governing remedies and their practical effects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates how changes or lax application of procedural/adjudicative rules affect enforcement of contractual promises in a regulated context, and Paper B analyzes a concrete conflict between UCC provisions (market damages vs. expectancy/lost profits) and the practical economic consequences for nonbreaching parties.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 20hofstralrev757!!SYMPOSIUM: THE FUTURE OF LAW AND ECONOMICS: POST-REVOLUTIONARY LAW AND ECONOMICS: A FOREWORD TO THE SYMPOSIUM *© 1992 Anthony D'Amato..
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE FUTURE OF LAW AND ECONOMICS: POST-REVOLUTIONARY LAW AND ECONOMICS: A FOREWORD TO THE SYMPOSIUM *© 1992 Anthony D'Amato..

shared_topics.topic: the appropriateness of monetizing remedies by reference to market prices (market-damages vs lost-profits)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes whether market-price differential or lost-profit measurement better compensates a middleman under the UCC when a seller breaches, while Paper B critiques the broader Law & Economics tendency to reduce legal questions to dollar comparisons and market valuations as the primary decision rule.

shared_topics.topic: normative goals of legal decisionmaking: compensation versus economic-efficiency/policy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages the normative aim of contract remedies (placing the nonbreaching party in the position of full performance) and its tension with market-based awards, whereas Paper B questions whether Law & Economics’ efficiency-oriented normative framework should displace other legal aims and how policy goals should guide judicial outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: use of economic analysis to increase predictability and standardization in doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A wrestles with conflicting UCC provisions and the predictable consequences of applying market-damage rules to resellers, while Paper B evaluates the claim that economic quantification yields greater predictability and less subjective judicial decisionmaking.

shared_topics.topic: resolving doctrinal or statutory conflicts through economic reasoning
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the clash between UCC §2-713 (market damages) and §1-106 (expectancy principle) and considers commentator and reform proposals, and Paper B addresses how the Law & Economics movement seeks to reshape or resolve legal doctrines by applying economic theory and empirical analysis.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83lawcontempprob151!!ARTICLE: BLACK MARKETS AND THE EXCHANGE STRUCTURE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BLACK MARKETS AND THE EXCHANGE STRUCTURE

shared_topics.topic: how law structures permissible exchanges and thereby shapes markets
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that law (through disabilities, price rules, spatial/temporal limits, etc.) defines which exchanges are lawful and thus creates black markets for prohibited transactions; Paper B examines how contract law (UCC provisions and damages rules) structures permissible commercial conduct by defining the legal consequences for nondelivery and thereby influences how market trades are conducted.

shared_topics.topic: the comparative use of disabling rules versus remedial sanctions to police transgressive exchanges
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes legal 'disabilities' (voiding or making transactions unenforceable) from 'kickers' (supracompensatory civil/criminal sanctions) as distinct tools to deter or block prohibited exchanges; Paper B engages this same choice at the civil-law level by debating whether breaches should be policed through market-price damages or limited to lost-profit compensation, i.e., different remedial intensities that shape behavior.

shared_topics.topic: preserving transaction structure and parties' expectations as an explicit legal objective
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the idea that legal rules (including criminalization) are used to preserve an established exchange structure and prevent conversion of consensual bargaining norms; Paper B invokes the expectancy-interest goal of contract remedies (UCC §1-106) and debates how damages doctrines should protect the nonbreaching party's expected position to maintain reliable contracting.

shared_topics.topic: the normative tension between efficiency and fairness in choosing remedies for exchange violations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques purely efficiency-based defenses of criminalizing certain exchanges and emphasizes fairness/system-survival rationales (Calabresi/Melamed, Dworkin); Paper B analyzes whether market damages (efficiency-promoting, sometimes producing windfalls) or lost profits (fair reflection of the injured party's expectancy) better serve the normative aims of contract law.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 117michlrev885!!ARTICLE: Moral Diversity and Efficient Breach
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Moral Diversity and Efficient Breach

shared_topics.topic: the normative aim and proper measure of expectation damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses expectation damages as the legal remedy that supposedly substitutes for performance (and how firms view damages as exhausting liability), while Paper B directly debates whether market-price damages or lost-profit measures better fulfill the normative goal of placing the nonbreaching party in the position of full performance.

shared_topics.topic: how damage rules shape incentives to breach (the efficient-breach question)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the efficient-breach doctrine—how expectation damages enable Holmesian firms to breach when profitable and how individuals' moral views prevent efficient breaches—and Paper B analyzes how different damage measures (market damages vs lost profits and the availability of cover) change actors' incentives and whether those rules lead to efficient or distorted outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: distributional consequences of remedial doctrines across types of contracting parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how the current remedial regime advantages sophisticated commercial actors relative to morally-constrained individuals, producing vertical and horizontal unfairness, while Paper B highlights a distributional conflict between producers and middlemen when market damages can produce windfalls to intermediaries that exceed their actual lost profits.

shared_topics.topic: the role of contract terms, statutory provisions, and choice architecture in determining remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates how contract drafting (exit clauses, liquidated-damages clauses, specific-performance terms) and choice-architecture solutions can alter perceived obligations and breach behavior, and Paper B scrutinizes how UCC provisions (e.g., sections 2-713 and 1-106) and their interaction determine which remedial measure governs and thus what remedies contracting parties can expect.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 60lalrev233!!ARTICLE: The Wasted Sacrifice of Lessors' Lost Profit Claims in Bankruptcy
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Wasted Sacrifice of Lessors' Lost Profit Claims in Bankruptcy

shared_topics.topic: limits on expectation damages (market-price awards versus lost profits)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the conflict where a middleman can recover market damages that far exceed its actual resale profit and whether recovery should be capped at lost profits; Paper B analyzes how bankruptcy §502(b)(6) effectively caps lessors' breach claims, truncating their expectancy-like recovery and eliminating portions of lost-profit claims.

shared_topics.topic: whether specialized statutes or doctrines should displace ordinary contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the tension between general expectancy principles (UCC §1-106) and the specific market-damage rule in UCC §2-713 and proposed Article 2 revisions, while Paper B critiques how the Bankruptcy Code disallows parts of lessors' contract damages, asking whether bankruptcy law lawfully and fairly overrides nonbankruptcy remedies.

shared_topics.topic: normative and policy critiques of treating certain claimants differently (middlemen, lessors)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions the conceptual validity and fairness of denying a middleman full market recovery in favor of a profit cap, and Paper B argues that §502(b)(6)'s disallowance reflects an irrational bias against real property lessors and contradicts principles of equal treatment among creditors.

shared_topics.topic: use of historical, doctrinal, and legislative analysis to reassess damage rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys case law, commentator positions, and proposed revisions to Article 2 to evaluate damage rules for middlemen, and Paper B traces the history and political/economic forces behind §502(b)(6) to assess the legitimacy of the statutory damage cap.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45flastulrev923!!ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: II. THE BEST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: Hadley v. Baxendale: A Bayesian Analysis of the Hadley Rule
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: II. THE BEST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: Hadley v. Baxendale: A Bayesian Analysis of the Hadley Rule

shared_topics.topic: normative justification for limiting contract damages (foreseeability and caps)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze doctrines that restrict the scope of recoverable contract damages—Paper A defends the Hadley foreseeability limitation via a Bayesian/ex ante welfare argument, while Paper B critiques or defends limits that would cap a middleman's recovery (market damages vs. lost profits) and examines whether such caps are normatively justified.

shared_topics.topic: ex ante perspective on selecting remedial rules to allocate risk
shared_topics.justification: Both works frame remedial rules in terms of their ex ante effects: Paper A uses the veil-of-ignorance/Bayesian original-position model to show why parties would choose a foreseeability rule, and Paper B evaluates whether market versus lost-profit measures better reflect the ex ante expectancy interests and risk allocation of contracting parties.

shared_topics.topic: tension between different damage measures (market price differential versus expectation/lost profits)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage the concrete question of which damage metric should govern when breach occurs—Paper A discusses the welfare implications of broad versus narrow liability rules, and Paper B directly contrasts awards measured by market-price differentials with awards approximating the claimant's actual lost profits/expectancy.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial rules affect parties' incentives to mitigate, disclose information, or choose strategies
shared_topics.justification: Both articles consider incentive effects of damage rules: Paper A links the Hadley rule to incentives about information disclosure and risk-bearing under uncertainty, while Paper B discusses how damages (and alternatives like cover) influence a middleman's behavior, choices to mitigate or resell, and sellers' incentives.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 46amulrev1!!ARTICLE: THE MEANING OF VALUE IN CONTRACT DAMAGES AND CONTRACT THEORY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE MEANING OF VALUE IN CONTRACT DAMAGES AND CONTRACT THEORY

shared_topics.topic: market-price (UCC §2-713) versus lost-profit measures of damages
shared_topics.justification: Both papers confront the tension between awarding damages measured by the market-price differential and awarding only the nonbreaching party's lost profits: Paper A analyzes case law and UCC provisions that produce this conflict for middlemen, while Paper B critiques existing damage measures and proposes a surplus/lost-profit–focused alternative.

shared_topics.topic: expectancy interest and the normative goal of placing the injured party in the position of full performance
shared_topics.justification: Each paper centers the traditional expectancy doctrine as the normative benchmark for remedies—Paper A treats the expectation interest as the core rule generating the dispute over which statutory provision should control, and Paper B reframes expectancy in terms of lost surplus and net benefit to clarify what 'placing the party in the same position' should mean.

shared_topics.topic: the meaning of 'value' and surplus versus total value in damage doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with how 'value' should be understood for calculating damages—Paper B provides an extended critique of conflicting legal and economic definitions and promotes a surplus-based measure, while Paper A implicitly relies on this debate when contrasting market-value awards with the middleman's small contractual profit.

shared_topics.topic: how damage rules apply to intermediaries, substitute transactions (cover/resale), and forward-resale relationships
shared_topics.justification: Both papers address how remedies should operate in resale/forward-contract contexts: Paper A uses a middleman/reseller example and surveys case law about cover and resale remedies, and Paper B explicitly treats substitute transactions (including cover and resale) when advocating a surplus-based, cost-inclusive damage rule.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 71califlrev56!!ARTICLE: The Collateral Source Rule and Contract Damages.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Collateral Source Rule and Contract Damages.

shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage the question of how to measure contract damages: Paper A confronts the tension between awarding market damages (market price minus contract price) and limiting recovery to the middleman's lost profits, while Paper B treats whether collateral benefits should reduce or otherwise alter the monetary recovery a contract plaintiff receives, i.e., the net measure of damages payable by the breaching party.

shared_topics.topic: avoidance of windfalls and allocation of loss between obligors/benefit-holders
shared_topics.justification: Both articles analyze whether damage awards produce impermissible windfalls and who should bear the cost of compensation: Paper A asks whether a middleman should reap a windfall from market-price damages or be limited to actual profit, and Paper B asks whether an independent collateral payment produces a windfall to the plaintiff (or whether the collateral source or defendant should instead be the primary obligor via subrogation).

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal disagreement and the need for principled rules in contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both papers survey divided case law and seek principled resolution: Paper A catalogs conflicting judicial treatment of UCC sections (market damages versus expectancy) and commentators' positions, while Paper B documents inconsistent applications of the collateral source rule in contract cases and advocates for coherent guiding principles.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of external events or third-party payments on an aggrieved party's expectancy interest
shared_topics.justification: Both works examine how events outside the contract affect the goal of placing the nonbreaching party in the position of full performance: Paper A focuses on external market-price changes that inflate market damages relative to expected profit, and Paper B focuses on collateral-source payments that may independently compensate the claimant and thus interact with expectancy-based recovery.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM:Instrumental Theories of Compensation: A Survey

shared_topics.topic: tension between compensatory/expectancy remedies and instrumental/efficiency goals
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the conceptual divide between corrective-justice claims that compensation is an axiom and economic analysis that chooses damages to optimize incentives, while Paper B illustrates that tension in practice by showing how the normative goal of restoring expectancy can conflict with market-damage awards that may be larger or more efficient.

shared_topics.topic: expectation damages/expectancy interest in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses expectation damages as an early economic result that could be characterized as compensatory, and Paper B directly analyzes the middleman's expectancy interest—how expectation-based remedies should be enforced and measured under the UCC.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between doctrinal rules/statutes and economic arguments about optimal remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts moral versus economic justificatory frameworks for remedies and argues economics provides an instrumental method for answering remedial questions; Paper B analyzes conflicting UCC provisions, case law, and commentary to assess whether doctrinal rules (and proposed statutory revisions) correctly implement normative or economic principles regarding damages.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Formal and Operative Rules in Overliquidation Per Se Cases

shared_topics.topic: judicial inconsistency and the gap between formal rules and how courts actually decide damages cases
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents that courts are divided when UCC provisions point to different remedies and evaluates case law outcomes; Paper B explicitly applies the formal-vs-operative-rules framework to show how doctrine (the penalty test or Code rules) often fails to predict judicial results in overliquidation cases.

shared_topics.topic: how to measure and limit contract damages (market-price measures, lost profits, and stipulated/ liquidated sums)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether market-price differentials or lost profits should cap a middleman's recovery under the UCC; Paper B addresses enforceability and reasonableness of agreed damages clauses when they produce overcompensation and discusses standards for limiting recovery.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between statutory (Code/UCC) provisions and common-law doctrines in shaping remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on conflicting UCC sections (e.g., 2-713, 2-712, 1-106) and possible Article 2 revisions affecting remedial outcomes; Paper B considers both the Code and common-law penalty doctrine and how statutory text and judicially developed tests are applied (or sidestepped) in damages cases.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 94bulrev55!!ARTICLE: DO THE RIGHT THING: INDIRECT REMEDIES IN PRIVATE LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DO THE RIGHT THING: INDIRECT REMEDIES IN PRIVATE LAW

shared_topics.topic: selection among alternative contractual damage measures (market differential vs lost profits)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly debates whether buyers/middlemen should receive market-price differential damages or be limited to their actual lost profits under the UCC, while Paper B provides a broader framework about choosing remedies (direct vs indirect) and discusses when monetary remedies should be designed or calibrated to achieve the law's objectives.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the normative aim of placing the nonbreaching party in the position of full performance (expectancy) and the fairness tensions that arise when that aim conflicts with market-based measures, and Paper B systematically analyzes normative reasons (autonomy, reduced animosity, educative/expressive effects) for preferring indirect remedies in certain contexts.

shared_topics.topic: role of measurement error and miscalculation risk in choosing remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper B argues that indirect remedies are preferable when there is a high risk of miscalculating a direct remedy, and Paper A illustrates this problem concretely—how market damages can greatly diverge from a middleman's true lost profit—raising the same concern about remedial mismeasurement and rule design.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial rules shape parties' incentives and strategic behavior (including self-compliance vs litigation choices)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how awarding market damages or limiting recovery affects a middleman's decisions (e.g., whether to cover or sue) and the producer's incentives, while Paper B foregrounds that indirect remedies function by inducing voluntary compliance and therefore evaluates remedies by their incentive effects.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 33uclalrev1565!!ARTICLE: PUNITIVE AND NONPECUNIARY DAMAGES IN ACTIONS BASED UPON CONTRACT: TOWARD ACHIEVING THE OBJECTIVE OF FULL COMPENSATION.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PUNITIVE AND NONPECUNIARY DAMAGES IN ACTIONS BASED UPON CONTRACT: TOWARD ACHIEVING THE OBJECTIVE OF FULL COMPENSATION.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal conflict among remedial rules and authorities (statutory provisions, Restatements, and case law divergence)
shared_topics.justification: Each paper examines how competing doctrines and authorities produce inconsistent outcomes — Paper B focuses on conflicts between UCC sections (e.g., 2-713 v. 1-106) and split case law, and Paper A addresses tensions among traditional contract rules, Restatement pronouncements, and newer case law allowing punitive or nonpecuniary recovery.

shared_topics.topic: evidentiary and doctrinal limits on recoverable losses (foreseeability, certainty, mitigation, and allocation of risk of error)
shared_topics.justification: Both discuss the legal standards that limit damages: Paper A surveys foreseeability, certainty, mitigation, and who bears the risk of imperfect proof leading to undercompensation, while Paper B’s debate over market versus lost-profit measures implicates those same concerns about certainty, proof of expectancy, and which party absorbs risk when damages are hard to calculate.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 20hofstralrev941!!SYMPOSIUM: THE FUTURE OF LAW AND ECONOMICS: THE NEGLIGENCE-OPPORTUNISM TRADEOFF IN CONTRACT LAW.
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE FUTURE OF LAW AND ECONOMICS: THE NEGLIGENCE-OPPORTUNISM TRADEOFF IN CONTRACT LAW.

shared_topics.topic: the normative role of the expectancy interest (placing the aggrieved party in the position of full performance) in economic analyses of contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes doctrine-focused approaches and emphasizes economic goals in shaping contract rules, and Paper B directly interrogates the expectancy-interest principle (UCC §1-106) versus market-differential damages, questioning which economic norm should control remedies.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames a general negligence–opportunism tradeoff and urges integrating divergent tort-style and opportunism-based approaches, while Paper B examines the concrete conflict between UCC §§2-713 and 1-106 and surveys case law and proposed revisions to resolve that doctrinal inconsistency.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules shape parties' incentives and the efficiency of contracting (including intermediaries' strategic choices)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that rules should be organized to promote trust and efficient behavior by influencing parties' incentives against opportunism, and Paper B studies how the choice between market damages and lost-profit measures affects a middleman's decision to cover, resell, or litigate, thereby altering ex ante and ex post behavior.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PEEVYHOUSE V. GARLAND COAL & MINING CO. REVISITED: THE BALLAD OF WILLIE AND LUCILLE

shared_topics.topic: appropriate measure of expectation damages (market differential vs lost profits/cost of performance/diminution in value)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers grapple with which monetary measure properly protects the plaintiff's expectancy interest — Paper A analyzes the tension between UCC market damages and a middleman's actual lost profits, while Paper B contrasts diminution-in-value and cost-to-repair remedies (and defends cost measures) in Peevyhouse.

shared_topics.topic: the normative aim of placing the nonbreaching party in the position of full performance and conflicts between doctrines that yield different results
shared_topics.justification: Both articles interrogate the foundational remedial goal of making the injured party whole (expectation interest) and show how different doctrinal rules or statutory provisions can conflict with that aim — Paper A via UCC sections giving divergent results, Paper B via the Peevyhouse court's choice that arguably frustrated the plaintiffs' expectancy.

shared_topics.topic: evidentiary and proof problems that lead courts to limit or choose particular damage measures
shared_topics.justification: Each paper emphasizes how factual record limitations and difficulties proving subjective loss or speculative profits affect damage awards — Paper A discusses cases where courts weigh a middleman's actual profit against market measures, while Paper B reconstructs how a scant record and proof problems contributed to the Peevyhouse diminution ruling.

shared_topics.topic: selection among alternative remedies (monetary measures, restitution, cover, or specific performance) and doctrinal guidance for electing remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both works consider plaintiffs' remedial options and the consequences of those choices — Paper A treats remedies under the UCC (market damages vs cover/lost profits), and Paper B discusses alternative paths (cost of performance, restitution, and urging courts toward specific performance) and how electing different remedies would have affected recovery.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 46sandiegolrev705!!Article: The Collateral Source Rule in Contract Cases
compared_to.partner_title: Article: The Collateral Source Rule in Contract Cases

shared_topics.topic: measure of contract damages to protect the expectancy interest
shared_topics.justification: Both papers centrally engage with how to measure damages to place the nonbreaching party in the position they would have occupied had the contract been performed: Paper A examines whether collateral receipts should alter that expectancy recovery, and Paper B analyzes whether a middleman’s market-differential damages should be replaced by its lost-profit expectancy.

shared_topics.topic: whether damage awards should be reduced or limited to avoid double recovery/overcompensation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks whether recoveries should be reduced by payments from collateral sources (insurance, savings), while Paper B questions whether market damages that exceed a plaintiff’s actual profit should be capped at lost profits to prevent overcompensation.

shared_topics.topic: tension between general remedial principles and specialized rules/statutes
shared_topics.justification: Both pieces analyze conflicts between broad contract-law norms and more specific doctrines or rules—for Paper A, the tort-origin collateral source doctrine and Restatement/treatise treatments versus its application in contract, and for Paper B, the apparent conflict between UCC section 2-713 (market damages) and UCC section 1-106 (normative goal of full performance).

shared_topics.topic: normative policy justifications for damage rules (fairness, loss allocation, and deterrence)
shared_topics.justification: Each article probes the policy aims underlying damages—Paper A evaluates whether policies that justify the collateral source rule in tort should apply in contract contexts, and Paper B weighs normative goals (placing the aggrieved in the performance position) against concerns about fairness and proper allocation of loss between contracting parties.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 59ohiostlj339!!ARTICLE: Disproportionality and the Law of Consequential Damages: Default Theory and Cognitive Reality
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Disproportionality and the Law of Consequential Damages: Default Theory and Cognitive Reality

shared_topics.topic: the tension between protecting the nonbreaching party's expectancy interest (placing the party in the position of full performance) and doctrines that limit recovery
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the dispute as one between the traditional expectancy‑protection principle and a lost‑profits cap, while Paper B treats whether and when limits like disproportionality are justified given the goal of appropriately compensating foreseeable losses.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes case law and whether proposed revisions to Article 2 resolve conflicts between sections (e.g., 2‑713 vs 1‑106); Paper B traces Restatement §351 and the draft revised Article 2’s insertion of a disproportionality limit and analyzes the doctrinal and practical consequences.

shared_topics.topic: normative and theoretical defenses for limiting consequential damages (efficiency, conceptual validity, and behavioral considerations)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A promises an analysis of the conceptual validity of competing positions on damage measures, while Paper B explicitly evaluates disproportionality using default‑rule economic theory and supplements that with cognitive/behavioral evidence to justify when limits on damages may be appropriate.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1349!!ARTICLE: LET US NEVER BLAME A CONTRACT BREAKER
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: LET US NEVER BLAME A CONTRACT BREAKER

shared_topics.topic: measure of damages for breach — market-price differential versus lost profits

shared_topics.topic: middlemen 'windfall' problem when resale/forward contracts exist

shared_topics.topic: normative purpose of contract remedies — expectation protection versus fault, insurance, and efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the dispute as a tension between the traditional expectancy goal (placing the aggrieved party where full performance would have) and the potentially excessive market award; Paper B develops a broader normative account defending a no-fault, insurance-style, efficiency-oriented regime in which damages are strict, serve to allocate risk, and enable efficient breaches.

shared_topics.topic: mitigation/cover duties and their effect on available damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the buyer/middleman's right to cover under UCC §2-712 and the implications of a plaintiff's choice not to cover before seeking market damages; Paper B analyzes the duty to mitigate (and related concepts like cover) as an institutional rule preventing exploitation of the contract-conferred bilateral monopoly and shaping what damages the breach victim can recover.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: LAW AND EQUITY IN CONTRACT ENFORCEMENT

shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly confronts the choice between market-price damages under UCC §2-713 and a lost-profits measure for a middleman, questioning which better places the nonbreaching party in the position of full performance; Paper B analyzes when damages (the legal remedy) adequately protect expectation interests versus when specific performance is needed, probing the adequacy of money as a substitute for promised performance.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal indeterminacy and judicial discretion in remedies for breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights split authority and uncertainty in courts about which UCC provision should control when measures diverge, inviting judicial choice; Paper B emphasizes the indeterminate, fact-sensitive fairness defense in equity and how that discretion leads courts to particularistic outcomes when deciding whether to grant specific performance.

shared_topics.topic: the role of the type of contract or good (fungible/marketed goods versus unique/idiosyncratic items) in selecting remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on resale/middleman scenarios involving fungible commodities and how market-price damages can overcompensate compared to lost profits; Paper B contrasts fungible goods (where damages normally suffice) with unique or idiosyncratic items (where specific performance and equitable considerations arise), using the nature of the subject matter to explain remedial differences.

shared_topics.topic: divergent judicial approaches and case-law analysis about proper remedial limits
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys sparse and divided case law on how courts have treated avoidable, unforeseeable, and uncertain losses when evaluating liquidated damages clauses and offers a recommended interpretive approach; Paper B surveys and analyzes split judicial authority about whether courts should permit market damages for middlemen or limit recovery to lost profits, assessing the conceptual validity of competing lines of cases.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE EXPECTATION MEASURE AND ITS DISCONTENTS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys case law divisions and proposed Article 2 revisions and assesses doctrinal resolution of conflicts between UCC provisions, while Paper B explicitly analyzes the administrability and institutional fit of alternative economic models and remedial regimes when assessing whether to retain or revise the expectation measure.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how section 104's tax-exemption interacts with tort damage awards and the practical consequences for plaintiffs' recovery, and Paper B analyzes the interaction and conflict between specific UCC provisions (e.g., §§2-713 and 1-106) that determine which remedial measure applies.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a structured framework recommending that courts tie non-enforcement to a showing of harm and account for ambiguity and evasive pricing, while Paper B surveys case law, commentator positions, and proposed revisions to Article 2 to assess and recommend how damages rules should be clarified or reformed.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Markets as a Moral Foundation for Contract Law

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that legal rules and remedies are part of what makes markets healthy and impersonal exchange viable, and Paper B analyzes how awarding market-price damages versus limiting recovery to lost profits alters middlemen's incentives to cover, resell, and participate in market transactions.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the importance of open entry and organizations that enable exchange among many actors, and Paper B uses the middleman/reseller scenario to scrutinize whether contract doctrine properly protects intermediaries' expectations or distorts their role in supply chains.

shared_topics.topic: the role of legal institutions and enforcement rules (including statutory interpretation) in enabling market development and preventing predation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses property rights, enforcement against expropriation, and institutional prerequisites for markets (illustrated by Russia's transition), while Paper B focuses on how UCC provisions and divergent judicial interpretations of those statutory rules function as institutional mechanisms that shape market outcomes.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Divorce Law: Exclusions and Disproportionate Divisions of Marital Estate

shared_topics.topic: how courts apply and reconcile statutes (case-law development)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys and critiques the divergent judicial approaches to choosing between conflicting UCC provisions, and Paper B likewise examines judicial application and interpretation of the statutory exclusion in divorce cases and the resulting doctrinal development.

shared_topics.topic: financial allocation and the monetary consequences of legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how damage measures (market damages vs. lost profits) change a middleman's monetary position, while Paper B addresses how statutory exclusions and division rules affect the monetary division of the marital estate between spouses.

shared_topics.topic: normative and efficiency justifications for expectation-based remedies (efficient breach, Coasean bargaining, and investment/transaction-cost considerations)

shared_topics.justification: Paper A presents empirical evidence that heuristics and biases in negotiation affect the shape and desirability of penalty clauses and argues context should determine enforceability; Paper B focuses on the transactional context (a middleman's forward resale and decision not to cover) to ask whether that conduct should limit recovery to lost profits rather than market differentials.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Moral Judgment and Moral Heuristics in Breach of Contract

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM:Instrumental Theories of Compensation: A Survey

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Income Tax Considerations in Florida Personal Injury Actions

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE FALLACY OF FULL COMPENSATION

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE CORRESPONDENCE OF CONTRACT AND PROMISE
