papers.node_id: 28gastulrev559!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT BREACHES AND THE CRIMINAL/CIVIL DIVIDE: AN INTER-COMMON LAW ANALYSIS
papers.title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT BREACHES AND THE CRIMINAL/CIVIL DIVIDE: AN INTER-COMMON LAW ANALYSIS
papers.abstract:
Scholars have long debated why certain common law breaches in American jurisprudence receive criminal punishment (imprisonment) while others only receive civil sanctions (monetary damages).These scholars, however, have focused only on torts and crimes and have largely left out contract breaches--a significant part of common law doctrine. Like its tort counterpart, this breach also only receives civil liability. What explains the similar treatment? This Article makes an original contribution to the literature by systematically introducing contract breaches into this debate on the criminal/civil divide.
It is important to say something about harms. Any meaningful comparison of these three common law breaches requires equalizing the harms involved. Otherwise, the analogy will break down. For example, murdering someone is obviously worse than negligently destroying property or failing to contractually deliver a good or service. Explaining why only murder gets criminal punishment in this case does not seem particularly difficult. The harms involved are very different. Homicide is qualitatively worse than any damage to property or loss of particular service. This assumption about harm is important. This Article seeks to understand why, everything else being equal, crimes alone receive criminal punishment, while both tort and contract breaches only trigger monetary sanctions.
This Article works out thisceteris paribusclaim by appealing to laws that safeguard property. A person may not steal your property (a crime); she cannot treat your property negligently (a tort); and she may not breach a contract by failing to compensate you for your property (a contract breach). Take the following three cases:
Scenario (1): You are sitting in a coffee shopwriting an essay on your recently purchased laptop that costs $ 1,000. You leave to go to the bathroom. In your absence, someone quickly steals your computer(a crime).
Scenario (2): As you are typing your essay on your recently purchased laptop that cost $ 1,000, someone negligently knocks it over. You had taken reasonable care to place it squarely on the table so it would not fall.It breaks completely and is now worth nothing (tort breach).
Scenario (3): Wanting to sell your laptop, you contract with an individual to sell it for $ 1,000. You give the computer to this person and await delivery of the money at the coffee shop (per the contract terms). To your dismay, this individual breaches the contract by failing to bring the money. The person intentionally decided not to honor the terms of the contract. At the time the contract was made, this person fully intended to pay you $ 1,000 and said as much. The individual simply changed her mind, even though she had the ability to satisfy the terms of the contract (contract breach).
In all three cases (collectively, the "Scenarios"), you lose the value of the computer. That is, in all Scenarios, you suffer the same monetary harm--a loss of $ 1,000.Nevertheless, only in Scenario (1), the criminal act, could the perpetrator suffer possible imprisonment at the discretion of the state. The perpetrators in Scenarios (2) and (3) (the tort and contract breach, respectively)would only be subject to monetary damages.They will not suffer any imprisonment, even though these individuals have caused the same harm to you as the criminal in Scenario (1). While this distinction may be familiar to us, what explains it?
The major theories used to account for the varying treatment of these breaches can be grouped roughly into two camps: the economic-based and moral-based models.The economic model relies on deterrence and efficiency to explain why torts receive monetary damages but crimes receive criminal punishment.According to these scholars, society has a greater economic incentive to deter criminal activity than tortious activity. The common phrase used here is that "criminal law punishes while tort law prices."The moral-based camp has questioned the explanatory power of the economic-based arguments. These scholars have argued, instead, that the real distinction between crimes and torts lies in the moral condemnation of the former but not the latter.Crimes generallyconstitute purposeful conduct, making them morally worse than the carelessness typified by tortious activity.
Yet, scholars on both sides of the debate have neglected to apply their theories to contract breaches. Perhaps, the thinking is that because contract law involves voluntary behavior, it is readily understandable why such breaches are not criminally punished and nothing more needs to be said. At a conceptual level, it is not clear how merely invoking voluntariness, without more, automatically vitiates the need for criminal punishment. The victim of a contract breach certainly has not consented to the deprivation of her property without compensation. Additional explanation seems necessary, particularly when economic or moral principles underlie the general explanation for the criminal/civil divide.
To be clear, many scholars have used economics and moral principles to analyze contract law. The notion of efficient breach has generated significant discussion and holds that breaking a contract is sometimes the economically preferable course of action.Perhaps, less well known is the notion that a contract corresponds to a moral obligation to uphold this promise.But all of these discussions--whether economic or moral--center on the internal mechanics of contract law (i.e. the analysis occursintra-contract law). Thesescholars have not engaged in the broader discussion of why contract breaches--like their tort counterparts--only receive civil liability. Here, the scholarship has been restricted to the tort/crime dichotomy.
Thus, this Article makes an original contribution by applying the aforementioned economic and moral-based theories to all three types of breaches and explains why crimes alone receive criminal punishment. The aim of the Article is not to recommend specific normative changes. Perhaps, certain contract breaches should be criminalized or some crimes not punished. This Article simply seeks to understandwhat explains whywe criminalize one but not the others.
The economic model predictably explains why contract breaches are treated like tort breaches. Contracts and torts share an underlying efficiency that is in sharp contrast to crimes. The moral-based position, however, is not as straightforward and cannot readily account for the difference. A contract breach--as intentional-based conduct--would also seem to elicit the same moral condemnation as a crime and thus warrant criminal punishment.This is particularly true if one includes contract breaches based on fraudulent inducement as to an intended obligation; these instances of deception or trickery also typically do not receive criminal punishment.What is missing from the moral-based model is recognizing the unique nature of the underlying responsibility in a contract breach. For this, this Article distinguishes between a "non-voluntary obligation" and a "voluntary obligation."The former automatically applies to allmembers of society, and thus, corresponds to tort and criminal legal duties. On the other hand, a voluntary obligation must be affirmatively undertaken, much like contractual responsibilities. Recognizing this fundamental difference can save the moral-based model. Understood in this way, the moral-based and economic-based theories can actually be integrated into a unified model.
There are limitations to this analysis. It does not attempt to explain the law's varying treatment ofallcrimes versusalltorts or contract breaches. Instead, its focus is on the prototypical common law breach.There are various indeterminacies within these bodies of law that prevent any analysis from being true in all circumstances. For instance, most jurisdictions today rely on a statutory criminal framework in lieu of common law.This framework includes a host of various violations, many of which are considered regulatory in nature.This Article seeks to explain the treatment of those familiar common law origin crimes against property or person that require criminal intent.
The Article is divided into five parts. Part I lays out the parameters of each respective common law breach, as well as three related scenarios involving the safeguarding of property. Part II focuses on the economic model and how it handily explains the respective sanctions all three common law breaches receive. Parts III and IV analyze the moral-based approach and its shortcomings when it comes to contract breaches. Finally, Part V explores the distinctionbetween voluntary and non-voluntary obligations, in an effort to rehabilitate the moral-based model and explain the treatment of contract breaches.

papers.node_id: 69tennlrev837!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT DAMAGES IN TENNESSEE
papers.title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT DAMAGES IN TENNESSEE
papers.abstract:
For the practicing lawyer, the law of damages is the most important area of contract law. It is what makes the difference between a case that is worth pursuing and a case where the client's best option is to walk away and content herself knowing that she has learned an expensive lesson. Despite its importance, the subject of how damages are determined has received little attention from writers.The lack of attention to damages has existed since the earliest days of American contract law when William Wetmore Story, the son of the renowned Justice Joseph Story, wrote one of the earliest American treatises on contracts. In a book of almost 500 pages, he only spent two pages discussing damages.
Generally, the subject of damages is downplayed in law school as well. Law students dislike the subject of damages because it deals with numbers, and contracts courses often give it short shrift. The result is that most law students graduate without a clear understanding of how to estimate their clients' damages.
The purpose of this article is to outline the principles governing contract damages in Tennessee and to suggest areas in which the law might be improved. I do not suggest any radical changes in the law of contract damages, but I do suggest that Tennessee courts be more liberal in awarding damages in order to more closely approach the theoretical goal of putting the non-breaching party in the same economic position that performance would have. This article is intended to serve as a guide for lawyers and for the courts. Part I is a brief overview of the principles on which contract damages are awarded. Part II is a detailed discussion of the benefit of the bargain rule, which is the basis on which the vast majority of contract damages are calculated. Part II also contains a detailed description of the way Tennesseecourts have determined each element of damages. Part III discusses the special rules of the Uniform Commercial Code, which are designed to provide more equitable compensation in cases involving the sale of goods. Part IV describes the way that Tennessee courts have applied the requirements of foreseeability, certainty, and non- avoidability to limit damage recoveries. Finally, Part V describes alternative methods of determining damages that are useful in a limited number of cases.

questions.question: How do Tennessee courts determine and calculate monetary damages for breach of contract-i.e., how do they measure the non-breaching party's economic loss?

To what extent do limits on recoverable damages (requirements about which losses are foreseeable, provable with sufficient certainty, and avoidable by the injured party) reduce awards below full compensation, and should courts be more liberal to better put the non-breaching party in the position performance would have afforded?
How do the special rules that apply to sale-of-goods contracts affect the calculation and fairness of damage awards compared with other types of contracts?

matched_themes: What counterfactual baseline should courts use to measure plaintiffs' losses for compensation purposes?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
Do limits on recoverable damages (foreseeability, certainty, avoidability) substantially reduce awards below full compensation, and should courts liberalize those limits?

papers.node_id: 24jlegalstud139!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT REMEDIES AND OPTIONS PRICING
papers.title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT REMEDIES AND OPTIONS PRICING
papers.abstract:
ONE of the most interesting questions in contract law is also one of the most basic: what is the appropriate remedy for breach of contract? The common law's answer is fairly simple. Money damages is the favored remedy, and specific performance is reserved for particular types of cases in which money damages are thought to be inadequate.
This remedial pattern is easier to describe than to explain. The most widely used explanation is that the choice between money damages and specific performance turns on the transaction costs associated with each.Specifically, damage awards may be systematically undercompensatory, leading to excessive breach and causing us to prefer specific performance. Other types of transaction costs, including the cost of negotiating around a specific performance award when nonperformance would be more efficient, lead to excessive performance and cause us to prefer money damages. Absent these particular transaction costs, the choice of remedy would not matter from an efficiency standpoint. The choice of remedy depends on which types of transaction costs dominate in particular situations.
Even when the choice of remedy has no allocative consequences, however, it has distributional consequences that may affect the risk borne by each of the contracting parties.This article attempts to determine how those distributional effects would influence the preferences of contracting parties between money damages and specific performance. It does so by characterizing money damages as an option. Specifically, the availability of money damages is tantamount to granting the promisor (or Seller)an option to buy back his performance by paying an amount of money awarded by the court. Where specific performance is awarded, Seller lacks this option. The benefit of the option approach is that it provides a framework for considering the extra value of the contract to Seller when the remedy will be money damages rather than specific performance.To the extent the parties can quantify that extra value, they can adjust the contract price depending on the remedy in such a way as to make riskneutral parties indifferent between the two remedies. Risk-averse parties, however, would not be indifferent, because the two remedies introduce different levels of variability into the parties' returns from the contract. Where transaction costs are low or nonexistent, the variability associated with money damages will be less than that associated with specific performance for both parties, and risk-averse parties will therefore prefer money damages. The same result holds, with some exceptions, when more substantial transaction costs are introduced, so long as neither typeof transaction cost dominates. The option approach, I will argue, provides a plausible explanation for the common law's choice of money damages as the usual remedy, as well as for some of the significant exceptions to that rule.
Section II briefly describes the transaction costs approach. Section III sets out the option framework. It considers first a situation in which there are no transaction costs of the type that create an excessive breach problem or an excessive performance problem. It then examines situations in which such transaction costs are present. Section IV argues that the results reached using the option framework are broadly consistent with the choice of remedy in reported cases. Section V concludes.

matched_themes: Do courts actually prefer monetary damages over specific (in-kind) remedies, or do they grant specific relief except when independent reasons exist to deny it?
When should courts order specific performance (in-kind relief) versus awarding monetary damages?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?

Do contracting parties prefer in-kind remedies or monetary damages, and how do risk preferences, transaction costs, and contracting experience (laypersons versus businesspeople) shape that preference?
Should the promisor or the promisee have the default right to choose between performance and payment to achieve allocative efficiency?
Should parties be presumptively permitted to contractually specify nonstandard damage remedies, or should courts retain authority to impose defaults?
Does making in-kind performance the legal default (rather than monetary compensation) change parties' enforcement choices, moral judgments, and economic efficiency?
When should courts prefer or enforce in-kind (specific) performance rather than monetary damages for breach of contract?
How do transaction costs, enforcement frictions, and institutional realities alter the theoretical efficiency of breach-plus-compensation?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
When is an indirect remedy (one that induces self-compliance) preferable to a direct remedy that delivers the outcome?

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Convergence in Contort: Landlord Liability for Defective Premises in Comparative Perspective

papers.node_id: 118wvalrev369!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT REMEDIES IN ACTION: SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE
papers.title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT REMEDIES IN ACTION: SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE
papers.abstract:
How is a right to specific performance of a contract used by parties? Despite longstanding scholarly interest in the topic, this question has been largely left unexplored. This Article presents a qualitative study of parties and attorneys involved in specific performance litigation. It investigates how parties choose between remedies, whether they negotiate after judgment for specific performance, whether specific performance is implemented, and the difficulties involved in its implementation.
The findings reveal important theoretical oversights and challenges to prevailing law. In practice, many plaintiffs opt out of specific performance. This is puzzling as expectation damages are notoriously under compensatory relative to performance. A primary explanation is that it is harder to execute specific relief than a money judgment. Focusing attention on execution provides a valuable lesson: in exactly these circumstances where U.S. law grants specific performance - unique goods - it is least valuable due to a lack of clear standards by which to evaluate performance. Another explanation is lawyer's bias: attorneys will often advise clients to sue for money damages to ensure easy collection of their own fees.
Another set of findings reveal that parties think about specific performance in ways that are inconsistent with both economic and rights-based theories. Sometimes plaintiffs will not negotiate a judgment as they will be reluctant to commodify it, in contrast to economic theories, and other times they will treat specific performance instrumentally, to achieve other ends but performance of the contractual promise, which is in tension with rights-based theories. The Article concludes by discussing the theoretical and policy implications of these findings, and highlights the ways in which qualitative research could enrich, challenge, and contextualize contract theory.
A central debate in modern contract theory concerns the choice of remedies for breach of contract - should courts award money damages orspecific relief? This debate is seen as central because it involves some of the most fundamental dilemmas of contract law:whether the law should protect rights or promote efficiency, bind parties to past commitments or evolve in light of new information, ensure proper compensation or create optimal incentives, etc.
This debate is often understood as being between normative economic analysis and an assortment of moral philosophies, which can be grouped, for convenience, under the heading of rights-based theories.The economic analysis stresses efficiency and social welfare, while rights-based theories are more concerned with the morality of actions and intentions.Beyond this primary normative distinction, these theories base their respective legal prescriptions on contrasting assumptions about the world in which people contract: their motivations, understandings, and expectations.
For concreteness, rights-based theories often favor specific performance because it is supposed to offer better compensation to victims of breach than money damages. Additionally, giving the promisee what was promised in the contract is deemed important, and it is supposed that specific performance will be used to achieve performance and not instrumentally to other ends. Economic theories alternatively assume that judgments are used instrumentally to maximize victim's welfare rather than coercing performance. As a corollary, victims will prefer specific performance to expectation damages, because it can be used either to demand performance or as leverage in negotiations to extract higher value payment. Lastly, both theories omit from consideration the choice that victims have between remedies, implicitly assuming that the choice has no impact on the legal process. If judges, for example, draw inferences from the choice of remedies on the merit of the case, or if lawyers are biased in favor of one of these remedies, providing victims a choice has broader implications than recognized. These assumptions, while not always explicit, are fundamental to justifying the legal prescriptions thatfollow, and their exploration promises a hope of advancing the debate beyond a normative stalemate.
It is therefore disappointing that despite a growing empirical literature on contract remedies,much is still unknown about the empirical validity of these assumptions.An important missing piece of the puzzle is an examination of the parties' internal point of view: What are parties' expectations, motivations, reasons, and actual behaviors with respect to the legal remedy of specific performance? How do they put remedies into use, and what is their practical significance? How do they implement the remedies? The answers to all of these questions are frustratingly scarce.
This Article makes explicit some of these assumptions and explores their validity. Its main contribution is a qualitative investigation, consisting of interviews with litigants and their lawyers who were involved in specific performance litigation.
A preliminary design issue is the choice of jurisdiction, because in the United States specific relief is only awarded in exceptional circumstances. As a result, the conclusions of any domestic investigation might be limited to these circumstances rather than the actual nature of specific performance. To overcome that, what is needed is a jurisdiction where contract law is sufficiently close to American contract law but nonetheless has specific performance set as the default remedy. Israel presents exactly such an opportunity.
The results are grouped by the chronological stage in the life of a litigated contract case: choice of remedies, post-judgment renegotiation, and the implementation and execution of the judgment. Working backwards, the Article describes, in each stage, findings that challenge traditional assumptions of contract theory.
Starting with the execution of specific performance awards, enforcement is found to be rife with practical problems, which are most pronounced when goods are unique.The principal problem is that performance, unlike damages, often requires the good will of the performing party - which, by the time the trial is over, is often non-existent and may actually turn into spite and bad faith. When there are no clear standards by which to judge the quality of performance, courts lack means of ensuring quality. When goods are unique, it generally means that clear quality standards are absent, meaning that in exactly these circumstances where specific performance is available under American law, it will be hardest to enforce. The Article also addresses the role of plaintiffs' and promisors' liquidity, and explains that specific performance is not a silver bullet against a promisee's insolvency. Social norms and reputation are important leverages, but their effects are not always in the direction of greater enforcement.
Before the judgment is implemented, economic theory predicts that the parties will negotiate over the decree if performance is inefficient. A surprising finding is that some parties (although not all) have refrained from negotiation despite the existence of an ostensible financial incentive to do so. The explanation seems to be derived, first, from the litigation dynamics that often contribute to the animosity between the parties and, second, from the cognitive perception of specific performance decrees as being qualitatively different from other goods on the market that may be freely traded. The framing of these decrees as default rights seems to affect parties' willingness to negotiate over them.
Despite a general theoretical expectation that, given the choice of remedies, plaintiffs will sue for specific performance, it was found that many opt-out of the default in favor of money damages.Of the reasons identified,one that stands out is lawyer's bias. Attorneys have a general preference for money damages out of concern for their own fees and their ability to collect them, which is harder in the case of specific performance decrees.
Of course, not all plaintiffs choose to opt-out. This is predicted by mainstream theory and may therefore seem to be of lesser interest, but delving deeper into plaintiffs' motivations suggests a more involved story. First, because the plaintiffs are given a choice between different contract remedies, courts may draw inferences from the choices made and use them to assess the merits of the case. Lawyers reported that a belief that opting out of specific performance sends a signal of bad faith to the court, as if the plaintiff is behaving opportunistically and only cares about money, not performance. Second, specific performance may be sued for to speed up the resolution of the case and to reduce the costs of litigation, because the costs of proving damages are spared. Third, parties occasionally sue for specific performance to use it as a bargaining chip.
The Article concludes by discussing various theoretical and legal implications of these findings. It is argued that rights-based theory should directly address the instrumental uses that parties make of specific performance judgments, as they create a wedge between what was promised and what is legally prescribed. The under-compensatory nature of specific performance should be recognized within corrective justice theories of contract law, and due attention should be given to the fact that the problem will not vanish simply by giving the promisee a choice between damages and enforcement. These findings suggest new areas for exploration for economic theories - primarily, the signaling effects of remedies and the attorney's influence on choice of remedies. The aversion to post-judgment renegotiation suggests that judgments are sticky and parties should not be trusted to renegotiate as a general matter. Concerns with a flood of litigation following a more liberal approach to specific performance should also be alleviated. Finally, it is explained that specific performance is not a silver bullet against a promisor's insolvency. Regarding the law, it is argued that limiting the scope of specific performance to cases of unique goods is non-constructive, as these are the cases where enforcement is most likely to be ineffective. Additionally, it is argued that lawyers should pay much closer attention to enforcement mechanisms.
The organization of this Article is as follows: Part II lays out the necessary theoretical framework. Specifically, it points out the relevant empirical assumptions and the role they play in theory. Part III presents stylized facts about Israeli and U.S. contract law, emphasizing the similarity of the systems in the context of this Article. Part IV delves into the methodology and explains the research protocol. Parts V, VI, and VII discuss the primaryfindings of the study. These Parts cover three time periods: the parties' choices before and during litigation, the parties' post-judgment renegotiations, and, finally, the implementation of the judgment in these cases where no post-judgment settlement has occurred. The final Part considers the chief theoretical and legal implications of these findings.

questions.question: When given the choice between in-kind enforcement and monetary compensation for a breached contract, do plaintiffs sue for and obtain specific (in-kind) performance or opt for money damages?
After a court orders in-kind performance, do parties renegotiate or settle the decree instead of implementing it, and what factors make post-judgment renegotiation more or less likely?

Are court-ordered in-kind remedies actually implemented and enforced in practice, and are they harder to execute than money judgments (for example, when the subject matter is unique or quality standards are unclear)?

matched_themes: Does giving the promisee a unilateral right to demand performance or elect a damages measure that captures promisor's forgone gains vindicate moral intuitions while preserving ex post efficiency?
When should courts order specific performance (in-kind relief) versus awarding monetary damages?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?

Do contracting parties prefer in-kind remedies or monetary damages, and how do risk preferences, transaction costs, and contracting experience (laypersons versus businesspeople) shape that preference?
Should the promisor or the promisee have the default right to choose between performance and payment to achieve allocative efficiency?
Does making in-kind performance the legal default (rather than monetary compensation) change parties' enforcement choices, moral judgments, and economic efficiency?
When should courts prefer or enforce in-kind (specific) performance rather than monetary damages for breach of contract?

Should remedies and contract law be structured to preserve conditions necessary for moral agency and promissory responsibility, rather than treating promises solely as instruments of economic cooperation?
Can costless ex-post renegotiation eliminate or preserve the ex-ante incentive effects of remedial rules on precaution, contract formation, and pricing?
How do transaction costs, enforcement frictions, and institutional realities alter the theoretical efficiency of breach-plus-compensation?

Can party-designed enforcement mechanisms (pre-agreed penalties, arbitration, bonding, reputational systems) reliably produce efficient breach outcomes without judicial intervention, and when do they fail?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
How should remedial and enforcement rules be structured to achieve efficient behavior when populations include both internalizers and externalizers?
To what extent does empirical uncertainty about measuring gains and losses limit courts' ability to design remedies that reflect non-welfare ethical preferences without sacrificing efficiency?
Are court-ordered in-kind remedies actually implemented and practically enforceable compared with money judgments?
Do courts consider the breaching party's blameworthiness or opportunistic behavior when selecting among compensatory remedies?
To what extent should moral blameworthiness and non-economic considerations influence the design and application of contract remedies?
When is an indirect remedy (one that induces self-compliance) preferable to a direct remedy that delivers the outcome?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 82columlrev1365!!ARTICLE: In Defense of Money Damages for Breach of Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: In Defense of Money Damages for Breach of Contract

shared_topics.topic: whether specific performance should be the default remedy versus money damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues against making specific performance the normal remedy and defends money damages as the preferable baseline, while Paper B empirically studies a jurisdiction with specific performance as the default and shows many plaintiffs opt out and that defaulting to specific performance raises practical problems.

shared_topics.topic: enforceability and practical implementation of specific performance awards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the difficulty and risk of error in formulating and enforcing specific performance and the loss of flexibility that a universal rule would entail; Paper B supplies qualitative evidence that specific performance is often hard to execute, lacks clear quality standards, and depends on the performing party's good will, especially for unique goods.

shared_topics.topic: efficiency versus rights‑based (moral) justifications for remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages both the moral (promise-keeping) and economic-efficiency arguments for specific performance and critiques the efficiency claim, while Paper B frames the remedies debate as economic versus rights-based and shows parties' behavior often departs from the assumptions of both theories.

shared_topics.topic: design and reform of remedy rules (including improving money damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A urges selective modification of money-damages rules rather than adopting routine specific performance; Paper B identifies concrete institutional problems (attorney incentives, signaling, enforcement) that bear on how remedy rules should be designed or reformed.

shared_topics.topic: parties' strategic choice of remedies, post-judgment negotiation, and signaling effects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A stresses that remedy rules shape parties' incentives and that a single remedy would blunt legal responsiveness, while Paper B empirically examines how plaintiffs and lawyers strategically choose damages or specific performance, use judgments as bargaining chips, avoid renegotiation, and consider signaling to courts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83lawcontempprob151!!ARTICLE: BLACK MARKETS AND THE EXCHANGE STRUCTURE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BLACK MARKETS AND THE EXCHANGE STRUCTURE

shared_topics.topic: how law and legal rules shape, enable, or disable private exchanges
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how the availability and framing of the judicial remedy of specific performance affects parties' bargaining, willingness to transact, and post‑judgment behavior; Paper B theorizes how legal rules and disabilities (not just criminal penalties) actively create and delimit 'black' versus licit exchanges by restricting the terms on which parties may lawfully trade.

shared_topics.topic: limits and practical difficulties of legal enforcement as a means of securing transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents practical enforcement problems in implementing specific performance (especially for unique goods) and shows that judicial decrees often cannot secure actual performance, while Paper B analyzes the limited deterrent role of criminal sanctions and emphasizes that disabilities and ‘‘hands‑tying’’ often function as the primary instruments to prevent or contain transgressive exchanges.

shared_topics.topic: the interplay between formal law and social/reputational or nonlegal sanctions in sustaining exchange norms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how social norms and reputation operate as levers (and sometimes fail) in inducing performance or settlement, and Paper B situates nonlegal normative regimes and civil sanctions alongside criminal law as components that preserve an exchange structure and discipline transgressive bargaining.

shared_topics.topic: how legal classification, remedy choice, or official responses signal and reshape actors' incentives and beliefs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that plaintiffs' choice of remedy (opting out of specific performance) and attorneys' advice can signal credibility or opportunism to courts and affect negotiation dynamics; Paper B argues that labeling exchanges as prohibited (or selectively enforcing them) changes participants' expectations and preserves the established transaction structure by signaling what exchanges are permitted.

shared_topics.topic: the inadequacy of pure efficiency/economic accounts to fully justify legal responses to transgressive exchanges
shared_topics.justification: Paper A challenges standard economic assumptions about remedy choice and instrumental uses of judgments, showing behaviors inconsistent with simple efficiency models, while Paper B rejects efficiency alone as a full explanation for criminalizing consensual exchanges and foregrounds system‑preservation, fairness, and normative considerations (Calabresi/Melamed) as complementary rationales.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 117michlrev885!!ARTICLE: Moral Diversity and Efficient Breach
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Moral Diversity and Efficient Breach

shared_topics.topic: moral status of breach and promise-keeping
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage the question whether breaching a contract is a moral wrong (a failure to keep a promise) or merely a legal contingency: Paper A documents and theorizes moral heterogeneity (individuals as promise‑moralists vs firms as Holmesian), while Paper B situates specific performance within rights-based theories that treat promises as morally salient and shows parties sometimes act on non‑economic, moral considerations.

shared_topics.topic: efficiency versus rights-based justifications for remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both examine the tension between efficiency (expectation damages, bargaining) and rights-based aims (enforcement of the promise): Paper A argues the existing damages regime interacts with moral beliefs to produce inefficiencies and distributional harms, and Paper B compares economic and rights-based theories to show empirical departures from both in parties' remedy choices and bargaining behavior.

shared_topics.topic: how available remedies and contract termsshape parties' choices and signaling
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how the presence or absence of particular contractual mechanisms or remedies affects behavior and perceptions: Paper A proposes modifying contract wording (mandatory exit clauses) to change moral perceptions and induce efficient exit, while Paper B shows that choosing between damages and specific performance sends signals, affects litigant framing, and influences willingness to negotiate.

shared_topics.topic: practical enforceability and implementation limits of non-monetary relief
shared_topics.justification: Both grapple with the real-world difficulties of forcing performance rather than awarding money: Paper A considers and rejects specific performance as an effective means to align moral actors and markets, and Paper B documents empirical implementation problems, measurement standards, and the unwillingness or inability to execute specific performance in practice.

shared_topics.topic: role of institutional actors and incentives (firms, lawyers, courts) in shaping breach/remedy outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Both analyze how institutional incentives change behavior around breach and remedies: Paper A contrasts firm (Holmesian) behavior with individual moralists and discusses market and regulatory responses, while Paper B documents attorneys' fee-driven preferences for damages, courts' inferences from remedy choices, and how these institutional forces affect whether specific performance is pursued or enforced.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 100yalelj369!!ARTICLE: The Myth that Promisees Prefer Supracompensatory Remedies: An Analysis of Contracting for Damage Measures.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Myth that Promisees Prefer Supracompensatory Remedies: An Analysis of Contracting for Damage Measures.

shared_topics.topic: promisees' choice between specific performance and expectation (money) damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A challenges the assumption that promisees prefer supracompensatory remedies and argues promisees generally prefer compensatory monetary remedies; Paper B empirically documents that many plaintiffs opt out of specific performance in favor of money damages and analyzes the reasons for that choice (enforcement difficulty, lawyer bias, signaling, etc.).

shared_topics.topic: practical enforceability and implementation problems of specific performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers whether courts should permit parties to contract for specific relief and questions judicial policing given enforcement realities, while Paper B provides qualitative evidence that specific performance is often hard to implement—especially for unique goods—due to lack of quality standards, bad faith, and execution obstacles.

shared_topics.topic: judicial review and contractual policing of remedial clauses (liquidated damages, penalties, specific performance clauses)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues against judicial policing of ex ante and ex post liquidated-damage clauses and for allowing specific-performance clauses, whereas Paper B questions current doctrinal limits (e.g., restricting specific performance to unique goods), highlighting how legal defaults and enforcement rules affect parties' behavior and outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: instrumental uses of remedies (leverage, signaling, and attorney influence) and implications for theory
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions the positive premise that promisees seek supracompensatory remedies to exploit promisors and discusses how remedial rules interact with parties' incentives, while Paper B documents that parties and lawyers often use specific performance instrumentally—as bargaining leverage, a signal to courts, or shaped by attorney preferences—challenging core assumptions in both economic and rights-based contract theories.

shared_topics.topic: policy and normative implications for remedy design in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A derives normative prescriptions (e.g., restore punitive-damages bar, allow contracting for specific relief, repeal liquidated-damage review), and Paper B draws policy conclusions from empirical findings (e.g., rethinking the uniqueness rule, attending to enforcement mechanisms, and factoring attorney incentives), with both engaging the question of how remedial doctrine should be reformed given parties' actual behavior and enforcement realities.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 104marqlrev141!!ARTICLE: THE MYTH OF OPTIMAL EXPECTATION DAMAGES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE MYTH OF OPTIMAL EXPECTATION DAMAGES

shared_topics.topic: choice between expectation damages and specific performance as remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage the core question of how and why parties end up with money damages rather than specific performance: Paper A empirically studies litigants' and lawyers' decisions to sue for or opt out of specific performance, while Paper B theorizes about the default role of expectation damages and whether that default matches parties' optimal preferences.

shared_topics.topic: heterogeneity of parties' preferences over remedy rules
shared_topics.justification: Both works challenge the assumption of a single, uniform optimal remedy: Paper B argues that optimal damages vary with parties' characteristics and bargaining context, and Paper A documents varied, context-dependent plaintiff motivations and uses of specific performance that diverge from standard economic or rights-based assumptions.

shared_topics.topic: strategic and signaling uses of remedies and negotiated/delegated outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Both papers consider remedies as strategic instruments rather than mere compensation mechanisms: Paper A shows parties use specific performance instrumentally (as bargaining chips) and that remedy choice can signal merits to courts, while Paper B frames damages as a priced termination option that parties may strategically select or contract over.

shared_topics.topic: role of attorneys and courts in shaping remedy selection and enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Both studies examine non-ideal actors and institutions affecting remedies: Paper A documents attorneys' biases toward money judgments and courts' inferences from remedy choices, and Paper B analyzes how courts enforce or limit contracted-for damages and the implications of judicially imposed default rules for parties' contracting autonomy.

shared_topics.topic: gap between economic theory assumptions and real-world enforceability/implementation of remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both papers critique the empirical validity of standard law-and-economics assumptions: Paper B questions assumptions (full information, contractibility) that justify expectation damages as optimal, and Paper A provides empirical evidence that enforcement difficulties, lack of clear performance standards, and social dynamics undermine theoretical predictions about specific performance.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 39urichlrev627!!ARTICLE:AN ALTERNATIVE PARADIGM FOR VALUING BREACH OF REGISTRATION RIGHTS AND LOSS OF LIQUIDITY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:AN ALTERNATIVE PARADIGM FOR VALUING BREACH OF REGISTRATION RIGHTS AND LOSS OF LIQUIDITY

shared_topics.topic: adequacy and measurement of remedies for breach of contract (money damages vs non‑monetary relief)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops and defends a specific damages formula for loss of registration/liquidity rights and critiques existing ad hoc measures, while Paper B empirically interrogates when parties seek money damages versus specific performance and highlights shortcomings of each remedy in practice.

shared_topics.topic: role of liquidity and solvency in shaping remedy choice and effectiveness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on loss of liquidity (registration rights) as the central harm and derives damages tied to foregone liquidity, and Paper B analyzes how plaintiffs' and defendants' liquidity or insolvency affect the attractiveness, enforceability, and practical value of specific performance or money judgments.

shared_topics.topic: practical enforceability and feasibility constraints on supposed legal solutions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes market and regulatory constraints (e.g., inability to short, limits on mitigation transactions) that make some theoretical damage measures infeasible, while Paper B documents real‑world execution problems and enforcement gaps that make specific performance hard to implement, especially for unique goods.

shared_topics.topic: tension between doctrinal theory and litigant behavior/strategic choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that courts lack a textured doctrinal principle and that case law yields inconsistent outcomes, and Paper B shows litigants and lawyers routinely act in ways that diverge from economic and rights‑based theories (e.g., opting out of specific performance or avoiding renegotiation), exposing gaps between doctrine and practice.

shared_topics.topic: mitigation duties and strategic responses to breach (including post‑breach negotiation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines a promisee's mitigation dilemma (resale in private market versus waiting for registration) and how that affects damages, and Paper B studies post‑judgment renegotiation and the strategic refusal or use of remedies as bargaining leverage, showing how mitigation and negotiation choices shape legal outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68amulrev1751!!ARTICLE: SOMETHING ELSE: SPECIFIC RELIEF FOR BREACH OF HUMAN RIGHTS TERMS IN SUPPLY CHAIN AGREEMENTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SOMETHING ELSE: SPECIFIC RELIEF FOR BREACH OF HUMAN RIGHTS TERMS IN SUPPLY CHAIN AGREEMENTS

shared_topics.topic: practical enforceability of specific performance / specific relief orders
shared_topics.justification: Both papers investigate how courts and parties struggle to execute specific relief in practice — highlighting problems like lack of clear performance standards, reliance on the performing party's goodwill, limits of contempt/enforcement, and attendant practical obstacles to achieving the court-ordered outcome.

shared_topics.topic: parties' choice between monetary damages and specific relief and its signaling/incentive effects
shared_topics.justification: Both examine why contracting parties (and their lawyers) opt for damages or specific relief, including attorney fee/collection concerns, bargaining leverage, reputational signaling to courts, and how remedy selection shapes negotiation and litigation dynamics.

shared_topics.topic: using contract remedies to pursue non-commercial or rights-based objectives
shared_topics.justification: Both papers consider using traditional contract remedies to achieve goals beyond pure expectation enforcement — Paper A situates specific performance within rights-based versus economic theories, while Paper B analyzes employing specific relief to enforce human-rights terms in supply-chain contracts.

shared_topics.topic: need for institutional or procedural mechanisms (monitors, experts) to implement specific relief
shared_topics.justification: Both identify that courts often lack the means to assess compliance and suggest that implementation may require institutional devices — e.g., monitoring, neutral experts, quality-assurance mechanisms or other enforcement-oriented procedures — to make specific relief effective.

shared_topics.topic: comparative and cross-jurisdictional constraints on the availability and effectiveness of specific relief
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with how jurisdictional rules and cross-border realities affect specific relief: Paper A uses an Israeli comparative setting to study a default-for-specific-performance regime, while Paper B addresses choice-of-law, foreign defendants, and transnational enforcement limits that constrain remedies for HR clauses in supply-chain agreements.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 71califlrev56!!ARTICLE: The Collateral Source Rule and Contract Damages.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Collateral Source Rule and Contract Damages.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of the compensatory burden between the contracting defendant and third-party/payor sources
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes whether collateral-source payments should reduce contract damages or whether the collateral payor (via subrogation) should bear primary responsibility, while Paper B examines who ultimately absorbs loss (promisee, promisor, creditors, or other levers) when remedies like specific performance fail or the promisor is insolvent.

shared_topics.topic: comparative adequacy of remedies (money damages versus specific performance) in providing compensation for breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions how collateral benefits affect the adequacy and fairness of monetary contract damages, and Paper B empirically investigates whether specific performance actually provides better compensation than money damages in practice and finds important shortcomings.

shared_topics.topic: role of enforcement, collection, and subrogation mechanisms in shaping remedy outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes repayment/subrogation as a preferred way to allocate recovery and avoid windfalls, whereas Paper B shows that practical enforcement problems, collection difficulties, and liquidity constraints materially determine whether a remedy (especially specific performance) yields the intended relief.

shared_topics.topic: how remedy rules and parties' remedy choices influence incentives, signaling, and lawyer behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates policy justifications and incentive effects underlying the collateral source rule (and potential windfalls), while Paper B documents that remedy choices carry signaling effects, are shaped by attorneys' incentives (fee/collectability), and influence bargaining and litigation strategies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 28setonhalllrev390!!ARTICLE: Attaching Tort Claims to Contract Actions: An Economic Analysis of Contort
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Attaching Tort Claims to Contract Actions: An Economic Analysis of Contort

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy of expectation damages to compensate breach victims
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically documents that expectation damages are often under‑compensatory relative to performance and explores why plaintiffs nonetheless shy away from specific performance; Paper B develops an economic model evaluating whether traditional contract damages achieve their remedial and incentive goals and explains doctrinal limits on those damages.

shared_topics.topic: plaintiffs' strategic choice among remedies (money damages, specific performance, and tort claims)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates empirically how plaintiffs and lawyers choose between specific performance and money judgments and how those choices are used instrumentally or signalingly; Paper B analyzes the legal and economic implications of allowing plaintiffs to attach tort causes of action to contract breaches, thereby changing the available remedial options and strategic calculus.

shared_topics.topic: economic analysis of remedy design and incentive effects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques assumptions of economic contract theory and highlights empirical phenomena (signaling, attorney incentives, renegotiation aversion) that affect remedy outcomes; Paper B explicitly uses an economic framework to assess how remedies (and expanding them via tort claims) influence incentives and welfare.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal limits on available remedies and their policy implications
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions doctrines that limit specific performance to 'unique' goods and stresses enforcement and implementation problems that undermine its value; Paper B examines common‑law tests and limits on contract damages and proposes alternative doctrinal frameworks for when tort remedies should be attached to contract actions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 4wmmarybuslrev493!!ARTICLE: CLASHING POLICIES OR CONFUSING PRECEDENTS: THE "GROSS NEGLIGENCE" EXCEPTION TO CONSEQUENTIAL DAMAGES DISCLAIMERS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CLASHING POLICIES OR CONFUSING PRECEDENTS: THE "GROSS NEGLIGENCE" EXCEPTION TO CONSEQUENTIAL DAMAGES DISCLAIMERS

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of agreed contractual remedies and limits on liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when courts will enforce or invalidate contractual limitations of liability (especially consequential damages disclaimers) under the UCC and common law, while Paper B empirically studies how courts and parties actually obtain, implement, or abandon an alternative contractual remedy—specific performance—highlighting practical and doctrinal limits on the effectiveness of agreed remedies.

shared_topics.topic: tension between freedom of contract and public‑policy or judicial intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly addresses the conflict between upholding negotiated risk allocations among sophisticated parties and courts refusing enforcement on public‑policy grounds (gross negligence, unconscionability), and Paper B probes how judicial default rules (e.g., availability of specific performance) and enforcement practices constrain parties' contractual expectations and choices.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal vagueness and ambiguous legal standards affecting predictability of outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents judicial confusion and split authority over what constitutes gross negligence, recklessness, or willful misconduct that can void liability limits, while Paper B documents the lack of clear standards for assessing the quality and enforceability of specific performance—both showing how vagueness undermines predictable enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: parties' strategic negotiation choices, bargaining power, and the role of counsel in shaping remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses negotiated contract drafting examples (inclusion/exclusion of gross‑negligence carveouts) to show how parties and counsel attempt to allocate risk, and Paper B provides empirical evidence that litigants and lawyers strategically choose (or avoid) specific performance, use remedies as bargaining chips, and that lawyers' incentives affect remedy selection and enforcement outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2004wislrev507!!SYMPOSIUM: PROMISSORY FRAUD WITHOUT BREACH
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: PROMISSORY FRAUD WITHOUT BREACH

shared_topics.topic: when and how the law should enforce promises (choice among remedies vs alternative liability)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically interrogates parties' and lawyers' choices between enforcement via specific performance and money damages and the practical consequences of those choices; Paper B examines when promissory fraud (a non-contractual tort or crime) should be available as an alternative or supplement to contract remedies, including situations where contract enforcement is unavailable.

shared_topics.topic: how inferences about intent and signaling affect legal outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper B centers on the promisor's present intent and how insincere promises operate as misrepresentations, while Paper A highlights signaling effects of a plaintiff's choice of remedy (e.g., opting out of specific performance may signal opportunism) and calls attention to how remedies themselves communicate information to courts and counterparts.

shared_topics.topic: the gap between doctrinal rules and practical enforceability of promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents practical obstacles to implementing court-ordered specific performance (especially for unique goods) and how those obstacles undermine doctrinal assumptions; Paper B probes doctrinal limits of promissory fraud and shows that formal contract remedies can fail to capture real harms from insincere promises, motivating non-contractual liability.

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations for imposing liability for broken or insincere promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A tests and challenges economic versus rights-based theories about whether the law should coerce performance or compensate loss, while Paper B questions the theoretical basis for promissory fraud liability (and when it should coexist with or replace contractual nonenforcement), contributing to debates about remedial and moral justifications for responding to promises.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 61scallrev629!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT REMEDIES, RENEGOTIATION, AND THE THEORY OF EFFICIENT BREACH.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT REMEDIES, RENEGOTIATION, AND THE THEORY OF EFFICIENT BREACH.

shared_topics.topic: how contract remedies shape the perform-or-breach decision (including the economic question of efficient breach)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates empirically whether parties choose specific performance or damages and how that choice affects incentives to obtain performance, while Paper B develops the economic theory of efficient breach, analyzing when remedies should induce promisors to perform or to breach for efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: the role of renegotiation (including post-judgment bargaining) in determining remedy outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies parties' actual willingness to renegotiate after judgment and finds stickiness and aversion to post-judgment deals, while Paper B centrally analyzes how ex post renegotiation costs affect which remedies are efficient and whether remedy effects disappear when renegotiation is easy.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy of economic assumptions about parties' behavior (motives, signaling, and bargaining) used in contract-remedies theory
shared_topics.justification: Paper A provides qualitative evidence that parties and lawyers often behave in ways inconsistent with standard economic and rights-based assumptions (e.g., reluctance to commodify judgments, lawyers' fee-driven advice, signaling to courts), while Paper B criticizes narrow economic models for relying on simplifying behavioral assumptions (e.g., that the perform-or-breach choice is the only relevant decision and that renegotiation will reliably restore efficiency).

shared_topics.topic: comparative assessment of specific performance versus money damages in terms of efficiency, enforcement, and practical effects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents practical enforcement problems, limited value, and strategic uses of specific performance compared to damages, while Paper B treats specific performance as a canonical remedy in its analysis of how different remedies affect incentives, precaution, contracting, and distributional outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 46amulrev1!!ARTICLE: THE MEANING OF VALUE IN CONTRACT DAMAGES AND CONTRACT THEORY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE MEANING OF VALUE IN CONTRACT DAMAGES AND CONTRACT THEORY

shared_topics.topic: choice between specific performance and monetary damages as competing remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically studies why parties and lawyers opt for money damages rather than specific performance (and how specific performance is litigated and executed), while Paper B situates remedies within damage-measure theory by analyzing how monetary awards should be defined and when they serve as the appropriate legal response to breach.

shared_topics.topic: adequacy and measurement of damages (expectation compensation versus lost surplus)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents that expectation damages often undercompensate relative to actual performance and highlights practical consequences of that shortfall, whereas Paper B critiques conflicting legal definitions of 'value' and proposes a surplus-based damage rule to more accurately measure the injured party's loss.

shared_topics.topic: assumptions and implications of efficient-breach theory for remedy design
shared_topics.justification: Paper B explicates efficient breach theory and reframes damages in terms of allocating resources to the most surplus-generating uses, and Paper A tests core behavioral assumptions of that theory (about parties' motivations, renegotiation, and instrumentality of judgments) with empirical evidence that challenges those assumptions.

shared_topics.topic: how remedy choice affects bargaining, signaling, and post-judgment renegotiation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A provides empirical findings on how suing for specific performance or damages influences negotiation dynamics, signaling to courts, and stickiness of judgments, while Paper B analyzes how different damage rules create incentives that influence parties' decisions to breach, perform, or reallocate contracts to alternative uses.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 65vandlrev829!!ARTICLE: Loss Aversion and the Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Loss Aversion and the Law

shared_topics.topic: theoretical foundations and goals of contract remedies (expectation vs reliance vs disgorgement; rights-based vs economic justifications)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes why contract law persistently frames remedies around expectation and reliance interests and why disgorgement is marginal, discussing normative theories for remedies; Paper B empirically interrogates the central remedies debate by studying why parties choose specific performance or damages and how those choices align or conflict with rights-based and economic theories.

shared_topics.topic: psychological factors (loss aversion, reference points, framing, status quo bias) shaping litigant behavior and doctrinal design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a general account of how reference points and loss aversion explain core legal patterns and should influence legal policy; Paper B provides empirical evidence that framing (e.g., treating decrees as default rights), cognitive perceptions, and aversion to renegotiation affect parties' willingness to seek or settle for specific performance.

shared_topics.topic: practical incentives, enforcement difficulties, and litigation dynamics affecting remedy choice and doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A offers an evolutionary/plaintiff-selection explanation for why doctrines addressing losses are more developed than those addressing gains, emphasizing plaintiffs' incentives in shaping law; Paper B documents how enforcement problems (difficulty executing specific performance), attorneys' fee incentives, liquidity, reputation, and court inference dynamics lead many plaintiffs to opt for damages and thus shape how remedies operate in practice.

shared_topics.topic: stickiness of legal outcomes and the law's power to shape perceptions — implications for reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues the law both mirrors and creates reference points, making baseline changes sticky and cautioning about reform; Paper B finds judgments and decrees are 'sticky' (parties are averse to renegotiation and courts' decrees influence bargaining), highlighting practical limits and unintended effects of changing remedial regimes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2013michstlrev1!!ARTICLE: THE EXPECTATION MEASURE AND ITS DISCONTENTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE EXPECTATION MEASURE AND ITS DISCONTENTS

shared_topics.topic: choice between expectation damages and specific performance as remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the expectation measure (money damages) and critiques/alternatives to it as the central remedial rule, while Paper B empirically investigates how parties actually choose between money damages and specific performance and the practical consequences of that choice.

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations of remedy choice — efficiency versus rights/corrective justice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the expectation measure in terms of the indifference principle and efficiency and canvasses alternative goals that might justify different remedies; Paper B contrasts economic (efficiency) and rights-based theories and tests their empirical assumptions about why parties would prefer one remedy over another.

shared_topics.topic: administrability and institutional fit of remedial rules (enforceability and implementation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly examines the administrability of proposed models and the congruence between remedial regimes and institutional capacities, and Paper B documents practical enforcement problems, implementation difficulties, and institutional barriers in executing specific performance awards.

shared_topics.topic: evaluation of alternative remedial regimes to the expectation measure
shared_topics.justification: Paper A substantively analyzes and critiques prominent alternative models and remedial regimes to the expectation measure, and Paper B performs an in‑depth empirical assessment of one key alternative (specific performance), highlighting its strengths and weaknesses in practice.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 55amjcompl721!!ARTICLE: Why No "Efficient Breach" in the Civil Law?: A Comparative Assessment of the Doctrine of Efficient Breach of Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Why No "Efficient Breach" in the Civil Law?: A Comparative Assessment of the Doctrine of Efficient Breach of Contract

shared_topics.topic: choice between money damages and specific performance as competing contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the doctrine of efficient breach — which presumes expectation damages (allowing breach when socially beneficial) — against civil law tendencies that favor performance; Paper B empirically investigates how parties and lawyers actually choose between suing for specific performance versus suing for money damages and the practical consequences of those choices.

shared_topics.topic: theoretical tension between economic-efficiency justifications and rights-based/moral justifications for remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts law-and-economics' efficient-breach rationale with civil-law moral commitments (pacta sunt servanda and good faith) that resist treating breach as efficient; Paper B frames and tests the debate between economic (efficiency/instrumental use of remedies) and rights-based (promises and corrective justice) theories, showing parties' behaviors that challenge both.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal rules and enforcement/implementation realities shape the practical availability and value of remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes structural doctrinal hurdles in civil-law systems (doctrines, remedies, and institutional design) that limit the attractiveness of efficient-breach reasoning, while Paper B documents enforcement and implementation problems (difficulty securing performance, lack of quality-standards for unique goods) that make specific performance less valuable in practice.

shared_topics.topic: the role of legal culture, norms, and attorney behavior in determining remedy adoption and use
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights pervasive cultural and normative obstacles in civil-law jurisdictions (good faith, moral meanings of contract) that impede acceptance of efficient breach, and Paper B shows how lawyers' incentives, signaling concerns, and parties' normative perceptions influence whether plaintiffs opt for or abstain from specific performance.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 116wvalrev363!!ARTICLE: HYPOTHETICAL EFFICIENCY IS NOT GROUNDS FOR BREACH
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: HYPOTHETICAL EFFICIENCY IS NOT GROUNDS FOR BREACH

shared_topics.topic: adequacy of monetary damages versus specific performance as remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically investigates whether expectation damages adequately compensate promisees and finds damages often under-compensatory relative to actual performance (and that many plaintiffs nonetheless opt for damages), while Paper B critiques the idea that paying compensatory damages makes breach morally permissible, arguing damages are not a sufficient moral or normative substitute for performance.

shared_topics.topic: how parties choose between performing, breaching, or renegotiating
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies litigants' and lawyers' real-world decisions about suing for specific performance, opting for money judgments, or negotiating post-judgment, documenting factors that drive those choices; Paper B analyzes the normative options facing firms (perform, breach and pay damages, or renegotiate) and argues for staying in relationship or seeking alternatives to efficiency-driven breach.

shared_topics.topic: tension between economic/efficiency reasoning and rights- or morality-based views of contract obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the remedies debate as pitting economic efficiency against rights-based theories and presents empirical findings that challenge assumptions of both approaches, while Paper B directly rejects an efficiency-based moral justification for breach and defends rights/moral considerations (and limits to economic reasoning) in guiding contractual behavior.

shared_topics.topic: limits of enforcement and the role of post-contractal behavior (renegotiation, good faith, and practical enforceability)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents practical enforcement problems for specific performance (especially with unique goods) and shows reluctance or obstacles to post-judgment renegotiation, whereas Paper B emphasizes the normative importance of implied duties (good faith, relational obligations) and advocates relational or normative constraints on exploiting legal remedies in lieu of continued performance or cooperative renegotiation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 93califlrev975!!ARTICLE: Actual and Virtual Specific Performance, the Theory of Efficient Breach, and the Indifference Principle in Contract Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Actual and Virtual Specific Performance, the Theory of Efficient Breach, and the Indifference Principle in Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: choice between specific performance and expectation damages / the indifference principle
shared_topics.justification: Both papers centrally examine when parties and courts should choose specific performance versus money damages: Paper B analyzes the indifference principle and argues expectation damages systematically fall short of making promisees indifferent, while Paper A provides empirical evidence that plaintiffs often opt out of specific performance and that real-world choices diverge from both economic and rights-based assumptions.

shared_topics.topic: adequacy and limits of expectation damages
shared_topics.justification: Both works question whether expectation damages actually compensate or incentivize the right outcomes: Paper B demonstrates a theoretical shortfall of expectation damages relative to the indifference principle and the implications for efficient breach, while Paper A documents empirically that damages are frequently under‑compensatory in practice and that this perception shapes litigant behavior and remedy choice.

shared_topics.topic: practical enforceability and implementation problems of specific performance
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage with the real-world limits of implementing specific performance: Paper A documents enforcement difficulties—quality standards, need for good will, and problems when goods are unique—while Paper B highlights practical drawbacks of actual specific performance (coerciveness, error, mitigation and opportunism) that counsel against routine awards.

shared_topics.topic: substitutability, unique goods, and the role of market cover (virtual specific performance)
shared_topics.justification: Both treat substitutability as central to remedy selection: Paper B develops the concept of virtual specific performance/cover when market substitutes exist and prescribes rules for cover damages, while Paper A empirically shows that specific performance is commonly available for ‘unique’ goods yet is often least valuable there because clear standards and market substitutes are lacking.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1501!!ARTICLE: WHEN IS A WILLFUL BREACH "WILLFUL"? THE LINK BETWEEN DEFINITIONS AND DAMAGES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: WHEN IS A WILLFUL BREACH "WILLFUL"? THE LINK BETWEEN DEFINITIONS AND DAMAGES

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal labels and parties' remedy-choices signal case merit and affect judicial relief
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows empirically that plaintiffs' choices between specific performance and damages (and lawyers' advice) are used as signals in litigation and can influence judicial inferences; Paper B analyzes how labels like 'willful' or 'bad faith' are indeterminate yet consequential, affecting when courts treat breaches differently and thus signaling heightened culpability to justify enhanced relief.

shared_topics.topic: whether and how culpability (e.g., 'willful' or 'bad faith') should alter the measure or form of remedy for breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper B argues that 'willful' breach cannot be defined solely by mental state and that any definition must be tied to how much damages should be increased, while Paper A engages this theme by contrasting economic and rights-based rationales for specific performance and documenting instances where courts and parties treat culpability and intentions as relevant to remedy selection.

shared_topics.topic: the evidentiary and fact-finding burdens different remedial doctrines impose and the practical consequences for enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper B emphasizes that any choice of a definition for 'willful' breach carries distinct fact-finding demands that affect court capacity to award enhanced damages, and Paper A documents empirically that proving and enforcing specific performance (or proving damages) entails different evidentiary costs and standards that shape parties' strategic choices and the feasibility of relief.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between normative aims (compensation, deterrence/punishment, and practical enforceability) when setting remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the remedies debate as a conflict between efficiency (compensation) and rights-based aims and shows practical enforcement limitations that undermine theoretical prescriptions, while Paper B connects the decision to raise damages for culpable breaches to underlying normative goals (how high damages should be for willful conduct) and the attendant practical implications of implementing those goals.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2012utahlrev861!!ARTICLE: Taking Outcomes Seriously
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Taking Outcomes Seriously

shared_topics.topic: diminished value of compelled performance / 'unwilling giving'
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that specific performance often yields less practical value because coerced performance lacks the promisor's goodwill and is hard to execute, while Paper B experimentally demonstrates that recipients value transfers less when they are obtained unwillingly or by coercion, even when pecuniary losses are compensated.

shared_topics.topic: inadequacy of standard monetary damages as a full measure of compensation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that expectation damages can be under‑compensatory relative to performance and that plaintiffs and lawyers treat remedies instrumentally, while Paper B argues (with experimental evidence) that wealth‑only measures miss important components (e.g., a compelled‑giving premium), producing systematic undercompensation.

shared_topics.topic: importance of non‑pecuniary factors (intentionality, identity, cooperation) in evaluating outcomes and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how reputation, animosity, framing, and the qualitative nature of performance affect negotiation, enforcement, and remedy choice; Paper B finds that intentionality, the actor's identity (friend vs. stranger), and cooperative vs. unwilling transfers materially change how people value otherwise identical end results.
