papers.node_id: 117yalelj2!!ARTICLE: Contracting for Cooperation in Recovery
papers.title: ARTICLE: Contracting for Cooperation in Recovery
papers.abstract:
In 1984, the city of Richmond contracted with McDevitt Street Bovis for the construction of a new baseball stadium. The stadium was built, but a decade later the city discovered deterioration in the concrete tubes supporting the cantilevered roof, caused by McDevitt's breach of its contractual duty to fill the tubes with grout. The city sued, claiming both breach of contract and fraud, the latter based on false certificates of completion and other documents McDevitt had submitted. In Richmond Metropolitan Authority v. McDevitt Street Bovis, Inc., the Virginia Supreme Court held that because the contract required McDevitt to provide the certificates and other documents, misrepresentations in them might give the city a right to damages for breach, but could not give rise to liability in fraud.
McDevitt is a good example of how courts police the border between contract and tort, protecting contract against, among other things, incursion by the punitive damages available in tort. But consider the holding's effect on Virginia contractors' decisions whether to submit accurate certificates of completion. Restricting recovery to the compensatory measures available in contract means that a Virginia builder who has breached its construction duties incurs little or no additional liability when it files a false certificate. The false certificate harms the purchaser first and foremost if it prevents her from discovering and recovering for nonconforming work.To prove that harm - and even that the certificate was false - the purchaser must first show that the work was nonconforming, i.e., that but for the false certificate, she would have recovered for breach. But if the purchaser can show nonconforming work, then she already has a winning claim for breach of the underlying construction duty, which will compensate her for her losses. That is, if the purchaser can show that the false certificate harmed her, it did not. The Virginia Supreme Court's decision to limit recovery for false certificates of completion to the compensatory damages available in contract renders legal liability for breach of the certification requirement irrelevant.
This strange situation is not limited to certificates of completion in the building industry. The above argument, or one like it, applies to any contractterm whose purpose is to make it easier for the promisee to discover and prove breach. Common examples include royalty reports, recordkeeping requirements, certificates of compliance, and auditing rights. Such terms belong to a hitherto underappreciated genus of contract terms: duties to undertake acts that promote the other side's recovery for breach. I will use "obstruction of recovery" or "obstruction" to refer both to promisor actions that aim to avoid legal liability and to the failure to act in ways that would assist in the recovery of damages due where there is a duty to do so. I will use "cooperation in recovery," or simply "cooperation," to designate nonobstruction.Where one side is particularly worried that she might be unable to recover for any breach, the other side might offer to undertake a contractual duty to cooperate in recovery - to agree, for instance, not to hide nonperformance, to keep complete records, or to provide information about performance.
But here's the problem: to recover compensatory damages for the breach of a duty to cooperate, a plaintiff must be able to demonstrate harm. The primary harm of an obstructive breach is that it prevents the promisee from recovering for breach of the underlying, or first-order, duty. Showing that harm requires independent proof of first-order breach - that the plaintiff was entitled to the damages she did not recover. But if the plaintiff can prove first-order breach, she can recover on that basis - which means that the obstructive breach has not harmed her. The upshot is a catch-22: a plaintiff can show obstructive harm only if she has not suffered it.
The way to break out of the circle is to attach extracompensatory remedies - remedies that are not tied to the plaintiff's verifiable losses - to obstructive breach. While the received wisdom is that optimal remedies for breach are always at or near the expectation measure, this cannot be so when it comes to duties to cooperate in recovery.If such contract terms are to make a practical difference, they must be backed by punitive damages, penalties or other remedies neither conditioned on nor limited to compensation for harm done.
At present, courts will not enforce a penalty or punitive damages clause, which brings the analysis back to the potentially positive role of fraud liability. There is a longstanding debate within the courts and legal scholarship about whether parties should be able to contract out of liability for their fraudulent misrepresentations.What has not been noticed is that many agreements are structured to opt into such liability using terms that require one party to represent that it is not in breach (by submitting, for example, a certificate of completion). When false, such representations not only breach the contract, but can satisfy the elements of fraud and support a claim for punitive damages. The contractual duty to share information about performance can be secured by the extracompensatory remedies available in fraud.
The existence of such contract terms suggests that parties want effective duties to cooperate in recovery. And their utility provides additional support for a thesis Ian Ayres and I have developed elsewhere: that the extracompensatory remedies available in tort can have "well-defined functions within the apparatus of the law of contracts."Yet, as exemplified in McDevitt, many courts are uncomfortable with this incursion of extracompensatory remedies into the world of contracts and have found ways to exclude fraud liability for acts that are also breaches. The most recent trend in this direction involves an expansive reading of the economic loss rule to bar liability for fraud in the performance. This Article argues that such rulings are mistaken and that courts should recognize the positive role fraud liability can play in contracts. But the fraud solution is second best. A better solution would be an exception to the rules against penalties and punitive damages when those remedies are attached to contractual duties to cooperate in recovery.
Robert Scott and George Triantis have recently observed that "contracts scholars [have focused] principally on the substantive terms and not on the ability of the parties to regulate the procedural course of their futureenforcement."This is confirmed by the scholarly neglect of duties to cooperate in recovery. Such duties are attempts to regulate contract enforcement. This Article therefore fills in the picture of how parties contract for the case of breach.
The Article's conclusions also bear on an old dispute about Holmes's famous dictum that "the duty to keep a contract at common law means a prediction that you must pay damages if you do not keep it, - and nothing else."This "Holmesian heresy" is sometimes read to mean that, as far as the law is concerned, the promisor does not have a duty to perform, but an option to perform or pay damages.Holmes himself rejected the alternative-promise reading, explaining that "the statement that the effect of a contract is the assumption of the risk of a future event does not mean that there is a second subsidiary promise to assume that risk, but that the assumption follows as a consequence directly enforced by the law, without the promisor's co-operation."This Article examines what happens when the parties do make a "second subsidiary promise" to pay damages - or at least to cooperate in their recovery. Its surprising result is that mandatory rules limiting contract damages to compensatory measures mean that even when there is a second subsidiary promise, legal liability for its breach does not make a practical difference.
Part I of the Article describes why some parties, including promisors who know they might breach, should want to contract for legally enforceable duties not to obstruct recovery, and explains why currently available contract remedies - which are limited to compensation for actual losses - are often insufficient to enforce such duties. The core reason is the catch-22 described above: the promisee who can prove obstructive harm has not suffered it. In some cases, the effects of the catch-22 can be reduced through recovery for other harms of obstructive breach, such as delayed compensation and higher litigation costs, or by liquidating damages. But these alternative grounds of recovery do not sufficiently protect against obstruction in all contexts.
Part II considers three forms that contractually specified extracompensatory remedies for obstructive breach might take: the right to terminate the contract, an adverse inference with respect to first-order breach, and penalties or punitive damages. The right to terminate works only where the promisor attaches significant value to the continued existence of the contract, and where the promisee is not likely already to have the right to terminate based on a showing of first-order breach. Nor is the adverse inference solution effective where the promisee has separate proof of first-order breach. I conclude that only penalties and punitive damages provide generally effective remedies for obstructive breach. The law of most states presently prevents parties from contracting for either.
Part III describes how, with no contractual solution available, duties to cooperate might be secured through the law of torts. The most important judicial step in this direction was California's failed experiment with punitive damages for postbreach obstruction in Seaman's Direct Buying Service v. Standard Oil Co. of California.A more promising approach can be found in parties' attempts to contract for representations of performance backed by fraud liability, though many courts have closed off this path by adopting expansive readings of the economic loss rule or similar doctrines. Finally, theparties can secure limited benefits with representations of intent to cooperate in recovery, again backed by the law of fraud.
Part IV completes the analysis by arguing that not only are extracompensatory remedies necessary for effective no-obstruct duties, but the benefits of cooperative duties are worth the costs of those remedies. Many familiar costs of penalties and punitive damages, such as deterring efficient breach, do not apply when they are attached to obstructive breach. And no-obstruct clauses backed by penalties or punitive damages are often a cheaper alternative than a more familiar solution to underenforcement: damage multipliers.
Before jumping into the analysis, a few words about method. My argument employs a broadly instrumentalist perspective, in that it assumes that among contract law's primary aims is facilitating transactions that would otherwise be prevented by lack of trust.In order to capture practical reasoning in the absence of trust, I employ nontechnical economic analysis of the self-interested calculations of individuals entering into and acting within legally binding agreements. I assume both that each party engages in such cost-benefit analysis to decide whether to enter into and how to perform under the contract, and that each tries to anticipate and influence the cost-benefit analysis of his or her counterpart. In undertaking this analysis, I generally assume that the only curbs on self-interest are legal ones - that is, the prospect of legal liability for bad acts. This is of course a theoretical fiction: extralegal norms, sanctions, and other consequences also enter into the mix. Nor is every decision in a contractual relationship based on such heartless cost-benefit analysis. But if contract law has a function in structuring the ongoing relationship between the parties, it is to substitute where nonlegal mechanisms for coordination, cooperation, or collaboration do not suffice. Ignoring extralegal norms, incentives, and reasons is an analytic device for exploring how legal mechanisms might substitute for them.

questions.question: Do ordinary compensatory contract remedies (expectation damages) adequately deter and compensate breaches of contractual duties to assist the other party's recovery (for example, by providing accurate certificates, records, or reports), or do those remedies create a catch-22 that makes such cooperative duties effectively unenforceable?

Would allowing extracompensatory remedies (such as penalties, punitive damages, termination rights, or evidentiary shifts) for breaches of duties to cooperate in recovery improve compliance and social welfare compared with the current rule limiting contract damages to compensation?

Can tort-based remedies for intentional or fraudulent misrepresentations serve as an effective and appropriate substitute for contractual extracompensatory remedies in enforcing cooperation duties, and what are the trade-offs of relying on tort law rather than contract law?

matched_themes: Should courts allow punitive or other extracompensatory damages for willful or abusive contract breaches, and what are the efficiency and fairness trade-offs?
How should legal doctrine treat contractual waivers (e.g., waivers of fraud claims or other torts)-do courts enforce such waivers or decide cases on alternative grounds?
When should courts permit plaintiffs to pursue tort claims alongside or instead of contract claims to obtain broader remedies, and how does allowing tort claims change damages outcomes?
Should parties and courts adopt fault-based remedial regimes that distinguish among breaches by reason when allocating remedies?
When a breaching party's intentional or grossly negligent misconduct is severe, should courts invalidate agreed contractual limits on liability in commercial contracts?
What counterfactual baseline should courts use to measure plaintiffs' losses for compensation purposes?
How should default liability rules interact with parties' freedom to allocate risks by contract and duties of disclosure to achieve efficient and fair risk allocation?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?
What standards and procedural safeguards should govern awards of punitive and other nonpecuniary damages in contract disputes to balance compensation and protection against abuse?
Should the promisor or the promisee have the default right to choose between performance and payment to achieve allocative efficiency?
How do institutional features-court capacity, procedural devices, and evidentiary rules-affect the substantive development and practical application of contract remedies?
Should parties be presumptively permitted to contractually specify nonstandard damage remedies, or should courts retain authority to impose defaults?
How do transaction costs, enforcement frictions, and institutional realities alter the theoretical efficiency of breach-plus-compensation?

Can party-designed enforcement mechanisms (pre-agreed penalties, arbitration, bonding, reputational systems) reliably produce efficient breach outcomes without judicial intervention, and when do they fail?
When do deceptive statements about present intent to perform give rise to liability in the absence of an enforceable contract?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
Should courts police and limit supracompensatory contractual remedies (penalty-like clauses), or does allowing parties to contract for such terms respect autonomy and promote efficient contracting?
How should remedial and enforcement rules be structured to achieve efficient behavior when populations include both internalizers and externalizers?
How do inequalities in litigation resources, legal representation, and factual records distort judicial factfinding and remedy outcomes in contract disputes?
To what extent does empirical uncertainty about measuring gains and losses limit courts' ability to design remedies that reflect non-welfare ethical preferences without sacrificing efficiency?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
Do parties and courts actually choose heterogeneous, context-tailored damage provisions in contracting, and under what conditions would such customization be voluntarily chosen or socially desirable?
Do limits on recoverable damages (foreseeability, certainty, avoidability) substantially reduce awards below full compensation, and should courts liberalize those limits?
When and under what standards should courts award disgorgement or remedies that strip gains from breaching parties?

Should contractual clauses that impose predetermined monetary payments for breach be treated as punitive (unenforceable) or as enforceable measures of compensation, and what factors predict courts' enforcement decisions?

Do repeat players, contract drafting strategies, secrecy about dispute outcomes, and presentation techniques enable stronger parties to extract one-sided terms and undermine the protective aims of contract law?
To what extent should moral blameworthiness and non-economic considerations influence the design and application of contract remedies?
When is an indirect remedy (one that induces self-compliance) preferable to a direct remedy that delivers the outcome?

papers.abstract: This fable is about promises. It takes place in a principality where, once upon a time, making promises -- and keeping them -was very important. A place where long-settled rules about the process of making sure promises are kept are now disregarded by many parties. A place where it may no longer be clear what those rules are. It is a rather small story within a very large story. The small story cannot be fully understood, however, without knowing the larger story. Therefore, that is where we shall begin.

papers.node_id: 85tullrev413!!ARTICLE: Convergence in Contort: Landlord Liability for Defective Premises in Comparative Perspective
papers.title: ARTICLE: Convergence in Contort: Landlord Liability for Defective Premises in Comparative Perspective
papers.abstract:
Let us imagine a tenant living in a rented apartment. Unbeknownst to the tenant or the landlord, the circuit breaker in the apartment is faulty. While the tenant plays with her small child in the apartment one afternoon, the apartment catches fire. Although the tenant and her child are able to escape the burning apartment, both suffer severe physical injury and emotional distress. According to the residential landlord-tenant law of most American jurisdictions, our landlord has breached a contractual obligation imposed by the lease - the implied warranty of habitability - by failing to maintain the apartment circuitry in a safe condition. And yet, because the harm suffered takes the form of physical injury and emotional distress, this breach appears to fit more squarely within the framework of tort law. The classification of the tenant's cause of action as either contractual or tort-based is essential: the rules governing the personal injury claims of the tenant and her child may be vastly different depending upon whether a court characterizes them as sounding in contract or in tort. Contractual liability likely exposes our landlord to strict liability, whereas liability in tort may be either strict or fault-based. Contractual recovery may not include damages for pain and suffering or emotional distress, whereas these damages would be awarded freely in tort. An exculpation clause may insulate the landlord from contractual, but not tort-based, liability. The statute of limitations may differ widely between the two causes of action. Moreover, a contractual theory of recovery would likely extend only to the tenant due to the rule of contractual privity, whereas a tort theory would extend equally to the tenant and the tenant's child.
In cases such as this one, only a small minority of American jurisdictions have employed a contract theory to hold a landlord liable for personal injuries. The overwhelming majority of American courts have found contract inapplicable to tenants' personal injury lawsuits and instead apply a tort-based negligence analysis. The American majority approach to landlord liability is the result of decades of debate that followed the "revolution" of residential landlord-tenant law - the reconceptualization of the residential lease as a contract andthe adoption of the implied warranty of habitability.Although a contract model was initially chosen to implement this newfound tenant-protection device, contract law strains to contain this state-imposed obligation relating not to economic expectations, but to physical safety and emotional security. American jurisdictions have dealt with the problem of contract law's awkward fit with legally imposed duties by adopting a bifurcated approach to landlord liability. Economic harm is compensated in contract; physical injury is compensated in tort.As a result, depending on the type of harm suffered, a tenant may have two very different claims against the landlord based on the same wrongful act. Now that the dust has settled following the landlord-tenant revolution, the time is ripe for assessing whether this bifurcated approach is optimal, or whether an alternative model would better address the needs of residential tenants, who comprise nearly thirty percent of the American population.
The relatively recent transformation of landlord-tenant law has imported into the common law landlord-tenant relationship a number of obligations that have been recognized in civil law leases for centuries.Thus the common law's embrace of an implied warranty of habitability closed a long-existing gulf between the two legal traditions' approaches to the obligations of residential landlords. In both traditions today, breach of the landlord's obligation to provide a safe and habitable dwelling gives rise to traditional contractual remedies, including termination of the lease and damages.However, the treatment of personal injuries, property damage, and nonpecuniary losses continues to differ across jurisdictional lines. While American tenants who suffer such losses are largely restricted to a tort theory of recovery, civil law tenants have both contractual and tort theories at their disposal.This Article turns to the civilian tradition to determinewhether this concurrent approach to landlord liability better allocates the risk of harm between residential landlords and their tenants.
The increasing convergence among the oft-polarized common law and civil law traditions has been of late a subject of great interest.Comparative scholarship not only provides fodder for legal reform, but also furthers understanding of differences, whether they result from history, social policy, or sheer chance.And yet, comparative examination of residential landlord-tenant law is relatively scarce.The paucity of comparative research in this area likely stems from the fact that regulation of residential leases is inextricably intertwined with housing policy, a matter generally thought of as local in character.Moreover, the fact that landlord-tenant relations, like many consumer protection regimes, are governed by an amalgam of contract, property, administrative, tort, and occasionally, constitutional law, makes them particularly difficult to study even in the domestic context, much less comparatively. Nonetheless, comparative study of tenancy law is critical. Such analysis allows for the pooling of knowledge,and it permits the study of more recent common law reforms against a backdrop of legal systems that have applied similar concepts for many years.To that end, this Article endeavors both to fill a gap in the comparative literature and to provide a critical appraisal, through a comparative lens, of the American approach to habitability in residential lease.
A close examination of the apparently disparate regimes governing the obligations of residential landlords reveals that the action against the landlord who has breached the obligation to maintain the premises, whether classified as contract-or tort-based, is treated similarly in many respects across jurisdictional lines. Where differences between the approaches exist, they stem primarily from the rules governing the distinction between contract and tort. Moreover, regardless of the theory of recovery employed, each system suffers from unique anomalies and injustices. These difficulties are a direct product of the system of classification and the interplay between contract and tort. Comparative observation leads to the conclusion that the landlord's liability for defective premises has been shaped more by the arbitrary dividing line between contract and tort than by reasoned policy making. Thus this Article argues that landlord liability for defective premises is best characterized as "contort," a hybrid obligation whose contours reflect elements of both contract and tort.In so doing, this author seeks to anchor the landlord's obligation to maintain the premises among other contorts, including, for example, legal malpractice, medical malpractice, and products liability.These and other examples illustrate that recasting an obligation as contort emancipates it from the confines of classification and permits lawmakers to choose the attributes that best suit social policy, regardless of taxonomy. Landlord liability for defective premises could benefit from similar liberation.
Part II of this Article traces the development of the American approach to landlord liability for the condition of the premises, from its historical roots through its twentieth-century revolution to its modern application. In so doing, Part II highlights the reasons for the American approach and its resulting anomalies. Part III examines the approaches of several "mixed" jurisdictions whose landlord-tenant law is grounded in the civilian tradition.This analysis demonstrates that each of these jurisdictions has struggled with the nature of a landlord's obligation for the condition of the premises, and explores the difficulties each jurisdiction has encountered at the border between contract and tort. Part IV revisits the timeless struggle to define contract and tort as two distinct types of obligations, and reviews the recognition of "contorts" - obligations that defy classification by their very nature. Part IV concludes that landlord liability for defective premises is best characterized as contort and argues that such recasting is necessary to eliminate the conceptual difficulties and practical injustices that to date have infected the regimes of not only some civilian jurisdictions, but those of the United States.

questions.question: Whether residential landlord liability for defective premises should be treated as a contract claim, a tort claim, or a hybrid obligation (a 'contort') to achieve a fairer and more coherent allocation of risk, remedies, and damages.

Whether a concurrent contract-and-tort approach (as found in some civil-law or mixed jurisdictions) allocates risk and remedies between landlords and tenants more effectively than the predominant common-law bifurcated approach.

Whether the line-drawing decision to classify claims as contract or tort-rather than underlying policy objectives-accounts for the anomalies and injustices in outcomes for tenants injured by defective premises.

matched_themes: When should courts permit plaintiffs to pursue tort claims alongside or instead of contract claims to obtain broader remedies, and how does allowing tort claims change damages outcomes?
Should parties and courts adopt fault-based remedial regimes that distinguish among breaches by reason when allocating remedies?
How have historical, geographic, institutional, and transnational influences shaped the evolution and transplantation of contract doctrines and remedies?
How should default liability rules interact with parties' freedom to allocate risks by contract and duties of disclosure to achieve efficient and fair risk allocation?
Should plaintiffs be permitted to recover non-pecuniary harms such as mental distress in breach-of-contract cases?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
Should residential landlord liability for defective premises be treated as contract, tort, or a hybrid obligation to allocate risk, remedies, and damages more coherently?
To what extent should moral blameworthiness and non-economic considerations influence the design and application of contract remedies?

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:The Shadow Code

shared_topics.topic: coherence and unification of contract remedies/damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes a single surplus-based rule to unify the fragmented damages formulas in the U.C.C. and the Restatement, while Paper B criticizes the bifurcated treatment of landlord harms and explores whether a more coherent allocation of remedies (contractual, tort, or hybrid) would better serve residential tenants.

shared_topics.topic: the effects of doctrinal classification on available remedies (contract vs tort)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how Restatement and U.C.C. distinctions (e.g., expectation vs reliance) affect what losses are recoverable, and Paper B centrally examines how classifying landlord duties as contract or tort dramatically changes liability, recoverable damages, and who may sue.

shared_topics.topic: compensatory goals, risk allocation, and incentives created by remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds damages in a welfare/compensatory surplus framework and emphasizes how remedies shape incentives to perform and mitigate losses, while Paper B evaluates how different liability regimes allocate risk between landlords and tenants and affect policy goals like safety, deterrence, and tenant protection.

shared_topics.topic: need for clearer doctrinal terminology and conceptual clarity
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for replacing ambiguous terms (profit, incidental/consequential) with a surplus-based vocabulary and clearer cost categories, and Paper B highlights conceptual confusion at the contract/tort border and proposes the 'contort' concept to remove classificatory anomalies.

shared_topics.topic: critique of existing doctrinal frameworks and proposals for principled reform (including comparative interpretation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques how U.C.C. and Restatement rules obscure underlying goals and offers a principled reinterpretation that preserves outcomes while clarifying method, and Paper B uses comparative (civilian vs common law) analysis to critique American approaches and to propose reconceptualizing landlord liability to better align doctrine with policy.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 80valrev1225!!ARTICLE: THE FAULT LINES IN CONTRACT DAMAGES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE FAULT LINES IN CONTRACT DAMAGES

shared_topics.topic: how classification between contract and tort determines available remedies and liability rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally analyzes how courts' choice to treat landlord obligations as contract versus tort alters liability regimes (strict vs fault, privity, statutes of limitation) for defective premises; Paper B similarly shows that doctrinal classification of breaches influences which damage measure courts apply and thus the legal consequences of breach.

shared_topics.topic: strict‑liability versus fault‑based approach to damages and liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that contract-based landlord liability tends toward strict liability while tort may be fault‑based, raising substantive differences in recovery; Paper B explicitly rejects a universal strict‑liability model for contract damages and develops a fault‑based economic theory to explain and justify variation in damage measures.

shared_topics.topic: using damages and remedial rules to allocate risk and create incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the choice between contract and tort (or a hybrid 'contort') affects how risk of harm is allocated between landlords and tenants and can be chosen to serve policy goals; Paper B frames damage rules as incentive‑creating devices and explains how different measures (expectation, reliance, restitution, market damages) are used to produce desirable contracting behavior.

shared_topics.topic: normative critique of existing doctrines and proposals for doctrinal reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the bifurcated American approach and proposes reconceptualizing landlord obligations as a hybrid 'contort' to better align law and policy; Paper B critiques the dominant strict‑liability/efficient‑breach account and proposes a fault‑sensitive economic theory to better explain and guide courts' use of damage measures.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal choice affects the scope and type of recoverable losses (economic vs nonpecuniary)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that classification as contract or tort determines whether plaintiffs can recover nonpecuniary harms (pain and suffering, emotional distress) and who may recover; Paper B analyzes why courts select different compensatory interests (expectation, reliance, restitution) and how those choices produce varying coverage of economic versus other losses.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 63vandlrev1003!!ARTICLE: Breach Is For Suckers
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Breach Is For Suckers

shared_topics.topic: mismatch between legal classification (contract vs tort) and social expectations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how classifying landlord obligations as either contract or tort produces doctrinal anomalies and fails to capture the social policies behind habitability protections, while Paper B shows that orthodox contract doctrine (treating breach as merely a monetary prediction) conflicts with lay moral intuitions about breach, arguing doctrinal categories misdescribe the harms at issue.

shared_topics.topic: adequacy of remedies — whether damages capture the full wrong and the role of specific performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts contractual remedies (which may exclude pain and suffering) with tort remedies and shows how classification determines the available relief for tenants, and Paper B critiques expectation damages as normatively inadequate compared with specific performance and other responses that would reflect moral culpability for breach.

shared_topics.topic: role of fault, strict liability, and moral blame in assigning legal responsibility
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how contract-based strict liability and tort-based fault doctrines produce different consequences for landlord liability, and Paper B investigates how perceptions of willfulness and culpability (e.g., willful vs efficient breach) drive moral outrage and should inform how the law treats breaches.

shared_topics.topic: compensating non-economic harms (emotional distress, moral injury, 'being suckered') arising from failures of performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on tenants' physical injuries and emotional distress that fall awkwardly between contract and tort remedies, while Paper B documents psychological harms—regret, embarrassment, feeling 'suckered'—that ordinary breach damages do not address, arguing the law should account for these non-pecuniary losses.

shared_topics.topic: using comparative or empirical analysis to challenge doctrine and propose reforms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses comparative (civilian vs common law) analysis to argue for reconceptualizing landlord obligations as a hybrid 'contort,' and Paper B uses original psychological experiments and existing empirical literature to argue doctrinal reforms that better align contract law with social-psychological realities.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DISGORGING EMOLUMENTS

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal classification (contract vs tort vs constitutional/statutory) shapes available remedies and liability rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how labeling landlord obligations as contract or tort determines applicable remedies (strict liability, damages types, privity, statutes of limitation) and creates anomalies, while Paper B examines how the characterization of emoluments violations (constitutional/statutory) leaves a remedial gap and affects what relief plaintiffs can obtain.

shared_topics.topic: the choice and design of remedies to achieve policy goals (including restitutionary relief)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates which remedies (contractual termination/damages versus tort recovery for pain and suffering) best allocate risk and protect tenants and argues for a hybrid approach to select suitable attributes, and Paper B argues that restitutionary disgorgement is the proper remedial design to deter officials, prevent unjust enrichment, and fill constitutional remedial gaps.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of existing legal regimes and advocacy for doctrinal or institutional reform/alternative frameworks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes recasting landlord liability as a 'contort'—a hybrid doctrinal framework freeing obligations from rigid classification—and Paper B proposes statutory and common-law paths to operationalize disgorgement, both advocating doctrinal reform to better serve underlying substantive aims.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk, responsibility, and prevention of unjust enrichment or harmful conduct
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is concerned with who should bear the cost when premises defects cause economic loss or personal injury (landlord vs tenant) and the role of liability doctrines in preventing under- or over-inclusive risk allocation, while Paper B focuses on preventing public officials from being unjustly enriched by emoluments and ensuring accountability through remedies that reallocate gains back to the public.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A UNIFYING THEORY OF CONTRACT DAMAGE RULES

shared_topics.topic: the significance of the contract-versus-tort classification for liability and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on how labeling landlord obligations as contract or tort reshapes available remedies (strict liability, emotional-distress damages, privity limits, statutes of limitation), while Paper B addresses how contract-status determines which damage formulas and principles apply and urges a single rule to govern breaches currently parsed by different doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: principles and measurement of damages for breaches of duty/obligation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how contractual treatment of habitability claims produces different damage outcomes than tort law (e.g., exclusion of pain-and-suffering), and Paper B develops a surplus-based computational principle (the Shadow Code) to unify how damages are calculated across contract breaches.

shared_topics.topic: diagnosis of fragmentation and the call for systemic reform/unification

shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores alternative allocations of contractual entitlements and associated remedies to demonstrate multiple doctrinal configurations can yield efficiency, while Paper B examines the contract/tort divide for defective premises claims and proposes treating such obligations as a hybrid 'contort' to escape the constraints imposed by strict classification.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that efficiency does not mandate a single entitlement/remedy structure and that competing allocations can be normatively acceptable, suggesting scope for doctrinal redesign; Paper B uses comparative (common law vs civil law) analysis to recommend recasting landlord obligations (and other 'contorts') so lawmakers can choose attributes that better achieve social policy objectives.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Fixer Upper: Buyer Deposits in Residential Real Estate Transactions

shared_topics.justification: Both critique how existing legal classifications produce unjust outcomes in housing: Paper A shows how the contract/tort divide misallocates remedies for tenant injuries, and Paper B demonstrates that liquidated-damages treatment of deposits often bears no relation to sellers' actual losses or contracting realities.

shared_topics.topic: use of contract doctrines to allocate risk in residential relationships
shared_topics.justification: Each paper analyzes how contractual rules assign financial risk in home-related transactions: Paper A examines how the implied warranty of habitability and privity principles shape which parties can recover and what losses are compensated, while Paper B scrutinizes deposit and liquidated-damages clauses as mechanisms that shift breach risk (and often large sums) onto buyers.

shared_topics.justification: Both authors question deferring to private ordering in the residential context and advocate corrective action: Paper A calls for reconceptualizing landlord obligations (a 'contort') to free policy choices from rigid taxonomy, and Paper B urges statutory regulation of deposits to curb the harsh effects of unfettered contract terms.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Disproportionality and the Law of Consequential Damages: Default Theory and Cognitive Reality

shared_topics.topic: reconceptualizing doctrine to better align law with policy and cognitive realities
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes recasting landlord liability as a hybrid 'contort' to free the obligation from rigid contract/tort taxonomy and better achieve policy goals; Paper B argues that traditional default‑rule (rational actor) analysis misjustifies disproportionality and proposes adjusting remedial default rules to account for cognitive biases in risk perception.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: WHEN IS A WILLFUL BREACH "WILLFUL"? THE LINK BETWEEN DEFINITIONS AND DAMAGES

shared_topics.topic: the role of culpability and mental state in setting liability standards

shared_topics.topic: problems caused by vague doctrinal labels and the need for doctrinal reform or reconceptualization
shared_topics.justification: Paper A diagnoses conceptual anomalies and injustices created by the shaky contract/tort dividing line and proposes recasting certain obligations as a hybrid 'contort' to better align rules with policy; Paper B criticizes the unexamined use of vague adverbial culpability labels (like 'willful') and calls for clearer definitions tied to damages and fact-finding implications.

shared_topics.topic: attention to courts' institutional and evidentiary burdens when applying enhanced liability rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how court-made classifications produce practical anomalies (different statutes of limitation, privity rules, evidentiary consequences) and thus implicate administrative and policy trade-offs; Paper B emphasizes that any choice about the definition of 'willful' and associated damages must account for the fact‑finding demands those choices impose on courts.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: What the Efficient Performance Hypothesis Means for Contracts Scholarship

shared_topics.topic: designing contract remedies to reconcile efficiency with ethical or policy goals
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that alternative remedies (e.g., a promisee-disgorgement/option) can achieve the same incentive efficiency as expectation damages while better respecting non‑welfarist ethical rights, and Paper B argues that recasting landlord obligations as a hybrid allows lawmakers to pick remedial attributes that better serve tenant‑protection policy rather than being constrained by doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and incentives between parties via remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how allocating the 'option' (promisor vs promisee) and which party receives gains or losses changes incentives to perform or breach, while Paper B shows that classifying landlord claims as contract or tort (and attendant rules like strict liability, damages for pain and privity) materially shifts which party bears the risk of defective premises.

shared_topics.topic: use of empirical and comparative evidence (and uncertainty) to choose or justify remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that empirical uncertainty about how to measure gains and losses determines whether one remedial rule is truly superior, and Paper B uses comparative (civilian vs common law) evidence to evaluate which remedial approaches better allocate harms and to reveal anomalies produced by doctrinal choices.

shared_topics.topic: advocating novel or hybrid remedial frameworks beyond established doctrinal categories
shared_topics.justification: Paper A spotlights previously overlooked promisee‑option/disgorgement remedies as legitimate alternatives to traditional remedies, and Paper B advances the 'contort' (contract‑tort hybrid) category to free obligations from rigid classification so policymakers can craft remedial attributes that better meet social aims.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Boundaries of Extracompensatory Relief for Abusive Breach of Contract

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal boundary between contract and tort and its remedial consequences
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how classifying an obligation as contract or tort changes available remedies and liability: Paper A examines limits on awarding extracompensatory (punitive) relief within contract doctrine and the consequences of stretching contract remedies, while Paper B treats the contract/tort distinction as central to landlord liability for personal injury and shows how classification decisively alters damages, privity, and statutes of limitation.

shared_topics.topic: whether specific categories of transactions can or should be treated differently from general contract doctrine (severability of subcategories)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues extracompensatory remedies are viable only when limited to conceptually severable subcategories (e.g., insurance) so risk won't ‘leak’ into the general contracting pool; Paper B similarly treats landlord–tenant relations as a distinct category (a potential ‘contort’) deserving tailored rules separate from ordinary contract law to better allocate risk and remedy harms.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between predictability of contracting costs and the need to respond to abusive or non‑economic harms
shared_topics.justification: Both articles engage the tradeoff between the contract law goal of predictable, administrable rules that encourage exchange and the countervailing desire to address abusive breaches or physical/nonpecuniary harms — Paper A frames this as a justification-limitation for extracompensatory damages, while Paper B shows how the implied warranty of habitability and ensuing harms expose strains in a predictability-focused contract model.

shared_topics.topic: appropriate institutional paths for doctrinal change (legislation, common law, and comparative borrowing)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that the viability of moderate-severability reforms depends on the process of implementation and grants important advantages to legislative solutions over ad hoc common-law innovations; Paper B likewise looks to comparative (civil vs common law) experience and legislative choices as sources for reforming landlord liability and for freeing obligations from rigid classification.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal classification or model choice affects available remedies and legal consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that classifying a landlord's obligation as contract or tort changes remedies (availability of pain and suffering, strict liability, privity defenses, statutes of limitation, exculpation clauses), whereas Paper B interrogates remedial structures (discretionary remedialism versus specified remedies) and measures how different legal models produce different remedial and outcome patterns.

shared_topics.topic: trade‑off between predictability/determinacy (detailed rules) and flexibility/individualized justice (broad principles or discretionary remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B centers on the jurisprudential debate over whether broad principles or detailed rules yield more predictable and fair outcomes and empirically tests that question across models; Paper A similarly critiques rigid doctrinal classification (contract vs tort) for producing arbitrary or unjust results and advocates a flexible reconceptualization (contort) to better achieve policy goals.

shared_topics.topic: the boundary between contract and tort and its consequences for remedies and liability
shared_topics.justification: Both articles focus on how classification (contract vs. tort) shapes available remedies, liability rules (strict vs. fault), privity, limitation periods, and the scope of recovery—Paper A examines how contract doctrine (and its commercial assumptions) blocks intangible recovery, and Paper B centers on how landlord liability is split or transformed by treating the same harms as contractual or tortious.

shared_topics.topic: critical appraisal of doctrinal limitations and proposals for reform
shared_topics.justification: Each paper argues that existing doctrines produce anomalies and injustice and proposes doctrinal change—Paper A urges abandoning the rigid general rule against intangible losses in favor of promise‑based analysis, while Paper B argues for reconceptualizing landlord obligations as a hybrid 'contort' to escape rigid classification and better allocate risk.

shared_topics.topic: comparative and cross‑jurisdictional analysis to inform domestic reform
shared_topics.justification: Both works deploy comparative jurisprudence (Paper A compares U.S., Canadian and U.K. authorities; Paper B contrasts common law and civil law regimes and mixed jurisdictions) to show differing treatments of non‑pecuniary harms and to draw lessons for improving domestic contract/landlord liability law.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Critique of the Efficient Performance Hypothesis

shared_topics.topic: normative tension between economic efficiency and moral or justice-based concerns in remedy design

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Your Loss or My Gain? The Dilemma of the Disgorgement Principle in Breach of Contract.

shared_topics.topic: the shaping effect of remedial doctrines on substantive duties and policy choices
shared_topics.justification: Both argue that remedial rules (expectation damages, restitution/disgorgement, tort damages, strict liability) influence the substance and enforcement of obligations—Paper A contends that the contract/tort divide has produced anomalies in landlord duties and advocates recasting obligations to allow policy-driven remedies, while Paper B assesses when disgorgement should be used to prevent undercompensation or unjust enrichment and when it is inappropriate.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: LET US NEVER BLAME A CONTRACT BREAKER

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal boundary between contract and tort and its consequences

shared_topics.topic: how default liability rules allocate risk and the economic efficiency of those allocations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that classification-driven rules have allocated risk between landlords and tenants in ways that may be arbitrary and proposes a hybrid approach to better serve social policy, whereas Paper B analyzes contract defaults (strict liability for breach, insurance role, mitigation, efficient breach) as economically efficient risk‑allocation mechanisms.

shared_topics.topic: the remedial regime (available remedies and limits) and its practical effects on who recovers and what harms are compensated
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how remedy differences—strict contractual recovery versus tort damages, privity limits, emotional distress awards, exculpation clauses, and statutes of limitations—alter victims' relief, while Paper B analyzes the consequences of awarding damages versus specific performance, restitution, punitive damages, and how those remedies affect incentives, bargaining costs, and third‑party consequences.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: IN (PARTIAL) DEFENSE OF STRICT LIABILITY IN CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: choice of liability regime (strict liability vs fault) and its normative effects

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal classification affects available remedies and parties' rights

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Moral Judgment and Moral Heuristics in Breach of Contract

shared_topics.topic: how classification as contract versus tort shapes liability, available remedies, and who may recover
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on how courts’ choice to treat defective‑premises claims as contract or tort determines strictness of liability, damages (e.g., emotional distress), statutes of limitation, and privity rules; Paper B interrogates the legal indifference to moral distinctions (intentional vs negligent breach) and demonstrates that people would treat breaches more like tortious intentional harms when assigning blame and higher awards.

shared_topics.topic: the role of intent, motive, and fault in assigning culpability and damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts strict contractual liability under the implied warranty with fault‑based tort standards and discusses how that affects exculpation and recovery; Paper B experimentally shows that subjects punish breaches more when motivated by greed or willfulness than when motivated by avoidance of loss, favoring higher (even punitive) awards for intentional breaches.

shared_topics.topic: policy tradeoffs between doctrinal consistency, risk allocation, and moral intuitions (efficiency versus fairness)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates whether the bifurcated contract/tort approach optimally allocates risk between landlords and tenants and proposes a hybrid 'contort' to better serve policy goals; Paper B highlights the tension between the efficiency rationale for limited contract damages (e.g., efficient breach) and lay moral intuitions that favor fairness and punishment, with implications for legal rule design.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT REMEDIES AND OPTIONS PRICING

shared_topics.topic: comparison of monetary damages versus non-monetary relief and their doctrinal consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts contractual remedies (lease termination, contractual damages) with tort remedies (compensation for pain and suffering, strict vs fault liability) in defective-premises cases, and Paper B analyzes money damages relative to specific performance, exploring how each remedy produces different incentives and outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the role of policy, efficiency, and transaction-cost considerations in shaping doctrinal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper B explicitly uses a transaction-cost and option framework to explain why courts favor damages or specific performance in different circumstances; Paper A evaluates how historical policy choices and doctrinal classification (contract vs tort) — rather than always principled policy design — have produced the modern allocation of landlord liability and argues for reform grounded in social-policy reasoning.

shared_topics.topic: who can enforce rights and recover under different doctrinal labels and how that affects outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes effects of privity and doctrinal classification on who (tenant versus tenant's child) can recover and what types of losses are compensable, while Paper B examines how the availability of a damages remedy changes parties' bargaining positions and contract pricing, implicating which parties effectively benefit or bear costs under different remedial regimes.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A COMPARATIVE FAULT DEFENSE IN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: allocation of losses and apportionment of fault between parties in non-performance or harm
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advocates a comparative-fault defense in contract to apportion damages when promisees contribute to their losses (through noncooperation or overreliance), and Paper B examines how contract-versus-tort classification affects who bears risk for defective premises and how injuries and damages are allocated between landlords and tenants.

shared_topics.topic: incentives to prevent harm or mitigate losses (efficient cooperation and avoidance of overreliance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds its argument for comparative fault in the need to incentivize promisees to cooperate and avoid inefficient reliance, and Paper B considers how different regimes (contractual warranty, tort duties, or contort framing) shape landlords' and tenants' incentives to maintain safety and prevent injuries.

shared_topics.topic: comparative/cross-jurisdictional analysis to inform domestic reform

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Liquidated Damages for Delay in Completion of Commercial Construction Projects: Are They Recoverable by the Owner When the Owner Contributes to the Delay?

shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on enforcement and drafting of liquidated damages provisions to fix compensation for delay and who bears the risk when performance is late; Paper B examines exculpation clauses, the implied warranty of habitability, and whether contractual limitations can shield landlords from claims or are displaced by tort law, thereby assessing contractual limits on liability.

shared_topics.topic: jurisdictional and doctrinal variation producing uncertainty in outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys conflicting California appellate decisions and other jurisdictions regarding recoverability and apportionment of liquidated damages; Paper B offers a comparative (common law vs civil law/mixed jurisdictions) account of how different systems treat landlord liability and shows how doctrinal differences yield divergent results.

shared_topics.topic: reform or drafting strategies to resolve doctrinal anomalies and better allocate risk
shared_topics.justification: Paper A concludes with practical drafting suggestions for owners and contractors to reduce uncertainty over liquidated damages; Paper B advocates conceptual and doctrinal reform (recasting obligations as 'contort') to free lawmakers from rigid contract/tort classifications and to better distribute risk and remedies in landlord‑tenant relationships.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 129yalelj1148!!ARTICLE: Reflective Remedies
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Reflective Remedies

shared_topics.topic: how uncertain legal standards and doctrinal boundaries affect predictability of obligations and liabilities
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that balancing tests and vague standards produce uncertainty about permissible conduct and enforcement, motivating remedial design; Paper B shows that the blurred line between contract and tort (and divergent jurisdictional precedents) creates unpredictable outcomes for tenants and landlords and produces doctrinal anomalies.

shared_topics.topic: judicial or regulatory modification of contractual remedies/terms as a corrective tool
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly contemplates courts 'reflecting' contractual terms (e.g., shortening a noncompete) or imposing reflective damages to correct overreach; Paper B examines how courts and systems alter the effects of leases (termination, implied warranties, overlap with tort) and ultimately advocates recasting obligations (a 'contort') to permit selecting remedial attributes independently of taxonomy.

shared_topics.topic: normative reform through comparative and functional analysis of remedies and doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A offers a policy proposal for remedy design (reflective penalties) grounded in incentive analysis to address shortcomings of uncertain rules, while Paper B uses comparative (common law vs civil law) and functional analysis to argue normative reform—recharacterizing landlord liability as a hybrid obligation to better achieve policy goals.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 41ambuslj503!!ARTICLE: Formal and Operative Rules in Overliquidation Per Se Cases
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Formal and Operative Rules in Overliquidation Per Se Cases

papers.node_id: 107michlrev1551!!ARTICLE: COULD BREACH OF CONTRACT BE IMMORAL?
papers.title: ARTICLE: COULD BREACH OF CONTRACT BE IMMORAL?
papers.abstract:
In a recent article,I argued that we should reconsider an oft-cited rationale for the contract law's strong traditional bar on punitive damages for intentional, gratuitous breach of contract. Further, this reconsideration should, perhaps, lead us to reevaluate the merits of maintaining the strong traditional bar. Morality, I claimed, correctly regards some breaches of promise as morally wrong and as warranting not only compensation but the administration of morality's punitive remedies, including blame, criticism, recrimination, and avoidance.The contract law invokes promise as the fundamental componentof a contractbut, puzzlingly, does not subject gratuitous breaches of contract (and hence breaches of promise) to the distinctive punitive measures endorsed and administered by law, save when those breaches are also torts.
If the law's rationale for the bar on punitive damages is that the prospect of punitive damages might discourage efficient breach of contract - I label this the efficient-breach rationale - then the divergence between morality's response to breach and the law's response to breach is problematic in ways that morally decent citizens cannot accept. The efficient-breach rationale forwards a justification for a legal doctrine that consists in the claim that barring punitive damages would encourage and facilitate certain breaching behavior. But this behavior is condemned by morality. To the extent the law adopts and embodies this rationale, it thereby embraces and tries to encourage and facilitate immoral behavior. Although the law need not enforce morality as such, it is problematic when the law, either directly, or by way of the justifications underlying the law, embraces and encourages immoral action. Citizens, who in a democratic polity must be thought of as partial authors of the law, cannot, in all consistency, accept such laws and their justifications while simultaneously acting and reasoning as moral agents.The law ought not to be structured or justified in ways that place citizens in such an untenable position: it must accommodate the needs of moral agency even if it need not or should not enforce morality directly.
My argument against the efficient-breach rationale presupposes that there are occasions on which breach of contract is immoral because the contractual breach is a relevant instance of an immoral form of breach of promise. This presupposition has most recently been criticized, at least with respect to incomplete contracts, by Steven Shavell.Shavell argues that breach of contract is not immoral under certain conditions. His strategy is to argue that when breach of contract occurs - at least with respect to an incomplete contract and in an appropriate legal context - the very occurrence of the contractual breach paradoxically demonstrates that there is no breachof promise - much less an immoral breach of promise.The contracts that Shavell imagines are incomplete in the respect that they do not explicitly address the conduct at issue; there is a contractual breach not because explicit language has been defied but because the background, gap-filling law supplies a missing term that is not fulfilled. Because the promise contained in the contract did not explicitly address the conduct, to assess whether contractual breaches of this sort also represent promissory breaches, we must interpret the underlying promise.
Briefly put, Shavell's argument is that because the parties had not made specific, explicit promissory arrangements to address the contractual-breaching conduct (for the contract is incomplete in this respect), the appropriate way to interpret the underlying promise is to ask what the parties would have agreed to had they considered the matter.In the relevant circumstances, he argues, the contractual breach itself reveals that the parties would have agreed to permit the breaching behavior had they considered the matter. Therefore, the underlying promise does not forbid the conduct in question and the contractual breach is not immoral, at least not because it is any sort of promissory breach.
Shavell's argument holds special interest in some part because it does not, at least on its surface, flow from a direct consequentialist analysis of the social welfare value of permitting or facilitating breach in relevant contexts. Rather, Shavell seems to be arguing that breach may be morally innocuous even if we assign moral pride of place to the significance of agreement as such.In relevant legal contexts, Shavell concludes, the values associated with promissory fidelity are not impugned by contractual breach.
In this Article, I begin by answering Shavell. I then use the issues that arise from this dispute as a springboard to examine the significance of performance as such to the morality of promising more generally. In Part I, I describe Shavell's position, explore some questions of interpretation of his position, and then register some direct criticisms of the strongestinterpretation of his view. In Part II, I proceed to the larger underlying issue: what, if anything, is morally special about performance?
My conclusion is neither that all deliberate breaches of promise are immoral, nor that all immoral breaches of promise should be punished by contract law.In this short Article, I mean only to defuse one source of resistance to the claim that some deliberate breaches of contract are immoral and to motivate one moral source of some promisees' claims to performance as such. A key theme in my argument is that it is a mistake to regard the available remedy for breach of contract as fully exhausting the content of the duty that one assumes when one promises (or when one contracts).
. Shavell's Argument that Breach of Contract Cannot Be Immoral
Shavell contends that where expectation damages are readily available,breach of contract is not immoral. Instead, breach reflects the behavior that the parties would have agreed to had they directly faced the circumstances that gave rise to the breach.It seems as though Shavell believes there is no real breach of promise in these circumstances. The promise and the contract it gave rise to were both silent about what to do in such cases, he supposes. And had the parties filled in the gap, the term they would have supplied would not require performance.
According to Shavell, a failure to perform is immoral only if it contravenes what the parties did agree to or would have agreed to had they explicitly contracted about the circumstances that gave rise to the breach.At least with respect to cases involving the actions of rational agents, Shavell thinks, the circumstances that give rise to breach are ones that the parties would have agreed excused nonperformance had they explicitly faced the question.Nonperformance in these situations, therefore, is not immoral.
If a contract explicitly provides for performance in the event of a particular contingency, then Shavell would allow that there is a moral duty to perform should that contingency occur.If it explicitly excuses performance in that contingency, then Shavell would say there is no moral duty to perform.If the contingency is not explicitly addressed, then in Shavell's view, "the moral duty of a party … is determined by what the contract would have said had it provided explicitly for the contingency."In his illustrative example, A contracts to shovel B's snow for a fee, say $ 150. If A's snow-shovel is stolen but the contract did not address A's duty in the case of theft, then A has a moral duty to locate a replacement and to shovel only if A and B would have explicitly specified that A must perform in cases of the theft of A's standard equipment.
Where the background law would award payment of expectation damages to B for A's failure to perform in this contingency, Shavell argues that if A and B did not explicitly require performance and A breaches, then the parties would not have specified that A must perform.For, according to Shavell, if A breaches, then A's cost of performance must exceed the cost of expectation damages.Suppose that the expected value to B was $ 200. If the cost of renting equipment in a snowstorm would be $ 500, then A may be expected to breach. Further, A, rationally, would not have agreed to perform in such a contingency, for it would be cheaper for A to pay expectation damages than to perform. Presumably, since the value to B is only $ 200, B would not have offered to pay more for A's shoveling to cover the cost of the rental. Had they addressed the contingency, they would have agreed to excuse A from performance where A's equipment fails. Therefore, A's failure to perform is not immoral.
Shavell's argument is unconvincing. It is unclear, for instance, why he assumes only certain aspects of the background law will infuse parties' hypothetical agreements and mutual understandings, but not others. A more consistent position on the background law might well yield a different result. Further, Shavell's hypothetical agreements fail to account for some of the probable effects of negotiating contingencies on the contract as a whole. I detail these and other problems with Shavell's position below.

questions.question: Is a deliberate breach of contract (or promise) morally wrong even when monetary expectation damages are available, particularly in cases where the contract is incomplete and the breach responds to a contingency not explicitly addressed?

Do legal rules or justifications that limit punitive responses to breach (thereby permitting or facilitating breach) wrongly endorse or encourage immoral behavior and place citizens in conflict with their duties as moral agents?
Is performance itself morally special such that promisees have a moral claim to specific performance beyond what is satisfied by monetary compensation?

matched_themes: Should courts allow punitive or other extracompensatory damages for willful or abusive contract breaches, and what are the efficiency and fairness trade-offs?
Should parties and courts adopt fault-based remedial regimes that distinguish among breaches by reason when allocating remedies?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?
Should the promisor or the promisee have the default right to choose between performance and payment to achieve allocative efficiency?
Should the availability of legal remedies or contractual incompleteness change the moral assessment of a party who breaches under unanticipated circumstances?

Should remedies and contract law be structured to preserve conditions necessary for moral agency and promissory responsibility, rather than treating promises solely as instruments of economic cooperation?

When and under what standards should courts award disgorgement or remedies that strip gains from breaching parties?
To what extent should moral blameworthiness and non-economic considerations influence the design and application of contract remedies?

papers.abstract: The Luten Bridge case,so thoroughly plumbed by the author, raised salient issues of past political affiliation, concern for the economic development of North Carolina and the South, and good government at state and national levels for Judge John J. Parker. Which values would prove decisive in this case involving construction of a controversial bridge, bereft of a connecting road?Parker's values encompassed links to all three. He was politically linked, albeit indirectly, to Rockingham County.In his pre-judicial political career, and as a judge nurturing a pro-South constitutional jurisprudence, Parker articulated an industrial development policy for the state and for the region.Simultaneously, however, he promoted good government in the progressive tradition, embodying the virtues of democracy, responsibility, accountability, efficiency, and conservation of resources.Parker must have found highly perplexingthe appearance on his court's docket of a case involving a member of the business-oriented North Carolina Republican Party, Benjamin Franklin Mebane, Jr.(the leading advocate of the Luten Bridge), an economic development strategy gone awry, and a dysfunctional county government.
