papers.node_id: 42ambuslj97!!ARTICLE: Cry Me a River: Recovery of Mental Distress Damages in a Breach of Contract Action--A North American Perspective
papers.title: ARTICLE: Cry Me a River: Recovery of Mental Distress Damages in a Breach of Contract Action--A North American Perspective
papers.abstract:
Both American and Canadian courts have manifested a historic, but nonetheless problematical, reluctance to award mental distress damages in contract. Both jurisdictions share an identical rule: general damages for mental distress are not ordinarily recoverable in a breach of contract action.The rationales for such a long-standing rule are multiple and, attimes, inconsistent. For instance, some judges contend that mental distress damages cannot be awarded in contract because they are not foreseeable according to the test in the landmark case ofHadley v. Baxendale.Other courts refuse to award such damages because virtually any breach of contract brings with it disappointment and upset and thus virtuallyeveryaction for breach of contract would have a mental distress recovery component. On this basis, courts regularly identify fear of opening the floodgates as a justification for the general rule against recovery.
Courts also cite the role and nature of contract law as a reason for denying mental distress damages. In short, judges are significantly concerned that if mental distress damages were recoverable, then contract law would lose some of its tough-minded, commercial focus. For instance, the Supreme Court of North Carolina justified the rule against recovery on the basis that contracts generally concern business or professional interests where the "[p]ecuniary interest is dominant."Canadian and Englishjudges have expressed similar sentiments.Indeed, Lord Cooke of Thorndon of the House of Lords recently articulated this conclusion in the following way: "[c]ontract-breaking is treated as an incident of commercial life which players in the game are expected to meet with mental fortitude."
In fashioning the general rule, courts appear to favor the attitudes and expectations of the "reasonable businessman" who either presumably would not experience distress in face of breach, or if he did, would not regard this as a risk borne by the other side. This perspective creates the implicit background for the following statement by the Supreme Court of Idaho:Life in the competitive world has at least equal capacity to bestow ruin as benefit, and it is presumed that those who enter this world do so willingly, accepting the risk of encountering the former as part of the cost of achieving the latter. Absent clear evidence to the contrary we will not presume that theparties to a contract such as the one before us meant to insure each other's emotional tranquility.
Life in the competitive world has at least equal capacity to bestow ruin as benefit, and it is presumed that those who enter this world do so willingly, accepting the risk of encountering the former as part of the cost of achieving the latter. Absent clear evidence to the contrary we will not presume that theparties to a contract such as the one before us meant to insure each other's emotional tranquility.
Despite reluctance to award recovery for mental distress damages in contract cases, courts in Canada and the United States provide such awards under two circumstances. The first such circumstance goes to themannerof breach. As discussed in Part IV, when the defendant acts outrageously or reprehensibly at thetimeof breach, damages for mental distress are recoverable. Such an award reflects the court's recognition that the defendant has not merely breached the contract; he or she has done so in amannerthat requires additional recompense or punishment. The second circumstance permitting recovery for mental distress goes to thefactof breach. The general rule against recovery for the fact of breach would not ordinarily warrant mental distress damages, but a burgeoning set of exceptions has now emerged. As discussed in Part V, there are two main approaches to this matter within American and Canadian jurisprudence. First, some courts have determined that mental distress damages are recoverable if the contract at bar fits within a special category.Other courts, in more direct defiance of the general rule, are prepared to assess the matter on the basis of foreseeability alone.If mental distress damages are a reasonably foreseeable consequence of breach, they are recoverable. As this article will show, the judicial approach to exceptions is unstable, leading to needless complexity in the law.
This article challenges the general rule against recovery for mental distress damages, arguing that the current patchwork of exceptions is unworkable.That is, while the general rule presupposes that contracts are not intended to ensure the plaintiff's "emotional tranquility,"it wouldappear that the informing rule is not sufficiently robust to be useful. Put another way, if the general rule were genuinely descriptive of most contracts, then there would not be so many exceptions. The better alternative is to treat all contracts on an equal footing instead of relegating "nontraditional" contracts to an inferior legal position. In this way, recovery for mental distress damages would follow ordinary principles of contract law instead of being relegated to an exception-based approach.
The process of developing a better alternative to the status quo has already begun in some courts. In a recent decision in the United Kingdom,Farley v. Skinner,Lord Steyn took a less rigid approach to the question of recoverability for mental distress damages in contract cases. According to Lord Steyn, the plaintiff is entitled to secure damages for intangible lossprovided that an important part of the contract is to provide "pleasure, relaxation, or peace of mind."The Supreme Court of Hawaii inFrancis v. Lee Enterprises, Inc.took a similar approach, reversing a ruling which forbade noneconomic damages in contract.The Hawaiian court stated that courts ought to focus on the nature of the contract itself and permit mental distress damages where such a loss is foreseeable.
Building on the approach and conclusions inFarley v. SkinnerandFrancis v. Lee Enterprises, this article argues that courts in both the United States and Canada should abandon the general rule against recovery for intangibles. Part II provides some brief historical context by considering recovery for mental distress damages in tort cases. The strict barriers to recovery in this area appear to indicate a generalized judicial skepticism about the legitimacy of intangible injury and act as a preview of how the courts respond to claims in contract.Part III provides necessary contextfor examining mental distress damages in the contractual arena by assessing this topic in relation to theRestatement (Second) of Contracts. It concludes that aspects of theRestatementare actuallymoreexacting on the plaintiff seeking mental distress recovery than the common law. This heightened standard betrays the anxiety with which claims for intangibles continue to be met.
Part IV focuses on recovery for mental distress in contract law through punitive or aggravated damages. This section concludes that, while such avenues of recovery are essential, courts have set the bar exceedingly high for recovery--perhaps another outgrowth of the judiciary's discomfort with intangible loss. This part underscores the ideas that recovery formannerof breach does not provide recompense to the plaintiff who is upset due to the defendant's breach alone, but only where the breach has been accompanied by high-handed or outrageous conduct.
Part V discusses the law concerning recovery based on thefactof breach. It is in such contexts that the general rule against recovery for mental distress damages operates. This part illustrates and critiques the various strategies courts have followed in order to prevent the general rule from working an injustice in a given case. The first most commonly followed strategy, which permits recovery when the contract fits within a special category, is impeachable on logic alone. As Professor Edward Veitch has observed, once is it acknowledged that mental distress damages are recoverable in certain circumstances, it is difficult to justify any limitation on those categories.The second approach, permitting recovery only on the basis of reasonable foreseeability, is one followed by numerous courts in Canada and advocated for in the United States by Professor Douglas Whaley.The difficulty with this rule is simply contextual. To the extent that the judge makes the classical assumption (namely, that contracts are unlikely to contain intangible content) that assumption propels the conclusion that the contract in question contains no such content. Such a mindset, in turn, makes it much less likely that mental distress damages willpass the foreseeability test ofHadley v. Baxendale.In short, the second approach to recovery--while appearing to be flexible--may actually produce the same outcome as if the general rule against recovery had been applied at the outset.
Part VI offers suggestions for reform, including how a court might most effectively approach claims for intangible loss in contract. That is, rather than coming to the question of recovery with categories and presuppositions in mind, the court would simply begin by asking the unadorned but elegant question at the foundation of all contract law: "What did the contract promise?" Part VII provides a brief conclusion.

questions.question: Whether plaintiffs should be permitted to recover damages for mental distress (noneconomic or intangible loss) resulting from a breach of contract.

Under what circumstances or doctrinal framework courts should award mental distress damages for breach of contract - for example, whether recovery should turn on the nature of the breach, the foreseeability of distress, or the contractual purpose and expectations.

matched_themes: Should courts allow punitive or other extracompensatory damages for willful or abusive contract breaches, and what are the efficiency and fairness trade-offs?
Should parties and courts adopt fault-based remedial regimes that distinguish among breaches by reason when allocating remedies?
What standards and procedural safeguards should govern awards of punitive and other nonpecuniary damages in contract disputes to balance compensation and protection against abuse?

Should remedies and contract law be structured to preserve conditions necessary for moral agency and promissory responsibility, rather than treating promises solely as instruments of economic cooperation?
Should plaintiffs be permitted to recover non-pecuniary harms such as mental distress in breach-of-contract cases?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
Do limits on recoverable damages (foreseeability, certainty, avoidability) substantially reduce awards below full compensation, and should courts liberalize those limits?
Do courts consider the breaching party's blameworthiness or opportunistic behavior when selecting among compensatory remedies?
To what extent should moral blameworthiness and non-economic considerations influence the design and application of contract remedies?

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: PROMISSORY FRAUD WITHOUT BREACH

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that allowing promissory fraud claims in certain nonenforcement contexts preserves freedom from contract while still punishing insincere promisors; Paper B surveys judicial concern about preserving a tough-minded commercial contract regime and the ‘floodgates’ risk, and argues for recalibrating that balance to address intangible harms.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: INSTRUCTING JURIES ON NONECONOMIC CONTRACT DAMAGES

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PENALTIES AS RATIONAL RESPONSE TO BARGAINING IRRATIONALITY

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Moral Diversity and Efficient Breach

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Collateral Source Rule and Contract Damages.

papers.node_id: 12jempiricallegalstud29!!ARTICLE: Damages Versus Specific Performance: Lessons from Commercial Contracts
papers.title: ARTICLE: Damages Versus Specific Performance: Lessons from Commercial Contracts
papers.abstract:
Black-letter law holds that an injunction--specific performance--is available in an action for breach of contract only in cases where damages are inadequate.This rule has a hoary lineage, with antecedents in the early common law of England.It is endorsed by courtsthroughout the United States and elsewhere in the English-speaking world. The subordination of specific performance is firmly embedded in the jurisprudence of contract law, and generally accepted in the courts.
Yet the rule preferring damages over specific performance is also mysterious. Its intellectual underpinnings are far from clear--as evidenced by a vigorous debate among contract theorists regarding the utility of the rule.The black-letter law of many countries with modern systems of contract law does not prefer damages over specific performance.Even in the United States, long a citadel of support for the rule, the foundations appear to be eroding; courts do not always adhere rigidly to the rule,and some have argued that the measure of damages actually awarded is closer to the breaching party's profit from breach than to the nonbreaching party's lost profits--a measure that emulates, in some respects, the supposedly disfavored specific performance remedy.
This article studies the rule on specific performance from a different perspective than those employed previously. Instead of theorizing about the rule, we examine the actual behavior of contracting parties.Specifically, we analyze a data set of 2,347 contracts filed as exhibits with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) in connection with reports of material events by reporting companies on Form 8-K, the "current report" form companies must file with the SEC to announce major events of which shareholders should be aware.This data set offers the advantage that it contains important contracts entered into by sophisticated economic actors whose incentives are to agree to rules that generate joint value for the transaction. Because of these features, there is reason to believe that the contract terms observed in this data set reflect efficient solutions to the contracting problem.
We examine the contracts in this data set to identify and analyze efforts by the counterparties to contract around the traditional rule preferring damages over specific performance.If nothing is said in the contract about this issue, the ordinary background rule of contract law will apply, but the parties can attempt to avoid the application of this rule by including language that seeks to influence how a court will treat the choice among contract remedies--for example, by stipulating that damages are not an adequate remedy for breach and agreeing that specific performance is appropriate. Although it is not clear that this language will be binding on the courts--the parties' ex ante agreement on this point will surely have an influence, perhaps a decisive influence, on how a court rules in an actual dispute.Thus, clauses providing for specific performance have the potential to cause a court that would otherwise award damages to award specific performance instead.
Our reason for studying these clauses is that sophisticated parties' contractual silence concerning specific performance suggests that they do not have strong objections to damages as the preferred remedy in the event of breach--and have adjusted other contract terms (such as price) to account for the relative impacts of a damages regime on their expected payoffs from the deal.Parties concerned about contractual silence's negative inference concerning the availability of specific performance can expressly negate the inference. For example, an asset sale agreement states that conditions authorizing termination of an agreement shall not be deemed "to impair the right of any party to compel specific performance by another party of its obligations under this Agreement."
The inference of the acceptability of damages, of course, is not true by necessity; possibly the observed behavior of contracting parties on the question of remedies reflects inattention, complacency, or a simple lack of imagination. However, given the sophistication of the parties in our data set, the importance of the contracts involved, and the fact that many of these contracts contain other clauses governing disputes under the contract, it is plausible to suppose that the parties' silence on the matter of contract remedies usually is meaningful. When, on the other hand, the parties have attempted to opt out of damages relief and into the specific performance remedy, it can be inferred that their judgment is that the value of the contract ex ante will be maximized if the courts will award specific performance in the event of breach rather than awarding contract damages. Thus, it is useful to study cases where parties have specifically expressed a preference for specific performance as a remedy, since we can infer from their behavior that they believe that specific performance is the remedy that maximizes joint profits ex ante. This article performs such a study.
In brief, our study supports the inference that sophisticated contracting parties often do prefer specific performance to contract damages and they prefer it a majority of the time in contracts involving corporate combinations. Thus, while a majority of contracts, 68.5 percent,do not refer to specific performance, substantial variation exists in the rates of including specific performance clauses. High rates of specific performance use in the area of corporate combinations through merger (53.4 percent) or assets sales (45.1 percent), inclusion of specific performance in some contracts of every type, and much lower use of it in loan agreements suggest that theories of contractual remedy should expressly account for contract type variation. Analysis of other variables reveals that specific performance is not strongly correlated with the presence of a non-U.S. party to a contract and is associated with relational contracts (but this result is sensitive to specific types). Inclusion of specific performance clauses is significantly associated with the presence of other contract terms departing from default dispute resolution clause treatment.
This article is structured as follows. Section II sets forth the traditional rule and explores the arguments for and against its efficiency as compared with specific performance. Section III outlines the prior empirical literature. Section IV describes the data set and sets forth the hypotheses we test. Section V analyzes the results and Section VI concludes.

questions.question: Whether sophisticated parties to important commercial contracts prefer in-kind (specific/performance-equivalent) remedies over monetary damages when allocating remedies ex ante.

Whether the likelihood of contracting for an in-kind remedy (versus leaving the default monetary remedy) varies with contract characteristics such as transaction type (e.g., mergers, asset sales, loans), cross-border parties, relational contracting features, and other deviations from default dispute-resolution terms.

matched_themes: Does giving the promisee a unilateral right to demand performance or elect a damages measure that captures promisor's forgone gains vindicate moral intuitions while preserving ex post efficiency?
Do courts actually prefer monetary damages over specific (in-kind) remedies, or do they grant specific relief except when independent reasons exist to deny it?
When should courts order specific performance (in-kind relief) versus awarding monetary damages?
Should the promisor or the promisee have the default right to choose between performance and payment to achieve allocative efficiency?
Should parties be presumptively permitted to contractually specify nonstandard damage remedies, or should courts retain authority to impose defaults?
When should courts prefer or enforce in-kind (specific) performance rather than monetary damages for breach of contract?
How should courts treat and enforce stipulated remedies (liquidated damages clauses) versus substituting judicial remedies?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
When is an indirect remedy (one that induces self-compliance) preferable to a direct remedy that delivers the outcome?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 78mdlrev147!!ARTICLE: THE ERROR THEORY OF CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE ERROR THEORY OF CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: specific performance versus damages as the default contractual remedy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates lay beliefs about whether specific performance or damages is the typical remedy and emphasizes how that belief shapes perceived implicit terms of bargains, while Paper B empirically analyzes commercial contracts to measure how often parties affirmatively choose specific performance over damages and what that reveals about the operation of the default rule.

shared_topics.topic: empirical study of remedy-related behavior and beliefs to inform doctrinal claims
shared_topics.justification: Both papers deploy empirical evidence—Paper A via a nationally representative survey of non-lawyers' beliefs and Paper B via a large dataset of SEC-filed commercial contracts—to draw normative and doctrinal inferences about how remedy rules function in practice.

shared_topics.topic: parties contracting around default remedial rules (opt-out/contracting-in of specific performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how false beliefs about background doctrine affect consent to legally implied remedial terms and the significance of implied default rules, while Paper B examines explicit contractual clauses that attempt to displace the default preference for damages by stipulating specific performance.

shared_topics.topic: implications of remedy rules for normative foundations of contract law (autonomy/consent vs efficiency)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that widespread false beliefs about remedies undermine promise/consent-based autonomy justifications for contract law, and Paper B evaluates whether empirical patterns of contracting (e.g., when parties opt for specific performance) bear on theoretical defenses of the damages-preference rule, including efficiency arguments.

shared_topics.topic: the role of parties' knowledge and sophistication in shaping remedial outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how non-lawyers' ignorance or mistaken beliefs about remedies affects their consent and the fairness of enforcing implied terms, while Paper B studies how sophisticated commercial actors respond to remedial defaults in drafting, showing variation by contract type and suggesting knowledge/sophistication matters for remedy selection.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 75minnlrev1445!!ARTICLE: Of Spoil Pits and Swimming Pools: Reconsidering the Measure of Damages for Construction Contracts.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Of Spoil Pits and Swimming Pools: Reconsidering the Measure of Damages for Construction Contracts.

shared_topics.topic: when are damages an adequate remedy versus when should courts compel specific performance or award cost-to-complete
shared_topics.justification: Both papers confront the core remedial question of when ordinary damages suffice and when an alternative remedy is required—Paper A studies parties' contractual choices to opt into specific performance versus relying on damages, while Paper B analyzes doctrinal tests (e.g., Jacob & Youngs and Peevyhouse) for choosing between cost-to-complete and diminution-in-value remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the economic efficiency implications of different remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Both works evaluate remedies through an efficiency lens—Paper A infers that sophisticated parties' inclusion or omission of specific-performance clauses reflects efficient ex ante tradeoffs, and Paper B critiques current remedial discretion as economically inefficient and proposes rules intended to improve certainty and compensation.

shared_topics.topic: the role of parties' ex ante agreements and expressed intentions in determining remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both articles examine how contracting parties' expressed preferences or intentions affect remedial outcomes—Paper A empirically analyzes contractual clauses that stipulate adequacy of damages or entitlement to specific performance, while Paper B recommends that courts give weight to an owner's intent to use an award to complete performance when selecting cost-to-complete damages.

shared_topics.topic: judicial doctrine, discretion, and inconsistency in applying remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage with the doctrine and practice of courts in remedial selection—Paper A documents how the traditional rule favoring damages is applied unevenly and sometimes contracted around, and Paper B criticizes judicial subjectivity and inconsistent application of the cost-to-complete versus diminution rules and proposes clearer standards.

shared_topics.topic: sensitivity of remedy choice to contract type and factual context
shared_topics.justification: Both studies emphasize that remedy selection depends on the type of contract and case-specific facts—Paper A shows empirical variation in inclusion of specific-performance clauses across contract types (e.g., mergers, asset sales, loans), and Paper B illustrates how factual differences (e.g., Kent vs. Peevyhouse) drive different remedial outcomes and complicate bright-line rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 103harvlrev687!!ARTICLE: THE DEATH OF THE IRREPARABLE INJURY RULE.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE DEATH OF THE IRREPARABLE INJURY RULE.

shared_topics.topic: the comparative desirability of damages versus specific performance as contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both papers centrally engage the question whether courts and contracting parties should (and do) prefer damages over specific performance — Paper A empirically examines when sophisticated parties stipulate for specific performance in contracts, while Paper B doctrinally argues that the conventional presumption favoring damages is misleading and that courts routinely award specific relief when appropriate.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy-of-damages / irreparable-injury concept as the doctrinal gatekeeper for equitable relief
shared_topics.justification: Both works analyze how the notion that damages are an 'adequate' remedy (or that injury is 'irreparable') operates in practice — Paper A studies when parties contractually assert that damages are inadequate, and Paper B critiques the irreparable-injury rule, showing courts redefine 'adequacy' to permit specific relief.

shared_topics.topic: the extent to which parties' contractual allocations of remedial rights affect judicial remedy outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Both papers examine the role of ex ante contracting in shaping remedy results — Paper A empirically measures how often and in what contract types parties include clauses to secure specific performance, while Paper B discusses how courts respond to such considerations and the practical relevance of party expectations in remedy decisions.

shared_topics.topic: the divergence between formal remedial doctrine and actual practice and the need for functional/contextual analysis
shared_topics.justification: Both authors confront a gap between black-letter rules and on-the-ground outcomes: Paper A uses contract data to infer efficient remedial choices by market actors that may contradict doctrinal presumptions, and Paper B documents case law showing judges rely on narrower, functional factors (fungibility, preliminary vs permanent relief, hardship) rather than the formal irreparable-injury rubric.

shared_topics.topic: contextual factors that determine when specific relief is appropriate (e.g., contract type, fungibility, preliminary vs permanent relief)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage the idea that remedy choice depends on context: Paper A finds variation in inclusion of specific-performance clauses across contract types (mergers, asset sales, loans), and Paper B elaborates doctrinally on contexts—fungible goods, preliminary versus permanent injunctions, hardship and superviseability—that make damages adequate or inadequate.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: An Examination of Judicial Reasoning - When a Penalty Is Not a Penalty

shared_topics.topic: judicial doctrine and reasoning in evolving remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes and critiques courts' incremental, and at times muddled, reasoning in cases like Cavendish-ParkingEye when reassessing the penalty rule, and Paper B discusses courts' historical preference for damages, signs of doctrinal erosion, and how judges may treat contractual language that tries to dictate remedies.

shared_topics.topic: efficiency and economic justification for remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for greater flexibility (and implicitly efficiency) in enforcing penalty/liquidated-damages clauses and criticizes per se invalidation as economically irrational, while Paper B uses empirical contract data to infer that sophisticated parties' choices about specific performance reflect ex ante efficiency-maximizing solutions and variation across contract types.

shared_topics.topic: the compensatory vs. punitive nature of contract remedies and the measurement of damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the distinction between compensatory damages and supracompensatory 'penalties' as the doctrinal rationale for invalidating clauses, and Paper B engages with whether damages awards (or parties' preferences for specific performance) align with compensatory aims or approximate breacher profits or other non-compensatory outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 55syracuselrev495!!ARTICLE: A UNIFYING THEORY OF CONTRACT DAMAGE RULES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A UNIFYING THEORY OF CONTRACT DAMAGE RULES

shared_topics.topic: how default legal rules interact with parties' ability to contract around remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically studies contractual clauses that attempt to alter the background rule preferring damages over specific performance, and Paper B discusses a black-letter Shadow Code as the governing default for damages while addressing how existing statutory or doctrinal elections and party choices affect remedy outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: how damages should be measured and the terminology/formulas for computing loss (expectation/reliance/lost profit/consequential/incidental)

shared_topics.topic: variation in remedy rules across contract types and the case for harmonization
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents systematic variation in inclusion of specific performance clauses across transaction types (e.g., mergers, asset sales, loans), while Paper B criticizes the multiplicity of context-specific damage rules (UCC vs Restatement, buyers vs sellers) and proposes a single rule intended to apply uniformly across contract types.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Role of the State in Contract Law: The Common-Civil Law Divide

shared_topics.justification: Paper A attributes cross‑jurisdictional doctrinal differences to distinct roles of the State in policing terms and calibrating remedies, and Paper B examines the black‑letter rule (courts' preference for damages) and how that background enforcement regime influences parties' ex ante contract choices.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how civil law's mandatory rules limit private ordering while common law allows more freedom (but with weaker remedies), and Paper B studies explicit contractual attempts to opt into specific performance (i.e., to alter the default remedial regime) and the prevalence of such opt‑outs across contract types.

shared_topics.topic: the value of empirical, 'law in action' study of contract doctrines and terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A calls for more empirical research to assess the practical import of doctrinal differences, and Paper B supplies such empirical evidence by analyzing thousands of real commercial contracts to reveal how remedy rules operate in practice.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Fixer Upper: Buyer Deposits in Residential Real Estate Transactions

shared_topics.topic: interaction between ex ante contracting choices and ex post judicial enforcement

shared_topics.justification: Each paper evaluates whether prevailing remedial rules produce desirable outcomes—Paper A asks whether specific performance or damages leads to joint value maximization in different contract types, while Paper B argues that deposit forfeitures often do not correspond to seller harm and thus raise normative concerns warranting consumer‑protection reforms.

shared_topics.topic: discrepancy between doctrinal defaults and real‑world contracting practices (empirical focus on contract type and market norms)
shared_topics.justification: Both works emphasize the importance of observed market practices relative to default doctrine: Paper A uses an SEC contract dataset to show variation across contract types in remedy clauses, and Paper B documents how residential real estate market norms (e.g., deposit sizes in hot markets) drive clause design and diverge from liquidated‑damages theory.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SOMETHING ELSE: SPECIFIC RELIEF FOR BREACH OF HUMAN RIGHTS TERMS IN SUPPLY CHAIN AGREEMENTS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the Model Contract Clauses' explicit inclusion of specific-relief remedies for HR breaches and how those clauses function as a means to secure nonstandard remedies, and Paper B analyzes contractual language parties use to 'contract around' the default damages-preference rule (e.g., stipulating damages are inadequate or that specific performance is warranted).

shared_topics.justification: Paper A diagnoses legal barriers (the anxieties of indenture and entanglement, enforcement problems across borders) that make courts reluctant or constrained in crafting specific relief for HR breaches, and Paper B treats the traditional doctrinal rule (specific performance only when damages inadequate) and its uneven application by courts as central to understanding remedy outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: how remedy choice affects ex ante incentives and contract performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that including specific-relief HR terms can shape parties' behavior, monitoring, and relational performance in supply chains (even if enforcement is imperfect), while Paper B infers from contract terms that sophisticated parties choose remedies (including specific performance) when those choices maximize joint value and thus influence contracting incentives and expected outcomes.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Loss Aversion and the Law

shared_topics.justification: Paper A employs a large empirical dataset of SEC-filed contracts to test hypotheses about remedy selection, and Paper B applies behavioral economics (prospect theory, loss aversion) to explain longstanding legal puzzles and to draw descriptive and normative conclusions about legal doctrine.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: Intentions, Guilt and Social Interactions

shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates how social norms of sincerity, guilt and insincerity aversion influence whether mutually beneficial social exchanges occur, and Paper B examines how the legal default favoring damages (versus explicit contractual stipulations for specific performance) affects parties' contracting behavior and the likely judicial remedy.

papers.node_id: 52tullrev659!!ARTICLE: Dependent Promises in the History of Leases and Other Contracts
papers.title: ARTICLE: Dependent Promises in the History of Leases and Other Contracts
papers.abstract:
One of the most perplexing problems in the law of contract is whether a breach by one party justifies a refusal to perform by the other. In a sale of goods, for example, is the buyer's duty to pay the price dependent on, or independent of, the seller's performance of his obligation to deliver? The general consensus is that, historically, promises were treated as independent until the time of Lord Mansfield, Chief Justice of England from 1756 to 1788. As Williston observed, "it was settled law for centuries that mutual promises unless containing express conditions were independent . . . . Lord Mansfield, contrary to three centuries of opposing precedents, changed the rule . . . ."This view did not originate in modern times. In 1744 Chief Justice Willes expressed his "dislike of those cases" holding promises to be independent, but added that "they are too many to be now over-ruled."In 1792, however, Chief Justice Kenyon remarked that "it would be absurd to say that the purchaser might enforce a conveyance without payment . . . . The old cases . . . outrage common sense."And a few years later Justice Grose suggested that "the older cases leaning to construe covenants of this sort to be independent"had been superseded.This view of the historical development is not without relevance today. A common explanation for covenants in a lease being held independent is that "the law of property crystallized before the development of mutually dependent covenants in contract law."Since promises are generally held to be dependent today, application of contract principles to leases is thought to require that covenants in a lease should also be dependent.
A similar movement from independent to dependent promises is said to have taken place in France. Whereas Roman law did not permit a seller to rescind if the price was not paid unless the contract so provided, modern French law, under the influence of canon law, implies a "resolutory condition" in all contracts, which allows one party to terminate if the other does not perform.Is this development related to the English experience? Can we say that as law progresses promises originally independent come to be treated as dependent? If so, what is the explanation for this?
This article will attempt to show that in fact no such development took place, either in France or in England; that many promises have been held dependent from a very early period; and that, conversely, many are held independent even today, for good reasons. The reasons for holding promises dependent or independent will be analyzed, and I hope to demonstrate that these reasons have not substantially changed over the centuries.

questions.question: Whether, historically, contractual promises were treated as independent and later came to be treated as mutually dependent (i.e., whether nonperformance by one party justifies the other's refusal to perform).
What reasons or policy considerations explain why particular promises are classified as dependent or independent, and whether those reasons have changed over time.
Whether similar changes in the treatment of promises across different legal systems are related or arose independently (i.e., to what extent developments in one jurisdiction influenced others).

matched_themes: What standard should courts apply to determine whether a party's deviation from contractual obligations is significant enough to excuse the other party's performance?
How have historical, geographic, institutional, and transnational influences shaped the evolution and transplantation of contract doctrines and remedies?
Should the promisor or the promisee have the default right to choose between performance and payment to achieve allocative efficiency?
When and to what extent should private self-help (withholding performance, repossession, or force) be permitted as a contract-enforcement mechanism?
When is an indirect remedy (one that induces self-compliance) preferable to a direct remedy that delivers the outcome?

papers.node_id: 103marqlrev1!!ARTICLE: DISGORGING EMOLUMENTS
papers.title: ARTICLE: DISGORGING EMOLUMENTS
papers.abstract:
disgorge: Yield or give up (funds, especially when dishonestly acquired)"they were made to disgorge all the profits made from the record"
One of the basic tenets of good government is that public officials act on behalf of the public interest rather than to enrich themselves at the public's expense. No doubt since the founding of America, government officials have engaged in behavior that risks violation of constitutional, statutory, and ethical prohibitions against certain emoluments. Issues of conflicts of interest, improper gains, and recusal are not unique to modern times. Historically, such matters have generated public criticism, advisory opinions by the Office of Legal Counsel, administrative corrective actions, statutory amendments, enhanced regulations, and sometimes governmental censures. These forces include separation-of-powers tension that may help, along with accountability to voters, lead to a satisfactory resolution of the arguably problematic conduct. Government actors and challengers have sought regulatory and ethical clarification of what constitutes an unlawful emolument, but this subject has never been litigated until now.
The sitting President of the United States maintains financial interests in companies with hotels bearing his last name. One such hotel is in Washington, D.C., not far from the White House. The President continues to receive profits from that hotel, which allegedly welcomes foreign diplomats as guests. These profits are emoluments as most broadly defined: any gain, benefit, advantage, or profit.Such profits, however, may or may not be unconstitutional or otherwise unlawful. The Justice Department maintains that such profits are not unlawful as there is no proof that the President has done anything in exchange for such profits.Government officials of prior administrations - Democratic and Republican - have engaged in behavior raising ethical questions thatsometimes also triggered emoluments concerns, if not, violations.None of the prior allegations, however, rose to litigation over whether certain emoluments were in fact unlawful. Several lawsuits filed against President Trump seek to prove that receipt of such profits - regardless of any lack of quid pro quo - are unlawful emoluments warranting relief.
Such emoluments controversies fill the news.Whether emoluments are improper as alleged is hotly debated among scholars and pundits.Scholarshipcontinues to mount on the meaning of constitutional emoluments and modern applications to alleged violations.These debates leave a gap in the literature with respect to addressing the remedies question. The relevant constitutional provisions state no remedies. Assume constitutional emoluments violations exist, what are we going to do about it? This Article offers answers to that core question and pathways to achieve desired goals of the underlying laws.
Putting aside the precise boundary on the impropriety of certain emoluments, what is the proper remedy? Which remedy will achieve the primary aims of the governing laws? This inquiry is vital for accountability of this and future administrations. If our laws - especially constitutional ones - lack bite, the temptation to engage in improper conduct, downplay arguable conflicts, and cover up questionable behavior will rise. Where unjust emoluments are proven, this Article explains why restitutionary disgorgement is a well-suited remedy to serve the goals of unjust enrichment and anti-corruption laws.
This Article introduces the constitutional boundaries for emoluments and the Framers' goals. Next, it summarizes the pending emoluments cases - all of which fail to allege an unjust enrichment claim or remedy. In Part III, it situates the disgorgement remedy within restitution law. This Article address challenges, but ultimately promotes restitutionary disgorgement as a powerful remedy to serve preferred goals. Part IV operationalizes potential paths for pursuing the disgorgement remedy against government officials including a statutory solution and a common law path. The Article concludes that restitutionary disgorgement is the optimal remedy to deter corruption and self-dealing, as well as prevent unjust enrichment.

questions.question: Whether restitutionary disgorgement is an appropriate and effective remedy to deter corruption and remedy unjust enrichment when public officials receive improper financial benefits.

How disgorgement remedies can be operationalized against public officials-through available legal pathways such as statutory reform or common-law claims-to secure restitution for improperly received benefits.

matched_themes: How do remedial rules for potentially illegal contracts affect parties' incentives to enter socially harmful or beneficial agreements?
Is restitutionary disgorgement an appropriate remedy to deter corruption and remedy unjust enrichment when public officials receive improper financial benefits?
Do courts actually prefer monetary damages over specific (in-kind) remedies, or do they grant specific relief except when independent reasons exist to deny it?
Should courts award disgorgement or force surrender of breacher gains in addition to compensation to deter opportunistic breaches?
Can reflective remedies or penalty-adjustment devices that 'reflect' excess conduct across uncertain legal caps produce better ex-ante incentives when legal standards are uncertain?
When and under what standards should courts award disgorgement or remedies that strip gains from breaching parties?
Should courts more readily grant equitable relief to compel performance when monetary damages undercompensate and public interests are implicated?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68flalrev1413!!ARTICLE: SUPREME DISGORGEMENT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SUPREME DISGORGEMENT

shared_topics.topic: disgorgement as a remedy to deter unjust enrichment and wrongdoing
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze disgorgement not merely as restitution but as a prophylactic and deterrent remedy — Paper A argues restitutionary disgorgement is optimal to deter corruption and prevent unjust enrichment by public officials, while Paper B treats the Supreme Court's award as authorizing disgorgement to deter opportunistic breaches and stabilize public agreements.

shared_topics.topic: situating disgorgement within restitution and unjust enrichment doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Both works connect disgorgement to the broader law of restitution/unjust enrichment — Paper A explicitly locates disgorgement within restitution law for emoluments claims, and Paper B links the Court's reasoning to Restatement Third restitution principles and the extension of disgorgement in contract contexts.

shared_topics.topic: when equitable disgorgement is available (law-versus-equity and insufficiency of other remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Each paper wrestles with the law-equity determination and the justification for awarding disgorgement beyond compensatory relief — Paper B highlights the presumption of equity and the Court's view that other remedies were insufficient, while Paper A discusses remedies pathways (statutory and common law/equitable) for obtaining disgorgement against officials.

shared_topics.topic: required mental state or causal showing for disgorgement (knowing breach, quid pro quo, or mere receipt)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the contours of the requisite mens rea or factual showing for disgorgement — Paper B emphasizes that knowing misconduct satisfies the intent requirement for disgorgement, and Paper A confronts whether receipt of profits without proof of quid pro quo can nonetheless warrant disgorgement in emoluments cases.

shared_topics.topic: use of disgorgement in public or quasi‑public disputes (public officials, states, and public compacts)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers focus on disgorgement in public-actor contexts rather than private commercial disputes — Paper A addresses disgorgement against a sitting President and the public-law dimensions of emoluments, and Paper B examines the Court's disgorgement award between states under a public water-allocation compact.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68flalrev1413!!ARTICLE: SUPREME DISGORGEMENT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SUPREME DISGORGEMENT

shared_topics.topic: disgorgement as an appropriate remedial tool
shared_topics.justification: Both papers argue for disgorgement as a viable remedy — Paper A advocates restitutionary disgorgement against public officials who improperly receive emoluments, while Paper B analyzes the Supreme Court's authorization of disgorgement in Kansas v. Nebraska and its broader remedial implications.

shared_topics.topic: restitution and unjust enrichment as the doctrinal basis for disgorgement
shared_topics.justification: Both works situate disgorgement within restitution/unjust enrichment law — Paper A develops disgorgement as a restitutionary remedy for emoluments, and Paper B treats the Supreme Court's award as grounded in restitutionary principles for opportunistic breaches.

shared_topics.topic: deterrence and the insufficiency of conventional remedies
shared_topics.justification: Each paper emphasizes that disgorgement can serve deterrent purposes and may be justified where compensatory or injunctive relief is inadequate — Paper A frames disgorgement as necessary to deter corruption and self-dealing, and Paper B lists deterrence and remedy insufficiency among the Court's reasons for disgorgement.

shared_topics.topic: the role of intent or quid pro quo/knowledge in awarding disgorgement
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the required mental element for disgorgement — Paper A grapples with whether profits absent demonstrable quid pro quo are unlawful and thus subject to disgorgement, while Paper B identifies 'knowing' conduct as satisfying the intent necessary for disgorgement in the compact dispute.

shared_topics.topic: disgorgement in public-law contexts and questions about extending it to private disputes
shared_topics.justification: Both analyze disgorgement primarily in public settings — Paper A examines remedies against public officials under constitutional emoluments doctrine, and Paper B considers a State-v-State disgorgement award and explicitly questions the reach of that logic to private litigants.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 89nwulrev1341!!ARTICLE: PEEVYHOUSE V. GARLAND COAL & MINING CO. REVISITED: THE BALLAD OF WILLIE AND LUCILLE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PEEVYHOUSE V. GARLAND COAL & MINING CO. REVISITED: THE BALLAD OF WILLIE AND LUCILLE

shared_topics.topic: advocacy of restitutionary remedies/disgorgement as appropriate relief
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that restitutionary disgorgement is the optimal remedy for unconstitutional or improper emoluments to prevent unjust enrichment and deter corruption, and Paper B identifies restitution (and the restitutionary value of benefits received) as an alternative recovery that plaintiffs could have pursued in Peevyhouse and which may better protect injured parties than diminution-of-value awards.

shared_topics.topic: comparative evaluation of remedial measures (cost-to-repair vs diminution vs equitable relief)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A weighs disgorgement against other possible remedies to determine which best serves constitutional and anti‑corruption goals, while Paper B undertakes a detailed comparison of cost-of-performance (repair), diminution-in-value, and specific performance/equitable relief in contract remediation disputes and argues for when each measure is appropriate.

shared_topics.topic: procedural and evidentiary obstacles to obtaining appropriate remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that existing emoluments litigation has failed to allege or pursue unjust enrichment claims and discusses separation-of-powers and litigation barriers to relief, and Paper B recounts how a deficient trial record, counsel strategy, and systemic adversary-system problems distorted fact-finding and yielded inadequate remedies in Peevyhouse.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between statutory reform, common-law remedies, and public policy goals
shared_topics.justification: Paper A outlines both statutory solutions and common-law paths for pursuing disgorgement to achieve accountability and deterrence, and Paper B traces statutory reclamation reforms, discusses how courts might fashion equitable remedies (like specific performance), and situates remedial choices in broader public-interest and policy contexts.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Convergence in Contort: Landlord Liability for Defective Premises in Comparative Perspective

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how labeling landlord obligations as contract or tort determines applicable remedies (strict liability, damages types, privity, statutes of limitation) and creates anomalies, while Paper B examines how the characterization of emoluments violations (constitutional/statutory) leaves a remedial gap and affects what relief plaintiffs can obtain.

shared_topics.topic: the choice and design of remedies to achieve policy goals (including restitutionary relief)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates which remedies (contractual termination/damages versus tort recovery for pain and suffering) best allocate risk and protect tenants and argues for a hybrid approach to select suitable attributes, and Paper B argues that restitutionary disgorgement is the proper remedial design to deter officials, prevent unjust enrichment, and fill constitutional remedial gaps.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of existing legal regimes and advocacy for doctrinal or institutional reform/alternative frameworks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes recasting landlord liability as a 'contort'—a hybrid doctrinal framework freeing obligations from rigid classification—and Paper B proposes statutory and common-law paths to operationalize disgorgement, both advocating doctrinal reform to better serve underlying substantive aims.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk, responsibility, and prevention of unjust enrichment or harmful conduct
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is concerned with who should bear the cost when premises defects cause economic loss or personal injury (landlord vs tenant) and the role of liability doctrines in preventing under- or over-inclusive risk allocation, while Paper B focuses on preventing public officials from being unjustly enriched by emoluments and ensuring accountability through remedies that reallocate gains back to the public.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: How Law Frames Moral Intuitions: The Expressive Effect of Specific Performance

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that restitutionary disgorgement best serves anti‑corruption and unjust enrichment goals by deterring self‑dealing and restoring gains, while Paper B analyzes whether damages or specific performance better advance contract law's aims (efficiency, protection of expectations, and fairness) and how the remedial choice affects legal outcomes.

shared_topics.justification: Paper B presents experimental evidence that the availability of specific performance alters promisees' moral intuitions and increases resentment toward breach; Paper A likewise grounds its remedial recommendation in the idea that disgorgement will change public officials' incentives and norms, using remedy design as a tool to influence conduct.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between normative/legal principles and remedial doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links remedial design to constitutional framers' anti‑corruption objectives and normative commitments against unjust enrichment, while Paper B interrogates deontological and utilitarian justifications for specific performance, showing that normative claims about promises are affected by which remedies the law provides.

shared_topics.topic: institutional and doctrinal routes for creating and enforcing remedies (statutory vs common law/judicial remedies and default rules)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores statutory solutions and common‑law paths for imposing disgorgement against officials and discusses separation‑of‑powers and enforcement challenges, while Paper B focuses on judicially created default remedies (damages vs specific performance), enforcement mechanisms, and the policy implications of courts' remedial choices.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 116yaleljonline414!!ARTICLE: Who Chooses and Who Gets What: Efficient Breach and Efficient Performance Hypotheses hypothesis.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Who Chooses and Who Gets What: Efficient Breach and Efficient Performance Hypotheses hypothesis.

shared_topics.topic: use of disgorgement/restitutionary disgorgement as a remedy for wrongful gains
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines disgorgement as one of the remedial tools that can reallocate profits when a promisor elects not to perform, and Paper B situates and advocates restitutionary disgorgement as the appropriate remedy to strip officials of illicit emolument profits.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial rules (damages, specific performance, disgorgement) shape incentives and policy goals
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that different remedies (expectation damages, specific performance, disgorgement) can all produce efficient performance by orienting the chooser's cost–benefit calculus, while Paper B analyzes which remedies best deter corruption and prevent unjust enrichment under emoluments law and how remedy choice advances accountability.

shared_topics.topic: redistribution or capture of gains from wrongful/non-performance conduct (unjust enrichment)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats the distribution of gains from non-performance (who captures profits when contracts are broken) as central to efficiency and fairness, and Paper B treats the disgorgement of profits from emoluments as a mechanism to prevent unjust enrichment by public officials.

shared_topics.topic: the interaction between legal entitlements/rights and remedial design in producing enforcement outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares competing allocations of legal rights (promisor's option to pay or perform versus promisee's right to compel performance) together with remedies to show how rights-plus-remedies determine efficiency, and Paper B similarly emphasizes that constitutional entitlements lack specified remedies and explores statutory and common-law remedial paths to make emoluments rules enforceable.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Actual and Virtual Specific Performance, the Theory of Efficient Breach, and the Indifference Principle in Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: adequacy of monetary damages versus equitable/coercive remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates whether expectation (monetary) damages adequately substitute for specific performance and develops the notion of 'virtual specific performance' as a monetary-market alternative; Paper B similarly assesses whether disgorgement (a monetary restitutionary remedy) is the appropriate and sufficient remedy for unlawful emoluments, comparing money relief to other forms of accountability.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial rules shape behavior (efficiency versus deterrence)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the theory of efficient breach and how different remedial doctrines (damages vs specific performance) create incentives for promisors and promisees, while Paper B argues that disgorgement is necessary to deter corruption and self-dealing by changing officials' cost–benefit calculus.

shared_topics.topic: restitution and unjust enrichment: measuring and reclaiming gains
shared_topics.justification: Paper A probes the shortfall of expectation damages relative to the promisee's lost position and considers market-based 'cover' as a way to achieve equivalent outcomes, whereas Paper B situates disgorgement within restitution law and develops doctrines and pathways to quantify and recover unjust gains (emoluments).

shared_topics.topic: institutional and normative constraints on remedies (coercion, error, procedural and constitutional limits)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A weighs the intrusiveness, error risks, jury-avoidance, and opportunism problems of ordering specific performance, and Paper B examines separation-of-powers, constitutional boundaries, statutory versus common-law routes, and litigation challenges that constrain the choice and application of disgorgement remedies.

shared_topics.topic: design and adequacy of legal remedies to achieve substantive policy goals
shared_topics.justification: Both papers centrally examine whether existing legal remedies effectively advance underlying policy aims — Paper A analyzes whether U.S. landlord‑tenant remedies (and proposed Anglo‑American reforms modeled on German law) actually alleviate substandard housing and protect low‑income tenants, while Paper B scrutinizes the lack of clear remedies for unconstitutional or unlawful emoluments and advocates restitutionary disgorgement as the proper remedy to deter corruption and prevent unjust enrichment.

shared_topics.topic: statutory reform versus common‑law solutions as pathways for change
shared_topics.justification: Each article weighs legislated statutes against judicially developed common‑law approaches — Paper A compares German statutory landlord‑tenant regimes to American law to assess possible statutory reforms, and Paper B outlines both a statutory route and a common‑law restitutionary path for pursuing disgorgement against public officials.

shared_topics.topic: using restitution/unjust‑enrichment principles and alternative remedies to remedy wrongdoing
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with restitutionary or compensatory concepts as tools for remedy: Paper A proposes alternative tenant remedies (e.g., withholding, repair remedies and other means of redress) to correct landlord failures and imbalance, and Paper B situates disgorgement within restitution law as the appropriate remedy to remedy unjust enrichment from emoluments.

shared_topics.topic: law as a mechanism to correct power imbalances and prevent exploitation/self‑dealing
shared_topics.justification: Each paper treats legal rules as instruments to reallocate power and deter exploitative conduct — Paper A focuses on how landlord‑tenant law can perpetuate or correct imbalances disadvantaging low‑income renters, while Paper B addresses how remedial doctrine can deter public‑official self‑dealing and protect the public interest.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 116columlrev2005!!ARTICLE: ECONOMIC ANALYSIS OF CONTRACT LAW FROM THE INTERNAL POINT OF VIEW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ECONOMIC ANALYSIS OF CONTRACT LAW FROM THE INTERNAL POINT OF VIEW

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how different monetary remedies—expectation damages, stipulated damages, and supercompensatory (penalty) awards—affect contracting behavior and social welfare given heterogeneous actors; Paper B argues for restitutionary disgorgement as the proper monetary remedy to deter emoluments, prevent unjust enrichment, and vindicate anti‑corruption aims.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules and remedies shape behavior through norms versus incentives (including crowding out)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops the internalizer/externalizer distinction and shows that doctrinal form (rules vs standards, perform‑or‑pay norms) can either guide behavior normatively or merely change incentives, sometimes crowding out moral motivations; Paper B treats remedies and constitutional proscriptions as instruments to influence officials' conduct and public norms, assessing whether disgorgement and other sanctions will effectively deter or alter behavior.

shared_topics.topic: aligning doctrinal choice with the underlying goals or values of the law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks whether contract doctrines should be designed to maximize social welfare or to express promissory morality and shows the choice affects optimal doctrine; Paper B situates emoluments remedies in the Framers' anti‑corruption and accountability goals and uses that purposive inquiry to justify disgorgement as the appropriate remedy.

shared_topics.topic: practical doctrinal and institutional paths to operationalize remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines concrete doctrinal mechanisms (penalty rule, willful breach, duress, stipulated damages) and how their formulation speaks to different actor types; Paper B maps out statutory and common‑law pathways to implement disgorgement and discusses the doctrinal and institutional choices needed to make the remedy operative.

shared_topics.topic: choosing the appropriate remedial theory to achieve policy goals (deterrence, restitution, compensation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that restitutionary disgorgement best serves anti-corruption and unjust-enrichment goals when officials receive improper emoluments, while Paper B analyzes whether conversion, specific performance, expectation damages, or liquidated damages best compensate a venture fund denied a right of first refusal and deter managerial opportunism.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops disgorgement as a restitutionary remedy for unconstitutional or unlawful emoluments, and Paper B considers analogous equitable remedies (conversion, specific performance) and when non‑pecuniary or restitution-like relief should supplant ordinary expectation damages in the venture capital ROFR context.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines both statutory reforms and common‑law pathways to enable disgorgement against public officials, while Paper B evaluates contractual design (standardizing liquidated damages clauses) as a practical alternative to changing remedial doctrines for breaches of rights of first refusal.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses political checks, separation‑of‑powers tensions, and voter accountability as imperfect restraints on emoluments conduct, and Paper B assesses reputation as an enforcement mechanism in venture capital and when legal remedies must supplement reputational enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: whether third‑party payments or benefits should reduce a defendant's liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates disgorgement of profits received by an official (arguing for stripping those gains irrespective of quid pro quo), and Paper B directly analyzes the collateral source question of whether payments from insurers, savings, or other third parties should diminish the primary defendant's recovery exposure.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A operationalizes both statutory solutions and common‑law routes for pursuing disgorgement against officials, and Paper B surveys how courts, the Restatement, treatises, and statutes have shaped and could alter application of the collateral source rule in contract cases.

shared_topics.topic: use of historical and doctrinal analysis to justify remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds its argument in constitutional history and Framers' goals to justify disgorgement as a remedy, while Paper B traces treatises, Restatement authority, and case law history to argue for or against applying the collateral source rule in contract disputes.

compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:COMMENTARY BREACH AND PENALTY AS CONTRACTUAL NORM AND CONTRACTUAL ANOMIE

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for restitutionary disgorgement as the appropriate monetary remedy to strip unlawfully obtained gains from public officials, while Paper B empirically examines the widespread use and judicial tolerance of contractual penalty clauses as monetary remedies for breach in Russia.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes separation-of-powers constraints, DOJ policy, and political accountability that affect whether emoluments remedies can be pursued, and Paper B documents how judicial tolerance, legal-system disorganization, and extra-legal forces (e.g., gangsterism) influence the enforcement and operation of contract remedies.

shared_topics.topic: deterrence versus efficiency trade-offs in remedial design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames disgorgement in terms of deterring corruption and preventing unjust enrichment, assessing whether the remedy serves the substantive goals of anti-corruption norms, while Paper B tests whether penalty clauses serve a deterrent function and whether their use is inconsistent with the economic notion of 'efficient breach.'

shared_topics.topic: appropriate remedial responses and limits on recovery
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes what remedy (restitutionary disgorgement) best serves emoluments and anti-corruption laws and explores statutory and common-law paths and constraints for imposing that remedy; Paper B analyzes the proper measure of recovery in contract law, showing how Hadley v. Baxendale limits damages to foreseeable losses and thus constrains the scope of remedial relief.

shared_topics.topic: policy goals that should guide remedies (deterrence, fairness, prevention of unjust enrichment)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues disgorgement is the optimal remedy to deter corruption, prevent unjust enrichment, and preserve accountability; Paper B applies the Hadley foreseeability rule as a policy-driven limitation designed to balance fairness to defendants with protection of plaintiffs’ expectations.

shared_topics.topic: use of precedent and historical doctrinal interpretation to define legal boundaries
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages historical constitutional text and prior advisory opinions and cases to define the emoluments doctrine and remedial possibilities; Paper B centers its analysis on the seminal Hadley v. Baxendale precedent to articulate when lost profits are recoverable under contract law.

shared_topics.topic: how uncertainty and probability affect entitlement to relief
shared_topics.justification: Paper A confronts uncertainty about when receipt of profits qualifies as an unlawful emolument and whether remedial relief is appropriate absent quid pro quo, while Paper B hinges recovery on the low probability of the specific long‑shot winnings and the Hadley probability/foreseeability standard that bars speculative losses.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 52wmmarylrev1181!!ARTICLE: YOU DO HAVE TO KEEP YOUR PROMISES: A DISGORGEMENT THEORY OF CONTRACT REMEDIES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: YOU DO HAVE TO KEEP YOUR PROMISES: A DISGORGEMENT THEORY OF CONTRACT REMEDIES

shared_topics.topic: disgorgement as an appropriate legal remedy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a disgorgement-centered theory of contract remedies, arguing for remedial structures that require recoupment of gains, while Paper B advocates restitutionary disgorgement as the correct remedy for unlawful emoluments and explains how disgorgement serves anti‑corruption and unjust enrichment goals.

shared_topics.topic: restitution/unjust enrichment versus compensatory damages
shared_topics.justification: Both papers interrogate the limits of traditional compensatory damages and situate disgorgement within restitution law — Paper A by reconceptualizing contract remedies around disgorgement, and Paper B by arguing that emoluments disputes require restitutionary (not merely compensatory) relief to prevent unjust enrichment.

shared_topics.topic: remedies as instruments of deterrence and public policy
shared_topics.justification: Each article links remedial choice to broader policy aims: Paper A ties remedy design in contract law to assuring promise‑keeping and appropriate incentives, and Paper B emphasizes disgorgement’s role in deterring corruption, self‑dealing, and weakening incentives for officials to profit improperly.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal and procedural pathways and limits for imposing disgorgement
shared_topics.justification: Both works engage with how disgorgement can be operationalized and constrained within existing legal frameworks — Paper A by situating a disgorgement theory within contract doctrine, and Paper B by mapping statutory and common‑law routes and addressing doctrinal challenges to obtaining disgorgement for emoluments.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83uchilrevonline190!!ARTICLE: The Demands of an Interpretive Theory of Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Demands of an Interpretive Theory of Contract

shared_topics.topic: interpretive legal theory and the normative/descriptive interplay
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advances an interpretive theory of contract law that rejects a strict descriptive/normative dichotomy and insists legal doctrine must be read and justified on moral grounds, while Paper B engages in constitutional and remedial interpretation (Framers' goals, scope of the emoluments clauses) and continually weighs interpretive choices against normative aims such as accountability and deterrence.

shared_topics.topic: justification of legal doctrines in light of underlying moral or policy aims
shared_topics.justification: Paper A seeks a unified moral justification for core contract doctrines (e.g., consideration, enforcement) so the whole doctrine coheres, and Paper B evaluates and selects remedies (restitutionary disgorgement) because they best serve the moral and policy aims of anti‑corruption and unjust‑enrichment rules.

shared_topics.topic: how law compels compliance and provides remedies to enforce obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that contract law creates legally obligatory (coercive) obligations that must be justified and enforced, and Paper B focuses on remedial mechanisms (disgorgement, statutory and common‑law paths) to compel compliance, prevent unjust enrichment, and hold public officials accountable.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 80brooklynlrev173!!ARTICLE: The Compensation Myth and U.C.C. Section 2-713
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Compensation Myth and U.C.C. Section 2-713

shared_topics.topic: the normative aims of remedies (deterrence vs compensation/unjust enrichment)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers interrogate what legal remedies should accomplish: Paper A argues disgorgement best serves anti-corruption goals by deterring misconduct and preventing unjust enrichment, while Paper B critiques the compensatory assumptions behind U.C.C. §2-713 and analyzes whether monetary damages actually achieve deterrence or full compensation in contract contexts.

shared_topics.topic: whether and how remedial rules should be changed by interpretation versus statutory amendment
shared_topics.justification: Both articles weigh the choice between leaving statutory text intact and reshaping outcomes through interpretation or common-law paths: Paper A explores statutory and common-law avenues to operationalize disgorgement for emoluments, whereas Paper B resists repeal of §2-713 and advocates interpretive strategies to adapt the statute to modern commercial practice.

shared_topics.topic: using historical and doctrinal foundations to justify remedial interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Both works ground their remedial proposals in historical and doctrinal inquiry: Paper A invokes constitutional text and the Framers' goals to delimit emoluments remedies, while Paper B surveys the U.C.C.'s historical roots and pre-Code doctrine to question prevailing assumptions about market-price damages.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE FAULT THAT LIES WITHIN OUR CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: how notions of fault/responsibility should determine liability and relief
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates when profits received by public officials should be treated as unlawful emoluments and argues for disgorgement as the appropriate remedy tied to notions of unjust enrichment and culpability; Paper B contends that fault (rather than a strict-liability model) is an indispensable element of contract doctrine that determines when and how parties should be held liable and what relief is appropriate.

shared_topics.topic: normative/theoretical critique of prevailing doctrinal assumptions
shared_topics.justification: Both papers undertake a critical, theory-driven interrogation of widely held doctrinal assumptions—Paper A questions implicit assumptions in emoluments litigation about whether and how constitutional provisions should be enforced and remedied, and Paper B disputes the prevailing myth that contract law is or should be strict liability—each proposing reframings grounded in legal theory and policy.

shared_topics.topic: designing remedies and enforcement to achieve legal objectives (deterrence, fairness, prevention of unjust enrichment)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on which remedy (restitutionary disgorgement) best serves anti-corruption and unjust-enrichment goals in emoluments cases, while Paper B links the proper allocation of fault within contract law to the effective operation of enforcement and remedial regimes that produce fair and deterrent outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the connection between legal rules about wrongdoing and the remedial/ normative aims of law (accountability, deterrence, preventing unjust enrichment)

papers.node_id: 59ohiostlj339!!ARTICLE: Disproportionality and the Law of Consequential Damages: Default Theory and Cognitive Reality
papers.title: ARTICLE: Disproportionality and the Law of Consequential Damages: Default Theory and Cognitive Reality
papers.abstract:
Hadley v. Baxendale's limits on a plaintiff's ability to recover consequential damages resulting from a breach of contract by now are quite familiar. Less familiar, but increasingly important, is an additional limit which focuses on the disproportionality between the contract price charged and the consequential damages which that breach induced. This limit, which has a long history, may be found in the Restatement (Second) of Contracts, and has been adopted by a good many states; moreover, the current draft of revised Article 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code contains it.
Disproportionality is largely, if not entirely, unjustifiable when looked at with the standard economic tools of default rule analysis, in particular problem- solving default analysis and information-forcing default rule analysis. Under either, Hadley by itself is more efficient than Hadley with disproportionality, at least under the great majority of plausible scenarios-those with a high-magnitude, low- probability risk.
Standard default theory, however, assumes that economic actors will behave rationally. Recent work in cognitive psychology and experimental economics suggests otherwise. Even seasoned businesspeople will frequently underestimate remote risk, which would cause them to charge too low a premium for bearing the risk.
