The types of risk that are most prone to underestimation-those that the promisor finds infrequent, remote, obscure, and unfamiliar-are the ones that are hence most appropriate for a disproportionality test, though one that focuses on the disparity between the size of the risk and the size of the premium charged to bear it.
Hadley v. Baxendaleis probably the one case that every common-law lawyer may be assumed to have read.Its facts-a miller sent his brokenmillshaft for repair, and the carrier's delay cost him lost profits from the mill's closure-may be all too familiar, evoking Kingsfieldian memories of a first-year contracts class. More importantly, we still look to Hadley as the key to the law of consequential damages, with every law student at some point learning the two tests from Hadley: that a party seeking consequential damages must show either (1) that the damages flowed naturally from the breach of contract, or (2) that the damages, though not flowing naturally, were nevertheless foreseeable by the contracting parties at the time of contracting.And, as usual in contract law, we can look to the Uniform Commercial Code (U.C.C.) and the Restatement (Second) of Contracts for clear statements of familiar black-letter law.
Or can we? Consider first the Restatement (Second). True, the pertinent section- number 351-starts with something like the test we know and love.Its first subsection starts with an oddly negative version of a foreseeability test: "Damages are not recoverable for loss that the party in breach did not have reason to foresee as a probable result of the breach when the contract was made."Of course, foreseeability is an elusive term, with its meaning dependent upon the legal context in which it is used.So the next subsection defines a foreseeable loss as one that "follows from the breach (a) in the ordinary course of events, or (b) as a result of special circumstances, beyond the ordinary course of events, that the party in breach had reason to know."Put together, these subsections amount to little more than Hadley, somewhatloosened, with the two familiar tests in the familiar order. But then we come to the third subsection, which may surprise even those who remember clearly their contracts class. There we get a limit on the two familiar tests: that even foreseeable consequential damages may not be recoverable if the court "concludes that in the circumstances justice so requires in order to avoid disproportionate compensation."What is this? Surely nothing from Hadley. Nor does the comment orient us any better, with its references to the informality of dealing and the commercial nature of the parties as factors in determining whether liability should be placed on the promisor.
Perplexed, we flip quickly to Article 2 of the U.C.C. There we breathe a sigh of relief, seeing something like the traditional Hadley rule firmly in place.But, aware that Article 2 is being revised, and now wary of over- reliance on our recollections, we look up the current draft of Article 2.What do we find when we see the revised text? The disproportionality language from the Restatement (Second).
Now, wait just a moment. For a case so well known as Hadley, and a doctrine so firmly established, this review has turned up more surprises than one would have thought. After all, contracts classes usually do not reach this disproportionality analysis,and the assiduous reader of law reviews-if anysuch person exists-would have little to recall on the issue.So is disproportionality a weird academic fancy, of little interest to practical lawyers? Actually, no. Bear in mind that revised Article 2 of the U.C.C. is likely to contain disproportionality as a part of its rules on consequential damages.The U.C.C. is not merely precatory; it is the law of all our common-law states.Should the revision enjoy the popularity of the original, then virtually all domestic sellers of goods will have to face this rule.And we finddisproportionality used more and more at home. Cases of this sort appear as far back as Roman times, and over two dozen times in the last two decades.
So perhaps it is time to pay some attention to disproportionality. Consequential damages for breach of contract are so important an element of contract remedies that if defendants can invoke disproportionality to have these damages reduced or effaced, they can significantly limit this major source of liability. It thus becomes important to know just when disproportionality analysis may properly be invoked. Unfortunately, there seems to be no consensus here. The writers on disproportionality tend to view it as more or less an equitable limitation on consequential damages, with all the flexibility and vagueness that this invocation of equity suggests, and the Restatement (Second) and the case law provide scarcely more guidance.
Hence this Article. Part II briefly traces the history of disproportionality analysis in contract remedies and describes the current state of the law and literature. Part III looks at disproportionality from the vantage of default rule theory; because the law of consequential damages is almost entirely composed of default rules, disproportionality is sensible to the extent that it makes a sensible default rule. As we shall see, though, the case for disproportionality under classic default rule theory is slight at best. An unconstrained rule would probably prove highly inefficient in practice, and it is hard, if not impossible, to define a class of cases for which disproportionality would prove efficient.
This rather gloomy scenario does not, however, end our analysis. Part IV employs modern cognitive psychology to provide and define a role for disproportionality as an adjunct to Hadley. Standard default rule theory tends to assume, as does the bulk of microeconomic analysis, that economic agents are basically rational-that they employ a coherent set of preferences for risk, and that they use these preferences consistently and efficiently, maximizing their gains to the extent possible. But, as a good many empirical studies have shown, these assumptions are often, perhaps usually, ill-founded. In fact, we carry around a good many departures from rational choice theory. For example, most people tend to undervalue remote risks; overvalue vivid data and undervalue drab data; take risks to avoid loss, but avoid them to protect gains; and many others.
These cognitive biases greatly affect our response to risk, which is at the center of much of law. Hence the recent efflorescence of legal literatureemploying cognitive analysis.Oddly, though, relatively little of it has dealt with its implications for contract and commercial law-oddly, because much of the purpose of contracts in practice is to diminish and allocate risks of market shifts, product and labor scarcity, and the like. If, contrary to the assumptions of standard law-and-economics analysts, those who enter into contracts cannot be assumed to act rationally, in the sense of making coherent decisions to maximize wealth, perhaps the law's expectations should be adjusted. More particularly, what if parties to a contract systematically tend to undervalue remote risk-the sort of risk at the core of disproportionality analysis? Then the law of consequential damages might properly take into account the possibility that these remote risks might not have been allocated to the breaching party, even though they were foreseeable. If the parties undervalue the risk, they will not assign it a large enough risk premium. The party bearing the risk would thus not be sufficiently compensated if it had to bear the full risk. This undervaluation is the focus of Part IV, which surveys the data supporting its presence and its varying strength and endurance.
Part V considers just where disproportionality analysis might sensibly be used. It ought not be ubiquitous; its presence adds greatly to commercial uncertainty and hence commercial cost, and in any case there are a good many types of contracting parties that should be assumed to have dealt satisfactorily with remote risk. Rather, its use should largely be confined to those breachers who deal but infrequently with the risk in question, who lack substantial experience with the risk, and for whom the risk is insufficiently salient to overcome the natural tendency to underestimate remote risk. Interestingly, this result does in fact explain most modern disproportionality decisions, but runs flatly against many of the earliest such cases-including a Cardozo opinion thathelped trigger, with some delay, the modern explosion in disproportionality.

questions.question: Whether imposing a legal limit on recovery of consequential damages that are disproportionately large relative to the contract price produces greater economic efficiency than leaving liability governed solely by a foreseeability-based rule.

Whether systematic cognitive biases-particularly the tendency to undervalue low-probability, high-magnitude risks-lead contracting parties to underprice risk, and thus whether a disproportionality-based limitation would correct such behavioral market failures.

Which kinds of transactions or contracting parties (for example, infrequent or inexperienced actors versus sophisticated, repeat players) should appropriately be subject to a disproportionality limitation to balance risk allocation, fairness, and commercial certainty.

matched_themes: How should default liability rules interact with parties' freedom to allocate risks by contract and duties of disclosure to achieve efficient and fair risk allocation?
Should parties be presumptively permitted to contractually specify nonstandard damage remedies, or should courts retain authority to impose defaults?
Should courts limit recoverable consequential damages that are grossly disproportionate to the contract price, and would such limits promote economic efficiency?
Should courts police and limit supracompensatory contractual remedies (penalty-like clauses), or does allowing parties to contract for such terms respect autonomy and promote efficient contracting?
How should remedial and enforcement rules be structured to achieve efficient behavior when populations include both internalizers and externalizers?
Can courts reliably determine ex post whether a breach would increase social welfare so that remedy choice can be used to promote efficiency?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
Do parties and courts actually choose heterogeneous, context-tailored damage provisions in contracting, and under what conditions would such customization be voluntarily chosen or socially desirable?
Do limits on recoverable damages (foreseeability, certainty, avoidability) substantially reduce awards below full compensation, and should courts liberalize those limits?
Can reflective remedies or penalty-adjustment devices that 'reflect' excess conduct across uncertain legal caps produce better ex-ante incentives when legal standards are uncertain?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 100yalelj369!!ARTICLE: The Myth that Promisees Prefer Supracompensatory Remedies: An Analysis of Contracting for Damage Measures.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Myth that Promisees Prefer Supracompensatory Remedies: An Analysis of Contracting for Damage Measures.

shared_topics.topic: limits on contractual remedies that produce supracompensatory outcomes (penalty clauses, punitive damages, liquidated damages, specific performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the doctrinal rules that bar or police penalty clauses, punitive awards, and specific-performance clauses and argues courts should relax ex ante/ex post policing because promisees do not prefer supracompensatory remedies; Paper B examines the doctrinally similar disproportionality limitation on consequential damages and assesses when courts should deny recovery to avoid disproportionate compensation.

shared_topics.topic: the justification of judicial policing vs leaving remedial terms as defaults (efficiency and default-rule analysis)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A weighs normative and positive premises and questions the need for judicial review of liquidated-damage and specific-performance clauses on efficiency and default-rule grounds; Paper B applies classic default-rule theory to disproportionality and then modifies that analysis using behavioral findings to determine when a legal default limiting damages is efficient.

shared_topics.topic: ex ante versus ex post assessment of damages clauses and parties' estimates of risk and loss
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes ex ante and ex post branches of the liquidated-damages rule and critiques courts' post-hoc reassessment of parties' estimates of harm; Paper B similarly contrasts foreseeability/prior allocation of risk with later assessment of disproportionality, focusing on how parties' ex ante pricing of risk may be inadequate.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of parties' bounded rationality or mistaken beliefs about risk on optimal remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A challenges the positive assumption that promisees will seek supracompensatory remedies and discusses how error (e.g., misestimates or collection costs) should affect judicial intervention; Paper B brings cognitive psychology and experimental economics to show parties systematically misestimate remote risks and argues the law should account for those biases when deciding whether to apply a disproportionality constraint.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of remote, low-probability/high-magnitude risks and when the law should limit recovery for such risks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses situations where party estimates of future harm may err and whether courts should prevent parties from contracting for remedies that would exploit such errors; Paper B focuses on the class of remote, infrequent, and non-salient risks that parties tend to undervalue and argues disproportionality should be available to limit liability in those contexts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 80ohiostlj1149!!ARTICLE: Fixer Upper: Buyer Deposits in Residential Real Estate Transactions
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Fixer Upper: Buyer Deposits in Residential Real Estate Transactions

shared_topics.topic: normative evaluation of contractual damages doctrines as default rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A assesses disproportionality and Hadley through default-rule and law-and-economics frameworks (arguing classic default theory poorly justifies disproportionality), and Paper B interrogates liquidated-damages/deposit doctrines against their stated compensatory purpose and argues doctrinal and statutory reform, treating these doctrines as default allocations of risk that merit normative scrutiny.

shared_topics.topic: whether contractual terms (deposits or consequential-damages rules) actually allocate risk and reflect expected harm
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on whether consequential-damage rules (including a disproportionality limit) properly allocate low-probability/high-loss risks between parties, while Paper B shows earnest-money deposits commonly bear little relation to sellers' actual losses and therefore fail to accurately allocate or predict harm.

shared_topics.topic: judicial treatment and standards for evaluating enforceability of damages clauses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how courts and instruments (Restatement, UCC revisions) incorporate a disproportionality/equitable limit on recoverable consequential damages, and Paper B documents courts' routine enforcement (or rubber-stamping) of deposit/liquidated-damages clauses and critiques the doctrinal tests used to justify that enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: the need to adjust legal rules to real-world and cognitive realities of contracting parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A marshals cognitive psychology and experimental economics to argue parties systematically misperceive remote risks and thus supports a limited role for disproportionality to protect against misallocated risk, while Paper B emphasizes real-world market practices and informational asymmetries in residential transactions and calls for statutory consumer-protective adjustments to deposit law.

shared_topics.topic: critique of the gap between doctrinal theory and market practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the disconnect between standard economic (rational-actor) justifications for defaults and observed behavior (undervaluation of remote risk), and Paper B highlights the disconnect between the theoretical purpose of liquidated damages and the actual, market-driven use of deposits that often bear no relation to sellers' damages.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 84nclrev1927!!ARTICLE: A BRIDGE, A TAX REVOLT, AND THE STRUGGLE TO INDUSTRIALIZE: A COMMENT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A BRIDGE, A TAX REVOLT, AND THE STRUGGLE TO INDUSTRIALIZE: A COMMENT

shared_topics.topic: limits and measurement of damages for breach of contract (anticipatory breach, mitigation, consequential damages, and disproportionality)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the Luten Bridge decision's rule on anticipatory breach and the restrictive measure of damages and duty to mitigate, while Paper B interrogates limits on recovery for consequential damages (Hadley) and the added constraint of disproportionality in measuring recoverable losses.

shared_topics.topic: judicial development and doctrinal evolution of contract remedies (role of courts, Restatements, and the UCC)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how judges and case law produce and adapt American common-law contract doctrines (illustrated by Luten Bridge), and Paper B traces doctrinal change in consequential-damages law through cases, the Restatement (Second), and proposed revisions to Article 2 of the UCC.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk between contracting parties and the normative justification for rules that reassign losses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the obligation to perform versus the duty to pay damages (and related migration of contract principles into property law) as questions about who bears contractual risk, while Paper B analyzes whether disproportionality should operate as a default rule to correct inefficient or misallocated risk-bearing, especially given behavioral tendencies.

shared_topics.topic: use of historical and contextual facts to explain why breaches occur and why doctrines arise
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates the county's breach in the economic and political history of the New South to explain the parties' conduct and the case's significance, and Paper B situates disproportionality within a longue durée of case law (even Roman antecedents) and commercial practice to explain the doctrine's emergence and variation.

shared_topics.topic: the pedagogical and canonical status of landmark cases in shaping understanding of contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends the case method and shows how the Luten Bridge case is edited in teaching to emphasize certain doctrines, while Paper B treats Hadley v. Baxendale as the canonical pedagogical touchstone for consequential-damages rules and criticizes how standard teaching omits significant doctrinal nuances like disproportionality.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2013uilllrev151!!ARTICLE: CAN'T BUY ME LOVE: MONETARY VERSUS IN-KIND REMEDIES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CAN'T BUY ME LOVE: MONETARY VERSUS IN-KIND REMEDIES

shared_topics.topic: adequacy of monetary damages to make injured parties whole versus in-kind relief
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically tests and finds a strong preference for in-kind remedies, arguing monetary awards often fail to restore the claimant's welfare; Paper B interrogates limits on monetary consequential damages (disproportionality), effectively questioning when money is an adequate substitute for losses caused by breach.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal criteria for when courts should require performance or limit monetary recovery (specific performance, Hadley foreseeability, disproportionality, option-theory)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A challenges the option-theory and urges more liberal use of specific performance and injunctions instead of defaulting to money; Paper B analyzes Hadley and the Restatement/UCC disproportionality clause to specify when courts should curtail consequential monetary awards and thereby indirectly when non-monetary expectations ought to be protected.

shared_topics.topic: use of behavioral and experimental evidence to revise law-and-economics assumptions about contracting parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A provides experimental data on laypeople and businesspeople's remedial preferences to challenge orthodox assumptions of indifference between money and in-kind remedies; Paper B draws on cognitive psychology and experimental findings about risk underestimation to justify a doctrinal exception (disproportionality) that standard rational-actor default theory would not support.

shared_topics.topic: implications for default-rule design in contract remedies weighing efficiency against unrecognized preference or behavioral costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues remedy defaults should account for the welfare loss when plaintiffs prefer in-kind relief and suggests premiums or more in-kind awards; Paper B examines default-rule theory and contends that cognitive biases may warrant a limited default (disproportionality) to avoid inefficient allocations of remote risks.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 93valrev59!!ARTICLE: THE MISSING INTEREST: RESTORATION OF THE CONTRACTUAL EQUIVALENCE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE MISSING INTEREST: RESTORATION OF THE CONTRACTUAL EQUIVALENCE

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal recognition of nontraditional contract remedies (disproportionality and the restoration interest)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes 'disproportionality' as an additional, often overlooked limitation on recovery of consequential damages beyond Hadley, assessing when courts should invoke it; Paper B likewise argues for doctrinal recognition of a previously neglected remedial goal—the 'restoration of contractual equivalence'—and recommends more systematic availability of such restoration remedies.

shared_topics.topic: use of law-and-economics / default-rule efficiency analysis to assess remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates disproportionality using default-rule theory and information‑forcing defaults to ask whether adding disproportionality increases efficiency, while Paper B subjects the proposed restoration interest to economic-efficiency analysis (alongside other normative theories) to justify its adoption and scope.

shared_topics.topic: how remedies allocate risk and loss when performance deviates or harms are nonstandard
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how foreseeability and disproportionality should operate to allocate high‑magnitude, low‑probability or remote risks (and whether premiums reflect those risks), whereas Paper B examines how restoration remedies reallocate losses from partial, defective, or delayed performance so as to preserve contractual equivalence rather than strictly enforcing expectation or restitution outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the relevance of parties' subjective valuations, contracting behavior, and transactional context to remedy design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws on cognitive psychology to show parties systematically undervalue remote risks and argues remedial rules (disproportionality) should account for that behavioral reality; Paper B emphasizes parties' subjective valuations, cooperative relationships, and practical transaction costs in arguing restoration remedies better track parties' expectations and performance incentives.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 87tullrev1075!!SYMPOSIUM: MODERN MARINE INSURANCE: COVERAGES, CURRENT ISSUES, AND CONNECTIONS:Reform of the Insurance Law of England and Wales - Separate Laws for the Different Needs of Businesses and Consumers
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: MODERN MARINE INSURANCE: COVERAGES, CURRENT ISSUES, AND CONNECTIONS:Reform of the Insurance Law of England and Wales - Separate Laws for the Different Needs of Businesses and Consumers

shared_topics.topic: limits on recovery of consequential damages and doctrinal tests for liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes doctrinal limits on recovery (Hadley foreseeability and the Restatement/UCC 'disproportionality' carve‑out) and when courts should deny consequential damages; Paper B substantively addresses consequential damages in the context of business insurance and how proposed statutory reforms would treat insurer liability for consequential losses.

shared_topics.topic: economic and efficiency analysis of legal rule reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates disproportionality through default‑rule economic theory and behavioral economics (arguing standard efficiency analysis is incomplete without cognitive biases), while Paper B assesses proposed insurance‑law reforms in light of economic consequences for commerce and the U.K. economy.

shared_topics.topic: whether legal standards should be tailored to types of parties (consumer vs sophisticated/commercial)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues disproportionality should be applied selectively — focused on parties inexperienced with or inattentive to a risk — rather than universally; Paper B directly debates creating separate statutory rules for consumers and businesses in insurance law and the costs/benefits of differentiated regimes.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk via foreseeability, disclosure, and warranty rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on foreseeability as the traditional mechanism for allocating consequential risks and highlights parties' systematic underestimation of remote risks; Paper B engages with disclosure and warranty doctrines (and reform proposals) as mechanisms that allocate risk between insureds and insurers.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 28gastulrev559!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT BREACHES AND THE CRIMINAL/CIVIL DIVIDE: AN INTER-COMMON LAW ANALYSIS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT BREACHES AND THE CRIMINAL/CIVIL DIVIDE: AN INTER-COMMON LAW ANALYSIS

shared_topics.topic: economic-efficiency explanations for why contract breaches get monetary (not criminal) sanctions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A applies law-and-economics reasoning (deterrence and efficiency) to explain why contract breaches, like torts, are typically met with monetary damages rather than imprisonment; Paper B uses default-rule economic analysis to evaluate whether a disproportionality limit on consequential damages is economically justified and how it affects efficient risk allocation.

shared_topics.topic: foreseeability, risk allocation, and consequential damages in contract breach remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A equalizes harms across tort, contract, and crime scenarios to probe why contract violations yield only monetary recovery and discusses how contractual obligations allocate losses; Paper B analyzes Hadley v. Baxendale and the Restatement/UCC rules on foreseeability and disproportionality to determine when consequential damages should be recoverable and how risks are or should be allocated between parties.

shared_topics.topic: limits of classical rational-actor assumptions and the role of moral/behavioral considerations in shaping contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques purely economic or purely moral accounts and introduces a voluntariness distinction to reconcile moral blameworthiness with contractual contexts; Paper B rejects standard rational-choice predictions for contracting parties, invoking cognitive psychology (systematic underestimation of remote risks) to justify a behavioral amendment (targeted disproportionality) to classical default-rule prescriptions.

shared_topics.topic: argument for doctrinal refinement—tailoring legal rules for contract breaches rather than blanket categorization
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues the criminal/civil divide cannot be fully explained without distinguishing voluntary versus non‑voluntary obligations and integrating models to refine when punishment is appropriate; Paper B likewise argues disproportionality should not be a ubiquitous equitable fudge but instead be constrained to contexts (infrequent, non‑salient risks, inexperienced parties) where behavioral realities make standard defaults inappropriate.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1569!!ARTICLE: WHY BREACH OF CONTRACT MAY NOT BE IMMORAL GIVEN THE INCOMPLETENESS OF CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: WHY BREACH OF CONTRACT MAY NOT BE IMMORAL GIVEN THE INCOMPLETENESS OF CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: contractual incompleteness and unforeseen contingencies in assessing breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that many breaches arise from contingencies that incomplete contracts did not intend to govern, and thus may not be immoral; Paper B explores how the law (foreseeability and disproportionality doctrines) responds when consequential harms arise from risks that parties did not or could not meaningfully anticipate.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and mispricing of remote risks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats breach as potentially permissible where contracts failed to allocate a particular contingency (i.e., the risk was not assigned); Paper B analyzes how parties systematically underprice remote or unfamiliar risks and how the law might correct misallocation via a disproportionality test to avoid imposing uncompensated burdens.

shared_topics.topic: normative justification for permitting breach or limiting remedies (justice/equity)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages the moral question whether breach should be condemned when contracts are incomplete and suggests permissibility in many cases; Paper B examines whether equitable limits (disproportionality) on consequential damages are normatively justified to avoid disproportionate compensation and to achieve just outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: role of parties' knowledge, intent, and foreseeability in determining liability and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on whether a promisor intended the contract/promise to cover the contingency that produced the breach, while Paper B centers on Hadley-style foreseeability and whether the breaching party had reason to know of special circumstances, using those factors to limit damages.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 71califlrev56!!ARTICLE: The Collateral Source Rule and Contract Damages.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Collateral Source Rule and Contract Damages.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of loss and risk between contracting parties
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how losses should be allocated when a breach occurs: Paper A examines whether promissors should bear low-probability/high-magnitude risks (and when a disproportionality limit should reallocate such risks), while Paper B examines whether the defendant or an independent collateral source should be treated as the primary obligor for compensating contractual losses.

shared_topics.topic: normative and policy justifications for limiting or adjusting contract damages
shared_topics.justification: Both articles evaluate the justification for doctrines that restrict full recovery—Paper A critiques disproportionality under standard default-rule (efficiency) analysis and then reconsiders it under cognitive-psychology informed policy, while Paper B surveys the policy rationales for the collateral source rule and whether those rationales warrant different treatment in contract versus tort.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal tools that modify a plaintiff's net recovery (avoiding windfalls or double recovery)
shared_topics.justification: Each paper focuses on legal mechanisms that change the plaintiff's ultimate recovery: Paper A studies the disproportionality doctrine as a means to reduce consequential damages when compensation would be extreme relative to contract price, and Paper B analyzes the collateral source rule and subrogation as doctrines that either preserve or reassign independent payments in measuring contract damages.

shared_topics.topic: the relevance of the type or characteristics of the loss in applying remedial doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Both works stress that the nature of the harm affects rule application—Paper A emphasizes characteristics like remoteness, magnitude, and salience (e.g., rare high-loss risks) in deciding when disproportionality should apply, while Paper B distinguishes personal injury, property, and economic loss (and considers breach type) in assessing whether and how the collateral source rule should operate.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 73washulq145!!ARTICLE: THE FALLACY OF FULL COMPENSATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE FALLACY OF FULL COMPENSATION

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal limits on awarding full or consequential compensation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the 'disproportionality' constraint that courts use to limit recovery of consequential contract damages, while Paper B examines the legal reluctance to award full-compensation 'prohibitory' remedies (specific performance, injunctions) and surveys doctrines (irreparable injury, uniqueness) that restrict such remedies.

shared_topics.topic: whether economic-efficiency and transaction-cost arguments justify denying full remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates disproportionality against standard default-rule and law-and-economics efficiency reasoning (finding little support absent behavioral departures), and Paper B assesses and critiques transactions-cost and efficiency defenses for favoring damages over full compensatory remedies.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and the role of foreseeability versus risk-imposition in remedy design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how parties price and allocate remote risks (foreseeability, underpriced risk premiums) and proposes disproportionality as a check when risk is underestimated, while Paper B contrasts harm-based damages with risk-based prohibitory remedies and interrogates when courts should prohibit risk-imposing transactions rather than merely price them.

shared_topics.topic: criteria for when exceptional, nonstandard remedies should apply
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes limiting disproportionality relief to situations involving infrequent or non-salient risks and inexperienced parties, and Paper B develops normative and practical frameworks (and relegation doctrines) for when prohibitory/full-compensation remedies are appropriate versus when damages should remain primary.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 63notredamelrev247!!ARTICLE:A Newly Identified Contract Unconscionability: Unconsionability of Remedy
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:A Newly Identified Contract Unconscionability: Unconsionability of Remedy

shared_topics.topic: disproportionality as a doctrinal limit on consequential damages
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze the doctrine that courts may limit or refuse recovery of foreseeable consequential damages when those damages are disproportionately large compared to the contract price, treating that limit as a significant constraint on Hadley-style recovery.

shared_topics.topic: the role of Restatement §351(3) and revised UCC Article 2 in endorsing disproportionality
shared_topics.justification: Both discuss the appearance of disproportionality language in Restatement (Second) §351(3) and in drafts of revised UCC Article 2, evaluating the provision's novelty, scope, and likely practical impact on commercial law.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between disproportionality and traditional rules (foreseeability, certainty, mitigation)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers trace how courts historically used foreseeability, certainty, and mitigation doctrines to achieve similar limiting results and debate whether §351(3) simply labels an existing practice or creates a distinct, overt ground for curtailing damages.

shared_topics.topic: competing normative justifications and criteria for invoking the limit (efficiency vs fairness/unconscionability; when to apply it)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the question whether disproportionality should be justified on efficiency/default-rule grounds or as a form of remedy-focused unconscionability to avoid extreme unfairness, and both offer—or evaluate—criteria for when courts should apply the doctrine (e.g., extreme disparity between price and liability, allocation of risk at contracting, relative experience and salience of the risk).

compared_to.partner_node_id: 84texlrev831!!Article: Specific Performance Versus Damages for Breach of Contract: An Economic Analysis
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Specific Performance Versus Damages for Breach of Contract: An Economic Analysis

shared_topics.topic: parties' misvaluation or underestimation of risk/valuation and its effect on remedy choice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses cognitive psychology and experimental economics to argue that contracting parties systematically undervalue remote or unfamiliar risks, which supports a disproportionality constraint on consequential damages; Paper B shows that underestimation of the value of performance (or outside-bid uncertainty) can make expectation damages produce joint losses and thus favors specific performance for conveyance contracts.

shared_topics.topic: economic/default-rule analysis to choose or justify remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates disproportionality through standard default-rule and information-forcing default analyses (then supplements with behavioral findings), while Paper B uses an ex ante joint-value maximizing economic framework to determine when parties would prefer damages versus specific performance.

shared_topics.topic: limits and adequacy of expectation/damages remedies and doctrinal responses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates a doctrinal limit (disproportionality) that restricts recovery of consequential damages despite foreseeability; Paper B analyzes when expectation damages are inadequate (or lead to inefficiency) and when legal doctrine should instead grant specific performance.

shared_topics.topic: the role of foreseeability, knowledge, and informational asymmetries in allocating loss
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on Hadley-style foreseeability and 'special circumstances' versus a disproportionality test tied to what parties knew or should have priced, while Paper B examines informational uncertainty about outside bids and parties' beliefs about value as critical determinants of whether damages or specific performance better allocates loss.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 23uclalrev501!!ARTICLE: THE HISTORICAL CONCEPTION OF A LEASE FOR YEARS *
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE HISTORICAL CONCEPTION OF A LEASE FOR YEARS *

shared_topics.topic: historical evolution of legal doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the development of lease law from medieval writs to modern doctrines, showing how remedies and classifications changed over centuries; Paper B similarly traces the history of disproportionality limits from Roman times through Hadley, the Restatement, and the UCC, using historical development to explain contemporary rules.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal innovation to fill gaps when existing categories fail
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how new writs and remedies were invented because existing property categories (freehold vs chattel) left lessees unprotected; Paper B shows how courts and restatements have added a disproportionality constraint beyond Hadley to address situations the traditional foreseeability tests leave unresolved.

shared_topics.topic: design of remedial rules to balance competing risks of liability and under-protection
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes trade-offs—fear of double liability for third parties versus inadequate protection of lessees—and how that shaped remedies; Paper B analyzes trade-offs between placing loss on breachers versus limiting liability through disproportionality, using efficiency and fairness reasons to justify limiting consequential damages.

shared_topics.topic: skepticism of formal classifications and emphasis on pragmatic considerations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that labels like 'freehold' versus 'contract' overstate what mattered, with practical concerns driving outcomes; Paper B critiques purely formal economic default-rule justifications and instead grounds disproportionality in cognitive and practical realities of how parties perceive and price risk.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 85tullrev413!!ARTICLE: Convergence in Contort: Landlord Liability for Defective Premises in Comparative Perspective
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Convergence in Contort: Landlord Liability for Defective Premises in Comparative Perspective

shared_topics.topic: foreseeability/proximate‑cause as a doctrinal limit on recovery
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how the contract/tort classification (implied warranty of habitability versus negligence) changes which harms are recoverable and how doctrines like proximate cause and foreseeability operate differently across those labels; Paper B analyzes Hadley-style foreseeability and how courts and restatements use foreseeability (and an added disproportionality check) to limit recovery for consequential damages.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk between parties through form and remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that treating landlord duties as contract versus tort allocates risks (strict liability, privity, who bears loss) differently between landlords and tenants; Paper B studies how disproportionality and premium pricing concerns allocate rare, high-magnitude risks between promisor and promisee and when the law should relieve parties of extraordinary liability.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal limits on damages and their policy justification (e.g., exclusion of non‑pecuniary loss, disproportionality, exculpation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores how contractual labeling can bar recovery for pain and suffering or be defeated by exculpatory clauses, producing unequal remedial outcomes, while Paper B investigates judicial and Restatement/UCC limits (disproportionality) that reduce or deny consequential damages and asks when those limits are justified.

shared_topics.topic: reconceptualizing doctrine to better align law with policy and cognitive realities
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes recasting landlord liability as a hybrid 'contort' to free the obligation from rigid contract/tort taxonomy and better achieve policy goals; Paper B argues that traditional default‑rule (rational actor) analysis misjustifies disproportionality and proposes adjusting remedial default rules to account for cognitive biases in risk perception.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 94tullrev925!!SYMPOSIUM: Contract Lore as Heuristic Starting Points
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: Contract Lore as Heuristic Starting Points

shared_topics.topic: behavioral critique of the rational-actor model in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A marshals cognitive psychology and experimental economics to show that parties systematically misperceive remote risks (undervaluing them), undermining standard default-rule analyses that assume rational actors; Paper B engages cognitive explanations too—criticizing Hillman's invocation of cognitive dissonance for persistence of 'contract lore' and offering alternative behavioral-framed accounts (heuristics) for why doctrinal beliefs persist.

shared_topics.topic: the validity and limits of traditional remedial doctrines (foreseeability/Hadley and expectation damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reevaluates Hadley v. Baxendale, the Restatement, and proposed UCC language by introducing a disproportionality limit on recoverable consequential damages and questioning the sufficiency of classic foreseeability rules; Paper B interrogates commonly held beliefs about remedies (e.g., expectation damages) and other staple contract doctrines, labeling some as myths or oversimplifications and urging closer scrutiny.

shared_topics.topic: the role of heuristics/default rules in doctrinal practice and instruction
shared_topics.justification: Paper B explicitly frames 'contract lore' as heuristic starting points useful for teaching and initial legal analysis; Paper A analyzes the law of consequential damages as composed largely of default rules and considers whether an added doctrinal heuristic (disproportionality) could correct behavioral biases in contracting.

shared_topics.topic: implications for doctrinal reform and how to justify changes in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that empirical cognitive evidence should inform when and how disproportionality limits are applied (and supports targeted doctrinal change, including UCC revision); Paper B treats identification of 'lore' versus justified doctrine as a tool for prompting law reform and discusses criteria for when doctrinal statements warrant revision.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83nyulrev1679!!ARTICLE: EFFICIENT BREACH THEORY THROUGH THE LOOKING GLASS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EFFICIENT BREACH THEORY THROUGH THE LOOKING GLASS

shared_topics.topic: economic (law-and-economics) evaluation of contract damages rules
shared_topics.justification: Both papers apply economic theory to assess remedial rules for breach: Paper A uses efficiency/expectation-damages analysis to question the disallowance of awards to breaching parties (negative damages), while Paper B applies default-rule economic analysis to evaluate the justification for a disproportionality limit on consequential damages.

shared_topics.topic: how remedies allocate surplus and risk between promisor and promisee after breach
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the question of who should capture the gains or bear losses from breach—Paper A asks why the breaching party is barred from recovering benefits when breach confers a net gain and whether awarding such benefits improves incentives, and Paper B examines whether consequential losses were properly allocated given the contract price and whether disproportionality should limit recovery when risks were mispriced.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between default legal rules and express contractual allocations (contract design)
shared_topics.justification: Both investigate the degree to which parties can or should contract around remedial defaults: Paper A analyzes the doctrinal impediments and alternatives (express negative-damages clauses, liquidated damages, specific performance) to the default expectation remedy, while Paper B treats disproportionality as a default rule and asks when parties could or should have allocated remote risk explicitly.

shared_topics.topic: the effects of imperfect information or cognitive limitations on efficient breach and damage allocation
shared_topics.justification: Both papers consider information problems: Paper A studies complete- versus incomplete-information settings and how allowing negative damages might improve ex ante investment and ex post breach decisions, and Paper B draws on cognitive psychology to argue parties systematically undervalue remote risks, which can justify a disproportionality constraint on consequential damages.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 55amjcompl721!!ARTICLE: Why No "Efficient Breach" in the Civil Law?: A Comparative Assessment of the Doctrine of Efficient Breach of Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Why No "Efficient Breach" in the Civil Law?: A Comparative Assessment of the Doctrine of Efficient Breach of Contract

shared_topics.topic: damages as the functional substitute for performance and their effect on breach incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the 'efficient breach' claim that expectation damages allow profitable breaches while leaving injured parties no worse off, and Paper B analyzes how rules on consequential damages (including limits like disproportionality) change the incentives to allocate risk and to perform versus breach.

shared_topics.topic: economic (law-and-economics / default-rule) evaluation of contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates the efficient breach doctrine within the law-and-economics tradition and contrasts legal systems by their structural support for efficiency reasoning, while Paper B explicitly applies default-rule and economic analysis to assess whether disproportionality is an efficient limitation on consequential damages.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal rules should respond to non‑legal realities (cultural or cognitive constraints)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines cultural and institutional obstacles in civil‑law systems (e.g., good faith, pacta sunt servanda) that make efficiency‑focused doctrines less attractive, and Paper B uses findings from cognitive psychology about biased risk perception to argue for doctrinal adjustments (disproportionality) that depart from standard rational‑actor assumptions.

shared_topics.topic: allocation and pricing of risk (foreseeability, premiums, and adequacy of compensation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that efficient breach requires the breaching party to be able to compensate the non‑breaching party (i.e., correct allocation/payment for risk), and Paper B examines how parties may misprice low‑probability high‑magnitude risks and how disproportionality tests relate to whether contractual prices/premiums adequately allocated those risks.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 116wvalrev363!!ARTICLE: HYPOTHETICAL EFFICIENCY IS NOT GROUNDS FOR BREACH
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: HYPOTHETICAL EFFICIENCY IS NOT GROUNDS FOR BREACH

shared_topics.topic: the normative role of economic efficiency in contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly challenges the claim that efficiency (the ‘efficient breach’ thesis) can morally justify breaching contracts, while Paper B evaluates whether efficiency-based default-rule analysis justifies a disproportionality limit on consequential damages, treating efficiency as a central justificatory criterion.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy and limits of damages as the sole remedy for breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks whether payment of compensatory damages renders breach morally permissible and rejects that consequence as a blanket justification, while Paper B examines legal limits (disproportionality/Hadley) on awarding consequential damages and whether damages adequately allocate risk in practice.

shared_topics.topic: the status and scope of implied/default contract terms versus express provisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques efforts to imply an ‘efficiency’ obligation or hypothetical-contract terms into agreements and distinguishes such implied covenants from express terms and good-faith doctrines, while Paper B treats the law of consequential damages as composed of default rules (including Restatement/U.C.C. formulations) and questions when courts should imply limits like disproportionality.

shared_topics.topic: incorporating human behavior, moral norms, or cognitive limitations into doctrinal design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that moral norms from interpersonal relationships (not just economic calculation) should guide business decisions and contractual obligations, while Paper B draws on cognitive psychology to argue that predictable biases (e.g., underestimating remote risks) should inform when disproportionality limits or adjusted default rules are appropriate.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 80brooklynlrev173!!ARTICLE: The Compensation Myth and U.C.C. Section 2-713
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Compensation Myth and U.C.C. Section 2-713

shared_topics.topic: the normative foundations of contract damages (compensation vs efficiency/deterrence)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers question the standard justification for contract damages: Paper A interrogates whether default-rule/efficiency rationales justify a disproportionality limit and incorporates cognitive biases to show departures from rational-actor assumptions, while Paper B challenges the ‘compensation myth’ behind the market-price/contract-price formula in UCC §2-713 and probes whether monetary awards actually achieve full compensation or efficient deterrence.

shared_topics.topic: how default rules and statutory remedies allocate risk between contracting parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes consequential-damages doctrines (Hadley and disproportionality) through default-rule theory and information-forcing analysis to see how rules allocate remote risks, and Paper B scrutinizes §2-713’s market-price remedy as a statutory mechanism for allocating loss when a seller breaches, questioning the assumptions about the relevant market and risk allocation implicit in that remedy.

shared_topics.topic: limits on damages and when courts should adjust or deny awards (foreseeability, disproportionality, market-price adjustments)
shared_topics.justification: Both works engage with doctrinal limits on recovery — Paper A with the Restatement/UCC-inspired disproportionality and Hadley foreseeability constraints on consequential damages, and Paper B with judicial and doctrinal treatment of the market-price/contract-price formula under §2-713 and circumstances in which market damages may over- or under-compensate.

shared_topics.topic: interpretation versus revision of U.C.C. Article 2 and practical consequences for commercial parties and courts
shared_topics.justification: Each article addresses Article 2’s treatment of remedies — Paper A highlights that revised Article 2 adopts a disproportionality provision and examines its practical impact, while Paper B resists statutory repeal and advocates interpretive strategies to adapt §2-713 to contemporary commercial realities, emphasizing the effects of textual change versus judicial interpretation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 70bulrev623!!ARTICLE: EQUITY TRANSFORMED: PRELIMINARY INJUNCTIONS TO REQUIRE THE PAYMENT OF MONEY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EQUITY TRANSFORMED: PRELIMINARY INJUNCTIONS TO REQUIRE THE PAYMENT OF MONEY

shared_topics.topic: reforming remedial doctrines to meet contemporary needs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates whether courts should add or recalibrate a disproportionality constraint on consequential damages, while Paper B argues for expanding equitable practice to allow preliminary injunctions for interim monetary payments; both call for doctrinal change to make remedies fit present-day realities.

shared_topics.topic: judicially-created limits on monetary relief (equity vs default legal rules)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes a judge-invoked disproportionality limitation as a default-rule constraint on contract damages, and Paper B scrutinizes historical equitable limits (e.g., 'no adequate remedy at law') that prevent courts from ordering interim monetary relief—each examines when courts may or should impose extra-statutory limits or alternatives to standard legal damages.

shared_topics.topic: incorporating behavioral and socioeconomic realities into remedial design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A invokes cognitive psychology (systematic underestimation of remote risk) to justify tailoring the scope of consequential damages, while Paper B foregrounds plaintiffs' socioeconomic vulnerability (indigence, uninsured status, social isolation) to justify interim equitable relief; both advocate adjusting remedial rules in light of non‑ideal human behavior and social conditions.

shared_topics.topic: who bears and when they must bear monetary risk or compensation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on which contracting party should bear low-probability, high-loss risks (and how pricing/premia reflect that allocation), whereas Paper B addresses the temporal allocation of monetary burden by proposing that defendants be required to pay portions of expected damages before trial; both grapple with allocating financial responsibility between parties in monetary remedies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 84nclrev1841!!ARTICLE: A BRIDGE, A TAX REVOLT, AND THE STRUGGLE TO INDUSTRIALIZE: THE STORY AND LEGACY OF ROCKINGHAM COUNTY v. LUTEN BRIDGE CO.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A BRIDGE, A TAX REVOLT, AND THE STRUGGLE TO INDUSTRIALIZE: THE STORY AND LEGACY OF ROCKINGHAM COUNTY v. LUTEN BRIDGE CO.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal limits on recovery for breach (mitigation and disproportionality)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze judicially-created limits on contract remedies: Paper A examines Rockingham County v. Luten Bridge Co. as the paradigmatic duty-to-mitigate decision, while Paper B analyzes the separate limit of disproportionality on recovery of consequential damages (as in the Restatement and draft U.C.C.).

shared_topics.topic: economic and risk-allocation rationales for damages rules
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with how damages doctrines allocate risk and affect economic behavior: Paper A situates the Luten dispute within the economic pressures of industrialization and local finance, and Paper B evaluates disproportionality through default-rule economic analysis and behavioral evidence about how parties price (or underprice) remote risks.

shared_topics.topic: the role of canonical cases in shaping contracts doctrine and pedagogy
shared_topics.justification: Both discuss how particular opinions become touchstones in contract law teaching and practice: Paper A traces Luten's elevation into standard contracts casebooks, and Paper B focuses on Hadley v. Baxendale as the archetypal (and widely taught) source for consequential damages doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: historical evolution and socio-political context of contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both articles historicize the development of remedies rules—Paper A by reconstructing the original political, local-government, and industrial context behind Luten, and Paper B by tracing the long history of disproportionality (from early precedent through Restatement and U.C.C. revisions) and situating doctrinal change in broader legal and cognitive developments.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 24geojlegalethics357!!ARTICLE: A Crisis of Confidence and Legal Theory: Why the Economic Downturn Should Help Signal the End of the Doctrine of Efficient Breach
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Crisis of Confidence and Legal Theory: Why the Economic Downturn Should Help Signal the End of the Doctrine of Efficient Breach

shared_topics.topic: limits of law-and-economics rational-actor assumptions in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Both papers problematize standard law-and-economics assumptions that parties are fully rational: Paper A argues the efficient-breach doctrine relies on narrow economic calculus and ignores real human incentives and moral psychology, while Paper B shows default-rule analyses (e.g., Hadley) misfire when cognitive biases (like underestimating remote risks) make contracting parties behave irrationally.

shared_topics.topic: whether compensatory damages adequately allocate risk and make victims whole
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with the adequacy of damages as the primary remedy: Paper A contends compensatory damages under efficient-breach theory fail to fully redress the non-breaching party and produce perverse incentives, and Paper B examines limits on consequential damages (disproportionality) as a response to mismatches between contract price, risk premiums, and the true burden of consequential loss.

shared_topics.topic: the role of trust, social norms, and psychological factors in shaping contractual behavior and legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Both authors emphasize non-price factors that influence contracting outcomes—Paper A foregrounds trust, reciprocity, and social norms as necessary predicates for reliable contracting and market stability, while Paper B draws on cognitive psychology to show how biases (salience, undervaluation of remote risk) should inform when courts apply doctrinal limits like disproportionality.

shared_topics.topic: when and why courts or scholars should constrain efficiency-driven doctrines because of broader systemic effects
shared_topics.justification: Each paper asks whether doctrines justified by narrow efficiency (efficient breach; unconstrained Hadley) should be restrained: Paper A argues efficient-breach norms fuel opportunism and systemic harms (e.g., depletion of market confidence), and Paper B argues disproportionality may be justified in targeted circumstances to avoid distorted risk allocation and excessive commercial uncertainty.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 40hastingslj907!!ARTICLE: Administrative Collateral Estoppel in California: A Critical Evaluation of People v. Sims.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Administrative Collateral Estoppel in California: A Critical Evaluation of People v. Sims.

shared_topics.topic: narrowing broad equitable doctrines to particular contexts to preserve fairness and predictability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the disproportionality limit on consequential damages should be confined to cases involving promissors who rarely face a given remote risk (to avoid commercial uncertainty), and Paper B argues that the People v. Sims rule of administrative collateral estoppel should be restricted to minor matters (or barred in serious criminal cases) to avoid unfair surprise and excessive litigation burdens on agencies.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between judicially-created doctrines and legislative or restatement reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces how disproportionality has migrated into the Restatement and the revised U.C.C. drafts and warns of broad adoption, while Paper B documents legislative and appellate reactions to Sims and analyzes statutory carve-outs adopted to blunt the case's effects.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules alter actors' incentives, behavior, and institutional costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how adopting a disproportionality rule changes contracting behavior, risk-pricing, and commercial certainty (and may inefficiently distort premiums), and Paper B examines how administrative preclusion under Sims changes litigant and agency behavior, increasing litigation of minor matters and affecting prosecutors and hearing officers.

shared_topics.topic: critical analysis of the policy and theoretical justifications for doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques classic default-rule economic justifications and offers cognitive-psychology-based reasons for a disproportionality test, while Paper B critiques Sims' asserted public-policy basis and argues the decision's rationale fails to justify its consequences.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 11texwesleyanlrev505!!SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:FORESEEABILITY AND DAMAGES:HADLEY V. BAXENDALE: CONTRACT DOCTRINE OR COMPENSATION RULE?
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:FORESEEABILITY AND DAMAGES:HADLEY V. BAXENDALE: CONTRACT DOCTRINE OR COMPENSATION RULE?

shared_topics.topic: Hadley v. Baxendale as the canonical rule limiting recovery of consequential damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats Hadley as the watershed case that crystallized a foreseeability/remoteness test for contract damages and traces its doctrinal influence, while Paper B takes Hadley as the central starting point for modern consequential-damages doctrine and frames its inquiry as whether and how other limits should sit alongside Hadley.

shared_topics.topic: The role of foreseeability/remoteness in limiting recovery and the contract–tort distinction
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how courts applied and later separated remoteness/foreseeability tests in contract versus tort (including the emergence of a laxer tort test), and Paper B engages the foreseeability limb of Hadley (Restatement §351/UCC formulations) and asks when foreseeability should or should not permit recovery in contract.

shared_topics.topic: Doctrinal history and evolution of limits on consequential damages in common law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A provides a historical narrative from early English cases through nineteenth- and twentieth-century authority explaining how remoteness doctrine developed, and Paper B likewise surveys the history of disproportionality limits (from ancient sources through modern Restatement and U.C.C. revisions) as part of that evolving remedial landscape.

shared_topics.topic: The use of supplementary limits to Hadley (e.g., disproportionality, thin‑skull/doctrine-driven exceptions) and their policy justification
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses doctrinal exceptions and pressures (the thin‑skull rule, duty of care) that animated a divergence from Hadley in tort and the policy concern about open‑ended liability, while Paper B investigates disproportionality as an additional equitable limit and evaluates its normative foundations through law‑and‑economics and cognitive psychology.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 18upajbusl315!!ARTICLE: Recovery of Damages for Lost Profits: The Historical Development
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Recovery of Damages for Lost Profits: The Historical Development

shared_topics.topic: the Hadley v. Baxendale foreseeability test as the central rule for consequential damages
shared_topics.justification: Both papers focus on Hadley’s two-part foreseeability test as the key organizing doctrine for recovery of consequential damages: Paper A traces the historical reception and reputed primacy of the Hadley rule, while Paper B analyzes how modern instruments (Restatement, U.C.C.) and doctrine continue to treat the Hadley tests as the baseline limit on consequential damages.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal limits on recovery of lost profits/consequential damages beyond Hadley
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with additional legal constraints that operate alongside or instead of Hadley — Paper A emphasizes the development and eventual primacy of the ‘reasonable certainty’ proof requirement in lost-profits awards, while Paper B examines the rising use of a disproportionality limitation (in Restatement/U.C.C. drafts and cases) that can bar otherwise-foreseeable consequential damages.

shared_topics.topic: historical origins and transnational migration of consequential-damages rules (Roman law, Pothier, common law development)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers trace the genealogy of consequential-damages doctrines across time and jurisdictions: Paper A gives a detailed account from Roman law through Pothier to Anglo‑American practice (including the surprising U.S.–to–U.K. migration of Hadley), and Paper B situates disproportionality in a long lineage of doctrinal practice reaching back to Roman times and early common-law opinions.

shared_topics.topic: policy and economic justifications for limiting consequential damages and risk-allocation concerns
shared_topics.justification: Both works evaluate limits on damages in light of broader policy/economic considerations: Paper A critiques popular economic-historical narratives (e.g., Victorian free-trade explanations) for doctrinal change, while Paper B applies law-and-economics default-rule analysis and behavioral (cognitive) evidence to assess when and why doctrines like disproportionality should constrain risk allocation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1997detclrev993!!ARTICLE: Capping Market Damages at Lost Profit: An Unwarranted Limitation on a Middleman's Expectancy Interest
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Capping Market Damages at Lost Profit: An Unwarranted Limitation on a Middleman's Expectancy Interest

shared_topics.topic: whether market‑price (UCC §2‑713) damages should be limited to a middleman's lost profits
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly poses this question through the middleman/reseller hypo (market damages vs the actual resale profit), arguing courts are split; Paper B addresses the closely related concern by examining limits on large consequential awards (disproportionality) when damages are large relative to the contract price or expected return.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between protecting the nonbreaching party's expectancy interest (placing the party in the position of full performance) and doctrines that limit recovery
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the dispute as one between the traditional expectancy‑protection principle and a lost‑profits cap, while Paper B treats whether and when limits like disproportionality are justified given the goal of appropriately compensating foreseeable losses.

shared_topics.topic: the role of UCC Article 2 and the Restatement in shaping and reforming rules on consequential/market damages (including proposed revisions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes case law and whether proposed revisions to Article 2 resolve conflicts between sections (e.g., 2‑713 vs 1‑106); Paper B traces Restatement §351 and the draft revised Article 2’s insertion of a disproportionality limit and analyzes the doctrinal and practical consequences.

shared_topics.topic: normative and theoretical defenses for limiting consequential damages (efficiency, conceptual validity, and behavioral considerations)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A promises an analysis of the conceptual validity of competing positions on damage measures, while Paper B explicitly evaluates disproportionality using default‑rule economic theory and supplements that with cognitive/behavioral evidence to justify when limits on damages may be appropriate.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2006michstlrev883!!ARTICLE: PENALTIES AS RATIONAL RESPONSE TO BARGAINING IRRATIONALITY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PENALTIES AS RATIONAL RESPONSE TO BARGAINING IRRATIONALITY

shared_topics.topic: use of behavioral economics / cognitive biases to reassess contract remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Both papers deploy insights from behavioral decision theory and cognitive psychology to challenge the classical rational-actor assumptions underlying contract law: Paper A uses experimental surveys showing heuristics (availability, status quo, signaling) in negotiators to argue for changing liquidated-damages doctrine, while Paper B surveys cognitive and experimental evidence (e.g., systematic underestimation of remote risks) to motivate a tailored disproportionality limit on consequential damages.

shared_topics.topic: whether and how the law should limit parties' freedom of contract in light of bounded rationality
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the tension between freedom-of-contract/consent and paternalistic or systemic limits: Paper A debates enforcing negotiated penalty clauses versus the traditional voiding of penalties, arguing that bargaining irrationality can justify enforcement; Paper B examines whether a disproportionality default (a legal limit on recovery) can be justified given parties' cognitive failures in pricing rare risks.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial doctrines allocate risk for low‑probability, high‑loss events and affect efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Each paper analyzes remedial rules as mechanisms for allocating rare but large risks: Paper A considers penalty/liquidated-damage clauses as responses to parties' risk calculations and their relation to efficient-breach theory, while Paper B focuses on Hadley/disproportionality and how undervaluation of remote risks implies mispriced risk-bearing that may warrant doctrinal adjustment.

shared_topics.topic: importance of contracting context (negotiation, experience, bargaining power, salience) in applying doctrinal rules
shared_topics.justification: Both works argue doctrinal application should depend on contextual factors: Paper A stresses distinctions between negotiated bespoke clauses and standard-form/unequal-bargaining scenarios when assessing penalty clauses, and Paper B recommends limiting disproportionality's use to cases involving parties with little experience or where the risk was insufficiently salient to them.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45flastulrev912!!ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: II. THE BEST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: Kingston v. Preston (and Goodisson v. Nunn, sort of)
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: II. THE BEST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: Kingston v. Preston (and Goodisson v. Nunn, sort of)

shared_topics.topic: default rules and implied contractual terms/conditions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes disproportionality as a potential default rule in the law of consequential damages and assesses it using default-rule theory; Paper B examines the judicial creation of implied (constructive) conditions that operate as legal defaults governing the dependence or concurrency of mutual promises.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and credit between contracting parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how parties allocate low‑probability/high‑magnitude risks (and how cognitive biases can cause underpricing of risk, suggesting a role for disproportionality), while Paper B studies how doctrines like dependence/independence, security requirements, and constructive conditions shift credit risk and who must perform first.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal limits on remedies for breach (foreseeability, proportionality, material breach, anticipatory repudiation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the Hadley foreseeability test and the disproportionality limitation on recovery of consequential damages; Paper B traces how implied conditions, the doctrine of material breach, and anticipatory repudiation operate to limit or excuse performance and shape available remedies.

shared_topics.topic: historical development and judicially‑crafted doctrines in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the history and recent resurgence of disproportionality rhetoric in Restatements and the U.C.C. drafts, assessing its doctrinal placement; Paper B provides a historical account of Kingston (and antecedent cases) and how judges (notably Lord Mansfield) fashioned implied conditions that reoriented modern contract doctrine.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 73califlrev1!!ARTICLE: Unity in Tort, Contract, and Property: The Model of Precaution.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Unity in Tort, Contract, and Property: The Model of Precaution.

shared_topics.topic: balancing compensation of victims with incentives for efficient precautions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A formulates the compensation principle versus the marginal (efficiency) principle and analyzes legal mechanisms that both compensate victims and preserve incentives to take precautions; Paper B analyzes how limits on consequential damages (disproportionality) affect the allocation of losses and incentives under contract law and whether such limits can sensibly reduce over- or under-compensation without distorting behavior.

shared_topics.topic: use of economic/default-rule analysis to evaluate liability doctrines across doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops an economic 'model of precaution' and applies it uniformly to tort, contract, and property rules to explain doctrinal choices, while Paper B evaluates the disproportionality constraint using default-rule theory from law-and-economics to assess whether that constraint makes sense as a legal default.

shared_topics.topic: the role of risk, foreseeability, and information in allocating liability and damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A isolates direct harms and the cost of precautions (and initially abstracts from information and risk-aversion) to show how liability rules affect precaution choices, and Paper B centers on foreseeability (Hadley) and the mismatch between contract price and consequential damages—especially for low-probability/high-loss events—highlighting how information about risk conditions liability outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: limits of standard rational-actor assumptions (information costs and cognitive biases) and their implications for rule design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A acknowledges that relaxing simplifying assumptions about risk aversion and information costs changes the model's predictions and discusses consequences, while Paper B brings empirical cognitive-psychology evidence that parties systematically underestimate remote risks and argues that such departures from rationality justify doctrinal adjustments like a disproportionality test.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 71califlrev56!!ARTICLE: The Collateral Source Rule and Contract Damages.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Collateral Source Rule and Contract Damages.

shared_topics.topic: limits on recoverable consequential damages to avoid disproportionate or windfall outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the doctrinal and policy basis for a disproportionality limit on consequential damages (when damages greatly exceed the contract price), while Paper B examines how the collateral source rule and subrogation limit recoveries so as to avoid windfalls or improper double recovery in contract cases.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and responsibility for losses after a breach
shared_topics.justification: Both papers wrestle with which actor should ultimately bear loss from a breach: Paper A considers when law should shift or limit liability because parties mispriced or failed to allocate remote risks, and Paper B asks whether the defendant or an independent collateral source should be the primary obligor to compensate the injured promisee.

shared_topics.topic: policy justifications for doctrinal rules governing contract remedies (efficiency, equity, fairness)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates disproportionality through default-rule efficiency analysis and cognitive-psychology-informed fairness, and Paper B surveys doctrinal outcomes against policy aims (preventing windfalls, assigning primary responsibility), arguing for principled application of collateral source rules in contract law.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between private risk-bearing mechanisms (pricing, insurance/subrogation) and legal damages rules
