shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how parties' risk pricing (and cognitive biases that underprice remote risks) affects whether courts should impose a disproportionality constraint, while Paper B analyzes how collateral payments and subrogation rights (private risk-transfer mechanisms) should affect the measure and allocation of contractual damages.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 69tennlrev837!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT DAMAGES IN TENNESSEE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT DAMAGES IN TENNESSEE

shared_topics.topic: limits on recovery of consequential damages (foreseeability and related doctrines)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze the doctrines that constrain recovery of consequential damages—Paper A centers on Hadley v. Baxendale and the foreseeability test (and an added disproportionality limit), while Paper B examines how Tennessee courts apply foreseeability as a limiting rule when awarding contract damages.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal sources shaping damages law (Restatement and the U.C.C.)
shared_topics.justification: Both articles rely on and critique black‑letter authorities: Paper A traces how the Restatement (Second) and the revised draft of UCC Article 2 incorporate a disproportionality limit, and Paper B treats the UCC and state case law as governing frameworks for how Tennessee calculates and limits contract damages.

shared_topics.topic: the goal and measurement of contract damages (expectation/benefit‑of‑the‑bargain and calculation methods)
shared_topics.justification: Both works engage with the normative aim of contract remedies—putting the non‑breaching party in the position performance would have done—Paper B by explaining and advocating application of the benefit‑of‑the‑bargain rule in Tennessee, and Paper A by evaluating whether default rules for consequential damages achieve efficient allocation and fair compensation.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal limits that affect ascertainability of damages (certainty and avoidability/non‑mitigation)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers address legal constraints that prevent or reduce awards when damages are uncertain or could have been avoided: Paper B treats certainty and non‑avoidability/mitigation as core limits on recoverable damages in Tennessee, while Paper A considers how risk magnitude/probability and evidentiary concerns factor into when courts should restrict consequential awards.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 63fordhamlrev665!!ARTICLE: CONSEQUENTIAL DAMAGES FOR COMMERCIAL LOSS: AN ALTERNATIVE TO HADLEY v. BAXENDALE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONSEQUENTIAL DAMAGES FOR COMMERCIAL LOSS: AN ALTERNATIVE TO HADLEY v. BAXENDALE

shared_topics.topic: limits and adequacy of Hadley v. Baxendale's foreseeability rule for consequential damages
shared_topics.justification: Both papers re-examine Hadley as the governing test for recovering consequential damages — Paper A argues the single, inflexible Hadley standard is flawed and ill-suited to varying contractual circumstances, while Paper B analyzes an additional doctrinal limit (disproportionality) that supplements or complicates Hadley.

shared_topics.topic: situationally varying scope of liability for consequential damages
shared_topics.justification: Both works contend that liability should not be uniform across all contracts — Paper A proposes a trifurcated standard that varies the scope of liability by situation, and Paper B argues for a constrained, context-dependent use of disproportionality (e.g., for remote or infrequent risks and inexperienced parties).

shared_topics.topic: policy-based evaluation of consequential-damages doctrine (efficiency, fairness, commercial certainty)
shared_topics.justification: Each paper grounds its critique and proposals in policy analysis — Paper A identifies and evaluates the relevant policies underlying recovery rules and tailors standards accordingly, while Paper B weighs economic default-rule efficiency against cognitive-psychology concerns to determine when doctrinal limits are justified.

shared_topics.topic: proposals for doctrinal reform or supplementation of existing contract-remedy rules
shared_topics.justification: Both articles offer concrete reforms to the law of consequential damages beyond traditional doctrine — Paper A advances a new trifurcated liability standard as an alternative to Hadley, and Paper B recommends incorporating a limited disproportionality test as an adjunct to Hadley with specified criteria for its application.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 10jempiricallegalstud512!!ARTICLE: Reference Points and Contractual Choices: An Experimental Examination
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Reference Points and Contractual Choices: An Experimental Examination

shared_topics.topic: behavioral critique of the rational-actor model in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Both papers challenge the standard law-and-economics assumption that contracting parties behave as fully rational, wealth‑maximizing actors: Paper A marshals cognitive psychology and experimental economics to show systematic departures (e.g., risk underestimation), while Paper B experimentally demonstrates framing/reference‑point effects on contractual choices and performance incentives.

shared_topics.topic: cognitive biases (risk underestimation and framing) shaping how parties perceive, allocate, and interpret contractual obligations and consequential losses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how people tend to undervalue remote, infrequent, or non‑salient risks and how that misperception undermines efficient allocation of consequential damages, while Paper B shows that gain/loss framing and reference points lead parties to adopt self‑serving interpretations or different effort levels under objectively identical contracts.

shared_topics.topic: implications for legal rule design (defaults, remedies, and drafting) to account for actual human decision-making
shared_topics.justification: Both papers draw normative implications for doctrine and contract practice: Paper A argues for a targeted disproportionality/default rule to correct predictable cognitive errors in risk premia, and Paper B explores how framing and ambiguity ought to inform contract drafting, enforcement incentives, and legal responses to interpretive disputes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 39urichlrev627!!ARTICLE:AN ALTERNATIVE PARADIGM FOR VALUING BREACH OF REGISTRATION RIGHTS AND LOSS OF LIQUIDITY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:AN ALTERNATIVE PARADIGM FOR VALUING BREACH OF REGISTRATION RIGHTS AND LOSS OF LIQUIDITY

shared_topics.topic: principled measurement of damages for breach of contract
shared_topics.justification: Both papers diagnose failures in existing doctrinal rules for awarding damages following a contractual breach and propose a more textured, principled measure: Paper A develops a specific damage formula (price decline plus hypothetical interest) for loss of registration rights/liquidity, while Paper B critiques Hadley and argues for a constrained disproportionality rule to govern when consequential damages should be limited.

shared_topics.topic: using economic and financial theory to inform legal rules on damages
shared_topics.justification: Both articles ground their recommended legal rules in economic/financial reasoning rather than purely equitable intuition: Paper A draws on financial engineering (synthetic instruments, critiques of option-pricing and short-sale proxies) to value lost liquidity, and Paper B applies default-rule economics and behavioral economic findings about risk perception to justify when disproportionality limits should apply.

shared_topics.topic: addressing uncertainty, volatility, and mitigation in assessing loss
shared_topics.justification: Each paper confronts how uncertainty and market volatility complicate damage computation and mitigation choices: Paper A examines fluctuating security prices, duration uncertainty, and the reasonableness of private resale as mitigation when registration is breached; Paper B analyzes how low‑probability/high‑magnitude risks and parties' systematic misperception of remote risks should affect allocation of risk and the availability or reduction of consequential damages.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 61scallrev629!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT REMEDIES, RENEGOTIATION, AND THE THEORY OF EFFICIENT BREACH.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT REMEDIES, RENEGOTIATION, AND THE THEORY OF EFFICIENT BREACH.

shared_topics.topic: how contract remedies affect parties' ex ante decisions (precautions, contract formation, and pricing)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that remedies influence more than the perform-or-breach choice — they affect how much promisors spend on precautions, whether they consent to contracts, and what prices they set — and that these effects do not vanish with costless renegotiation. Paper B likewise examines how damages rules (and a disproportionality limit) interact with parties' pricing of risk and the premiums charged to bear remote risks, showing that damages rules shape ex ante allocation and pricing decisions.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and consequential damages limits (including disproportionality) as distributional and incentive devices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that contract remedies have distributional effects that determine who gains or loses when breach occurs and thus affect behavior. Paper B focuses on limits on consequential damages — notably disproportionality — as a mechanism that reallocates or limits liability for remote risks, analyzing when such limits are justified and how they alter who bears losses.

shared_topics.topic: use of economic/default-rule analysis to evaluate the efficiency of contract remedies and damage rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques early economic treatments that narrowly analyzed perform-or-breach outcomes and stresses broader economic inquiry into how remedies change incentives and welfare. Paper B applies default-rule and law-and-economics reasoning to assess whether adding a disproportionality rule to Hadley is efficient, and then supplements that analysis with behavioral evidence where standard economic assumptions fail.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 103harvlrev687!!ARTICLE: THE DEATH OF THE IRREPARABLE INJURY RULE.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE DEATH OF THE IRREPARABLE INJURY RULE.

shared_topics.topic: when monetary damages are adequate or should be limited
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines doctrinal and normative limits on awarding consequential (monetary) damages—particularly the disproportionality constraint that can reduce recovery—and asks when courts should deny full monetary compensation; Paper B analyzes the irreparable-injury/adequacy doctrine to show when courts treat damages as an inadequate remedy and instead grant specific (equitable) relief, identifying the real reasons courts deny monetary compensation.

shared_topics.topic: economic/transaction‑cost analysis of remedial doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A applies default‑rule and law‑and‑economics reasoning (including information‑forcing defaults) to assess whether disproportionality promotes efficient contract risk allocation, while Paper B surveys and critiques economic and transaction‑cost arguments (and debates) about the wisdom of preferring damages over specific relief.

shared_topics.topic: critique of formal doctrinal rules and advocacy for a functional/behavioral approach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that standard default theory's rational‑actor assumptions misfit actual contracting behavior and therefore doctrinal rules (like disproportionality) should account for cognitive biases; Paper B argues that the traditional irreparable‑injury rule is a formalistic misdescription of practice and urges replacing it with functional, case‑sensitive rules that reflect what courts actually do.

papers.node_id: 76marqlrev519!!ARTICLE: Divorce Law: Exclusions and Disproportionate Divisions of Marital Estate
papers.title: ARTICLE: Divorce Law: Exclusions and Disproportionate Divisions of Marital Estate
papers.abstract: This Article examines the exclusion of gifted and inherited assets from the divisible marital estate upon divorce, under Section 767.255 of the Wisconsin Statutes.It discusses each of the following important areas:

questions.question: Whether and under what circumstances gifted or inherited assets should be treated as separate from marital property and excluded from division at divorce

Whether excluding gifted or inherited assets justifies making disproportionate divisions of the remaining marital estate (i.e., awarding one spouse more than an equal share), and what standards should govern such disproportionate allocations

compared_to.partner_node_id: 116yaleljonline438!!ARTICLE: What the Efficient Performance Hypothesis Means for Contracts Scholarship
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: What the Efficient Performance Hypothesis Means for Contracts Scholarship

shared_topics.topic: allocation of property/entitlements upon dissolution of a relationship
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes who should hold the 'option' to determine allocation of contract performance (promisor vs promisee) and how that affects who ends up with the economic benefit when a contract relationship breaks; Paper B examines which assets (e.g., gifts and inheritances) should be excluded from the divisible marital estate and how property is allocated between spouses on divorce.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoff between efficiency and non‑welfarist ethical or fairness considerations in designing legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly contrasts efficiency-maximizing remedies (expectation damages) with remedies that reflect ethical claims (promisee-disgorgement) and argues courts might accommodate both; Paper B engages with fairness concerns (disproportionate divisions, protections for gifted/inherited property) that can conflict with simple economic or equal-sharing rules.

shared_topics.topic: measurement and valuation problems in applying remedies or dividing assets
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes empirical uncertainty in measuring promisee losses versus promisor gains as central to choosing the efficient remedy; Paper B involves practical valuation and evidentiary issues in determining the value and divisibility of gifted or inherited assets and in justifying disproportionate divisions.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts/doctrine in structuring remedial or property-division rules given empirical and normative uncertainty
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how courts must pick remedial structures (expectation damages, specific performance, or promisee-option remedies) and how empirical limits constrain that choice; Paper B analyzes statutory and doctrinal rules (e.g., Wisconsin §767.255) and how judges implement exclusions and disproportionate divisions when balancing competing legal and normative claims.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 23uclalrev501!!ARTICLE: THE HISTORICAL CONCEPTION OF A LEASE FOR YEARS *
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE HISTORICAL CONCEPTION OF A LEASE FOR YEARS *

shared_topics.topic: how legal classification of property affects substantive rights and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how labeling a lease as a 'freehold' versus a contract/chattel determined whether a lessee could bring the principal action to recover land and thus governed available remedies; Paper B analyzes how statutory classification of gifted and inherited assets as excluded from the marital estate determines spouses' entitlements on divorce.

shared_topics.topic: the gap between formal doctrinal categories and practical fairness or protection of parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that pragmatic concerns (avoiding double liability, protecting lessees) drove changes despite rigid doctrinal labels; Paper B examines whether the statutory exclusion of gifts and inheritances produces disproportionate or unfair divisions in practice, highlighting tensions between formal rules and equitable outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: development or adaptation of legal rules to fill remedial gaps
shared_topics.justification: Paper A describes the invention of new writs to protect lessees when existing actions were inadequate; Paper B engages with statutory and doctrinal mechanisms (and likely judicial responses) that determine how separate assets are treated to address perceived injustices in marital division.

shared_topics.topic: who bears loss or liability based on property status (allocation of rights between parties and third parties)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers how allowing both lessor and lessee to sue would affect third-party liability and who ultimately bears loss from dispossession; Paper B addresses how labeling an asset as separate versus marital allocates financial loss or gain between spouses upon divorce.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 94bulrev55!!ARTICLE: DO THE RIGHT THING: INDIRECT REMEDIES IN PRIVATE LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DO THE RIGHT THING: INDIRECT REMEDIES IN PRIVATE LAW

shared_topics.topic: remedial design in family law/divorce

papers.node_id: 108michlrev633!!ARTICLE: DO LIQUIDATED DAMAGES ENCOURAGE BREACH? A PSYCHOLOGICAL EXPERIMENT
papers.title: ARTICLE: DO LIQUIDATED DAMAGES ENCOURAGE BREACH? A PSYCHOLOGICAL EXPERIMENT
papers.abstract:
Economists claim that the theory of efficient breach allows us to predict when parties will choose to breach a contract if the legal remedy for breach is expectation damages.Relying on the assumption that individuals are rational wealth maximizers, law-and-economics scholars argue that promisors are indifferent as between performance and breach,that promisees andpromisors alike favor the rule of expectation damages,and that penalty clauses will deter efficient breach by imposing extra costs on the promisor.In other words, an economic prediction of human behavior says that when a promisor can make one extra dollar by breaching his contract, he will breach the contract.
As a descriptive model of human behavior, this set of premises and predictions lacks empirical support. Although the model of the rational actor is a useful tool in certain domains, it fails to capture important, shared, nonmonetary values and incentives that shape behavior in predictable ways. When interpersonal obligations - like contracts - are informal or underspecified, people act in accordance with shared community norms.However, when sanctions for uncooperative behavior are specified, codified, or otherwise formalized, behavior becomes more strategic and more self-interested.
Consider the following anecdote: In December of 2001, the Boston Fire Department changed its sick-leave policy to allow 15 sick days per year. The previous system had allowed unlimited sick time, and the new rule was part of an initiative to bring professional management tools to the department.In 2001, firefighters took a total of 6432 days. In 2002, the total number of sick days rose to 13,431 - more than double the previous year.
The new system was ostensibly more rigid, with a higher penalty for taking sick days - each sick day brought workers closer to the prospect of unpaid time off. The old system, by contrast, had no explicit penalty at all for sick time. The old system had something powerful in its favor, though: the firefighters had a tradition of "toughing it out" through illness, showingup for work even when it hurt.The new policy made sick leave into a contractual entitlement rather than a breach of protocol.
The penalty for missing a day under the new system was not big enough to deter absenteeism on its own (15 days of illness per year is, after all, a lot - most people do not need to worry that they will need all of those days), but it changed the social norm in such a way that firefighters were willing to miss work in situations in which they otherwise would have felt obligated to show up. In the firefighters' case, the policy was costly, insofar as it encouraged workers to stay home even when they could have worked - the policy encouraged workers to breach in cases in which breach was overall more costly than performance. But what would happen if the incentives were more carefully calibrated, such that parties would breach only if it were efficient to do so? What if the Fire Department had been able to set the number of sick days at a level that would deter malingerers from exploiting the policy but encourage contagious workers to stay at home in cases in which they might otherwise have felt social pressure to show up for work? In that case, the formalization of the sick-leave policy might have done some good by reducing the effect of the social norm in cases in which it was arguably counterproductive. Put differently, formalizing the sanction for breach of an agreement might be a means of encouraging breach when it is otherwise efficient to do so.
This Article uses the analytical framework suggested by the firefighters' sick-time policy to map the relationship between liquidated-damages clauses in contracts and the parties' propensities to breach. The experiments reported here offer evidence for a positive relationship between the presence of a liquidated-damages clause in a contract and parties' willingness to breach a contract when breach is profitable. In other words, when the penalty for breach is formally included in the agreement between the parties - like the firefighters and the Fire Department - parties are more likely to choose to breach.
Liquidated damages are a means of making the sanction for breach explicit within a contract. Decision researchers have found experimental evidence that, when social norms are in conflict with efficiency incentives, a more explicit incentive structure leads to more self-interested behavior.Even when the law of contracts is arguably clear itself on the legal remedy for breach, moral intuition differentiates between a background law like the rule of expectation damages and an obligation to pay damages included as a clause in the body of the contract. When parties stipulate damages, they clarify the respective expectations of the parties, permitting efficient breach without repudiation of the mutual understanding.
These experiments offer an account of the psychology of legal decisionmaking at the intersection of moral rules of promise and legal rules of contract. Considerable evidence suggests that most people think that there is a moral element to contract law and breach of contract.In behavioral studies, participants routinely report that a contract is a promise, that breach of contract is immoral, and that breach is a moral harm even when the promisee is fully compensated for the expected benefit of the contract.People think that the moral obligation is to perform as specified, not to confer a benefit as great as the value of the promised performance.It seems that most people believe that the content of the promise is the text of the contract. In this Article, I will focus on cases in which the moral aversion to breach of contract is in tension with economic incentives - efficient-breach opportunities. In some cases, breach is more profitable than performance. However, under most common-sense moral theories of contract, performance is morally preferable and perhaps even obligatory.
A moral aversion to breach may prevent exploitation of apparently wealth-maximizing opportunities. However, I will offer evidence in these experiments that moral intuitions about contract are not immutable. Psychologists and behavioral economists have observed in many contexts that actors are more likely to defy a social norm when the penalty for their noncooperation is real and explicit, but not so harsh as to deter the behavior on its own terms.I argue here that weak sanctions in economics games serve the same function as liquidated-damages clauses in efficient breach situations. The liquidated-damages clause makes the remedy for breach explicit but not unduly punitive. Under these conditions, I predicted that people would be more willing to breach a contract, an action normally dictated against by social and moral norms. Data reported here suggests that people prefer to breach a contract with a liquidated-damages clause to one with an identical remedy provided by the rule of expectation damages. One interpretation of these results, supported by both descriptive and normative scholarship in this field, is that liquidated-damages clauses encourage efficient breach by changing the parties' understanding of the content of the promise.
In Part I, I review descriptive and normative scholarship on efficient breach and liquidated-damages clauses, and claim that drafting liquidated-damages clauses may encourage parties to think deliberatively about the costs and benefits of their contractual agreements. In Part II, Ianalyze the possible effects of liquidated damages in light of evidence from experimental psychology and economics on behavioral responses to incomplete contracts and mild sanctions. In Part III, I report findings from three short experiments. In the first experiment, I find that subjects require a bigger financial incentive to breach a contract without a liquidated-damages clause than a contract with a liquidated-damages clause. Second, I replicate this effect with a penalty clause, showing that subjects prefer to breach a contract with a liquidated-damages clause even when it is more costly (e.g., the damages are higher) than paying the expectation-level damages in a contract without stipulated damages. In the third experiment, I find that subjects' willingness to breach a contract with a liquidated-damages clause is driven by the belief that the clause changes the promisee's subjective probability of breach. Subjects think that breaching a contract when the other party expects breach is less immoral and will lead to fewer reputation costs. In Part IV, I discuss the implications of this research, including the use of liquidated damages as a debiasing mechanism and possible policy prescriptions suggested by these results. I suggest that liquidated damages may offer a means of reconciling two normatively valuable goals: wealth maximization on the one hand and maintenance of a moral culture of promise on the other.

questions.question: Whether including an explicit monetary-damage term in a contract makes parties more willing to breach for financial gain than when the same monetary consequence exists only as an external or background remedy.

Whether the explicitness of a contractual sanction (a stipulated but not overly punitive payment for breach) lowers the non-monetary moral aversion to breaching and thus reduces the financial incentive required to choose breach over performance.

Whether any increased willingness to breach when damages are stipulated is driven by changes in actors' beliefs about social norms, perceived immorality, and expected reputational or enforcement responses by the counterparty.

matched_themes: How should courts treat pre-agreed breach payments and liquidated damages clauses (enforce, reform, apportion, or void)?
Do pre-agreed breach-payment clauses (liquidated damages) change parties' beliefs about norms and moral aversion to breach, and do such clauses increase or decrease the willingness to breach?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?
Should the promisor or the promisee have the default right to choose between performance and payment to achieve allocative efficiency?
Should parties be presumptively permitted to contractually specify nonstandard damage remedies, or should courts retain authority to impose defaults?
Should the availability of legal remedies or contractual incompleteness change the moral assessment of a party who breaches under unanticipated circumstances?

Should remedies and contract law be structured to preserve conditions necessary for moral agency and promissory responsibility, rather than treating promises solely as instruments of economic cooperation?
How should courts treat and enforce stipulated remedies (liquidated damages clauses) versus substituting judicial remedies?

Can party-designed enforcement mechanisms (pre-agreed penalties, arbitration, bonding, reputational systems) reliably produce efficient breach outcomes without judicial intervention, and when do they fail?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
Should courts police and limit supracompensatory contractual remedies (penalty-like clauses), or does allowing parties to contract for such terms respect autonomy and promote efficient contracting?
Do enforceable contractual damage remedies substitute for or complement informal relational governance in franchise and other repeated relationships?
How should remedial and enforcement rules be structured to achieve efficient behavior when populations include both internalizers and externalizers?
Do behavioral biases and heuristics affect how parties draft, negotiate, and accept pre-agreed breach-payment clauses, and can contract design mitigate those biases?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
Do parties and courts actually choose heterogeneous, context-tailored damage provisions in contracting, and under what conditions would such customization be voluntarily chosen or socially desirable?
To what extent should moral blameworthiness and non-economic considerations influence the design and application of contract remedies?
How do differences in wording, formatting, and contract presentation influence non-drafting parties' post-execution behavior by evoking emotions or exploiting cognitive biases?
When is an indirect remedy (one that induces self-compliance) preferable to a direct remedy that delivers the outcome?

papers.node_id: 94bulrev55!!ARTICLE: DO THE RIGHT THING: INDIRECT REMEDIES IN PRIVATE LAW
papers.title: ARTICLE: DO THE RIGHT THING: INDIRECT REMEDIES IN PRIVATE LAW
papers.abstract:
All legal systems must design remedies for rights violations. The vast literature on this subject has offered several classifications of remedies. We are well familiar with the distinction between compensatory and punitive remedies,monetary and nonmonetary remedies,and extrajudicial and court-awarded remedies.These classifications differ in terms of their content, aims, and scope. Yet we intuitively assume that all remedies have a common denominator: they attain the desired outcome directly.
Take, for instance, the distinction between monetary and nonmonetary remedies. When the strived-for outcome is that the promisee receive expectation damages from the promisor, the remedy directly realizes this goal by ordering payment of the sum. Alternatively, when the desired outcome is that the contracted-for asset be delivered in-kind, the promisee is awarded specific performance. Thus, regardless of whether the law aims at a monetary or a nonmonetary outcome, the remedy embodies the desired result.
The same seems to be true for the other classifications as well. Once we have determined whether the wrongdoer should pay compensatory or punitive damages, the remedy requires the wrongdoer to pay the chosen amount. Likewise, if the injured party is entitled to exercise self-help in lieu of suing in court, one intuitively assumes that both the extrajudicial and the judicial remedies attain the end result in a similar way. Thus, when a trespasser has wrongfully ousted a possessor, both the self-help measure and the state-enforced injunction directly restore possession through forceful expulsion of the wrongdoer.
The direct correlation between remedies and outcomes seems not only descriptively accurate, but also normatively sound. If the law is to save time and money for all the parties - plaintiffs, defendants, and courts - should not it always grant the remedy that embodies the desired outcome?
This Article argues that this ostensibly rhetorical question should often be answered in the negative. It introduces a novel classification of remedies, one that distinguishes between "direct" and "indirect" forms of redress. Indirect remedies (IRs) are unique in that their immediate product is not the end result that the law aims to achieve. Specifically, an IR attains the desired outcome by inducing the injurer to self-comply.
To illustrate, when a car mechanic exercises a possessory lien, the sought-after result is not that the vehicle remain in the mechanic's hands. The mechanic is not interested in the car itself and is not free to use it. Rather, the lien encourages the owner of the car to volunteer remuneration for the services rendered. Similarly, when a tenant withholds the rent, the ultimate goal of the remedy is not to save the tenant money, but to induce the landlord to repair defects in the apartment or remove other obstacles to the tenant's enjoyment. Likewise, when a declaratory judgment states that a certain contingency iscovered by an insurance policy, it does not seek merely to point out the true state of affairs, but to prompt the insurance company to pay willingly the insured what is due her. Other examples of IRs include suspension of contractual performance to induce fulfillment of the counter-performance, preliminary injunctions that bring about the resolution of the conflict, and damages awards in defamation suits that incentivize libelers to apologize. The heretofore overlooked category of IRs cuts across all the familiar classifications. IRs can be monetary or nonmonetary, compensatory or punitive, self-help or court awarded.
This Article aims to be both descriptive and normative. Descriptively, it demonstrates that IRs are prevalent in diverse fields of private law and identifies indirectness as a common denominator of seemingly unrelated legal remedies. It offers a taxonomy of IRs, highlighting their diversity and ingenuity. As the above examples illustrate, an in-kind IR may aim at a monetary outcome (possessory lien), a monetary IR may attempt to induce an in-kind result (rent-withholding), a declaratory IR may strive for a monetary or nonmonetary end-product, and so forth and so on.
Normatively, this Article justifies the use of IRs in appropriate circumstances by addressing the basic puzzle that such remedies pose: Why grant a remedy that is likely to achieve the desired outcome in two steps instead of one? IRs offer several advantages over direct remedies. Generally speaking, IRs incentivize both potential and actual wrongdoers to do the right thing of their own accord, rather than order them to behave in the way that would realize the desired outcome. Self-compliance is highly beneficial. First, it interferes less with the autonomy of the right-infringer and at the same time enhances the value of what has been received in the eyes of the right-holder. Second, cognitive-dissonance theory suggests that IRs, as compared with direct remedies, would more effectively educate people to cooperate and to consider others' interests. To the extent that the law seeks to play an educative role,it should consider the relative efficacy of its educational devices. Third, indirect enforcement tends to reduce animosity and expressive harms, thereby promoting the preservation of ongoing relationships between the parties - or at least minimizing the nonpecuniary costs of the conflict. Finally, IRs typically require less involvement on the part of the legal system and are therefore less costly to administer than direct remedies. Consequently, IRs can mitigate the distorting effect of wealth on the vindication of rights and improve access to justice.
While the literature has discussed each of the remedies I characterize as indirect in isolation, it has not focused attention on IRs as a distinct category.My analysis facilitates the more appropriate use of IRs and sets guidelines for designing IRs in new contexts. For instance, IRs are particularly well-suited to cases where there is (a) a low risk of error regarding the existence of a right and its infringement, and (b) a high risk of miscalculating a direct remedy. In addition, to avoid charges of unfairness or arbitrariness, there should be a recognizable relationship between the content of the IR and the injury to the right-holder.
Two caveats are in order. First, I do not argue that as a rule IRs should supplant direct remedies. A remedy that directly aims at the sought-after outcome may be the best response to an infringement of a right. Awareness of the existence of IRs and a better understanding of their various advantages and limitations can, however, improve the legal response to rights violations. Second, since my project focuses on the ways to vindicate rights, I will not address the justifications for any of the substantive rights discussed here. I assume that the right itself is well founded, and therefore concentrate on the indirect and direct ways of remedying its infringement.
This Article proceeds as follows. Part I provides a general taxonomy of IRs. It demonstrates the wealth of remedial possibilities with examples from property, contract, tort, intellectual property, and family law. Part II elaborates on the abovementioned advantages of indirect rights enforcement. This discussion establishes the need to articulate the circumstances in which IRs are appropriate and to choose between different types of indirect relief. Part III addresses such considerations as the costs of errors, the risk of ineffectiveness, the identity of the right-infringer (private individual versus public entity), the type of interaction involved (ongoing relations versus end-game or one-shot game), and the presence or absence of a direct remedy for the harm.

shared_topics.topic: whether money damages or specific performance should be the presumptive remedy for contract breaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly defends keeping money damages (expectation damages) as the normal remedy and criticizes proposals to make specific performance routine; Paper B treats specific performance as a paradigmatic direct remedy and analyzes it against alternative (indirect) remedial designs, comparing their costs and benefits.

shared_topics.topic: efficiency and fairness trade-offs in selecting remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A weighs economic efficiency and fairness costs of shifting to routine specific performance versus the flexibility of money damages; Paper B develops normative criteria showing how indirect remedies can improve efficiency, reduce costs, and avoid certain fairness harms compared with direct remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the role of error costs and valuation difficulty in remedy choice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the difficulty and risk of error in quantifying subjective losses (e.g., restoration of land) as central to whether money damages or specific performance is preferable; Paper B similarly highlights that indirect remedies are especially attractive where there is low error about rights but high risk of miscalculating a direct remedy, making error-cost analysis central to remedial design.

shared_topics.topic: how remedies influence parties' incentives, autonomy, and ongoing relationships
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the moral obligations of promise and how remedies (money damages vs specific performance) affect respect for promises and relational outcomes; Paper B argues indirect remedies promote self-compliance, reduce animosity, preserve relationships, and respect the autonomy of wrongdoers more than some direct remedies.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Capping Market Damages at Lost Profit: An Unwarranted Limitation on a Middleman's Expectancy Interest

shared_topics.topic: selection among alternative contractual damage measures (market differential vs lost profits)

shared_topics.topic: normative principles and goals guiding remedial design (expectancy, fairness, relational and expressive concerns)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the normative aim of placing the nonbreaching party in the position of full performance (expectancy) and the fairness tensions that arise when that aim conflicts with market-based measures, and Paper B systematically analyzes normative reasons (autonomy, reduced animosity, educative/expressive effects) for preferring indirect remedies in certain contexts.

shared_topics.topic: role of measurement error and miscalculation risk in choosing remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper B argues that indirect remedies are preferable when there is a high risk of miscalculating a direct remedy, and Paper A illustrates this problem concretely—how market damages can greatly diverge from a middleman's true lost profit—raising the same concern about remedial mismeasurement and rule design.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial rules shape parties' incentives and strategic behavior (including self-compliance vs litigation choices)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how awarding market damages or limiting recovery affects a middleman's decisions (e.g., whether to cover or sue) and the producer's incentives, while Paper B foregrounds that indirect remedies function by inducing voluntary compliance and therefore evaluates remedies by their incentive effects.

compared_to.partner_title: Article: Specific Performance Versus Damages for Breach of Contract: An Economic Analysis

shared_topics.topic: choice between monetary (damages) and non‑monetary (specific performance) remedies in contract law

shared_topics.topic: how remedies shape incentives and induce self‑compliance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A's central claim is that many remedies operate indirectly by inducing injurers to self‑comply rather than by directly producing the end state, while Paper B analyzes how damages versus specific performance create different incentives for breach, costly avoidance, and negotiation.

shared_topics.topic: enforcement, bargaining and transaction costs as determinants of remedy choice

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE FUTURE OF LAW AND ECONOMICS: THE NEGLIGENCE-OPPORTUNISM TRADEOFF IN CONTRACT LAW.

shared_topics.topic: how remedies shape parties' incentives to comply

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs among enforcement objectives (deterrence, inducement, and relationship preservation)

shared_topics.topic: the role of trust and ongoing relationships in choosing legal responses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that indirect remedies preserve relationships and reduce expressive harms, whereas Paper B argues prioritizing deterrence of opportunism is necessary to sustain the trust foundations of efficient contracting — both link remedial design to the preservation of relational value and trust.

shared_topics.topic: economic/efficiency reasoning in designing remedial or doctrinal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses cost, administrative burden, and educative/behavioral benefits to normatively justify indirect remedies in appropriate contexts, while Paper B invokes efficiency to argue for presumptive priority in deterring opportunism over negligence; both deploy law-and-economics reasoning to evaluate what rules/remedies should be used.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1413!!ARTICLE: THE ROLE OF FAULT IN CONTRACT LAW: UNCONSCIONABILITY, UNEXPECTED CIRCUMSTANCES, INTERPRETATION, MISTAKE, AND NONPERFORMANCE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE ROLE OF FAULT IN CONTRACT LAW: UNCONSCIONABILITY, UNEXPECTED CIRCUMSTANCES, INTERPRETATION, MISTAKE, AND NONPERFORMANCE

shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds its normative defense of indirect remedies in values like autonomy, education, fairness, and preservation of relationships; Paper B argues that fault (including moral blameworthiness and negligence) should be a central building block of contract law and thus centrally shapes doctrines and remedies.

shared_topics.topic: whether law should induce voluntary self‑compliance versus impose direct, strict obligations

shared_topics.topic: contextual criteria for choosing between different remedial or doctrinal responses (costs of error, efficacy, and fairness)

shared_topics.topic: treatment of mistakes, unexpected circumstances, and the effect of relationship dynamics on liability and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the type of interaction (ongoing relations vs one-shot) and the risk of error should affect whether indirect enforcement is used; Paper B analyzes doctrines dealing with mistake and unexpected circumstances and how such errors and the nature of the parties' relationship should inform fault assessments and remedial outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: incentive effects and economic efficiency of remedies

shared_topics.topic: the need for decision rules versus judicial discretion in remedy selection

shared_topics.topic: role of context, party identity, and non-market or subjective harms in setting remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with how contextual factors matter: Paper A stresses the identity of the injurer, ongoing versus one-shot interactions, and non-pecuniary harms (autonomy, relationship preservation) in designing remedies, while Paper B contrasts fact patterns (e.g., Kent vs. Peevyhouse), owner intent, and the problem that market-value measures may fail to capture restoration or subjective/environmental interests.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: IN (PARTIAL) DEFENSE OF STRICT LIABILITY IN CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: efficiency, allocative consequences, and administrative/error costs in choosing remedies

shared_topics.topic: the influence of legal entitlements/rights allocation on remedy design and outcomes

shared_topics.justification: Paper A grapples with uncertainty (e.g., whether invoice submission is a condition) and highlights courts' fairness-driven constructions to avoid arbitrary forfeitures and administrability problems in accrual recognition; Paper B articulates when indirect remedies are appropriate by analyzing risks of error, miscalculation of direct remedies, fairness concerns, and administrative costs.

shared_topics.topic: the importance of transaction structure and ongoing relationships in tailoring legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on bilateral contractual contexts (invoices, recurring services) and how those relational features affect whether substantial performance fixes rights for tax purposes; Paper B identifies ongoing interactions versus one-shot encounters as a key determinant favoring indirect remedies that preserve cooperation and minimize relational breakdown.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: LAW AND EQUITY IN CONTRACT ENFORCEMENT

shared_topics.topic: practical administration costs, enforcement difficulties, and third‑party/efficiency effects of remedial choices

shared_topics.topic: why some legal wrongs trigger monetary civil remedies while others trigger coercive punishment
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes why torts and contract breaches typically yield monetary damages while crimes can produce imprisonment, comparing harms, intent, and institutional aims; Paper B interrogates the design of remedies and when the law should award direct monetary or nonmonetary relief versus other forms of redress that achieve outcomes indirectly.

shared_topics.topic: the role of incentives and efficiency in designing legal responses to rights violations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A deploys an economic/deterrence model to explain the civil/criminal divide (arguing that efficiency concerns drive differences in sanctions), while Paper B defends indirect remedies in part because they create incentives for self-compliance and lower enforcement costs, emphasizing efficiency trade-offs in remedial choice.

shared_topics.topic: the interaction between moral/expressive considerations and instrumental rationales in choosing remedies or punishments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts moral-based accounts (condemnation, culpability) with economic accounts to explain why certain breaches are criminalized, and Paper B discusses expressive harms, educative effects, and how indirect remedies may better promote normative change or reduce moral hostility compared with direct coercion.

shared_topics.topic: how voluntariness or the relational context of obligations affects remedial or punitive design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes voluntary (contractual) obligations from non‑voluntary duties to explain why breach of voluntarily assumed obligations is treated differently from crimes or torts, and Paper B singles out ongoing relationships and the nature of interactions as crucial factors favoring indirect remedies that preserve cooperation and minimize relational damage.

shared_topics.topic: limits and calculation of contractual damages (foreseeability and measurement)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on Hadley v. Baxendale's foreseeability rule that limits recovery of lost profits absent communicated special circumstances, and Paper B analyzes when direct monetary remedies are appropriate versus indirect remedies, emphasizing the risk of miscalculating a direct remedy and the difficulties of measuring damages.

shared_topics.topic: the role of party communication/notice in shaping remedial outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats the Hadley rule as hinging on what special circumstances were communicated or contemplated by the parties, while Paper B highlights that effective indirect remedies require a recognisable relationship between the remedy's content and the injury and often operate by prompting voluntary responses contingent on information and expectations.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial rules influence party behaviour and encourage self-compliance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses Hadley as part of the common law's broader function and flexibility in shaping contractual conduct across contexts, and Paper B theorises that indirect remedies work normatively by inducing injurers to self-comply, reducing conflict and preserving relationships.

shared_topics.topic: comparative/doctrinal analysis of private-law remedies across contexts and time
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates Hadley within nineteenth- and twenty‑first‑century common-law practice and cross-jurisdictional influence, and Paper B surveys and taxonomises indirect remedies across property, contract, tort, IP, and family law to draw doctrinal and normative lessons for designing remedies.

shared_topics.topic: remedies in contract law (use and design of specific performance, suspension/withholding, liens etc.)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A catalogues and theorizes contract-related indirect remedies (e.g., suspension of performance, rent-withholding, possessory liens) as mechanisms to induce the counterparty to comply, while Paper B focuses on the common law of contracts and the broader remedial frameworks (including whether remedies should be flexible or prescribed), so both substantively engage with how contract law selects, structures, and applies remedies.

shared_topics.topic: trade-offs between determinacy/predictability and flexibility/relational or efficiency goals in remedial design
shared_topics.justification: Paper B investigates whether detailed rules yield greater predictability and efficiency compared with broad principles that allow individualized justice, whereas Paper A evaluates the normative costs and benefits of indirect remedies—highlighting gains in autonomy, relationship preservation, and reduced administration alongside risks of error or ineffectiveness—so both analyze the same policy trade-offs in designing private-law remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the availability and character of specific performance (the right to require performance) in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the 'right to require performance' under the UN Convention for the International Sale of Goods and how that right should be interpreted internationally; Paper B treats specific performance as the paradigmatic direct remedy and contrasts it with indirect remedies such as suspension of performance, examining when courts should order in-kind relief versus alternatives.

shared_topics.topic: remedies designed to induce voluntary compliance (indirect enforcement mechanisms to secure contractual performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages with enforcement questions under the CISG about how a buyer or seller can secure performance across borders, while Paper B develops a taxonomy and normative account of indirect remedies (e.g., suspension of performance, liens, withholding) that aim to induce the counterparty to self-comply rather than achieve the outcome directly.

shared_topics.topic: how to choose among remedial regimes across different legal traditions and contexts (comparative/interpretive design of remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on producing an international interpretation of remedial rules through UNCITRAL's cross‑jurisdictional drafting process, reconciling civil/common-law approaches to performance remedies; Paper B offers cross-field criteria and guidelines for when indirect versus direct remedies are appropriate, thereby addressing how remedial rules should be designed and applied across diverse legal settings.

shared_topics.topic: incentives and behavioral effects of private‑law rules and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that many remedies operate indirectly by inducing injurers to self‑comply and evaluates remedies by their incentive and educative effects (reduced animosity, autonomy, compliance), while Paper B analyzes how shifts between fault‑based and strict‑liability regimes in contract and tort shaped incentives for care and compensation, particularly in products liability contexts.

shared_topics.topic: the boundary between contract and tort and its implications for remedy design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys remedial techniques across contract, tort, property and other fields and emphasizes choosing remedies (direct vs indirect) according to the substantive context, whereas Paper B interrogates the historical and conceptual separation of contract and tort (and its public/private ordering consequences) and how that separation influences which doctrines and remedies apply at the contract‑tort interface.

shared_topics.topic: classification/taxonomy of private‑law doctrines and their normative consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a novel taxonomy distinguishing 'direct' and 'indirect' remedies and draws normative lessons for when each is appropriate, while Paper B provides a periodization and conceptual taxonomy of fault's role in the modernization of contract and tort and argues that those classificatory choices have long‑run normative and doctrinal effects.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A is an explicit symposium piece critiquing and reflecting on the future and 'troubles' of the law-and-economics project; Paper B applies law-and-economics reasoning to remedial design while also spelling out the circumstances and limits in which an economically-inflected tool (indirect remedies) is appropriate.

shared_topics.topic: the distinction between descriptive and normative claims in legal theory
shared_topics.justification: Paper B frames its contribution as both descriptive (taxonomizing indirect remedies) and normative (justifying when to use them); Paper A, as a methodological critique of law-and-economics, likewise engages with the boundary and interplay between positive description and normative prescription in legal scholarship.

papers.node_id: 46hofstralrev827!!ARTICLE: DOES FAILURE TO MITIGATE DAMAGES BAR RECOVERY OF THE COSTS OF MITIGATION?
papers.title: ARTICLE: DOES FAILURE TO MITIGATE DAMAGES BAR RECOVERY OF THE COSTS OF MITIGATION?
papers.abstract:
It is well established that if a person injured by a breach of contract has the opportunity to mitigate her damages without thereby bearing undue risk, burden, or humiliation, but does not do so, then that person will be denied recovery of those damages that she could have so avoided.It is also well established that a person may as a general matter recover the cost of reasonable mitigation efforts, along with her other recoverable losses.The law is also clear that if a person makes reasonable efforts to mitigate damages, but those efforts prove to be unsuccessful, she still is entitled as a general matter to recover the cost of those mitigation efforts.
There is another and more subtle question related to the mitigation of damages, however, for which the answer is unfortunately not quite so clear. If a person injured by the breach of a contract is in a position to reasonably mitigate damages, but does not do so, that person as noted above will not be able to recover the damages that could have been so avoided.But under those circumstances, will that person nevertheless still be able to recover the probable costs of those reasonable mitigation efforts had they been undertaken,even though the person did not actually incur those costs? In other words, should the penalty for a person that does not take reasonable steps to mitigate her damages be the loss of the right to recover all of the damages that could have been so avoided, without any offset of the probable costs that such mitigation efforts would entailfrom this reduction in her award? Or should the party only lose the right to recover the net reduction of damages that could have been achieved by those mitigation efforts, after offsetting the probable costs of those efforts from the reduction in damages that would have resulted?
Let me try to clarify the scope of this question with a simple illustration. Consider the situation that arises if a person can mitigate her losses from a breach of contract by $ 10,000 by taking reasonable mitigation measures that would probably cost only about $ 500. If she takes those measures, so that her damages are thereby reduced by $ 10,000, she will then be able to recover her remaining damages, including as an element of incidental damages the $ 500 cost of those mitigation efforts. But what if that person does not take those mitigation efforts, and her losses are consequently $ 10,000 greater than they might have been? Should one's recovery then be reduced by the full $ 10,000 of avoidable losses as a result of one's failure to take those reasonable mitigation efforts, or instead only by the $ 9500 net savings that would have resulted from the mitigation efforts once the $ 500 probable costs of mitigation are also taken into account and offset? In this brief Article, I will consider this narrow and seemingly simple but actually rather difficult question.
Let me preface my analysis by making clear my views as to the proper resolution of this question, as a matter of policy. I believe that courts should not reduce the damages that they assess against a party who breaches a contract, when the injured party fails to reasonably mitigate, by any more than is necessary to uphold the basic avoidability of damages principle. I also believe, however, that courts should also attempt to provide sufficient incentive for future injured parties to behave efficiently after breach. These two goals could both be accomplished by courts reducing the recovery of an injured person who fails to mitigate by only the net reduction in damages that would have resulted had reasonable mitigation efforts been undertaken. They should offset from the reduction in damages that they impose to deny recovery for losses, that could have been avoided through reasonable mitigation efforts, the probable costs that would have been incurred in carrying out those mitigation efforts.
Such a result would be fair to the contract breacher in that it would prevent him from obtaining an undeserved windfall reduction in his damages when the injured party fails to make reasonable mitigation efforts, as compared to the compensatory damages that he would be obligated to pay had reasonable mitigation efforts been undertaken and the losses caused by the breach thereby reduced, and the cost of mitigation then included in the recovery as an incidental cost of the breach. In addition, an injured person who fails to make reasonable efforts to mitigate damages would be denied only the recovery of the net amount of damages that could have been avoided through those mitigation efforts, once the probable cost of those efforts is taken into account and offset, an appropriate result since that is how much those mitigation efforts would have saved.
Reducing the recovery of an injured person who fails to mitigate by only the net rather than the gross reduction in damages that would have resulted from mitigation efforts, had they been undertaken, is also relatively efficient in that it would preserve (although concededly would slightly weaken) the economic incentive for persons to mitigate damages whenever it is cost-effective for them to do so. Even with this smaller reduction in her recovery, a person would still be better off if she made reasonable efforts to mitigate damages than if she did not. Cost-effective mitigation efforts would still be encouraged.
find convincing on both fairness and efficiency grounds these arguments for reducing the damages awarded to a person who fails to take reasonable efforts to mitigate by only the net rather than the gross reduction in damages that would probably result from the mitigation efforts. However, this position is not unassailable and reasonable persons might disagree with my conclusions. It is possible to envision a court first denying recovery of those damages that could have been avoided through reasonable mitigation efforts that were not undertaken, applying standard avoidability principles to reach this result, and then also denying recovery of the probable cost of those mitigation efforts as an offset to that reduction in damages.
A court might reach this seemingly harsh result - one that appears to both undercompensate the injured person that fails to mitigate and also confer an undeserved windfall reduction in damages to the contract breacher - on one or more of several possible bases. First of all, since those probable mitigation costs were not actually incurred by the injured person, a court might rather simplistically conclude on that basis alone that those costs are not losses that merit recovery, even if only as an offset against a larger damages reduction that would be imposed due to the failure to reasonably mitigate. While there is some support to be found in contract law generally for awarding damages under circumstances when no out-of-pocket losses have been incurred,courts in most contracts cases are only called upon to award damages where actual losses can be proven,and may therefore be uncomfortable with the somewhat counterintuitive concept of ordering reimbursement of expenses that were not actually incurred.
, those probable mitigation costs, since they were not actually incurred, are only estimated costs. Such estimates may, under some circumstances, not be reasonably certain in their magnitude, and an injured person perhaps may be denied recovery by a court for that reason alone. Now the costs of mitigating damages, particularly the costs of typical covering purchases or subsequent resales, or of short-term financing-type arrangements entered into to offset temporary cash shortfalls after breach, can often be established with a fair degree of precision, and will not pose the same significant uncertainty problems as do, for example, claims based upon lost future profits or foregone opportunities. However, probable mitigation expenses that were not incurred are inherently less certain in amount than are actually incurred expenses, and in some instances their magnitude may pose substantial questions that a court would deem sufficient to justify denying their recovery.
, allowing such an offset from the reduction of damages for failure to mitigate will concededly undercut, to some extent, the incentive for future contracting parties to take reasonable efforts to mitigate damages in the event of breach, since if such an offset is allowed then the penalty for failure to mitigate is reduced to that extent. This reduction in the incentive to mitigate may give some courts concern. However, mitigation efforts are generally regarded as being "reasonable" efforts for avoidability of damages purposes only in instances where the magnitude of the avoidable losses substantially exceeds the costs of mitigation. Under those circumstances, even if the probable costs of mitigation are offset against the much larger damages reduction that will be imposed for the failure to mitigate the injured person would still have been far better off had she undertaken those mitigation efforts and avoided those larger damages. The allowance of this relatively minor recovery of the probable costs of mitigation efforts that were not undertaken would still leave in place a sufficiently strong incentive to take all clearly cost-effective mitigation efforts.
Despite the problems that I have pointed out with each of these bases for denying recovery of probable mitigation costs that were not incurred, a court may for one or more of those reasons decide that it is better policy to reduce the recovery of an injured person who has failed to take reasonable mitigation efforts by the full amount of damages avoidable through those mitigation efforts, rather than by the smaller net amount of damages reduction that would have occurred had those mitigation efforts taken place and the probable costs of those mitigation efforts then been offset from those avoidable losses.
have discussed some of the relevant policy considerations and offered my opinion as to the better result, but what is the actual state of the law? There is surprisingly little authority to be found that addresses this question. Several major single-volume contract law treatises that I have reviewed all closely agree on the general framework of mitigation of damages law, as one would expect, but none of them address this particular question regarding the right to recover probable mitigation costs that were not incurred, nor cite any precedents or statutes that would apply to these circumstances.Moreover, those treatises in their rather brief discussions of mitigation issues do not always distinguish between the application of avoidability principles to sale of goods contracts and to other contracts not governed by U.C.C. Article 2 - a distinction which could arguably be significant in this context given the different treatment of seller consequential damages under U.C.C. Article 2 as compared to common law.
In addition, these several treatise discussions all overlook what may be an important distinction between what I describe as the "primary" mitigation efforts that a person may undertake to directly reduce the amount of damages that she will suffer from a breach, and that person's possible "secondary" mitigation efforts to obtain external financing of any cash shortfall resulting from the breach that may persist even after those primary damages mitigation efforts have been undertaken, until settlement compensation or a judgment award is paid.Such secondary mitigation efforts may be undertaken so as to avoid the risk of further consequential losses that might result from that shortfall. Such consequential losses may result, for example, from defaults by the injured person upon other obligations that take place because of the financial constraints imposed by the shortfall, or from consequent financial restrictions on the ability to pursue other profitable opportunities, until a settlement payment or damages award is received from the contract breacher. As I will discuss below, a court may choose to deal differently between primary and secondary mitigation efforts with regard to allowing recovery of probable mitigation costs when those mitigation efforts are not undertaken.
Nor do any of these treatises consider the possible significance of applicable prejudgment interest statutes for the right to recover the probable costs of such secondary mitigation financial arrangements that are not undertaken. As I will discuss below, prejudgment interest statutes may well be regarded by some courts as having some bearing on the scope of recovery rights, both for the recovery of costs incurred for secondary mitigation measures, and for the probable costs of secondary mitigation measures that are not undertaken.
In Part II of this Article, I more fully elaborate on this distinction between primary and secondary efforts to mitigate damages,and on the potential significance of prejudgment interest statutes on the right to recover the probable costs of secondary mitigation efforts that are not undertaken.Having developed this analytical framework, in Part III, I address the question of the right of a person who fails to take reasonable efforts to mitigate her damages, after the breach of a sale of goods contract that is governed by state statutes implementing U.C.C. Article 2, to recover the probable costs of those mitigation efforts.I will separately consider the circumstances of seller breach and buyer breach of such sale contracts, and with regard to primary and secondary mitigation efforts,and will also take into account the effect of prejudgment interest statutes.In Part IV, I address these same questions with regard to those contracts not governed by U.C.C. Article 2, using the applicable provisions of the Restatement (Second) of Contracts as a general articulation of the governing common law principles.Part V presents a brief overall conclusion.
. Primary and Secondary Mitigation Efforts, and the Significance of Prejudgment Interest Statutes for Recovery of the Probable Cost of Secondary Mitigation Efforts that Are Not Undertaken

Does the answer to that question differ depending on the type of mitigation (direct actions that reduce loss versus secondary financial measures to bridge cash shortfalls) and the legal treatment of interest on delayed compensation?

matched_themes: Should courts allow apportionment of contractual damages when the non-breaching party's reliance or failure to cooperate contributed to the loss?
What counterfactual baseline should courts use to measure plaintiffs' losses for compensation purposes?
To what extent does empirical uncertainty about measuring gains and losses limit courts' ability to design remedies that reflect non-welfare ethical preferences without sacrificing efficiency?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
Do limits on recoverable damages (foreseeability, certainty, avoidability) substantially reduce awards below full compensation, and should courts liberalize those limits?
When is an indirect remedy (one that induces self-compliance) preferable to a direct remedy that delivers the outcome?

shared_topics.topic: whether breaches of contract can (or should) attract non‑compensatory or exceptional treatment (punitive remedies, nondischargeability)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly asks whether willful and malicious breaches should be treated like tortious wrongs and thus rendered nondischargeable under §523(a)(6), while Paper B examines doctrinal lines that can produce unusually harsh remedial outcomes (e.g., denying recovery or offsets for mitigation) and contemplates when courts may properly impose such nonstandard consequences.

shared_topics.topic: how to measure and compose recoverable damages (incidental costs, offsets, net vs gross reductions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates when contract damages should be characterized or expanded (for example by punitive elements) for purposes like nondischargeability, and Paper B analyzes the precise arithmetic of damages after breach—whether courts should reduce awards by the gross avoidable loss or only the net avoidable loss after probable mitigation costs are accounted for.

shared_topics.topic: the role of policy trade‑offs (fairness, creditor/debtor fresh start, efficiency and mitigation incentives) in shaping remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames nondischargeability as a policy choice balancing a debtor's fresh start against creditor protection and punishment for wrongful conduct, and Paper B explicitly weighs fairness and economic efficiency when deciding how failure to mitigate should affect the size of a plaintiff's recovery.

shared_topics.topic: interaction of contract remedies with other legal regimes or doctrines (bankruptcy, tort law, UCC, prejudgment interest)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates contract breaches within bankruptcy law and tort doctrines to determine nondischargeability, while Paper B examines how U.C.C. Article 2, prejudgment interest statutes, and distinctions between primary/secondary mitigation affect the scope and calculation of contract damages.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal uncertainty and the need for clearer rules (circuit splits, gaps in treatises/authority)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A catalogs circuit splits and ambiguous Supreme Court guidance about §523(a)(6) in contract contexts, and Paper B documents the surprising scarcity of authority or treatise treatment on whether unincurred probable mitigation costs should be recoverable, calling for doctrinal clarification.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 55amjcompl721!!ARTICLE: Why No "Efficient Breach" in the Civil Law?: A Comparative Assessment of the Doctrine of Efficient Breach of Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Why No "Efficient Breach" in the Civil Law?: A Comparative Assessment of the Doctrine of Efficient Breach of Contract

shared_topics.topic: use of economic efficiency to justify contract damages rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A weighs the efficiency consequences of reducing recovery by the net versus the gross avoidable loss when a plaintiff fails to mitigate, arguing that offsetting probable mitigation costs preserves mitigation incentives; Paper B centers on the economic theory of 'efficient breach,' assessing whether allowing breaches that raise total surplus should be encouraged by the law.

shared_topics.topic: what compensatory (expectation) damages should include—especially mitigation costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes whether probable but unincurred mitigation expenses should be recoverable or offset when mitigation is not undertaken, treating such costs as part of incidental/expectation recovery; Paper B treats expectation damages as the compensation mechanism that makes a non-breaching party whole and thus enables or prevents efficient breaches.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial rules shape incentives to mitigate or to breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how different damage-offset rules affect a harmed party's incentive to take cost-effective mitigation steps after breach; Paper B studies how damages doctrines (and their doctrinal framing) influence a contracting party's incentive to perform or to breach when a better opportunity arises.

shared_topics.topic: tension between fairness/moral norms and economic rationale in remedy design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses fairness concerns (risk of undercompensating injured parties or giving breachers windfalls) alongside efficiency goals when deciding whether to allow offsets for unincurred mitigation costs; Paper B examines the civil‑law moral and good‑faith resistance to the utilitarian arguments of efficient breach despite their economic appeal.

shared_topics.topic: role of doctrinal and institutional context (UCC/common law vs civil law) in shaping damages outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares UCC Article 2 and common‑law/Restatement approaches and considers statutory issues like prejudgment interest in determining recoverable mitigation costs; Paper B compares common‑law receptiveness to efficient breach with civil‑law traditions (notably France and Germany) and identifies structural and cultural doctrinal hurdles to adopting efficiency‑based remedial rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 33uclalrev1565!!ARTICLE: PUNITIVE AND NONPECUNIARY DAMAGES IN ACTIONS BASED UPON CONTRACT: TOWARD ACHIEVING THE OBJECTIVE OF FULL COMPENSATION.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PUNITIVE AND NONPECUNIARY DAMAGES IN ACTIONS BASED UPON CONTRACT: TOWARD ACHIEVING THE OBJECTIVE OF FULL COMPENSATION.

shared_topics.topic: systematic undercompensation of contract plaintiffs by damages doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A diagnoses how traditional contract rules (foreseeability, certainty, mitigation, limited nonpecuniary and punitive awards, and denial of attorneys' fees) cumulatively leave plaintiffs undercompensated; Paper B examines one key doctrinal limiter—mitigation doctrine—and how its operation (and the treatment of mitigation costs) can further reduce plaintiff recovery.

shared_topics.topic: tension between full compensation and efficiency/deterrence objectives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames a central conflict between the goal of fully compensating breach victims and the corollary aim of avoiding overcompensation to preserve efficient commercial activity, and argues for rethinking punitive/nonpecuniary awards; Paper B explicitly weighs fairness against incentives, arguing mitigation offsets should preserve efficient incentives while avoiding excessive forfeiture of compensation.

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal and evidentiary role of mitigation (including how to measure and offset mitigation costs)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats mitigation as a major rule that limits recoverable damages and contributes to undercompensation, while Paper B is devoted to the precise question of how mitigation should be measured—whether courts should deduct gross avoidable loss or net avoidable loss after probable mitigation costs—and distinguishes primary versus secondary mitigation.

shared_topics.topic: the significance of uncertainty, burden of proof, and prejudgment interest in calculating damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how requirements of reasonable certainty and courts' allocation of the risk of error to plaintiffs reduce awards (and notes restricted prejudgment interest), whereas Paper B analyzes how the uncertainty of probable (not incurred) mitigation costs and the interplay with prejudgment interest statutes affect whether and how such estimated costs should be credited or denied.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2013uilllrev151!!ARTICLE: CAN'T BUY ME LOVE: MONETARY VERSUS IN-KIND REMEDIES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CAN'T BUY ME LOVE: MONETARY VERSUS IN-KIND REMEDIES
