shared_topics.topic: normative aims of contract remedies (expectancy vs deterrence and harm-reduction)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the default non-enforcement remedy for illegal contracts for ignoring social-harm and deterrence goals and argues remedies should be tied to the harm the contract creates; Paper B interrogates the UCC's goal of protecting the aggrieved party's expectancy interest by asking whether market damages or lost profits better serve that normative aim in middleman resale cases.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial rules shape parties' ex ante incentives and transactional choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how non-enforcement, restitution, and other remedies create incentives (including overdeterrence or underdeterrence) and how parties may price or structure deals to evade those incentives; Paper B examines how a middleman's choice to cover or sue for market damages versus lost profits reflects strategic behavior driven by the available remedial measures.

shared_topics.topic: legal uncertainty and doctrinal conflict over which remedial rule applies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes ambiguity in defining illegality (statutes, public policy, Restatement factors) and how that uncertainty amplifies deterrent effects; Paper B focuses on doctrinal conflict between UCC section 2-713 (market damages) and section 1-106 (expectancy principle) and the resulting case-law division that creates uncertainty about recoverable damages.

shared_topics.topic: scholarly and reformist engagement with remedy doctrine and proposed fixes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a structured framework recommending that courts tie non-enforcement to a showing of harm and account for ambiguity and evasive pricing, while Paper B surveys case law, commentator positions, and proposed revisions to Article 2 to assess and recommend how damages rules should be clarified or reformed.

shared_topics.topic: the effects of legal uncertainty and proof requirements on contracting and deterrence

shared_topics.topic: historical and doctrinal development of remedial rules in contract law

shared_topics.topic: the normative/economic justification for limiting or permitting monetary recovery (deterrence and social-welfare concerns)

papers.node_id: 54arizlrev673!!ARTICLE: How Law Frames Moral Intuitions: The Expressive Effect of Specific Performance
papers.title: ARTICLE: How Law Frames Moral Intuitions: The Expressive Effect of Specific Performance
papers.abstract:
A long-standing controversy exists regarding whether courts should grant relief to a disappointed contract promisee in the form of damages or specific performance.
Under American law, a damage remedy is the applicable default rule;injured contract parties have a right to damages for unexcused breaches by promisors.If damages are adequate to protect the expectation interest of the injured contract party, courts will not award specific performance or an injunction.Influenced by the economic approach to law, contract scholars reached a consensus in the early 1980s that the expectation damage remedy is the appropriate default remedy for a breach of contract.Expectation damages, it was argued, induce breach only if the cost of performance for the promisor exceeds the value of performance for the promisee.As a result, performance occurs if and only if it is efficient.By enhancing efficient breach, the expectation damage remedy prevents excessive performance when the costs of performance outweigh the value of performance or when the promisor could sell to a higher outside bidder.Other scholars have argued in favor of damage remediesbecause performance is often more intrusive and harmful to personal freedom than the damage remedy.Following Mill's harm principle,performance should beawarded only when the less intrusive remedial measure of damage compensation cannot fully redress the harm caused by the violation of the promisee's rights.
Some modern contract theorists, however, favor specific performance as the more appropriate default remedy.Specific performance is the fulfillment of the performance due in the contract as nearly as practicable, by the party in breach.Two very distinct strands of scholarship advocate specific performance as a default remedy. First, ethical theorists favor a specific performance default, because it aligns with the moral obligation that promises should be kept. Second, under the consent theory of contracts, for instance, contract rights cannot be waived unilaterally, unless the contract specifies otherwise.
Other scholars promote specific performance on economic grounds.From an efficiency perspective, expectation damages may impose unnecessary costs.If contracting parties are rational, they will design an optimal contract and courts should enforce these terms "rather than give the parties an option(expectation damages) when they did not bargain for it."Moreover, expectation damages may induce socially wasteful breaches of contracts because courts tend to underestimate the value of performance to promisees.By contrast, specific performance forces a promisor to negotiate with the promisee to seek removal from his or her contractual duties.To some economists, specific performance eliminates much of the ethical concerns about efficient breach.First, it leaves the decision of whether a breach can take place with the innocent promisee. Second, because the promisee knows exactly the value of performance, contracts will be breached only on terms that meet or exceed the promisee's interest in the original contract.
In this Article, we claim that contract scholarship overlooks an important interdependence between contract norms and default remedies. When scholars argue that the morality of performance or bargaining benefits are a sufficient justification for specific performance, they ignore how moral evaluations and bargaining costs are themselves strongly affected by whether specific performance is available as a default remedy. When expressed as a legal default, the legal right to insist on performance increases a promisee's sense of entitlement and resentment against breach.
We posit that specific performance as a legal default may create aversion against breach even when performance is inefficient. This insight is based on empirical evidence that we obtained in a novel study for this Article.We conducted an incentive-compatible laboratory experiment where participants signed and performed valid legal contracts that were legally enforceable.Participants understood that their decisions would impact their earnings as stipulated in the contract(s) that they entered into with other participants.
Participants entered into a contract that stipulated a joint task (adjustment of sliders on a computer screen) and the distribution of gains when the contract was completed. While one of the participants (the promisee) commenced the contractual task, his or her counterpart (the promisor) received an outside offer from a third party that would require the promisor to breach the original contract. The outside offer presented an opportunity for efficient breach: The gains realizedby the new offer were more than sufficient to fully compensate the expectation damages of the promisee.
We measured the decisions and motivations of participants regarding the performance, breach, and enforcement of the legally enforceable contracts entered into by participants. First, a promisor had to decide whether she would breach or honor the original contract. Second, a promisee could enforce the original contract or accept damage compensation. After we observed the behavior of the participants, we examined their motivations in three additional stages of the experiment. First, we provided promisors and promisees with an endowment that could only be used to make a donation to the other contract party. We measured how the actions of one contracting party influenced the amount the other party donated. Second, participants could generate additional income by making a wager on the prediction that the other party would breach or enforce the original contract. Third, we used questionnaires to ask participants what motivated their behavior in the experiment.
Our experiment focused on the availability of specific performance as the default remedy. All promisees in the experiment could prevent the breach of contract without relying on a legal remedy. A promisee could always instruct that the outside offer be withdrawn.But one group of participants could also prevent breach by relying on a specific performance default.In other words, all contracting parties could enforce the contract, but only one group of participants in the experiment could do so on the basis of the legal remedy.
A number of interesting findings emerged. First, we observed that, when specific performance was the default remedy, promisees demonstrated a strong preference to enforce the original contract. In fact, participants sacrificed a substantial part of their earnings in the experiment to obstruct the efficient breach when specific performance was available.By comparison, promisees in the control group did not object to the efficient breach. The mere availability of specific performance caused players in the experimental group to insist on the inefficient performance.
, we observed substantially smaller donations whenever promisees were entitled to specific performance. This suggests that when specific performance is the applicable default, efficient breaches induce stronger resentment and even a desire to punish the promisor.
Third, the results show that the specific performance default triggered conflicting moral intuitions about contract breach among contracting parties. Specific performance made the ethical norm to adhere to the contract more salient to promisees, whereas promisors focused on the efficiency of the breach. Promisees adopted the principled position that promises must be kept and strongly resented the efficient breach, whereas promisors evaluated the contract on utilitarian grounds and were much more accepting of efficient breaches of the contract.
Finally, our data indicated that promisors failed to anticipate how the specific performance remedy created resentment about the efficient breach among promisees.
This Article contests both the economic and deontological argument for specific performance. First, we advance an empirical understanding of the ethics of contract breach. Deontological concepts of contract theory often assume that individuals have a principled aversion against promise breaking.As an empirical matter, it appears from our study that the moral obligation to keep one's promise is context dependent. Individuals seem to have conflicting and contradicting moral intuitions about contract breach that can be triggered by the legal frame. A default of specific performance makes the ethical norm to perform the contract more salient.When specific performance was available, breach was evaluated negatively in light of fairness considerations regarding cooperation and defection. Without the specific performance default, participants in our study perceived the breach in a more utilitarian sense, focusing on the gains from trade. The results of the survey questionnaires confirm that the default remedy triggered the moral intuitions of promisees and induced a sense of entitlement.
, we offer new insights into the relative transaction costs generated by different remedies for breach of contract.Specifically, our findings challenge the notion that a specific performance default remedy leads to "more mutually beneficial promises … exchanged at a lower cost than under any other contractremedy."Although some economic theorists argue that specific performance is the favored remedy if no significant bargaining impediments are present, we posit that the availability of specific performance may negatively affect bargaining conditions in the following ways: First, instead of viewing contractual rights as a means to an end, a legal remedy itself may create intrinsic value in carrying out contractual promises. Second, by boosting the salience of performance, a specific performance default may cause promisees to insist on performance even when it is in their material interest to accept the efficient breach. Third, when specific performance has an expressive effect on the moral intuitions of contract promisees,the resulting opposition to breach increases the burden on promisors when they negotiate to obtain release from inefficient contractual obligations. A promisor must compensate the promisee not only for the material costs of breach. The promisor must also obtain forgiveness for violating the statutory entitlement to performance. If the contract breach is perceived as an insult, material compensation might not be satisfactory.In other words, by fueling promisees' moral aversion to breach, specific performance might lead parties into conflict rater than negotiation. Overall, because the economic case for specific performance largely rests on the ability of parties to renegotiate a mutually beneficial outcome, our findings weaken the efficiency argument in favor of specific performance.
The Article proceeds as follows. In Part I, we provide a brief historical review of the leading perspectives on optimal contract remedies. Part II describes the design and implementation of our study. In Part III, we report and discuss our findings. Part IV derives policy implications for contract theory in particular and legal regulation more generally.

questions.question: Whether making in-kind performance the legal default (rather than monetary compensation) causes promisees to insist on enforcement and resist otherwise efficient breaches of contract.

Whether the availability of an in-kind performance default changes contracting parties' moral judgments, punitive or prosocial responses (e.g., donations or punishment), and acceptance of efficient breaches.

Whether an in-kind performance default affects bargaining dynamics and transaction costs by increasing promisees' entitlement and resentment, thereby making renegotiation and mutually beneficial settlements harder (and whether promisors anticipate these effects).

matched_themes: Does giving the promisee a unilateral right to demand performance or elect a damages measure that captures promisor's forgone gains vindicate moral intuitions while preserving ex post efficiency?

Should the promisor or the promisee have the default right to choose between performance and payment to achieve allocative efficiency?

Does making in-kind performance the legal default (rather than monetary compensation) change parties' enforcement choices, moral judgments, and economic efficiency?
When should courts prefer or enforce in-kind (specific) performance rather than monetary damages for breach of contract?
Should the availability of legal remedies or contractual incompleteness change the moral assessment of a party who breaches under unanticipated circumstances?

shared_topics.topic: applicability of extraordinary remedies across public and private contracting contexts
shared_topics.justification: Both papers consider how remedial doctrines apply differently in public versus private settings—Paper A highlights that the Supreme Court's public, interstate compact context leaves open questions about private litigants seeking disgorgement, while Paper B studies private contracting behavior and draws implications for remedy policy in civilian contracts.

papers.node_id: 116wvalrev363!!ARTICLE: HYPOTHETICAL EFFICIENCY IS NOT GROUNDS FOR BREACH
papers.title: ARTICLE: HYPOTHETICAL EFFICIENCY IS NOT GROUNDS FOR BREACH
papers.abstract:
Parties contemplating breaching a contract face an intractably difficult situation. They may be legally bound by the terms of their agreement, but - perhaps as a result of a new opportunity - continued performance is no longer efficient. In such instances, some firms will simply breach and pay damages. Others will comply with the terms of their contracts or seek to renegotiate. But, in all events, it seems legitimate to ask, if the only penalty the law imposes for breach is the payment of compensatory damages, and the breaching firm pays those damages, is it morally permissible to breach a contract whenever it is efficient to do so? This question, although hotly debated among leading commentators,remains unresolved, and, as a result, business leaders are left without sufficient guidance.
This Article rejects efficient breach by showing how the arguments of one of its leading proponents, Steven Shavell,fail and, in doing so, lays out a new path for parties to remain in relationship even where considerations of efficiency would call for breach and payment of damages. To be clear, Shavell does not contend that there is no moral obligation to keep promises.He would, however, limit that obligation to those instances where the parties' agreement expressly provides for the contingency at issue. He maintains that, if one adopts his definition of moral behavior, where a contingency occurs that is not expressly set forth in the contract, breach is moral so long as the cost of performance exceeds its value to the promisee and the promisor pays damages.
begin by explaining why the law cannot be read to favor breach plus the payment of damages even in the more limited situations Shavell identifies, and I explore and reject the use of hypothetical contracts as a basis to support efficient breach. I then distinguish the covenant of good faith and other contract terms implied by law from an implied covenant of efficiency, which is what those advocating efficient breach would imply into every contract. I maintain that although economic considerations may provide information that may help business leaders consider normative questions, economics cannot serve as an effective moral compass for business decisions. Instead, business leaders should be guided by the values they use when making normative decisions in their interpersonal relationships, and avoid distancing themselves from such matters by viewing them as involving "just business" decisions.That is so because such distancing does not permit them to escape responsibility for their actions or the harm that they may do.

questions.question: Is it morally permissible for a party to breach a contract and pay compensatory damages whenever doing so is economically efficient?

Does the law or ordinary contract interpretation justify or favor allowing breach-plus-damages on grounds of efficiency, or alternatively imply an obligation to perform even when performance is economically inefficient?
Should business leaders rely on economic efficiency as the appropriate moral guide when deciding whether to breach contracts, or should interpersonal moral values govern those decisions instead?

matched_themes: Should parties and courts adopt fault-based remedial regimes that distinguish among breaches by reason when allocating remedies?

What moral and legal limits should constrain the commodification of promises-i.e., which promises ought not be treated as market commodities and how should the law reflect anti-commodification concerns?
How should default liability rules interact with parties' freedom to allocate risks by contract and duties of disclosure to achieve efficient and fair risk allocation?
Do courts actually prefer monetary damages over specific (in-kind) remedies, or do they grant specific relief except when independent reasons exist to deny it?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?
Should the promisor or the promisee have the default right to choose between performance and payment to achieve allocative efficiency?
Should parties be presumptively permitted to contractually specify nonstandard damage remedies, or should courts retain authority to impose defaults?
Should the availability of legal remedies or contractual incompleteness change the moral assessment of a party who breaches under unanticipated circumstances?

Should remedies and contract law be structured to preserve conditions necessary for moral agency and promissory responsibility, rather than treating promises solely as instruments of economic cooperation?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
Should courts police and limit supracompensatory contractual remedies (penalty-like clauses), or does allowing parties to contract for such terms respect autonomy and promote efficient contracting?
Do enforceable contractual damage remedies substitute for or complement informal relational governance in franchise and other repeated relationships?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
To what extent should moral blameworthiness and non-economic considerations influence the design and application of contract remedies?
When is an indirect remedy (one that induces self-compliance) preferable to a direct remedy that delivers the outcome?

papers.node_id: 107michlrev1381!!ARTICLE: IN (PARTIAL) DEFENSE OF STRICT LIABILITY IN CONTRACT
papers.title: ARTICLE: IN (PARTIAL) DEFENSE OF STRICT LIABILITY IN CONTRACT
papers.abstract:
The Restatement's oft-quoted assertion about the nature of contract liability is one of the most imprecise generalizations ever made about the common law of contract. Numerous scholars have pointed out that, in fact, there are many notions of fault that infuse contract law, ranging from prescriptions against intentional "bad behavior," to assessments of the reasonableness of an actor's behavior in assessing both liability and damages. But while there are indeed many "fault lines" in contract,speaking atthat level of generality has little analytic purchase.In short, from a distance the fault lines in contract appear broken and indistinct.
In this Article, I propose to defend the notion of strict liability that lies at the core of the Restatement's claim. By its terms, the Restatement does not rule out fault-based considerations for claims based on promissory estoppel, fraud, bad faith, mistake, excuse or a host of other issues. But the availability of these principles only in select circumstances justifies a core no-fault regime.This core regime is based on two key prongs: (1) the promisor is liable to the promisee for breach, and that liability is unaffected by the promisor's exercise of due care or failure to take efficient precautions; and (2) the promisor's liability is unaffected by the fact that the promisee, prior to the breach, has failed to take cost-effective precautions to reduce the consequences of nonperformance.In terms of the Restatement conception, then, contract law is strict liability without a contributory negligence defense.
Notwithstanding the many illustrations of fault lines in contract, the Restatement's assertion, as limited above, is descriptively accurate. The core of contract law as applied in the courts is a no-fault regime. This is so even though theorists mount powerful arguments on efficiency grounds for a cost-benefit analysis of promisor and promisee behavior in particular cases, and even though contract doctrine appears to invite just such an analysis. For example, if the promisor carelessly fails to take efficient precautions ex ante that result in breach ex post, the "willful breach doctrine" invites courts to increase damages to deter such inefficient behavior. Similarly, if the promisee fails to take efficient precautions prior to the breach that would reduce or eliminate losses, the mitigation principle invites courts to apply a "contributory negligence" bar to recovery. However, a large sample of cases shows that courts decline to employ the willful breach doctrine to deter an inefficient breach. And despite evidence that the promisee has failed to take precautions prior to breach that would have reduced losses, courts adhere strictly to the rule that the promisee's mitigation responsibility is not triggered until the promisor breaches.
The courts' reluctance to adopt a comparative fault standard in assessing the core question of liability for breach is all the more surprising given that comparative fault principles are found elsewhere in contract law, most notably in the doctrines of unjust enrichment and unilateral mistake.Viewed in this light, the question is not why contract law fails to acknowledge explicitly the many different fault principles that it embraces implicitly. Rather,the puzzle is why courts adhere to a no-fault regime at the core of contract liability even though contract doctrine invites them to consider fault in other instances.
In Part I of this Article, I set out the case that courts are committed to a strict liability regime at what I call the "core" of contract law. This Part focuses on the evidence of strict liability as demonstrated by (a) courts' reluctance to use the willful breach doctrine to deter inefficient breach by promisors, and (b) courts' reluctance to use the mitigation principle to deter inefficient overreliance by promisees. In Part II, I offer two complementary normative justifications for contract law's stubborn resistance to fault principles at its core. I argue that there are unappreciated ways in which courts' adherence to strict liability doctrine reduces contracting costs. In addition, I argue that a strict liability core best supports parties' efforts to access informal or relational modes of contracting, especially where key information is unverifiable. I conclude, therefore, that both autonomy and efficiency values support the claim that commercial parties will prefer strict liability rules to fault-based rules for assessing performance and the response to nonperformance.

questions.question: Whether the central regime governing breach of contract operates as a no-fault (strict liability) system - that is, whether a promisor is held liable for breach regardless of the promisor's exercise of care and regardless of the promisee's pre-breach precautions.

Why courts maintain a no-fault core in contract liability despite economic and doctrinal reasons that could justify allocating losses according to fault (i.e., what explains judicial resistance to comparative-fault approaches in core contract cases).

Whether and how a strict-liability core in contract law affects contracting behavior - specifically, whether strict liability reduces contracting costs and better facilitates informal or relational contracting when key information is unverifiable.

papers.node_id: 82columlrev1365!!ARTICLE: In Defense of Money Damages for Breach of Contract
papers.title: ARTICLE: In Defense of Money Damages for Breach of Contract
papers.abstract:
In recent years a body of literature has appeared advocating the adoption of specific performance as the normal remedy for breach of contract.Two principal justifications have been offered to support specific performance, one founded on the moral obligation of promise,the other on the economic efficiency of specific prformance compared with money damages.The view that a promise creates a moral obligation to perform is not novel.Indeed, the moral obligation of the promisor may be one of the primary reasons why under the common law a promisee generally recovers expectation damages for the promisor's breach -- that is, damages that put the promisee in the position in which he would have been had the promisor fulfilled his promise.Although an award of compensatory money damages may sufficiently support the principles of trust and respect for another's word that underlie a moral obligation theory,a rule requiring specific performance of a contractualpromise would undoubtedly strengthen the ethical notion that a promisor ought to keep his promise.  What is novel and surprising, then, about the recent literature supporting specific performance is not the conclusion that specific performance buttresses the moral obligation of promise, but rather the contention that routinely granting specific performance to promisees who request it would be more efficientthan the current system under which money damages are the normal remedy.
This Article will challenge the thesis that the remedy for breach of contract should be specific performance in cases in which it has not traditionally been granted.  Part I will examine the arguments for making specific performance routinely available to promisees on request and will show that giving promisees that right would be inadvisable for reasons of both fairness and efficiency.  Part II will investigate the recurrent problem of formulating an appropriate remedy for breach of a promise to restore land at the end of a lease.  The difficulty in this context of accurately quantifying the promisee's subjective loss, and the resulting risk of undercompensation, constitute perhaps the strongest arguments for specific performance where it is not now granted.Part II will show, however, that even in these cases, if an invariable remedy were to be adopted to ensure the promisee adequate compensation, a carefully chosen money damages rule would be preferable to specific performance.
Part III will explore what is perhaps the most serious objection to making specific performance the usual remedy for breach of contract.  In light of the difficulty and risk of error involved in trying to compensate the promisee with money damages in some cases, it is not surprising that specific performance would be viewed as a simple and direct way of correcting the perceived defects of a money damages system.  But the allure of any routine remedy for breach of contract, especially specific performance, is deceptive, for the issues that arise in the formulation of contract remedies are so diverse and complex thatthey do not yield to any universal solution.  One significant asset of the current system of money damages is its ability to respond satisfactorily to the varied ethical and economic considerations relevant to difficult contract cases.  Much of this flexibility and responsiveness is likely to be lost if specific performance becomes the paradigmatic remedy for breach of contract.  This Article will urge, therefore, that instead of making specific performance routinely available, the legal system should selectively modify those money damages rules that thwart the underlying objectives of contract law.

questions.question: Whether courts should make in-kind enforcement (specific performance) the normal/default remedy for breach of contract instead of monetary compensation.
Whether routinely granting in-kind remedies would be more economically efficient and substantively fair than retaining money damages as the usual remedy.

In cases where the promisee's loss is hard to quantify (for example, subjective or nonmarket losses), whether in-kind remedies are superior to carefully tailored monetary damages or whether money damages can be reformed to achieve adequate compensation.

matched_themes: What counterfactual baseline should courts use to measure plaintiffs' losses for compensation purposes?
Does giving the promisee a unilateral right to demand performance or elect a damages measure that captures promisor's forgone gains vindicate moral intuitions while preserving ex post efficiency?
Do courts actually prefer monetary damages over specific (in-kind) remedies, or do they grant specific relief except when independent reasons exist to deny it?
When should courts order specific performance (in-kind relief) versus awarding monetary damages?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?
Should the promisor or the promisee have the default right to choose between performance and payment to achieve allocative efficiency?
Does making in-kind performance the legal default (rather than monetary compensation) change parties' enforcement choices, moral judgments, and economic efficiency?
When should courts prefer or enforce in-kind (specific) performance rather than monetary damages for breach of contract?
Should the availability of legal remedies or contractual incompleteness change the moral assessment of a party who breaches under unanticipated circumstances?

Should remedies and contract law be structured to preserve conditions necessary for moral agency and promissory responsibility, rather than treating promises solely as instruments of economic cooperation?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
How should remedial and enforcement rules be structured to achieve efficient behavior when populations include both internalizers and externalizers?
Can courts reliably determine ex post whether a breach would increase social welfare so that remedy choice can be used to promote efficiency?
To what extent does empirical uncertainty about measuring gains and losses limit courts' ability to design remedies that reflect non-welfare ethical preferences without sacrificing efficiency?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
Do courts consider the breaching party's blameworthiness or opportunistic behavior when selecting among compensatory remedies?
To what extent should moral blameworthiness and non-economic considerations influence the design and application of contract remedies?
When is an indirect remedy (one that induces self-compliance) preferable to a direct remedy that delivers the outcome?
Should courts more readily grant equitable relief to compel performance when monetary damages undercompensate and public interests are implicated?

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BLACK MARKETS AND THE EXCHANGE STRUCTURE

shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents historical practice in seventeenth-century English courts that limited damage remedies and favored liquidated, sum-certain recoveries (including bonds) instead of flexible in-action damage adjustments, while Paper B directly debates whether money damages should remain the normal remedy or be supplanted by specific performance, defending money damages as the preferable default.

shared_topics.topic: difficulties of quantifying damages and institutional responses to avoid complex assessments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows courts used procedural devices (pleading limits, bonds, sum-certain rules) to avoid in-trial jury assessments of competing damages, and Paper B highlights the practical problem of accurately measuring subjective losses (e.g., lease-restoration cases) and argues for carefully tailored money-damages rules rather than routine specific performance.

shared_topics.topic: how procedural and administrative constraints shape substantive contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A's central claim is that administrative capacity, jury control, and pleading rules drove substantive doctrines like the strict law of conditions; Paper B likewise reasons that the practicability of administering remedies (errors, enforcement burdens, need for flexibility) should determine whether courts favor damages or specific performance.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between formalism (predictable, administrable rules) and economic/fairness efficiency in contract enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links the emergence of formal, administrable contract doctrines to judicial incentives and institutional preservation (sometimes at the expense of commercial expectations), while Paper B weighs the efficiency and fairness consequences of adopting a more rigid remedy rule (specific performance) versus retaining the more flexible, sometimes less formal money-damages regime.

shared_topics.topic: the role and scope of expectation (money) damages as the default remedy for breach of contract
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates its proposed valuation rule within the expectation-damages tradition (arguing for a textured money-damages formula for loss of registration/liquidity), while Paper B defends money damages as the normal remedy and explicates the theoretical foundations of expectation relief against proposals to expand specific performance.

shared_topics.topic: the difficulty of quantifying damages when the promised performance or asset value is hard to value
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes valuation problems for assets with fluctuating market prices and loss of liquidity (showing traditional formulas are inadequate and proposing a synthetic-rights measure), and Paper B examines contexts (e.g., lease-restoration and other subjective losses) where money damages are hard to quantify and the risk of undercompensation supports careful remedial design.

shared_topics.topic: the need for contextual, 'textured' remedial rules rather than a one-size-fits-all remedy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the general expectation principle lacks sufficient texture for registration-rights cases and develops a bespoke damages rule for that context, while Paper B argues against making specific performance the universal remedy and urges selective modification of money-damages rules to fit distinct factual and ethical concerns.

shared_topics.topic: weighing normative considerations (fairness/moral obligation) against efficiency when choosing remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds its proposed monetary formula in historical and equitable principles (seeking to fairly compensate the promisee for loss of liquidity), and Paper B directly debates the moral- obligation and economic-efficiency justifications for specific performance versus money damages, balancing fairness and efficiency in remedial choice.

shared_topics.justification: Both works analyze situations where the promisee's loss is hard to measure—Paper B treats long-shot, probabilistic betting winnings as speculative and therefore nonrecoverable beyond the ticket price, and Paper A highlights subjective or hard-to-quantify losses (e.g., lease restoration) as a central reason specific performance is sometimes invoked or money-damages rules need adjustment.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between efficiency and fairness in designing contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both papers weigh economic efficiency against fairness: Paper A debates whether specific performance would be more efficient than money damages and warns about fairness/efficiency costs of making it the default, while Paper B implicitly balances compensating a plaintiff's windfall loss against limits that promote predictable, administrable damages rules.

shared_topics.topic: rule-based limits versus case-by-case remedial discretion in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the question of whether bright-line remedial rules are desirable: Paper B demonstrates application of a doctrinal rule (Hadley) to deny unlikely losses, and Paper A explicitly argues against adopting a single universal remedy (specific performance) in favor of selectively modifying damages rules to preserve flexibility.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:SELF-HELP IN CONTRACT LAW: AN EXPLORATION AND PROPOSAL

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: FAULT AT THE CONTRACT-TORT INTERFACE

papers.title: ARTICLE: Income Tax Considerations in Florida Personal Injury Actions
papers.abstract: provides that the amount of any damages received in compensation for personal injuries is not taxable income.As a result of this provision, two distinct tax issues typically arise whenever a personal injury case is presented to a jury.  First, is evidence showing the effect of the section 104 tax exemption on the plaintiff's claim for lost future earningsadmissible?  Second, should the jury be instructed that any damages it awards for the personal injury are tax exempt?  In some cases the courts have confused these two questions, even though they are analytically distinct.

questions.question: Whether evidence about the tax-exempt status of personal injury damages may be presented to the jury and considered when calculating lost future earnings.
Whether juries should be instructed that damages awarded for personal injuries are not subject to income tax.

papers.node_id: 37umiamilrev93!!ARTICLE: Inflation and the Present Value of Future Economic Damages
papers.title: ARTICLE: Inflation and the Present Value of Future Economic Damages
papers.authors: William F. Landsea; David L. Roberts
papers.abstract:
The practice of awarding plaintiffs in personal injury cases a current sum of money as compensation for future loss of earnings or medical care makes the assessment of economic damages a difficult task.  The assessment necessarily involves (1) forecasting the future damages and (2) discounting these damages to determine their present value.  Discounting the expected future damages is requiredbecause the plaintiff may invest the current award and earn additional income until actual expense is incurred.  The anticipated rate of future price inflation affects both the rate at which future damages are expected to grow and the rate at which future damages should be discounted.  Incomes, medical expenses, and returns on investments all tend to increase during inflationary periods.
Judges, attorneys and jurors ordinarily do not have the training, skills and knowledge required to forecast and calculate the present value of future economic damages.  As a result, the legal system is often forced to rely on the testimony of "expert" witnesses.  Unfortunately, these experts are sometimes less expert than their credentials imply.  In addition, the competition for lucrative expert witness employment often puts pressure upon experts to become advocates for the party that employs them.  It is not surprising, therefore, that federal and state courts have accepted a variety of different approaches to determining the present value of future damages, based on alternative methods of incorporating anticipated price inflation.  Similarly, it is not surprising that, for a given set of conditions and assumptions, these alternative methods of calculating present value often result in dramatic differences in calculated values of damages.  The inability of the legal system to evaluate objectively the methodology of economic experts has led to substantial inequities in the settlement of personal injury cases.
The apparent difficulty for some within the legal community to appreciate the economic complexities involved in accurate damages assessment is evident in certain opinions of the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.  InJohnson v. Penrod Drilling Co.,theCircuit prohibited the consideration of expected future price inflation in determining the present value of future economic damages.  The court's position was that the "influence on future damages of possible inflation or deflation is too speculative a matter for judicial determination"and, therefore, triers of fact "should not be instructed to take into account future inflationary or deflationary trends in computing future lost earnings, nor should the jury be advised to consider such alternative descriptions of inflationary and deflationary trends as the purchasing power of the dollar or the consumer price index."In practice, this positionbecame an inflexible standard that forbade any evidence of price inflation in assessing economic damages and often led to substantial understatements in present value awards.
InCulver v. Slater Boat Co.,theCircuit overruled the precedent established inPenrodand evaluated a number of alternative methods of assessing the present value of future damages.  The different methods discussed are widely used in other federal circuits and in the state courts.  InCulver,the court concluded: "[W]e have discussed several acceptable methods that are useful in the consideration of the likely effect of inflation,"but warned that those methodologies were "only suggested approaches, and not strait-jackets, for courts to use in determining future earnings."For the same set of conditions and assumptions, these several "acceptable" methods often produce substantially different present values.
The purpose of this article is to provide a convenient reference on present value calculations in personal injury cases that will be useful in evaluating and comparing the alternative methods often employed by expert witnesses and accepted by the courts.  In Part II a "preferred" method of calculating present value is presented and explained.  Part III explores the effects on present value of changing such factors as the expected growth rate of damages or the discount rate.  In Part IV the relationships between the expected rate of price inflation and the expected growth and discount rates for damages are explained, and Part V presents evaluations of the more widely used methods of calculating present values and illustrates the errors to which these approaches often lead.

shared_topics.topic: the role of economic analysis versus moral or corrective justice considerations in structuring remedies

shared_topics.topic: normative critique of existing doctrine and proposals for reform to prevent inequitable outcomes

shared_topics.topic: methodology for determining monetary remedies (how damages are measured and awarded)

shared_topics.topic: the role and capacity of courts (versus experts) to make complex factual and economic determinations when awarding remedies

shared_topics.topic: use of economic reasoning to justify or structure legal remedies (incentives, deterrence, and efficiency)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly frames expectation and reliance damages in economic terms—deterrence of breach versus deterrence of wrongful contracting—arguing remedies should respond to economic reasons for breach; Paper B applies economic principles (discounting, inflation expectations, investment returns) to determine present value and link award size to incentives and fairness in compensation.

shared_topics.topic: uncertainty and forecasting about future events and its impact on award fairness and doctrinal choice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how the reason for breach and factual uncertainty should affect remedy selection (and whether a fault-based regime is feasible), whereas Paper B focuses on uncertainty in forecasting future earnings, medical costs, and inflation and shows how different assumptions and methods produce substantially different awards and settlement inequities.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between legal rules and economic principles (discounting, growth, caps)

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE FALLACY OF FULL COMPENSATION

papers.node_id: 81fordhamlrev1221!!ARTICLE: INSTRUCTING JURIES ON NONECONOMIC CONTRACT DAMAGES
papers.title: ARTICLE: INSTRUCTING JURIES ON NONECONOMIC CONTRACT DAMAGES
papers.authors: David A. Hoffman; Alexander S. Radus
papers.abstract:
What are the natural and probable consequences of breach of contract? Please illustrate/define/exemplify?
Juries may not award noneconomic damages for breach of contract.The point is often expressed in the major contracts treatises, casebooks, and the Restatement (First) and Restatement (Second) of Contracts, with copious supporting documentation.And yet, venerable authorities acknowledge that such losses may be real,foreseeable,or even likelyconsequences ofcontract breach. Corbin takes it a step further, noting that contract breach "practically always causes mental vexation and feelings of disappointment by the plaintiff."
With a few exceptions,this conventional wisdom thus concludes that frustrated promisees routinely are denied the opportunity to seek and recover noneconomic damages. This remedial gap is not an accident or a bug of contract adjudication - it is built into the very structure of the system.
The problem with this story is that it overgeneralizes and, consequently, misleads at two levels. First, "contract law" is legion: each state has its own peculiar contracting tradition, doctrine, and practice. Commentators de-emphasize regional variety in finding a broad exclusive doctrine against noneconomic losses.This kind of monistic approach to contract law is common. Our understandings of purportedly uniform contract doctrines - like interpretationand remedies- are impoverished when we mistake the Restatement's certainty for the diversity that exists across the states.
But much more significantly, the conventional wisdom operates at the wrong level of analysis. It misses the actual mechanism by which contract damages are shaped in real cases - jury instructions. This Article remedies that failure by conducting the first comprehensive academic study of pattern contract jury instructions in all fifty states and the District of Columbia. Such pattern instructions form the preapproved baseline against which real jury instructions are drafted and exert significant influence at trial.Analysis of these pattern instructions results in a more muddled picture than the treatises would have led us to believe. We find that there are four basic approaches to contract remedy instructions, which guide - or fail to guide -juries through the process of awarding general damages in significantly different ways.
We couple this research with a preliminary psychological experiment in which we test how lay people react to these different pattern jury instructions. In each category, we find jurors eager to "overcompensate" plaintiffs. Most interestingly - and perhaps surprisingly - we find some evidence that this overcompensation is closely linked to more general principles of jury control and may best be explained as an award for noneconomic losses. Therefore, in the majority of American jurisdictions, juries instructed with the pattern instructions may be likely to include noneconomic damages for breach as a matter of course. Indeed, in eight jurisdictions,jurors hearing contract cases are instructed to award damages in a way that is very hard to distinguish from ordinary tort remedies.
Looking carefully at pattern instructions thus excavates the hidden diversity in contract doctrine, as well as jurisdictions' surprising flexibility regarding damages. Although it may be true that in many (but not all) states a judge would deny a claim for noneconomic losses if it were squarely presented in a motion, most juries will be instructed in a way that makes the award of noneconomic damages likely. Thus, noneconomic damages in contract cases are not the exception - they are probably the norm.
We proceed as follows. Part I details the conventional wisdom on contract remedies as collected in treatises, casebooks, and court opinions. Part II describes pattern jury instructions, a remarkably neglected source of information about contract law. Part III categorizes existing contract jury instructions on noneconomic losses. Finally, Part IV uses these categories to generate a survey experiment suggesting how lay people will respond to different instructions. Part IV also describes the significance of these results for conventional understandings of the law of contract remedies.

questions.question: Whether the wording of standard (pattern) jury instructions in different jurisdictions causes juries to award noneconomic damages for breach of contract.
How much variation exists across jurisdictions in their standard jury instructions regarding contract remedies, and how that variation affects the likelihood of noneconomic damages being awarded.

How lay jurors respond to different formulations of contract jury instructions-specifically, whether certain instruction types lead jurors to 'overcompensate' and include noneconomic losses in awards.

matched_themes: How have historical, geographic, institutional, and transnational influences shaped the evolution and transplantation of contract doctrines and remedies?
How do institutional features-court capacity, procedural devices, and evidentiary rules-affect the substantive development and practical application of contract remedies?
How do transaction costs, enforcement frictions, and institutional realities alter the theoretical efficiency of breach-plus-compensation?
Should plaintiffs be permitted to recover non-pecuniary harms such as mental distress in breach-of-contract cases?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
To what extent should moral blameworthiness and non-economic considerations influence the design and application of contract remedies?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 63vandlrev1003!!ARTICLE: Breach Is For Suckers
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Breach Is For Suckers

shared_topics.topic: lay moral intuitions about breach leading to noneconomic or emotional awards
shared_topics.justification: Both papers present experimental evidence showing that ordinary people view breach as morally significant and are inclined to award or sympathize with noneconomic harms (emotional distress, disappointment), with Paper A finding jurors tend to 'overcompensate' and Paper B documenting moral reactions that demand remedies beyond pure expectation loss.

shared_topics.topic: mismatch between doctrinal rules (Holmes/Restatement) and how people actually think about remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both critique the conventional doctrinal view that breach is a mere prediction of liability and that expectation damages suffice, documenting a gap between that legal orthodoxy and lay/jury intuitions about blame, culpability, and appropriate relief.

shared_topics.topic: psychological mechanisms driving punitive or compensatory responses to breach (exploitation/'sucker' schema and jury control effects)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with psychological explanations for why people punish breachers or award extra damages — Paper B develops the 'sucker'/exploitation framework (consent, perceived profiteering, intentionality) and Paper A links juror overcompensation to general principles of jury control and perceptions consistent with noneconomic loss.

shared_topics.topic: how procedural framing and instructions shape remedial outcomes in contract cases
shared_topics.justification: Both papers consider the influence of how cases are presented on outcomes: Paper A empirically analyzes pattern jury instructions across jurisdictions and shows how instruction wording produces divergent likelihoods of noneconomic awards, while Paper B's experiments and doctrinal discussion imply that framing of remedies (monetary vs specific performance, moral framing) affects lay preferences and judgments.

shared_topics.topic: use of empirical/experimental methods to inform contract doctrine and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both employ original experiments and empirical analysis to question existing doctrines and to propose that empirical findings about lay responses should inform doctrinal understanding and potential reform of contract remedies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68amulrev1751!!ARTICLE: SOMETHING ELSE: SPECIFIC RELIEF FOR BREACH OF HUMAN RIGHTS TERMS IN SUPPLY CHAIN AGREEMENTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SOMETHING ELSE: SPECIFIC RELIEF FOR BREACH OF HUMAN RIGHTS TERMS IN SUPPLY CHAIN AGREEMENTS

shared_topics.topic: adequacy of expectation damages for non‑pecuniary or reputational harms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that expectation damages poorly capture harms from breaches of human‑rights production clauses (e.g., reputational injury when goods conform but were produced with forced labor), and Paper B empirically interrogates whether contract law's conventional bar on noneconomic damages masks a reality in which juries nevertheless compensate non‑pecuniary loss.

shared_topics.topic: judicial reluctance and doctrinal limits on awarding non‑monetary relief in contract cases
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes judicial anxieties (indenture and entanglement) that constrain courts from granting specific relief (injunctions, orders to change employment practices), while Paper B shows how judges' remedial frameworks and instructions shape whether juries effectively award noneconomic relief, highlighting courts' central gatekeeping role over remedies.

shared_topics.topic: using contracts to address social or extra‑commercial objectives and the enforceability problems that creates
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies model human‑rights clauses in supply agreements and the practical and doctrinal obstacles to enforcing social‑purpose contractual promises, and Paper B addresses how contract remedies (and the way they are presented to juries) can produce awards that reach beyond purely economic loss, bearing on contracts that aim to secure noncommercial expectations.

shared_topics.topic: procedural and institutional mechanisms to implement remedies (monitors, experts, and instruction language/jury control)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes adapting institutional‑reform tools—monitors, neutral experts, quality‑assurance mechanisms—to make specific relief for HR clauses practicable, and Paper B demonstrates that the wording of pattern jury instructions and broader jury control practices function as procedural instruments that determine whether and how noneconomic contract harms are compensated.

shared_topics.topic: jurisdictional variation in remedial practice and its impact on enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights obstacles under U.S. law (and cross‑border enforcement challenges) to remedying breaches of HR clauses, while Paper B documents wide state‑by‑state variation in pattern jury instructions and shows that remedial outcomes depend heavily on local doctrinal and procedural differences.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 93califlrev975!!ARTICLE: Actual and Virtual Specific Performance, the Theory of Efficient Breach, and the Indifference Principle in Contract Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Actual and Virtual Specific Performance, the Theory of Efficient Breach, and the Indifference Principle in Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: whether monetary damages (particularly expectation damages) actually make promisees indifferent between performance and legal relief (the indifference principle)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a detailed critique showing a systematic shortfall of expectation damages relative to the indifference principle and explores specific performance and cover as remedies to fill that gap; Paper B shows that in practice juries often award additional (including noneconomic) sums under pattern instructions, a fact that materially affects whether monetary awards can achieve indifference in real cases.

shared_topics.topic: when and why courts should award specific performance versus monetary relief or market substitutes (cover/virtual specific performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly theorizes criteria for awarding actual specific performance and for permitting 'virtual' specific performance via cover, weighing moral, policy, and practical objections; Paper B, by analyzing pattern jury instructions and remedial practice across jurisdictions, engages with the practical availability and shape of nonstandard remedial outcomes that functionally alter the choice and effect of remedies in contract disputes.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial rules shape parties' incentives and the normative case for or against doctrines like efficient breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages the theory of efficient breach and argues that prevailing remedial rules (and modifications like routine specific performance) have important efficiency tradeoffs, sometimes promoting inefficiency, while Paper B documents that juries and instruction regimes frequently produce awards (including noneconomic components) that will influence contracting incentives in ways that diverge from textbook efficiency predictions.

shared_topics.topic: the mismatch between doctrinal prescriptions (Restatements/treatises) and actual remedial practice in courts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights tensions between canonical doctrines (expectation damages, rarity of specific performance) and the realities of bargaining and market remedies, and Paper B empirically demonstrates that Restatement-based conventional wisdom disguises substantial state-by-state and jury-instruction-driven variation in what relief is actually awarded.

shared_topics.topic: the substantive scope and measurement of recoverable contract losses (expectation, cover, and noneconomic harms)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how expectation damages and cover relate to what losses are measured and how virtual specific performance can replicate performance, while Paper B interrogates whether noneconomic losses are recoverable in contract cases and shows that many jurisdictions' instructions effectively allow juries to compensate for such harms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 42ambuslj97!!ARTICLE: Cry Me a River: Recovery of Mental Distress Damages in a Breach of Contract Action--A North American Perspective
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Cry Me a River: Recovery of Mental Distress Damages in a Breach of Contract Action--A North American Perspective

shared_topics.topic: recoverability of noneconomic/mental distress damages for breach of contract
shared_topics.justification: Both papers center on whether plaintiffs can recover noneconomic losses (mental distress, emotional harm) for contract breaches, critically examining the traditional rule that such damages are ordinarily not recoverable and questioning that rule's doctrinal and practical foundations.

shared_topics.topic: the role of foreseeability (Hadley v. Baxendale) and Restatement standards in limiting recovery
shared_topics.justification: Both works analyze how foreseeability doctrines—especially Hadley v. Baxendale and formulations in the Restatements—are used to permit or bar noneconomic damages, including critiques of how these tests operate in practice.

shared_topics.topic: exceptions permitting recovery (manner of breach, special-contract categories, punitive/aggravated damages)
shared_topics.justification: Each paper surveys the exception regimes—awards where the defendant's conduct is outrageous (manner of breach), when the contract contemplates emotional benefits (special categories), or via punitive/aggravated damages—and assesses their scope, instability, and logical problems.

shared_topics.topic: jurisdictional diversity and doctrinal inconsistency across courts
shared_topics.justification: Both articles document and criticize the patchwork of approaches across jurisdictions (states, and U.S./Canadian/UK courts), arguing that there is significant variation and instability rather than a single uniform rule on noneconomic recovery.

shared_topics.topic: procedural and instructional mechanisms shaping substantive awards (e.g., jury instructions, judicial framing)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with how courtroom processes and doctrinal framing influence outcomes—Paper A by empirically studying pattern jury instructions and their tendency to produce noneconomic awards, and Paper B by discussing how judicial attitudes, rules, and framing (including categorical presumptions) practically determine when such damages are allowed.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 24geojlegalethics357!!ARTICLE: A Crisis of Confidence and Legal Theory: Why the Economic Downturn Should Help Signal the End of the Doctrine of Efficient Breach
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Crisis of Confidence and Legal Theory: Why the Economic Downturn Should Help Signal the End of the Doctrine of Efficient Breach

shared_topics.topic: the limits of law-and-economics (efficiency) as the governing rationale for contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly attacks the doctrine of efficient breach and the law-and-economics claim that efficiency alone should govern contract choices, while Paper B undermines the strict economic model by showing that actual jury practices produce awards (including noneconomic items) that are not neatly explained by efficiency reasoning.

shared_topics.topic: the scope of compensatory damages and whether non‑economic harms belong in contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the compensatory damages framework (noting its indifference to motive and its failure to address broader harms), and Paper B empirically examines how pattern jury instructions and lay jurors often result in awards that include noneconomic losses despite the conventional rule excluding them.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of behavioral, psychological, and social norms (trust, reciprocity, lay perceptions) on contract enforcement and remedies

papers.node_id: 98neblrev926!!ARTICLE: Irrevocable Gift Promises and Promises Inducing Reliance: A Mandate for the Return of the Seal in Contract Law
papers.title: ARTICLE: Irrevocable Gift Promises and Promises Inducing Reliance: A Mandate for the Return of the Seal in Contract Law
papers.abstract:
All too often the statement is made and accepted that one cannot legally make an enforceable gift promise. In other words, it is stated and accepted that an individual cannot bind one's future self to make a donative transfer that will be enforced by the court should the future self opt not to honor the previously promised gift transaction. However, not all agree that this is an acceptable state of affairs. A case in point: the great contracts scholar Williston once wrote that the ability to make an enforceable donative promise "is something that a person ought to be able ... if he wishes to do it ... create a legal obligation to make a gift. Why not? ... I don't see why a man should not be able to make himself liable if he wishes to do so."
Of course, a thorough examination of the history of contract doctrine and transactions reveals that Williston's statement is somewhat inaccurate. This is because at common law, a donor could make such an enforceable promise using a "sealed" agreement.Indeed, in a few states that have adopted the position of the Restatement (Second) of Contracts, one can still use the seal to make and deliver an enforceable promise.However, in a majority of jurisdictions in which the use of the seal is prohibited, it is often stated and accepted that a donor cannot make an enforceable donative promise. Thus, as contract law has evolved, one initially could make an enforceable donative promise via a seal, but for reasons that are peripheral to the issues addressed in this Article, eventually that avenue was blocked.
By and large, contract law does not currently provide a legal avenue for enforcement of gratuitous promises that require future performance. Indeed, contract law has largely become irrelevant when analyzing the enforceability of donative promises because gifts and the enforceability of donative promises are the province of the law of property. In order to make a valid gift, property law requires the donor to intend to make a gift, deliver the gift, and that the gift be accepted by the donee.
Furthermore, it is hornbook lawthat a mere promise to make a gift in the future without delivery made contemporaneously with or shortly after the expression of intent to make the gift will not be enforced as a gift no matter how sincere the promise was when made.Thus, one can make an enforceable gift transfer if the donor and donee meet the three requirements of intent, delivery, and acceptance.What apparently cannot be done is to enforce against the donor her mere promise to make a gift in the future if the donor subsequentlychanges her mind and opts not to make the gift transfer or delivery. The donor cannot make a valid and enforceable contractual agreement that binds herself alone to complete the donative transaction.
Despite broad acceptance of the rules described above, the statement that one cannot make an enforceable donative promise is incorrect as a legal conclusion. An examination of the law and legal doctrine beyond the province of gift or the law of property demonstrates that there do exist enforceable donative promises. In terms of the donor's intent (i.e., her desire to bind her future self to an act for which there is no consideration or reciprocity), enforceable donative promises are effectively indistinguishable from so-called unenforceable donative promises. These enforceable donative promises are not denominated as gifts and, thus, when the issue of the enforceability of so-called gift promises is addressed, they are often ignored.
It is quite common in other related areas of the law - particularly contracts and trusts and estates law - for courts to enforce donative promises lacking consideration. These enforceable donative promises, however, are not analyzed per this requirement and are therefore beyond the imprimatur of contract. Hence, the presence or absence of consideration is irrelevant. Indeed, it is possible to make inter vivos gift promises and testamentary promises that are enforceable.One interesting fact about these enforceable promises that create donative transfers is that the person ultimately making the transfer is not the donor, the person who makes an enforceable promise.Instead, theperson ultimately making the transfer is an agent of the donor usually acting in a fiduciary capacity.
To be clear, examining trusts and estates law, donors may use irrevocable inter vivos trusts to make donative promises that are enforceable against the donor during the donor's life.Putative donors can also make certain inter vivos gifts without complying with the requisite formalities attendant to the creation of an irrevocable inter vivos trust by intending to make a future gift but dying before being able to act upon that intent. Under the contractual doctrine of reliance or promissory estoppel, courts will indeed enforce certain uncompleted gift promises against the putative donor (actually, the donor's estate) if the court finds reasonable and foreseeable reliance on the part of the donee.
Just as importantly, a donor can make donative promises that are enforceable after the donor's death by executing a valid and enforceable will.Upon execution of an enforceable will, the donor makes an inter vivos promise regarding the disposition of assets following the donor's death. These promises will later be enforced by the courts through an agent of the donor as long as the donor has not revoked her will or revoked the gift before dying.These donative promises made in a will are herein labeled transitive. This is because when the promise is made in a will, it is unenforceable because wills are not irrevocable.The promise may subsequently be revoked by the putative donor. However, if unrevoked or unchanged at the putative donor's death, the unenforceable promise is now transformed (hence, the denominationtransitive) into an enforceable promise against the donor's estate.
Once it is accepted that three types of donative promises - those made in trust, those made in a valid will, and those that induce reliance - are enforceable while others are not, the seminal question and issue becomes: Why are these promises deemed enforceable and others are not? What makes irrevocable inter vivos trust donative promises - promises that induce reliance on the part of the donee - and promises made in a will enforceable, while other simple or future gift donative promises are not?
The primary purpose of this Article is answering that question. Part II briefly details the state of the law as it pertains to the enforceability of donative promises (i.e., gifts) - plowing ground that has been well-furrowed by numerous prominent scholars. However, this Article goes beyond describing and defining these pedestrian gift transactions in Part II by expanding the definition of donative promises and demonstrating that certain transactions made in irrevocable inter vivos trusts, promises that induce reliance, and solemn promises made in a will are also the product of donative promises, yet are enforced.
In Part II, this Article explains another puzzle regarding the line that divides donative promises that are enforceable and those that are not. The dispositive factor is the formalities attendant at the execution of the promise. These formalities provide courts with sufficient evidence to affirm and enforce the promise efficiently (i.e., at little or low cost and with attendant low error costs). In effect, they serve the same purpose and act as a substitute for the doctrine of consideration in contract law.
The formalities associated with an irrevocable inter vivos trust and a valid will are well documented and require little explanation. On the contrary, the formalities associated with promises that induce reliance and are enforced pursuant to theare somewhat opaque and require detailed explication in Part II. Indeed, focusing on the formalities supplied by the putative donee who relies on the donor promises, this Article provides a coherent normative thesis for enforceable reliance promises that heretofore has been lacking.
Part III parses the distinction between enforceable and unenforceable donative promises, including those premised on reliance, as a product of the functional formalities associated with enforceable donative promises and the lack of same with unenforceable donative promises. The conclusion is buttressed with a brief recitation of theuse of the seal at common law and how it served as a functional formality in the context of an irrevocable inter vivos trust or a will.
Part III then explores the distinction between donative promises to prove that the different formalities required to validate the different promises rationally reflect the different types of relationships that produce donative versus bargained-for promises. Part III pays particular attention to promises that induce reliance and are therefore enforceable. The formalities supplied by reliance on the part of the donee do not seem similar to the formalities supplied by inter vivos trusts and wills, yet focusing on their functional purpose, these formalities serve the same purpose of allowing courts to enforce promises with remedial certainty (efficiently) and with low error costs (collectively, low adjudicative costs).
Part IV focuses on the remedy sought for breach of a promise and calls for an expansion - or rather the resurrection - of use of the seal to supply requisite formalities to bind a gratuitous promisor to complete the promise they have made by making that promise enforceable.This is consistent with the current economic theory of contracts that convincingly posits that promises should be enforceable when the parties intend them to be enforceable.The seal allows courts to efficiently and effectively determine when the donor intends to be bound and, just as importantly, provides proof of what the promisor is bound to do.
Given the formalities associated with the common law execution of the seal, this Article proposes to expand upon these inter vivos gifts by adding future gifts made pursuant to a seal. Consequently, when the putative donor intends a gift and satisfies the requisite formalities of sealing, the gift should be given effect. The seal, like the other irrevocable and enforceable gifts, satisfies the requirements of functional formality. Indeed, it is the epitome of functional formality that served as green light to an enforceable agreement that predated the development and use of the doctrine of consideration to demarcate an enforceable contract or agreement.
The use of a seal to validate a future gift of a present interest or a future interest in a present asset will satisfy the channeling, ritualistic, and evidentiary functions served by the requirements for a completed inter vivos gift and, relatedly, a testamentary gift via a properly executed will. These three types of enforceable donativepromises - completed gifts, inter vivos gifts accomplished pursuant to an irrevocable inter vivos trust, and testamentary promises in a valid will - are widely accepted and noncontroversial.
Consequently, this Article concludes that donors should have five vehicles by which they can complete donative transactions, three of which result in the enforceability of mere donative promises: (1) If the putative donor is interested in making an inter vivos transfer, the putative donor can validate the donative intent by making a delivery and effectuating a completed gift. If, however, the donor chooses to make a future gift, putative donors can use: (2) inter vivos irrevocable trusts; (3) promises that are reasonably relied on; and (4) transitive promises (designated as such because the donor can amend or revoke the promise) made in a validly executed and subsequently enforced will. In addition, putative donors or contracting parties should be able to make enforceable promises pursuant to (5) a sealed agreement.
Thus, the concluding portion of Part IV builds upon the insights gleaned in Part III to propose a fifth type of future non-testamentary transfer via the use of a seal. This Article defends the expanded use of a seal by the functional formalities it provides to the arbiter and the safe harbor it provides to putative donors acting as the equivalent of legal version of a simple inter vivos trust. The original functional purpose of the seal informed both parties to the bilateral transaction that they were entering into an enforceable agreement - more specifically, an agreement enforceable by the state should one of the parties choose not to honor the promise(s) embodied in the seal. This Article contends that there is no viable reason not to employ the same functional formalities to validate a unilateral promise even if that promise is a mere gift or donative promise.
Proving that the doctrine of consideration is largely tautological and circular,expanding the use of the seal in contractual agreements as well as donative transactions will provide contractual certainty to agreements when the parties both desire that it be enforceable.In other words, the inherent tautological character of consideration provides no certainty that a court will later determine that there was valid consideration and enforce a disputed promise. The court may, for whatever reason it deems acceptable, choose to find or not find that there is consideration.
By recognizing sealed promises as enforceable promises, parties can guarantee that their promises will later be honored by a court. Furthermore, once the seal is universally available and enforceable, other benefits may flow therefrom. The so-called trichotomy of reliance promises - implied good faith in business relationship, uncompleted gift transfers, and public policy cases - can be reduced to the sole category of public policy cases.Thus, if parties wish to make an enforceable gift or enter into an enforceable promise before a final and formal contract is executed, they may do so through the use of the seal eliminating any reliance or reliance promises (pun intended). Moreover, the illusory and highly chimerical distinction between gifts and contract transactions will dissipate.
