papers.node_id: 10flataxrev459!!Article: Just Enough: Substantial Performance, Ministerial Acts and the All Events Tests for Income and Expense Accruals
papers.title: Article: Just Enough: Substantial Performance, Ministerial Acts and the All Events Tests for Income and Expense Accruals
papers.abstract:
The tax law sets unrealistic expectations for accruing many income and expense items arising out of bilateral contracts. Under an accrual method, a taxpayer generally takes an income item into account when the taxpayer has a fixed right to receive it and takes an expense item into account when the taxpayer has a fixed liability to pay it.The tax law thus expects the taxpayer to determine when all events have occurred to make the right or liability unconditional.The taxpayer might find this determination easy if it were to exchange only one promise for one promise (e.g., seller only promises to perform services and buyer only promises to pay), use words establishing conditional relationships (e.g., the buyer promises to pay if and only if the seller performs the services), and experience nothing short of complete performance (e.g., the seller never provides nonconforming services). But the taxpayer probably doesn't engage in those transactions very often.
For most transactions, the taxpayer will find it difficult to determine whether all events have occurred to fix rights and liabilities from bilateral contracts. For example, consider a contract that contains a typical explicit requirement that a service provider submit an invoice to a client to receive payment for rendered services. Once the services have been performed, the accrual method rules contemplate that the parties will determine whether the submission of the invoice represents an event that must occur to fix the service provider's right to income and the client's liability to pay under the contract. That determination might prove difficult because some authorities and guidance have disregarded requirements to submit documentationwhereas others have treated the satisfaction of such requirements as a prerequisite to any finding of fixed rights and liabilities.Aside from raising questions about how to reconcile the authorities and guidance, the differences in treatment highlight a larger issue that tax accounting rules occasionally require, but do not always permit-accruals prior to the full performance of all promises contained in bilateral contracts. As a consequence, taxpayers need to consider whether the occurrence of substantial performance, rather than full performance, represents the last event that must occur to fix rights and liabilities for tax purposes.
This Article explores the role of substantial performance under the all events tests of sections 451 and 461 by placing particular emphasis on its application to ministerial acts. Because these Code sections focus on unconditional rights and liabilities, Part II starts with a discussion of conditions constructed by courts to preserve expectations and avoid forfeitures in accordance with promises contained in bilateral contracts. This discussion of contract law then describes why, in response to additional concerns about fairness, courts treat the substantial performance of certain promises as satisfying the conditions that the courts construct. The discussion illustrates how a party's substantial performance, rather than full performance, can establish unconditional rights and obligations under a contract.

questions.question: Whether a party's substantial (but not complete) performance of contractual obligations is sufficient to fix taxable income and deductible expenses under accrual accounting methods.

Whether ministerial, administrative, or documentary formalities (for example, routine invoice submission) must occur before rights and liabilities are treated as fixed for accrual purposes, or whether such formalities can be disregarded so accruals arise earlier.

papers.node_id: 45umemlrev59!!Article: Justice and Harsh Results: Beyond Individualism and Collectivism in Contracts
papers.title: Article: Justice and Harsh Results: Beyond Individualism and Collectivism in Contracts
papers.abstract:
The strict enforcement of contract terms can have harsh results. Whether such harsh results should be imposed by law has generally been addressed from one of two perspectives: either an individualist perspective, in which individual autonomy is given priority, or a collectivist perspective, in which social values are given priority.Each of these perspectives on the issue of harsh results is represented in the famous contracts case of Jacob & Youngs, Inc. v. Kent.
Jacob & Youngs was a construction firm that agreed to build a mansion for George Kent, a New York lawyer.The contract specified that the mansion's plumbing would consist of a certain brand of wrought-iron pipe called Reading pipe.But instead of installing Reading pipe, Jacob & Youngs used a different brand, which was probably of equivalent quality and value.Claiming breach of contract, Kent refused to pay the outstanding balance.Jacob & Youngs sued, and the case came before the New York Court of Appeals.
Writing from the collectivist perspective, Judge Benjamin Cardozo reasoned that justice would not sanction the harsh result of Jacob & Youngs forfeiting payment over a trivial breach.Writing from the individualist perspective, Judge Chester McLaughlin argued that whether the terms were fair was for the parties to decide, and justice required the court to enforce the contract as written.
This Article argues that each judge's reasoning was wrong. Neither the individualist nor the collectivist approach adequately addresses the issues raised by the prospect of enforcing a harsh contractual term. The individualist relies on flawed accounts of human autonomy and contractual fairness, in which any terms on which the parties agree should be deemed fair. And the collectivist ultimately disregards the will of the parties and ignores the voluntary nature of contracts. This Article argues that a Thomist approach combines the strengths and avoids the weaknesses of the individualist and collectivist approaches by holding that a contract is a voluntary act of commutative justice which vindicates both the voluntary nature of contracts and the need for substantive fairnessin exchanges. A Thomist approach emphasizes the purpose of contracts, the common good, and the necessary means for achieving such purposes, namely promise-keeping. This Article applies a Thomist approach to the Jacob & Youngs case, arguing the Reading pipe term should have been enforced. This Article also calls for a re-characterization of this canonical case because a review of the record and precedent demonstrates that the case was wrongly decided on the basis of Judge Cardozo's material misrepresentations of fact and law.
Part II of this Article describes the surprising facts of Jacob & Youngs, drawing attention to the material misrepresentations of fact and law in Judge Cardozo's opinion. Part III presents a central philosophical question in contract theory: why do promises create moral obligations? It considers representative answers to this question from the individualist and collectivist perspectives, focusing on works by Charles Fried and P.S. Atiyah, and explores the implications of these perspectives for Jacob & Youngs. Part IV presents a Thomist perspective on why promises create moral obligations, focusing on works by James Gordley, and demonstrates the superiority of this approach to individualist and collectivist approaches. And Part V applies this Thomist perspective to Jacob & Youngs v. Kent, arguing that justice requires the enforcement of the Reading pipe term, though not for the reasons stated in Judge McLaughlin's dissenting opinion.
This Article's use of the term "Thomist" is a broad rubric for associating the thought of numerous thinkers from Aristotle and Aquinas to medieval scholastics and Spanish natural lawyers to John Finnis and James Gordley. The term should be accurate, but this Article makes no descriptive claims about the relationships, similarities, or differences among these thinkers.

papers.title: ARTICLE: Landlord-Tenant Law in the United States and West Germany--A Comparison of Legal Approaches ++ We are grateful to Lawrence Friedman, Bruce J. Gould, Herbert Jacob, Zigurds Zile and Dietmar Seiler for their helpful comments on a draft of this paper. This research was supported by funds granted to the Institute for Research on Poverty of the University of Wisconsin, pursuant to the provisions of the Economic Opportunity Act of 1964.
papers.abstract:
Recent interest in the general welfare of low-income groups has again directed attention to the problem of housing for the poor. This attention has focused upon the difficulties encountered by low-income residents in utilizing existing remedies, and the problems encountered by public agencies in utilizing existing governmental programs to alleviate substandard housing conditions.In analysing the influence of present legal relations on the problems of substandard housing, some writers have noted the apparent imbalance between the legal rights available to landlords and those which are in reality available to tenants.
While we would agree with recent commentators who have argued that substantial progress in housing conditions can only come with substantial allocation of funds for low-income housing purposes,we are also persuaded that it would be useful to consider the extent to which landlord-tenant legal relations in America may currently contribute to the development of substandard housing and act to inhibit the development of solutions to substandard housing through suppression of initiative. To gain perspective on proposals for reform of the fundamental landlord-tenant legal relationin America, we have examined the law of lease in Germany and compared the German legal relationship to the American problems and experiences. This analysis of the German lawprovides a method whereby many recently advocated Anglo-American statutory reforms in landlord-tenant relations may be studied within a legal system in which they have been operable for many years.
Such an investigation illuminates the possibility of developing in the United States a law of landlord and tenant which would be based upon the mutuality of obligation found in contract law and which would correct the often criticized lack of mutuality which currently characterizes American landlord-tenant relations.Additionally, examination of the German landlord-tenant law provides stimulating suggestions for developing alternative legal remedies for tenants faced with reluctant landlords who fail to provide required services or who retaliate against tenants seeking to exercise available remedies.
Regrettably, the paucity of available data on the workings of the German law has hampered the development of a truly comparative analysis. We recognize the desirability of studying the practical impact of the German legal arrangements in order to fully understand the effect of legally authorized norms on the German landlord-tenant relationships. However, the striking differences between the American and German statutes, as well as the recent extensive American advocacy of legal reforms which would closely correspond to the German law, indicate that it would be useful to explicate comparisons between the two legal systems as they exist theoretically. In recognition of the limitations inherent in such comparisons, we have attempted to limit our discussion to the insights into American landlord-tenant problems which may emerge from examining the structure of the German landlord-tenant statutes.
Throughout the discussion, we have concentrated upon American problems which particularly affect the low-income tenant. Analytically, however, it is misleading to suggest that American tenants encounter difficulties solely because of their poverty status. It is more useful to conceive of the problems discussed in this paperas relating to all tenants to some extent, but which tend to have greater saliency for tenants in inverse relation to their incomesandin inverse relation to the openness of the housing market in which the tenant searches for shelter. Where middle class rental units are scarce relative to demand, many of the problems described in this paper as resulting from the imbalance in the relationship between landlord and tenant may have equal relevance to the middle income renter.

questions.question: Whether the structure of landlord-tenant legal relations-specifically the degree of mutual obligations and the availability of tenant remedies-affects the prevalence of substandard housing and tenants' ability to obtain repairs and services.

Whether adopting legal approaches from another legal system that emphasize greater mutuality of obligation and alternative tenant remedies would reduce landlord reluctance and retaliation and thereby improve housing conditions.

How different landlord-tenant legal regimes shape the behavior and bargaining power of tenants (especially low-income tenants) and influence their use of governmental programs to remedy substandard housing.

matched_themes: To what extent does variation in state involvement across legal systems explain cross-jurisdictional differences in contract rules and remedies?
How do landlord-tenant legal regimes and tenant-remedy structures affect tenant bargaining power, housing conditions, and use of governmental relief programs?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 38ambuslj633!!ARTICLE: A THEORY OF EFFICIENT PENALTY: ELIMINATING THE LAW OF LIQUIDATED DAMAGES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A THEORY OF EFFICIENT PENALTY: ELIMINATING THE LAW OF LIQUIDATED DAMAGES

shared_topics.topic: limits on freedom of contract and judicial intervention in private agreements
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze when courts or statutes should override private bargains: Paper A critiques how American landlord-tenant law and judicial doctrines produce an imbalance that limits tenants' effective contractual rights, while Paper B critiques the common‑law rule voiding penalty clauses and argues for greater enforcement of parties' agreed remedies except in cases of inefficient or unconscionable bargains.

shared_topics.topic: comparative law as a tool for domestic reform
shared_topics.justification: Both articles use cross‑jurisdictional comparison to inform reform: Paper A systematically compares U.S. landlord‑tenant law with West German statutes to draw reform lessons for tenant remedies and mutual obligations, while Paper B reviews civil‑law and English approaches to penalties and UCC revision efforts to justify doctrinal change on liquidated damages.

shared_topics.topic: design and role of remedial doctrines in shaping incentives and behavior
shared_topics.justification: Each paper focuses on how remedial rules influence actors' incentives: Paper A examines how landlord and tenant remedies (and the lack thereof) affect landlords' maintenance behavior and tenants' willingness to seek redress, and Paper B analyzes how enforcement or nullification of liquidated damages clauses alters contracting, performance incentives, and settlement behavior.

shared_topics.topic: statutory and doctrinal reform proposals to better align law with policy goals
shared_topics.justification: Both propose specific legal reforms: Paper A evaluates adopting German‑style mutuality and alternative tenant remedies in U.S. statutes to improve housing outcomes, while Paper B proposes eliminating the tripartite liquidated‑damages rule in favor of presumptive enforcement plus unconscionability and reformation as regulatory mechanisms.

shared_topics.topic: protection of weaker or disadvantaged contracting parties
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with how legal rules affect vulnerable parties: Paper A centers on low‑income tenants harmed by imbalanced landlord‑tenant relations and limited remedies, and Paper B addresses how penalty doctrines and doctrines like unconscionability should police unfair bargaining outcomes that disadvantage one party.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 64hastingslj679!!Article: Consenting Under Stress
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Consenting Under Stress

shared_topics.topic: limits of existing doctrines to address coercion or imbalance (duress, unconscionability, landlord remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes narrow judicial treatments of duress/unconscionability that ignore stress-induced impairment, while Paper B critiques American landlord-tenant rules for failing to correct the imbalance between landlords and tenants and suppressing tenant remedies.

shared_topics.topic: use of non‑legal evidence or comparative insights to reform legal standards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws on biology, neuroscience, sociology, and psychology to inform a stress‑sensitive approach to consent, and Paper B uses comparative study of West German statutes and practice to illuminate alternative statutory reforms for landlord‑tenant relations.

shared_topics.topic: designing remedial frameworks to prevent exploitation and restore fair consent/relations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes a four‑element analytic framework for adjudicating consent undermined by stress and suggests when courts should grant relief, whereas Paper B discusses statutory and remedial structures (mutual obligations, tenant remedies, anti‑retaliation) that could correct exploitative landlord‑tenant dynamics.

shared_topics.topic: how socioeconomic conditions affect the ability to exercise rights and make meaningful choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on consent obtained under financial need or crisis-related stress that impairs decisionmaking, and Paper B focuses on how low income and tight housing markets limit tenants' practical ability to assert rights or avoid substandard housing.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Role of the State in Contract Law: The Common-Civil Law Divide

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that civil-law jurisdictions involve stronger legislative and judicial policing of contract terms to enforce social values, and Paper B examines how German statutory landlord-tenant rules (a form of state intervention) advance housing welfare and tenant protection relative to the U.S.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes differences in the prevalence of mandatory contract rules and duties of good faith in civil versus common law, while Paper B highlights the German law's emphasis on mutual obligations in leases and suggests U.S. reforms to correct the American imbalance between landlords and tenants.

shared_topics.topic: remedies and enforcement mechanisms available for breach or nonperformance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares remedies (e.g., enforcement of penalty clauses, availability of specific performance, bankruptcy discharge) across legal families to show differing calibrations of sanctioning, and Paper B focuses on tenant remedies and alternative legal sanctions against landlords under German law versus U.S. practice.

shared_topics.topic: call for studying 'law in action' and the empirical impact of doctrinal differences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A stresses the need for empirical work to assess the practical effects of doctrinal contract differences, and Paper B likewise laments paucity of data on the operation of German tenant laws and urges investigation of their real-world impact on housing outcomes.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A THEORY OF SELF-HELP REMEDIES IN CONTRACT

shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how the prospect of litigation and remedial rules influence parties' use of informal agreements, settlements, and threats to resolve disputes outside court; Paper B uses a comparative lens to ask how German statutory structures affect tenants' and landlords' real‑world practices and whether legal rules crowd out or support informal problem‑solving.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE FAULT THAT LIES WITHIN OUR CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: critique of prevailing doctrinal paradigms and exploration of alternative frameworks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares Anglo-American and German statutory/regulatory approaches to suggest reforms for landlord-tenant law, and Paper B rejects the prevailing 'strict liability' myth in contract law and argues for retaining fault-based conceptions, with both papers advancing normative arguments for changing dominant legal frameworks.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Critique of the Efficient Performance Hypothesis

shared_topics.topic: tension between moral obligations to perform and efficiency-based remedies

shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how current U.S. landlord‑tenant doctrines create an imbalance of power disadvantaging tenants and considers German rules that assign different entitlements, whereas Paper B frames remedies as allocating the right to choose performance (call vs put option) and studies how those allocations affect who controls whether performance occurs.

shared_topics.topic: comparative evaluation of alternative legal remedies and reforms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A undertakes a cross‑jurisdictional comparison (U.S. vs West Germany) to assess whether different statutory designs produce more effective tenant protections, and Paper B evaluates and proposes alternative remedies (Schwartz's election rule, Brooks's hypothetical disgorgement) comparing their normative and efficiency consequences.

papers.node_id: 50mdlrev253!!ARTICLE: LAW AND EQUITY IN CONTRACT ENFORCEMENT
papers.title: ARTICLE: LAW AND EQUITY IN CONTRACT ENFORCEMENT
papers.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: A DESCRIPTION OF THE PROBLEM
According to traditional doctrine, a contract plaintiff is entitled to legal damage remedies for breach of contract unless the defendant establishes a distinct defense such as fraud.But the equitableremedy of specific performance is not available unless the contract isfair.In the following pages, I will consider why this is so.
Traditionally, the remedy of specific performance has been subject to an extra layer of defenses that do not apply to legal contract remedies.Some defenses to specific performance are based on the practical difficulties of administering specific relief.But another type of equitable defense, which I will call a fairness defense, rests on moral standards that have no obvious relation to the mechanics of the remedy.  Equity is said to operate on a higher moral plane than law: it demands more meticulous conduct and a greater degree of altruism between contracting parties, and it will not assist one party in taking unfair advantage of the other.As a result, a courtmay deny specific performance on the basis of "hardship," or "sharp practice," although the defect in the transaction is not concrete enough to establish a defense at law.
Panco v. Rogersis a good example.  An elderly couple (the Pancos) signed an agreement to sell their home to the Rogers for $ 5500.The court valued the property at $ 10,000.Mr. Panco, an elderly carpenter, was hard of hearing and lacked business experience; Mrs. Panco was "of foreign extraction" and may not have been fluent in English.The Pancos thought the price in the contract was$ 12,500, but they signed without discovering their error.The Rogers did nothing palpably wrong and believed the price asked was $ 5500, as stated in the written agreement.The court found no basis to set aside the contract; at most there was a unilateral mistake by the Pancos and no concrete evidence that the Rogers were aware of the mistake.Nevertheless, it denied specific performance.It explained that before granting an equitable remedy, "the court must be satisfied that the claim is fair, reasonable and equal in all its parts."If enforcement of the contract would be "harsh, oppressive or manifestly unjust" to the promisor, the equitable remedy should be withheld.
It is difficult to describe the content of the fairness defense because the defense is very fluid.  Typically, the decision to deny specific performance is based on a combination of one party's mistake or lack of sophistication, unverified suspicions that the other was aware of her advantage, and an unequal exchange of value.In particular cases, one or another element may predominate; the court may be moved by hardships that arose after the contract was made,the promisor's disabilities at the time of negotiation,thepromisee's disposition to take advantage,or the discrepancy in values exchanged.
One feature that characterizes all versions of the fairness defense is their indeterminacy.Traditional legal defenses to contract enforcement, such as fraud, mistake, or incapacity, are relatively well defined.The fairness defense is an open-endedstandard that reaches an additional level of unfairness outside the categories recognized at law.Its lack of definition invites the judge to respond in a more particularistic way to the facts of each case.
The fairness defense is equitable in the sense that it applies only to the equitable remedy of specific performance, and does not disturb the underlying contract obligation.  A promisor who establishes a defense of fraud is entitled to a decree of rescission, which nullifies the contract.In contrast, a less concrete claim of unfairnessordinarily does not support rescission, although it may persuade the court to deny specific performance.When a court follows this pattern -- refusing the promisee's claim for specific performance but also refusing the promisor's claim for rescission -- the contract remains in place.  As a result, the promisee can sue for damages for breach, measured by the lost value of her bargain.Equitable enforcement is barred, but a legal damage remedy is not.
The special treatment of equitable relief is highlighted by the procedural merger of law and equity.  Almost everywhere, law and equity are now administered in a single court.  When a merged court recognizes a fairness defense to specific performance, one judge is applying two different standards of morality, depending onthe remedy sought.
This double standard is hard to understand.  At least in theory, specific performance and damages are simply two means of accomplishing the same result.  Specific performance protects the plaintiff's expectation interest in a contract by delivering the promised performance.  The standard measure of damages for breach of contract protects the same interest, forcing the defendant to pay the monetary equivalent of the promised performance.Why, then, do courts apply (or claim to apply) a different standard to specific performance?
The double standard of morality for legal and equitable contract remedies has been the subject of some scathing criticism in scholarly writing.Courts, too, seem less enthusiastic than theyonce were about the special moral status of specific performance.  There are few reported decisions in recent years in which courts have denied specific performance and also refused rescission or granted damages.Yet courts continue to say there is a distinction in the moral standards applicable to legal and equitable relief; opinions repeatedly assert that specific performance is discretionary and may be withheld on the basis of unfairness that would not affect a damage remedy.The secondRestatementalso preserves the special standard for equitable relief in unquestioning terms.
The purpose of this Article is to consider whether there is any coherent explanation or justification for a morally inspired defense that is uniquely applicable to specific enforcement of contracts.  Is there anything about the equitable remedy that calls for a stricter standard of behavior, or a greater degree of altruism between parties?Is there any other reason, apart from the nature of the legal and equitable remedies, why courts preserve a distinction in the defenses available?
My analysis begins in Part I by identifying different values represented by legal and equitable standards for enforcement of contracts.  Legal and equitable defenses correspond to opposing theories of contract obligation.  They also follow different formal approaches to law.
In Part II, I consider three ways of explaining the persistence of a dual standard.  First, there are some real differences in the operation of specific and substitutional relief as a means of protecting contract expectations.In certain situations, specific performance and damages have different effects on the interests of third parties, on efficiency in resource allocation, and on the distribution of wealth between the parties.  These effects, however, are not present in all cases, and so do not justify a generally applicable fairness defense to equitable relief.
, courts may use the fairness defense to achieve a compromise remedy when they sense that protection of the promisee's expectations is not appropriate.The compromise is possible because, although contract damages are supposed to protect the promisee's expectations, they often fall short of this objective.  In many cases, especially those that fall within the traditional scope of the specific performance remedy, doctrinal limits and practical difficulties of proof prevent the promisee from recovering the economic equivalent of her bargain through a legal damage remedy.  As a result, a fairness defense to specific performance tends to undermine the expectancy measure and push the remedy toward reliance, without altogether extinguishing the promisor's liability.  If this is the function of the fairness defense, however, a more direct solution is needed.
A third possible explanation of the separate standards for legal and equitable enforcement of contracts is that courts have used the equitable fairness defense as a device to resolve a persistent conflict between the utilitarian benefits of stability in contract law and the impulse to impose altruist values in particular cases.The institution of private exchange requires a legal foundation with the appearance of security for future transactions.  A nebulous defense to contract liability that cannot be captured in a rule undermines that foundation.  But the utility of contract law is a function of the message judicial decisions send to the market, rather than the decisions themselves.  When the courts' power to give relief on the basis of fairness is wrapped in the obscure form of an equitable defense, there may be a sufficient degree of "acoustic separation"to preserve the appearance that contracts are reliable.  In other words, the court may be able to accomplish both goals (stability and altruism) at once.  This may in fact work quite well.  But is it acceptable?
My analysis of these issues is framed against the background of existing limitations on the scope of the specific performance remedy.  Prevailing doctrine holds that specific performance is available only when damages are inadequate (or relatively inadequate) as a means of protecting the promisee's expectation interest.Professor Douglas Laycock has demonstrated that this rule is now so dilutedthat it has little practical meaning.Nevertheless, equitable defenses are not likely to arise in the context of a consumer transaction or other sale of fungible goods, because specific performance will not be at issue.They will appear mainly in connection with sales of land, sales of things likely to have idiosyncratic value, sales of things for which there is no ready substitute, and long-term contractual relations.Most cases discussed in this Article fall into the first three of these categories, and arise from discrete exchanges negotiated on an individual basis.  This Article touches only briefly on long-term contracts, which are a separate species of transaction and require a different type of analysis.

questions.question: Is there a coherent justification for applying a stricter fairness-based defense to remedies that compel a party to perform (in-kind enforcement) than to remedies that award monetary compensation?

Why do courts persist in treating in-kind enforcement differently from monetary remedies-e.g., is the separate fairness defense explained by real differences in third-party effects, efficiency or distributional consequences, by its role as a compromise when monetary damages fail to protect expectations, or by a desire to balance market stability with ad hoc moral considerations?

matched_themes: Should parties and courts adopt fault-based remedial regimes that distinguish among breaches by reason when allocating remedies?
What counterfactual baseline should courts use to measure plaintiffs' losses for compensation purposes?
Do courts actually prefer monetary damages over specific (in-kind) remedies, or do they grant specific relief except when independent reasons exist to deny it?
When should courts order specific performance (in-kind relief) versus awarding monetary damages?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?
How do institutional features-court capacity, procedural devices, and evidentiary rules-affect the substantive development and practical application of contract remedies?
Does making in-kind performance the legal default (rather than monetary compensation) change parties' enforcement choices, moral judgments, and economic efficiency?
When should courts prefer or enforce in-kind (specific) performance rather than monetary damages for breach of contract?
Should the availability of legal remedies or contractual incompleteness change the moral assessment of a party who breaches under unanticipated circumstances?

Should remedies and contract law be structured to preserve conditions necessary for moral agency and promissory responsibility, rather than treating promises solely as instruments of economic cooperation?
How do transaction costs, enforcement frictions, and institutional realities alter the theoretical efficiency of breach-plus-compensation?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
How should remedial and enforcement rules be structured to achieve efficient behavior when populations include both internalizers and externalizers?
Can courts reliably determine ex post whether a breach would increase social welfare so that remedy choice can be used to promote efficiency?
To what extent does empirical uncertainty about measuring gains and losses limit courts' ability to design remedies that reflect non-welfare ethical preferences without sacrificing efficiency?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
Do limits on recoverable damages (foreseeability, certainty, avoidability) substantially reduce awards below full compensation, and should courts liberalize those limits?
Do courts consider the breaching party's blameworthiness or opportunistic behavior when selecting among compensatory remedies?
To what extent should moral blameworthiness and non-economic considerations influence the design and application of contract remedies?
When is an indirect remedy (one that induces self-compliance) preferable to a direct remedy that delivers the outcome?
Should courts more readily grant equitable relief to compel performance when monetary damages undercompensate and public interests are implicated?

shared_topics.topic: the differential treatment of remedies (specific performance vs damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes why courts apply a distinct, more exacting fairness standard to equitable relief (specific performance) than to legal remedies (damages) and surveys doctrinal limits on when specific performance is granted; Paper B empirically documents widespread false beliefs that specific performance is the typical remedy and uses those beliefs to critique doctrinal and normative consequences of remedial defaults.

shared_topics.topic: the role of mistake (especially unilateral mistake) in contract enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how courts invoke fairness or mistake-related considerations to deny equitable relief (often in unilateral mistake settings) while leaving contracts intact and subject to damages; Paper B argues that pervasive false beliefs about contract law would, under autonomy-based consent doctrines, make many bargains voidable for mistake, creating doctrinal and policy problems.

shared_topics.topic: competing normative foundations for contract law (promise/consent vs utilitarian/law-and-economics)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames legal vs equitable defenses as reflecting opposing theories of contractual obligation and considers utilitarian explanations for doctrinal choices; Paper B directly challenges the promise/consent (autonomy) justification—because of widespread error—and urges consideration of consequentialist or second-best normative accounts like law-and-economics.

shared_topics.topic: fairness, unconscionability, and the court's policing of unequal or exploitative bargains
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the equitable 'fairness' defense that courts invoke to withhold specific performance when a bargain seems harsh or exploitative; Paper B engages with related doctrines (unconscionability and boilerplate regulation), arguing the real problem is substantively one-sided terms and proposing regulation to address unfairness.

shared_topics.topic: the need for stability and predictability in contract law and the market effects of doctrinal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A worries that an opaque equitable fairness defense can undermine market confidence yet may be retained for its ability to reconcile stability with ad hoc moral corrections; Paper B shows that widespread legal ignorance threatens transactional reliability (e.g., making many contracts voidable under autonomy reasoning) and therefore recommends doctrinal or normative shifts to preserve predictable commercial ordering.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 89nwulrev1341!!ARTICLE: PEEVYHOUSE V. GARLAND COAL & MINING CO. REVISITED: THE BALLAD OF WILLIE AND LUCILLE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PEEVYHOUSE V. GARLAND COAL & MINING CO. REVISITED: THE BALLAD OF WILLIE AND LUCILLE

shared_topics.topic: when specific performance should be awarded versus monetary damages (adequacy of damages and choice among diminution-in-value, cost-to-repair, or expectation measures)

shared_topics.topic: equitable fairness defenses and the indeterminacy of denying specific performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes factual assumptions and doctrinal choices that led courts to deny full equitable relief in Peevyhouse and urges courts to consider fairness in granting specific remediation; Paper B provides a theoretical account of the 'fairness' defense unique to equity, documenting its fluid, judge-driven nature and questioning whether its indeterminacy is justifiable.

shared_topics.topic: contract enforcement for unique land-related bargains and remedial implications of idiosyncratic property
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is an extended case study of a strip‑mining lease where land-specific harm and reclamation make the adequacy of damages and availability of equitable relief central; Paper B highlights that disputes over sales or transfers of land and other idiosyncratic goods are precisely the contexts in which specific performance and special equitable considerations typically arise.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of the factual record, litigation process, and judicial discretion on remedy outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how a scant or distorted trial record, unequal counsel resources, and procedural realities produced the contested Peevyhouse outcome and may have led to doctrinally questionable relief; Paper B examines how the open-ended fairness defense and equitable discretion allow judges to resolve cases particularistically, raising concerns about inconsistent application and the rule-of-law implications of fact-sensitive equitable judgments.

shared_topics.topic: use of alternative remedial doctrines (restitution, reliance, or equitable compromise) when expectancy relief is problematic
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores alternative remedies—restitution, more ready use of specific performance, and statutory reclamation—that could have better compensated the Peevyhouses when expectation measures failed; Paper B considers how courts sometimes use the fairness defense to yield compromise remedies that approximate reliance or partial protection when full expectancy relief seems inappropriate, and calls for clearer doctrinal responses.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE DISGORGEMENT INTEREST IN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: the remedial interests that contract law should protect (expectation, reliance, restitution, disgorgement)

shared_topics.topic: whether different remedies should be subject to different doctrinal or moral standards (damages vs specific performance vs disgorgement)

shared_topics.topic: critique of Restatement Second and established remedial doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A notes and questions the Second Restatement's preservation of a special equitable standard for specific performance, while Paper B focuses on the deliberate exclusion of disgorgement from Restatement Second and challenges the doctrinal choices reflected there.

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations of remedy rules, including efficiency, distributional effects, and moral considerations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A weighs utilitarian aims (market stability, efficiency) against equitable/altruistic moral impulses as explanations for the fairness defense and its effects on wealth allocation; Paper B critiques reliance on efficient-breach reasoning and develops normative arguments for disgorgement based on fairness and appropriate allocation of gains from breach.

shared_topics.topic: practical and doctrinal limits on administering nonstandard remedies (proof, third‑party effects, rarity of cases)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses practical administration problems, third‑party impacts, and evidentiary constraints that limit when specific performance and equity defenses arise; Paper B examines practical reasons and doctrinal obstacles why disgorgement is uncommon and when courts have in fact imposed profit‑stripping remedies.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Capping Market Damages at Lost Profit: An Unwarranted Limitation on a Middleman's Expectancy Interest

shared_topics.topic: conflicts between different remedial rules (market damages vs lost profits; damages vs specific performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines a direct statutory and doctrinal conflict when UCC section 2-713 market damages produce an award larger than the buyer's forward-contract profits, and Paper B analyzes the broader doctrinal tension between monetary damages and equitable specific performance and why different standards are applied to each remedy.

shared_topics.topic: use of normative/fairness considerations to limit or reshape legal remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates whether normative goals (placing the aggrieved party in the position of full performance) should cap market damages at lost profits, and Paper B analyzes the 'fairness' defense in equity, showing how moral judgments uniquely restrict availability of specific performance even when legal remedies remain available.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal indeterminacy and judicial division in applying remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both papers document and analyze inconsistent judicial responses: Paper A surveys case law division over whether market damages or lost-profit limits control, while Paper B emphasizes the fluid, indeterminate nature of the equitable fairness defense and courts' variable application of different standards to legal and equitable relief.

shared_topics.topic: policy trade-offs between efficiency, reliance, and equitable values in choosing remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers the normative and conceptual validity of alternative damage measures (and implications of proposed Article 2 revisions), and Paper B explicitly weighs utilitarian concerns (efficiency, market stability, third‑party effects) against altruistic or fairness-based impulses in explaining why courts differentiate remedies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 120harvlrev708!!ARTICLE: THE DIVERGENCE OF CONTRACT AND PROMISE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE DIVERGENCE OF CONTRACT AND PROMISE

shared_topics.topic: the normative significance of remedies (specific performance vs damages) for reflecting moral wrongs

shared_topics.justification: Paper B analyzes the discretionary fairness defense in equity as an instrument courts use to deny enforcement on moral grounds and considers its justification, and Paper A asks more broadly whether contract law should accommodate interpersonal morality or at least be compatible with conditions for moral agency, evaluating when legal norms should reflect altruistic or moral expectations.

shared_topics.topic: effects of contract doctrine on moral agency, social norms, and market stability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues contract law can inhibit or undermine moral agency and virtues like fidelity, and Paper B discusses how an indeterminate fairness doctrine balances the utilitarian need for predictable contract enforcement against impulses to impose altruistic standards, both assessing how doctrinal choices shape behavior and social culture.

shared_topics.topic: indeterminacy and judicial discretion in applying moral standards within contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper B highlights the fluid, open-ended nature of the equitable fairness defense and its invitation to particularistic judicial responses, and Paper A criticizes aspects of contract doctrine and its justifications as potentially unknowable or unacceptable to self-consciously moral agents, raising concerns about doctrinal indeterminacy and legitimacy.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: WILLFULNESS VERSUS EXPECTATION: A PROMISOR-BASED DEFENSE OF WILLFUL BREACH DOCTRINE

shared_topics.topic: use of moral or fairness considerations (fairness defense, willfulness) to calibrate remedies

shared_topics.topic: how remedy rules affect ex ante incentives, bargaining and market stability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers whether separate equitable standards preserve market stability or allow courts to impose altruistic values without destabilizing contracting, while Paper B grounds willful-breach doctrines in the need to let promisors credibly commit (and thus raise the price of promises) so as to produce efficient ex ante contracting incentives.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal indeterminacy and the rules-versus-standards problem in contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the open-ended, fluid nature of the fairness defense and its invitation to particularistic judicial responses, and Paper B notes ambiguity in what constitutes 'willfulness' and defends doctrines that necessarily rely on judicial screening of opportunistic, avoidable breaches.

shared_topics.topic: typical factual contexts where alternative remedies arise (land, unique goods, cost-of-completion/diminution-in-value disputes)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that equitable defenses and specific performance issues mainly arise in sales of land or idiosyncratic goods and discrete bilateral exchanges, and Paper B analyzes case clusters (e.g., market-difference and cost-of-completion/diminution-in-value cases) where courts choose between awarding the promisee's expectation or denying the promisor benefits from breach.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE FUTURE OF LAW AND ECONOMICS: THE STRANGEST ATTACK YET ON LAW AND ECONOMICS.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: FORCE MAJEURE, VIS MAJOR, IMPOSSIBILITY, AND IMPRACTICABILITY UNDER OHIO LAW BEFORE AND AFTER COVID-19

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the role of boilerplate force majeure clauses and how contract language shapes outcomes in pandemic-related breaches, and Paper B shows that the nature of the transaction (land, unique goods, long-term contracts) drives whether specific performance is at issue and how equitable defenses operate; both link contract form and subject matter to which remedies or defenses are applicable.

shared_topics.topic: law-and-economics and policy tradeoffs between stability, efficiency, and fairness in contract enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A invokes law-and-economics principles when assessing how doctrines should apply post-COVID to preserve transactional stability, while Paper B explicitly analyzes utilitarian benefits of contract stability versus the impulse to impose altruistic fairness through equitable defenses; both use economic and policy reasoning to evaluate doctrinal design and remedial choice.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EFFICIENT BREACH THEORY THROUGH THE LOOKING GLASS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how awarding or denying 'negative damages' would change breach versus performance decisions and investment incentives both before and after contract formation, and Paper B considers how availability or denial of specific performance (versus damages) affects efficiency in resource allocation, third‑party interests, and the distributional consequences of enforcement, making incentive effects central to both analyses.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Commodified Promises and Contract Theory

shared_topics.topic: how remedies should be allocated (specific performance versus damages and what justifies them)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the special defenses and moral standards that lead courts to deny specific performance while awarding damages, analyzing doctrinal and practical distinctions; Paper B explicitly lists 'remedies' as a domain its commodification theory aims to explain and justify, connecting the market character of promises to appropriate remedial responses.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between moral/deontological promissory values and instrumental/market (utilitarian) values in contract law

compared_to.partner_node_id: 71vandlrev61!!ARTICLE: Contract as Commodified Promise
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contract as Commodified Promise

shared_topics.topic: criteria for when courts should enforce promises (commerciality vs moral/fairness limits)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a market-based account that courts should primarily enforce commercial (commodified) promises and proposes presumptive enforceability when parties treat promises as marketables; Paper B interrogates the separate, more demanding fairness standard that courts apply to equitable enforcement (specific performance), asking when moral considerations should bar enforcement even though legal damages remain available.

shared_topics.topic: moral or anti-commodification constraints on contract enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly analyzes anti-commodification norms (e.g., bans on selling certain things, the rule against enforcing donative promises) as principled limits on what contracts should be enforced; Paper B treats the fairness defense to specific performance as an expression of moral standards that may justify withholding equitable relief to avoid exploiting vulnerable parties.

shared_topics.topic: how choice of remedy (specific performance vs damages) interacts with normative and doctrinal standards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reframes debates over contract remedies by showing how commodification and promissory norms bear on appropriate remedies and enforcement doctrines; Paper B focuses on the doctrinal and normative split between damages and specific performance, asking why equitable relief is subject to a distinct, stricter fairness inquiry and what that implies for doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: the instrumental role of contract law in supporting market stability and how doctrines communicate norms to markets
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds contract enforcement in a market-instrumental justification—enforcing commodified promises to sustain markets and liberal values—while Paper B analyzes the utilitarian value of doctrinal stability (and the idea of 'acoustic separation') whereby courts balance market confidence against case-by-case altruistic intervention via equitable defenses.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1583!!ARTICLE: THE FAULT PRINCIPLE AS THE CHAMELEON OF CONTRACT LAW: A MARKET FUNCTION APPROACH
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE FAULT PRINCIPLE AS THE CHAMELEON OF CONTRACT LAW: A MARKET FUNCTION APPROACH

shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly examines the tradeoffs between strict liability and fault liability regimes in contract law (including how CISG/PECL/Unidroit adopt or mix them), while Paper B addresses a related question by asking why courts treat equitable enforcement (specific performance) differently from legal damages and impose additional fairness constraints that effectively alter the promisor's remedial exposure.

shared_topics.topic: when harsh or non‑monetary sanctions (e.g., specific performance, termination) are appropriate versus monetary damages or softened sanctions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses limiting the most onerous sanctions via devices like Nachfrist (a 'second chance') and differentiating obligations by market function, while Paper B analyzes the doctrinal and policy reasons courts deny specific performance (yet allow damages), and when damages are inadequate to vindicate expectations.

shared_topics.topic: the role of market expectations and transactional function in shaping contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly proposes a market‑function approach to combine strict and fault liability based on parties' expectations and transaction types, and Paper B considers how judicial doctrines (including the fairness defense) send signals to markets and balance stability of private exchange against ad hoc equitable interventions.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that contemporary systems use nuanced mixtures of strict and fault regimes (and devices like Nachfrist) to adapt to different transaction types, while Paper B shows courts use the equitable ‘fairness’ defense and discretionary denial of specific performance as a hybrid tool to reconcile utilitarian contract stability with case‑specific notions of fairness.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 13nyujlbus393!!Article: FREEDOM TO MISLEAD: THE FICTITIOUS FREEDOM TO CONTRACT AROUND FRAUD UNDER DELAWARE LAW
compared_to.partner_title: Article: FREEDOM TO MISLEAD: THE FICTITIOUS FREEDOM TO CONTRACT AROUND FRAUD UNDER DELAWARE LAW

shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly analyzes Delaware decisions holding that clear anti-reliance or integration clauses can preclude extra‑contractual fraud claims; Paper B engages the related issue by examining when equitable doctrines (like the fairness defense) or traditional defenses such as fraud should nevertheless affect enforcement, i.e., whether contractual form should be overridden by substantive unfairness.

shared_topics.topic: the role of party sophistication, bargaining power, and negotiation context in enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats sophistication and extensive negotiation as key preconditions for permitting parties to 'contract around' fraud via disclaimers; Paper B repeatedly cites parties' lack of sophistication, mistakes, or unequal bargaining positions as central reasons courts invoke equitable defenses to refuse specific performance.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between freedom of contract/efficiency and equitable fairness or moral constraints
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques judicial arguments that prioritize freedom of contract and efficiency to uphold exculpatory clauses for fraud, while Paper B analyzes the broader institutional and moral tension between utilitarian goals (stability and predictability) and equity's impulse to deny relief in unfair transactions.

shared_topics.topic: the remedial distinction between legal damages and equitable relief (specific performance/rescission) in unfair or fraudulent transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on whether fraud claims can survive contractual disclaimers and thus affect available remedies, and Paper B examines why courts apply different standards and defenses to specific performance versus damages (and how fraud or fairness claims influence availability of rescission or equitable relief).

compared_to.partner_node_id: 94tullrev925!!SYMPOSIUM: Contract Lore as Heuristic Starting Points
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: Contract Lore as Heuristic Starting Points

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy and role of expectation damages/expectation interest
shared_topics.justification: Paper A scrutinizes the 'lore' that expectation damages put the aggrieved party in the position they would have been absent breach and labels that claim a myth in many instances; Paper B treats the expectation interest as the common objective of damages and specific performance and analyzes when damages actually protect that interest (and when they fall short).

shared_topics.topic: the gap between doctrinal statements and actual practice (doctrine–practice mismatch)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that many widely recited propositions of 'contract lore' do not accurately describe how contract law operates in practice and may serve as simplified starting points, while Paper B documents dilution and indeterminacy in doctrines (e.g., the rule limiting specific performance to cases where damages are inadequate) and asks why courts continue to assert formal distinctions that diverge from practice.

shared_topics.topic: the function of doctrinal rules and heuristics as starting points or signals for lawyers, judges, students, and markets
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly characterizes commonly repeated contract propositions as heuristic starting points used in teaching and initial analysis, and Paper B examines how vague equitable doctrines (and the formal law/equity distinction) can be used as a device or signal—e.g., to preserve market stability or achieve compromise outcomes—rather than as precise, rule-like constraints.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between efficiency/utilitarian goals and fairness or aspirational moral values in contract enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores the idea that 'lore' may reflect the normative aspirations of contracts scholars about how the law should operate, while Paper B analyzes courts' use of an equitable fairness defense as embodying altruistic moral standards that sometimes conflict with utilitarian aims of predictability and efficient enforcement.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83uchilrevonline190!!ARTICLE: The Demands of an Interpretive Theory of Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Demands of an Interpretive Theory of Contract

shared_topics.topic: moral justification for equitable defenses distinct from legal remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates whether the fairness defense that uniquely bars specific performance (but not damages) has any coherent moral or doctrinal foundation, while Paper B develops an interpretive, moral theory of contract law (Contract as Empowerment) seeking to justify why particular doctrines and remedies should be coercively enforced on moral grounds.

shared_topics.topic: the normative significance of different remedies (specific performance versus damages) for expectation and reliance interests
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how specific performance and damages differently protect expectation interests, can shift outcomes toward reliance, and generate distributional and third‑party effects; Paper B similarly confronts how rival normative theories (promissory, reliance, consideration‑based) account for remedies and seeks a unified account that explains the place of those remedies within contract doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: the role of fairness and reasonableness between contracting parties in shaping doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on an indeterminate 'fairness' standard in equity that courts invoke to deny specific performance, and Paper B advances a nondistributive conception of what is reasonable and fair between parties as central to an interpretive theory that aims to justify contract rules.

shared_topics.topic: the ambition to reconcile disparate contract doctrines within a coherent theoretical framework balancing stability and moral aims
shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks whether courts use equitable doctrines instrumentally to balance market stability and ad hoc moral impulses (e.g., 'acoustic separation'), while Paper B explicitly aims to produce a unified interpretive theory that harmonizes central doctrinal challenges and reconciles descriptive and normative perspectives.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 60lalrev233!!ARTICLE: The Wasted Sacrifice of Lessors' Lost Profit Claims in Bankruptcy
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Wasted Sacrifice of Lessors' Lost Profit Claims in Bankruptcy

shared_topics.topic: whether doctrinal distinctions between types of remedies justify treating similar contract claims differently
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques Section 502(b)(6) for singling out lessors' damage claims (a monetary remedy) for partial disallowance in bankruptcy, arguing the statute illegitimately demotes certain damages claims; Paper B analyzes the longstanding rule that equitable relief (specific performance) may be withheld on fairness grounds even when legal damages remain available, questioning whether a different moral standard for different remedies is coherent or justified.

shared_topics.topic: the exceptional legal treatment of real property contracts (sales and leases)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on real property lessors' lost profit claims and how bankruptcy law (§502(b)(6)) treats lease damages differently from other contractual claims; Paper B emphasizes that specific performance doctrines and fairness defenses arise most often in land-sales and other idiosyncratic property transactions, treating real property as a special category in contract enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: normative concerns about unequal or discriminatory treatment of parties under doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that §502(b)(6)'s partial disallowance reflects an irrational bias against lessors and violates the principle that like-situated creditors should be treated alike; Paper B criticizes the double moral standard courts apply to equitable versus legal remedies and questions whether that asymmetry can be coherently defended.

shared_topics.topic: the role of economic and policy considerations (efficiency, stability, distribution) in shaping and justifying legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the political, economic, and legal forces behind §502(b)(6) and evaluates its consequences for contractual theory and bankruptcy policy; Paper B evaluates utilitarian effects of specific performance versus damages, including efficiency, third-party impacts, and the tension between market stability and ad hoc equitable interventions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 103harvlrev687!!ARTICLE: THE DEATH OF THE IRREPARABLE INJURY RULE.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE DEATH OF THE IRREPARABLE INJURY RULE.

shared_topics.topic: when damages are 'adequate' as a bar to equitable relief (i.e., the adequacy-of-damages/irreparable-injury rule)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically challenges the traditional irreparable-injury rule, arguing courts treat damages as inadequate except in narrow fungible-market cases; Paper B analyzes the doctrinal rule that specific performance is available only when damages are inadequate and surveys its dilution and practical implications for contract enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: equitable-only defenses (the 'fairness' or undue-hardship rationale) that deny specific performance but leave legal remedies intact
shared_topics.justification: Paper B carefully analyzes the indeterminate 'fairness' defense unique to specific performance—how courts deny equitable relief for hardship or sharp practice while allowing damages—while Paper A catalogues comparable equitable exceptions (undue hardship, interference with rights, impractical supervision) and shows courts invoke such reasons to deny injunctions or specific relief.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues historical law/equity categories are dysfunctional and advocates replacing them with functional questions (specific v. substitutionary, preliminary v. permanent); Paper B highlights the procedural merger of law and equity and questions the coherence of applying different moral standards depending on the remedy, searching for a principled explanation.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents that courts routinely redefine 'adequate' and 'irreparable' to justify results and urges explicit attention to the real policy reasons behind decisions; Paper B likewise notes courts continue to profess a special moral standard for equitable relief even as decisions increasingly blur or contradict that rhetoric, and it evaluates possible justifications for that judicial behavior.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 52ucdavislrev637!!ARTICLE: Retribution in Contract Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Retribution in Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: How remedial discretion functions to reconcile efficiency/stability with fairness or deterrence goals in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the efficient-breach idea and examines courts' use of remedies (including disgorgement) to deter opportunistic breaches, and Paper B explores how equity's fairness defense may serve as a judicial device to balance utilitarian market stability against ad hoc altruistic or moral interventions.

shared_topics.topic: The role of doctrinal limitations on damages (e.g., inadequacy, certainty, avoidability, foreseeability) and courts' willingness to relax or apply them depending on context
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how judges modulate traditional damage limitations based on breacher behavior when choosing between compensatory remedies, and Paper B situates the fairness defense against the backdrop of the inadequacy-of-damages rule for specific performance and shows how doctrinal dilution and practical limits create space for equitable defenses.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:CO-INVEST AT YOUR OWN RISK: AN EXPLORATION OF POTENTIAL REMEDIAL THEORIES FOR BREACHES OF RIGHTS OF FIRST REFUSAL IN THE VENTURE CAPITAL CONTEXT

shared_topics.justification: Paper A confronts the valuation problem presented by a fund's missed chance to invest in a high‑growth startup and examines analogies to stock/option damages; Paper B highlights the classic rule that specific performance is tied to situations where damages are inadequate (land, unique goods, idiosyncratic value) and analyzes the limits of monetary relief.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers equitable remedial theories (including specific performance) and how non‑legal enforcement mechanisms like reputation interact with remedies for breaches in VC settings; Paper B extensively interrogates the fairness defense—why courts may deny specific performance on equitable grounds even when legal damages remain available.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1997detclrev993!!ARTICLE: Capping Market Damages at Lost Profit: An Unwarranted Limitation on a Middleman's Expectancy Interest
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Capping Market Damages at Lost Profit: An Unwarranted Limitation on a Middleman's Expectancy Interest

shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the conceptual validity of conflicting provisions in the UCC (e.g., §2-713 versus §1-106) and whether statutory rules square with the normative goal of expectancy protection; Paper B questions the moral and doctrinal basis for treating equitable remedies (specific performance) under a different normative standard than legal damages and asks whether that distinction is justified.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal indeterminacy and judicial discretion in remedies for breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights split authority and uncertainty in courts about which UCC provision should control when measures diverge, inviting judicial choice; Paper B emphasizes the indeterminate, fact-sensitive fairness defense in equity and how that discretion leads courts to particularistic outcomes when deciding whether to grant specific performance.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on resale/middleman scenarios involving fungible commodities and how market-price damages can overcompensate compared to lost profits; Paper B contrasts fungible goods (where damages normally suffice) with unique or idiosyncratic items (where specific performance and equitable considerations arise), using the nature of the subject matter to explain remedial differences.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 33uclalrev1565!!ARTICLE: PUNITIVE AND NONPECUNIARY DAMAGES IN ACTIONS BASED UPON CONTRACT: TOWARD ACHIEVING THE OBJECTIVE OF FULL COMPENSATION.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PUNITIVE AND NONPECUNIARY DAMAGES IN ACTIONS BASED UPON CONTRACT: TOWARD ACHIEVING THE OBJECTIVE OF FULL COMPENSATION.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how traditional damage doctrines (foreseeability, certainty, mitigation, limits on nonpecuniary recovery and attorneys' fees) systematically undercompensate contract plaintiffs and urges broadened punitive/nonpecuniary awards to achieve full compensation; Paper B analyzes how courts treat damages as sometimes inadequate to vindicate expectation interests and therefore turn to equitable relief (or deny it via fairness defenses) in cases involving unique or idiosyncratic subject matter.

shared_topics.topic: judicial discretion and doctrinal limits on extraordinary remedies (punitive/nonpecuniary damages vs specific performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques restrictive doctrines that limit punitive and nonpecuniary awards in contract and calls for reform and procedural safeguards when such awards are permitted; Paper B explores the indeterminate, discretionary fairness defense that uniquely governs specific performance and highlights how open-ended equitable standards differ from legal defenses.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between full compensation/punishment and economic efficiency/avoidance of overcompensation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames limits on recovery as driven by concerns that excessive liability deters productive economic activity and so has historically constrained full compensation; Paper B similarly situates the fairness defense as a judicial response balancing market stability and utilitarian goals against impulses to impose moral or altruistic corrections in particular cases.

shared_topics.topic: concerns about indeterminacy and the need for clearer standards or procedural safeguards when courts grant or withhold nonstandard relief
shared_topics.justification: Paper A warns of risks of abuse and overcompensation if courts expand punitive and nonpecuniary awards and recommends careful standards and procedural protections; Paper B emphasizes the vague, fluid nature of the equitable fairness defense and questions whether its indeterminacy can be justified or should be replaced by more coherent rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 67hastingslj407!!Article: Remedial Clauses: The Overprivatization of Private Law
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Remedial Clauses: The Overprivatization of Private Law

shared_topics.justification: Both engage the question whether parties should be free to pre‑specify remedial outcomes: Paper B argues remedial clauses risk overprivatizing remedial decisionmaking and displacing the judiciary and rule‑of‑law values, while Paper A shows courts use equitable doctrines (e.g., fairness defenses) to check privately negotiated bargains when granting specific performance, reflecting judicial control over remedial outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the normative tension between fairness/equity and utilitarian/efficiency considerations in remedy design
shared_topics.justification: Each paper weighs moral/ethical constraints against efficiency and market considerations — Paper A interrogates the moral (fairness) defense unique to equity versus efficiency/stability goals of contract law, and Paper B critiques law‑and‑economics calls to enforce remedial clauses that prioritize contracting efficiency over fairness and public adjudicative values.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial rules and doctrines affect market stability, third‑party interests, and the signaling function of judicial decisions
shared_topics.justification: Both works consider remedies' broader systemic effects: Paper A argues that an indeterminate fairness defense may preserve market stability by providing 'acoustic separation' between equity and law, while Paper B contends that enforcing private remedial terms can insulate private relations from public oversight and undermine the judiciary's signaling and stabilizing role.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 65vandlrev829!!ARTICLE: Loss Aversion and the Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Loss Aversion and the Law

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes broader patterns in which law more readily rectifies losses than confers gains (e.g., torts vs unjust enrichment, takings vs givings) and uses loss aversion to explain remedial asymmetries; Paper B interrogates the specific asymmetry between equitable relief (specific performance) and legal damages, asking why a stricter fairness standard attaches to specific performance even when both remedies aim to protect expectation interests.

shared_topics.topic: role of moral norms and commonsense morality in shaping legal standards and defenses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that commonsense morality and deontological intuitions (baseline-based thinking, prohibition on harming over duty to help) help explain why legal doctrines focus on losses; Paper B describes the fairness defense as an expression of a higher moral plane in equity—requiring greater altruism and enabling courts to deny specific performance on moral/fairness grounds.

shared_topics.topic: how indeterminate standards and judicial discretion function and affect legal predictability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that reference points are malleable and that law can set or reshape baselines (with cautions about manipulability), while Paper B emphasizes the fluid, open-ended nature of the fairness defense that invites particularistic judicial responses and serves as an instrument of discretionary equitable relief.

shared_topics.topic: normative trade-offs for lawmaking between efficiency/stability and moral or psychological considerations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws normative implications from behavioral facts (e.g., weighting losses more heavily, caution in reforms that change baselines) and contemplates conservative and progressive responses; Paper B weighs the utility of preserving contractual stability against the impulse to impose fairness/altruistic values (and considers devices like 'acoustic separation' to manage these trade-offs).

compared_to.partner_node_id: 94bulrev55!!ARTICLE: DO THE RIGHT THING: INDIRECT REMEDIES IN PRIVATE LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DO THE RIGHT THING: INDIRECT REMEDIES IN PRIVATE LAW

shared_topics.topic: criteria for choosing between specific performance/damages and direct/indirect remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze when courts should award an in-kind, direct remedy versus an alternative form of relief — Paper A examines doctrinal and functional tests for granting specific performance instead of damages (adequacy of monetary relief, idiosyncratic goods), while Paper B develops a general framework for when indirect remedies (that induce self-compliance) are preferable to direct remedies (low error risk, high risk of miscalculating a direct remedy).

shared_topics.topic: the role of non‑compensatory values (fairness, education, relationship preservation) in remedy design
shared_topics.justification: Both works defend remedy doctrines that incorporate moral or relational aims beyond mere compensation — Paper A interrogates the equitable 'fairness' defense and its moral standards unique to specific performance, and Paper B argues that indirect remedies can better promote autonomy, educate actors, reduce animosity, and preserve ongoing relationships.

shared_topics.topic: indeterminacy, judicial discretion, and the need for normative limits on equitable remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both papers confront the problem of vague remedial standards and judicial discretion — Paper A emphasizes the open‑ended, fact‑sensitive nature of the fairness defense to specific performance and worries about arbitrary application, while Paper B acknowledges risks of arbitrariness in indirect remedies and sets out design criteria (errors, effectiveness, relation between remedy and injury) to constrain discretion.

shared_topics.topic: practical administration costs, enforcement difficulties, and third‑party/efficiency effects of remedial choices
shared_topics.justification: Both articles consider pragmatic consequences of remedy selection — Paper A discusses administrative difficulties of specific performance and how remedies affect third parties, efficiency, and wealth distribution, while Paper B highlights that indirect remedies can lower enforcement costs, reduce court involvement, and may have different efficiency and distributional implications than direct relief.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 100yalelj369!!ARTICLE: The Myth that Promisees Prefer Supracompensatory Remedies: An Analysis of Contracting for Damage Measures.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Myth that Promisees Prefer Supracompensatory Remedies: An Analysis of Contracting for Damage Measures.
