BAXENDALE:FORESEEABILITY AND DAMAGES:THE COMMON-LAW HISTORY OF NON-ECONOMIC DAMAGES IN BREACH OF CONTRACT ACTIONS VERSUS WILLFUL BREACH OF CONTRACT ACTIONS

shared_topics.topic: how undercompensatory damages distort contracting incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces how courts limited recoverability of non-economic damages and the resulting gaps between harm and legal recovery, while Paper B shows that undercompensatory damage rules create incentives for parties (particularly promisees) to modify contracts or seek performance outside the remedial scheme.

shared_topics.topic: judicial control over remedies and verdicts to curb excessive or inadequate awards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the historical progression of courts constraining juries and devising rules to prevent excessive or inadequate non-economic awards, and Paper B focuses on the judicial role in defining and policing remedies (like specific performance) to prevent parties from circumventing the remedial system.

shared_topics.topic: opportunistic exploitation of remedial rules in contract modification and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper B centers on promisee opportunism through 'self-help' modifications to secure performance, and Paper A engages the related concern that remedial uncertainty and lax limits on non-economic recovery can produce opportunistic or inconsistent verdicts that courts seek to regulate.

shared_topics.topic: availability and limits of non-pecuniary or non-monetary remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the history and modern limits on awarding non-economic (emotional/mental) damages in breach cases, and Paper B examines when non-monetary relief (specific performance) is justified as a remedy and the problems that arise when parties use modification to obtain such relief informally.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal evolution of common-law remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A provides a long-run common-law history of damages rules from early Anglo-Saxon practice to modern American limitations, while Paper B traces the modern doctrinal development of the modification doctrine and its reconciliation with traditional remedial principles.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 75minnlrev1445!!ARTICLE: Of Spoil Pits and Swimming Pools: Reconsidering the Measure of Damages for Construction Contracts.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Of Spoil Pits and Swimming Pools: Reconsidering the Measure of Damages for Construction Contracts.

shared_topics.topic: undercompensation of damages and its behavioral consequences
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze situations in which traditional monetary remedies fail to make the non-breaching party whole — Paper A shows that undercompensatory damage rules incentivize promisees to seek contract modifications and use performance-plus-later-contestation as a self-help way to obtain more than damages; Paper B shows that awarding only diminution in value (rather than cost to complete) can leave owners undercompensated and explores the consequences and corrections for that shortfall.

shared_topics.topic: choice among remedial measures (specific performance versus monetary measures like cost-to-complete or diminution in value)
shared_topics.justification: Both works grapple with which remedy is appropriate when contracts are breached — Paper A focuses on when specific performance (including 'self-help' performance obtained via modification) can or cannot be justified, while Paper B addresses the choice between awarding cost-to-complete (a substitute for forcing performance) and awarding diminution in market value and when each is appropriate.

shared_topics.topic: judicial discretion, doctrinal uncertainty, and calls for reform of remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Each paper critiques current remedial doctrine for producing inconsistent or subjective outcomes and proposes doctrinal adjustments — Paper A urges integrating self-help enforcement into the general remedial framework to police opportunism, and Paper B criticizes courts' ad hoc rejection of cost-to-complete and proposes a clearer rule to bring predictability and better compensation.

shared_topics.topic: opportunism and exploitation of remedial rules by contracting parties
shared_topics.justification: Both examine how parties can exploit remedial doctrines for advantage — Paper A highlights 'promisee opportunism' where a promisee leverages modification and subsequent contest to gain more than entitled, while Paper B analyzes cases (e.g., Jacob & Youngs and Peevyhouse) where parties' motives and strategic use of contract specs or remedial gaps affect whether courts constrain opportunistic or unfair recoveries.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83uchilrevonline190!!ARTICLE: The Demands of an Interpretive Theory of Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Demands of an Interpretive Theory of Contract

shared_topics.topic: the normative justification of contract enforcement remedies (specific performance vs damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critically examines how modification doctrine can functionally grant promisees a self-help form of specific performance and argues when such a remedy is or is not justified relative to the ordinary substitutional damages remedy; Paper B engages this issue at a theoretical level by defending an interpretive account of contract law that must explain why and when contract obligations should be given coercive legal force and thus how remedial choices (enforcement versus damages) fit within a moral framework for the law of contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal role and explanation of consideration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces modern modification doctrine’s move away from formalistic consideration rules and explores how those rules interact with modification, performance, and opportunism; Paper B foregrounds the centrality of the consideration requirement and seeks an interpretive, moral explanation for why consideration operates as a core doctrine of contract law.

shared_topics.topic: opportunism, bargaining leverage, and fairness in contractual adjustments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes promisee and promisor opportunism when parties modify contracts (including how undercompensatory damages create incentives to exploit modifications); Paper B addresses similar concerns more abstractly by aiming to justify contract doctrines in terms of what is reasonable and fair between contracting parties and by confronting how a general theory should police opportunistic behavior.

shared_topics.topic: the need to integrate disparate contract doctrines into a coherent theoretical framework
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that self-help enforcement measures and modification rules must be integrated into the broader remedial structure of contract law rather than treated as special exceptions; Paper B proposes a unified interpretive theory of contract law designed to account for and harmonize the main doctrines (including remedies, consideration, and obligations) within a single moral framework.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 29yalejonreg1!!ARTICLE: Self-Help and the Rules of Engagement
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Self-Help and the Rules of Engagement

shared_topics.topic: self-help remedies in contract law and their normative limits
shared_topics.justification: Paper A identifies and critiques a specific form of contractual self-help—the 'self-help specific performance remedy' that promisees can exploit via modifications—and argues self-help measures must be integrated into the general remedial scheme; Paper B develops a general framework for when the law should permit self-help (versus mandatory process), explicitly applying that framework to contractual contexts such as repossession and eviction.

shared_topics.topic: how the choice between damages and specific performance affects parties' incentives to exploit contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how undercompensatory damages and the availability (or not) of specific performance drive promisees to induce performance via modification and then renege; Paper B similarly connects the form and clarity of legal entitlements (including capped monetary remedies versus retaking specific property) to when confrontational self-help is allowed and how parties will behave.

shared_topics.topic: the role of administrative costs, accuracy, and judicial process in channeling disputes away from self-help
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that self-help that yields more than the remedial system allows should be constrained and integrated with judicial remedies, effectively requiring judicial process where necessary; Paper B foregrounds administrative costs, the accuracy benefits of adjudication, and delay as key variables that justify prohibiting self-help or requiring verification by courts.

shared_topics.topic: strategic opportunism and manipulation of self-help rules by parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights promisee opportunism—modifying to secure performance and later contesting the modification—as an underexplored problem; Paper B analyzes related strategic behaviors (e.g., debtors staging breaches of the peace or otherwise exploiting repo/eviction rules) and how rule design affects such manipulation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 41houslrev1579!!ARTICLE:MEASURING "ACTUAL HARM" FOR THE PURPOSE OF DETERMINING THE ENFORCEABILITY OF LIQUIDATED DAMAGES CLAUSES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:MEASURING "ACTUAL HARM" FOR THE PURPOSE OF DETERMINING THE ENFORCEABILITY OF LIQUIDATED DAMAGES CLAUSES

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy of the damages remedy and its effects on contracting behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how limits on expectation damages (avoidability, foreseeability, certainty) affect the measurement of 'actual harm' for enforcing liquidated damages clauses; Paper B shows that undercompensatory damages create incentives for parties to seek modifications or self-help routes (e.g., inducing performance) and argues remedies should account for that incentive structure.

shared_topics.topic: party opportunism created by remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is concerned that allowing unrecoverable losses to be counted as 'actual harm' could enable parties to recover amounts beyond what ordinary damages law would permit; Paper B examines promisee opportunism where a party exploits modification doctrine and remedial gaps to obtain more than the legal entitlement (the 'self-help specific performance' problem).

shared_topics.topic: whether and how remedial doctrines should constrain contractual enforcement and interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grapples with how the avoidability/foreseeability/certainty limits of damages should constrain courts' review of liquidated damages clauses under the U.C.C. and Restatement; Paper B argues that self-help remedies and modification doctrine must be reconciled with the general remedial system so that equitable and legal remedies coherently constrain parties' post‑contract behavior.

shared_topics.topic: the proper boundaries of recoverable losses (what counts as 'actual harm' or adequate relief)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks which categories of loss (reasonably avoidable, unforeseeable, or uncertain) should be included when computing 'actual harm' for clause enforcement; Paper B addresses when damages are legally inadequate and when specific performance (or other relief) is appropriate, raising the same central question of which losses warrant which remedial forms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 99minnlrevheadnotes141!!ARTICLE: The Limitations of Economic Reasoning in Analyzing Duress
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Limitations of Economic Reasoning in Analyzing Duress

shared_topics.topic: opportunistic exploitation in contract modification/duress
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how one party can exploit the contractual relationship to extract concessions: Paper A critiques attempts to reduce duress to simple rent‑seeking explanations of opportunism in modification cases, and Paper B documents and theorizes a concrete form of opportunism (promisee self‑help specific performance) that arises when parties modify contracts under threat of breach.

shared_topics.topic: bargaining leverage as a source of redistribution (rent‑seeking) versus productive adjustment
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the question whether hold‑up or modification rents are mere redistribution rather than wealth‑creating adjustments: Paper A evaluates the proposal to frame duress as 'rentseeking' (redistribution), while Paper B investigates how leverage in the contractual relationship can be used to reallocate value through modifications and when that reallocation is opportunistic.

shared_topics.topic: limits and role of economic reasoning in doctrinal design
shared_topics.justification: Both papers question how far economic models should drive doctrinal rules: Paper A explicitly critiques reducing duress doctrine to an economic rent‑seeking formula, and Paper B applies incentive/damage‑compensation reasoning to argue for integrating self‑help remedies into the remedial system while warning of the distortions that follow from simplistic economic assumptions.

shared_topics.topic: how contract law doctrine and remedies should be structured to police opportunism
shared_topics.justification: Both discuss doctrinal responses to opportunistic modification — Paper A argues that simple economic reductions will not satisfactorily serve the functional or instrumental goals of contract law, and Paper B prescribes that courts should align modification doctrine and remedial rules (specific performance vs damages) to prevent promisee and promisor opportunism.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 11texwesleyanlrev627!!SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:THE BOUNDARIES OF CONTRACT IN A GLOBAL ECONOMY:HADLEY V. BAXENDALE AND OTHER COMMON LAW BORROWINGS FROM THE CIVIL LAW
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:THE BOUNDARIES OF CONTRACT IN A GLOBAL ECONOMY:HADLEY V. BAXENDALE AND OTHER COMMON LAW BORROWINGS FROM THE CIVIL LAW

shared_topics.topic: limits on contractual remedies and the adequacy of damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes Hadley v. Baxendale as a foundational judicial rule that limits recovery of contractual damages (foreseeability), while Paper B focuses on the remedial structure of contract law—how undercompensatory damages create incentives for opportunistic modification and when specific performance is or is not justified.

shared_topics.topic: balancing contractual flexibility with policing opportunism in modification and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper B directly addresses the tension between allowing parties to adjust contracts and preventing opportunistic self-help modifications; Paper A likewise examines how the Hadley foreseeability rule and other borrowed doctrines function to constrain parties' claims and limit opportunistic recovery under contract.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts in shaping and reformulating contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions whether the Hadley rule was a judicial invention or a transplant from civil law and situates it in judicial law‑making, and Paper B critiques modern judicial approaches to modification and remedial decisionmaking, arguing courts must integrate self-help measures into the broader remedial framework.

shared_topics.topic: the alignment of contract rules with commercial and social context
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates Hadley in the exigencies of commerce and explores how legal transplants interact with societal context, while Paper B grounds the evolution of modification doctrine in the parties' need for flexibility in changing commercial conditions and the practical adequacy of remedies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 12jempiricallegalstud29!!ARTICLE: Damages Versus Specific Performance: Lessons from Commercial Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Damages Versus Specific Performance: Lessons from Commercial Contracts

shared_topics.topic: contracting around default remedial rules (express clauses vs doctrinal workarounds)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically analyzes how sophisticated parties include contractual clauses (e.g., stipulating that damages are inadequate or that specific performance is available) to alter courts' default remedial rules, while Paper B shows doctrinally how parties can achieve similar outcomes through contract modification and 'self-help' practices that functionally alter available remedies.

shared_topics.topic: adequacy of damages as a driver of parties' behavior
shared_topics.justification: Both papers treat the insufficiency of damages as a central trigger: Paper A infers that parties' silence or inclusion of specific-performance clauses reflects judgments about whether damages will be adequate, and Paper B argues that undercompensatory damages create incentives for promisees to seek modifications that yield performance effectively unavailable through damages alone.

shared_topics.topic: specific performance versus substitutional damages as competing remedial regimes and efficiency implications
shared_topics.justification: Paper A assesses, with empirical data, when parties prefer specific performance to damages (and in which contract types), while Paper B theorizes how allowing or denying specific performance affects incentives to modify contracts and the potential for opportunistic exploitation, thereby engaging the efficiency tradeoffs between the two remedies.

shared_topics.topic: strategic/opportunistic behavior around modification and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Both articles focus on strategic responses to remedy rules: Paper A interprets contractual drafting choices as strategic attempts to secure preferred remedies, and Paper B develops the concept of promisee opportunism through post-contract modification and enforcement tactics that exploit the remedial structure.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 108michlrev633!!ARTICLE: DO LIQUIDATED DAMAGES ENCOURAGE BREACH? A PSYCHOLOGICAL EXPERIMENT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DO LIQUIDATED DAMAGES ENCOURAGE BREACH? A PSYCHOLOGICAL EXPERIMENT

shared_topics.topic: how remedial rules and contractual clauses alter incentives to breach or perform
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how the design of remedies (specific performance versus expectation damages in Paper A; liquidated-damages clauses versus expectation damages in Paper B) changes parties' incentives to perform or to breach and thereby influences contracting behavior.

shared_topics.topic: opportunistic exploitation of contractual structures
shared_topics.justification: Each paper studies opportunism enabled by contract law: Paper A identifies promisee opportunism through post‑modification self‑help specific performance, while Paper B shows that explicit penalty clauses can encourage promisor opportunism (breach) when profitable.

shared_topics.topic: the interaction between formal legal provisions and moral or social norms governing promises
shared_topics.justification: Both works investigate how formalization of remedies or clauses reshapes moral perceptions and norms—Paper A argues self‑help remedies must fit within substantive remedial norms, and Paper B demonstrates that liquidated damages change parties' moral judgments about the obligation to perform.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy of damages as a corrective and its effects on contracting choices
shared_topics.justification: Each article interrogates whether damages adequately compensate and thereby whether alternative remedial structures are justified or produce behavioral changes—Paper A highlights undercompensatory damages driving modification strategies, and Paper B compares expectation damages to stipulated damages and their behavioral consequences.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1397!!ARTICLE: A COMPARATIVE FAULT DEFENSE IN CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A COMPARATIVE FAULT DEFENSE IN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: incentive effects of remedial rules on contracting parties' behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that adopting a comparative-fault defense in contract law would create incentives for promisees to cooperate and avoid inefficient reliance while preserving promisor incentives to perform; Paper B analyzes how the choice between performance and damages (and modification doctrine) shapes parties' incentives to seek, resist, or exploit contractual changes.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy of damages versus specific performance and its impact on strategic conduct
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques existing contractual remedies for failing to motivate efficient cooperative or reliance-avoidance behavior and advocates apportionment of loss; Paper B focuses on the gap between the value of performance and available damages, showing that undercompensation creates incentives for promisee self-help and opportunistic modification.

shared_topics.topic: opportunism and allocation of loss when both parties contribute to adverse outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A identifies situations where promisee fault (noncooperation or overreliance) should reduce recovery and thus share losses, framing such allocation as a guard against inefficient conduct; Paper B documents promisee opportunism (using post-performance contestation of modifications) and treats extra-remedial gains as opportunistic allocations that contract doctrine should police.

shared_topics.topic: aligning remedial doctrine with substantive contract duties and transactional flexibility
shared_topics.justification: Paper A seeks to expand substantive contract doctrine by importing comparative-fault rules to better match duties to cooperate/avoid reliance with remedies, while Paper B argues that modification and self-help remedies must be integrated into the broader remedial scheme so that flexibility to adjust contractual terms does not undermine the underlying structure of contract law.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 39umiamilrev847!!ARTICLE: Stability in the Present Value Determination of Future Lost Earnings: An Historical Perspective with Implications for Predictability
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Stability in the Present Value Determination of Future Lost Earnings: An Historical Perspective with Implications for Predictability

shared_topics.topic: use of economic theory and empirical evidence to set legal remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses economic theory and historical after-tax data to recommend a stable benchmark differential discount rate for calculating present value of future lost earnings, while Paper B employs economic reasoning about incentives and undercompensation to argue how modification doctrine and self-help specific performance should be limited and structured.

shared_topics.topic: concern with predictability and stability of remedial standards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts should adopt a stable, benchmark differential discount rate to make awards predictable across cases and occupations, and Paper B seeks clearer doctrinal limits on when self-help specific performance is permissible to reduce opportunistic and unpredictable outcomes from ad hoc contract modifications.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial rules create incentives that can produce opportunism or inequity
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that wide judicial variation in choosing discount rates can create large, inequitable differences in awards, and Paper B analyzes how inadequate damage remedies incentivize promisees to exploit modification opportunities (self-help) to obtain more than their contractual entitlement.

shared_topics.topic: tension between uniform/formulaic benchmarks and judicial discretion in remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques courts' refusal to adopt a single methodology and proposes a benchmark rate to reduce divergent awards, while Paper B critiques the flexible, case-by-case modification doctrine and advocates for principled limits tying self-help remedies to the broader remedial scheme.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 57scallrev667!!ARTICLE: A LITTLE ESSAY IN PARTIAL DEFENSE OF THE CONTRACT-MARKET DIFFERENTIAL AS A REMEDY FOR BUYERS.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A LITTLE ESSAY IN PARTIAL DEFENSE OF THE CONTRACT-MARKET DIFFERENTIAL AS A REMEDY FOR BUYERS.

shared_topics.topic: whether contract remedies (damages vs specific performance) actually compensate parties for their losses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends the contract-market differential as an accurate compensatory damages measure for buyers in sale-of-goods disputes, while Paper B interrogates when specific performance versus damages yields adequate compensation and argues self-help specific performance can misalign with remedial goals.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial rules create incentives for opportunistic behavior by contracting parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines buyer behavior (cover, resale) and the risk of overcompensation under the contract-market differential, and Paper B analyzes promisee opportunism arising from modification (inducing performance and then contesting obligations) when the remedial structure undercompensates or permits self-help gains.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of timing and market conditions on measuring remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses problems created by time lapses and anomalous market conditions in computing the contract-market differential, and Paper B highlights discrepancies between the value of performance and the available damage remedy (including limits due to judicial administration) that depend on timing and market valuation.

shared_topics.topic: the gap between theoretical doctrine and judicial practice in remedial law and the need to align doctrine with practical enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts scholarly theoretical critiques of the contract-market differential with courts' consistent use of it and offers rebuttals, while Paper B critiques modern modification doctrine and urges integrating self-help remedies into the general remedial framework to prevent doctrinally inconsistent opportunism.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1397!!ARTICLE: A COMPARATIVE FAULT DEFENSE IN CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A COMPARATIVE FAULT DEFENSE IN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: incentive effects of remedial rules (damages, specific performance, or apportionment) on contracting behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how adopting a comparative fault defense in contract law would change parties' incentives—encouraging efficient cooperation and reliance while preserving promisor incentives to perform—whereas Paper B examines how remedial structure (undercompensatory damages vs self-help specific performance) creates incentives for promisees to seek opportunistic alterations and argues remedies should be calibrated to avoid such distortions.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal reform to police opportunism and promote efficient performance-stage behavior
shared_topics.justification: Both articles propose changes to contract doctrine to curb inefficient or opportunistic conduct: Paper A argues for introducing CFD into American contract law to deter noncooperation and overreliance, and Paper B argues for rethinking modification doctrine and limiting a promisee's self-help specific-performance remedy to prevent promisee opportunism.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of losses between promisor and promisee when promisee's conduct contributes to harm
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally advocates apportioning damages when a promisee fails to cooperate or avoids overreliance, and Paper B engages the same allocation problem indirectly by showing how current remedial gaps let promisees obtain more than the contractual entitlement (via modification and performance), thus distorting the proper distribution of loss and benefit.

shared_topics.topic: the role and limits of promisee cooperation and reliance duties during contract performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A identifies categories where the promisee has a legal burden to cooperate or avoid overreliance and ties liability to those duties; Paper B addresses the performance phase dynamic in which promisees may induce performance through modification and then challenge obligations, highlighting tensions around parties' duties and strategic reliance during performance.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 97valrev1939!!ARTICLE: THE MYTH OF EFFICIENT BREACH: NEW DEFENSES OF THE EXPECTATION INTEREST
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE MYTH OF EFFICIENT BREACH: NEW DEFENSES OF THE EXPECTATION INTEREST

shared_topics.topic: specific performance versus monetary damages as the appropriate remedy for breach
shared_topics.justification: Both papers center on the remedial choice between specific performance (a property-rule) and expectation damages (a liability-rule). Paper A analyzes how contractual modification can produce a de facto self-help specific performance remedy and argues when that remedy is or is not justifiable, while Paper B frames the broader property-rule vs liability-rule debate, defending damages (and the dual-performance view) against calls to make specific performance the default.

shared_topics.topic: how undercompensatory damages shape parties' incentives and create opportunistic behavior
shared_topics.justification: Both articles engage the problem that damages may undercompensate promisees and thus distort incentives: Paper A argues undercompensatory damage rules induce promisees to seek modifications to secure performance and then contest them (promisee opportunism), while Paper B analyzes critiques that damages unfairly allocate breach gains to promisors (and considers disgorgement/ gain-based remedies) and shows how pricing and damages affect surplus-sharing.

shared_topics.topic: the role of renegotiation and contract modification in delivering efficient or inequitable outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Both works examine renegotiation/modification dynamics—Paper A focuses on doctrinal rules governing modification and the risk that modification will be used opportunistically by either party, whereas Paper B explores how renegotiation under property vs liability rules (and Coasean bargaining) affects whether breaches or performance are efficient and how default remedies alter incentives to renegotiate.

shared_topics.topic: selection and normative justification of default remedial rules and integrating remedies into contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Each paper addresses which remedial default the law should supply and why: Paper A argues self-help enforcement measures must be integrated into the general remedial fabric and limits when self-help specific performance can be justified, while Paper B develops theoretical and moral defenses for liability-rule expectation damages as the appropriate default and analyzes the consequences of shifting to property or restitutionary rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 7jempiricallegalstud743!!ARTICLE: Relational Governance and Contract Damages: Evidence from Franchising
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Relational Governance and Contract Damages: Evidence from Franchising

shared_topics.topic: how the structure of legal remedies (liquidated damages, damages, specific performance) shapes parties' incentives and opportunistic behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically studies how the presence or absence of liquidated-damages clauses in franchise contracts affects franchisee incentives and the use of informal governance; Paper B analyzes how the availability (or legal unavailability) of specific performance and the undercompensatory nature of damages create incentives for promisees to seek self-help modification and opportunistically extract performance.

shared_topics.topic: substitution and complementarity between formal legal enforcement and informal or self-help governance mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A tests whether formal contract remedies and relational (informal) governance act as substitutes or complements in franchising; Paper B treats self-help specific performance as an informal enforcement pathway that parties may use to bypass formal remedial limits, raising similar substitution/complementarity concerns between courts-based remedies and party-driven enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of enforcement costs, remedial limits, and judicial doctrine on ex ante contracting choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how litigation costs, franchisor experience, and court treatment of liquidated damages influence whether franchisors include formal damage terms or rely on relational controls; Paper B argues that limits in judicial administration and doctrinal choices about modification and specific performance alter parties' ex ante and ex post behavior, encouraging or deterring opportunistic modifications.

shared_topics.topic: concerns about opportunism in long-term principal–agent or bilateral contracting relationships and how contract design mitigates it
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames franchising as a principal–agent problem where contract terms and relational rewards deter franchisee shirking; Paper B focuses on opportunism arising from contract modification and shows how remedies and doctrinal rules must be designed to prevent one party (here, the promisee) from exploiting the relationship.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 84texlrev831!!Article: Specific Performance Versus Damages for Breach of Contract: An Economic Analysis
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Specific Performance Versus Damages for Breach of Contract: An Economic Analysis

shared_topics.topic: economic criteria for when specific performance is preferable to expectation damages
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze when courts (or parties) should prefer specific performance over damages: Paper A offers an economic taxonomy (contracts to produce vs conveyance of existing property) showing when specific performance maximizes joint value, while Paper B evaluates when specific performance is a justifiable remedy (including as a self-help outcome of modification) and when it should be denied.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial rules shape parties' incentives and opportunistic behavior
shared_topics.justification: Both works study how the availability or absence of specific performance affects strategic behavior: Paper A shows specific performance can create wasteful avoidance, risk-bearing, and bargaining dynamics for sellers, while Paper B focuses on promisee opportunism (using modification to extract performance and then contesting the change) that remedies can enable.

shared_topics.topic: the significance of damages' inadequacy (undercompensation) for remedy choice and contracting outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Both papers treat inadequacy of the damage remedy as a central problem: Paper A explains how expectation damages may fail when buyer valuations are underestimated (leading to joint losses and a case for specific performance in conveyances), and Paper B argues undercompensation of damages motivates parties to modify contracts and seek self-help specific performance.

shared_topics.topic: the role of bargaining/modification costs and limits of judicial enforcement in determining remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both analyses incorporate transaction costs and enforcement constraints into remedy choice: Paper A emphasizes bargaining costs for releases, enforcement difficulties of compelled production, and comparative ease of enforcing conveyances, while Paper B centers on the modification process, bargaining leverage, and judicial-administrative limits that affect whether specific performance (or self-help substitutes) is appropriate.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 104marqlrev141!!ARTICLE: THE MYTH OF OPTIMAL EXPECTATION DAMAGES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE MYTH OF OPTIMAL EXPECTATION DAMAGES

shared_topics.topic: adequacy and optimality of expectation damages versus alternative remedies (including specific performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions whether expectation damages are the universally optimal default and surveys critiques that expectation damages can be under- or over-compensatory; Paper B analyzes when damages are legally inadequate and argues that reliance on substitutionary damages creates pressures that make specific performance or other remedies salient and sometimes necessary.

shared_topics.topic: remedial rules create strategic incentives and opportunistic behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how the expectation-damages regime can distort parties' investment and performance incentives (e.g., causing overinvestment or misaligned breach decisions); Paper B shows how undercompensatory damages and current modification doctrine create promisee opportunism (the 'self-help specific performance' problem) and strategic modification behavior.

shared_topics.topic: limits on parties' freedom to contract around remedial defaults and courts' role policing remedial terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes 'damages exceptionalism' whereby courts strike down or limit contracted-for damages provisions and questions why damages are harder to contract around than other terms; Paper B critiques modification doctrine and judicial enforcement practices, arguing courts must integrate remedial limits into doctrine to prevent parties from using modifications to evade the remedial system.

shared_topics.topic: treating remedial entitlements (damages/specific performance) as priced contract terms or termination options that affect bargaining and contract design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames damages as part of the contract's pricing scheme and as the price of a termination option that sophisticated parties would negotiate; Paper B examines how modification and the availability (or absence) of particular remedies change the effective value of performance and breach, and thus alter parties' bargaining incentives and the structure of agreements.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 11texwesleyanlrev481!!SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. shared_topics.topic: the relationship between damages and specific performance as competing contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the substitutional character of the damage remedy versus specific performance, arguing that modification doctrine can create a de facto self-help specific performance that circumvents remedial limits; Paper B situates damages within a broader remedial philosophy shift and examines how courts have constrained types of recoverable damages, informing which remedies are preferred or limited in practice.

shared_topics.topic: how the adequacy or limits of damages shape party incentives and outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues undercompensatory damage rules create incentives for promisees to seek modifications and exploit performance, while Paper B documents courts' adoption of limiting rules for non-economic damages based on concerns about excessive or inadequate awards—both discuss how damage rules influence contracting behavior and litigation outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: judicial and doctrinal efforts to police remedies and prevent opportunistic or excessive awards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A calls for integrating self-help enforcement into the general remedial scheme and for doctrine that polices opportunistic modifications; Paper B traces historical mechanisms by which courts controlled juries and developed rules to constrain damage awards, reflecting a shared focus on doctrinal controls over remedies.

shared_topics.topic: historical evolution of contract remedial doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces modern shifts in modification doctrine away from formalistic consideration-based theories toward approaches addressing opportunism, and Paper B offers a long-run history of damages law from early common law to modern limitations—both engage with how remedial doctrines have developed over time.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1569!!ARTICLE: WHY BREACH OF CONTRACT MAY NOT BE IMMORAL GIVEN THE INCOMPLETENESS OF CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: WHY BREACH OF CONTRACT MAY NOT BE IMMORAL GIVEN THE INCOMPLETENESS OF CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: normative assessment of breach (lawful breach vs moral wrongdoing)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates when contractual modification and self-help enforcement allow parties to obtain more than their contractual rights and treats such opportunism as normatively suspect; Paper B directly asks when breach should be considered immoral given legal permissibility and argues that moral condemnation is attenuated by factual and contractual context.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy and role of remedies (damages versus specific performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on how undercompensatory damages and the availability of specific performance shape incentives to modify and to engage in promisee self-help; Paper B highlights that the law typically permits breach conditional on paying damages and uses that remedial structure as a key premise in assessing the moral status of breach.

shared_topics.topic: contractual incompleteness and its implications for enforcement and adjustment
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats modification doctrine as a response to parties' need for flexibility when contracts do not perfectly allocate future risks, while also policing opportunism; Paper B’s core argument is that contracts are often incomplete and that this incompleteness affects whether breaches should be seen as violations of promise.

shared_topics.topic: strategic opportunism around modification or breach in unforeseen contingencies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes strategic behavior by promisees and promisors (especially promisee opportunism in inducing performance via modification and later contesting it); Paper B examines when breaches in contingencies not specified by incomplete contracts may be strategically chosen and whether such choices are morally blameworthy.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 103harvlrev687!!ARTICLE: THE DEATH OF THE IRREPARABLE INJURY RULE.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE DEATH OF THE IRREPARABLE INJURY RULE.

shared_topics.topic: when specific performance (or other equitable relief) is appropriate given the inadequacy of damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how undercompensatory damages create incentives for promisees to engineer modifications to secure performance and later contest them, arguing specific performance should only be allowed when it would be justified at suit or when damages are legally inadequate; Paper B analyzes the irreparable-injury doctrine and shows courts treat damages as inadequate in most non‑fungible contexts, documenting when judges prefer specific relief over substitutionary damages.

shared_topics.topic: strategic or opportunistic behavior by parties exploiting remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on 'promisee opportunism' — parties using contract modification to obtain performance they could not secure at law — and treats self-help specific performance as a potential opportunistic tactic; Paper B documents how parties and courts manipulate notions of adequacy and irreparability, and how remedial labels are used strategically in preliminary and permanent relief disputes.

shared_topics.topic: critique of formalistic remedial doctrines and advocacy for a functional, integrated approach to remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues self-help remedies must be integrated into the general fabric of contract remedy rather than treated as special exceptions rooted in formal rules; Paper B similarly argues against the archaic irreparable-injury rhetoric and for asking functional questions (specific vs substitutionary, preliminary vs permanent) to guide remedial choice.

shared_topics.topic: the role of judicial doctrine and balancing (practical constraints) in policing fairness and limiting exploitative remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the challenge courts face in allowing contractual flexibility while policing opportunistic modifications and defining the proper scope of specific-performance remedies; Paper B catalogs the real reasons courts deny equitable relief (hardship, supervision costs, competing rights, preliminary-stage risk balancing) and shows courts effectively balance these considerations rather than mechanically applying the irreparable-injury rule.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 58drakelrev177!!ARTICLE: AUTONOMY AND ACCOUNTABILITY IN THE LAW OF CONTRACTS: A RESPONSE TO PROFESSOR SHIFFRIN
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: AUTONOMY AND ACCOUNTABILITY IN THE LAW OF CONTRACTS: A RESPONSE TO PROFESSOR SHIFFRIN

shared_topics.topic: the choice between specific performance and expectation damages as contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on how modification can create a de facto self-help specific performance remedy and argues when such a remedy is justified relative to the normal damage remedy; Paper B surveys doctrinal and normative debates over damages versus specific performance, documenting when courts grant specific performance and how that choice relates to the moral enforcement of promises.

shared_topics.topic: how inadequacy of damages shapes party incentives (including inducements to modify or breach)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that undercompensatory damage rules create incentives for promisees to induce performance via modification and then contest the modification, while Paper B examines whether the availability and size of damages (and doctrines like efficient breach) align with moral and legal expectations and influence promisor behavior.

shared_topics.topic: opportunism and the need to police abusive tactics in contractual relations (including the role of doctrine to prevent exploitation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes promisee opportunism arising from modification and calls for integrating self-help remedies into the remedial framework to prevent exploitation; Paper B addresses promisor and promisee accountability through doctrines such as the implied covenant of good faith, promissory estoppel, and punitive damages as mechanisms to deter opportunistic breaches and abusive conduct.

shared_topics.topic: the moral and legal status of breach (whether breach is wrongful or permissible and how law should treat intentional breaches)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats the promisor's threat to breach and the resulting strategic responses as central to modification doctrine and remedy allocation, while Paper B directly interrogates whether intentional breach is morally and legally permissible, analyzing doctrines (efficient breach, Holmes's 'pay or perform') that frame breach as a choice with legal and moral consequences.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 62bclrevesupp32!!ARTICLE: THE COST OF GUILTY BREACH: WILLFUL BREACH IN M&A CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE COST OF GUILTY BREACH: WILLFUL BREACH IN M&A CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: the role of fault/intentionality and opportunism in setting contractual liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents that sophisticated parties routinely distinguish willful breaches and escalate liability based on fault, while Paper B analyzes promisee and promisor opportunism (intentional exploitation) in modification contexts and treats self-help measures as potentially opportunistic conduct to be policed.

shared_topics.topic: how perceived inadequacy of damages (vs specific performance) shapes contracting and post-contract behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A’s findings about parties preferring fault-based allocation of liability imply dissatisfaction with baseline damage rules, and Paper B argues that undercompensatory damage remedies motivate promisees to seek modifications and self-help performance, linking remedial shortcomings to strategic behavior.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between party autonomy/flexibility and judicial/doctrinal limits to prevent exploitation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts parties' real-world contractual preferences (e.g., willful-breach clauses) with black‑letter doctrine’s strict‑liability and courts' resistance to punitive arrangements, while Paper B examines courts' effort to allow contract modification flexibility yet police opportunistic or coercive modifications.

shared_topics.topic: how sophisticated contract drafting and doctrinal design aim to manage post-contractual strategic behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses empirical review and interviews to show M&A drafting choices (fault distinctions) as tools to allocate risk and deter opportunism, and Paper B considers doctrinal rules on modification and self-help specific performance as mechanisms to constrain or permit strategic post-agreement adjustments.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 98iowalrev183!!ARTICLE: Markets as a Moral Foundation for Contract Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Markets as a Moral Foundation for Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: how legal remedies and remedy rules shape incentives in market exchange
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that functioning markets depend on legal rules (property protection, prohibition of expropriation) that shape actors' incentives to engage in impersonal exchange, and Paper B shows how the design of contract remedies (damages versus specific performance and modification doctrine) creates incentives for promisors and promisees to behave opportunistically or cooperatively.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy of enforcement mechanisms to sustain commerce
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that markets require effective enforcement against predation and expropriation to permit broad impersonal trade, while Paper B analyzes how undercompensatory damage remedies and limitations on specific performance can distort enforcement and lead parties to use self-help modifications that undermine contractual stability.

shared_topics.topic: opportunism, exploitation, and their effects on transactional regimes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how predation and capture (e.g., Russian oligarchs) can prevent healthy markets from emerging, and Paper B studies a different form of opportunism—promisee or promisor exploitation via contract modification—that corrodes fair contractual relationships and market functioning.

shared_topics.topic: institutional design and the rule of law as prerequisites for reliable contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A identifies institutional features (open entry, protection of property rights, prohibition on violence) needed for impersonal market exchange, and Paper B interrogates how doctrinal choices about modification and remedies should be integrated into the legal framework to produce predictable, non-exploitative contracting institutions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1583!!ARTICLE: THE FAULT PRINCIPLE AS THE CHAMELEON OF CONTRACT LAW: A MARKET FUNCTION APPROACH
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE FAULT PRINCIPLE AS THE CHAMELEON OF CONTRACT LAW: A MARKET FUNCTION APPROACH

shared_topics.topic: adequacy and choice of remedies (specific performance versus damages)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers substantively engage with how remedial rules shape contractual outcomes: Paper A examines how liability regimes and sanctions (including limits on the most onerous sanctions) affect enforcement, while Paper B analyzes when specific performance is justified versus substitutionary damages and how undercompensation by damages drives strategic behavior.

shared_topics.topic: party opportunism when doctrines allow post‑contractual adjustment
shared_topics.justification: Both works confront opportunistic exploitation of contractual rules — Paper A by arguing for a nuanced liability mix to avoid misuse of strict or fault regimes in different market contexts, and Paper B by diagnosing promisee opportunism in modification (the 'self‑help specific performance' problem) and proposing doctrinal responses.

shared_topics.topic: need to balance contractual flexibility with safeguards against exploitation
shared_topics.justification: Each paper grapples with permitting parties to adapt to changing conditions while constraining abusive adjustments: Paper A advocates a market‑function approach to calibrate strict/fault elements to market expectations, and Paper B seeks doctrines that permit legitimate modification but police coercive or opportunistic amendments.

shared_topics.topic: how allocation of the promisor's choice between performance and breach affects incentives
shared_topics.justification: Both analyze the behavioral consequences of giving promisors a practical choice between performing and breaching (with damages): Paper A considers how liability regimes signal expected performance obligations, and Paper B treats that choice as central to why promisees may seek modifications to secure performance and later contest them.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 53lalrev1257!!ARTICLE: Comparative Ruminations on the Foreseeability of Damages in Contract Law. Dedicated to Professor Jurgen Basedow, Augsburg University, School of Law.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Comparative Ruminations on the Foreseeability of Damages in Contract Law. Dedicated to Professor Jurgen Basedow, Augsburg University, School of Law.

shared_topics.topic: limits on recoverable contract damages and the role of foreseeability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the historical and comparative rule that contractual liability is limited to damages that were foreseeable or in the parties' contemplation (e.g., Hadley v. Baxendale and its French-law origins), while Paper B examines how the undercompensation of damages within the remedial system creates incentives to seek modified performance and thus interrogates the boundaries of what damages should compensate in contract law.

shared_topics.topic: choice of remedies in contract law (damages versus specific performance) and when each is justified
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts contractual and tortious compensation rules and emphasizes legal limits on compensation in contract cases, and Paper B directly evaluates when specific performance—as opposed to substitutionary damages—should be available or treated as a permissible self-help remedy in modification contexts.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal development and comparative/historical origins of contract-law rules limiting liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the history and comparative origins of the foreseeability/‘contemplation’ limitation across civil-law systems and common-law formulations, and Paper B surveys the modern evolution of modification doctrine away from formalistic consideration doctrines toward frameworks aimed at policing opportunism, situating contemporary rules in their doctrinal trajectory.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial rules allocate risk and shape party incentives (including opportunistic behavior)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that foreseeability limits and other remedial distinctions (statutes of limitation, burden of proof, interest rules) function to allocate risk between contracting parties, and Paper B analyzes how the structure of remedies—particularly inadequate damages or lack of specific performance—creates incentives for promisees or promisors to exploit modification opportunities.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83columlrev35!!ARTICLE: THE STRUCTURE OF JUDICIAL ADMINISTRATION AND THE DEVELOPMENT OF CONTRACT LAW IN SEVENTEENTH-CENTURY ENGLAND Copyright © 1983 by Clinton W. Francis.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE STRUCTURE OF JUDICIAL ADMINISTRATION AND THE DEVELOPMENT OF CONTRACT LAW IN SEVENTEENTH-CENTURY ENGLAND Copyright © 1983 by Clinton W. Francis.

shared_topics.topic: how the availability and structure of contract remedies (specific performance vs damages vs bonds) shape party incentives and opportunistic behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the relative availability of specific performance and undercompensatory damages incentivizes promisees to induce performance via modifications and then contest those modifications, while Paper B examines seventeenth-century practices (bonds, sums certain, limits on damages) showing how remedy design directed litigant behavior and the enforcement of contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of judicial-administrative constraints on substantive contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that self-help remedies and modification rules must be integrated with the broader remedial system and are affected by limitations in judicial administration, and Paper B documents how the courts' administrative needs and controlled-delegation produced substantive contract rules (e.g., law of conditions) to manage caseloads.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between doctrinal formalism and the need for contractual flexibility in preventing opportunism
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques formalistic modification theories and seeks a doctrine that permits adjustment while policing opportunistic self-help, whereas Paper B shows how the common law's formal procedures (strict conditions, pleading rules) traded off flexibility for administrability and thereby influenced opportunities for exploitation.

shared_topics.topic: the inadequacy of damages as a remedial default and institutional responses to secure performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that substitutionary damages often fail to compensate promisees and thus drive strategic modification/self-help, while Paper B highlights historical mechanisms (contract bonds, liquidated sums, procedural limitations) that courts promoted to substitute for or limit ad hoc damages assessments and secure performance.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 118wvalrev369!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT REMEDIES IN ACTION: SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT REMEDIES IN ACTION: SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between money damages being undercompensatory and parties' incentives to seek or manipulate specific performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that undercompensatory expectation damages create incentives for promisees to induce performance via contract modification and then contest the modification (a form of promisee opportunism); Paper B empirically documents that expectation damages are often undercompensatory and explores how that fact shapes parties' (sometimes counterintuitive) choices between suing for specific performance or for money.

shared_topics.topic: practical enforcement and implementation problems of specific performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that specific performance is often unavailable or undesirable in judicial enforcement and that self-help uses of specific performance must be assessed against the remedial system; Paper B provides qualitative evidence of real-world enforcement difficulties—especially in unique-goods cases—highlighting lack of clear quality standards, need for good will, and obstacles to execution.

shared_topics.topic: strategic, opportunistic, and instrumental uses of remedy choices, including renegotiation dynamics
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes promisee opportunism via modification (using the threat or promise of performance strategically) and argues doctrine must police such behavior; Paper B shows through interviews that parties and lawyers treat remedy choices instrumentally (e.g., bargaining leverage, signaling to courts), that attorneys' incentives affect remedy selection, and that post-judgment renegotiation is often avoided or constrained by litigation dynamics.

shared_topics.topic: normative and doctrinal implications for limiting or shaping the scope of specific performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues self-help specific performance should be limited to contexts where specific performance would be appropriate in court and integrated into the overall remedial framework; Paper B critiques the prevailing doctrinal focus (e.g., limiting specific performance to unique goods), arguing empirical enforcement realities and behavioral factors should inform doctrinal reform and policy debates.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 117yalelj2!!ARTICLE: Contracting for Cooperation in Recovery
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contracting for Cooperation in Recovery

shared_topics.topic: incentives and opportunistic behavior in contractual performance and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how parties exploit gaps in the remedial system—Paper A considers promisors who benefit from obstructing discovery and recovery (e.g., false certificates) while Paper B focuses on promisees who use modifications to obtain performance and then contest obligations—treating opportunism as central to how contracts are actually enforced.

shared_topics.topic: the inadequacy of compensatory damages and the need for extracompensatory or alternative remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that compensatory damages often cannot deter or remedy obstructive breaches and thus supports extracompensatory remedies (penalties, punitive damages, fraud liability) for no-obstruct duties; Paper B likewise emphasizes that the damage remedy can be undercompensatory, producing pressure for a self-help specific performance remedy and requiring doctrinal adjustment.

shared_topics.topic: the role of nonstandard remedies (equitable, tort, or punitive remedies) in contract law and the doctrinal boundary between remedial regimes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines invoking tort/fraud and punitive remedies to enforce contract duties to cooperate, and critiques courts' attempts to exclude such incursions (economic loss rule); Paper B examines the place of specific performance (an equitable remedy) relative to the default substitutional damages regime and argues for integrating or limiting self-help equitable relief within contract doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: normative doctrinal reform to police opportunism and better align enforcement with contracting parties' needs
shared_topics.justification: Both articles propose changes to doctrine—Paper A proposes exceptions to rules against penalties or recognition of fraud-based extracompensatory remedies to make cooperation clauses effective, while Paper B proposes limiting or defining the permissible scope of a self-help specific performance remedy so modification doctrine does not enable promisee opportunism.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 84nclrev1841!!ARTICLE: A BRIDGE, A TAX REVOLT, AND THE STRUGGLE TO INDUSTRIALIZE: THE STORY AND LEGACY OF ROCKINGHAM COUNTY v. LUTEN BRIDGE CO.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A BRIDGE, A TAX REVOLT, AND THE STRUGGLE TO INDUSTRIALIZE: THE STORY AND LEGACY OF ROCKINGHAM COUNTY v. LUTEN BRIDGE CO.

shared_topics.topic: how inadequacy of monetary damages versus specific performance shapes parties' incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that undercompensatory damage rules encourage promisees to induce performance through modification and then contest the modification (a ‘self-help specific performance’ problem), and Paper B centers on Rockingham County v. Luten Bridge Co. as a canonical disputes about damage remedies—particularly the duty to mitigate—and how the choice/limits of monetary relief governs contracting behavior.

shared_topics.topic: judicial decisions and doctrinal development as drivers of contract-remedy rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes modern doctrinal shifts and codification efforts that reframe modification and remedy rules, while Paper B historicizes a single influential judicial opinion (Luten Bridge) to show how a court decision shaped teaching and practice around mitigation and damages.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal limits on opportunistic recovery and the allocation of risk after breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is centrally concerned with policing promisee opportunism and integrating self-help remedies into the remedial scheme to prevent unjust enrichment, and Paper B examines the duty to mitigate and the court's refusal to compensate for avoidable performance as a doctrinal mechanism to prevent improvident or opportunistic recoveries.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between remedial doctrine and broader economic or administrative realities
shared_topics.justification: Paper A notes that limits in judicial administration and commercial realities affect whether specific performance or damages are appropriate and influence modification behavior, and Paper B situates the mitigation/damages dispute within the economic and political context of industrialization and local government finance, showing how social conditions shape remedial controversies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1501!!ARTICLE: WHEN IS A WILLFUL BREACH "WILLFUL"? THE LINK BETWEEN DEFINITIONS AND DAMAGES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: WHEN IS A WILLFUL BREACH "WILLFUL"? THE LINK BETWEEN DEFINITIONS AND DAMAGES

shared_topics.topic: how remedial choices (damages vs specific performance) shape parties' opportunistic behavior and breach incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A connects the availability and magnitude of damages to whether courts should treat certain breaches as 'willful' and thus justify higher awards, while Paper B analyzes how the prospect of specific performance (or its absence) creates incentives for promisees or promisors to seek opportunistic modifications or self-help remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the role of doctrinal definitions/labels in determining remedial consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that labels like 'willful' lack a clear definition yet drive higher damages outcomes, and Paper B shows that how modification doctrine is defined (and characterized) determines whether parties can secure de facto specific performance or exploit the contract, meaning doctrinal language directly affects remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the problem of undercompensation of damages as a driver of strategic behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links the decision to treat breaches as especially culpable (and increase damages) to the inadequacy of ordinary damage rules in some contexts, while Paper B demonstrates that undercompensatory damage remedies motivate promisees to induce performance via modification and then litigate to capture more than damages would have provided.

shared_topics.topic: judicial fact‑finding and administrative limits as constraints on doctrinal design

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: WHY BREACH OF CONTRACT MAY NOT BE IMMORAL GIVEN THE INCOMPLETENESS OF CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: the consequences of contractual incompleteness / need for flexibility in adjusting terms to unforeseen contingencies

shared_topics.topic: how the remedial structure (damages vs specific performance) shapes parties' incentives and justifies or condemns conduct
shared_topics.justification: Paper A notes that law commonly permits breach by allowing damages and uses that gap between moral intuitions and legal remedies to frame its argument; Paper B develops this theme in detail, arguing that undercompensatory damages and the unavailability of specific performance create incentives for both promisors and promisees to engage in opportunistic modifications.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate relationship between moral/promissory norms and legal doctrine in judging contractual behavior

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: YOU DO HAVE TO KEEP YOUR PROMISES: A DISGORGEMENT THEORY OF CONTRACT REMEDIES

shared_topics.topic: how remedial rules shape parties' incentives to perform or breach
shared_topics.justification: Both works treat remedy rules as determinant of contracting behavior: Paper A emphasizes that awarding damages effectively gives promisors an option to breach, and Paper B analyzes how that 'choice' (and inadequacy of damages) leads promisors and promisees to pursue strategic modifications or self-help enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: the need for coherence between individual self-help measures and the broader remedial system

shared_topics.justification: Paper A tests whether stronger parties use penalty clauses to extract advantage and whether legal activism breeds remedial opportunism, while Paper B theorizes and demonstrates promisee opportunism (self-help specific performance) that arises when parties can extract more than their contractual entitlement via modification.

shared_topics.topic: how judicial doctrine and enforcement shape contracting practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents high judicial tolerance for penalties in Russia and links firms' use of penalties to legal activism and the local legal environment; Paper B focuses on doctrinal rules (availability of specific performance, limits of damages, and judicial administration) and argues these rules determine whether self-help modifications will be opportunistically available.

shared_topics.topic: norms and legitimacy of breach as a determinant of remedial design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates whether efficient breach is regarded as legitimate in Russian contracting and how that norm correlates with penalty use, whereas Paper B questions whether remedial doctrine (preferring substitutional damages over specific performance) coheres with the normative goals of allowing or deterring breaches and modifications.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DOES FAILURE TO MITIGATE DAMAGES BAR RECOVERY OF THE COSTS OF MITIGATION?

shared_topics.topic: how remedial rules create strategic or opportunistic behavior by contracting parties

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts must allow contractual flexibility while policing opportunism and calibrate when self-help specific performance is justified, and Paper B advances a policy choice (net vs. gross offset) designed to fairly compensate victims while preserving efficient incentives to mitigate.

shared_topics.topic: interaction of remedy rules with broader statutory and doctrinal frameworks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends that self-help remedies must be integrated into the general architecture of contract remedial law, and Paper B explicitly examines how recoverability of mitigation costs interacts with U.C.C. Article 2, the Restatement (Second) of Contracts, and prejudgment interest statutes.

shared_topics.topic: opportunistic behavior by contracting parties exploiting procedural or remedial gaps

shared_topics.topic: the role of institutional choice (courts vs administrative adjudication) in shaping enforcement outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes limitations in judicial administration and how those limits affect the availability and desirability of specific performance, while Paper B focuses on administrative adjudication as the forum for enforcing qualifying facility contracts, so both interrogate how the chosen enforcement forum and its procedures influence contractual rights and remedies.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial limits, judicial constraints, and legal ambiguity affect contracting choices
