papers.node_id: 117michlrev885!!ARTICLE: Moral Diversity and Efficient Breach
papers.title: ARTICLE: Moral Diversity and Efficient Breach
papers.abstract:
Individuals and firms have sharply different moral views about whether it is permissible to breach a contract. Most people think it is wrong to breach even if it is in their economic interest to do so.Contracts, in the eyes ofmany, are promises. When you enter a contract, people believe, you make a promise to perform.And because people also tend to think that breaking a promise is wrong,they think they are subject to a corresponding moral obligation to perform the contract.As a result, contracting parties who hold this view will perform their express obligations under a contract even if they would be better off economically by breaching and paying damages to their counterparty.
But firms often don't hold that view. Instead, they typically view a contract simply as a legal obligation to perform, the violation of which is not a moral wrong to be avoided but rather a legal contingency to be navigated.Justice Holmes famously claimed that "[t]he duty to keep a contract at common law means a prediction that you must pay damages if you do not keep it,-- and nothing else."According to the view associated with Holmes,law provides the remedy for breach of contract through expectation damages, and submitting to that remedy exhausts both the moral and legal liability of a breacher. For a Holmesian firm, then, there is no further moral obligation to perform rather than to breach and pay damages.As a result, the Holmesian firm will breach and pay damages whenever it is in its interest to do so.
This asymmetry in moral belief has profound practical consequences. Consider the aftermath of the housing crisis in 2008. Mortgage contracts require monthly payments of the principal and interest that, over the life of the loan, amount to much more than the original loan amount. After housing prices plummeted in 2008, millions of homeowners owed more on their mortgages than their houses were worth.Their mortgage contracts were "underwater," and it would have been financially beneficial for many of them to breach those contracts. This was particularly true because many of the contracts were from nontraditional loans, which had become popular before the crisis.Those loans often included balloon payments, teaser interest rates that increased dramatically after an introductory period, and other features that made those loans especially costly after the first several years of the loan term.Underwater homeowners thus faced a choice between continuing to make rapidly escalating monthly payments and breaching their mortgage contract. The primary consequence of breach is that the borrower must turn over the house that served as collateral for the loan.When the house is worth less than the balance of the mortgage, and thus worth much less than the homeowner would ultimately have to pay over the life of a nontraditional loan because of interest, the homeowner often best serves her financial interests by breaching the mortgage contract and turning over the house.
Yet hundreds of thousands--or more--of underwater homeowners refused to breach their mortgage contracts. The numbers are staggering. Research by the Federal Reserve indicates that only about 5% of households with negative equity (that is, with underwater mortgages) who could affordto make their monthly paymentschose to default on their mortgages.If a million homeowners could have saved $ 100,000 each by walking away from their underwater mortgages, in aggregate their choices not to do so cost them $ 100 billion. Homeowners incurred that astounding cost--to the direct benefit of large financial institutions--in large part because of their perceived moral obligation to make good on the promise they made to pay their mortgage.Those same large financial institutions, by contrast, breached their own contractual obligations--both to the homeowners who were going underwater and to the investors to whom they sold securitized mortgages.
This Article thus examines a question the literature has neither recognized nor addressed: how the law and regulation of contracts should account for the fact that legal actors are guided by differing views about the moral permissibility of breach. The Article proceeds in four Parts. Part I situates the phenomenon of moral diversity within the philosophical and economic debate about the morality of breach. It shows that the debate revolves around a disagreement about the moral scope of the promise generated by a facially unqualified contract--that is, a contract that states a primary obligation to perform without providing an explicit alternative like a liquidated-damages clause. Some theorists view such contracts to give rise to categorical promises, but others take those contracts to give rise only to promises-in-the-alternative to perform or pay. That disagreement about the moral scope of a promise, in turn, mirrors the moral diversity among contracting parties: individuals, but not firms, think that a contract generates a promise to perform, not a promise to perform or pay.
Part II presents recent empirical research revealing the asymmetry in moral belief among different types of parties regarding the moral permissibility of breach. Section II.A presents the experimental evidence supporting the conclusion that individual actors tend to view breach as immoral. It extracts from that research two further important conclusions: first, that even among individuals there is substantial heterogeneity in moral belief about breach; and second, that individuals tend to determine the moral scope of their contractual promise by reference to the express terms of the contract. Section II.B presents the evidence that sophisticated parties like commercial firms tend to view a contract as generating alternative options to perform orto pay. It presents both the experimental evidence on the breaching beliefs and behavior of sophisticated commercial actors and the theoretical considerations that have led many scholars to conclude that such commercial actors tend to behave as Holmesians.
Part III argues that this asymmetry is normatively problematic. This Part addresses two normative frameworks: economic efficiency, and fairness and distribution. Section III.A argues that the existing legal framework, in conjunction with individuals' moral beliefs, results in those individuals forgoing efficient breaches. That legal framework thus leads to outcomes that are not Pareto optimal and fails to maximize social welfare. Section III.A then considers and rejects the counterargument that some of the forgone breaches would have been opportunistic but not efficient. Section III.B argues that the existing legal framework is distributionally unfair because it facilitates sophisticated commercial actors to systematically exercise economically advantageous legal options that individuals with different moral beliefs would view as morally foreclosed. The distributional consequences are problematic both vertically, between moralist individuals and Holmesian sophisticated commercial actors, and horizontally, between individuals who will breach and those who refuse to breach on moral grounds. The Part then considers and largely rejects the objection that the market will eliminate the distributional disadvantage for the moralist by pricing contracts between firms and individuals to account for individuals' propensity not to breach on moral grounds.
Part IV proposes a novel solution to the problem of moral diversity about breach based on the conceptual framework of choice architecture and demonstrates the solution's viability using empirical data from two new studies I performed. Sections IV.A and IV.B consider the traditional tools the law might use to address the asymmetry: reducing expectation damages to induce individual moralists to breach, adopting specific performance as remedy for breach to require sophisticated Holmesians to perform, and providing disclosure requirements to inform individuals of their legal rights. The Sections show how these tools would be ineffective to address moral diversity and efficient breach. Section IV.C then presents a proposal based on the conceptual framework of choice architecture. My proposal requires contracts to include an exit clause that creates a contractual option not to perform and to pay instead. Because individuals judge the scope of the promise arising from a contract based on the contract's express terms, this proposal would alter the substance of individual moralists' perceived moral obligation to align with the view of sophisticated Holmesians. Finally, this Part presents the results of two new experimental studies I performed that demonstrate the impact of exit clauses. The first study indicates that individuals are more willing to exercise an exit clause than they are to breach a contract with a liquidated-damages clause or a facially unqualified contract with neither an exit clause nor a liquidated-damages clause. The second study indicates that individuals are also more willing to exercise an exit option in a mortgage than they are to default on a mortgage without an exit clause. Indeed, the data indicates that millions more homeowners with underwater mortgagesmight have strategically breached during the housing crisis if mortgage contracts contained exit clauses. These empirical results suggest that a mandatory exit clause could be an effective solution to the problem of moral diversity about breach in a wide range of contractual contexts.

questions.question: Does moral heterogeneity between individual contracting parties and firms - specifically that many individuals view breach as a moral wrong while firms view breach as an economically permissible option - cause individuals to forgo efficient breaches and produce welfare-reducing and distributionally unfair outcomes under current contract regimes?

Can requiring an explicit contractual exit option (an express term that permits nonperformance in exchange for a specified payment) change individuals' moral judgments and increase their willingness to exercise efficient breaches, thereby increasing overall efficiency and reducing distributional bias?

Do contracting parties determine the moral scope of their obligation by reference to the express terms of the contract, and does that process systematically differ between individual (non-sophisticated) actors and sophisticated commercial actors?

matched_themes: Do pre-agreed breach-payment clauses (liquidated damages) change parties' beliefs about norms and moral aversion to breach, and do such clauses increase or decrease the willingness to breach?
How should default liability rules interact with parties' freedom to allocate risks by contract and duties of disclosure to achieve efficient and fair risk allocation?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?
Should the promisor or the promisee have the default right to choose between performance and payment to achieve allocative efficiency?
Should parties be presumptively permitted to contractually specify nonstandard damage remedies, or should courts retain authority to impose defaults?
Does making in-kind performance the legal default (rather than monetary compensation) change parties' enforcement choices, moral judgments, and economic efficiency?
Should the availability of legal remedies or contractual incompleteness change the moral assessment of a party who breaches under unanticipated circumstances?

Should remedies and contract law be structured to preserve conditions necessary for moral agency and promissory responsibility, rather than treating promises solely as instruments of economic cooperation?

Can party-designed enforcement mechanisms (pre-agreed penalties, arbitration, bonding, reputational systems) reliably produce efficient breach outcomes without judicial intervention, and when do they fail?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
How should remedial and enforcement rules be structured to achieve efficient behavior when populations include both internalizers and externalizers?
Do behavioral biases and heuristics affect how parties draft, negotiate, and accept pre-agreed breach-payment clauses, and can contract design mitigate those biases?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?

Do repeat players, contract drafting strategies, secrecy about dispute outcomes, and presentation techniques enable stronger parties to extract one-sided terms and undermine the protective aims of contract law?
To what extent should moral blameworthiness and non-economic considerations influence the design and application of contract remedies?
Do laypersons and experienced businesspeople differ in their preference for in-kind remedies versus money damages, and how does business experience shape these preferences?
How do differences in wording, formatting, and contract presentation influence non-drafting parties' post-execution behavior by evoking emotions or exploiting cognitive biases?
When is an indirect remedy (one that induces self-compliance) preferable to a direct remedy that delivers the outcome?
Should courts more readily grant equitable relief to compel performance when monetary damages undercompensate and public interests are implicated?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 118wvalrev369!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT REMEDIES IN ACTION: SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT REMEDIES IN ACTION: SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE

shared_topics.topic: moral status of breach and promise-keeping
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage the question whether breaching a contract is a moral wrong (a failure to keep a promise) or merely a legal contingency: Paper A documents and theorizes moral heterogeneity (individuals as promise‑moralists vs firms as Holmesian), while Paper B situates specific performance within rights-based theories that treat promises as morally salient and shows parties sometimes act on non‑economic, moral considerations.

shared_topics.topic: efficiency versus rights-based justifications for remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both examine the tension between efficiency (expectation damages, bargaining) and rights-based aims (enforcement of the promise): Paper A argues the existing damages regime interacts with moral beliefs to produce inefficiencies and distributional harms, and Paper B compares economic and rights-based theories to show empirical departures from both in parties' remedy choices and bargaining behavior.

shared_topics.topic: how available remedies and contract termsshape parties' choices and signaling
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how the presence or absence of particular contractual mechanisms or remedies affects behavior and perceptions: Paper A proposes modifying contract wording (mandatory exit clauses) to change moral perceptions and induce efficient exit, while Paper B shows that choosing between damages and specific performance sends signals, affects litigant framing, and influences willingness to negotiate.

shared_topics.topic: practical enforceability and implementation limits of non-monetary relief
shared_topics.justification: Both grapple with the real-world difficulties of forcing performance rather than awarding money: Paper A considers and rejects specific performance as an effective means to align moral actors and markets, and Paper B documents empirical implementation problems, measurement standards, and the unwillingness or inability to execute specific performance in practice.

shared_topics.topic: role of institutional actors and incentives (firms, lawyers, courts) in shaping breach/remedy outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Both analyze how institutional incentives change behavior around breach and remedies: Paper A contrasts firm (Holmesian) behavior with individual moralists and discusses market and regulatory responses, while Paper B documents attorneys' fee-driven preferences for damages, courts' inferences from remedy choices, and how these institutional forces affect whether specific performance is pursued or enforced.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2013uilllrev151!!ARTICLE: CAN'T BUY ME LOVE: MONETARY VERSUS IN-KIND REMEDIES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CAN'T BUY ME LOVE: MONETARY VERSUS IN-KIND REMEDIES

shared_topics.topic: contracting parties' preferences and moral beliefs about breach and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both papers present empirical/experimental evidence showing that individuals and firms differ in how they view breaches and remedies: Paper A shows a general preference for in-kind remedies (shared by laypersons and businesspeople), while Paper B documents moral heterogeneity—individuals tend to view breach as morally wrong whereas firms act as Holmesian 'breach-and-pay' actors.

shared_topics.topic: adequacy of monetary (expectation) damages versus in-kind relief
shared_topics.justification: Both engage substantively with whether monetary compensation rightly substitutes for performance: Paper A finds monetary remedies often fail to restore welfare compared with in-kind relief and may be undercompensatory, and Paper B analyzes how the legal reliance on expectation damages interacts with moral commitments and can lead to inefficient or distributionally unfair outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the role and limits of specific performance and other remedy doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Each paper examines specific performance and related remedial doctrines as alternatives to money: Paper A argues courts should more liberally award in-kind relief (specific performance, injunctions), while Paper B evaluates and ultimately rejects simple reliance on specific performance as an effective fix for moral-diversity problems, comparing it to other tools.

shared_topics.topic: how contractual language and default/express terms shape behavior and perceived obligations (liquidated damages, exit clauses)
shared_topics.justification: Both discuss how contract terms alter parties' choices and moral perceptions: Paper A studies ex ante choices among entitlements and the effect of terms on remedy preferences (and cautions re: liquidated-damages clauses), and Paper B shows that express exit clauses or liquidated-damages language change individuals' perceived moral scope and can increase willingness to exercise an option not to perform.

shared_topics.topic: using empirical/experimental methods to inform contract-law policy reforms
shared_topics.justification: Both papers rely on experimental data and translate those findings into normative recommendations for doctrinal or regulatory change—Paper A on awarding remedies and compensatory premiums, and Paper B on choice-architecture reforms like mandatory exit clauses to address moral diversity.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2006michstlrev883!!ARTICLE: PENALTIES AS RATIONAL RESPONSE TO BARGAINING IRRATIONALITY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PENALTIES AS RATIONAL RESPONSE TO BARGAINING IRRATIONALITY

shared_topics.topic: the normative status and practical effects of efficient-breach theory
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage directly with the efficient-breach idea: Paper A critiques the use of efficient-breach reasoning to invalidate liquidated-damage (penalty) clauses and shows its limits, while Paper B documents how moral resistance to breach prevents many individually efficient breaches and analyzes how law should respond to that inefficiency.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of behavioral and psychological factors on contracting and breach decisions
shared_topics.justification: Both articles draw on behavioral insights — Paper A studies heuristics and biases (availability, status-quo, reputational and signaling effects) affecting negotiators, and Paper B documents moral beliefs and psychological heterogeneity about whether breach is morally permissible and how those beliefs shape real-world breach choices.

shared_topics.topic: contract design (choice of clauses) as a tool to align incentives and correct behavioral/moral frictions
shared_topics.justification: Both papers evaluate specific contractual devices as responses to behavioral or moral frictions: Paper A argues for allowing negotiated penalty/liquidated-damages clauses as rational responses to bargaining irrationality, while Paper B proposes and tests an exit clause (contractual option to pay rather than perform) to reconcile moralists' behavior with efficient outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the proper role of legal intervention versus freedom of contract (paternalism vs consent) in structuring remedies and enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Both authors debate whether courts should impose bright-line rules or let parties' choices govern outcomes — Paper A frames the penalty-rule as tension between freedom of contract and systemic paternalism, and Paper B evaluates legal remedies (damages reduction, specific performance, mandatory clauses) and argues for choice-architecture solutions that respect parties' moral views while addressing distributional concerns.

shared_topics.topic: use of empirical/experimental methods to inform contract-law doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Both papers rely on original or recent experimental evidence to support doctrinal recommendations: Paper A reports two surveys testing heuristics in negotiated penalty clauses, and Paper B presents empirical studies (and new experiments) demonstrating moral heterogeneity and the effects of exit clauses on willingness to breach.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 116columlrev2005!!ARTICLE: ECONOMIC ANALYSIS OF CONTRACT LAW FROM THE INTERNAL POINT OF VIEW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ECONOMIC ANALYSIS OF CONTRACT LAW FROM THE INTERNAL POINT OF VIEW

shared_topics.topic: whether contractual obligations are perceived as moral promises versus perform-or-pay legal options
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze the empirical and conceptual distinction between parties who treat contracts as moral promises that oblige performance (internalizers/moralists, often individuals) and parties who treat contracts as legal obligations that can be discharged by paying damages (externalizers/Holmesian firms), and how that difference affects breach decisions.

shared_topics.topic: heterogeneity of parties (individuals vs firms; internalizers vs externalizers) and its behavioral consequences
shared_topics.justification: Both papers emphasize that populations are mixed—some actors internalize legal norms while others respond only to incentives—and explore how that heterogeneity produces systematically different breach behavior and strategic choices in contracting contexts.

shared_topics.topic: normative and efficiency implications of moral diversity for contract law design
shared_topics.justification: Both works consider how moral diversity among contracting parties undermines standard efficiency prescriptions and argue that contract doctrine and regulation should account for differing moral motivations to avoid Pareto-inefficient outcomes and unfair distributions of costs and benefits.

shared_topics.topic: the role of remedial and contractual mechanisms (damages, liquidated/stipulated damages, specific performance, exit clauses) in shaping parties' perceptions and actions
shared_topics.justification: Each paper examines how remedies and contract terms—expectation damages, liquidated/stipulated damages, specific performance, and proposed exit/choice-architecture clauses—can alter what internalizers perceive as their duty and thereby change the incidence of performance versus breach.

shared_topics.topic: crowding out: whether legal rules can undermine or reshape moral motivations to keep promises
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage with the idea that legal norms and doctrines can 'crowd out' moral motives to perform—either by signaling that breach-for-pay is acceptable or by providing interpretive cues—and analyze the implications of that crowding out for legal doctrine and policy.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 13nyujlbus393!!Article: FREEDOM TO MISLEAD: THE FICTITIOUS FREEDOM TO CONTRACT AROUND FRAUD UNDER DELAWARE LAW
compared_to.partner_title: Article: FREEDOM TO MISLEAD: THE FICTITIOUS FREEDOM TO CONTRACT AROUND FRAUD UNDER DELAWARE LAW

shared_topics.topic: treatment of sophisticated commercial parties versus individuals in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes Delaware decisions that give deference to integration/disclaimer clauses where contracting parties are 'sophisticated' and negotiated at arm's length; Paper B empirically and normatively distinguishes firms (Holmesian, sophisticated actors) from individual moralists and shows how that asymmetry affects contracting behavior and legal outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: freedom of contract and the ability to contract around legal liabilities (fraud, breach, or moral obligations)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates whether and when parties may 'contract around' fraud through disclaimers and integration clauses under Delaware law; Paper B examines how contract design (e.g., exit clauses, liquidated damages) can permit or constrain breaches and morally/economically reallocate liability, and evaluates whether such freedom should be constrained.

shared_topics.topic: impact of explicit contractual language on parties' perceived obligations and available remedies (reliance, anti‑reliance, exit clauses)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how anti‑reliance and integration language is said to negate extra‑contractual reliance and bar fraud claims; Paper B shows individuals derive the moral scope of their promise from express terms and that adding exit clauses or specific language changes willingness to perform or accept breach.

shared_topics.topic: use of economic efficiency arguments to justify contract doctrines and their distributive consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques Delaware judges' and commentators' reliance on freedom of contract and efficiency rationales to uphold clauses that allegedly preclude fraud claims; Paper B engages economic-efficiency reasoning about 'efficient breach,' argues existing rules produce Pareto-inefficient and distributively unfair outcomes, and assesses reforms accordingly.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1533!!ARTICLE: FAULT AT THE CONTRACT-TORT INTERFACE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: FAULT AT THE CONTRACT-TORT INTERFACE

shared_topics.topic: the normative role of moral concepts (promising, fault) in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically and normatively examines how parties' moral beliefs about promises affect decisions to breach contracts, while Paper B traces how the concept of fault historically shaped (and was diminished in) contract doctrine; both treat moral or moral-analogous concepts as central to understanding contractual obligations.

shared_topics.topic: Holmesian/strict‑liability conception of contract versus a promise‑based conception and its doctrinal consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts a Holmesian view (contracts as legal contingencies permitting breach-and-pay) with a promise-based moral view and analyzes distributional and efficiency consequences, while Paper B documents the nineteenth‑century shift toward treating contract as operating with reduced relevance of fault (a form of strict liability) and explores the conceptual and practical effects of that shift.

shared_topics.topic: how liability rules and remedies shape private actors' behavior and social welfare
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates how remedies (expectation damages, specific performance, exit clauses) interact with moral beliefs to produce (inefficient) breach behavior and proposes contract design to alter outcomes, whereas Paper B examines how treating fault differently in contract and tort affects liability allocation and the functioning of modern private law, implicating behavioral and welfare consequences.

shared_topics.topic: the boundary between private ordering and public regulation in allocating responsibility
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes regulatory or doctrinal interventions (mandatory exit clauses, disclosure) to reconcile moral diversity among contracting parties, and Paper B critiques the historical conceptualization that aligned the contract–tort boundary with a private ordering vs public regulation divide, so both analyze how legal structures allocate responsibility between private parties and public law.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 53lalrev1257!!ARTICLE: Comparative Ruminations on the Foreseeability of Damages in Contract Law. Dedicated to Professor Jurgen Basedow, Augsburg University, School of Law.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Comparative Ruminations on the Foreseeability of Damages in Contract Law. Dedicated to Professor Jurgen Basedow, Augsburg University, School of Law.

shared_topics.topic: limitations on recoverable contract damages (foreseeability, contemplation, and expectation damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the ‘foreseeability’/‘contemplation’ limitation on recoverable contract damages (including Hadley v. Baxendale and its French-law origins), while Paper B analyzes how the law’s default remedy of expectation damages (and limits on recovery) shapes parties' breach decisions and distributive outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of parties' expectations and contract wording at formation on liability and obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on what losses were foreseeable or in the parties' contemplation at contract formation as the basis for liability, and Paper B shows empirically that individuals determine the moral scope of their contractual promise by reference to the contract's express terms and proposes modifying those terms (exit clauses) to change behavior.

shared_topics.topic: comparison and policy evaluation of remedies for breach (damages vs specific performance vs contractual alternatives)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts civil-law and common-law rules governing damages and related remedies (including differing rules on delay interest and compensation), and Paper B evaluates remedy choices—expectation damages, specific performance, liquidated-damages clauses—and proposes an institutional change (mandatory exit clauses) as a policy response.

shared_topics.topic: foundational justifications for contractual liability (legal doctrine history versus moral theory of promises)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the historical/legal origins and doctrinal justification for distinctions and rules in contract liability across legal systems, while Paper B engages with the philosophical debate about whether contracts generate categorical promises or merely legal-predictive obligations and the practical implications of that disagreement.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45umemlrev59!!Article: Justice and Harsh Results: Beyond Individualism and Collectivism in Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Justice and Harsh Results: Beyond Individualism and Collectivism in Contracts

shared_topics.topic: moral foundations of contractual promises and obligations
shared_topics.justification: Both papers centrally analyze why promises generate moral duties: Paper A surveys and critiques individualist and collectivist accounts and advances a Thomist account of promissory obligation, while Paper B interrogates whether ordinary contracts create categorical promises or ‘perform-or-pay’ promises and documents how those conceptions drive actors' moral judgments about breach.

shared_topics.topic: enforcement of formal contractual terms versus fairness-focused discretion
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the question whether courts should rigidly enforce contract terms or temper enforcement for substantive fairness: Paper A debates strict enforcement in Jacob & Youngs and argues for a Thomist balance that vindicates promise-keeping while ensuring fairness, and Paper B examines how the existing remedy structure (expectation damages, specific performance) produces inefficient and distributionally unfair outcomes and evaluates alternative remedial rules.

shared_topics.topic: the role of parties' moral beliefs and voluntariness in shaping contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Both inquire how the will and moral views of contracting parties should affect legal treatment of contracts: Paper A criticizes simplistic appeals to party autonomy or social values and proposes an account that respects voluntary commitments while demanding substantive fairness; Paper B documents moral heterogeneity (individual moralists vs Holmesian firms) and argues contract law should be designed to account for those differing beliefs.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal or regulatory reforms to correct inefficiency and unfairness in contract outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Both propose normative and doctrinal interventions grounded in theory and facts: Paper A applies its Thomist framework to re-characterize Jacob & Youngs and correct errors in precedent, while Paper B empirically proposes mandatory exit clauses and choice-architecture reforms to align moral perceptions, increase efficient breaches, and mitigate distributional harms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68valrev947!!ARTICLE: EFFICIENT BREACH OF CONTRACT: CIRCLES IN THE SKY Copyright (c) 1982 by Ian R. Macneil.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EFFICIENT BREACH OF CONTRACT: CIRCLES IN THE SKY Copyright (c) 1982 by Ian R. Macneil.

shared_topics.topic: normative critique of the 'efficient breach' doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Both papers interrogate whether the standard economic defense of breach (breach when breach gains exceed promisee losses) is normatively defensible: Paper A exposes a fallacy in the simple-efficient-breach analysis and argues the rule must be restated, while Paper B shows that moral heterogeneity and distributional concerns mean the law's current treatment of breach produces welfare and fairness problems that the doctrine overlooks.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy of remedies—expectation damages versus specific performance
shared_topics.justification: Both engage substantively with how courts should remediate breach: Paper A focuses on the specific performance versus damages choice and how that affects the efficiency argument, and Paper B analyzes expectation-damages reduction and specific performance as traditional tools (finding them ineffective in practice) before proposing alternative contractual design solutions.

shared_topics.topic: moral/promise theory versus legal/Holmesian conceptions of contract
shared_topics.justification: Both papers contrast moral views of contracts as categorical promises (pacta sunt servanda) with instrumental legal views that treat contracts as entitling parties to choose performance or pay damages; Paper A highlights the moral tension with efficient breach, and Paper B develops and empirically documents the divergence between individuals' promise-based morality and firms' Holmesian stance.

shared_topics.topic: limits of the simple-efficiency model due to real-world frictions (transaction costs, behavioral heterogeneity, market failures)
shared_topics.justification: Both criticize treating efficient breach in a frictionless model: Paper A distinguishes and rejects the 'simple' frictionless efficient-breach analysis (emphasizing transaction costs and other real-world considerations), and Paper B documents behavioral heterogeneity and market/pricing failures (e.g., mortgage defaults) that prevent the simple-efficiency outcome from obtaining in practice.

compared_to.partner_title: LAW AND LITERATURE SYMPOSIUM: "SOME SORT OF CHRONICLER I AM": NARRATION AND THE POETRY OF LAWRENCE JOSEPH: ARTICLE: RESTITUTIONARY DISGORGEMENT AS A MORAL COMPASS FOR BREACH OF CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: conflict between the efficient-breach (choice) model and a moral obligation to keep promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how Restatement (Third) §39's disgorgement remedy departs from Holmesian/efficient-breach assumptions by importing moral condemnation and incentives to keep promises, while Paper B documents that many individuals view contracts as moral promises and shows how that moral belief produces departures from the efficient-breach outcome.

shared_topics.topic: design of remedies for breach (disgorgement, expectation damages, specific performance, exit clauses) and their incentive/fairness effects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on restitutionary disgorgement for 'opportunistic' breaches and its potential to reallocate profits away from breachers, whereas Paper B critically examines expectation damages and specific performance and proposes mandatory exit clauses as an alternative contractual mechanism to align incentives and address distributional concerns.

shared_topics.topic: role of the breacher's moral state or mens rea (conscious advantage-taking/opportunism) in allocating legal remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers §39's requirement to assess deliberate, opportunistic conduct (mens rea) to justify disgorgement, and Paper B empirically contrasts actor types (individual moralists vs Holmesian firms) to show how differing moral beliefs about breach should affect legal response and remedy design.

shared_topics.topic: legal or doctrinal interventions (restatements, contract terms, choice architecture) to reshape contracting behavior and address moral diversity or opportunism
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates the Restatement's new doctrine as a formal legal intervention likely to change contract-law norms and behavior, while Paper B proposes and tests contract-drafting reforms (mandatory exit clauses) and evaluates legal tools as choice architecture to harmonize moral diversity and produce more efficient or fair outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1997detclrev993!!ARTICLE: Capping Market Damages at Lost Profit: An Unwarranted Limitation on a Middleman's Expectancy Interest
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Capping Market Damages at Lost Profit: An Unwarranted Limitation on a Middleman's Expectancy Interest

shared_topics.topic: the normative aim and proper measure of expectation damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses expectation damages as the legal remedy that supposedly substitutes for performance (and how firms view damages as exhausting liability), while Paper B directly debates whether market-price damages or lost-profit measures better fulfill the normative goal of placing the nonbreaching party in the position of full performance.

shared_topics.topic: how damage rules shape incentives to breach (the efficient-breach question)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the efficient-breach doctrine—how expectation damages enable Holmesian firms to breach when profitable and how individuals' moral views prevent efficient breaches—and Paper B analyzes how different damage measures (market damages vs lost profits and the availability of cover) change actors' incentives and whether those rules lead to efficient or distorted outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: distributional consequences of remedial doctrines across types of contracting parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how the current remedial regime advantages sophisticated commercial actors relative to morally-constrained individuals, producing vertical and horizontal unfairness, while Paper B highlights a distributional conflict between producers and middlemen when market damages can produce windfalls to intermediaries that exceed their actual lost profits.

shared_topics.topic: the role of contract terms, statutory provisions, and choice architecture in determining remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates how contract drafting (exit clauses, liquidated-damages clauses, specific-performance terms) and choice-architecture solutions can alter perceived obligations and breach behavior, and Paper B scrutinizes how UCC provisions (e.g., sections 2-713 and 1-106) and their interaction determine which remedial measure governs and thus what remedies contracting parties can expect.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 42ambuslj97!!ARTICLE: Cry Me a River: Recovery of Mental Distress Damages in a Breach of Contract Action--A North American Perspective
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Cry Me a River: Recovery of Mental Distress Damages in a Breach of Contract Action--A North American Perspective

shared_topics.topic: the moral or normative significance of contractual promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes whether ordinary contracts generate categorical moral promises (explaining individuals often treat contracts as moral commitments) while Paper B interrogates judicial assumptions about whether contracts are meant to secure non‑economic goods like "emotional tranquility," urging courts to ask what the contract actually promised.

shared_topics.topic: how legal remedies shape behavior and justice in contract breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates how expectation damages versus specific performance and mandatory exit clauses affect breach decisions, efficiency, and distributional fairness; Paper B critiques the limited availability of non‑pecuniary (mental distress, punitive/aggravated) damages and how remedial doctrines influence who is compensated and how courts respond to breach.

shared_topics.topic: the importance of express contract terms in delimiting obligations and recoverable harms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A presents empirical evidence that individuals infer the moral scope of their obligation from express terms and proposes mandated exit clauses to alter perceived duties, while Paper B recommends determining recoverability of intangible loss by focusing on the contract's nature and what it expressly promised.

shared_topics.topic: the problem of 'nontraditional' contracts and doctrinal exceptions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how nontraditional loan terms (balloon payments, teaser rates, etc.) and clause types (liquidated damages vs exit clauses) change actors' choices and moral judgments, whereas Paper B examines how courts carve out special categories or exceptions for certain contracts to allow mental distress damages and criticizes the instability of that exception‑based approach.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A UNIFYING THEORY OF CONTRACT DAMAGE RULES

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy of expectation/lost-surplus damages as the primary remedy for breach
shared_topics.justification: Both papers centrally engage the remedial goal of contract law to compensate injured parties — Paper A critiques how expectation-damages regimes interact with parties' moral beliefs and can fail to produce desirable behavior, while Paper B reconceptualizes damages as a single surplus-based (lost-surplus) rule that formalizes and justifies the expectation/compensation objective across contexts.

shared_topics.topic: efficient breach and economic cost–benefit analysis as a justification for remedy rules
shared_topics.justification: Both works treat efficiency as a core lens for evaluating remedies — Paper A focuses on how moral heterogeneity prevents efficient breaches and argues for contract design to enable Pareto-improving breaches, whereas Paper B grounds its Shadow Code in an economic surplus comparison that balances costs and benefits of performance versus breach.

shared_topics.topic: the design and computation of damages and doctrinal limits (mitigation, foreseeability, consequential and incidental losses, liquidated damages)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage substantively with how damages are calculated and constrained: Paper B systematizes and clarifies computational formulas and doctrinal limits (mitigation, foreseeability, exclusions of subjective losses), while Paper A evaluates existing doctrinal tools (expectation damages, liquidated-damages clauses, specific performance) as mechanisms that shape parties' incentives and moral judgments.

shared_topics.topic: how remedy and contract-term architecture shape party behavior and distributional outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Both articles examine how legal design choices change behavior and allocation: Paper A empirically and normatively analyzes how different remedy regimes and contract clauses (e.g., exit clauses, liquidated damages, specific performance) alter individuals' propensity to breach and create distributional effects between firms and consumers, while Paper B argues that clearer, unified remedy rules will better align incentives and avoid inconsistent outcomes across types of parties and transactions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 69tennlrev837!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT DAMAGES IN TENNESSEE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT DAMAGES IN TENNESSEE

shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers expectation damages as the legal mechanism that renders breach an economically navigable option for firms (the 'Holmesian' view) and examines how that remedy interacts with moral beliefs; Paper B is devoted to how expectation (benefit-of-the-bargain) damages are calculated in Tennessee and treats them as the primary tool for compensating non-breaching parties.

shared_topics.topic: how remedies influence parties' incentives and the efficiency of breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the existing remedial regime (especially damages) combined with moral heterogeneity leads individuals to forgo efficient breaches and produces distributional consequences; Paper B emphasizes that damages rules (and their adequacy) determine whether cases are pursued and seeks to align awards with the goal of placing the non-breaching party in the position of performance, thereby affecting incentives.

shared_topics.topic: legal constraints and limits on recoverable damages (foreseeability, certainty, avoidability) and their normative consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers whether altering damages (e.g., reducing expectation damages) would change behavior and rejects some such fixes; Paper B gives detailed treatment to how Tennessee courts apply foreseeability, certainty, and non-avoidability to limit recoveries and discusses the impact of those limits on compensation.

shared_topics.topic: comparative assessment of remedies and alternative measures (expectation vs specific performance, reliance, restitution, or other methods)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates specific performance, liquidated damages, and proposes a contractual exit clause as an alternative choice-architecture solution to align moral beliefs and outcomes; Paper B discusses alternative methods of determining damages (beyond the benefit-of-the-bargain) and UCC-specific rules as different remedial approaches to achieve fair compensation.

compared_to.partner_title: Article: FREEDOM TO MISLEAD: THE FICTITIOUS FREEDOM TO CONTRACT AROUND FRAUD UNDER DELAWARE LAW

shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically and doctrinally contrasts how firms (Holmesian actors) and individual moralists differ in views and behavior regarding breach, while Paper B focuses on how courts treat 'sophisticated' commercial parties when enforcing integration/disclaimer clauses and evaluating fraud claims.

shared_topics.topic: tension between freedom of contract and protective doctrines (efficiency vs fairness)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the existing legal framework enabling expectation damages and breach options produces efficiency and distributional concerns between moralist individuals and firms, and Paper B critiques Delaware decisions that uphold contractual disclaimers on the ground of freedom/efficiency versus the need to protect parties from fraudulent inducement.

shared_topics.topic: how express contractual language shapes obligations, remedies, and parties' perceptions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that individuals infer the moral scope of promises from express contract terms and proposes mandatory exit clauses to change behavior, while Paper B examines the legal force of integration/anti-reliance and disclaimer clauses in determining whether extra-contractual representations can be the basis for fraud claims.

shared_topics.topic: judicial doctrines and their real-world effects on bargaining outcomes and reliance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates how current remedies (expectation damages, specific performance, liquidated damages) and possible choice-architecture reforms affect breach decisions and welfare, whereas Paper B evaluates Delaware jurisprudence on disclaimers and whether courts' interpretations realistically permit contracting around fraud or instead protect reliance.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 55syracuselrev495!!ARTICLE: A UNIFYING THEORY OF CONTRACT DAMAGE RULES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A UNIFYING THEORY OF CONTRACT DAMAGE RULES

shared_topics.topic: the role and formulation of damages remedies (expectation damages and alternatives)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a single surplus-based rule that subsumes and operationalizes expectation and reliance measures for calculating contract damages; Paper B centrally analyzes expectation damages as the default legal remedy, contrasts them with alternatives (specific performance, liquidated-damages clauses), and evaluates their normative consequences.

shared_topics.topic: damages, incentives, and the economic efficiency of breach decisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames damages as restoring the injured party's lost surplus—explicitly linking remedies to the costs/benefits that drive perform-or-breach decisions; Paper B studies how the existing remedial regime (and moral beliefs about breach) affects parties' incentives and can prevent economically efficient breaches, proposing institutional fixes to improve welfare.

shared_topics.topic: how contract terms and doctrinal language shape parties' behavior and perceived obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques inconsistent doctrinal terminology (e.g., incidental vs. consequential damages, lost profit) and argues that clearer rules better predict outcomes and incentives; Paper B shows that contracting parties (especially individuals) derive their moral obligations from express contract terms and demonstrates that clause design (e.g., exit clauses, liquidated-damages clauses) materially changes breach behavior.

shared_topics.topic: the need for legal or doctrinal reform to address shortcomings in current remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for a reformed, unified 'Shadow Code' to resolve ambiguities and simplify damages computation across the U.C.C. and Restatement; Paper B proposes a choice-architecture reform (mandatory exit clauses) because existing remedies and doctrines fail to account for moral diversity and produce unfair or inefficient outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 97marqlrev695!!ARTICLE: SHAME, REGRET, AND CONTRACT DESIGN
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SHAME, REGRET, AND CONTRACT DESIGN

shared_topics.topic: how contract wording and formal features shape parties' ex post decisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how formatting, framing, and specific clauses (e.g., reliance language, bold disclosures, arbitration provisions) are used to induce emotions or heuristics that alter post‑formation behavior; Paper B shows that explicit contractual terms (exit clauses, liquidated‑damages language, or facially unqualified promises) change whether individuals view breach as morally permissible and thus whether they will perform or pay.

shared_topics.topic: the role of moral beliefs and emotions in whether contracting parties perform or breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on inducing shame, guilt, and the perception of promises as moral duties to suppress challenges or breaches; Paper B documents moral diversity (individuals as promise‑minded vs. firms as Holmesian) and demonstrates that moral views drive large numbers of people to forgo economically efficient breaches.

shared_topics.topic: asymmetry between sophisticated repeat players (contract drafters/firms) and individual/non‑drafting parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that repeat contract preparers can design contracts to exploit cognitive biases and social norms to the detriment of individual non‑drafters; Paper B emphasizes that firms typically adopt a Holmesian view while individuals hold moralist views, producing systematic distributional and welfare consequences.

shared_topics.topic: law and policy responses to behavioral effects of contract design (choice architecture of contracts)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the normative implications and the need for scrutiny of contractual features that manipulate post‑formation behavior and social norms; Paper B proposes a choice‑architecture remedy (mandatory exit clauses) and evaluates other legal tools (damages, specific performance, disclosure) to address moral diversity and inefficient breach.

JOHN BARTLETT, BARTLETT'S FAMILIAR QUOTATIONS 447 (Geoffrey O'Brien ed., 18th ed. 2012) (quoting President Abraham Lincoln, Second Inaugural Address (March 4, 1865)). --DEFINING NONDISCHARGEABILITY OF DEBTS FOR WILLFUL AND MALICIOUS INJURY UNDER SECTION 523(A)(6) OF THE BANKRUPTCY CODE

shared_topics.topic: whether a contractual breach can (or should) give rise to heightened non‑compensatory consequences (punitive sanctions or nondischargeability)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes whether breaches of contract that are 'willful and malicious' can render debts nondischargeable under §523(a)(6), arguing for nondischargeability where the breacher knowingly causes harm without economic justification; Paper B examines when breach should be morally or legally condemned beyond payment of expectation damages, exploring how law might impose or avoid extra penalties to align incentives and fairness.

shared_topics.topic: the interface between contract law and tort principles (i.e., 'tortifying' breaches)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages the doctrinal question of whether and when contract breaches should be treated as tortious for purposes of bankruptcy nondischargeability, while Paper B addresses the broader debate about whether contracts generate categorical promises (a moral/tort-like prohibition on breach) versus mere legal contingencies, and how that affects enforcement and normativity.

shared_topics.topic: design and selection of remedies for breach (expectation damages, punitive damages, specific performance, liquidated damages, and contract design alternatives)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates how allowing punitive‑type consequences (and denying discharge) interacts with contract damages and policy, citing trends toward punitive awards in contract contexts; Paper B systematically examines existing remedies—expectation damages, specific performance, liquidated damages—and proposes a contractual 'exit clause' as a choice‑architecture remedy to reconcile moral diversity and promote efficient outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between efficiency, fairness, and moral/creditor protection in how the law treats breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames §523(a)(6) nondischargeability as a legislative policy choice balancing a debtor's fresh start against creditor protection and punitive aims, whereas Paper B analyzes how moral heterogeneity causes inefficiencies and distributional unfairness under current contract law and proposes reforms that weigh efficiency against moral and distributive concerns.

shared_topics.topic: enforcement of contractual remedies (liquidated damages, expectation damages, specific performance)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers substantively analyze how legal remedies for breach should operate: Paper A examines when courts enforce or refuse stipulated/ liquidated-damages clauses (especially where no loss occurred), and Paper B evaluates the effects of existing remedies (expectation damages, liquidated-damages clauses, specific performance) and proposes alternative contractual mechanisms (exit clauses) to change incentives.

shared_topics.topic: tension between freedom of contract (party autonomy) and other policy norms (just compensation, fairness, moral obligations)
shared_topics.justification: Both works grapple with conflicting normative goals that bear on enforcement: Paper A frames the core dilemma as freedom of contract versus the just-compensation/anti‑penalty impulse in overliquidation cases, while Paper B explores the conflict between contractual autonomy for firms and moral duties felt by individuals and the distributional/fairness consequences of allowing efficient breaches.

shared_topics.topic: the role of contractual language/clauses in shaping parties' conduct and legal/moral expectations
shared_topics.justification: Both papers emphasize that the specific terms of a contract (e.g., stipulated damages or an exit clause) materially alter behavior and perceptions: Paper A argues that how courts treat a stipulated damages clause (prospectively vs retrospectively) determines enforcement outcomes, and Paper B shows empirically that express clauses (liquidated damages vs exit option) change whether individuals view breach as permissible and thus whether they will perform or pay.

shared_topics.topic: favoring functional/empirical analysis over formal doctrinal labels to reform contract law
shared_topics.justification: Each article criticizes reliance on formal doctrinal tests and instead advances a functional or empirical approach: Paper A applies Warren's operative-rules methodology to explain inconsistent penalty‑doctrine outcomes, and Paper B uses experimental and empirical evidence to diagnose moral-diversity problems and to justify a choice‑architecture intervention (mandatory exit clauses).

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PUNITIVE AND NONPECUNIARY DAMAGES IN ACTIONS BASED UPON CONTRACT: TOWARD ACHIEVING THE OBJECTIVE OF FULL COMPENSATION.

shared_topics.topic: remedies for breach (expectation damages versus specific performance and alternative remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers centrally analyze the legal remedies available for contract breach — Paper A critiques the existing reliance on expectation damages and considers (and rejects) using specific performance or reduced damages to correct moral-diversity problems, while Paper B surveys monetary remedies (including prejudgment interest and the historical reluctance to award punitive or nonpecuniary damages) and argues for reforming remedy doctrine to better achieve compensatory goals.

shared_topics.topic: tension between full compensation and economic efficiency (the costs and incentives created by damage rules)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the tradeoff between compensating nonbreaching parties and preserving efficient reallocations: Paper A focuses on how individuals' moral constraints prevent efficient breach under current law and how the law's design affects aggregate welfare, while Paper B analyzes how doctrines limiting recovery (foreseeability, certainty, mitigation) are motivated by fears of overcompensation that could impede valuable economic activity and thus alter efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: distributional consequences and fairness between sophisticated parties and individuals
shared_topics.justification: Both papers address how remedial doctrines differentially affect parties: Paper A emphasizes how sophisticated Holmesian firms exploit the damages regime relative to moralist individuals, producing vertical and horizontal unfairness, and Paper B documents systematic undercompensation of contract plaintiffs (due to strict damage rules, limits on nonpecuniary and punitive awards, and denial of fees/interest), highlighting asymmetric burdens on victims of breach.

shared_topics.topic: the role of contract terms and allocations of risk in shaping liabilities and moral/legal expectations
shared_topics.justification: Both examine how express contractual provisions and presumptions about contractual scope determine liability and behavioral outcomes — Paper A focuses on how express terms (liquidated-damages clauses, exit clauses) shape individuals' perceived promises and willingness to breach, while Paper B emphasizes that damage limits turn on what losses the parties reasonably contemplated at contract formation and thus on the contract's risk allocation.

shared_topics.topic: using economic and empirical evidence to justify legal reform for predictability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A presents experimental data showing exit clauses change individuals' breach behavior and recommends choice-architecture reforms, and Paper B provides historical and economic analysis of after-tax differential discount rates to argue for a benchmark approach that increases predictability of lost-earnings awards.

shared_topics.topic: concern with inequity and variability produced by current judicial or market practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues existing contract law differentially disadvantages moralist individuals compared to firms and yields distributional unfairness, and Paper B documents wide variations in present-value awards across courts and methods, arguing that such variability produces inequitable outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: advocacy of rule-based solutions (mandatory or benchmark rules) to reduce harmful heterogeneity in outcomes

shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how liquidated-damages clauses, exit clauses, and facially unqualified contracts shape individuals' moral judgments about whether to perform or pay, while Paper B analyzes overliquidation per se cases—instances where stipulated damages are enforced despite no actual loss—and critiques how courts apply the penalty doctrine to such clauses.

shared_topics.topic: tension between economic efficiency and fairness/justice in breach remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames efficient breach against individuals' moral constraints and documents distributional unfairness when firms exploit legal remedies, whereas Paper B frames the conflict as freedom of contract versus just compensation and shows how selective enforcement of penalties produces unfair and economically inefficient outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: limits of formal doctrines and the need for doctrine or rule reform grounded in how contracts operate
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that classical remedies (expectation damages, specific performance, disclosure) fail to address moral heterogeneity and proposes an exit-clause choice-architecture reform supported by experiments, while Paper B shows the penalty/disproportion test lacks predictive content and proposes a prospective-only enforcement approach plus equitable evidence to align doctrine with actual case outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: how differences among contracting parties affect legal outcomes and policy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents moral and behavioral heterogeneity between individual 'moralists' and sophisticated Holmesian firms and analyzes how that heterogeneity interacts with contract terms, and Paper B, by highlighting selective enforcement and the practical consequences of permitting stipulated sums, engages with how the law's application differently advantages or disadvantages contracting parties depending on context and bargaining choices.

Nebraska's authorization of disgorgement (restitutionary relief) for a knowing breach of a public water‑allocation compact and explores its doctrinal implications; Paper B engages the same doctrinal space by contrasting expectation damages with alternative remedies (specific performance, liquidated‑damages, and contract design changes) and considers when non‑compensatory responses to breach are normatively appropriate.

shared_topics.topic: when compensatory damages are insufficient and courts should or should not reach beyond expectation relief
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues the Supreme Court justified disgorgement because compensatory relief and injunctions were insufficient to deter and stabilize the interstate compact; Paper B similarly interrogates the adequacy of expectation damages and examines (and rejects or accepts) tools like reduced damages or specific performance when monetary remedies fail to produce efficient or fair outcomes.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the public character of the dispute and raises the question whether the Court's disgorgement logic extends from a State‑versus‑State case to private litigants; Paper B documents and theorizes how sophisticated commercial actors (Holmesian firms) and individual moralist contracting parties differ in their breach behavior and argues the law should account for that asymmetry in remedy design.

shared_topics.topic: the role of mental state, culpability, or moral judgment in calibrating remedies for breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A identifies 'knowing' or reckless disregard as satisfying the intent element that justifies disgorgement and deterrence; Paper B focuses on moral beliefs about the permissibility of breach (individual conscience versus firm instrumentalism) and treats those beliefs as relevant to whether law should impose or relax remedial consequences to achieve efficiency and fairness.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes a choice-architecture solution—mandatory exit clauses—to align contract terms with diverse moral beliefs and facilitate efficient breach, and analyzes the (in)effectiveness of remedies like reduced expectation damages or specific performance; Paper B argues that courts and policymakers should reconsider awarding specific performance more readily, account for undercompensation from money awards (e.g., premiums), and be cautious about invalidating liquidated-damages clauses.
