papers.node_id: 2006michstlrev883!!ARTICLE: PENALTIES AS RATIONAL RESPONSE TO BARGAINING IRRATIONALITY
papers.title: ARTICLE: PENALTIES AS RATIONAL RESPONSE TO BARGAINING IRRATIONALITY
papers.abstract:
The contradiction which is the common law of liquidated damages continues, undeservedly so, to garner an inordinate amount of scholarly attention.This is because it remains an overt exception to the regime of freedom of contract. Whether one believes that the rhetorical banner of freedom of contract is at best a facsimile or a downright illusion, the surface outline of the debate presented here is clear. Freedom of contract dictates that courts fully enforce promises or their praxis -- contractual terms -- to their fullest. This is assuming that the generic requirements of genuineness of assent, consideration, capacity, and legality are met. The law of liquidated damages in its simplest form states that clauses imbued with the formal trappings of contract -- and to make the case the most clear, even clauses that are products of express negotiation between parties of relativelyequal bargaining power-- are not to be enforced if the clauses are deemed penalties post hoc.
The common law of contracts rests on two fundamental principles.The first principle, the bargain principle, holds that a contract freely entered into should be strictly enforced.The courts have a negative obligation not to judge the fairness of the terms in such contracts. The second principle is the indifference principle.It holds that, due to the compensatory nature of damages, parties should be indifferent between the option of performance and the option of receiving compensatory damages. The law of liquidated damages poses a quandary for both of these fundamental principles.The rule against penalties is essentially a substantive fairness determination in which the consent-based rationale of the bargain principle is discarded. The common use of liquidated damage clauses (penalty clauses) also questions the veracity of the indifference principle. Using a penalty clause reflects that parties are not indifferent between performance and damages. This is partially due to the under-compensatory nature of contract damages.
This freedom of contract-paternalism debate persists in a startling way into mainstream law and economics. On one side of the debate within law and economics scholarship are those arguing that any express contractual term, freely entered into, should be strictly enforced.The importance of consent as the foundation of contracts is fully embraced. The only reason to limit freedom of contract is when the genuineness of consent is questioned.Therefore, the development of a separate set of requirements and an attendant jurisprudence, as in the case of liquidated damages law, is antithetical to freedom of contract rationales. Furthermore, there are inevitable costs to be borne in the areas of transactions costs in the negotiation and enforcement of contracts, as well as to the simplicity and purity of contract law -- or, more appropriately, to the efficiency of contracting and to the efficiency of common law rules. The increased complexity of the legal regime produced by the creation of exceptions to rules (such as penalty clauses as unenforceable) inevitably lead to higher transaction costs.The higher transaction costs include the waste of costs incurred in the negotiation of unenforceable clauses and the costs expended in trying to negotiate around unenforceability.Moreover, the development of additional requirements and policing mechanisms for liquidated damage clauses is superfluous given the existence of general policing doctrines. Liquidated damages clauses that are the product of overreaching and that are unduly punitive in application are vulnerable to attack using the broad-based policing doctrines such as unconscionability, misrepresentation, duress, and mistake.
On the other side of the law and economics scholarship debate are scholars who assert that the efficiency of contract remedies is due to the compensatory nature of contract damages.The ability for a breachingparty to limit its liability to compensatory damages is what grounds efficient breach theory. Therefore, since liquidated damages that act as penalties are necessarily supra-compensatory, the current rules that invalidate such clauses are efficient.Penalties by their nature deter efficient breach and therefore need to be eradicated as a matter of law. This rationale serves a form of paternalism that is systemic in nature. Instead of the party-based paternalism found in the general policing doctrines, the paternalism here is that of systemic efficiency regardless of the context. In fact, the contextual factors that provide the rationales for so much of contract law's limitations on freedom of contract, such as the lack of genuine consent, overreaching, and inequality of bargaining power, are rendered irrelevant by the edict that all penalties are void ab initio.
The efficient breach rationale for liquidated damages law is faulty on two fronts. First, it assumes that any damages above those recognized in common law contracts are supra-compensatory and thereby punitive in nature. Second, such a black and white rule eliminates the importance of consent to the enforcement inquiry. The failure of liquidated damages law to distinguish a highly negotiated clause between parties of relatively equal bargaining power and a clause that is not a product of negotiation, such as in an adhesion contract between parties of unequal bargaining power, is contradictory to a system reliant on consent and personal autonomy.
In a previous critique of the law of liquidated damages,the author concluded that the legal distinction between the unenforceability of penalty clauses and enforceable liquidated damages clauses was irrational and inefficient.In addition, the author suggested using the tools of behavioral economics or behavioral decision theory (BDT)to better understand thepraxis of liquidated damages or penalty clauses.The author asserted that "behavioral decision theory offers insights into how contracting parties deal with . . . uncertainty."This Article reports the findings of two experimental surveys showing the prevalence in the use of behavioral heuristics and biasesby parties negotiating a contract for the purchase of a new home.
The heuristics or biases studied here are the availability bias, status quo bias, reputational effect, and signaling effect. The scenarios used for the survey represent the best case against the current state of the law of liquidated damages. The current law broadly groups all penalty clauses as unenforceable, whether negotiated (custom-designed) or not negotiated (standard form), paid-for or not paid-for, and whether products of equal bargaining power or unequal bargaining power. The parties in the scenarios possess relatively equal bargaining powers and enter into an open negotiation of a penalty clause in a home building contract. The party wanting the clause (homebuyer) is willing to compensate the other party (homebuilder) for its insertion. The law's inability or unwillingness to distinguish this type of scenario from the one involving no open bargaining, one-sided standard form insertion of the clause between parties of unequal bargaining powers, provides reason enough for changing the law.
Based upon the findings of the empirical surveys presented in this Article, two claims are made and studied. First, the use of heuristics by and the effect of biases on contract negotiators support the normative claim that the law of liquidated damages needs to be changed. The simplest and most efficient change would be the complete elimination of the specialized requirements for the enforceability of liquidated damages clauses.This is acontrary use of BDT to what is generally found in the literature. Often, BDT is used to justify judicial or governmental intervention to protect individuals from their own cognitive shortcomings.
This change in the law of liquidated damages acknowledges that the current bifurcation of liquidated damage clauses into legally enforceable liquidated damages and unenforceable penalties is overly simplistic. Instead, many penalty clauses are efficient and should be strictly enforced. Therefore, the law of liquidated damages is not justified and is an affront to freedom of contract rationales. Parties should be allowed to negotiate enforceable penalty clauses. Liquidated damage clauses, qua penalties, that are a product of overreaching can be monitored by contract law's general policing doctrines such as unconscionability and misrepresentation.
The second and broader claim is that the verification of the effects of behavioral heuristics and biases provides an avenue to discuss the meaning and importance of rationality, at least as defined by classical economic theory, in the realm of contract negotiation.As an ordering device, rationality serves as a guide as to how contracts and contract rules should appear in a perfect world. However, in the imperfect world exposed by BDT, there arerelative degrees of rational-irrational thought. Further, the systemic irrationality demonstrated by BDT is a natural component of rational beings.
With the rationality assumption discarded, this Article poses that contract law, represented by the private negotiation of a penalty clause, is a rational device for dealing with bargaining irrationality. A clause that responds to a contracting party's irrational calculation of risk and allows that person to enter into a contract warrants enforcement when it proves to be a Pareto efficient move in relation to a less efficient alternative. When the uncertainty of performance drives a party to a more inefficient alternative, a clause responding to such irrationality should not be lightly discarded by a hard rule of non-enforceability.
Part I of this Article presents the methodology of the experimental surveys including a discussion of the operative facts selected for the scenarios, the dependent and independent variables, and the hypotheses posed. Part II presents the statistical findings of the experimental surveys, using a logistic regression model to analyze the relative importance of the selected factors in the negotiation of penalty clauses. Part III analyzes the findings in order to better understand the issues, both practical and theoretical, that have been discussed in the debate over the enforceability of penalty clauses in the common law. Part IV concludes that the penalty clauses presented and selected in the surveys' scenarios represent a rational response to bargaining irrationality. This Part ventures some ideas regarding the insights that BDT offers to contract law. It argues that penalty clauses should be enforced as a rational response to the bargaining irrationality uncovered by the empirical findings of BDT.

questions.question: Whether contracting parties use behavioral heuristics and biases when negotiating pre-agreed breach-payment clauses, and how those biases affect the likelihood and terms of including such clauses.

Whether pre-agreed breach-payment clauses can operate as a rational, Pareto-improving response to negotiators' cognitive biases such that legal rules should permit their enforcement rather than categorically invalidating them.

matched_themes: Should courts allow punitive or other extracompensatory damages for willful or abusive contract breaches, and what are the efficiency and fairness trade-offs?
How should courts treat pre-agreed breach payments and liquidated damages clauses (enforce, reform, apportion, or void)?
How should default liability rules interact with parties' freedom to allocate risks by contract and duties of disclosure to achieve efficient and fair risk allocation?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?
What standards and procedural safeguards should govern awards of punitive and other nonpecuniary damages in contract disputes to balance compensation and protection against abuse?
Should the promisor or the promisee have the default right to choose between performance and payment to achieve allocative efficiency?
Should parties be presumptively permitted to contractually specify nonstandard damage remedies, or should courts retain authority to impose defaults?
How should courts treat and enforce stipulated remedies (liquidated damages clauses) versus substituting judicial remedies?
How do transaction costs, enforcement frictions, and institutional realities alter the theoretical efficiency of breach-plus-compensation?

Can party-designed enforcement mechanisms (pre-agreed penalties, arbitration, bonding, reputational systems) reliably produce efficient breach outcomes without judicial intervention, and when do they fail?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
Should courts police and limit supracompensatory contractual remedies (penalty-like clauses), or does allowing parties to contract for such terms respect autonomy and promote efficient contracting?
Do behavioral biases and heuristics affect how parties draft, negotiate, and accept pre-agreed breach-payment clauses, and can contract design mitigate those biases?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
Do parties and courts actually choose heterogeneous, context-tailored damage provisions in contracting, and under what conditions would such customization be voluntarily chosen or socially desirable?

Should contractual clauses that impose predetermined monetary payments for breach be treated as punitive (unenforceable) or as enforceable measures of compensation, and what factors predict courts' enforcement decisions?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1551!!ARTICLE: COULD BREACH OF CONTRACT BE IMMORAL?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: COULD BREACH OF CONTRACT BE IMMORAL?

shared_topics.topic: normative assessment of the 'efficient breach' rationale for limiting punitive or penalty remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly challenges the efficient-breach rationale that barring punitive damages promotes efficiency and thus justifies permitting breaches that morality condemns; Paper B critiques the same efficiency-based justification used to invalidate penalty clauses and liquidated damages, arguing the rationale is both conceptually and empirically problematic.

shared_topics.topic: whether expectation/compensatory damages fully discharge promissory duties (i.e., whether monetary damages exhaust the moral duty to perform)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats Shavell's claim that availability of expectation damages means breach is not a promissory wrong and contests whether money alone can capture the moral content of a promise; Paper B interrogates the compensatory nature of contract damages as central to the indifference principle and shows how supra‑compensatory clauses (penalties) reveal limits to the idea that damages make parties indifferent between performance and breach.

shared_topics.topic: appropriate enforceability of supra‑compensatory remedies (punitive damages, penalty or liquidated‑damage clauses)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether punitive legal remedies should ever apply to deliberate, gratuitous breaches of promise and whether the law's bar on punitive damages is defensible; Paper B assesses the doctrinal rule voiding penalty clauses, presenting empirical and normative arguments that many such supra‑compensatory clauses can be rational and should be enforceable.

shared_topics.topic: how to interpret parties' intentions and gap‑filling in incomplete or negotiated contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes Shavell's hypothetical‑consent approach—asking what parties would have agreed to when a contract is silent on a contingency—and disputes that such gap‑filling always immunizes breaches from moral fault; Paper B examines negotiated versus standard penalty clauses, the role of bargaining (including whether clauses reflect true intent), and how behavioral biases affect what contracting parties actually agree to or would have agreed to.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between consent/freedom of contract and paternalistic limits (including the role of bargaining power and irrationality)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the moral agency of citizens and objects to legal rationales that intentionally encourage immoral breach even if framed as socially efficient, implicating limits on policy that overrides promissory morality; Paper B frames the doctrine against penalties as a form of systemic paternalism opposing freedom of contract, and uses behavioral decision theory to argue for revising paternalistic rules where bargaining irrationality, not lack of consent, motivates protective intervention.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 89bulrev1397!!ARTICLE: A THEORY OF SELF-HELP REMEDIES IN CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A THEORY OF SELF-HELP REMEDIES IN CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: adequacy of damages as a substitute for specific performance and its effect on parties' incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that damages often inadequately compensate subjective or hard-to-measure losses, which explains why law tolerates self-help (withholding/refusal) and windfalls to protect performance rights; Paper B likewise treats the under‑compensatory nature of damages as central to why parties use supra‑compensatory penalty clauses and why the indifference principle fails in practice.

shared_topics.topic: limits on freedom of contract versus judicial paternalism in policing remedial terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages the normative dispute between economic (efficiency) and autonomy/formalism approaches in deciding which informal or uncertain agreements courts should enforce and how self‑help should be regulated; Paper B debates whether the special doctrine invalidating penalty clauses is an illegitimate paternalistic intrusion on freedom of contract and argues for relaxing that policing rule.

shared_topics.topic: how bargaining context, consent, and power shape enforcement of disputed contractual rights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how honest disputes, duress, reservation of rights, and unequal costs of nonperformance affect whether parties may withhold performance or must accept and litigate; Paper B empirically examines negotiation settings and bargaining power to argue the law should distinguish negotiated penalty clauses from one‑sided standard form impositions.

shared_topics.topic: use of contractual remedies and clauses as strategic bargaining tools
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies threats to withhold performance, accord and satisfaction, voluntary payment doctrine, and reservation of rights as mechanisms parties use to extract concessions or resolve disputes; Paper B treats liquidated‑damage/penalty clauses as deliberate contractual responses to perceived bargaining/risk preferences and behavioral biases that function as strategic instruments.

shared_topics.topic: the interplay between legal rules and actual contracting behavior (including behavioral considerations)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how remedial rules (material breach, mitigation, UCC §1‑308, duress doctrines) shape parties' real‑world decisions to perform, withhold, or settle; Paper B brings behavioral decision theory evidence that negotiators use heuristics and biases, arguing legal doctrine should respond to such real contracting behavior rather than assume classical rationality.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2013uilllrev151!!ARTICLE: CAN'T BUY ME LOVE: MONETARY VERSUS IN-KIND REMEDIES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CAN'T BUY ME LOVE: MONETARY VERSUS IN-KIND REMEDIES

shared_topics.topic: whether promisees (and contracting parties) are indifferent between specific performance and money
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reports experimental evidence that laypeople and businesspeople strongly prefer in-kind performance to monetary awards, directly challenging the indifference principle; Paper B marshals behavioral decision theory and survey evidence to argue that parties are not indifferent between performance and damages and that contractual terms (including penalties) reflect this non‑indifference.

shared_topics.topic: the proper treatment and enforceability of liquidated damages / penalty clauses
shared_topics.justification: Paper B is an extended empirical and normative critique of the common‑law rule that invalidates penalty clauses and argues many such clauses should be enforceable; Paper A discusses liquidated damages in its normative Part, warning courts to be cautious about invalidating liquidated damages and suggesting doctrinal implications given observed preferences for in‑kind remedies.

shared_topics.topic: use of behavioral and experimental evidence to inform contract remedial doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Both papers rely on experimental/survey methods and behavioral insights to question classical economic assumptions underlying contract law—Paper A uses experiments on remedial preferences to inform remedies doctrine, while Paper B uses behavioral decision theory surveys to explain bargaining behavior and to argue for changing the law on penalties.

shared_topics.topic: whether monetary damages adequately compensate and the efficiency implications of remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A finds monetary remedies often fail to restore the injured party’s welfare (undercompensatory compared to in‑kind relief) and recommends considering premiums or more in‑kind relief for efficiency; Paper B questions the efficient‑breach justification for limiting penalties, arguing that supra‑compensatory clauses can be Pareto‑efficient responses to bargaining irrationality and thus have different efficiency implications.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between freedom of contract (consent/autonomy) and paternalistic or welfare‑based intervention in remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper B frames liquidated damages law as a clash between freedom of contract and systemic paternalism that prohibits penalties, arguing for greater respect for negotiated consent; Paper A likewise weighs parties' autonomy and institutional costs against the welfare gains from honoring in‑kind preferences and suggests doctrinal adjustments to better respect injured parties' remedial preferences.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 70bulrev623!!ARTICLE: EQUITY TRANSFORMED: PRELIMINARY INJUNCTIONS TO REQUIRE THE PAYMENT OF MONEY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EQUITY TRANSFORMED: PRELIMINARY INJUNCTIONS TO REQUIRE THE PAYMENT OF MONEY

shared_topics.topic: reforming traditional doctrines that limit enforcement of monetary obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the common-law rule invalidating 'penalty' liquidated-damage clauses should be rethought and many such clauses enforced, while Paper B argues that historical equitable limits (refusing preliminary injunctions to order interim payment) should be relaxed so plaintiffs can obtain money sooner.

shared_topics.topic: when courts should override formal rules to address real-world inefficiencies and harms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A invokes behavioral decision theory to show bargaining irrationality and contends courts should allow contractual terms that respond to that irrationality, while Paper B contends courts should use equitable relief to prevent secondary harms caused by delays in legal remedies for impecunious plaintiffs.

shared_topics.topic: tension between freedom of contract/consent and paternalistic or systemic judicial intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the debate as freedom-of-contract arguments versus paternalistic elimination of penalties for systemic efficiency, and Paper B interrogates the doctrine that equity must yield to legal remedies—both papers explore limits on private ordering imposed by judicial doctrines and when intervention is justified.

shared_topics.topic: use of economic and efficiency reasoning to justify doctrinal change in remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the 'efficient breach'/compensatory damages rationale and advances Pareto-efficiency arguments (given behavioral biases) for enforcing certain clauses, while Paper B marshals social-need, harm-avoidance, and administrative-cost considerations to argue preliminary payments are efficient and legally appropriate.

shared_topics.topic: responding to imperfect or vulnerable parties in designing remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents contracting parties' cognitive biases and argues contract law should accommodate such imperfect decision-making, and Paper B focuses on indigent injured plaintiffs whose inability to wait for judgments requires adapting equitable remedies to protect vulnerable litigants.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 117michlrev885!!ARTICLE: Moral Diversity and Efficient Breach
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Moral Diversity and Efficient Breach

shared_topics.topic: the normative status and practical effects of efficient-breach theory
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage directly with the efficient-breach idea: Paper A critiques the use of efficient-breach reasoning to invalidate liquidated-damage (penalty) clauses and shows its limits, while Paper B documents how moral resistance to breach prevents many individually efficient breaches and analyzes how law should respond to that inefficiency.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of behavioral and psychological factors on contracting and breach decisions
shared_topics.justification: Both articles draw on behavioral insights — Paper A studies heuristics and biases (availability, status-quo, reputational and signaling effects) affecting negotiators, and Paper B documents moral beliefs and psychological heterogeneity about whether breach is morally permissible and how those beliefs shape real-world breach choices.

shared_topics.topic: contract design (choice of clauses) as a tool to align incentives and correct behavioral/moral frictions
shared_topics.justification: Both papers evaluate specific contractual devices as responses to behavioral or moral frictions: Paper A argues for allowing negotiated penalty/liquidated-damages clauses as rational responses to bargaining irrationality, while Paper B proposes and tests an exit clause (contractual option to pay rather than perform) to reconcile moralists' behavior with efficient outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the proper role of legal intervention versus freedom of contract (paternalism vs consent) in structuring remedies and enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Both authors debate whether courts should impose bright-line rules or let parties' choices govern outcomes — Paper A frames the penalty-rule as tension between freedom of contract and systemic paternalism, and Paper B evaluates legal remedies (damages reduction, specific performance, mandatory clauses) and argues for choice-architecture solutions that respect parties' moral views while addressing distributional concerns.

shared_topics.topic: use of empirical/experimental methods to inform contract-law doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Both papers rely on original or recent experimental evidence to support doctrinal recommendations: Paper A reports two surveys testing heuristics in negotiated penalty clauses, and Paper B presents empirical studies (and new experiments) demonstrating moral heterogeneity and the effects of exit clauses on willingness to breach.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 55amjcompl721!!ARTICLE: Why No "Efficient Breach" in the Civil Law?: A Comparative Assessment of the Doctrine of Efficient Breach of Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Why No "Efficient Breach" in the Civil Law?: A Comparative Assessment of the Doctrine of Efficient Breach of Contract

shared_topics.topic: whether contract law should favor damages over specific performance to enable 'efficient breach'
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the efficient breach doctrine and why civil law systems (France, Germany) resist treating damages as an acceptable substitute for performance, while Paper B interrogates the deterrent effect of supra‑compensatory remedies (penalty clauses) on breach and on the indifference between performance and damages.

shared_topics.topic: the normative tension between freedom of contract and judicial paternalism in policing contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts common‑law efficiency-driven doctrines with civil‑law norms (good faith, pacta sunt servanda) that morally constrain breach, and Paper B debates whether invalidating penalty clauses is a form of systemic paternalism that unjustifiably limits parties' autonomy.

shared_topics.topic: the legal status and efficiency effects of liquidated damages / penalty clauses as contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper B empirically and doctrinally evaluates when liquidated damages operate as penalties and whether they should be enforceable, and Paper A engages the broader question of how remedial rules (damages versus enforced performance) affect the plausibility of efficient breach in different legal traditions.

shared_topics.topic: use of economic analysis (law-and-economics) to assess contract remedies and incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates the efficient breach doctrine within the law‑and‑economics movement and examines structural elements that foster or impede efficiency reasoning in civil law, while Paper B uses economic efficiency arguments (and critiques them) to assess the rationale for invalidating or enforcing penalty clauses.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of nonlegal factors (cultural norms or behavioral biases) on contract doctrine and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights cultural and doctrinal obstacles in civil law—such as good faith and moral commitments to performance—that shape receptivity to efficient breach, and Paper B brings behavioral decision theory evidence (heuristics and biases in bargaining) to argue that certain clauses (including penalties) can be rational responses to bargaining irrationality.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 42ambuslj97!!ARTICLE: Cry Me a River: Recovery of Mental Distress Damages in a Breach of Contract Action--A North American Perspective
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Cry Me a River: Recovery of Mental Distress Damages in a Breach of Contract Action--A North American Perspective

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy and limits of contract damages as a remedial regime
shared_topics.justification: Both papers interrogate which kinds of losses contract law should compensate — Paper A critiques the rule that invalidates supra‑compensatory 'penalty' liquidated damages and defends parties' ability to contract for such terms, while Paper B scrutinizes the traditional bar on non‑pecuniary (mental distress) recoveries and whether intangible losses should be recoverable under ordinary contract remedies.

shared_topics.topic: tension between freedom of contract and judicial paternalism in policing contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Both articles address judicial intervention that overrides parties' bargains — Paper A frames the rule against penalties as a form of systemic paternalism that limits autonomy, and Paper B critiques courts' categorical rules denying emotional loss as unduly restrictive of parties' expectations and proposes treating contracts on equal footing.

shared_topics.topic: the role of doctrinal constraints (compensatory principle and foreseeability tests) in limiting recovery
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with foundational doctrinal rationales for restricting damages — Paper A centers the compensatory nature of contract damages and the efficient breach argument in debates over penalties, while Paper B focuses on foreseeability (Hadley v. Baxendale) and related tests that courts use to exclude mental distress damages.

shared_topics.topic: critique of exception‑based, fragmented doctrines and calls for doctrinal reform
shared_topics.justification: Both papers argue current rules produce an incoherent patchwork — Paper A calls the bifurcation between enforceable liquidated damages and void penalties overly simplistic and proposes relying on general policing doctrines, and Paper B labels the growing set of exceptions to the no‑recovery rule for mental distress as unworkable and advocates a clearer, promise‑focused approach.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 94tullrev925!!SYMPOSIUM: Contract Lore as Heuristic Starting Points
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: Contract Lore as Heuristic Starting Points

shared_topics.topic: the role of heuristics and behavioral biases in contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reconceptualizes commonly repeated 'contract lore' as heuristic starting points for legal analysis, and Paper B empirically documents specific behavioral heuristics (availability, status quo, reputational/signaling effects) shaping negotiators' choices.

shared_topics.topic: using behavioral insights to justify or guide contract-law reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats lore/heuristics as a device to identify areas where doctrine may need reform, while Paper B uses behavioral decision theory and experimental evidence to argue for changing the law of liquidated damages (e.g., enforcing some penalty clauses).

shared_topics.topic: the centrality of party intent/consent and freedom of contract in enforcement questions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the lore concerning the importance of parties' intent, and Paper B centers the bargain principle and consent-based rationales (and critiques their displacement by the penalty rule) in assessing when contractual terms should be enforced.

shared_topics.topic: skepticism of bright-line doctrinal rules in favor of nuanced or policing-based responses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that many 'lore' rules function as heuristic first steps rather than absolute rules and thus warrant nuanced inquiry, and Paper B criticizes the black‑and‑white rule invalidating all penalties, proposing reliance on contextual policing doctrines (e.g., unconscionability) instead of categorical invalidation.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM:What to Compensate? Some Surprisingly Unappreciated Reasons Why the Problem Is So Hard

shared_topics.topic: choosing the baseline for calculating damages (the relevant counterfactual 'but‑for' world)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages this insofar as it critiques how the indifference principle and compensatory-damages paradigm underpin doctrines on liquidated damages and efficient breach, while Paper B is explicitly devoted to the problem of selecting the appropriate baseline for compensation across tort and contract scenarios.

shared_topics.topic: whether remedies should be strictly compensatory versus serving deterrence or paternalistic goals (efficiency vs fairness/consent)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A pits the efficient-breach/efficiency rationale against freedom-of-contract and paternalism in the rule against penalties, arguing for preserving consent in many cases; Paper B surveys the normative dilemmas behind baseline choice, showing how different remedial aims (compensation, deterrence, distributive fairness) pull in different directions.

shared_topics.topic: role of parties' subjective welfare, preferences, and behavioral biases in determining appropriate relief
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reports experiments showing heuristics and biases in contract negotiation and argues such behavioral realities should affect enforceability of penalty clauses, and Paper B discusses cases where plaintiffs' subjective welfare changes (e.g., being better off after harm) that complicate what compensation should aim to restore.

shared_topics.topic: the inadequacy of bright-line doctrinal rules to account for contextual differences (negotiation context, bargaining power, fact-specific harms) in remedy decisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues the categorical invalidation of penalty clauses ignores distinctions like negotiated versus standard-form clauses and bargaining power, and Paper B demonstrates that different factual clusters (existence, counterfactual lives, changed preferences) require distinct baseline analyses rather than one-size-fits-all rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 29yalejonreg1!!ARTICLE: Self-Help and the Rules of Engagement
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Self-Help and the Rules of Engagement

shared_topics.topic: design of remedies and private enforcement versus court process
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze when the law should allow private enforcement (self-help or contractually specified penalties) versus require state process, with Paper A modeling the choice to permit repossession or force and Paper B critiquing the categorical invalidation of penalty clauses that would otherwise privately allocate consequences for breach.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs among enforcement costs — violence, delay, administrative costs, and transaction costs — in selecting legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly models how violence, administrative verification costs, mistakes, and delay interact to shape self-help doctrines, while Paper B evaluates how the transaction costs and efficiency consequences of invalidating or enforcing liquidated-damage clauses should factor into remedial rules.

shared_topics.topic: role of mistakes, informational asymmetries, and parties' knowledge in shaping doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how unclear rights and strategic knowledge of rules (e.g., breach-of-the-peace standards) affect the effectiveness of self-help, and Paper B uses behavioral decision theory and experiments to show how heuristics and imperfect bargaining information influence negotiated penalty clauses and thus the desirability of enforcing them.

shared_topics.topic: tension between party autonomy (freedom of contract) and paternalistic limits on enforceability of remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both papers confront limits on private ordering — Paper A explains when the law channels disputes into judicial process (restricting self-help) to reduce mistakes and social costs, and Paper B questions whether the common law rule invalidating penalty clauses is an unjustified paternalistic constraint on negotiated contractual autonomy given behavioral realities.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 42ambuslj97!!ARTICLE: Cry Me a River: Recovery of Mental Distress Damages in a Breach of Contract Action--A North American Perspective
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Cry Me a River: Recovery of Mental Distress Damages in a Breach of Contract Action--A North American Perspective

shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes the entrenched general rule (and its category-based exceptions) barring recovery for mental distress and shows how categorical limits produce doctrinal instability, advocating a focus on what the contract promised; Paper B attacks the black‑and‑white rule invalidating penalty clauses and argues for abandoning the specialized penalty test in favor of a more context-sensitive enforcement regime.

shared_topics.topic: whether supra‑compensatory or non‑pecuniary losses should be recognized or suppressed in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks whether intangible harms (mental distress) ought to be recoverable in breach actions and surveys doctrines (punitive/aggravated damages, special contract categories) that currently suppress such awards; Paper B interrogates the exclusion of supra‑compensatory (penalty) clauses as inconsistent with contractual autonomy and shows when such non‑compensatory terms can be efficient and should be enforced.

shared_topics.topic: the legitimacy and scope of judicial paternalism versus freedom of contract in policing contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents judicial reluctance to award emotional losses grounded in concerns about commercial expectations and 'reasonable businessman' attitudes, critiquing that paternalism; Paper B frames the penalty rule as a form of systemic paternalism opposed to freedom of contract and argues the rule improperly overrides parties' consent.

shared_topics.topic: the centrality of parties' intentions/expectations (consent) in determining remedial outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes resolving disputes about intangible recovery by asking 'what did the contract promise?' and emphasizes focusing on contract content and foreseeability of loss; Paper B locates the problem with the penalty doctrine in its failure to respect negotiated consent and advocates enforcement where clauses reflect genuine bargaining and negotiated risk allocations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 61scallrev629!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT REMEDIES, RENEGOTIATION, AND THE THEORY OF EFFICIENT BREACH.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT REMEDIES, RENEGOTIATION, AND THE THEORY OF EFFICIENT BREACH.

shared_topics.topic: the theory of efficient breach and whether remedies should promote breach when socially efficient
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques and challenges the 'efficient breach' rationale for invalidating penalty clauses, arguing it mischaracterizes supra‑compensatory payments and neglects consent and behavioral factors; Paper B explicates the efficient breach question more broadly, asking when remedies should encourage breach and how the theory has been applied to analyze particular remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the role and enforceability of liquidated damages / penalty clauses as contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on liquidated damages/penalty clauses, using behavioral experiments to argue many such clauses are rational and should be enforceable; Paper B treats liquidated damages as a central example in economic analyses of remedies and examines their efficiency implications in the renegotiation context.

shared_topics.topic: the importance of renegotiation and transaction costs in assessing remedy efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses transaction costs from specialized rules and the distinction between negotiated versus standard form clauses, emphasizing negotiation context; Paper B highlights how the ease or cost of ex post renegotiation influences whether particular remedies are efficient and critiques analyses that ignore these costs.

shared_topics.topic: how contract remedies influence parties' incentives beyond the simple perform-or-breach decision (precaution, entry, bargaining, distributional effects)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues penalty clauses reflect parties' risk calculations and can be a rational response to bargaining 'irrationality,' affecting contracting choices; Paper B stresses that remedies affect a range of decisions — spending on precautions, whether to enter a contract and at what price, bargaining behavior, and distributional outcomes — not just the decision to perform or breach.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE EXPECTATION MEASURE AND ITS DISCONTENTS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers the indifference principle (that promisees should be indifferent between performance and damages) to critique how liquidated damages and penalty rules conflict with that principle, while Paper B treats the indifference principle as the core justification for the expectation measure and surveys challenges to it.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the law-and-economics claim that penalties must be void because they deter efficient breach and argues some penalty clauses can be efficient, and Paper B analyzes how traditional efficiency arguments support the expectation measure and summarizes economic critiques proposing modifications or replacements on efficiency grounds.

shared_topics.topic: the role of rationality assumptions (and behavioral critiques) in shaping remedial doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically invokes behavioral decision theory to show bargaining heuristics and irrationality that undermine classical rational-actor assumptions and argues remedies should respond to that, while Paper B engages the methodological assumptions behind the indifference/expectation framework—implicitly raising the same question of whether classical rationality adequately justifies current remedial doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: administrability and institutional constraints on adopting alternative remedial regimes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses transaction costs, enforcement complexity, and reliance on general policing doctrines as practical limits on changing liquidated-damages law, and Paper B explicitly evaluates the administrability and institutional congruence of alternative models and remedial regimes to the expectation measure.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE CASE FOR PUNITIVE DAMAGES IN CONTRACTS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that many penalty clauses (liquidated damages characterized as penalties) should be enforceable because they can be Pareto-efficient responses to bargaining heuristics, while Paper B argues that punitive or in terrorem remedies should be available for willful breaches to deter opportunism and promote efficient bargaining.

shared_topics.justification: Paper B frames the availability of punitive damages as shifting contractual entitlements toward property-rule protection to encourage pre‑breach negotiation, and Paper A analyzes how the current specialized regime for liquidated damages raises transaction/negotiation costs and why negotiated penalty clauses may be more efficient to uphold.

shared_topics.topic: how contracting parties' behavioral characteristics (irrationality, heuristics, or opportunism) should influence remedy design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses behavioral decision theory and empirical surveys to show negotiators employ biases (availability, status quo, signaling) and argues remedies should accommodate such bargaining irrationality; Paper B distinguishes opportunistic willful breaches from efficient ones and recommends remedial rules (punitive damages) tailored to deter opportunism while preserving efficient outcomes.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DISGORGING EMOLUMENTS

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Why No "Efficient Breach" in the Civil Law?: A Comparative Assessment of the Doctrine of Efficient Breach of Contract

shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the common‑law rule invalidating penalty clauses as supra‑compensatory and questions that rule using empirical behavioral evidence, and Paper B engages the compensatory-damages premise underlying efficient breach (i.e., damages substituting for performance) when explaining when breaches can be socially efficient.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A brings behavioral decision theory to bear, showing heuristics and biases in contracting and arguing that contractual terms can be rational responses to bargaining irrationality, whereas Paper B highlights cultural and doctrinal (civil‑law) obstacles to treating contracts purely as economic exchange, thereby questioning the universal applicability of the law‑and‑economics account.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PUNITIVE AND NONPECUNIARY DAMAGES IN ACTIONS BASED UPON CONTRACT: TOWARD ACHIEVING THE OBJECTIVE OF FULL COMPENSATION.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT DAMAGES IN TENNESSEE

compared_to.partner_node_id: 28gastulrev559!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT BREACHES AND THE CRIMINAL/CIVIL DIVIDE: AN INTER-COMMON LAW ANALYSIS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT BREACHES AND THE CRIMINAL/CIVIL DIVIDE: AN INTER-COMMON LAW ANALYSIS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether specialized rules (the penalty doctrine) constitute unacceptable paternalism versus necessary protection given behavioral biases, and Paper B interrogates when state criminalization (a form of public intervention) is justified as opposed to leaving harms to civil resolution.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Damages Versus Specific Performance: Lessons from Commercial Contracts

papers.node_id: 101marqlrev87!!ARTICLE: PLURALISM APPLIED: A CONCORDANT APPROACH TO SELECTING CONTRACT RULES
papers.title: ARTICLE: PLURALISM APPLIED: A CONCORDANT APPROACH TO SELECTING CONTRACT RULES
papers.abstract:
One cannot tortiously interfere with one's own contract.Rather, according to the Restatement of Torts, only "one who intentionally and improperly interferes with the performance of a contract … between another and a third person" is liable in tort for causing a breach of contract.This stands to reason in a society grounded in freedom of contract because "along with the celebrated freedom to make contracts goes a considerable freedom to break them as well."Accordingly, courts do not generally punish or make an example of parties who breach a contract through the award of punitive damages.The breaching party should be ordered to compensate the victim of the breach for the harm causedby the broken promise,but society does not seek to punish and deter breach of contract in the same way that it seeks to punish and deter torts.
This black letter rule can be justified by two dominant theories of contract law: efficiency theory and rights-based theory.
Efficiency theory generally addresses problems in contract law by asking which solution increases overall social welfare by resulting in the most efficient use of resources and an increase in societal wealth.Efficiency theorists arguethat greater wealth or utility will sometimes result if a party breaches a contract than if the contractual promise is fulfilled.This happens when the gains to be made under an alternative contract (or through no contract at all) will be greater than the cost of compensating the victim of the breach for the harm to its expectation under the contract.It follows that efficiency theory favors a rule against punitive damages for a simple breach of contract.Punitive damages would deter these "efficient breaches" and result in a waste of the wealth and utility they would otherwise create.
Unlike efficiency theory, which is primarily concerned with how contract law can promote social welfare, rights-based theory views contract law as protecting the rights of the individual parties to the contract.In particular, contract law should protect the right of individuals to bind themselves through contracts (i.e., freedom of contract) by enforcing the promises enshrined in contracts, or by protecting the reliance interest individuals have in contracts.The pioneer of the promissory theory of contracts, Charles Fried, wrote that "the obligation to keep a promise is grounded not in arguments of utility but in respect for individual autonomy and in trust."It follows that if a party breaks a contractual promise, the only way to protect freedom of contract is for the law to enforce that promise; the breaching party "should be made to hand over the equivalent of the promised performance."The appropriate remedy for breach of contract is expectation damages because "the expectation standard gives the victim of a breach no more or less than he would have had had there been no breach - in other words, he gets the benefit of his bargain."Fried explains why damages for breach of contract should be no less than compensatory damages under a rights-based theory.
Daniel Markovits and Alan Schwartz complete the picture by explaining why a rights-based theory of contract counsels against supra-compensatory damages for breach of contract, such as punitive damages.Markovits and Schwartz hypothesize that a contract is a dual promise: "either to trade goods or services to buyers or to make a monetary transfer to buyers, equal to the value the buyers would realize from receiving the goods or services [i.e., an expectation value]."It follows that compensatory, expectation damages are favored over supra-compensatory, punitive damages because they do not impose an obligation greater than what the contracting parties agreed to and thereby protect the breaching party's freedom of contract.
Hence, there are strong theoretical arguments across dueling theories of contract law to justify the old chestnut of a principal that there are no punitive damages for a simple breach of contract.And it follows from this that one cannot tortiously interfere with one's own contract.Breach of contract is permitted, not punished.
But what of the more complicated situation where a parent company directs its wholly owned subsidiary to breach a contract? This might happen for a variety of reasons. When a parent acquires a subsidiary, the subsidiary brings with it various baggage, some good, some bad, including ongoing contractual obligations with other companies. The parent may seek to terminate the contract for legitimate, business related reasons. For example, the parent may be able to negotiate better terms with a different supplier, or may be able to satisfy the contract needs internally. On the other end of the spectrum, the parent may terminate a subsidiary's contract out of personal malice or spitetoward the victim of the breach, even if doing so is not in the best interest of the shareholders. Somewhere in between is the situation where a parent acquires a subsidiary for the purpose of terminating the subsidiary's contracts with competitors of the parent. Once the acquisition is made, this would appear to be in the business interest of the parent and subsidiary. To the extent such behavior harms competition, it would presumably be in the realm of antitrust law to deter such behavior. Is it nonetheless a tort that courts should punish under a theory of intentional interference with contract?
The courts are deeply divided on these questions, with conflicting views among the states' highest courts and among the federal courts of appeals applying state law.Part II of this Article: analyzes notable rulings from around the country to arrive at the conclusion that there are at least four different approaches to the question of whether and when a parent company may terminate the contract of a subsidiary.

papers.title: ARTICLE: PUNITIVE AND NONPECUNIARY DAMAGES IN ACTIONS BASED UPON CONTRACT: TOWARD ACHIEVING THE OBJECTIVE OF FULL COMPENSATION.
papers.abstract:
The stated objective of contract remedies is to compensate the aggrieved party fully for breach by putting her as closely as possible in the same position as she would have been had the contract been performed.Because of the traditional and still largely prevailing preference of Anglo-American law for substitutional remedies, courts seek to fulfill this full-compensation objective largely by awarding monetary damages rather than by granting specific performance or other equitable relief.It is now almost commonplace,however, to recognize that traditional contract damage remedies leave many victims of contract breach (probably a substantial majority) undercompensated.One reason for this situation is that there is an important and countervailing corollary to the principle of full compensation: Do not overcompensate the victim of contract breach.  As others have shown, this desire to avoid overcompensation has multifaceted origins.  Most important among these is the fear that excessive liability for contract breach may discourage valuable commercial and economic activity and thus create an undesirable barrier to the efficient reallocation of resources.Because of these concerns, the corollary of avoiding overcompensation has dominated the principle of full compensation for the past century.
The dominance of the corollary is manifest when one examines the major rules governing the determination of contract damages.  Almost all of these rules focus upon limiting the breacher's liability and assuring that the contract plaintiff is not placed in a better position than she would have been after full performance.  Damages are limited to the types of loss which the breacher, at the time of contract formation, had reason to know might be forthcoming.Thus, damage rules recognize the consensual basis of contract liability by limiting a contracting party's potential liability to those risks that might reasonably be deemed to have been assumed upon entering the contract.  The amount of loss must be established with a reasonable degree of certainty,and mitigation principles prevent plaintiff from recovering for losses that she reasonably might have avoided.Both the foreseeability and certainty requirements tend to be applied more frequently and strictly in contract actions than in tort.Moreover, by applying these requirements, courts often remove entire elements of claimed loss from the province of the jury.
The purpose of this Article is not to criticize per se these traditional limitations on contract recovery.  Rather, my object is to note their cumulative effect.  The traditional rules establish full compensation as the maximum potential recovery for a contract plaintiff, and they impose the primaryrisk of error in calculating damages on the aggrieved plaintiff rather than upon the breacher; thus they often preclude realizing full compensation.  The plaintiff's risk of not obtaining full compensation is then compounded by a variety of other rules, some particularly applicable to contract actions and others of more generality.  For example, contract plaintiffs normally may recover for emotional distress only infrequently and in narrowly restricted circumstances.This limitation effectively denies the contract plaintiff access to the open-ended "fund" of general damages, pain and suffering, that is regularly available to the tort plaintiff.  In tort, this pain and suffering fund ameliorates in part the risk of undercompensation with respect to other more specific elements of damage.  Courts in contract actions also tend to award prejudgment interest only in restricted situations, normally permitting such recoveries only if the quantum of damages could be determined with relative certainty at the time of breach.This rule is often justified as necessary to avoid penalizing one who in good faith seeks to litigate a dispute, but it is not well designed to achieve this objective,and it necessarily adds to the pervasive undercompensationof contract plaintiffs by not replacing the income that plaintiffs could have earned by investing the gains to which they were entitled under the contract.
Another important contributor to the undercompensation of contract plaintiffs is the American rule on attorneys' fees, which in most instances prevents the prevailing party from recovering attorneys' fees and the costs of litigation from the loser.These are often substantial costs for which the contract plaintiff is not easily recompensed, while the tort plaintiff frequently may obtain compensation for costs and attorneys' fees covertly, through a large pain and suffering or punitive damages award.Punitive damages have been much less freely available to contract plaintiffs than to tort plaintiffs.  Traditionally, punitive damages were said never to be available in contract actions.Even the recent Second Restatement of Contracts recognizes only one exception to the general prohibition: Punitive damages may be awarded for breach of contract only if "[t]he conduct constituting the breach is also a tort for which punitive damages are recoverable."
In recent years, however, there has been a notable trend toward permitting recovery of punitive damages in some actions based upon contract,together with some movement (albeit less marked) toward more frequent awards for nonpecuniary elements of loss such as mental anguish, inconvenience, and annoyance caused by breach of contract.This Article reviews the recent developments concerning punitive and nonpecuniary damages in actions founded upon breach of contract, regardless of whether the pleadings are framed in contract or in tort, and focuses on both the overt and the covert ways in which courts recently have permitted these recoveries.
In the course of this review, I argue for a broader and more overtrecognition of both nonpecuniary loss and punitive or supracompensatorydamages in contract.  Ultimately, however, I also suggest a substantial reformulation of objectives with respect to "punitive" damages in contract.  These new objectives would shift the primary focus from deterrence and punishment to complete and full compensation for contract plaintiffs, at least in situations involving egregious breach.I make these suggestions fully recognizing the risks of abuse and overcompensation inherent in permitting recovery for such open-ended items as mental distress and punitive damages and acknowledging that these risks are presently of substantial concern with respect to punitivedamage claims in tort actions.An appreciation of these risks and the recognition that they already may have become reality in some contract actions, particularly in some punitive damages awards against insurers for bad faith refusal to pay or settle claims,leads me to recommend that careful attention be paid to the standards for awarding nonpecuniary and punitive damages and that new procedural safeguards be employed when determining and awarding punitive damages.Before discussing these recommendations, however, it is necessary to examine more fully the ways and the extent to which traditional contract damage remedies systematically tend to undercompensate contract plaintiffs.

questions.question: Do traditional contract remedies systematically undercompensate injured parties by limiting recovery for nonpecuniary losses and punitive/supracompensatory awards?

Would broader recognition of nonpecuniary and punitive damages in contract cases help achieve full compensation for plaintiffs, especially in egregious breaches, without creating unacceptable risks of overcompensation or adverse economic effects?
What standards and procedural safeguards should govern awards of punitive and nonpecuniary damages in contract disputes to balance the goals of full compensation and protection against abuse?

matched_themes: Should courts allow punitive or other extracompensatory damages for willful or abusive contract breaches, and what are the efficiency and fairness trade-offs?
When should courts permit plaintiffs to pursue tort claims alongside or instead of contract claims to obtain broader remedies, and how does allowing tort claims change damages outcomes?
Should parties and courts adopt fault-based remedial regimes that distinguish among breaches by reason when allocating remedies?
What counterfactual baseline should courts use to measure plaintiffs' losses for compensation purposes?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?
What standards and procedural safeguards should govern awards of punitive and other nonpecuniary damages in contract disputes to balance compensation and protection against abuse?
How do institutional features-court capacity, procedural devices, and evidentiary rules-affect the substantive development and practical application of contract remedies?
How do transaction costs, enforcement frictions, and institutional realities alter the theoretical efficiency of breach-plus-compensation?
Should plaintiffs be permitted to recover non-pecuniary harms such as mental distress in breach-of-contract cases?
Should courts police and limit supracompensatory contractual remedies (penalty-like clauses), or does allowing parties to contract for such terms respect autonomy and promote efficient contracting?
How do inequalities in litigation resources, legal representation, and factual records distort judicial factfinding and remedy outcomes in contract disputes?
To what extent does empirical uncertainty about measuring gains and losses limit courts' ability to design remedies that reflect non-welfare ethical preferences without sacrificing efficiency?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
Do limits on recoverable damages (foreseeability, certainty, avoidability) substantially reduce awards below full compensation, and should courts liberalize those limits?
Do courts consider the breaching party's blameworthiness or opportunistic behavior when selecting among compensatory remedies?
To what extent should moral blameworthiness and non-economic considerations influence the design and application of contract remedies?

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Retribution in Contract Law

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE EXPECTATION MEASURE AND ITS DISCONTENTS

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE FALLACY OF FULL COMPENSATION

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: What the Efficient Performance Hypothesis Means for Contracts Scholarship

shared_topics.topic: proposals to reform doctrinal rules governing contract damages and the mechanisms to police abuse

compared_to.partner_node_id: 117michlrev885!!ARTICLE: Moral Diversity and Efficient Breach
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Moral Diversity and Efficient Breach

shared_topics.topic: remedies for breach (expectation damages versus specific performance and alternative remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers centrally analyze the legal remedies available for contract breach — Paper A critiques the existing reliance on expectation damages and considers (and rejects) using specific performance or reduced damages to correct moral-diversity problems, while Paper B surveys monetary remedies (including prejudgment interest and the historical reluctance to award punitive or nonpecuniary damages) and argues for reforming remedy doctrine to better achieve compensatory goals.

shared_topics.topic: tension between full compensation and economic efficiency (the costs and incentives created by damage rules)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the tradeoff between compensating nonbreaching parties and preserving efficient reallocations: Paper A focuses on how individuals' moral constraints prevent efficient breach under current law and how the law's design affects aggregate welfare, while Paper B analyzes how doctrines limiting recovery (foreseeability, certainty, mitigation) are motivated by fears of overcompensation that could impede valuable economic activity and thus alter efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: distributional consequences and fairness between sophisticated parties and individuals
shared_topics.justification: Both papers address how remedial doctrines differentially affect parties: Paper A emphasizes how sophisticated Holmesian firms exploit the damages regime relative to moralist individuals, producing vertical and horizontal unfairness, and Paper B documents systematic undercompensation of contract plaintiffs (due to strict damage rules, limits on nonpecuniary and punitive awards, and denial of fees/interest), highlighting asymmetric burdens on victims of breach.

shared_topics.topic: the role of contract terms and allocations of risk in shaping liabilities and moral/legal expectations

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1997detclrev993!!ARTICLE: Capping Market Damages at Lost Profit: An Unwarranted Limitation on a Middleman's Expectancy Interest
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Capping Market Damages at Lost Profit: An Unwarranted Limitation on a Middleman's Expectancy Interest

shared_topics.topic: evidentiary and doctrinal limits on recoverable losses (foreseeability, certainty, mitigation, and allocation of risk of error)

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE DISGORGEMENT INTEREST IN CONTRACT LAW

papers.node_id: 18upajbusl315!!ARTICLE: Recovery of Damages for Lost Profits: The Historical Development
papers.title: ARTICLE: Recovery of Damages for Lost Profits: The Historical Development
papers.authors: Robert M. Lloyd; Nicholas J. Chase
papers.abstract:
A popular myth holds that Hadley v. Baxendalewas part of a judicial trend toward limiting the power of juries to award damages for lost profits. According to this myth, pre-Hadley juries exercised unlimited power to award plaintiffs the damages they had suffered on account of contract breaches and other wrongs. One of the leading contracts textbooks goes so far as to say: "Prior to 1854 [the date of the Hadley opinion] there were almost no rules of contract damages. The assessment of damages was for the most part left to the unfettered discretion of the jury."
The myth goes on to hold that the Hadley rule was necessary so that the industrial enterprises that were developing at the time would not be exposed to excessive damage awards if a plaintiff convinced a jury that the defendant's breach had cost the plaintiff immense profits. Even the eminent damages scholar Professor Charles T. McCormick said that the Hadley rule "harmonized well with the free-trade economic philosophy of the Victorian era during which our law of contracts became systematized."
These myths fit nicely with the legal realist jurisprudence that was dominant in American legal scholarship for most of the twentieth century(and even better with the critical legal studies jurisprudence that took the position that legal rules had developed as tools for maintaining the dominance of the entrenched elites).Because these myths appeared to confirm what most American scholars already believed,those scholars accepted the myths with without question.
In fact, however, the law developed in quite a different way. Roman law made the first steps toward allowing plaintiffs to recover lost profits in the third century B.C.As the Roman economy developed, these rules on lost profits became more sophisticated and went on to become the core of the damages rules for the modern European civil law.Anglo-American law took a different course. Contrary to the myths, the common law had rigid rules limiting awards of damages, and common law judges held juries to these rules.But unlike the civil law rules, the common law rules made little allowance for the recovery of lost profits until a series of New York cases incorporated the civil law rules (as articulated by the French scholar Pothier) into American law years before the Hadley court famously relied on Pothier to postulate a rule already well known in America.
What is far more important than the fact that the Hadley rule actually migrated from the United States to Great Britain, rather than crossing the Atlantic in the other direction, is that the rule Hadley announced has become relatively unimportant as a limitation on damages. Far more important in modern law is a rule that developed alongside the Hadley rule - the rule that damages in general and lost profits in particular can be recovered only if they can be proven with reasonable certainty. This article will trace that rule, showing how it developed alongside the Hadley rule and ultimately overshadowed it.

questions.question: How did the legal rules governing recovery of lost profits develop over time across different legal traditions and jurisdictions?
To what extent were limits on awards for lost profits driven by concerns about jury discretion and the economic effects of industrialization versus other doctrinal or evidentiary changes?

Which type of limitation became more important in practice for restricting recovery of lost profits: limits based on how foreseeable the loss was at the time of the transaction, or limits based on the plaintiff's ability to prove the amount of the loss with reasonable precision?

matched_themes: How have historical, geographic, institutional, and transnational influences shaped the evolution and transplantation of contract doctrines and remedies?
How do institutional features-court capacity, procedural devices, and evidentiary rules-affect the substantive development and practical application of contract remedies?

shared_topics.topic: Hadley v. Baxendale's foreseeability rule as a limiter on recovery of consequential/lost profits
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the historical origins and reception of the Hadley rule, correcting myths about its emergence and noting its role in limiting jury awards; Paper B treats Hadley as the canonical foreseeability-based constraint on consequential damages that shaped Anglo‑American contract liability.

shared_topics.topic: Rules limiting recovery of lost profits (foreseeability and reasonable certainty)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that the modern constraint on lost‑profit awards is the requirement that such losses be proven with reasonable certainty (which developed alongside Hadley), while Paper B discusses limits on consequential/lost profits recovery under Hadley and subsequent statutory codifications.

shared_topics.topic: Transnational diffusion and codification of contract damages doctrine (civil law influences, Pothier, Sale of Goods Act, UCC)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents the movement of lost‑profits doctrines between Roman/civil law, French commentators (Pothier), U.S. decisions, and Hadley in England; Paper B examines Hadley’s export as a ‘world force’ and its incorporation into Commonwealth practice and codifying instruments like the Sale of Goods Act and the U.S. Uniform Commercial Code.

shared_topics.topic: Economic and policy effects of liability‑limiting damages rules on industry and business behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages the argument (and myth) that limiting damages was important to industrial development and constrained jury discretion, while Paper B analyzes how Hadley‑style liability limits influence firm location decisions, litigation costs, and broader commercial growth (including an analogy to fostering e‑commerce).

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy and limits of damages as a remedy

shared_topics.topic: discrepancy between formal rules and judicial practice

shared_topics.topic: policy and economic rationales behind remedial rules
