papers.title: ARTICLE: THE EFFICIENCY OF SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE: TOWARD A UNIFIED THEORY OF CONTRACT REMEDIES. I should like to thank Dan Farber of the University of Minnesota Law School and John Lopatka of the University of Illinois College of Law for their great help. Participants in the Contracts Seminar at Boalt Hall, University of California, Berkeley; the Faculty Workshop, Department of Economics, University of California, Davis; the Faculty Workshops in the Department of Economics and in the Law School, Louisiana State University; and Industrial Organization Workshop, Department of Economics, University of Illinois, all provided stimulating forums and helpful comments on earlier drafts of this paper. I owe a special debt to Thomas Wippman, Lon Carlson, Eric Blomquist, and David Waimon for their invaluable research assistance.
papers.abstract:
By invoking the notion of economic efficiency, economists and legal scholars have recently made great headway in developing a new and unified theory of contractual relationships.The key advance was the economists' recognition that there are circumstances in which at least one party can be made better off, without making anyone worse off, by one party's breaching rather than performing a contractual promise.This insight suggested that long-established rules for forming and enforcing contracts should be reexamined to see to what extent they fostered or hindered the efficient exchange of reciprocal promises.
The law, it has been urged, should not hinder the breaching of contracts where the breach offers a Pareto-superior outcome.This view suggests that a contract should not be enforced at law solely because to break it is morally repugnant, a repudiation of one's solemn oath.  Justice Holmes made the same point without the aid of economic analysis,viz.,that the common law should move away from a moral interpretation of contract:
The duty to keep a contract at common law means a prediction that you must pay damages if you do not keep it, and nothing else.  If you commit a tort, you are liable to pay a compensatory sum.  If you commit a contract, you are liable to pay a compensatory sum unless the promisedevent comes to pass, and that is all the difference.  But such a mode of looking at the matter stinks in the nostrils of those who think it advantageous to get as much ethics into the law as they can.
If we agree with Holmes and accept for the time being that contractual relations and breach of contract should be evaluated on efficiency grounds, we are led to consider, inter alia, the efficiency characteristics of various remedies for breach.  We should invoke those remedies that encourage breach when breach is Pareto-superior to performance and discourage it otherwise.  There is a long distance, however, between simply stating this goal with regard to remedies and deciding which among the numerous remedies is the most efficient.
The bulk of the scholarship on efficient remedies has concerned the award of money damages, and a consensus has been reached on the form of damages that is most likely to promote economic efficiency.Alternatives to money damages have not received the same attention from lawyers and economists who have written on the efficiency aspects of contract law.  For example, specific performance, the most notable alternative form of court-imposed remedy for breach of contract, has only rarely been subjected to the same sort of scrutiny under the efficiency criterion as has money damages.Nor has there been sufficient attention paid to what might be called party-designed or self-help means of achieving enforcement of value-maximizing reciprocal promises through, for example, liquidated damage clauses, arbitration, and bonding.  Nor has there been enough written on the role that market forces, such as a regard for one's future business reputation, might play in mitigating inefficient breach of contract.
The purpose of this essay is to begin the development of an integrated theory of contract remedies by delineating the circumstances under which courts should simply enforce a stipulated remedy clause or grant relief to the innocent party in the form of damages or specific performance.  The conclusion, in brief, is that in the absence of stipulated remedies in the contract that survive scrutiny on the usual formation defenses, specific performance is more likely than any form of money damages to achieve efficiency in the exchange and breach of reciprocal promises.  If specific performance is the routine remedy for breach, there are strong reasons for believing, first, that more mutually beneficial exchanges of promises will be concluded in the future andthat they will be exchanged at a lower cost than under any other contract remedy, and, second, that under specific performance postbreach adjustments to all contracts will be resolved in a manner most likely to lead to the promise being concluded in favor of the party who puts the highest value on the completed performance and at a lower cost than under any alternative.
The argument proceeds by examining the relationship between different contract remedies and the costs imposed on contracting parties and on society at the time that promises are exchanged and during negotiations, if any, after the breach.  A central tenet of the argument is that the transaction costs facing parties who have already concluded a contract are less, even if there has been a breach, than the costs of a court's resolving the dispute.
In Part I the notion of an efficient breach is explained and the theoretical literature on the efficiency aspects of remedies for breach other than specific performance are explored.  In Part II, I discuss the role of certain nonlegal, market forces (such as reputation) in obtaining efficient breach, the efficacy of self-help measures such as bonding, arbitration, and liquidated damages, and then, in Part III, the traditional measures of money damages -- restitution, reliance, and expectation.  Part IV makes the case for specific performance as the routine remedy for breach by discussing its effect on contract formation costs and on post-breach negotiation costs.  I also discuss what defenses a promisor might be allowed to mount against specific performance and, therefore, under what circumstances courts should award money damages rather than grant equitable relief to the nonbreaching party.

questions.question: Does routinely ordering actual completion of promised contractual performance rather than awarding money damages produce more efficient contracting outcomes (more mutually beneficial exchanges, lower transaction and renegotiation costs, and post-breach allocation to the party who values performance most)?

Can party-designed enforcement mechanisms and market forces (pre-agreed penalties, private arbitration, bonding, reputational incentives) reliably yield efficient breach outcomes without judicial intervention, and under what conditions do they succeed or fail?
When should courts enforce parties' stipulated remedies as written versus substitute judicial remedies (monetary or in-kind) in order to maximize overall economic efficiency?

matched_themes: How should courts treat pre-agreed breach payments and liquidated damages clauses (enforce, reform, apportion, or void)?
Should courts allow apportionment of contractual damages when the non-breaching party's reliance or failure to cooperate contributed to the loss?
What counterfactual baseline should courts use to measure plaintiffs' losses for compensation purposes?
Does giving the promisee a unilateral right to demand performance or elect a damages measure that captures promisor's forgone gains vindicate moral intuitions while preserving ex post efficiency?
Do pre-agreed breach-payment clauses (liquidated damages) change parties' beliefs about norms and moral aversion to breach, and do such clauses increase or decrease the willingness to breach?
Do courts actually prefer monetary damages over specific (in-kind) remedies, or do they grant specific relief except when independent reasons exist to deny it?
When should courts order specific performance (in-kind relief) versus awarding monetary damages?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?
Should the promisor or the promisee have the default right to choose between performance and payment to achieve allocative efficiency?
Should parties be presumptively permitted to contractually specify nonstandard damage remedies, or should courts retain authority to impose defaults?
Does making in-kind performance the legal default (rather than monetary compensation) change parties' enforcement choices, moral judgments, and economic efficiency?
When should courts prefer or enforce in-kind (specific) performance rather than monetary damages for breach of contract?
When and to what extent should private self-help (withholding performance, repossession, or force) be permitted as a contract-enforcement mechanism?
How should courts treat and enforce stipulated remedies (liquidated damages clauses) versus substituting judicial remedies?
How do transaction costs, enforcement frictions, and institutional realities alter the theoretical efficiency of breach-plus-compensation?

Can party-designed enforcement mechanisms (pre-agreed penalties, arbitration, bonding, reputational systems) reliably produce efficient breach outcomes without judicial intervention, and when do they fail?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
Should courts police and limit supracompensatory contractual remedies (penalty-like clauses), or does allowing parties to contract for such terms respect autonomy and promote efficient contracting?
Do enforceable contractual damage remedies substitute for or complement informal relational governance in franchise and other repeated relationships?
Should contract damages be measured as lost surplus (net benefit) rather than expectancy or market value as a general rule?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
Do parties and courts actually choose heterogeneous, context-tailored damage provisions in contracting, and under what conditions would such customization be voluntarily chosen or socially desirable?
Do courts consider the breaching party's blameworthiness or opportunistic behavior when selecting among compensatory remedies?

Should contractual clauses that impose predetermined monetary payments for breach be treated as punitive (unenforceable) or as enforceable measures of compensation, and what factors predict courts' enforcement decisions?
To what extent should moral blameworthiness and non-economic considerations influence the design and application of contract remedies?
When is an indirect remedy (one that induces self-compliance) preferable to a direct remedy that delivers the outcome?
Should courts more readily grant equitable relief to compel performance when monetary damages undercompensate and public interests are implicated?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83lawcontempprob151!!ARTICLE: BLACK MARKETS AND THE EXCHANGE STRUCTURE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BLACK MARKETS AND THE EXCHANGE STRUCTURE

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules define and delimit permissible exchanges
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that law (through disabilities, price rules, spatial/temporal limits, and person- or purpose-based restrictions) creates the domain of prohibited exchanges (black markets) and thereby shapes what exchanges can lawfully occur; Paper B examines how contract law (through remedies and enforceability doctrines) structures which promissory exchanges will be consummated or breached and thus influences what kinds of reciprocal promises parties will enter into.

shared_topics.topic: choice of enforcement mechanism (disabling rules versus remedial sanctions) and their effects on behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes between legal disabilities that tie actors' hands and 'kickers' (supracompensatory civil/criminal sanctions) used to deter transgressive exchanges; Paper B analyzes the efficiency consequences of alternative remedial responses to breach (specific performance versus money damages and stipulated remedies) and how those remedies influence parties' incentives to perform or breach.

shared_topics.topic: economic efficiency and transaction costs as criteria for legal design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages law-and-economics discussions (citing Posner, Calabresi/Melamed) about when criminalization or other legal responses are justified to preserve exchange structures, emphasizing system survival and costs of allowing conversions; Paper B develops a transaction-cost and Pareto-efficiency account to recommend which remedies (particularly specific performance) best minimize bargaining and enforcement costs and promote value-maximizing exchanges.

shared_topics.topic: the role of private ordering and nonlegal forces (reputation, self-help, norms) in governing exchanges
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that many exchanges occur without law and that nonlegal norms and private ordering help maintain exchange structures alongside legal disabilities and sanctions; Paper B examines market-based enforcement (reputation), party-designed devices (liquidated damages, bonding, arbitration), and their capacity to achieve efficient outcomes without judicial intervention.

shared_topics.topic: preserving established exchange norms and preventing private reordering of transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames criminal and civil responses as tools to prevent actors from converting or undermining society's established transaction structure; Paper B considers how default remedies (especially routine specific performance) or contractible stipulated remedies affect parties' ability to reallocate entitlements post-contract and thereby preserve or alter the prevailing pattern of exchanges.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 70bulrev623!!ARTICLE: EQUITY TRANSFORMED: PRELIMINARY INJUNCTIONS TO REQUIRE THE PAYMENT OF MONEY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EQUITY TRANSFORMED: PRELIMINARY INJUNCTIONS TO REQUIRE THE PAYMENT OF MONEY

shared_topics.topic: when equity should displace or supplement legal remedies (money damages)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage the question whether courts should grant equitable relief even when money damages are the ultimate legal remedy — Paper A argues for preliminary injunctions ordering interim payments to plaintiffs despite the availability of a later money judgment, and Paper B argues for routine use of specific performance (an equitable remedy) instead of monetary damages in many contract breaches.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy of money damages and the 'adequate remedy at law' doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Both works critically examine the doctrine that money damages are an adequate remedy: Paper A challenges the historical and doctrinal basis for denying equitable relief because a legal remedy exists, while Paper B analyzes when monetary damages suffice and when they should be rejected in favor of specific performance.

shared_topics.topic: use of nontraditional criteria (harm, efficiency, and transaction costs) to choose remedies
shared_topics.justification: Each paper urges that courts consider broader criteria beyond historical formality — Paper A emphasizes secondary harms, indigency, and contemporary social needs to justify interim equitable payments, while Paper B applies economic efficiency and transaction-cost analysis to explain when specific performance promotes socially desirable outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: effects of remedy rules on parties' incentives, settlement and performance behavior
shared_topics.justification: Both examine how the choice of remedy shapes behavior: Paper A notes preliminary payments can prevent coerced low-value settlements and mitigate plaintiffs' incentives to accept undervalued resolutions, whereas Paper B focuses on how specific performance versus damages affects parties' incentives to enter, perform, breach, or renegotiate contracts.

shared_topics.topic: administrability and procedural burdens of imposing equitable relief
shared_topics.justification: Each article addresses practical and procedural limits on equitable remedies: Paper A defends interim payments against concerns about judicial administrative burden, Seventh Amendment rights, and due process, while Paper B evaluates enforcement costs, post-breach negotiation burdens, and practical defenses that bear on whether courts should order specific performance.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 55amjcompl721!!ARTICLE: Why No "Efficient Breach" in the Civil Law?: A Comparative Assessment of the Doctrine of Efficient Breach of Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Why No "Efficient Breach" in the Civil Law?: A Comparative Assessment of the Doctrine of Efficient Breach of Contract

shared_topics.topic: the doctrine and economic theory of efficient breach of contract
shared_topics.justification: Both papers centrally engage the concept of an 'efficient breach'—Paper A analyzes the origins, logic, and applicability of the efficient-breach doctrine (and why it has not been embraced in civil law systems), while Paper B explicates the efficient-breach notion as the motivating criterion for evaluating which contractual remedies promote Pareto-superior outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: how remedies (damages versus specific performance) shape efficiency of breach and contracting
shared_topics.justification: Both works examine how the choice of remedy influences whether breaches that increase total value will occur or be discouraged—Paper A frames efficient breach in terms of compensatory damages enabling Pareto improvements, and Paper B compares money damages and specific performance (arguing specific performance may better promote efficient contracting and post-breach allocation).

shared_topics.topic: the impact of legal-institutional structures and doctrines on incentives to breach
shared_topics.justification: Both papers consider how doctrinal rules and institutional features affect parties' incentives—Paper A studies structural and doctrinal obstacles in civil-law systems (good faith, pacta sunt servanda) that impede acceptance of efficient breach, while Paper B studies how court remedial rules (and related defenses) and transaction-cost differences shape contracting and breach behavior.

shared_topics.topic: the interplay between legal remedies and non-legal mechanisms (morality, good faith, reputation, self-help) in preventing or enabling inefficient breaches
shared_topics.justification: Both discuss extra-judicial factors that interact with remedies—Paper A emphasizes moral norms and good-faith traditions in civil law that resist breach-for-profit, and Paper B analyzes market forces and self-help (reputation, bonding, liquidated damages, arbitration) as alternatives or complements to judicial remedies in achieving efficient outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: appropriate legal remedies for breach of contract (money damages vs alternative remedies such as specific performance, liquidated damages, or nondischargeability)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when contract-derivative claims should result in nondischargeable obligations under bankruptcy law (treating certain breach damages as excepted from discharge), while Paper B systematically compares money damages, specific performance, and self-help remedies (liquidated damages, bonding, arbitration) under an efficiency framework.

shared_topics.topic: whether and when a contractual breach should be treated as tortious or warrant punitive/non-compensatory consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses the doctrinal and policy question whether breaches can be 'willful and malicious' (a tort-like basis to deny discharge and justify punitive treatment), and Paper B contrasts moral/punitive views with the economic notion of efficient breach, asking when law should discourage versus permit or price breaches.

shared_topics.topic: use of policy and incentive analysis to allocate costs and shape remedies for breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A weighs competing policy goals (debtor's fresh start vs creditor protection) to argue when nondischargeability is appropriate, and Paper B uses transaction-cost and efficiency reasoning to recommend which remedies (e.g., specific performance) best align parties' incentives and minimize social costs.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between contract remedies and external institutional enforcement mechanisms (bankruptcy, market-based enforcement, and self-help)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates contract breaches within the bankruptcy regime—examining how discharge rules and exceptions affect enforcement of contractual liabilities—while Paper B examines how market forces (reputation), contractually-stipulated remedies, and self-help devices interact with court-imposed remedies to achieve enforcement and efficiency.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 52ucdavislrev637!!ARTICLE: Retribution in Contract Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Retribution in Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: the theory of efficient breach and its implications for remedy design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops and invokes the efficient-breach framework to evaluate which remedies (damages, specific performance, or stipulated clauses) best promote value-maximizing exchanges, and Paper B treats efficient-breach theory as the dominant orthodox account that it interrogates against alternative concerns like retribution and deterrence.

shared_topics.topic: whether courts should award specific performance or money damages to promote efficient outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that specific performance is often the remedy most likely to achieve efficiency in formation and post-breach renegotiation, while Paper B engages this choice by analyzing how courts select among performance-directed remedies (cost of completion, disgorgement) and monetary measures to incentivize or discourage performance.

shared_topics.topic: the role of promisor blameworthiness or moral considerations in selecting remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts Holmes' rejection of moralizing contract law with an economic efficiency approach (noting the moral repugnance of breach), and Paper B centrally examines how courts in practice and doctrine factor the breaching party's blameworthy or opportunistic behavior into remedy selection despite the formal compensation-only stance.

shared_topics.topic: judicial discretion and doctrinal limits on compensatory damages in light of parties' behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys traditional measures (expectation, reliance, restitution) and defenses to specific performance while assessing their efficiency effects, and Paper B analyzes case law showing that judges apply rules like certainty, foreseeability, and choice between alternative compensatory formulas differently depending on the breaching party's conduct and available remedial options (including disgorgement).

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2001wislrev681!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:COMMENTARY BREACH AND PENALTY AS CONTRACTUAL NORM AND CONTRACTUAL ANOMIE
compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:COMMENTARY BREACH AND PENALTY AS CONTRACTUAL NORM AND CONTRACTUAL ANOMIE

shared_topics.topic: use of contractual penalties and stipulated remedies (liquidated damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically documents the high prevalence and judicial tolerance of penalty clauses in Russian commercial contracts and analyzes factors predicting their use; Paper B treats stipulated remedies (including liquidated damages) as party-designed enforcement devices and evaluates their efficiency relative to damages and specific performance.

shared_topics.topic: the concept and legitimacy of efficient breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates whether Russian firms view efficient breach as legitimate and whether penalty use deters opportunistic refusal to perform, while Paper B centers on the efficient-breach framework and asks which remedies (damages, specific performance, or stipulated remedies) best promote Pareto-superior breaches.

shared_topics.topic: the role of nonlegal market mechanisms (reputation, long‑term relationships, self‑help) in achieving enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares legal activism to reliance on nonlegal remedies such as cooperation based on longstanding trading relationships and finds limited evidence that relationships reduce penalties; Paper B analyzes how market forces (reputation), bonding, arbitration, and other self-help arrangements can substitute for or complement judicial remedies to induce efficient performance.

shared_topics.topic: how institutional and judicial context shapes contracting behavior and remedy choice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links Russian institutional features — legal disorganization, judicial tolerance of penalties, and modes of legal activism — to distinctive contracting practices that depart from Western predictions; Paper B examines how courts' remedy rules (e.g., routine specific performance versus monetary damages) affect ex ante contract formation, ex post renegotiation costs, and the set of exchanges parties are willing to enter.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 54arizlrev673!!ARTICLE: How Law Frames Moral Intuitions: The Expressive Effect of Specific Performance
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: How Law Frames Moral Intuitions: The Expressive Effect of Specific Performance

shared_topics.topic: choice of default remedy: specific performance versus expectation damages
shared_topics.justification: Both papers address whether courts should make specific performance or expectation (money) damages the default legal remedy for breach; Paper A argues theoretically that specific performance can be the routine remedy to promote efficiency, while Paper B empirically interrogates and challenges the wisdom of making specific performance the default by showing its behavioral effects.

shared_topics.topic: the economic concept of 'efficient breach' and its implications for remedy design
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the efficient-breach framework—Paper A develops how different remedies (especially specific performance) affect parties' incentives to breach or perform and claims specific performance better aligns incentives, while Paper B tests and questions those efficiency claims by showing that legal framing can make promisees resist efficient breaches.

shared_topics.topic: how remedy rules affect contract formation and post‑breach renegotiation costs (transaction costs)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how remedy rules influence the costs of forming contracts and of negotiating after breach; Paper A argues specific performance reduces formation and post‑breach transaction costs and leads to lower‑cost, value‑maximizing exchanges, whereas Paper B examines (with experimental evidence) how a specific‑performance default can increase bargaining frictions and make renegotiation more costly by generating moral resistance.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between legal rules and moral/behavioral responses (expressive effects, reputation, and enforcement by private parties)
shared_topics.justification: Both works consider how law interacts with nonlegal forces and moral views—Paper A discusses moral interpretations of promises, reputation, and self‑help enforcement (liquidated damages, bonding, arbitration) as complements or substitutes to legal remedies, while Paper B empirically documents that the legal availability of specific performance alters moral intuitions and resentment, changing how parties behave and enforce contracts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1397!!ARTICLE: A COMPARATIVE FAULT DEFENSE IN CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A COMPARATIVE FAULT DEFENSE IN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: economic efficiency as the normative criterion for contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Both papers evaluate contract doctrines through an economic-efficiency lens — Paper A uses efficiency to compare remedies (specific performance vs money damages and self-help mechanisms), while Paper B argues for a comparative-fault defense because it would produce more efficient cooperation and reliance incentives.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules shape parties' incentives to perform, breach, cooperate, or avoid overreliance
shared_topics.justification: Both works analyze the incentive effects of doctrines — Paper A examines how remedies influence parties' choices to enter bargains and whether to breach or perform, and Paper B focuses on how apportioning fault would induce promisees to cooperate and avoid excessive reliance while preserving promisors' incentive to perform.

shared_topics.topic: allocation and apportionment of loss following breach

papers.node_id: 78mdlrev147!!ARTICLE: THE ERROR THEORY OF CONTRACT
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE ERROR THEORY OF CONTRACT
papers.abstract:
Many people have false beliefs about contract law. They falsely believe contract formation depends on the agreement being signed and in writing.They falsely believe unlawful terms, like a lease term that requires a tenant rather than the landlord to perform maintenance on an apartment, are legally enforceable.They may falsely believe subjective rather than objective meanings of contract terms are legally binding.And, they falsely believe specific performance rather than damages is the standard remedy for breach of contract.Moreover, the phenomenon of false beliefs about contract doctrine is heterogeneous. Not everyone has these false beliefs, and people who hold one such false belief sometimes do not hold others. But the phenomenon is pervasive. A substantial proportion of the population is mistaken about one or more of the major elements of contract doctrine.
Courts and scholars, with few exceptions,have largely ignored these pervasive patterns of false beliefs about contract law.Other areas of law, notably criminal law, have grappled with the potentially important implications of ignorance of law through their doctrines of mistake.Contract law, for its part, has well-developed doctrines to handle mistakes of fact but failedto address the problem of mistakes of law in a meaningful way.A constellation of doctrines designed to account for mistakes of fact guide courts in deciding cases involving false beliefs about the facts underlying a contract- for example, in the classic case, whether a cow the buyer purchased was barren.But the courts' treatment of mistake of law in contracts cases is limited to situations involving false beliefs about areas of law other than contract law - for example, where the parties were ignorant of the rule against perpetuities.In light of that limitation, contract doctrine does not concern itself with the question of whether the contracting parties know contract law or not. Scholarship on mistake in contract law mirrors that limitation by focusing on mistakes of fact to the exclusion of mistakes of law.Despite that neglect by courts and commentators, the phenomenon of legal ignorance about contract law has profound, if unrecognized, practical and theoretical implications.
This Article will advance the error theory of contract to fill that gap. Similar to other error theories advanced in analytic philosophy, the error theory of contract provides a conceptual framework for determining how widespread false beliefs undermine prevailing justificatory theories of contract.This Article's target is one of the most prominent and intuitive theories ofcontract law: the promise or consent theory of contract.According to the theory, often called the "autonomy" theory,the moral justification for the State holding people to contracts lies in their prior voluntary commitment to enter the agreement.The promise-or consent-based autonomy theory is deeply intuitive to many. We must agree to enter a contract. And, if that voluntary commitment to enter the contract is compromised, for example through coercion, we cannot justifiably be held to it - a contract made with a gun to your head is no contract at all. The essential ingredient of contracts, what makes them different from other legal obligations, is their voluntary character. For that reason, the promise-or consent-based autonomy theory serves as the primary theoretical alternative to the law and economics analysis that otherwise dominates the discussion on the foundations of contract law.
This Article will seek to show that the autonomy theory fails as a justification of existing contract law. To do so, this Article will establish three conclusions. First, there is pervasive error, a fact supported by empirically confirmable, robustly observed patterns of false beliefs about contract doctrine among non-lawyers. Second, pervasive error about contract doctrine undermines the viability of promise-and consent-based autonomy theories of contract in a wide range of cases. Third, the failure of those theories of contract has significant implications for ongoing disputes about contract doctrine and the problem of boilerplate.
This Article will proceed to those conclusions as follows. Part I will synthesize and contribute to the growing body of empirical evidence that many people have false beliefs about the content of contract doctrine. First, Section I.A will present the evidence of people's widespread false beliefs about contract formation. That evidence will show that people often think that a contract is formed when they formally sign the contract, rather than when (as contract doctrine holds) the parties manifest mutual assent. Section I.B will then present the existing evidence that many people have false beliefs about whether particular invalid contract terms are legally enforceable, using the context of residential leases as an example.
Finally, Section I.C will report the results of a new empirical study regarding people's beliefs about contract remedies. The study surveyed a nationally representative sample of 1,000 subjects about whether they believe specific performance or damages is the typical remedy for breach of contract. The results of the study, the first of its kind, will indicate that (1) a substantial portion of the population falsely believes specific performance is the standard remedy for breach and that (2) an additional significant portion is simply ignorant of the correct legal answer. Moreover, the study's results will show that meaningful inequalities in the distribution of false beliefs and ignorance about contract remedies across educational level, income level, and gender.
Part II will then argue that widespread false beliefs and legal ignorance about contract doctrine poses a fundamental challenge to promise-and consent-based autonomy theories of contract law. Section II.A will present the core challenge to those theories: Under an autonomy theory, it is morally unjustifiable for the State to hold people to bargains with implied terms, supplied by the law, about which they are critically mistaken. Because people have false beliefs about the content of contract doctrine, they have false beliefs about implicit, legally-implied terms of the contract that they often find important to the value of the contract. For example, when people falsely believe the remedy for breach is specific performance, they believe their contract includes an implicit remedial term that differs importantly from the implicit remedial term the law actually provides. Contract doctrine thus enforces a bargain that is materially different from the one to which they thought they agreed: People pay a contract price they think purchases them a guarantee of performance, but the law ultimately provides them only with money damages. As a result, the normative basis for contract doctrine cannot be grounded in the parties' actual promise or consent - because many people, due to their false beliefs about contract doctrine, often do not actually consent to the terms of the bargain that contract doctrine enforces.
Sections II.B and II.C will in turn argue that the two strategies adopted by promise and consent theories to justify default doctrinal rules falter in light of widespread false beliefs and ignorance about contract doctrine. First, Professor Randy Barnett's consent-by-reference approach, which supposes that people give blanket consent to whatever rules the law imposes regardless of their content,fails because people do not give blanket consent to terms that contradict their affirmatively false beliefs about the law. Second, Professor Charles Fried's appeal to secondary norms aside from autonomy, like efficiency or fairness,fails because in order to succeed, its appeal to secondarynorms would replace, not supplement, the autonomy norms that were supposed to be the core of the theory. Part II will, therefore, conclude that the promise-or consent-based autonomy theory fails to justify contract doctrine.
Finally, Part III will explore the practical implications of that failure of promise-and consent-based autonomy theories for ongoing debates about contract doctrine. Section III.A will argue that in light of pervasive false beliefs about important aspects of contract doctrine, the autonomy theory leads to the implication that vast numbers of contracts are voidable under the doctrine of unilateral mistake. That implication is unpalatable because it would undermine the reliable system of commercial transactions the law of contract must serve to support. For that reason, the proper move for the autonomy theorist is to turn to other, second-best normative theories as a foundation for contract law.
Section III.B will suggest that this argument may in turn provide a new basis for making progress in the long-running debate between different normative foundations for the doctrinal rules of contract. Those debates - most commonly between those who adopt an autonomy approach based on promissory morality and those who adopt a law and economics consequentialist approach - typically amount to fundamental disagreements about normative first premises. But if an autonomy theory cannot justify a workable system of contract, even on its own terms, then we may have no choice but to look to other norms to craft contract doctrine. That, in turn, has far-reaching doctrinal implications. Doctrines as diverse as consideration, mitigation, remedies, unconscionability, and the objective requirement of assent all plausibly depend on whether we start out with a promise-or consent-based normative foundation, or a law and economics foundation. The foundational failure of the autonomy theory might allow us to resolve those debates.
Section III.C will then explore the implications of legal ignorance about contract doctrine for the problem of boilerplate. One core problem with boilerplate, as several courts and scholars currently conceive it, is many people are ignorant of boilerplate terms and, therefore, do not consent to them. That focus misses the real problem. Because many people are also ignorant of the background contract doctrine that would apply in the absence of boilerplate terms, people are ignorant of, and, therefore, do not consent to, the relevant implicit or explicit terms either way. The unique problem presented by boilerplate is thus neither knowledge nor consent, but rather that boilerplate typically offers terms that are substantively slanted in favor of the firms that draft them. Once the actual problem comes into focus, we can see the crux of the solution is not to ban boilerplate, but to regulate its content so it is not so unfair. Finally, because non-lawyers often use the text of their contracts - even their boilerplate contracts - as reference tools to determine their legalrights once a problem or dispute arises, it may even be beneficial to encourage well-regulated boilerplate to help to ameliorate the problem of legal ignorance after the fact.
This Article's conclusion will set the agenda going forward. It first frames the theoretical questions about how a justificatory theory of contract law must respond to the error theory in order to salvage its normative accounts of contract doctrine. That path is challenging but well-trodden for the law and economics approach, which has in recent years adapted to other forms of bounded rationality developed by the behavioral law and economics movement. But the challenge for an autonomy theory is more profound. Finally, the conclusion will offer some preliminary remarks on how the error theory of contract might serve as a model for theoretical and practical accounts of false legal belief and legal ignorance in other private law contexts, including tort, bankruptcy, and corporate law.
I. The Empirical Evidence of False Beliefs About Contract Doctrine
The growing body of empirical evidence regarding people's beliefs about contract doctrine reveals a complicated factual landscape with contours of knowledge and ignorance. This Part synthesizes the existing empirical evidence on false beliefs and legal ignorance about contract law and contributes a new study to the literature. Sections I.A and I.B draw on empirical studies in the literature regarding people's beliefs about contract formation and the enforceability of certain unlawful contract terms. Section I.C presents the results of a new empirical study regarding people's false beliefs about contract remedies. In particular, the study tested whether people believe specific performance or damages is the remedy for breach of contract.

papers.node_id: 2013michstlrev1!!ARTICLE: THE EXPECTATION MEASURE AND ITS DISCONTENTS
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE EXPECTATION MEASURE AND ITS DISCONTENTS
papers.authors: Shawn J. Bayern; Melvin Aron Eisenberg
papers.abstract:
Under the indifference principle in contract law, the remedies for breach of contract should "leave the promisee absolutely indifferent, in subjective terms, between having the defendant breach and pay damages or having the defendant perform."This principle underlies the expectation-based remedies that are central to contract law--in particular, the expectation measure of damages, which serves as a surrogate for the "indifference principle."
Traditional economic analysis recognized that the expectation measure is supported by strong reasons of efficiency.Recently, however, some law-and-economists have criticized the expectation measure, and by implication the indifference principle, on instrumental grounds. The criticisms fall into two categories. Some critics argue that the goals of the indifference principle would be best served by modifying the expectation measure.Other critics argue that contract law should aim to achieve other goals entirely and then develop alternative economic models and remedial regimes based onthose goals.Part I of this Article briefly summarizes the strengths of the indifference principle and the expectation measure. Parts II and III consider prominent alternative models and remedial regimes.
This Article has a substantive and a methodological aspect. The substantive aspect analyzes the validity of the alternative models and regimes apart from questions of administrability and institutional issues. The methodological aspect examines the administrability of these models and regimes and the congruence between the models and regimes, on the one hand, and institutional considerations, on the other.

questions.question: Whether damages calculated to leave the promisee indifferent between breach-plus-payment and performance (i.e., expectation-based remedies) best promote the goals of contract law compared with alternative remedial objectives.

Whether alternative remedial models or objectives (including modified monetary measures or non-monetary remedies) are substantively justified and administrable given practical institutional constraints.

matched_themes: Should parties and courts adopt fault-based remedial regimes that distinguish among breaches by reason when allocating remedies?
What counterfactual baseline should courts use to measure plaintiffs' losses for compensation purposes?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?
Should the promisor or the promisee have the default right to choose between performance and payment to achieve allocative efficiency?
How do institutional features-court capacity, procedural devices, and evidentiary rules-affect the substantive development and practical application of contract remedies?
How do transaction costs, enforcement frictions, and institutional realities alter the theoretical efficiency of breach-plus-compensation?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
Can courts reliably determine ex post whether a breach would increase social welfare so that remedy choice can be used to promote efficiency?
To what extent does empirical uncertainty about measuring gains and losses limit courts' ability to design remedies that reflect non-welfare ethical preferences without sacrificing efficiency?
Are court-ordered in-kind remedies actually implemented and practically enforceable compared with money judgments?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
When is an indirect remedy (one that induces self-compliance) preferable to a direct remedy that delivers the outcome?

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the material-breach doctrine that permits a nonbreaching party to suspend or terminate its own performance (rather than continue and sue), while Paper B evaluates the expectation measure and alternative remedial regimes that determine when damages — instead of continued performance or other relief — should be the appropriate response to breach.

shared_topics.topic: normative goals of contract doctrine (efficiency versus good faith/fairness)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds its critique and proposed reform of material-breach doctrine in promoting good-faith performance and appropriate policy objectives, and Paper B interrogates the indifference/expectation principle's efficiency rationale and considers critiques that contract law should pursue other goals such as fairness or different social objectives.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal clarity, administrability, and the proper role of courts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes courts' inconsistent application of material-breach and constructive-condition doctrines and urges a clearer doctrinal framework (invoking Jacob & Youngs), while Paper B explicitly examines the administrability and institutional fit of the expectation measure and alternative remedial models, assessing how legal rules can be implemented by courts.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: PROMISSORY FRAUD WITHOUT BREACH

shared_topics.topic: limits of the expectation measure and when alternative remedies are appropriate

shared_topics.topic: the role of tort/fraud liability as a supplement or substitute for contract enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops promissory fraud as a tort-like doctrine that can impose compensatory and punitive liability where contract remedies are unavailable or inappropriate, and Paper B considers alternative remedial regimes (beyond pure expectation damages) that may serve similar corrective or deterrent functions.

shared_topics.topic: administrability, evidentiary burdens, and institutional fit of remedial doctrines (intent, causation, enforceability)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grapples with proving present intent, proximate causation for deceit damages, and how rules like the Statute of Frauds affect availability of remedies, while Paper B explicitly evaluates the administrability of alternative damage measures and the congruence between theoretical models of remedies and institutional/practical constraints.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: MODERN MARINE INSURANCE: COVERAGES, CURRENT ISSUES, AND CONNECTIONS:Reform of the Insurance Law of England and Wales - Separate Laws for the Different Needs of Businesses and Consumers

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Fixer Upper: Buyer Deposits in Residential Real Estate Transactions

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE FUTURE OF LAW AND ECONOMICS: THE TROUBLES WITH LAW AND ECONOMICS.

shared_topics.topic: the normative foundations and goals of legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A, through its critical, philosophical cast, questions the normative assumptions that underlie law-and-economics reasoning, while Paper B directly analyzes the normative basis of contract remedies (the indifference principle) and debates whether different substantive goals should drive remedial design.
