shared_topics.justification: Paper A's project—assessing the 'future' and 'troubles' of law-and-economics—raises concerns about how abstract economic reasoning maps onto legal practice and institutions; Paper B explicitly examines the administrability of alternative models and the congruence between theoretical remedies and institutional constraints.

papers.node_id: 73washulq145!!ARTICLE: THE FALLACY OF FULL COMPENSATION
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE FALLACY OF FULL COMPENSATION
papers.abstract:
The American legal system could provide full compensation if we wished. The civil remedies of specific performance, injunctions and restitution would accomplish the task in a wide variety of cases. Nevertheless, the civil system has been reluctant to employ these full compensation remedies, what this Article shall term "prohibitory remedies," opting repeatedly for obviously insufficient damages measured by plaintiff's loss. The civil system's preference for damages and concomitant reluctance to employ prohibitory remedies more regularly has been castigated as "materialistic,""niggardly,""amoral,"and showing "a marked solicitude for men who do not keep their promises."Indeed, the large weight of academic commentary is decidedly condemnatory.
Perhaps because of the rather dogmatic and monolithic bent of the academic commentary, the law's predilection for incomplete remedies has been largely without apologists, save for the economist-lawyers who have protested that remedies ensuring full compensation would be preferred were it not for the omnipresent transactions costs that stand in the way.Even this limited economic justification for the predominance of undercompensatory damages has been thoroughly challenged on the ground that the transactions costs of prohibitory remedies compare favorably with those of damages.
The more obvious line of defense has not been pursued. As Professor Schwartz has noted, one possible reason why full compensation, here referring to specific performance, is not routinely available is that "the law's commitment to the compensation goal may be less than complete; restricting specific performance may reflect an inarticulate reluctance to pursue the compensation goal fully."Schwartz, like others after him, declined to address that possibility, preferring to "presuppose[] the desirability of the compensation goal … [because] neither [a descriptive nor normative theory] exists at present and creating them is beyond the scope of this Article."
Yet it is this line of inquiry that appears most productive, for it promises to move the debate away from the bottomless speculation about transactions costs to the more significant and logically prior question of whether the law ought to be committed to providing full compensation as the proponents of prohibitory remedies assume. Taking up the challenge implicit in Schwartz's discussion, this Article attempts to provide a descriptive and normative theory for the law's apparent disinclination to provide fully compensatory remedies.
Understanding the reluctance of the remedial system to provide full compensation requires first a focus on the commentators' criticisms of the prevalent damages remedy. According to the critics, the traditional damages remedy should not continue to predominate because it fails to provide adequate deterrence against wrongdoing,because it fails to require full compensation,because it does not maximize wealth and achieve efficiency,because it lacks commensurability with the harm,because it signifies the "commodification" of personal rights and interests,and because it is simply not the right thing to do.
Instead of maintaining the dominance of the damages remedy, the legal system should, according to the critics, supplant it substantially with "prohibitory remedies" that prescribe a form of full compensation to be accorded the plaintiff. Prohibitory remedies differ from damages remedies in that they are designed to stop or undo completed transactions, even involuntary ones. Unlike damages, prohibitory remedies are not justified on the basis of harm caused, but rather on the basis of risk imposed; they seek not to channel private risk-taking, but to prohibit it; if substitutionary, they are measured not by harm, but by gain; they are not derived from private agreement or private markets, but by court decree; and they signify an attempt to generate appropriate, safety-producing behavior and adequate compensation by judicial order, and thus do not depend upon a defendant "correctly" configuring potential gains and potential losses prior to taking action.In short, prohibitory remedies attempt to "prohibit" harms;damages remedies "price" them.
There are two problems, one practical and one normative, with a remedial system that employs prohibitory remedies to provide full compensation. First, practically, prohibitory remedies will not necessarily produce deterrence, compensation, wealth, efficiency, or justice any better than do damages remedies; in fact, in many cases they may do worse. Second, normatively, the goal that underlies prohibitory remedies, that is, full compensation, is not the unblemished good that the critics have presumed it to be. Full compensation may only be achieved at a cost, not just to defendants but to society, and it may be a cost that society prefers not to bear. This practical and normative attack on full compensation also provides the practical and normative justification for its denial.
Parts II and III discuss the practical problem with prohibitory remedies, that they are in fact inadequate to the tasks the critics have posited for them. First, Part II outlines the central and pervasive dichotomy in the law of remedies between pricing remedies and prohibitory remedies, and attempts to characterize the remedies of injunctions, specific performance, restitution, and some others as prohibitory in nature. Next, Part III examines the effectiveness of prohibitory remedies at fulfilling the central tasks of the law of remedies, those of reducing the incidence of harm and assuring compensation. Regarding harm, it argues that the routine employment of prohibitory remedies will not only fail to reduce the risk of harm but may actually tend to increase the incidence of undesirable harm-causing activity. Similarly, it contends that the goal of full compensation will likewise tend to be frustrated by the widespread adoption of prohibitory remedies.
Parts IV and V present the normative justification for a remedial system that relegates prohibitory remedies, and thus full compensation, to a secondary role. First, Part IV questions the desirability of a remedial system that actually seeks to compensate plaintiffs fully. Prohibitory remedies represent a remedy that is at bottom a redistributional one, and not a corrective one; thus their implementation properly depends on allocational decisions that might sometimes disprefer a particular distribution, even one that appears "fully compensatory." Part V attempts a rehabilitation ofprohibitory remedies, suggesting a framework for their use that fulfills the more limited aims for which they are suited. Properly understood, prohibitory remedies provide needed deterrence in those cases where the predominate damages remedy is insufficient. This Part also suggests that the various "relegation doctrines" that traditionally inhibit the use of prohibitory remedies, such as the irreparable injury rule and the "uniqueness" test, properly maintain harm-based damages as the primary remedy and thus desirably limit compensation for the sake of maximizing social wealth and minimizing the needless infliction of harm.

questions.question: Are prohibitory or in-kind remedies that aim to provide full compensation more effective than monetary damages at deterring wrongful conduct and assuring victims are fully compensated?
Does pursuing full compensation through prohibitory remedies impose social or distributive costs that can justify restricting their routine use?
What normative framework should guide when courts should use prohibitory/in-kind remedies versus monetary damages to maximize social welfare and appropriate deterrence?

matched_themes: How do remedial rules for potentially illegal contracts affect parties' incentives to enter socially harmful or beneficial agreements?
Does giving the promisee a unilateral right to demand performance or elect a damages measure that captures promisor's forgone gains vindicate moral intuitions while preserving ex post efficiency?
Do courts actually prefer monetary damages over specific (in-kind) remedies, or do they grant specific relief except when independent reasons exist to deny it?
When should courts order specific performance (in-kind relief) versus awarding monetary damages?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?
Should the promisor or the promisee have the default right to choose between performance and payment to achieve allocative efficiency?
Does making in-kind performance the legal default (rather than monetary compensation) change parties' enforcement choices, moral judgments, and economic efficiency?
When should courts prefer or enforce in-kind (specific) performance rather than monetary damages for breach of contract?

Should remedies and contract law be structured to preserve conditions necessary for moral agency and promissory responsibility, rather than treating promises solely as instruments of economic cooperation?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
Should courts award disgorgement or force surrender of breacher gains in addition to compensation to deter opportunistic breaches?
Should courts limit recoverable consequential damages that are grossly disproportionate to the contract price, and would such limits promote economic efficiency?
Should courts strip breachers of gains (disgorgement) in opportunistic or deliberate breaches, and what are the doctrinal and incentive effects of allowing disgorgement remedies in contract law?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
When and under what standards should courts award disgorgement or remedies that strip gains from breaching parties?
To what extent should moral blameworthiness and non-economic considerations influence the design and application of contract remedies?
When is an indirect remedy (one that induces self-compliance) preferable to a direct remedy that delivers the outcome?
Should courts more readily grant equitable relief to compel performance when monetary damages undercompensate and public interests are implicated?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 80brooklynlrev173!!ARTICLE: The Compensation Myth and U.C.C. Section 2-713
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Compensation Myth and U.C.C. Section 2-713

shared_topics.topic: limits and desirability of full compensation/expectation damages
shared_topics.justification: Both papers question the assumption that legal remedies should or do provide full compensation — Paper A develops a normative and descriptive critique of seeking full compensation via prohibitory remedies, while Paper B calls the notion of market-based compensation a 'myth' and shows that the market-price formula in U.C.C. §2-713 does not reliably effect compensation.

shared_topics.topic: choice and limitation of remedial forms (pricing vs prohibitory remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Both examine why courts favor monetary (pricing) remedies over prohibitory relief and whether judicially limiting a plaintiff's or buyer's choice of remedy is justified — Paper A defends maintaining damages as primary over injunctions/specific performance, and Paper B analyzes judicial interference with buyers' remedy choices to prevent overcompensation under §2-713.

shared_topics.topic: how damages should be measured (harm-based vs gain-based and the role of market price)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the question of the proper metric for awards — Paper A contrasts harm-measured damages with gain-measured prohibitory remedies, and Paper B scrutinizes the assumption that the relevant market price (often cover price) is the correct measure under the U.C.C.'s market-price/contract-price formula.

shared_topics.topic: whether remedies achieve deterrence and economic efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Both papers interrogate the asserted economic functions of remedies: Paper A argues that prohibitory remedies may fail to reduce harm or improve wealth/efficiency, while Paper B demonstrates that expectation/market damages do not necessarily produce efficient incentives and that standard economic justifications for damages are flawed.

shared_topics.topic: practical and institutional constraints on changing remedial rules or statutes
shared_topics.justification: Both discuss the non-theoretical obstacles to remedial reform — Paper A defends doctrinal limits (e.g., irreparable injury, uniqueness) as socially and allocationally justified, and Paper B argues against repeal of §2-713 and for interpretive strategies because of drafting, political, and systemic consequences.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1349!!ARTICLE: LET US NEVER BLAME A CONTRACT BREAKER
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: LET US NEVER BLAME A CONTRACT BREAKER

shared_topics.topic: specific performance and other prohibitory remedies versus damages as the default remedy for breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends the common-law preference for damages and limits on specific performance (arguing contracts function as options and specific performance would thwart efficient breaches), while Paper B analyzes why courts systematically refrain from awarding specific performance, framing injunctions/restitution as 'prohibitory remedies' and defending the primacy of damages on practical and normative grounds.

shared_topics.topic: the economic efficiency of permitting 'efficient breaches' (allowing breach when social gains exceed plaintiff's loss)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly uses the efficient-breach argument to justify strict-liability damages and to oppose punitive or specific-performance remedies that would block socially beneficial reallocations; Paper B likewise evaluates how prohibitory remedies can frustrate wealth maximization and may produce worse deterrence or allocation outcomes than pricing remedies.

shared_topics.topic: restitution and disgorgement (awarding breacher's profits) as a remedial option in contract contexts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses restitution and windfall damages (including middleman profit awards and when disgorgement might be justified), arguing restraint because restitution can create a bilateral-monopoly problem, while Paper B treats restitution among the class of prohibitory remedies and assesses its redistributive consequences and limits on its desirability.

shared_topics.topic: transaction‑costs and default rules in allocating risk and choosing remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues strict liability for nonperformance functions as an insurance-like default that reduces transaction and litigation costs and allocates risk efficiently (with parties free to contract around it), whereas Paper B engages the transaction-costs defense of damages, critiques simplistic cost accounts, and incorporates transaction‑cost considerations into a defense of relegating prohibitory remedies to a secondary role.

shared_topics.topic: the normative foundations of remedial choice: moral fault/blame versus economic/allocative justifications
shared_topics.justification: Paper A rejects moralizing (fault/blame) in contract remedies and grounds rules in economic risk allocation and incentives, while Paper B questions the underlying normative commitment to 'full compensation' and argues remedial design should reflect redistributional and social‑welfare tradeoffs rather than a pure moral or compensationist dogma.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 116yaleljonline423!!ARTICLE: A Critique of the Efficient Performance Hypothesis
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Critique of the Efficient Performance Hypothesis

shared_topics.topic: whether specific performance (full compensation) should be the default or more widely available than expectation damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages this by evaluating Schwartz's proposal (and Brooks's variant) to give promisees stronger rights to performance and arguing that expectation damages better preserve ex post efficiency; Paper B addresses the same question by defending the law's reluctance to award full compensation and arguing that prohibitory remedies should be limited for practical and normative reasons.

shared_topics.topic: efficiency, deterrence, and transaction-cost tradeoffs between damages and prohibitory remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on ex post efficiency concerns—arguing that put-style remedies or hypothetical disgorgement can distort promisor opportunity-cost incentives—while Paper B systematically analyzes whether prohibitory remedies actually improve deterrence or social wealth compared with damages and whether transaction-cost explanations suffice.

shared_topics.topic: the conceptual framing of remedies as pricing/call options versus prohibitory/put options and the resulting allocation of choice rights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly applies option theory (call vs put) to show how expectation damages grant the promisor the choice to breach while put-like rules give the promisee choice, and Paper B advances a closely related dichotomy between 'pricing' remedies (damages) and 'prohibitory' remedies (specific performance, injunctions) and examines the consequences of that classification.

shared_topics.topic: normative/moral arguments about the nature of promises and redistributional consequences of awarding performance versus money
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates moral criticisms of expectation damages (the view that promises morally require performance) and whether remedies should respect promisees' moral right to performance, while Paper B questions whether full compensation is normatively desirable given its redistributive effects and social costs.

shared_topics.topic: the proposal that promisees be given an election between specific performance and expectation damages (Schwartz's rule) and its practical implications
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly analyzes and critiques Schwartz's elective rule (and Brooks's modifications), arguing about its moral appeal and efficiency costs; Paper B cites Schwartz's observation as motivation to ask whether the law should commit to full compensation and develops a descriptive and normative account of why the elective/full-compensation approach is not routinely adopted.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 55syracuselrev495!!ARTICLE: A UNIFYING THEORY OF CONTRACT DAMAGE RULES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A UNIFYING THEORY OF CONTRACT DAMAGE RULES

shared_topics.topic: the normative purposes of contract remedies (compensation vs deterrence vs efficiency)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers explicitly interrogate what remedies are meant to achieve: Paper A argues for a unifying, surplus-based compensatory rule that restores the injured party to the wellbeing they would have had after performance, while Paper B questions whether the law should pursue full compensation at all, weighing compensation against deterrence, wealth-maximization, and social costs.

shared_topics.topic: the role and justification of prohibitory (non-pricing) remedies such as specific performance and restitution
shared_topics.justification: Both engage substantively with non-damages remedies: Paper B centers its analysis on why courts limit specific performance, injunctions, and restitution and when they are normatively appropriate, and Paper A treats restitution and equitable principles as part of the remedial landscape while situating monetary damages (the Shadow Code) relative to these alternatives.

shared_topics.topic: economic and cost–benefit reasoning in designing remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Each paper uses economic-style reasoning to justify remedy design: Paper A frames damages as restoring anticipated surplus and analogizes to Learned Hand cost–benefit analysis, whereas Paper B evaluates the economic arguments for and against full-compensation prohibitory remedies, including transaction costs and aggregate wealth effects.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal limits on recovery and their justificatory basis (mitigation, foreseeability, irreparable-injury/uniqueness, proof certainty)
shared_topics.justification: Both works treat limitation doctrines as central to remedy law: Paper A codifies limitations such as mitigation, foreseeability, and reasonable-certainty proof in its Section 4, and Paper B analyzes and defends relegation doctrines like irreparable injury and uniqueness as proper constraints on granting full compensatory prohibitory relief.

shared_topics.topic: how compensation should be measured (plaintiff's loss versus defendant's gain / expectation vs gain-based measures)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers debate measurement of relief: Paper A operationalizes damages as the difference between anticipated and actual surplus (an expectation/loss-based metric), while Paper B contrasts damages measured by plaintiff loss with prohibitory remedies that are often measured by the defendant's gain and explores the normative implications of each measurement approach.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 56sclrev93!!ARTICLE:The Shadow Code
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:The Shadow Code

shared_topics.topic: the compensation goal of contract remedies — whether damages should aim at full compensation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers the compensatory goal by proposing a single surplus-based rule that puts an injured party in the position they would have occupied had performance occurred, while Paper B directly questions the desirability and practical advisability of providing full compensation (via prohibitory remedies) rather than relying primarily on damages.

shared_topics.topic: how to measure and compute monetary relief (surplus-based formulas versus pricing/prohibitory calculations)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a concrete formula—anticipated surplus minus actual surplus—as a unifying computational method for damages across breach contexts, and Paper B contrasts pricing (damages) with prohibitory remedies that are measured differently (by gain or forced restitution) and debates the implications of those different measurement approaches.

shared_topics.topic: incentive effects of remedial rules on parties' behavior (deterrence, promise-making/breaking, mitigation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that its surplus-based structure facilitates theoretical analysis of incentives (to make or break promises and to mitigate losses), while Paper B analyzes whether prohibitory remedies or damages better achieve deterrence and how different remedies influence the incidence of harmful behavior.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal limits on recovery and their justification (mitigation, foreseeability, certainty, irreparable-injury/uniqueness doctrines)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A codifies traditional limits on damages—reasonable certainty, mitigation, foreseeability—into its SC 4 and explains how they fit the surplus rule, while Paper B surveys and defends doctrines that limit the use of prohibitory remedies (irreparable injury, uniqueness) as legitimate constraints on full compensation.

shared_topics.topic: trade-offs between individual compensation and broader social welfare or efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that aligning remedial rules with the surplus/compensatory goal clarifies incentives and preserves efficiency analyses, and Paper B normatively defends limiting full compensation on grounds that widespread use of prohibitory remedies can reduce social wealth or impose redistributional costs society may prefer to avoid.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 116wvalrev363!!ARTICLE: HYPOTHETICAL EFFICIENCY IS NOT GROUNDS FOR BREACH
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: HYPOTHETICAL EFFICIENCY IS NOT GROUNDS FOR BREACH

shared_topics.topic: normative assessment of damages versus prohibitory remedies (specific performance, injunctions, restitution)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers directly debate whether the law should treat damages as the primary response to contractual breaches or instead compel full performance or other prohibitory remedies: Paper A interrogates whether paying compensatory damages morally justifies breach (rejecting the 'efficient breach' rationale), while Paper B analyzes and defends the remedial system's preference for damages over routinely awarding full-compensation prohibitory remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the role of economic efficiency in justifying breach and remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Both works engage with economic arguments for remedy selection and conduct: Paper A critiques the use of efficiency as a moral compass for deciding to breach (targeting Steven Shavell's efficiency-based defense of breach-plus-damages), and Paper B examines and pushes back on economic defenses (e.g., transaction-cost and wealth-maximization rationales) for favoring damages over prohibitory remedies.

shared_topics.topic: legal doctrines and implied obligations that limit or shape the right to breach
shared_topics.justification: Both articles consider doctrinal mechanisms that constrain unilateral breach beyond the written bargain: Paper A distinguishes implied covenants (like good faith) from an implied covenant of efficiency and rejects importing an efficiency obligation into every contract, while Paper B discusses 'relegation doctrines' (irreparable injury, uniqueness tests) and other legal limits that preserve damages as the primary remedy.

shared_topics.topic: interaction of moral/normative considerations with remedial policy in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Both papers ground their remedial recommendations in normative reasoning about promises, responsibility, and social costs: Paper A foregrounds moral obligations of promise-keeping and relational values against 'just business' efficiency claims, and Paper B provides a normative critique of full compensation—arguing that full compensatory remedies carry redistributive and social costs that may counsel limiting their use.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 11texwesleyanlrev627!!SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:THE BOUNDARIES OF CONTRACT IN A GLOBAL ECONOMY:HADLEY V. BAXENDALE AND OTHER COMMON LAW BORROWINGS FROM THE CIVIL LAW
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:THE BOUNDARIES OF CONTRACT IN A GLOBAL ECONOMY:HADLEY V. BAXENDALE AND OTHER COMMON LAW BORROWINGS FROM THE CIVIL LAW

shared_topics.topic: limits on recoverable damages and remedial constraints (e.g., foreseeability and the denial of specific performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the doctrinal and policy reasons courts favor damages over prohibitory remedies like specific performance, while Paper B analyzes Hadley v. Baxendale as a foundational rule that limits recovery in contract law (foreseeability) and thereby constrains the scope of damages.

shared_topics.topic: descriptive vs. normative explanations for why courts adopt particular remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops both descriptive and normative theories for the law's reluctance to provide full compensation, and Paper B historicizes Hadley (asking whether the rule was judicial invention or borrowed) and evaluates the origins and justifications of the foreseeability limitation.

shared_topics.topic: trade-offs among compensation, deterrence, and social costs in remedy design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that full compensation can impose broader social costs and may not achieve better deterrence or efficiency, and Paper B treats Hadley's limitation on damages as a rule that balances commercial predictability and allocative consequences of exposing defendants to open-ended liability.

shared_topics.topic: the role of judicial lawmaking and doctrinal borrowing in shaping remedies and limits on liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques and defends judicial doctrines (irreparable injury, uniqueness) that limit prohibitory remedies, and Paper B documents and assesses how common-law courts borrowed civil-law concepts to create or shape the Hadley rule limiting contract damages.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1583!!ARTICLE: THE FAULT PRINCIPLE AS THE CHAMELEON OF CONTRACT LAW: A MARKET FUNCTION APPROACH
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE FAULT PRINCIPLE AS THE CHAMELEON OF CONTRACT LAW: A MARKET FUNCTION APPROACH

shared_topics.topic: when to prefer damages (pricing) versus prohibitory/strict remedies (specific performance or strict liability)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the doctrinal and normative divide between damages (pricing remedies) and prohibitory remedies like specific performance or injunctions, arguing why the law routinely prefers undercompensatory damages; Paper B addresses the parallel choice in contract law between fault-based liability and strict (no-fault) liability, treating strict liability as the heavier sanction and asking when it should apply.

shared_topics.topic: efficiency, social costs, and transaction-cost-based justifications for remedial regimes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques transaction-cost and efficiency explanations for favoring or rejecting full-compensation prohibitory remedies and foregrounds broader social costs; Paper B evaluates liability regimes through economic and market-function lenses, weighing efficiency and transaction-cost considerations in choosing between strict and fault liability.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal devices that limit or temper the application of severe remedies (e.g., 'second chance' / Nachfrist, irreparable-injury/uniqueness tests)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends relegation doctrines (irreparable injury rule, uniqueness test) as proper limits on using prohibitory remedies; Paper B examines Nachfrist/the 'second chance' principle and other devices that similarly restrict when the harshest contractual sanctions (strict liability) should be imposed.

shared_topics.topic: comparative and normative assessment of remedy/liability regimes across legal systems
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a descriptive and normative theory explaining why common remedial choices prevail and when prohibitory remedies are normatively justified, while Paper B uses comparative law (civil/common law, CISG, European principles) to map how different systems blend strict and fault liability and to prescribe a market-function approach.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 59ohiostlj339!!ARTICLE: Disproportionality and the Law of Consequential Damages: Default Theory and Cognitive Reality
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Disproportionality and the Law of Consequential Damages: Default Theory and Cognitive Reality

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal limits on awarding full or consequential compensation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the 'disproportionality' constraint that courts use to limit recovery of consequential contract damages, while Paper B examines the legal reluctance to award full-compensation 'prohibitory' remedies (specific performance, injunctions) and surveys doctrines (irreparable injury, uniqueness) that restrict such remedies.

shared_topics.topic: whether economic-efficiency and transaction-cost arguments justify denying full remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates disproportionality against standard default-rule and law-and-economics efficiency reasoning (finding little support absent behavioral departures), and Paper B assesses and critiques transactions-cost and efficiency defenses for favoring damages over full compensatory remedies.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and the role of foreseeability versus risk-imposition in remedy design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how parties price and allocate remote risks (foreseeability, underpriced risk premiums) and proposes disproportionality as a check when risk is underestimated, while Paper B contrasts harm-based damages with risk-based prohibitory remedies and interrogates when courts should prohibit risk-imposing transactions rather than merely price them.

shared_topics.topic: criteria for when exceptional, nonstandard remedies should apply
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes limiting disproportionality relief to situations involving infrequent or non-salient risks and inexperienced parties, and Paper B develops normative and practical frameworks (and relegation doctrines) for when prohibitory/full-compensation remedies are appropriate versus when damages should remain primary.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 81fordhamlrev1221!!ARTICLE: INSTRUCTING JURIES ON NONECONOMIC CONTRACT DAMAGES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: INSTRUCTING JURIES ON NONECONOMIC CONTRACT DAMAGES

shared_topics.topic: whether damages alone adequately compensate and when non-pricing remedies are appropriate
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly contests the presumption that the law should aim for ‘full compensation,’ contrasting pricing remedies (damages) with prohibitory remedies (specific performance, injunctions, restitution) and arguing why damages may be preferred; Paper B examines the traditional exclusion of noneconomic contract damages and whether the damages remedy as applied (via juries) actually compensates the real, foreseeable harms plaintiffs suffer.

shared_topics.topic: discrepancy between doctrinal pronouncements and on-the-ground remedial outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the divergence between academic/ doctrinal advocacy for full-compensation remedies and the legal system's persistent reliance on damages; Paper B documents a similar divide by showing that treatises and Restatements often proclaim a rule against noneconomic contract damages while pattern jury instructions and actual jury behavior reveal substantial state-by-state variation and a tendency to award such losses.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules and procedural devices channel which remedies are available and awarded
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes relegation doctrines (irreparable-injury rule, uniqueness tests) and other doctrinal gates that systematically limit use of prohibitory remedies; Paper B studies pattern jury instructions as the procedural instrument that largely determines whether juries will include noneconomic losses in contract awards.

shared_topics.topic: conceptualization and measurement of compensable harm (loss vs gain; economic vs noneconomic) and the normative trade-offs involved
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts remedies measured by plaintiff loss (damages) with prohibitory remedies measured by defendant gain and interrogates normative trade-offs among compensation, deterrence, and social cost; Paper B interrogates the boundary between economic and noneconomic harms in contract law, how foreseeability and measurement doctrines treat mental distress, and the implications of juror overcompensation for remedial objectives.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 90ucinlrev283!!ARTICLE: FORCE MAJEURE, VIS MAJOR, IMPOSSIBILITY, AND IMPRACTICABILITY UNDER OHIO LAW BEFORE AND AFTER COVID-19
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: FORCE MAJEURE, VIS MAJOR, IMPOSSIBILITY, AND IMPRACTICABILITY UNDER OHIO LAW BEFORE AND AFTER COVID-19

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk for unforeseen, disruptive events in contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how force majeure, impossibility, and impracticability doctrines (and boilerplate clauses) allocate the economic risk of COVID-19 disruptions between contracting parties under Ohio law; Paper B examines how remedial rules (damages versus prohibitory remedies) allocate costs and redistribute losses after breaches, implicating who ultimately bears risk when performance or protection is contested.

shared_topics.topic: judicial doctrines and discretion in enforcing or excusing contractual obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how courts should interpret and apply judicial doctrines (force majeure, vis major, impossibility, impracticability) to excuse nonperformance in extraordinary circumstances; Paper B analyzes judicially-created 'relegation doctrines' (irreparable injury rule, uniqueness test) and the courts' discretionary role in limiting the availability of specific performance and other prohibitory remedies.

shared_topics.topic: law-and-economics reasoning (efficiency, transaction costs, deterrence) shaping doctrinal choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A invokes law-and-economics principles when assessing how Ohio courts likely would and should apply excuse doctrines to pandemic-related breaches; Paper B centrally evaluates economic justifications (transaction costs, efficiency, deterrence) both for and against privileging full compensation through prohibitory remedies over damage remedies.

shared_topics.topic: normative debate over full enforcement versus pragmatic limitation of remedies/obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages normative questions about whether doctrines should be applied leniently to excuse pandemic-driven nonperformance or strictly enforce contracts, and proposes how courts ought to balance fairness and predictability; Paper B explicitly challenges the desirability of pursuing 'full compensation' through prohibitory remedies and defends limiting full enforcement on practical and normative grounds (redistributional costs, social wealth maximization).

compared_to.partner_node_id: 117yalelj2!!ARTICLE: Contracting for Cooperation in Recovery
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contracting for Cooperation in Recovery

shared_topics.topic: the insufficiency of compensatory damages to police certain contractual breaches and the need for extracompensatory remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that compensatory expectation damages often cannot deter or remedy 'obstruction of recovery' (e.g., false certificates) and so calls for extracompensatory tools (penalties, punitive damages or fraud liability) to make cooperation clauses effective; Paper B similarly analyzes why ordinary damages leave victims undercompensated in many cases and evaluates whether non‑pricing 'prohibitory' remedies (specific performance, injunctions, restitution) should fill that gap.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs among deterrence, efficiency, and social costs when selecting remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses economic/instrumentalist reasoning to weigh the benefits of permitting punitive or liquidated remedies for no‑obstruct clauses against potential costs like overdeterrence, while Paper B develops a broader practical and normative account of how prohibitory remedies can increase social costs or perverse incentives and therefore why the law often prefers damages.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate boundary and interaction between contract remedies and other legal doctrines (tort, prohibitory doctrines, economic‑loss/relegation rules)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines when tort-based fraud remedies should supplement contractual enforcement (and critiques doctrines like the economic loss rule that bar such incursions), while Paper B interrogates doctrines that limit prohibitory remedies (irreparable injury, uniqueness) and more generally the institutional separation between pricing remedies and prohibitory/injunctive relief.

shared_topics.topic: whether and to what extent parties can or should shape their own enforcement regimes through contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on contract terms that seek to 'regulate the procedural course of future enforcement' (certificates, recordkeeping, no‑obstruct clauses) and the legal limits on contracting for penalties or punitive consequences, and Paper B considers the normative and doctrinal limits on shifting remedial outcomes (e.g., using specific performance or other prohibitory remedies) and when courts should honor or deny such redistributive enforcement outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 75texlrev293!!ARTICLE: A Primer on Prejudgment Interest
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Primer on Prejudgment Interest

shared_topics.topic: the normative and economic justification for providing 'full compensation' to plaintiffs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends assessing prejudgment interest as necessary to achieve full monetary compensation and the associated efficiency and deterrence goals; Paper B questions the desirability of pursuing full compensation (via prohibitory remedies) and develops normative and descriptive reasons why the law often stops short of full compensation.

shared_topics.topic: how remedies affect deterrence and parties' incentives (including delay incentives)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues prejudgment interest aligns incentives by preventing defendants from obtaining an interest-free delay and by ensuring proper deterrence through full compensation; Paper B analyzes whether substitutive or prohibitory remedies actually improve deterrence compared with damages and shows they can fail or worsen social outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: measurement and implementation of monetary remedies — how awards should be calculated to reflect losses or gains
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the correct financial methods for computing prejudgment interest (choice of rate, compounding, proxies) to ensure accurate compensation; Paper B treats damages as a pricing/measurement mechanism (versus prohibitory remedies) and scrutinizes how monetary measures map onto harm, gain, and efficient outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the role of legal rules, judicial discretion, and doctrinal limits in shaping which remedies are available and how they are applied
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents statutory variation and broad judicial discretion in selecting rates and methods for prejudgment interest and calls for constrained, principled rules; Paper B examines doctrinal limits (irreparable injury, uniqueness, relegation doctrines) that constrain prohibitory remedies and defends their normative role in preserving damages as primary.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 33uclalrev1565!!ARTICLE: PUNITIVE AND NONPECUNIARY DAMAGES IN ACTIONS BASED UPON CONTRACT: TOWARD ACHIEVING THE OBJECTIVE OF FULL COMPENSATION.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PUNITIVE AND NONPECUNIARY DAMAGES IN ACTIONS BASED UPON CONTRACT: TOWARD ACHIEVING THE OBJECTIVE OF FULL COMPENSATION.

shared_topics.topic: the legitimacy and desirability of 'full compensation' as the remedial goal in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Both papers interrogate whether the law should aim to make plaintiffs whole — Paper A critiques how orthodox rules nonetheless leave plaintiffs undercompensated and argues for rethinking remedial objectives in some cases, while Paper B offers a descriptive and normative challenge to the assumption that full compensation ought to be the central remedial goal.

shared_topics.topic: the choice between monetary (pricing) remedies and prohibitory/equitable remedies (specific performance, injunctions, restitution)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the tradeoff between awarding damages and ordering prohibitory remedies: Paper A discusses courts' preference for substitutionary monetary remedies and limited use of specific performance, and Paper B analyzes the distinction between pricing and prohibitory remedies and defends relegating prohibitory remedies to a secondary role.

shared_topics.topic: the role of deterrence, efficiency, and transaction‑cost considerations in designing remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both examine economic and policy rationales for limiting or expanding remedies — Paper A highlights concerns that excessive liability may chill productive activity and thus justifies limits on damages, while Paper B develops practical and normative arguments (including transactions costs and wealth-maximization) for why prohibitory/full‑compensation remedies may be undesirable or counterproductive.

shared_topics.topic: the availability, function, and limits of punitive and nonpecuniary damages in contract actions
shared_topics.justification: Both address supracompensatory awards and nonpecuniary losses: Paper A surveys recent trends toward allowing punitive and emotional‑distress recoveries in contract and proposes standards and safeguards, while Paper B raises normative objections to using remedies aimed at redistribution or deterrence (rather than harm‑based correction), which bears on when punitive or nonpecuniary awards are appropriate.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83lawcontempprob151!!ARTICLE: BLACK MARKETS AND THE EXCHANGE STRUCTURE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BLACK MARKETS AND THE EXCHANGE STRUCTURE

shared_topics.topic: legal disabilities and prohibitory remedies as tools to disable or undo exchanges
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that law primarily shapes markets by imposing legal disabilities that render transactions void, voidable, or unenforceable (tying actors' hands), while Paper B analyzes prohibitory remedies (injunctions, specific performance, restitution) as judicial tools that stop or undo transactions rather than merely price them, treating both as substantive mechanisms for disabling certain exchanges.

shared_topics.topic: using denial of enforcement or limited remedies to preserve exchange norms/structure
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends that authorities deny enforcement or impose disabilities (and sometimes criminal 'kickers') to protect an established exchange structure from being rewritten by individual conduct, and Paper B defends the civil system's reluctance to grant full compensatory (prohibitory) remedies on the grounds that limiting remedies can serve broader social allocation and systemic goals rather than merely compensating plaintiffs.

shared_topics.topic: skepticism about purely economic/transaction-cost explanations for remedial or prohibitory choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A rejects a purely law-and-economics account for why consensual exchanges are criminalized, arguing efficiency cannot fully explain disabilities and criminalization, while Paper B interrogates the economist-lawyer defense that transaction costs alone justify preferring damages over prohibitory remedies and develops normative reasons for that reluctance.

shared_topics.topic: the proper allocation between civil, criminal, and regulatory tools in controlling transgressive exchanges
shared_topics.justification: Paper A maps a spectrum of legal responses—from ignoring transgressive transactions to voiding them and imposing civil or criminal sanctions—and emphasizes that criminal law is only one tool among civil penalties and nonlegal sanctions, whereas Paper B focuses on the civil-remedies side of that spectrum, debating when courts should employ prohibitory (non-pricing) civil orders versus damages and how that choice interacts with broader enforcement policy.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 70bulrev623!!ARTICLE: EQUITY TRANSFORMED: PRELIMINARY INJUNCTIONS TO REQUIRE THE PAYMENT OF MONEY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EQUITY TRANSFORMED: PRELIMINARY INJUNCTIONS TO REQUIRE THE PAYMENT OF MONEY

shared_topics.topic: whether equitable remedies should substitute for or supplement money damages to provide interim or full compensation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advocates using preliminary injunctions to compel interim monetary payments to impecunious plaintiffs before trial, while Paper B analyzes and questions the broader proposition of using prohibitory/equitable remedies (specific performance, injunctions, restitution) to achieve full compensation instead of damages.

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal limits on equitable relief—especially the 'adequate remedy at law', irreparable injury, and uniqueness/relegation doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the traditional requirement that equity not act when an adequate remedy at law exists and challenges the irreparable-injury rule in the context of interim payments, and Paper B examines and defends the relegation doctrines (irreparable injury rule, uniqueness test) that restrict the availability of prohibitory remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the practical and normative tradeoffs between pricing (damages) and prohibitory/equitable remedies—deterrence, compensation, efficiency, administrative and constitutional concerns
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses practical and constitutional objections to ordering interim payments (administrative burdens, Seventh Amendment, due process) and argues they are manageable, while Paper B explores whether prohibitory remedies actually improve deterrence or compensation and raises normative concerns about social costs, redistribution, and efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: reassessing historical origins of remedy rules in light of contemporary societal conditions and needs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A calls for reexamination of historical limitations on equity (given modern problems like uninsured plaintiffs, lone households, and merged law/equity), and Paper B revisits the historical and normative bases for the law's reluctance to provide full compensation, asking whether those origins justify current doctrine.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 116yaleljonline414!!ARTICLE: Who Chooses and Who Gets What: Efficient Breach and Efficient Performance Hypotheses hypothesis.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Who Chooses and Who Gets What: Efficient Breach and Efficient Performance Hypotheses hypothesis.

shared_topics.topic: specific performance versus expectation damages as remedial tools
shared_topics.justification: Paper A juxtaposes expectation damages (which enable the promisor to internalize the cost of performance under the efficient breach framing) with specific performance (used in its efficient performance hypothesis to let the promisee internalize the value of performance), while Paper B analyzes specific performance as one of the 'prohibitory remedies' contrasted with damages and evaluates their practical and normative roles in the remedial system.

shared_topics.topic: whether and how different remedies produce economically efficient outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that both an efficient breach regime and an alternative efficient performance regime can produce efficient results by placing the chooser (promisor or promisee) in a position to weigh social costs and benefits, and Paper B critically examines claims that prohibitory remedies (full compensation) would improve deterrence, compensation, or wealth maximization compared to damages, concluding that damages may better promote social wealth in many cases.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial design allocates entitlements and redistributes gains from nonperformance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines competing allocations of rights (the promisor's Holmesian option versus a promisee's right to compel performance) and how remedies distribute the gains from nonperformance, while Paper B treats prohibitory remedies as fundamentally redistributional (measuring some remedies by gain rather than harm) and assesses the normative desirability of such redistributive remedial rules.

shared_topics.topic: normative and policy foundations for preferring one remedial regime over another
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses ethical and moral constraints that might favor giving the decision right to either promisor or promisee (or neither) and argues efficiency is compatible with multiple normative allocations, whereas Paper B interrogates the normative presumption that the law should pursue full compensation and offers practical and moral justifications for limiting prohibitory remedies in favor of harm-based damages.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1583!!ARTICLE: THE FAULT PRINCIPLE AS THE CHAMELEON OF CONTRACT LAW: A MARKET FUNCTION APPROACH
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE FAULT PRINCIPLE AS THE CHAMELEON OF CONTRACT LAW: A MARKET FUNCTION APPROACH

shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates Ernst Rabel's advocacy of a strict-liability regime (as embodied in CISG article 79 and European principles) and asks whether strict liability is superior, especially in sales versus services; Paper B critically examines the desirability of remedies that deliver full compensation (specific performance, injunctions, restitution) and argues against making such prohibitory remedies the default.

shared_topics.topic: how to allocate and combine different liability/remedy regimes based on market function, deterrence, and efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes a 'market function' approach to balance strict and fault liability depending on market expectations and the function of the contract (e.g., sales vs services); Paper B evaluates remedies by their effects on deterrence, compensation, wealth maximization, and transactions costs and proposes a framework limiting prohibitory remedies to contexts where they produce desirable social outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: use of limiting doctrines or graduated sanctions to avoid the harshest remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the German Nachfrist (a 'second chance' that limits the imposition of the most onerous sanctions) as part of a nuanced mix of liability rules; Paper B analyzes relegation doctrines (irreparable-injury rule, uniqueness test) that function to restrict the routine use of prohibitory/full-compensation remedies and preserve damages as primary.

shared_topics.topic: normative tradeoffs between corrective/compensatory aims and redistributional or social-cost considerations in remedy design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A weighs the promise-mirroring rationale for strict liability against contextual limits (e.g., services) and argues for market-sensitive combinations of liability rules; Paper B argues that full compensation is not an unalloyed normative good because it can impose social costs and effect redistributions that the legal system may rightly decline.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2004wislrev507!!SYMPOSIUM: PROMISSORY FRAUD WITHOUT BREACH
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: PROMISSORY FRAUD WITHOUT BREACH

shared_topics.topic: normative aims of remedies — compensation versus deterrence and redistribution
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly questions whether the law should aim for full compensation and argues that damages often better serve deterrence, wealth maximization, and social-cost tradeoffs than prohibitory (full‑compensation) remedies; Paper B analyzes promissory fraud remedies (compensatory, punitive, and criminal) and the normative role those remedies play in deterring insincere promises and policing the limits of contractual freedom.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal limits on enforcing promises and when non-contractual liability is appropriate
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines doctrines (irreparable‑injury rule, uniqueness, relegation doctrines) that restrict use of specific performance and injunctions and defends limiting prohibitory remedies; Paper B asks when promissory fraud liability should be imposed even where contract enforcement is unavailable, tying liability to the rationale for nonenforcement and explaining doctrinal boundaries between contract and tort/fraud.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts damages measured by plaintiff loss with prohibitory remedies measured by defendant gain or designed to remove risk, and critiques the assumed superiority of full‑compensation metrics; Paper B interrogates proximate causation and how misrepresentations about intent can cause harm (and thus justify damages) even absent nonperformance, engaging the question of what factual predicates and measurements justify relief.

shared_topics.topic: the legal significance of promises and promisor's present intent
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats promises as the source of remedial rights enforceable by specific performance or injunctions and evaluates when courts should compel promised performance; Paper B focuses on promises as communicative acts that can falsely describe a promisor's present intent (promissory misrepresentations), exploring when that factual claim about intent gives rise to tort or criminal liability independent of contractual breach.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 117yaleljpocketpart14!!ARTICLE: What Efficiency Demands: The Efficient Performance Hypothesis Defended
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: What Efficiency Demands: The Efficient Performance Hypothesis Defended

shared_topics.topic: comparative evaluation of damages versus prohibitory remedies (specific performance/injunctions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally critiques the push for routinely substituting damages with 'prohibitory remedies' (specific performance, injunctions, restitution), arguing they may worsen deterrence, compensation, and social welfare; Paper B likewise analyzes the economic role of specific performance versus monetary remedies, treating them as instruments that can be calibrated to achieve allocative efficiency under different entitlements.

shared_topics.topic: who holds the legal entitlement to choose performance or nonperformance and how that affects remedy design
shared_topics.justification: Paper B explicitly contrasts regimes in which the promisor or the promisee holds the right/option to choose nonperformance (efficient breach vs efficient performance) and shows how that entitlement reshapes which remedies produce efficient outcomes; Paper A likewise interrogates underlying assumptions about the law's commitment to full compensation and how remedial doctrines reflect and reinforce which parties' choices (performance vs breach) are systemically enabled.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of efficiency-based prescriptions due to transaction costs and empirical indeterminacy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques purely transaction-cost justifications for eschewing prohibitory remedies and explores broader practical limits on efficiency gains from such remedies; Paper B emphasizes that allocative efficiency is indeterminate in the abstract and that transaction costs, bargaining costs, and empirical contingencies are decisive in choosing among remedies.

shared_topics.topic: distributional or redistributive implications of remedial rules (compensation as redistribution)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that prohibitory/full-compensation remedies are at root redistributive (not purely corrective) and that society may justifiably limit them for allocational reasons; Paper B likewise recognizes that remedies have distributive consequences and that efficiency-consistent remedy choices can be fashioned to produce different distributions depending on which party bears rights or transfers.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 23uclalrev501!!ARTICLE: THE HISTORICAL CONCEPTION OF A LEASE FOR YEARS *
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE HISTORICAL CONCEPTION OF A LEASE FOR YEARS *

shared_topics.topic: practical/pragmatic considerations as primary drivers of legal doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that medieval treatment of leases (freehold vs contract) resulted from pragmatic concerns (e.g., double liability, adequate protection) rather than abstract taxonomy, and Paper B argues that the remedial system's reluctance to provide full compensation reflects practical and social-cost considerations rather than purely doctrinal commitments to compensation.

shared_topics.topic: development and design of remedies to protect private interests against third parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the historical invention of new writs to give lessees protection against third-party ejectors when traditional actions were unavailable, while Paper B analyzes why courts favor damages over prohibitory remedies (injunctions, specific performance, restitution) and how remedial doctrines structure plaintiffs' ability to obtain relief against others.

shared_topics.topic: trade-offs in imposing liability or relief (risk of double liability, social costs, and deterrence effects)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the trade-off between protecting lessees and exposing third parties to double liability, and Paper B evaluates how full-compensation prohibitory remedies can produce social costs, redistributional effects, and perverse deterrence, arguing these trade-offs justify limiting such remedies.

shared_topics.topic: critique of doctrinal labels and presumed normative goals in law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A challenges the significance commonly attributed to labels like 'freehold' versus 'chattel' or 'property' versus 'contract' as explanatory, while Paper B questions the often-unexamined normative assumption that the law should aim for full compensation and shows how that presupposition shapes remedial doctrine.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 116yaleljonline438!!ARTICLE: What the Efficient Performance Hypothesis Means for Contracts Scholarship
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: What the Efficient Performance Hypothesis Means for Contracts Scholarship

shared_topics.topic: comparison of pricing (damages/expectation) remedies and prohibitory/forced-performance remedies (specific performance, disgorgement-option)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers directly compare remedies that award money (expectation damages or loss-based damages) with remedies that compel or substitute performance (specific performance, injunctions, disgorgement-option), evaluating when each class of remedy is preferable and how they differ in aims and mechanics.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoff between efficiency (wealth-maximization) and non-welfarist or ethical considerations in remedy design
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage the tension between efficiency-based justifications for damages and ethical or rights-based reasons to insist on performance or fuller compensation, asking whether courts should and can design remedies that reconcile or prioritize those different values.

shared_topics.topic: empirical and transaction-cost constraints on choosing the optimal remedy (measurement problems and practical feasibility)
shared_topics.justification: Both works treat empirical uncertainty and practical measurement problems—e.g., difficulty measuring promisee lost profits versus promisor outside gains, or the transaction costs associated with enforcing prohibitory remedies—as central determinants of which remedy an efficiency-minded legal system can feasibly adopt.

shared_topics.topic: incentive and deterrence effects of different remedies (how remedies alter parties' behavior)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how remedies change incentives—Paper A shows how expectation damages and the disgorgement-option internalize gains and losses to induce efficient breach decisions, while Paper B critically assesses whether prohibitory remedies actually improve deterrence or might worsen harmful activity.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83uchilrev759!!Article: Contract as Empowerment
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Contract as Empowerment

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes why the law typically prefers damages to prohibitory remedies, questioning the practical and normative consequences of expanding specific performance and injunctions; Paper B treats expectation damages and specific performance as central remedial doctrines and explains their proper role under an "empowerment" theory of contract, including a reappraisal of damages' moral force.

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations for remedial and contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a descriptive and normative theory for the legal system's reluctance to provide full compensation, arguing that full compensation is not an unqualified normative good; Paper B offers a normative account—"contract as empowerment"—that seeks to unify and justify disparate contract doctrines and the law's remedial choices.

shared_topics.topic: tension between party autonomy (deference to subjective will) and judicial intervention for fairness/public policy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes doctrines that limit judicial imposition of prohibitory remedies (e.g., irreparable injury, uniqueness) and treats prohibitory relief as potentially redistributive and intrusive; Paper B addresses the doctrinal split between deferring to parties' subjective intentions and doctrines that permit courts to override agreements for fairness (e.g., unconscionability, objective interpretation), and integrates those interventions into its theory.

shared_topics.topic: limits of economic/efficiency explanations (transactions costs, efficient breach) for explaining remedies and contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the economist-lawyers' transactions-costs justification for damages and challenges the claim that prohibitory remedies are infeasibly costly or less efficient; Paper B rejects a simple "efficient breach" economic account of expectation damages and argues that economic theories alone do not capture the moral and empowering dimensions of contract law.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 105michlrev559!!ARTICLE: THE DISGORGEMENT INTEREST IN CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE DISGORGEMENT INTEREST IN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: harm-based (damages) versus gain-based (prohibitory/disgorgement) remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both papers directly contrast remedies measured by the plaintiff's loss (damages/pricing remedies) with remedies measured by the defendant's gain (specific performance/injunctions framed as prohibitory remedies in Paper A, and disgorgement in Paper B), examining the conceptual and practical differences between loss-based and gain-based relief.

shared_topics.topic: normative debate over whether the law should provide full compensation or disgorgement
shared_topics.justification: Each article engages the normative question of whether courts ought to aim for 'full compensation' or require disgorgement of breacher gains, challenging assumptions that full compensation (or disgorgement) is unambiguously desirable and exploring redistributional versus corrective goals of remedies.

shared_topics.topic: efficiency, deterrence, and economic justifications for remedial rules (including efficient breach and transaction costs)
shared_topics.justification: Both works evaluate economic arguments—Paper A interrogates transactions-cost and efficiency defenses of damages dominance and deterrence effects of prohibitory remedies, while Paper B critiques the efficient-breach rationale for rejecting disgorgement and develops economic-normative defenses of gain-based relief.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal prevalence and limits on non-damages relief (why courts/Restatements restrict prohibitory remedies or disgorgement)
