papers.node_id: 80valrev1225!!ARTICLE: THE FAULT LINES IN CONTRACT DAMAGES
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE FAULT LINES IN CONTRACT DAMAGES
papers.abstract:
THE fundamental premise of most theories of contract damages has been that contract damage law is a "strict liability" system; that is, the reason the breach occurs does not matter in determining the measure of damages.That premise is wrong. In fact, the reason the breach occurs has always influenced courts' determination of the proper measure of damages. And economic theory supports a damage regime that takes the reason for breach into account. I call such a damage regime "fault-based."
Traditional theories have not questioned the strict liability view of contract damages because they have focused on the goal of compensating the victim of the breach.The goal of compensation implies strict damage liability because if damages are to be measured by the plaintiff's loss, the reason for the breach must be irrelevant. But "compensation" is a term that is susceptible of various meanings. As all students of contracts know, Fuller and Perdue defined,and the Restatement enshrined,three compensatory "interests" that contract damages protect: expectation, restitu-tion, and reliance.Although Fuller and Perdue taught us that the pursuit of compensation requires an important choice, they didnot successfully teach us how to make it. If compensation canmean all these things, how do courts decide which damage measure to use?
Many traditional theories answer that there is and should be one predominant compensatory interest protected by contract remedies: that interest is expectation.These theories either minimizeor marginalize the role for the reliance and restitution interests.But these theories have never been satisfactory. Expectation theorists struggle to explain why, if protecting the expectation interest is the goal, contract damages so often undercompensate the expectation interest. Doctrines such as mitigation, foreseeability, and uncertainty, as well as the inability of the victim of the breach to recover attorney's fees or prejudgment interest at market rates, make contract damages undercompensatory from the perspective of the expectation interest.Expectation theorists also have trouble explaining why reliance and restitution measures are used at all. Their explanations of the plethora of damage measures haveusually been based on doctrinal categories,measurement difficulties,or ad hoc adjustments.
Not only have traditional scholars accepted the strict liability view of contract damages, but the most famous, and infamous, economic theory of contract damages - the theory of efficient breach - implicitly accepts the strict liability premise in offering a justification for the expectation damage measure.Strict liability in the efficient breach theory is not, however, a consequence of a particular definition of compensation; rather, strict liability grows out of the theory's commitment to limited court involvement in contract damage determination.The beauty of the pure efficientbreach theory is that a uniformly applied rule of expectation damages avoids costly court determinations of the nature of a particular breach, that is, whether a particular breach is efficient or inefficient. The reason is that a uniformly applied expectation damage remedy results in the occurrence of efficient, and only efficient, breaches with minimal court involvement. Inefficient breaches are deterred because the party contemplating breach knows that it cannot make more from breaching and paying damages than it can from performing. Efficient breaches are not deterred because the party contemplating breach knows that it can compensate the promisee fully and still be better off by breaching. The court's role with respect to damages is minimized: its only responsibility is to determine whether a contract has been made, whether a breach has occurred, and what the expectation damages are.
The efficient breach theory has enjoyed surprisingly wide acceptance by such traditional scholars as Professors Farnsworthand Eisenbergas well as the Restatement (Second) of Contracts.I would attribute this acceptance not only to the theory's strong defense of the expectation damage measure as the primary measure in contract law, but also to the theory's grounding in the traditional notion of a strict liability approach to contract damages.
The problem is that although the theory of efficient breach purports to explain why courts use expectation damages rather than reliance, restitution, or punitive damages for breach of contract, it fails as an explanatory or positive theory. It does not explain when courts actually use expectation damages or some other measure ina particular case.Although law and economics scholars have long recognized that efficient breach is only one component of an economic theory of contract damages, until now no one has offered a broader theory because no one has been willing to give up on strict liability. No economic theory has attempted to explain in a systematic way how courts actually do and should go about choosing among all the different damage measures available.
This paper attempts to fill that gap by rejecting the strict liability idea and developing instead a fault-based economic theory of contract damages that accurately describes the system we actually have, and normatively justifies this system as one that operates to promote efficient contracting behavior. My goals in the paper are threefold: to explain why courts have developed such a variety of contract damage measures; to understand the predominance of the expectation measure; and to connect the market damage measure to the general theory of contract damages.
The paper starts from the economic premises that all rules of contract law create incentives, and that courts use different rules in different situations to encourage desirable and discourage un-desirable conduct. Contract damage rules are but a subset ofall contract rules: they provide one way, though not the onlyway, for courts to affect contracting behavior. I argue that de-veloping damage rules that create the right incentives for bothparties requires an understanding of why contracts are breached.define and explain three broad categories of breaches: con-tracts that should not have been made; contracts that shouldnot be performed; and contracts that should not have beenbreached. I argue that courts tend to use larger damage measures,such as expectation and high-restitution,to deter promi-sorsfrom breaching contracts that should be performed, as well as from acting opportunistically in breaching other contracts. Courts tend to use smaller damage measures, such as reliance and low-restitution, to deter promisors from making accidental contracts that should not have been made, and to encourage promisors to take precautions against accidental contingencies resulting in contracts that should not be performed, but to avoid overdeterring promise-making and encouraging excessive precaution-taking. Courts also use various doctrines that reduce expectation and reliance damage awards to give promisees incentives to take precautions and mitigate. The theory also explains the centrality of the market damage measure to contract law, the relationship of that measure to the strict liability ideal, and the limits of strict liability in the market context.
I use case examples throughout to show that courts are in fact using different damage measures in ways that the fault-based theory explains better than the extant alternatives. Although many may wonder how courts can do what I suggest they should do, my answer is that they are already doing it. That does not mean that I believe courts always get it right; in fact, I discuss several cases with which I disagree. But by and large, the doctrinal contours of contract damages are explainable by the theory outlined here. Moreover, discussing cases that I think courts could have handled better helps demonstrate the usefulness of the theory. Courts always do better when they have a better idea of what it is that they should be looking for. So far, contract theorists have not provided much practical help. Unless an alternative theory based on strict liability can better explain the contract damage law we in fact have, the onus is on the proponents of strict liability to show why the law as it has developed is so misguided that we should abandon the system we have, and to show how an alternative system would work better.
. Damage Rules as Part of an Economic Approach to Contract Law
The economic approach to contract law aims to identify and justify rules that minimize the joint costs, or equivalently, maximize the joint profits of contracting.All contract law rules create incentives; the economic approach focuses on the question of what incentives these rules do and should create. Such an analysis requires an understanding of why contracts fail and what steps both contracting parties can take to facilitate successful contracts and prevent or reduce the costs of failed contracts. After discussing the general economic approach to contract damages, this Section will discuss three categories of contract breach: contracts that should not have been made; contracts that should not be performed; and contracts that should not have been breached. These Sections form the building blocks for a theory of how contract damage rules are and should be used to create optimal incentives in different breach situations.

questions.question: Whether the reason for a contractual breach (i.e., fault or cause of the breach) systematically affects which measure of damages courts apply.

Whether a damages regime that conditions awards on the reason for breach (a fault-based regime) produces more efficient contracting incentives and lower joint costs than a regime that ignores the reason for breach.
How courts should select among alternative damage measures to allocate incentives for promise-making, performance, breach, and precaution so as to minimize the total social costs of contracting.

matched_themes: Should parties and courts adopt fault-based remedial regimes that distinguish among breaches by reason when allocating remedies?
Should courts allow apportionment of contractual damages when the non-breaching party's reliance or failure to cooperate contributed to the loss?
What counterfactual baseline should courts use to measure plaintiffs' losses for compensation purposes?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?
Should the promisor or the promisee have the default right to choose between performance and payment to achieve allocative efficiency?
Does the promisor's motive for breaching (loss-avoiding vs gain-seeking) affect how much compensation promisees need to accept nonperformance?
How do transaction costs, enforcement frictions, and institutional realities alter the theoretical efficiency of breach-plus-compensation?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
Should courts award disgorgement or force surrender of breacher gains in addition to compensation to deter opportunistic breaches?
How should remedial and enforcement rules be structured to achieve efficient behavior when populations include both internalizers and externalizers?
Should courts strip breachers of gains (disgorgement) in opportunistic or deliberate breaches, and what are the doctrinal and incentive effects of allowing disgorgement remedies in contract law?
Can courts reliably determine ex post whether a breach would increase social welfare so that remedy choice can be used to promote efficiency?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
Do limits on recoverable damages (foreseeability, certainty, avoidability) substantially reduce awards below full compensation, and should courts liberalize those limits?
When is a market-difference (market-price differential) damages measure appropriate for buyers and resellers, and under what market conditions does it overcompensate or undercompensate?
Do courts consider the breaching party's blameworthiness or opportunistic behavior when selecting among compensatory remedies?
When and under what standards should courts award disgorgement or remedies that strip gains from breaching parties?
When is an indirect remedy (one that induces self-compliance) preferable to a direct remedy that delivers the outcome?

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Economic Theory and the Present Value of Future Lost Earnings: An Integration, Unification, and Simplification of Court Adopted Methodologies

shared_topics.topic: how damage rules affect incentives and behavior

compared_to.partner_node_id: 105michlrev559!!ARTICLE: THE DISGORGEMENT INTEREST IN CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE DISGORGEMENT INTEREST IN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates when disgorgement would improve incentives and prevent unjustified promisor gains from breach, including potential apportionment between parties; Paper B frames all damage rules as incentive devices, explaining how varying damage measures (and doctrinal limits) are used to deter inefficient breaches and encourage appropriate precautions and contract-formation decisions.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between Restatement doctrine, case law practice, and what remedies courts actually award
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates why Restatement Second omitted disgorgement despite recognitions of similar remedies outside contract law and examines case examples that award disgorgement; Paper B surveys case law to show that courts already use a variety of measures contrary to a strict-liability account and uses cases to support its fault-based explanatory framework.

shared_topics.topic: whether and when a promisor's gains from breach should be disgorged or apportioned between parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally asks when a promisor's gain attributable to breach should be disgorged or divided with the promisee and develops criteria and case discussions for apportionment; Paper B incorporates restitution and 'high/low' restitution measures into its taxonomy and explains when courts employ restitution-like awards (including limiting or apportioning gains) to achieve proper incentives.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 46amulrev1!!ARTICLE: THE MEANING OF VALUE IN CONTRACT DAMAGES AND CONTRACT THEORY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE MEANING OF VALUE IN CONTRACT DAMAGES AND CONTRACT THEORY

shared_topics.topic: choice among damage measures (expectation, reliance, restitution, and surplus-based alternatives)

shared_topics.topic: critique and reinterpretation of the efficient-breach rationale for damages

shared_topics.topic: damages as incentive devices that shape breach, performance, and resource allocation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats damage rules as part of contract law's incentive architecture—designing measures to deter inefficient breaches and avoid overdeterrence—while Paper B emphasizes that damage measures should be understood in terms of the incentives they create to reallocate resources to more profitable (surplus-maximizing) uses.

shared_topics.topic: conceptual ambiguity in core terms (e.g., 'compensation' and 'value') and doctrinal consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that 'compensation' can mean expectation, reliance, or restitution and that this ambiguity affects which remedy courts choose; Paper B documents conflicting legal and economic meanings of 'value' and shows how that confusion complicates the application of economic damage theory.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between doctrinal doctrines (mitigation, foreseeability, cover/resale, market measures) and economic measurement of damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explains how doctrines like mitigation, foreseeability, and uncertainty produce undercompensation relative to expectation and how courts use market measures to limit liability; Paper B discusses how substitute-transaction rules (cover/resale), warranty and partial-performance contexts, and cost recovery fit into a surplus-based framework for measuring damages.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 116yaleljonline438!!ARTICLE: What the Efficient Performance Hypothesis Means for Contracts Scholarship
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: What the Efficient Performance Hypothesis Means for Contracts Scholarship

shared_topics.topic: the normative and efficiency justification for expectation damages and the efficient-breach framework
shared_topics.justification: Both papers centrally engage the claim that expectation damages (and the efficient-breach story that justifies them) are efficiency-promoting: Paper A critiques the strict-liability/efficient-breach premise and develops a fault-based alternative that explains when expectation damages are used, while Paper B interrogates the efficient-performance/expectation rationale by showing that alternative remedial structures can be equally efficient under certain assumptions.

shared_topics.topic: when and why courts should use alternative remedial measures (reliance, restitution, specific performance, disgorgement) instead of expectation damages

shared_topics.topic: how damage rules create incentives that affect promisor and promisee behavior
shared_topics.justification: Both papers treat damage rules as instruments for shaping contracting behavior: Paper A builds a taxonomy of breaches and prescribes different damages to deter or encourage performance and care, while Paper B focuses on how giving the option to breach (promisor) or compel performance (promisee) produces equivalent incentive effects in the perform-or-breach model.

shared_topics.topic: the practical and empirical difficulties of measuring losses and gains that determine the optimal remedy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A repeatedly notes measurement problems (foreseeability, uncertainty, mitigation) and doctrinal adjustments that lead courts to under- or over-compensate, while Paper B emphasizes empirical uncertainty about whether courts can better measure promisee lost profits or promisor outside opportunities—an uncertainty that affects which remedy is actually superior.

shared_topics.topic: the role of non-efficiency (ethical or fault-based) considerations in designing or choosing damages
shared_topics.justification: Both papers consider normative concerns beyond pure welfare maximization: Paper A develops a fault-based theory that incorporates reasons for breach into damages, and Paper B argues that ethical preferences (e.g., whether the promisee or promisor should hold the performance option) can be accommodated without sacrificing efficiency under certain empirical conditions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 85tullrev413!!ARTICLE: Convergence in Contort: Landlord Liability for Defective Premises in Comparative Perspective
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Convergence in Contort: Landlord Liability for Defective Premises in Comparative Perspective

shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that contract-based landlord liability tends toward strict liability while tort may be fault‑based, raising substantive differences in recovery; Paper B explicitly rejects a universal strict‑liability model for contract damages and develops a fault‑based economic theory to explain and justify variation in damage measures.

shared_topics.topic: using damages and remedial rules to allocate risk and create incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the choice between contract and tort (or a hybrid 'contort') affects how risk of harm is allocated between landlords and tenants and can be chosen to serve policy goals; Paper B frames damage rules as incentive‑creating devices and explains how different measures (expectation, reliance, restitution, market damages) are used to produce desirable contracting behavior.

shared_topics.topic: normative critique of existing doctrines and proposals for doctrinal reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the bifurcated American approach and proposes reconceptualizing landlord obligations as a hybrid 'contort' to better align law and policy; Paper B critiques the dominant strict‑liability/efficient‑breach account and proposes a fault‑sensitive economic theory to better explain and guide courts' use of damage measures.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal choice affects the scope and type of recoverable losses (economic vs nonpecuniary)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that classification as contract or tort determines whether plaintiffs can recover nonpecuniary harms (pain and suffering, emotional distress) and who may recover; Paper B analyzes why courts select different compensatory interests (expectation, reliance, restitution) and how those choices produce varying coverage of economic versus other losses.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 71vandlrev61!!ARTICLE: Contract as Commodified Promise
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contract as Commodified Promise

shared_topics.justification: Paper A rejects a strict‑liability (uniform expectation) regime and explores limits of market damage rules to avoid overdeterrence and perverse incentives, while Paper B investigates anti‑commodification norms and moral limits (e.g., illegality, donative promises) that should constrain treating promises purely as market commodities.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal reform motivated by normative theory (reconceptualizing formation and liability doctrines)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes replacing the strict‑liability damage paradigm with a fault‑based, incentive‑sensitive framework for damages, and Paper B proposes doctrinal reforms—such as demoting consideration and presumptively enforcing commodified promises—grounded in a philosophical account of commerciality.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1583!!ARTICLE: THE FAULT PRINCIPLE AS THE CHAMELEON OF CONTRACT LAW: A MARKET FUNCTION APPROACH
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE FAULT PRINCIPLE AS THE CHAMELEON OF CONTRACT LAW: A MARKET FUNCTION APPROACH

compared_to.partner_node_id: 75texlrev293!!ARTICLE: A Primer on Prejudgment Interest
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Primer on Prejudgment Interest

shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a fault-based framework explaining when courts choose expectation, reliance, or restitution measures (and the centrality of market damages), and Paper B engages this same measurement problem for the time-value component of awards by analyzing how prejudgment interest should be computed and integrated into monetary judgments.

shared_topics.topic: economic/incentive-based justification for damage rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly builds an economic theory of contract damages that designs remedies to create optimal incentives (preventing inefficient breaches, encouraging precautions), and Paper B uses economic reasoning to justify prejudgment interest as necessary for correct incentive structures for prospective actors and to avoid perverse incentives to delay litigation.

shared_topics.topic: use of market-based rates or proxies in setting monetary awards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the importance of the market damage measure and the limits of strict liability in market contexts, and Paper B addresses the practical need to select market-rate proxies (and adjust them) when computing prejudgment interest to approximate correct financial compensation.

compared_to.partner_title: Article: The Collateral Source Rule in Contract Cases

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SUPREME DISGORGEMENT

shared_topics.topic: deterrence and incentive-function of remedial rules

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Commodified Promises and Contract Theory

shared_topics.justification: Paper A claims its commodification lens can explain and justify rules governing remedies among other doctrines, and Paper B is wholly devoted to explaining why courts use different damage measures (expectation, reliance, restitution, market damages) and how those choices should be normatively justified to shape incentives.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 105michlrev559!!ARTICLE: THE DISGORGEMENT INTEREST IN CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE DISGORGEMENT INTEREST IN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes why courts employ different damage measures (expectation, reliance, restitution) across breach types and how those choices create incentives; Paper B focuses on restitution-of-profits (disgorgement), arguing it is a distinct remedial interest that contract law should and sometimes does protect, thereby addressing the same doctrinal menu of remedies.

shared_topics.topic: critique of the efficient-breach justification for uniform expectation damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the efficient-breach story depends on a strict-liability premise and fails to explain the doctrinal variety of damages, while Paper B traces Restatement rejection of disgorgement in part to efficient-breach reasoning and argues that the theory cannot sustain exclusion of disgorgement.

shared_topics.topic: economic/incentive-based justification for designing damage rules (fault-based vs strict liability)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a fault-based economic theory of damages to align incentives in different categories of breach, contrasting that with strict-liability regimes; Paper B advances normative (including economic) arguments for protecting disgorgement to correct incentive and fairness problems left unresolved by existing rules.

shared_topics.topic: measurement and allocation of promisor gains, including market-based measures and apportionment
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the centrality of market damage measures and limits of strict liability in valuing losses, while Paper B examines disgorgement as restoring promisor gains and asks when and how a breacher's profits should be apportioned between promisor and promisee.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Economic Theory and the Present Value of Future Lost Earnings: An Integration, Unification, and Simplification of Court Adopted Methodologies

shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines whether forecasts of future earnings and inflation are necessary, arguing stable economic relationships make awards more predictable and reduce reliance on speculative forecasts; Paper B discusses doctrines (foreseeability, uncertainty, mitigation) that limit awards because of uncertainty about future losses and explains how different measures respond to forecasting limitations.

shared_topics.topic: comparative analysis of alternative damage formulas and their normative implications
shared_topics.justification: Paper A demonstrates mathematical equivalence (under correct parameter definitions) of several present‑value methods but evaluates them for conceptual soundness and practicality; Paper B compares expectation, reliance, and restitution measures, relating each to different breach types and assessing their normative effects on contracting behavior.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Critique of the Efficient Performance Hypothesis

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Attaching Tort Claims to Contract Actions: An Economic Analysis of Contort

shared_topics.justification: Both engage substantively with which damage measures courts apply, the reasons for limits on those measures, and how those measures compare to remedies available in tort (e.g., expanded consequential, emotional-distress, punitive awards).

shared_topics.topic: incentive effects of damages rules on contracting behavior (breach, performance, reliance, mitigation)
shared_topics.justification: Both investigate how different remedial regimes create incentives for parties — deterring inefficient breach, encouraging or discouraging contract formation, and motivating mitigation or precaution-taking — and evaluate doctrines accordingly.

shared_topics.justification: Both examine the interplay between contract and tort remedies: Paper B directly analyzes when tort claims can be attached to contract actions and Paper A’s fault-based account similarly reconsiders when fault (traditionally tort-like) should affect contract damages, with both critiquing existing tests and proposing alternative frameworks.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 55syracuselrev495!!ARTICLE: A UNIFYING THEORY OF CONTRACT DAMAGE RULES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A UNIFYING THEORY OF CONTRACT DAMAGE RULES

shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds its surplus‑based rule in an economic conception of wellbeing and monetizable costs/benefits to justify damage awards, while Paper B develops a fault‑based economic theory tying different damage measures to incentives that promote efficient contracting and deter undesirable breaches.

shared_topics.topic: reconciling new theoretical proposals with existing doctrines and judicial practice (UCC and Restatement)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A demonstrates the Shadow Code's equivalence to and improvements over the U.C.C. and the Restatement (Second) of Contracts and seeks to resolve their ambiguities, while Paper B critiques the efficient‑breach/strict liability reading of existing theory, links the market/expectation measure to those frameworks, and uses case law to show how courts actually apply different doctrines.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 20hofstralrev933!!SYMPOSIUM: THE FUTURE OF LAW AND ECONOMICS: THE STRANGEST ATTACK YET ON LAW AND ECONOMICS.
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE FUTURE OF LAW AND ECONOMICS: THE STRANGEST ATTACK YET ON LAW AND ECONOMICS.

shared_topics.topic: efficient breach and the remedial choice between expectation damages and specific performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the one‑size expectation‑damages approach implicit in the efficient‑breach literature and develops a fault‑based account explaining when courts use larger or smaller measures; Paper B centers on the efficient‑breach hypothetical and discusses (and defends) the remedial implications, contrasting damages with Jaffee's preference for specific performance.

shared_topics.topic: whether contract damages should be a strict‑liability (uniform expectation) regime or a fault‑sensitive regime
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly rejects the strict‑liability premise and proposes a fault‑based economic theory to explain doctrinal variation; Paper B engages this debate by treating efficient‑breach (and its strict‑liability flavor) as the target of Jaffee's attack and evaluating the coherence and desirability of abandoning that approach.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial rules function as incentive devices and interact with transaction and enforcement costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames damage rules as part of an economic toolkit to create incentives that minimize joint costs, explaining doctrines (mitigation, foreseeability) as incentive calibrators; Paper B likewise focuses on transaction costs, bilateral monopoly, and the costs of judicial inquiry/supervision when weighing damages against specific performance and other remedies.

shared_topics.topic: tension between economic‑efficiency rationales for remedies and non‑economic concerns (moral retribution, third‑party harms, demoralization)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates how different damage measures deter opportunism, encourage precautions, and allocate risk to promote efficient contracting, while Paper B catalogues moral and distributive objections to efficient breach—retributive satisfaction, third‑party harms, and demoralization—and examines whether economic reasoning adequately addresses these concerns.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 80ohiostlj1149!!ARTICLE: Fixer Upper: Buyer Deposits in Residential Real Estate Transactions
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Fixer Upper: Buyer Deposits in Residential Real Estate Transactions

shared_topics.topic: enforceability and normative justification of liquidated damages/deposit forfeitures
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a fault-based theory explaining when courts should apply different damage measures (expectation, restitution, reliance) to justify outcomes normatively; Paper B analyzes courts' widespread enforcement of buyer deposit forfeitures as liquidated damages and questions whether that enforcement is normatively appropriate given doctrinal aims.

shared_topics.topic: mismatch between stipulated damages (deposits) and actual harm and its implications for compensation and incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how different damage measures produce under- or over-compensation relative to parties' losses and uses incentive analysis to explain doctrinal variation; Paper B documents that residential earnest-money deposits often bear little relation to sellers' actual losses and explores the perverse incentive and fairness consequences.

shared_topics.topic: role of courts and doctrinal rules in choosing and applying damage measures to shape contracting behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how courts deploy different damage doctrines (mitigation, foreseeability, market measures) to create optimal incentives under different breach types; Paper B critiques how courts apply enforceability tests for liquidated-damages clauses (often rubber-stamping them) and how that judicial practice affects real-estate contracting incentives.

shared_topics.topic: trade-off between certainty/minimizing litigation costs and tailoring damages to the reason for breach (strict liability versus fault-based approaches)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts the strict-liability/efficient-breach model's appeal for administrative simplicity with a fault-based approach that tailors remedies to reasons for breach; Paper B describes how the perceived value of certainty (e.g., upholding standard deposit clauses) leads courts to favor simple, predictable outcomes even when they may misalign with the actual reasons for breach.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 116yaleljonline414!!ARTICLE: Who Chooses and Who Gets What: Efficient Breach and Efficient Performance Hypotheses hypothesis.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Who Chooses and Who Gets What: Efficient Breach and Efficient Performance Hypotheses hypothesis.

shared_topics.topic: the normative role of expectation damages versus alternative remedies in producing efficient outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions the view that expectation damages (and the promisor's option to pay) are necessary for efficiency by showing alternative mixes of rights and remedies (specific performance, disgorgement) can yield efficient choices; Paper B critiques the strict-liability/expectation-default view and explains when courts actually choose expectation versus reliance or restitution to promote desirable contracting incentives.

shared_topics.topic: how allocation of entitlements (promisor's option to breach vs promisee's right to compel performance) affects contracting incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly contrasts the Holmesian promisor-option with an entitlement giving promisees the power to compel performance and shows both can lead to efficiency; Paper B analyzes how different damage rules and entitlements create incentives that deter or encourage breaches and opportunism, linking entitlement structure to behavior.

shared_topics.topic: the design of remedies and damages as instruments to shape parties' precaution, mitigation, and contract-formation decisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes structuring remedies (specific performance, disgorgement) so the chooser internalizes costs/benefits of performance, while Paper B develops a broader fault-based taxonomy explaining why courts use larger or smaller damage measures to induce appropriate precaution, mitigation, and promise-making behavior.

shared_topics.topic: critiques of the orthodox 'efficient breach'/strict-liability account and proposals for alternative frameworks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A offers the 'efficient performance' hypothesis as an alternative showing efficiency need not depend on promisor-centered options or expectation damages; Paper B rejects strict liability in damages and advances a fault-based economic theory that better explains doctrinal diversity and when breaches should be deterred or permitted.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2012utahlrev861!!ARTICLE: Taking Outcomes Seriously
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Taking Outcomes Seriously

shared_topics.topic: whether the promisor's reason or intent should alter damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A presents experimental evidence that intentionality, motivation, and whether a transfer is voluntary affect recipients' valuation of outcomes and thus should be included in welfare/damage calculations; Paper B develops a fault-based theory arguing courts already and should continue to tailor damage measures based on the reason for breach rather than treating breach as strict liability.

shared_topics.topic: adequacy of monetary/expectation damages as a complete measure of welfare or outcome
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the narrow wealth-only conception of outcomes and urges broadening outcome measures beyond pecuniary end-results; Paper B criticizes the exclusive reliance on expectation damages and analyzes the roles of expectation, restitution, and reliance interests in capturing what compensation should mean.

shared_topics.topic: how damage rules should be designed to create proper incentives and promote efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that incorporating non-pecuniary elements (e.g., voluntariness, identity, intentionality) into outcome definitions can increase welfare and avoid inefficiencies; Paper B systematically explains how varying damage measures (larger for deterring opportunistic breaches, smaller for accidental contracts) create incentives that promote efficient contracting behavior.

shared_topics.topic: the special treatment of coerced or compelled transfers and implications for remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that unwilling or legally compelled transfers reduce recipients' valuation and suggests adding premiums to damages (e.g., 'compelled giving' premium) and rethinking remedies like liquidated damages and takings compensation; Paper B addresses when courts choose different remedial measures (expectation, restitution, reliance) and how doctrines like mitigation and market measures limit or modify awards in contexts involving enforcement and coerced outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 37umiamilrev93!!ARTICLE: Inflation and the Present Value of Future Economic Damages
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Inflation and the Present Value of Future Economic Damages

shared_topics.topic: methods for measuring monetary damages and present valuation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes alternative computational methods for converting forecasted future earnings and medical costs into a present-value award (including how inflation and discounting should be incorporated) and proposes a preferred calculation; Paper B analyzes and justifies different substantive damage measures (expectation, reliance, restitution, market) and explains when courts choose larger or smaller monetary measures to serve different objectives.

shared_topics.topic: judicial doctrine and discretion in selecting damage rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how courts have accepted divergent approaches (and sometimes excluded inflation evidence) and critiques the legal system's inconsistent treatment of present-value methodologies; Paper B examines how courts actually apply different damage doctrines and develops a theory (fault-based) explaining judicial selection among damage measures.

shared_topics.topic: economic modeling of incentives and parameters that affect awards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats economic parameters—expected inflation, growth rates, and discount rates—as central inputs that change the magnitude of awards and investment incentives for plaintiffs; Paper B uses economic incentive analysis (including efficient-breach logic) to argue how damage rules shape promisor and promisee behavior and which measures promote efficient contracting.

shared_topics.topic: uncertainty, forecasting, and the role of expert evidence in assessing damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the forecasting difficulties, uncertainty about future prices/returns, and the reliance on (often contested) expert witnesses to compute present values; Paper B addresses uncertainty and measurement difficulties as reasons courts sometimes reduce or alter damages (through doctrines like mitigation, foreseeability, and uncertainty) and motivates doctrinal rules that respond to informational limits.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 31sandiegolrev307!!ARTICLE: Contracts in Wonderland: A Fable Regarding the Administrative Adjudication of Qualifying Facility Contracts in California
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contracts in Wonderland: A Fable Regarding the Administrative Adjudication of Qualifying Facility Contracts in California

shared_topics.topic: who (which institutions) adjudicate and enforce contractual promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the role courts play in enforcing contracts and choosing damage measures, arguing that judicial rules create incentives for performance or breach; Paper B centers on administrative adjudication of qualifying-facility contracts and how that alternative institutional forum shapes whether promises are kept and how disputes are resolved.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules and remedies shape parties' expectations and contracting behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a fault-based economic theory showing that different damage measures (expectation, reliance, restitution, market measures) are used to create incentives for desirable contracting conduct; Paper B examines (through a fable) how changes in the rules and enforcement processes affect parties' expectations about promise-keeping and outcomes under contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the destabilization or erosion of settled contract norms and its practical consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents doctrinal variety in damage measures and explains why courts use different rules across contexts, highlighting doctrinal uncertainty; Paper B explicitly describes long-settled rules being disregarded and uncertainty about what the rules are, and explores the consequences for contracting in that environment.

shared_topics.topic: the procedural role of adjudication (courts vs administrative bodies) in producing legal outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes minimizing court involvement and how adjudicative roles influence the choice of uniform remedies like expectation damages; Paper B focuses on administrative adjudication as a forum for contract disputes and how procedural choices at the administrative level affect enforcement and the substance of contractual rights.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1381!!ARTICLE: IN (PARTIAL) DEFENSE OF STRICT LIABILITY IN CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: IN (PARTIAL) DEFENSE OF STRICT LIABILITY IN CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: the normative and descriptive debate over strict liability versus fault-based contract damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A rejects the strict-liability premise and develops a fault-based economic theory to explain and justify when courts use different damage measures; Paper B defends a core strict-liability regime and argues descriptively and normatively that courts preserve a no-fault core despite peripheral 'fault lines.'

shared_topics.topic: economic and incentive-based justifications for damage rules (efficiency, deterrence, contracting costs)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how different damage measures create incentives to deter inefficient breaches, overreliance, or accidental contracting and ties remedy choice to joint-cost minimization; Paper B offers complementary efficiency and transaction-cost arguments for why a strict-liability core lowers contracting costs and supports informal/relational contracting.

shared_topics.topic: the role and selection of specific remedial doctrines and damage measures (expectation, reliance, restitution, mitigation, willful breach, market damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explains why courts deploy expectation, reliance, restitution, and market measures differently across breach types and how doctrines like mitigation shape awards; Paper B focuses on the willful-breach and mitigation doctrines to show courts' resistance to comparative-fault adjustments and defends the resulting remedial structure.

shared_topics.topic: empirical/descriptive claims about how courts actually apply contract-damage rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that courts already vary damage measures in patterns consistent with a fault-based incentive theory and uses case examples to support this; Paper B surveys cases to argue the opposite descriptive conclusion—that courts maintain a strict-liability core and decline to apply comparative-fault modifications at the core of contract liability.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 90ucinlrev283!!ARTICLE: FORCE MAJEURE, VIS MAJOR, IMPOSSIBILITY, AND IMPRACTICABILITY UNDER OHIO LAW BEFORE AND AFTER COVID-19
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: FORCE MAJEURE, VIS MAJOR, IMPOSSIBILITY, AND IMPRACTICABILITY UNDER OHIO LAW BEFORE AND AFTER COVID-19

shared_topics.topic: how contract rules and clauses allocate risk and create incentives for performance versus breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a fault-based economic theory showing how different damage measures (expectation, reliance, restitution, market damages, mitigation doctrines) are used to deter or encourage performance and manage opportunistic breaches; Paper B analyzes force majeure clauses and related doctrines as contractual and common‑law tools that allocate risk and shape parties' incentives to perform or excuse nonperformance (especially during COVID-19).

shared_topics.topic: treatment of unforeseen events and excuse doctrines (impossibility, impracticability, force majeure) and their impact on remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A classifies breach types and explains why courts choose larger or smaller damage measures depending on whether contracts should have been performed, made, or breached in the face of contingencies; Paper B focuses on impossibility, impracticability, vis major, and force majeure, assessing when those doctrines excuse performance and how that changes the availability and measurement of damages after a large unforeseen shock like COVID‑19.

shared_topics.topic: judicial interpretation and adaptation of contract doctrine in response to systemic shocks or novel circumstances
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that courts already apply a variety of damage rules contextually and calls for a theory to explain and guide that case‑by‑case application; Paper B surveys Ohio precedent and projects how courts will interpret force majeure and excuse doctrines in the wake of the COVID‑19 pandemic, assessing how doctrines may be applied or should evolve.

shared_topics.topic: use of law-and-economics reasoning to evaluate and justify contract doctrines and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly frames its fault‑based damages theory in economic terms—focusing on incentives, joint costs, and efficiency in remedy selection; Paper B invokes law and economics principles in situating force majeure and excuse doctrines and in analyzing how courts should allocate losses and shape behavior in pandemic‑related contract disputes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 63notredamelrev247!!ARTICLE:A Newly Identified Contract Unconscionability: Unconsionability of Remedy
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:A Newly Identified Contract Unconscionability: Unconsionability of Remedy

shared_topics.topic: courts' use of foreseeability, certainty, and mitigation doctrines to limit large damage awards
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how traditional rules like foreseeability, certainty, and mitigation operate not merely as formal limits but as mechanisms courts use to reduce or shape damages — Paper A argues these doctrines have been covertly employed to avoid disproportionate remedies, and Paper B shows they function as tools to calibrate awards for incentive purposes within a fault-based damages framework.

shared_topics.topic: limiting disproportionate or unconscionable remedies (unconscionability of remedy)
shared_topics.justification: Both works engage the question whether courts should (and do) curb exceptionally large consequential damages as unjust or unconscionable — Paper A develops the explicit doctrine of 'unconscionability of remedy' (and §351(3)) to refuse or limit disproportionate compensation, while Paper B explains why smaller or capped measures are normatively appropriate in some breach contexts to avoid overdeterrence and unfair liability.

shared_topics.topic: the importance of risk allocation at the time of contract formation for determining damages
shared_topics.justification: Both papers emphasize that the fairness and proper magnitude of damages depend on the parties' allocation of risk when the contract was made — Paper A stresses that disproportionate liability reflects a failure to allocate risk and should be curtailed, and Paper B links damage rules to incentives for contracting parties to make, allocate, or avoid risky bargains.

shared_topics.topic: the justification and selection among different damage measures (expectation, reliance, restitution) to achieve normative goals
shared_topics.justification: Both articles address why courts sometimes choose measures other than full expectation damages: Paper A discusses curtailing remedies to avoid extreme unfairness (effectively selecting smaller measures), while Paper B provides an economic theory explaining when and why courts deploy expectation, reliance, or restitution to produce proper incentives and deterrence.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 55amjcompl721!!ARTICLE: Why No "Efficient Breach" in the Civil Law?: A Comparative Assessment of the Doctrine of Efficient Breach of Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Why No "Efficient Breach" in the Civil Law?: A Comparative Assessment of the Doctrine of Efficient Breach of Contract

shared_topics.topic: the theory of efficient breach of contract and its normative implications
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the doctrine of efficient breach comparatively, asking why the efficiency-based justification for breaching (and compensating) contracts has not taken root in civil law systems; Paper B critically engages with efficient breach as the dominant economic justification for expectation damages and explains its limits within a broader theory of contract damages.

shared_topics.topic: the role of expectation (and alternative) damage measures in enabling or discouraging breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A relies on the assumption that breachers can compensate promisees (typically via expectation damages) to make breaches efficient and examines whether civil law doctrines would permit that outcome; Paper B interrogates why courts use expectation, reliance, and restitution measures and proposes a fault-based account for when larger or smaller measures should be applied to shape behavior.

shared_topics.topic: how institutional, doctrinal, and cultural features of legal systems shape incentives and the adoption of economic doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes structural and cultural hurdles in civil law (e.g., pacta sunt servanda, good faith, doctrinal history in France and Germany) that impede acceptance of efficient-breach reasoning; Paper B examines how existing judicial doctrines and institutional constraints lead courts to choose different damage rules to create specific incentives and achieve efficient contracting behavior.

shared_topics.topic: a law-and-economics approach to designing contract rules to maximize joint welfare
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates efficient breach within the law-and-economics tradition and asks whether its efficiency rationale applies across legal families; Paper B explicitly uses economic incentive analysis to propose a fault-based damages regime intended to minimize joint costs and promote efficient contracting outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 60lalrev233!!ARTICLE: The Wasted Sacrifice of Lessors' Lost Profit Claims in Bankruptcy
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Wasted Sacrifice of Lessors' Lost Profit Claims in Bankruptcy

shared_topics.topic: legitimacy and measurement of expectation / lost‑profit damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when expectation (lost‑profit) damages are the appropriate remedy versus reliance or restitution and explains their predominance under different breach incentives; Paper B focuses on lessors' lost‑profit claims in bankruptcy, treating those claims as expectation damages and contesting statutory limits on their measurement and enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: economic and policy justifications for limiting or adjusting contract damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops an economic, fault‑based theory for tailoring damage measures to create optimal incentives (deterring inefficient breaches, avoiding overdeterrence), while Paper B evaluates the economic and policy rationales offered for the statutory cap on lessors' damages and finds them unconvincing.

shared_topics.topic: distributional consequences and fairness among claimants created by remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how different damage rules allocate risk and incentives between promisor and promisee (and influence behavior like precaution and mitigation), and Paper B argues that Section 502(b)(6)'s partial disallowance of lessors' claims produces unequal and unfair treatment of similarly situated creditors.

shared_topics.topic: interaction of doctrinal rules with economic/contract theory in shaping remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques existing doctrinal explanations (strict liability/efficient breach) and proposes a theory better aligned with doctrinal practice, while Paper B examines historical and doctrinal developments in bankruptcy law and contrasts contractual theory with statutory bankruptcy policy in justifying limits on remedies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 10flataxrev459!!Article: Just Enough: Substantial Performance, Ministerial Acts and the All Events Tests for Income and Expense Accruals
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Just Enough: Substantial Performance, Ministerial Acts and the All Events Tests for Income and Expense Accruals

shared_topics.topic: the legal significance of substantial or partial performance versus full performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how doctrines (like mitigation, foreseeability, and reductions in awards) reflect courts' willingness to treat less-than-complete performance differently when measuring damages, and Paper B examines whether substantial (rather than full) performance can satisfy contractual conditions so that rights and liabilities become fixed for tax accrual purposes.

shared_topics.topic: judicially crafted doctrines to avoid forfeiture and shape outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts employ a variety of damage measures and doctrinal adjustments to produce desirable incentives and avoid over- or under-deterrence, while Paper B traces how courts construct conditions and invoke substantial-performance doctrines to preserve expectations and avoid unfair forfeitures when applying the all-events tests.

shared_topics.topic: when contractual events trigger legal entitlements or liabilities (timing of fixity)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is centrally concerned with when different damage regimes should apply depending on the nature and timing of breach, and Paper B focuses on the ‘‘all events’’ accrual tests—asking when the occurrence of contractual events (including ministerial acts and substantial performance) makes rights or liabilities unconditional for tax accounting.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules create incentives for parties' behavior around performance, documentation, and breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops an economic, fault-based theory showing how different damage measures incentivize promise-making, performance, and precaution-taking, and Paper B considers how accrual/tax rules and the recognition of substantial performance influence taxpayers’ decisions about invoicing, documentation, and completion of contractual obligations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 34santaclaralrev1!!ARTICLE: Liquidated Damages for Delay in Completion of Commercial Construction Projects: Are They Recoverable by the Owner When the Owner Contributes to the Delay?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Liquidated Damages for Delay in Completion of Commercial Construction Projects: Are They Recoverable by the Owner When the Owner Contributes to the Delay?

shared_topics.topic: whether a promisee's own contribution to a breach bars or reduces recovery of contractual damages (e.g., liquidated damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes California case law on whether an owner who contributes to construction delay can still recover liquidated damages and how courts have either denied recovery or apportioned awards; Paper B develops a fault-based theory explaining why and when courts should reduce or limit damages based on the reason for breach and parties' fault.

shared_topics.topic: how courts should apportion damages where there are concurrent or overlapping causes of nonperformance (causation and concurrency of delay)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on scheduling-expert disputes and appellate decisions about causation and concurrency in construction delays and on methods courts use (or avoid) to allocate days of delay; Paper B theorizes more generally about using different damage measures and doctrines to allocate loss across parties when breaches arise from multiple causes.

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal choice between enforcing fixed contractual damage terms versus adjusting damages to reflect fairness and incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines judicial willingness to enforce liquidated-damage clauses strictly versus apportioning or denying them when the owner contributed to delay, and offers drafting strategies to manage that risk; Paper B critiques the strict-liability/expectation-damage approach and defends a fault-sensitive set of doctrines that adjust remedies to produce better incentives and fairer outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: use of contract design and legal rules to allocate risk and reduce litigation costs stemming from delay disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes contractual drafting techniques to avoid uncertainty and costly litigation over delay, causation, and liquidated damages; Paper B situates damages rules within an economic framework explaining how remedial rules can be shaped to create incentives, limit costly adjudication, and allocate risks between parties.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 10flataxrev459!!Article: Just Enough: Substantial Performance, Ministerial Acts and the All Events Tests for Income and Expense Accruals
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Just Enough: Substantial Performance, Ministerial Acts and the All Events Tests for Income and Expense Accruals

shared_topics.topic: when partial or "substantial" performance fixes legal rights and liabilities
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes whether substantial rather than full performance (including ministerial acts like invoicing) can satisfy contractual conditions so that income or expenses must be accrued for tax purposes; Paper B examines how degrees and reasons for nonperformance (and partial performance) influence the choice and size of contract-damage measures, treating performance quality and extent as central to remedial outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: how courts construe contractual conditions to avoid forfeiture and produce fair outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on judicially constructed conditions and the willingness of courts to treat substantial performance as satisfying contractual conditions to preserve expectations and avoid forfeiture in accrual timing; Paper B shows that courts select among damages doctrines and adjust remedies to balance parties' expectations and avoid harsh or overdeterrent results, effectively construing contractual obligations through remedial choices.

shared_topics.topic: the incentive effects of legal rules on contracting behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A concerns how tax accrual rules and the timing of recognizing income/expenses create incentives (or burdens) for contracting and billing practices, and whether allowing accrual on substantial performance changes those incentives; Paper B develops an economic, fault-based theory showing that different damage measures are used to create optimal incentives for promise-making, performance, breach, and precaution-taking.

shared_topics.topic: judicial use of doctrinal devices and discretion to temper formal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents divergent authorities treating documentary or ministerial requirements (e.g., invoices) as either prerequisites or irrelevant for fixing rights, highlighting judicial discretion in applying the all-events tests; Paper B documents doctrines (mitigation, foreseeability, uncertainty, selection among expectation/reliance/restitution) that courts deploy to modulate strict remedial rules and calibrate outcomes to situational fairness and efficiency.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 86tullrev135!!ARTICLE: False Efficiency and Missed Opportunities in Law and Economics
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: False Efficiency and Missed Opportunities in Law and Economics

shared_topics.topic: limits of the efficient-breach justification for expectation damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes the theory of efficient breach as a legal-economic argument that overlooks how rules permitting breach can misallocate activity and produce socially inferior incentives; Paper B directly rejects the strict‑liability/efficient‑breach account as an adequate theory of contract damages and develops a fault‑based alternative to explain when and why expectation damages are used.

shared_topics.topic: design of legal rules as incentive devices for contracting and tort behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that legal rules (e.g., Hand Formula, breach doctrines) create incentives that can push actors into particular activities and must be evaluated for those behavioral effects; Paper B explicitly treats damage rules as tools to create incentives, showing how different measures (expectation, reliance, restitution, market damages) are used to encourage or deter particular contracting conduct.

shared_topics.topic: opportunism, selection effects, and the opportunity costs of legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that permitting or encouraging an activity (or a remedy) can attract actors into opportunistic roles and divert capital/labor from more productive alternatives, producing selection effects; Paper B analyzes how damages deter opportunistic breaches and how particular damage rules influence parties' decisions to make contracts or position themselves to breach, with attendant allocation consequences.

shared_topics.topic: critique of law‑and‑economics models that rely on idealized market or institutional assumptions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues many law‑and‑economics conclusions depend on implausibly strong assumptions about capital, credit, and other market perfection and thus may misapply to real institutions; Paper B challenges the strict‑liability/efficient‑breach model's reliance on minimizing court involvement and related idealizations, arguing a more realistic, fault‑sensitive approach better fits actual doctrine and institutional constraints.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68valrev947!!ARTICLE: EFFICIENT BREACH OF CONTRACT: CIRCLES IN THE SKY Copyright (c) 1982 by Ian R. Macneil.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EFFICIENT BREACH OF CONTRACT: CIRCLES IN THE SKY Copyright (c) 1982 by Ian R. Macneil.

shared_topics.topic: limits of the ‘efficient breach’ doctrine and critiques of the simple-efficiency model
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly diagnoses a fallacy in the ‘simple-efficient-breach’ analysis and shows how that model is defective, while Paper B criticizes efficient-breach theory for relying on strict‑liability assumptions and limited court involvement and argues it fails to explain actual doctrinal practice.

shared_topics.topic: choice among remedies — expectation damages versus specific performance, reliance, and restitution
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the specific‑performance versus damages choice and how the rule must be stated to avoid the simple‑efficiency fallacy, and Paper B analyzes why courts use expectation, reliance, and restitution measures and how those remedies should be allocated under a fault‑sensitive regime.

shared_topics.topic: how damage rules create incentives that affect breach/perform decisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses the Athos/Porthos example and efficiency arguments about when breach increases social welfare and questions whether the simple model captures real incentives, while Paper B develops an explicit economic (fault‑based) theory showing how different damage measures are used to encourage or deter particular contracting behavior.

shared_topics.topic: role of transaction costs and real‑world doctrinal frictions in undermining idealized economic models
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes between a transaction‑cost‑free simple analysis and more realistic transaction‑cost‑sensitive accounts and locates the fallacy in ignoring those frictions, and Paper B points to doctrines (mitigation, foreseeability, uncertainty, market damages) and practical court practices as adjustments that reflect transaction costs and limit strict‑liability conclusions.

shared_topics.topic: distinguishing types/grades of fault (negligence, opportunism, accidental mistake) and tailoring doctrinal responses

papers.node_id: 107michlrev1583!!ARTICLE: THE FAULT PRINCIPLE AS THE CHAMELEON OF CONTRACT LAW: A MARKET FUNCTION APPROACH
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE FAULT PRINCIPLE AS THE CHAMELEON OF CONTRACT LAW: A MARKET FUNCTION APPROACH
papers.abstract:
Some seventy-five years ago, Ernst Rabel came from Berlin to the United States as director of the famous "Schloss Institutes" for comparative and international law, the forerunner of the Max Planck Institutes. Since Michigan became what was likely his strongest link to the United States, it seems fitting to begin with his contributions. Rabel brought with him his conception of comparative law as a discovery device for all countries,and sought to develop this international discussion into more concrete results, namely, into a unification of sales law as the core area of contract law.Moreover, when Rabel later wrote his treatises on international private law and (comparative) sales law- which became highly influential for the Hague Uniform Sales Law of 1964and subsequently the Vienna Convention on the International Sale of Goods of 1980 ("CISG")- one of the core questions where his new surroundings heavily influenced himwas fault. In fact, he strongly advocated a strict liability regime, a trademark of Anglo-American contract law, which was ultimately introduced into article 79 of the CISG. And because of the eminence of the CISG, this regime has remained on the international agenda; it is evident in more general sets of contract law principles developed over the last decades at the Unidroit leveland in Europe.The Principles of European Contract Law opt for a strict liability regime in which the only permissible excuse is force majeure,andthe breaching party bears the burden of proof.The Unidroit Principles share, in principle, this singular focus on force majeure,but they do so in a more refined manner: article 5.1.4 distinguishes "obligations de resultat" (promises of result) from "obligations de moyen" (promises of best efforts). The addition of this distinction is important. But it should be kept in mind that these terms could be bargained for in a contract under any regime.
The importance of another development for which Rabel strongly advocated, the introduction of the so-called German "Nachfrist" into the CISG regime, is less obvious. But in fact, this was no less influential on the current European regime than the incorporation of the strict liability approach. Nachfrist limits, in principle, the most onerous sanctions for breach of contract to those cases where the party not only breached but also did not cure when given a "second chance" (after an additional period of time), both in the CISG and in the current European system.
Several questions arise from this cross-Atlantic trip into history. The first is whether the example of Rabel and the contract law developments he spawned speak in favor of the superiority of a strict liability regime.The second question is whether the core argument advanced by Rabel, i.e., that only strict liability can mirror the promise initially given, is one that works particularly well in sales law (and in an industrial society), but less well in services (and in a service society). A third question is whether, instead of following Rabel's regime, all legal systems really follow a nuanced approach with a mixture of strict liability and fault liability elements, and utilize other governance devices such as the "second chance" principle. Finally, a fourth question is what guidelines can be given for a satisfactory combination of the two liability regimes.
This Article suggests that the answer to this final question is that market expectations should be the core criterion for combining strict and fault liability and that, therefore, legal scholarship and legal regimes should take a market function approach. Part I takes a comparative law approach to show the range of possibilities in choosing between liability regimes, and examines their relative advantages. Part II proposes a market function approachbased on these systems to balance elements of strict liability and fault liability.
. Nuance as the Common Denominator in a Comparative Law Perspective
The traditional view among contract scholars is that civil law systems opt for fault liability in contract law while common law systems opt for strict liability. Yet this impression is the result of too much abstraction on both sides. Upon closer inspection, the common denominator between civil and common law systems is that all systems opt for a nuanced combination of the two.Contract law development in Europe now often occurs at the European Community ("EC") level. EC contract law is an amalgam of the civil law and common law systems of its member states and thus provides a valuable additional perspective.

questions.question: Should liability for breach of contract depend on the breaching party's culpability or be imposed irrespective of culpability, and which approach better aligns with parties' promises and market expectations?

Does the suitability of a culpability-conditioned versus an outcome-conditioned liability regime vary between transactions that are result-oriented (e.g., sale of goods) and those that are effort- or service-oriented?

How should legal systems combine culpability-conditioned and outcome-conditioned liability rules (including governance devices that give breaching parties a 'second chance'), and should market-function or market-expectation criteria guide that combination?

matched_themes: What standard should courts apply to determine whether a party's deviation from contractual obligations is significant enough to excuse the other party's performance?
Should parties and courts adopt fault-based remedial regimes that distinguish among breaches by reason when allocating remedies?
How have historical, geographic, institutional, and transnational influences shaped the evolution and transplantation of contract doctrines and remedies?
Are civil-law systems less receptive than common-law systems to permitting breaches that increase overall welfare when compensation is possible?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
How should remedial and enforcement rules be structured to achieve efficient behavior when populations include both internalizers and externalizers?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
Do courts consider the breaching party's blameworthiness or opportunistic behavior when selecting among compensatory remedies?
How should international instruments reconcile divergent national traditions to create transnational rules on remedies for cross-border sales?
When is an indirect remedy (one that induces self-compliance) preferable to a direct remedy that delivers the outcome?

shared_topics.topic: the gap between stated contract doctrine and actual practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques 'contract lore' as myths or oversimplifications that diverge from how law actually operates, and Paper B likewise rejects an oversimple strict-vs-fault binary, showing across systems that doctrine is applied with many qualifications and mixtures.

shared_topics.topic: interpretive devices for making sense of contract rules (heuristics vs market-function)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes treating widely asserted contract propositions as heuristic starting points for analysis rather than literal truths, while Paper B advances a 'market function' approach as an interpretive and normative rule for choosing and combining liability regimes.

shared_topics.topic: criteria for when contract law should be reformed
shared_topics.justification: Paper A offers a lore/aspiration scale to flag statements of law that merit skepticism and possible reform, and Paper B proposes market expectations as the normative criterion to guide acceptable mixes of strict and fault liability and attendant reforms.

shared_topics.topic: how promises, performance expectations, and remedies should be allocated
shared_topics.justification: Paper A probes doctrines like expectation damages and the significance of party intent as aspirational or mythic accountings of what performance law should do, and Paper B analyzes distinctions between obligations of result vs means, strict liability, and remedial regimes (including Nachfrist) as ways to align legal consequences with the underlying promise and expectations.

shared_topics.topic: emphasis on nuance, exceptions, and 'second chance' governance devices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that many contested contract doctrines function as first-step heuristics that admit numerous exceptions and further inquiry, and Paper B documents and defends nuanced doctrinal devices (e.g., Nachfrist/second-chance rules and mixed liability regimes) rather than categorical rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1517!!ARTICLE: WILLFULNESS VERSUS EXPECTATION: A PROMISOR-BASED DEFENSE OF WILLFUL BREACH DOCTRINE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: WILLFULNESS VERSUS EXPECTATION: A PROMISOR-BASED DEFENSE OF WILLFUL BREACH DOCTRINE

shared_topics.topic: the relevance of promisor fault/willfulness in allocating liability for breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends special treatment for 'willful' breaches, arguing that willfulness (breaches avoidable at little or no cost) should change remedies; Paper B analyzes the role of fault versus strict liability in contract law and asks when fault-based rules should govern breaches rather than strict liability.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial design should shape promisor incentives (including disgorgement, expectation, and 'second chance' tools)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for promisor-centered disgorgement-style remedies to eliminate incentives for costless, willful breaches; Paper B evaluates remedial and procedural devices (e.g., Nachfrist/second chance and differentiated sanctions) as part of a regime that balances strict and fault liability to produce appropriate incentives.

shared_topics.topic: using ex ante market expectations and bargaining to determine the appropriate liability regime
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds the willful-breach rules in parties' ex ante bargaining and the premium a promisor can obtain by credibly committing not to commit costless breaches; Paper B proposes a 'market function' approach that selects between strict and fault liability based on what best mirrors market expectations for particular contractual contexts.

shared_topics.topic: tailoring liability rules to types of promises or the costs of performance (result vs means; costless avoidance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on breaches that could have been avoided at little or no cost to the promisor as the category warranting enhanced remedies; Paper B distinguishes obligations of result vs obligations of means and argues liability should vary with the nature of the promissory undertaking and the costs/risk of performance.

shared_topics.topic: comparative/legal-structural justification for mixing strict liability and fault elements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends doctrinal patchwork (willful-breach doctrines alongside expectation damages) as justified by promisor-market behavior and efficient outcomes; Paper B surveys national and transnational systems to argue that a nuanced mixture of strict and fault liability, guided by market function, is the preferable structural approach.

shared_topics.topic: strict liability versus fault-based liability regimes in contract law

shared_topics.topic: how courts choose among damage measures (expectation, reliance, restitution) based on the nature of breach

shared_topics.topic: economic/incentive-based justifications for damage rules (including critique of efficient breach)
