papers.title: ARTICLE: THE MYTH OF EFFICIENT BREACH: NEW DEFENSES OF THE EXPECTATION INTEREST
papers.abstract:
CONTRACT remedies have long sought to protect the gains that parties contract to realize. Although the Restatement recognizes three distinct contractual interests - expectation, reliance, and restitution - it expressly privileges the expectation interest over the other two. Courts "ordinarily … enforce[] the broken promise by protecting the expectation that the injured party had when he made the contract."
In recent years, both courts and scholars have begun to question how the law should protect a promisee's expectation. This question once had a conventional - indeed, assumed - answer. Courts, the Restatement observes, ordinarily protect the promisee's expectation "by attempting to put him in as good a position as he would have been in had the contract been performed";that is, by "giving the injured party the "benefit of the bargain.'"The Uniform Commercial Code similarly recites that contract remedies are designed to put the aggrieved party "in as good a position as if the other party had fully performed."Conventional contract law thus does not put the promisee in the position of receiving the promised performance but rather puts him "in as good a position" by requiring the promisor to pay money damages that equal the benefit of the promisee's lost bargain. In the current lexicon, contractual expectations conventionally receive liability rather than property rule protection.
That contract remedies should vindicate the expectation interest through liability rules has become controversial.The controversy is best introduced by clarifying basic terms.
A Liability Rule: The law protects an entitlement by a liability rule when it requires an infringer of the entitlement to pay the entitlement holder a sum of money fixed by a third party, typically a court. Under contract law, the promisee is entitled to the benefit of his bargain, which the promisor infringes by breaching. The law accords liability rule protection to the entitlement because a court or jury fixes the entitlement's value and requires the promisor to pay it as damages.
A Property Rule: The law protects an entitlement with a property rule when it makes the entitlement holder's acquiescence a necessary condition for transfer of the entitlement. Contract law would protect the expectation with a property rule if it required the promisor always to render the promised performance rather than a monetary substitute for it. Under property rule protection, the promisee could obtain specific performance as of right.
Both liability and property rule protection of a contractual expectation focus on the value that the promisee places on performance. Liability rule protection permits the promisor to "take" the entitlement and later pay, or comply with a court order requiring her to pay, the promisee's value. Property rule protection would permit the promisee to enjoin unconsented takings, thereby requiring the promisor to repurchase the entitlement from the promisee.
A Restitutionary Rule: In contrast to liability and property rules, a restitutionary rule such as disgorgementfocuses on any value the promisor possesses that is attributable to the promisee. The Restatementdescribes the promisee's restitutionary entitlement as his "interest in having restored to him any benefit that he has conferred on the other party."This benefit can include gains that the promisor realized from breach if the parties' contract contributed to their existence. A restitutionary rule is enforced by an order requiring the promisor to pay over the value in her hands.
Some critics, including both commentators and courts, argue that contract law should protect the expectation with a property rule. Other (and overlapping) critics support vindicating the restitution interest.The critics are beginning to have an impact on the positive law.The classical expectation remedy, long a fixed point of contract law, is coming under threat.
This Article rejects both categories of criticism in favor of defending contract law's conventional preference for protecting the expectation interest with a liability rule. Although we defend the (increasingly insecure) status quo, we do so by novel arguments. Novelty matters in this case. The familiar arguments in favor of current law do not quite address the revisionist wave. Our arguments refute the revisionists' claims head-on.
Before introducing these arguments, we make a further clarifying remark concerning renegotiation.Renegotiation is unnecessary when contract law protects the expectation with a liability rule. A promisor who rejects performance is required only to pay the promisee's foregone value. She therefore can make value-maximizing perform-or-breach decisions unilaterally. In contrast, parties may renegotiate under property rule or restitution protection. Promisor exit from a contract may, we show below, create a greater total gain than performance. In this event, a promisee with property rule protection has an incentive to renegotiate to a new arrangement, under which the promisor is permitted to exit in return for sharing with the promisee the larger gain that exit makes possible. Restitution protection permits the promisee to capturethe gain that exit from a contract can create. The promisor, however, can prevent this gain from coming into existence by performing. Hence, the promisee, again, has an incentive to permit promisor exit in return for a share of the gain. Though the restitution remedy and property rule protection of the expectation focus differently on the location of the gains from breach, the availability of renegotiation causes the two rules to generate the same payoffs for contracting parties. Recognizing this permits us, for convenience, to evaluate the expectation interest debate primarily by contrasting liability and property rules.
Taken together, these clarifications permit us now to state the core of our position: both the efficient administration of commercial exchange and the commercial morality of the exchange relation require that promisors' obligations be set according to promisees' gains from trade and that these obligations be vindicated by a mechanism in which courts assess the gains' monetary value. That is, contract law should retain its traditional commitment to vindicating the promisee's expectation interest and should protect this interest by a liability rule. But we should not get ahead of ourselves. Rather, we begin at the beginning, by rehearsing conventional defenses of contract law's decision to protect the expectation interest with a liability rule, in order to establish the background against which recent critics have attacked the law and against which we construct our novel defenses.
Contract remedies took their liability rule form many years ago, but until recently, the law lacked a theoretical justification. In the 1970s, law and economics scholars constructed an efficiency rationale that ranges over the three stages of a contractual relationship. Beginning at the last litigation stage, a court cannot protect the expectation unless it is informed of the promisee's gain: the value abuyer would have realizedor the cost the seller would have incurred.Parties inform courts, which makes the penultimate stage relevant. Then, the parties learn values and costs and make the performance/breach decision. Now let a seller, for example, discover an opportunity to sell to a third party or to redeploy her resources to some entirely distinct purpose, rather than perform under the initial contract. As long as the law requires the seller to pay the promisee's gain if she breaches, she will perform nevertheless unless her gain from breach would exceed the promisee's gain from performance. Protecting the expectation with a liability rule thus is ex post (that is, at the performance/breach stage) efficient. A promisor breaches only if breach would produce a greater gain overall than performance would have done; otherwise, she performs. Now turn to the initial, contracting stage. Parties would contract for liability rule protection of the expectation because this would maximize the expected contracting gain for the parties to share. This multi-stage justification for liability rule protection has a name - the "theory of efficient breach" - and it has become sufficiently familiar to appear in textbooks intended for students.
The theory of efficient breach is vacuous, however. To see why, focus initially on the penultimate stage, when the promisor decides whether to perform. The Coase Theorem teaches that when transaction costs are low and agents are informed, as in contracting situations, agents bargain to the efficient allocation of property rights if the status quo allocation is suboptimal. To apply the Theorem here, let the law protect the expectation with a property rule - specific performance - and assume that performance of the parties' original contract would be inefficient: the promisor's loss from performance would exceed the promisee's gain. In this circumstance, as just said, parties renegotiate to permit breach: that is, they renegotiate to the result that a liability rule would have yielded on its own. Now let a liability rule obtain and assume that performance would be efficient: the promisee's performance gain exceeds the promisor's performance loss. In this circumstance, the promisor performs, which is the result that a property rule would have directed.And to summarize, in the Coase Theorem environment that efficient breach theory assumes, efficient breach (and efficient performance) occurs under every rule type.
Efficient breach theory also fails at the contracting stage because it cannot explain why parties would agree to liability rule protection were they free to do so. If parties ex post capture the surplus that breach makes available under any remedy, all remedies are consistent with surplus maximization. The theory thus cannot show why parties would contract for any remedy in the feasible set rather than any other remedy. Indeed, liability rule protection appears particularly problematic from a contracting point of view. The remedy allocates the full gain from breach to the promisor, so the promisee apparently has no reason to agree to it. The morality of promising, furthermore, seems to vindicate the promisee's concern. Even when breach is efficient, a breaching promisor appears to disappoint his promisee and violate his contractual obligations. The expectation remedy, however, apparently permits the promisor to retain the gains from her breach. Efficiency is not generally regarded as a sufficient ground for the law to permit, and indeed encourage, such an apparent wrong. There are no analogous doctrines of efficient conversion or efficient theft, for example.
There are two ways to rescue liability rule protection of the expectation interest from this theoretical lacuna. First, transaction costs may be lower under a liability rule. Second, the remedy may better encourage the parties to invest in the deal their contract is meant to protect. Under either explanation, protecting the expectation with a liability rule increases net surplus and so permits the promisor to purchase the promisee's consent to the remedy. We later pursue the transaction cost idea, but it is important to note here that both explanations relax the two key assumptions that generate efficient breach theory. The first assumption is that transaction costs are zero (that is, contracting and renegotiation are costless). The second assumption is that parties do not invest in the contract.When these assumptions hold, however, the remedy is theoretically ungrounded.
In recent years, prominent critics, implicitly accepting the two assumptions that generate efficient breach theory, have stepped into the void to argue that the expectation interest remedy is the wrong rule. The critics make two related claims. First, they claim that liability rule protection of the expectation interest is unjust because it allocates the full gain from breach to the promisor. This claim assumes the promisee has a right to share in the gain that breach makes possible. The critics' second claim defends this assumption. According to the critics, a contract law that permits an agent to bind herself to perform but also permits the agent to breach if she pays a legally set price - the expectation - is incoherent. A law of contract must permit agents to bind themselves. Hence, the law is made coherent only if it protects the promisee's right to performance with a property rule. The default contract remedy thus should be specific performance. The analysis above illustrates how the critics' two claims are related. A promisee with a right to specific performance can capture a portion of the gain that breach makes possible by forcing the promisor to purchase the right to exit from the contract.
A legal rule whose theoretical foundation is shaky sometimes is replaced, so it is unsurprising that the expectation interest's critics have made real world progress. The Uniform Commercial Code liberalized the right to specific performance. Specific performance, however, sometimes is impractical: it takes too long to get. Specific performance also is impossible when the promisor has sold the property to a good faith purchaser. The disgorgement remedy ameliorates these difficulties because it requires the promisor to transfer her gain from breach to the promisee. The recently adopted Restatement of Restitution permits a court to replace the expectation remedy with disgorgement when the remedy is inadequate,and "gain based damages" are beginning to be awarded in England and Israel.American courts also increasingly exhibit distaste for restricting contract damages to the promisee's loss when the promisor benefitted from breach.Critics also argue that the promisee's right to performance sometimes should be protected with the strongest remedy: punitive damages.
This Article thus enters an academic debate - Can liability rule protection of the expectation interest be justified? - that has real world consequences. Much in contract law will change if the critics'position captures the day. The changes, we argue here, would be for the worse, both economically and morally.
Our argument rests on an old idea, to which we give a new name: the "dual performance hypothesis." The dual performance hypothesis justifies protecting the expectation with a damage remedy. The hypothesis holds that contracts typically impose alternative obligations on the promisor: either to supply goods or services for a specified price or to transfer to the promisee the gain the promisee would have made had those goods or services been supplied. Under the hypothesis, a promisor who fails to deliver the promised goods or services but instead transfers the gain to her promisee performs rather than breaches.The promisor breaches only if she neither delivers nor pays. A breach in this sense contradicts the promisee's actual expectation - to receive goods or money - and thus reduces agents' incentives to organize their economic affairs under contracts. On this view, "efficient breach" theorynot only is vacuous; "efficient breach" itself is a myth, because no true breach is efficient.
Contract theorists of both an economic and a philosophical bent commonly either ignore the dual performance hypothesis or reject it as being psychologically and perhaps also ethically implausible.A promisee, it is said, intends to contract for goods or services; he does not intend to sell an option that permits the promisor either to trade or to pay. Our argument against this view proceeds along two intertwined paths. One path, which is developed in Parts I and II, creates a simple model that rests on the two assumptions remarked above: transaction costs are zero, and parties do not invest. On these assumptions, the model permits us to make three points.
, a promisee's expected monetary payoff is at least as high under liability rule protection of the expectation as it would be under property rule protection. This result refutes criticisms of current law whose premise is that liability rule protection deprives promisees of the gains that they contracted to realize. To summarize the logic of this result, let the promisor be a seller and define two types of contracting gains. The trading gain is the difference between the value the promisee would realize from trade and the promisor's cost of trade.The nontrading gain is the difference between the cost of trade and the promisee's value.When a seller rejects trade, a buyer with a right to specific performance realizes his trading gain and a portion of the nontrading gain. The seller must pay the buyer his trading gain because it is the buyer's expectation, and the seller also must pay the buyer a share of the nontrading gain in the form of a bribe for permitting the seller to exit.A seller who rejects trade thus incurs a cost that is the sum of the trading gain and the bribe. Since prices include costs, the contract price when the buyer's expectation is protected with a property rule reflects both cost categories. Now, substitute the expectation remedy for the buyer's right to specific performance. Competition will then cause the price to fall by the magnitude of the bribe the seller no longer has to pay. Holding the buyer's value fixed, his damages increase as the price falls.And since the reduction in price equals the expected bribe, the damages remedy permits the buyer to share in the nontrading gain. The buyer thus does as well when his expectation is protected with a liability rule as when it is protected with a property rule.
This result also shows that the movement to protect the expectation with property rules is as theoretically ungrounded as the efficient breach defense of the expectation. If the promisee's gain under a contract is invariant to the remedy the law supplies to enforce that contract, every remedy is as good as every other remedy.We therefore ask here whether promisees have second order reasons for preferring to share in the nontrading gain through the price mechanism - that is, through expectation damages - or to share in that gain through the renegotiation mechanism - that is, through a specific-performance-induced bribe.
The second point the model supports is that contracting and bargaining costs do create such second order reasons. This point is best introduced by assuming that parties are free to write either a "property rule contract" or a "liability rule contract."Our first point implies that the promisee's gross payoff would be the same under either contract type. We show below - our second point - that the cost of creating a property rule contract would exceed thecost of creating a liability rule contract. Buyers/promisees thus would have an incentive to write liability rule contracts because these generate higher net payoffs. Further, when a promisor/seller rejects trade, the property rule contract forces the parties into a bilateral monopoly. Bargaining in this game is zero sum: every dollar the seller pays to the buyer is a dollar that the seller must lose. The seller's incentive to resist payment is increasing in the size of the payment the buyer seeks. Since, we show, the buyer has a higher ex post payoff under a property rule than under a liability rule, the seller bargains harder, and perhaps less ethically, to avoid paying him under the property rule. Reasoning such as this implies that current law is a better default than a property rule default.And the implication vindicates the dual performance hypothesis.
Another implication of the dual performance hypothesis - our third point - is that the distinction between liability and property rule protection of the expectation is artificial. To see why, consider a widespread view that parties have no preferences regarding the remedies that the law provides unless their contract contains an express remedy term, such as a liquidated damages clause. This claim is implausible because parties take prices into account and the price is partly a function of the applicable remedy. When the remedy is viewed as an implied term, contract law necessarily protectsthe expectation with a property rule. Under a property rule contract, the seller promises to deliver goods or services unless delivery is impractical. Courts specifically enforce this contract by ordering delivery. Under a liability rule contract, the seller promises to deliver goods or services or make a monetary transfer in the amount of the promisee's foregone gain. Courts specifically enforce this contract by ordering transfer.Thus, every contracting remedy is a form of specific performance.
The other path along which our argument travels, which is developed in Part III, seeks to connect the structure of surplus sharing that our model identifies to the normative structure of contractual obligation and the principles of promissory morality that contract law implicates. Our argument here involves two claims.
, the dual performance hypothesis is consistent with the normative structure of contractual obligation. Regarding theory, the dual performance hypothesis restores coherence to contract law. Contract law must permit parties to make binding promises. A law that restricts the promisee to the payment of a preset monetary sum is coherent if the promisor binds herself either to deliver goods or services or to pay that preset sum. Moreover, a promisee without a right to the promisor's performance has the same expected payoff, or a higher payoff, than the promisee with that right. Thus, current contract law is as distributionally just as the law that the critics favor. We therefore reject the familiar suggestions that the expectation remedy merely prices, rather than sanctions, breachand that contract law betrays its own normative commitments when it encourages promisor exit.
, the type of sharing associated with the dual performance hypothesis is morally appropriate for promisors and promisees who interact, as they do in contract, at arm's length. In making this argument, we take on the core moral objection to the dual performance hypothesis, which is (roughly) that the expectation remedy encourages promisors to behave, within the promise relation, in a self-interested way that betrays the solidarity that this relation should properly involve. We argue, to the contrary, that the thinner form of promissory solidarity associated with the dual performance hypothesis, in which the terms of contractual sharing are cabined by the parties' contract, is appropriate for commercial transactions in open, cosmopolitan economies.
These claims, like the claims elaborated along our argument's first path, are principally formal or analytic. We develop a representation result: a set of concepts that together characterize the practices, doctrines, and norms of commercial contracting. This result exhibits the surplus-sharing associated with contract doctrine's preference for protecting the expectation with a liability rule and elaborates the meaning of that sharing so as to render it consistent with the solidarity that contractual and promissory norms more generally require. These results thus answer the current criticisms of the expectation remedy because the criticisms themselves are largely formal and analytic.
We conclude this Introduction with two remarks and a methodological observation. First, we analyze commercial transactions. Our paradigm case is an agreement to produce a widget, not an agreement to cook dinner together on Thursday nights. This focus permits us to abstract from the familial and affective claims to which contracts in private circumstances may give rise. It would be a category mistake, for example, to offer $ 50 to a friend when circumstances caused you to cancel a dinner date with him. It is not a category mistake for the promisors in our analysis to offer money to promisees when the promisors fail to deliver goods.
Analyzing commercial transactions also permits us plausibly to assume that parties are competent to make contracts and to renegotiate them when circumstances change. We make this assumption not only for its realism but also for heuristic reasons. Current critiques of contract law implicitly assume full rationality. They do not claim that the law constitutes a trap for the weak-minded but rather that a rational promisor can use the law to deprive her rational promisee of the full nontrading gain. We analyze this core contracting case to show that the concern is misplaced.
Our second introductory remark is that we proceed by making explicit the assumptions that govern the current expectation interest debate and then pursuing their implications. Those assumptionshold: (a) parties know the values of the relevant economic parameters; (b) parties know what their contracts do;(c) courts can protect the expectation with either a liability or a property rule because courts: (i) interpret contracts to realize the parties' preferences and (ii) learn the costs and values that trade would have implicated; (d) the parties' contracting and bargaining costs are zero; and (e) parties do not invest in the subject matter of the contract. We make these five assumptions for heuristic purposes: that is, we ask how contract remedies would actually function in the idealized world that current critics inhabit. This analysis permits us to ask whether any remedy becomes preferable to any of the others when that world is made more realistic.
Finally, our formal model and our more discursive analyses are each constructed with the other in mind (this is why we say that the two paths of our argument are intertwined). The model's account of the structure of contractual sharing is developed to answer conceptual concerns about the relationship between contract remedies and contractual solidarity. And our interpretive engagement with the doctrinal, normative, and moral structure of contract aims to elaborate this structure in light of the instrumental interactions between contracting parties that our model highlights. We return to comment on this marriage between economics and philosophy in our conclusion.
Part I sets out a model of the parties' contracting problem, which Part II then solves. The model performs two functions. First, it shows formally that, on the Coase Theorem assumptions noted above, the promisee's expected return under a contract is invariant to the remedy the law supplies. Second, modeling commercial party preferences permits us to identify the circumstances in which parties prefer the liability rule contract, which permits the promisor either to trade or to transfer, or the circumstances in which parties prefer a property rule contract, which commits the promisor to trade. It is important to identify these circumstances because thesearch is for the appropriate default remedy. Part III then interprets the model's results to show how they clarify the normative issues that occupy the literature and that are beginning to affect the law.

questions.question: Whether courts should enforce contracts by compelling promised performance (an in-kind remedy) or by awarding monetary compensation (a liability-rule remedy), in terms of overall economic efficiency and parties' incentives to contract and perform.

Whether promisees receive as high or higher expected monetary payoffs under enforcement by monetary damages than under enforcement that entitles them to insist on performance, given assumptions about renegotiation, transaction costs, and investments.

Whether enforcing contracts by awarding monetary compensation is normatively defensible - i.e., coherent with promissory morality and fair sharing of gains when a promisor obtains benefits from breaching - compared with remedies that require the promisor to surrender breach-related gains or to perform.

matched_themes: What moral and legal limits should constrain the commodification of promises-i.e., which promises ought not be treated as market commodities and how should the law reflect anti-commodification concerns?
What counterfactual baseline should courts use to measure plaintiffs' losses for compensation purposes?
Does giving the promisee a unilateral right to demand performance or elect a damages measure that captures promisor's forgone gains vindicate moral intuitions while preserving ex post efficiency?
Do courts actually prefer monetary damages over specific (in-kind) remedies, or do they grant specific relief except when independent reasons exist to deny it?
When should courts order specific performance (in-kind relief) versus awarding monetary damages?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?
Should the promisor or the promisee have the default right to choose between performance and payment to achieve allocative efficiency?
Should parties be presumptively permitted to contractually specify nonstandard damage remedies, or should courts retain authority to impose defaults?
Does making in-kind performance the legal default (rather than monetary compensation) change parties' enforcement choices, moral judgments, and economic efficiency?
When should courts prefer or enforce in-kind (specific) performance rather than monetary damages for breach of contract?
Does the promisor's motive for breaching (loss-avoiding vs gain-seeking) affect how much compensation promisees need to accept nonperformance?
Should the availability of legal remedies or contractual incompleteness change the moral assessment of a party who breaches under unanticipated circumstances?
When and to what extent should private self-help (withholding performance, repossession, or force) be permitted as a contract-enforcement mechanism?

Should remedies and contract law be structured to preserve conditions necessary for moral agency and promissory responsibility, rather than treating promises solely as instruments of economic cooperation?
Can costless ex-post renegotiation eliminate or preserve the ex-ante incentive effects of remedial rules on precaution, contract formation, and pricing?
How should courts treat and enforce stipulated remedies (liquidated damages clauses) versus substituting judicial remedies?
How do transaction costs, enforcement frictions, and institutional realities alter the theoretical efficiency of breach-plus-compensation?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
Should courts award disgorgement or force surrender of breacher gains in addition to compensation to deter opportunistic breaches?
Should courts police and limit supracompensatory contractual remedies (penalty-like clauses), or does allowing parties to contract for such terms respect autonomy and promote efficient contracting?
Should contract damages be measured as lost surplus (net benefit) rather than expectancy or market value as a general rule?
Should courts strip breachers of gains (disgorgement) in opportunistic or deliberate breaches, and what are the doctrinal and incentive effects of allowing disgorgement remedies in contract law?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
Would a surplus-based (lost-surplus or net-benefit) formula for contract damages simplify and improve compensation and incentives compared with existing measures?
What are the conceptual and methodological limits of the law-and-economics approach, and has the movement materially changed judicial decision-making?
When and under what standards should courts award disgorgement or remedies that strip gains from breaching parties?
To what extent should moral blameworthiness and non-economic considerations influence the design and application of contract remedies?
When is an indirect remedy (one that induces self-compliance) preferable to a direct remedy that delivers the outcome?

shared_topics.topic: theoretical soundness of the 'efficient breach' thesis and whether expectation damages promote efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Both papers directly interrogate the theory that expectation damages (the ‘expectancy’ remedy) produce efficient breach outcomes — Paper A argues the concept is indeterminate and that prior analyses are too narrow to support efficiency claims, while Paper B critiques efficient-breach theory as vacuous and develops alternative defenses of expectation damages.

shared_topics.topic: choice between expectation damages (liability rule) and specific performance (property rule)
shared_topics.justification: Both works engage substantively with the comparative normative and doctrinal question of whether contract law should enforce promises by awarding money (liability rule) or by ordering performance (property rule), weighing how each remedy allocates gains from breach and affects incentives.

shared_topics.topic: role of renegotiation, transaction costs, and institutional assumptions in assessing remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how renegotiation and transaction-cost assumptions (including the Coase-theorem environment) affect conclusions about which remedial rule yields efficient or desirable outcomes — Paper B formalizes this with models and the Coase argument, and Paper A criticizes prior work for neglecting wider institutional and downstream effects.

shared_topics.topic: normative/moral claims about promissory obligation and how they interact with economic analysis
shared_topics.justification: Both articles consider the moral dimension of promising (deontological versus instrumental views) and whether economic remedies (damages) disrespect promissory solidarity — Paper A highlights critics who insist on a deontological value to promises, and Paper B develops a moral defense of liability-rule expectation protection (the dual performance hypothesis).

shared_topics.topic: limitations of standard economic assumptions (information, rationality, downstream impacts) for resolving remedy disputes
shared_topics.justification: Both papers emphasize limits of the idealized economic assumptions used in the literature — Paper A invokes behavioral economics, happiness studies, and downstream firm effects to show indeterminacy and false positives/negatives, while Paper B tests the remedies under and beyond idealized assumptions (information, zero transaction costs, no investment) to show when each rule is justified.

shared_topics.justification: Both papers centrally engage the efficient-breach literature: Paper A critiques courts' reliance on efficient-breach reasoning to bar punitive damages and argues efficiency supports allowing punitive damages for willful breaches, while Paper B directly challenges efficient-breach theory as vacuous (the "myth of efficient breach") and defends why liability-rule expectation damages remain justified.

shared_topics.topic: the Calabresi‑and‑Melamed distinction between property rules and liability rules as the right framework for contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both articles organize their arguments around property vs. liability rule protection of contractual entitlements: Paper A invokes Calabresi & Melamed to argue punitive damages and other property-rule protections better induce negotiation, whereas Paper B evaluates why expectation damages (a liability rule) are the appropriate default and when parties would prefer one rule over the other.

shared_topics.topic: the role of transaction costs and renegotiation in determining which remedy maximizes welfare
shared_topics.justification: Both works analyze how the costs of bargaining, negotiation, and litigation affect whether courts should allow unilateral breach with damages or force negotiation/specific performance: Paper A argues that negotiation costs are usually lower than litigation costs so property-rule inducement to negotiate is efficient, and Paper B studies when zero/positive transaction costs make liability or property rules preferable and how renegotiation undermines the efficient‑breach critique.

shared_topics.topic: the proper set of remedies for breach (expectation damages, specific performance, disgorgement/punitive damages) and their normative implications
shared_topics.justification: Both papers dispute contemporary moves to alter remedial regimes: Paper A advocates expanding access to punitive damages for willful breaches (and compares punitive damages to specific performance and penalty clauses), while Paper B defends traditional expectation damages against calls for broader specific‑performance, disgorgement or punitive remedies and analyzes the moral and distributive consequences of shifting remedies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 101marqlrev87!!ARTICLE: PLURALISM APPLIED: A CONCORDANT APPROACH TO SELECTING CONTRACT RULES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PLURALISM APPLIED: A CONCORDANT APPROACH TO SELECTING CONTRACT RULES

shared_topics.topic: theory of "efficient breach" and whether breach should be economically encouraged
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly critiques the law-and-economics "efficient breach" account, arguing it is vacuous under Coasean assumptions and developing alternative justifications for liability-rule enforcement; Paper B describes and deploys the efficiency-theory rationale that favors allowing breach (and disfavoring punitive damages) when breach increases social wealth, using that rationale to frame tortious-interference questions.

shared_topics.topic: liability-rule (expectation damages) versus property-rule (specific performance) protection of contractual expectations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the normative and economic implications of protecting contractual expectations by damages versus specific performance and defends liability-rule protection; Paper B discusses the expectation remedy as the standard compensatory remedy (and contrasts it with supra‑compensatory or punitive remedies) when assessing remedies for breach and related tort claims.

shared_topics.topic: the "dual performance" or "dual promise" conception of contracts (either perform or pay)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A introduces and defends the dual performance hypothesis — that contracts often implicitly promise performance or a monetary transfer — to justify damages remedies; Paper B cites and employs the dual promise formulation (Markovits & Schwartz) to explain why expectation damages, not punitive awards, align with contractual commitments.

shared_topics.topic: competing normative frameworks for contract law (efficiency/utilitarianism versus rights/promissory morality) and their implications for remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A juxtaposes economic efficiency and promissory-morality arguments to defend liability-rule remedies and to reconcile commercial solidarity with damages; Paper B explicitly frames the dispute between efficiency theory and rights-based (promissory) theory to explain when punitive or supra‑compensatory remedies should be disallowed and how that affects tortious-interference doctrines.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 53lalrev1257!!ARTICLE: Comparative Ruminations on the Foreseeability of Damages in Contract Law. Dedicated to Professor Jurgen Basedow, Augsburg University, School of Law.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Comparative Ruminations on the Foreseeability of Damages in Contract Law. Dedicated to Professor Jurgen Basedow, Augsburg University, School of Law.

shared_topics.topic: the role of monetary damages versus specific performance as the primary contract remedy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends expectation (money) damages and contrasts liability-rule damages with property-rule specific performance and restitution, arguing for damages as the default in commercial contracting; Paper B engages this theme indirectly by treating how contract systems allocate compensation (monetary awards) rather than other remedies, comparing how different legal traditions limit or grant non-monetary relief and emphasizing monetary compensation rules in contract law.

shared_topics.topic: limits on recoverable damages tied to parties' expectations at contract formation (foreseeability/contemplation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the promisee's expectation interest — the value the promisee placed on performance at formation — as the baseline for damages, while Paper B studies the foreseeability (contemplation) limitation that confines contract damages to losses foreseeable when the contract was made, comparing its historical and doctrinal roots across systems.

shared_topics.topic: the conceptual distinction and interaction between contractual and tortious liability and its effect on remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes types of entitlements and remedies (expectation, reliance, restitution) and situates contract remedies within broader rules about liability and property, whereas Paper B explicitly contrasts contractual and tortious liability rules (sources of obligation, burdens of proof, timing of interest, and differing damage rules), using that distinction to explain why contract remedies diverge from tort remedies.

shared_topics.topic: comparative/doctrinal analysis of how different legal systems treat contract remedies and damage rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A references Restatement, the UCC, and comparative moves in England and Israel while arguing doctrinally for liability-rule protection of expectations; Paper B performs a comparative analysis of civil-law and common-law approaches (French‑based, German, Italian, English doctrines like Hadley v. Baxendale) to foreseeability and compensatory rules, with both papers evaluating cross-jurisdictional doctrine to support normative claims about remedy design.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1533!!ARTICLE: FAULT AT THE CONTRACT-TORT INTERFACE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: FAULT AT THE CONTRACT-TORT INTERFACE

shared_topics.topic: choice between monetary liability and alternative remedial regimes (liability rules vs property rules/strict liability/fault)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the nineteenth-century shift that left tort tethered to fault and contract rhetorically oriented toward strict liability, exploring the doctrinal consequences of those remedial allocations; Paper B engages the same normative and doctrinal question in contemporary form by debating whether contractual expectations should be enforced by monetary liability (damages) or by property-style specific performance or restitutionary remedies, defending liability rules on economic and moral grounds.

shared_topics.topic: the contract–tort/restitution boundary and doctrinal blurring (e.g., warranty, products liability, disgorgement)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly analyzes the interface between contract and tort and how historical conceptualizations continue to muddle cases like products‑warranty liability, while Paper B examines the encroachment of restitutionary and gain‑based remedies into contract law (disgorgement, gain‑based damages) and the consequences for the dividing line between contractual and restitutionary/tort remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts and enforcement mechanisms in shaping private ordering
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that conceptualizations of fault and liability historically sketched a border between public regulation and private ordering that affects judicial decisionmaking, and Paper B focuses on courts' central role in valuing expectations, fixing damages, and thereby determining whether private contracting will produce efficient or equitable outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: historical and doctrinal evolution of private‑law categories and their normative effects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A offers a historical account of how contract and tort modernized in the nineteenth century and how that history still influences doctrinal thinking, while Paper B situates current remedial debates within the history of the Restatements, the UCC, and evolving remedies (specific performance, disgorgement), using doctrinal development to motivate normative conclusions about remedy defaults.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Capping Market Damages at Lost Profit: An Unwarranted Limitation on a Middleman's Expectancy Interest

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the concrete problem of a middleman whose market-price damages dwarf its actual resale profit and whether recovery should be capped at lost profits, and Paper B engages the same underlying question at a theoretical level by analyzing who should capture the gains from breach (promisor or promisee) and whether disgorgement or property remedies can/should reallocate those gains.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal and statutory tensions in contract remedies (UCC and Restatement provisions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines conflicting UCC provisions (e.g., §§2-713, 2-712, 1-106) and case law on which rule should govern market versus lost-profit damages, while Paper B discusses how the UCC and the Restatement (and reforms like disgorgement/gain-based damages) have shifted courts toward alternative remedies and the implications of those doctrinal changes.

shared_topics.topic: normative and efficiency justifications for expectation-based remedies (efficient breach, Coasean bargaining, and investment/transaction-cost considerations)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A promises to analyze the conceptual validity of competing positions about expectancy damages in particular fact patterns, and Paper B develops detailed economic and moral arguments (critiquing efficient-breach reasoning, advancing the 'dual performance hypothesis,' and invoking transaction costs and investment incentives) to justify why liability-rule expectation damages are preferable.

compared_to.partner_title: Article: Consenting Under Stress

shared_topics.topic: use of interdisciplinary (non-legal) evidence to inform contract doctrine

shared_topics.topic: how default doctrines/remedies allocate risks, incentives, and fairness between contracting parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques existing doctrinal defaults (duress, unconscionability, undue influence) and proposes a new framework to determine when stress warrants relief to prevent exploitation; Paper B defends liability-rule expectation damages as the proper default, arguing remedy choice (liability vs property vs restitution) materially shapes prices, bargaining positions, and surplus sharing.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally analyzes how severe stress impairs decisionmaking and the quality of consent that should inform relief; Paper B interrogates the common economic assumptions about parties' information and rationality (and how courts learn values), showing those assumptions materially affect whether particular remedies are justified.

shared_topics.topic: the role of alternatives and renegotiation in evaluating breach, consent, and appropriate relief
shared_topics.justification: Paper A challenges doctrinal requirements that a distressed party show reasonable alternatives, arguing stress undermines recognition of alternatives and should change legal assessment; Paper B models ex post renegotiation and shows how the availability and cost of renegotiation interacts with remedy choice (property vs liability) to determine efficient and equitable outcomes.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Recovery of Damages for Lost Profits: The Historical Development

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal limits on recovery of monetary damages (foreseeability, proof/certainty, and related constraints)

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that a liability rule depends on courts (or juries) fixing the promisee's monetary gain and analyzes informational implications for courts and contracting parties; Paper B corrects myths about jury freedom and shows the historical role of judges and evidentiary rules in controlling damage assessments, so both examine institutional allocation of fact‑finding and valuation authority.

shared_topics.topic: effects of damages rules on contracting behavior and economic incentives (including efficient breach debate)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages in an extended economic analysis of how expectation damages, specific performance, or disgorgement affect parties' performance/breach incentives, prices, and renegotiation (critiquing and defending 'efficient breach'); Paper B considers the motivating economic concerns behind limiting damage exposure in industrial contexts and how the evolution of damage rules redistributed risk and influenced contracting practices.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE FUTURE OF LAW AND ECONOMICS: THE NEGLIGENCE-OPPORTUNISM TRADEOFF IN CONTRACT LAW.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly debates liability-rule (expectation damages) versus property-rule (specific performance) and restitutionary alternatives, defending damages as the appropriate default; Paper B addresses how contract rules and remedies should punish and deter opportunistic breaches versus negligent conduct, which has direct implications for whether courts favor monetary damages, injunctions, or other sanctions to shape behavior.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE CORRESPONDENCE OF CONTRACT AND PROMISE

papers.node_id: 104marqlrev141!!ARTICLE: THE MYTH OF OPTIMAL EXPECTATION DAMAGES
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE MYTH OF OPTIMAL EXPECTATION DAMAGES
papers.authors: Theresa Arnold Amanda Dixon Madison Sherrill Mitu Gulati
papers.abstract:
One of the most debated questions in contract law is what the optimal measure of damages for a breach is. One might think that this question would largely be left to the parties themselves, since the possibility of breach is something that all parties to a contract should contemplate.However, for a variety of reasons, ranging from reluctance by contract parties to broach the uncomfortable subject of relationship failure to the fact that courts tend to second-guess the damages provisions that parties do contract for,parties often fail to explicitly provide their preferred remedies for breach of the contract.As a result, courts frequently have to determine the appropriate amount of damages for a contractual breach.And that makes the question about the optimal default rule for damages important.
The textbook answer has long been that courts should set damages at the amount that puts the jilted party in as good of a position as she would have been in had the contract been performed - expectation damages.For example, if Karishma, a whiskey distributor, promised to deliver twelve cases of Japanesewhiskey to Keegan's restaurant on January 31, 2019, but decides not to do so because she is able to find another buyer willing to pay a higher price, she should have to pay Keegan his cost to purchase an equivalent set of those cases from an alternate supplier, including any transaction costs that might be incurred in identifying and entering an agreement with such alternate supplier. In 1936, Lon Fuller and William Perdue famously asked the question of why the law favored expectation damages over the alternatives, reliance and restitution, setting up a debate over the optimal measure of damages that has continued to this day.
The clearest and loudest answer to the Fuller-Perdue puzzle came in the 1970s, with the emergence of the field of law and economics. One of the early projects of law and economics scholars was to use economic arguments to explain why certain common law doctrines were efficient. Given the question posed by Fuller and Perdue, the law's preference for expectation damages was a ripe topic.
Drawing from what is now known as the theory of efficient breach, a series of scholars argued that expectation damages are the measure that parties - assuming full information, equal bargaining power and so on - would rationally agree to.That is, expectation damages are the default rule because they are the measure that parties would have agreed to had they explicitly contracted for itex ante.The theoretical argument made in support of this claim is thatexpectation damages are the measure that causes the breaching party to internalize the costs of the breach, thereby setting up the right set of incentives when a party is making a determination of whether to perform under the contract or breach.Robert Hillman's Contract Law casebook explains:
Most writers explain the expectancy goal as the best method for encouraging people to make and rely on their contracts, which benefits them and society... . A damages measure any lower than lost expectancy would undermine people's confidence in their contracts, and a measure larger than expectancy would discourage them from making contracts because they would be wary of the extent of their liability for breach.
The foregoing economic explanation for why the law favors expectation damages has, over the years, garnered broad support.However, the field of law and economics itself has become skeptical of the simple theory of efficient breach.In particular, a number of scholars have offered critiques complicating the assumptions of the basic model supporting the optimality of expectation damages.For example, under certain circumstances, one party may be incentivized to sub-optimally over invest, without any adjustment forthe risk that the contract may not be performed, because of an expectation that the other party, if it breaches the contract, will have to pay expectation damages.Based on these complicating factors, some argue that expectation damages are under-compensatory and others argue that they are over-compensatory.
This theoretical debate over whether expectation damages or some other measure of damages is optimal rests on an assumption that there is one measure of damages that is optimal, regardless of variations in the types of parties and their economic relationship.This assumption is remarkable when compared with how we generally view contract terms. With respect to other contract terms, there is broad consensus - particularly in contracts among sophisticated commercial parties - that optimal contract terms are what the parties choose.After all, parties know what suits them best. Given that the bargain over contract rights and obligations among parties is inevitably a function of factors such as price, risk preferences, liquidity tolerance, and so on, it stands to reason that different sets of parties will contract for a range of different contract terms. There may be standard terms that develop for subsets of a particular market, but one would expect variation across different types of transactions. We would expect this for damages provisions just as we would for other contract terms.
To illustrate why we would expect variation in damages provisions, imagine a company in a highly volatile industry, with large fluctuations in profits and losses, and small capital reserves. Given these characteristics, this firm's negotiations with a prospective lender would probably result in a different pricing scheme than the one that could be negotiated by a highly capitalized firm in a low volatility industry. And if one were to view damages provisions as a component of this pricing scheme - which, as an economic matter, they are - one might expect to see variation in the types of damages provisions that different types of firms are able to negotiate. Put differently,one should see different prices for different types of damage provisions, if one were to hold the lender-borrower duo constant.
Although we would expect variation in damages provisions, the current system has so internalized compensation as a basis for damages that it goes beyond a mere default rule.Courts strike down explicitly contracted-for damages terms that they deem to be supra compensatory.Sophisticated parties in bespoke contracts are told by courts that they must be content with an off-the-rack damages measure (which presumably they would have contracted for themselves, had they been acting rationally).
A few legal scholars have questioned the damages exceptionalism that makes the default rule for damages more difficult to contract out of than other defaults.Questioning that a single optimal measure of damages exists and that parties typically contract for expectation damages, Robert Scott and George Triantis write:
Given the great variety of conditions under which parties contract for [the option to pay damages and exit the contract], it should not be surprising that commercial and consumer contracts contain a wide range of option prices. We explain the heterogeneity in [contracted for damages amounts] and argue that they are rarely equivalent to the measure of the seller's expectation in a completed sale.
Victor Goldberg echoes Scott and Triantis: "By framing the problem as one of pricing the termination option, it is clear that in a wide variety of contexts the efficient rule (i.e., [the] one that sophisticated parties would voluntarilychoose) bears no relation to the ones featured in the lawyer's rhetoric and the economist's model.

questions.question: Whether a single, uniform measure of contractual damages is optimal across different types of parties and transactions
Whether contracting parties would voluntarily choose heterogeneous damage provisions (different measures or prices for breach) tailored to their economic characteristics and risk preferences
Whether courts should permit parties to contractually specify nonstandard damage remedies rather than imposing a court-selected default

matched_themes: How should courts treat pre-agreed breach payments and liquidated damages clauses (enforce, reform, apportion, or void)?
What counterfactual baseline should courts use to measure plaintiffs' losses for compensation purposes?
How should default liability rules interact with parties' freedom to allocate risks by contract and duties of disclosure to achieve efficient and fair risk allocation?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?
Should parties be presumptively permitted to contractually specify nonstandard damage remedies, or should courts retain authority to impose defaults?
How should courts treat and enforce stipulated remedies (liquidated damages clauses) versus substituting judicial remedies?
How do transaction costs, enforcement frictions, and institutional realities alter the theoretical efficiency of breach-plus-compensation?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
Should courts police and limit supracompensatory contractual remedies (penalty-like clauses), or does allowing parties to contract for such terms respect autonomy and promote efficient contracting?
How should remedial and enforcement rules be structured to achieve efficient behavior when populations include both internalizers and externalizers?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
Do parties and courts actually choose heterogeneous, context-tailored damage provisions in contracting, and under what conditions would such customization be voluntarily chosen or socially desirable?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 56sclrev93!!ARTICLE:The Shadow Code
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:The Shadow Code

shared_topics.topic: whether expectation damages (a single uniform measure) are the optimal default rule for breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly critiques the canonical law-and-economics justification for a single optimal expectation-damages rule (the efficient-breach argument) and argues that a single default is implausible across heterogeneous parties; Paper B engages the same question by restating the compensatory goal in surplus terms and proposing a single surplus-based formula that it argues is normatively equivalent to expectation-based doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: how to compute damages in practice (formulas and components: anticipated v. actual benefits and costs, cover/resale, partial performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses what expectation damages should include (e.g., replacement costs and transaction costs) and highlights how different fact patterns can alter proper measurement; Paper B offers an explicit surplus-based computational formula (anticipated minus actual surplus) and maps that formula onto the various UCC/Restatement computations for cover, resale, partial performance and warranty cases.

shared_topics.topic: the role and treatment of various cost categories and limits (transaction costs, performance costs, breach‑related costs, consequential/incidental losses, mitigation and foreseeability)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises concerns about transaction costs and how expectation damages may over- or under-compensate when those costs or incentives are present; Paper B systematically classifies costs (performance, surplus‑enhancing, breach‑related) and codifies limitations such as mitigation, reasonable certainty, and foreseeability within its surplus framework.

shared_topics.topic: whether damages rules should be uniformly applied by courts or reflect parties' contractual choices and heterogeneity
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that sophisticated parties negotiate a variety of damages/termination prices and that courts’ resistance to contracting-out of damages is problematic; Paper B addresses the desirability of a unified, general principle (the Shadow Code) that applies across buyers, sellers, consumers and merchants, while situating that principle alongside existing contract terms and evidentiary choices.

shared_topics.topic: use of law-and-economics and incentive analysis to justify and critique damages doctrines (efficient breach, incentives to invest/rely/mitigate)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages the law-and-economics literature (efficient breach, incentive effects, over‑investment and reliance problems) to challenge the simple economic case for expectation damages; Paper B deploys an economic surplus model to reveal incentives and to show how a single surplus-based rule clarifies the incentive effects of remedies and aligns with UCC/Restatement goals.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 67hastingslj407!!Article: Remedial Clauses: The Overprivatization of Private Law
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Remedial Clauses: The Overprivatization of Private Law

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of stipulated/liquidated damages (remedial) clauses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses courts striking down explicit damages provisions and the exceptional treatment of damages as a default that parties may not fully contract around; Paper B directly analyzes the doctrinal treatment and evolving enforceability of remedial (liquidated/stipulated) clauses and the modern trend toward greater enforcement or invalidation as penalties.

shared_topics.topic: whether expectation damages should be the default or displaced by private contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the assumption that expectation damages are the single optimal default and questions why courts prevent parties from choosing alternative remedial pricing, while Paper B debates the permissive movement to allow parties to select remedies ex ante and defends retaining a strong default limiting such private displacement.

shared_topics.topic: tension between party autonomy (private ordering) and judicial/public oversight in remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that courts often second-guess or invalidate bargained-for damages terms despite parties' preferences, and Paper B frames remedial clauses as an overprivatization problem that displaces judicial remedial decisionmaking and public rule-of-law values.

shared_topics.topic: law-and-economics efficiency arguments versus doctrinal and normative limits on remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages with law-and-economics theories (efficient breach, internalizing breach costs) and scholarly critiques complicating those assumptions, and Paper B addresses and critiques the law-and-economics/libertarian rationale for enforcing remedial clauses, arguing doctrinal limits serve other public values.

shared_topics.topic: whether stipulated damages are compensatory versus punitive (penalty concerns and reasonableness)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys arguments that expectation damages may under- or over-compensate and discusses courts' aversion to supra-compensatory awards, while Paper B centers the line between reasonable compensatory liquidated damages and unenforceable penalties, using doctrinal tests of uncertainty and reasonableness.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 118wvalrev369!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT REMEDIES IN ACTION: SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT REMEDIES IN ACTION: SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE

shared_topics.topic: choice between expectation damages and specific performance as remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage the core question of how and why parties end up with money damages rather than specific performance: Paper A empirically studies litigants' and lawyers' decisions to sue for or opt out of specific performance, while Paper B theorizes about the default role of expectation damages and whether that default matches parties' optimal preferences.

shared_topics.topic: heterogeneity of parties' preferences over remedy rules
shared_topics.justification: Both works challenge the assumption of a single, uniform optimal remedy: Paper B argues that optimal damages vary with parties' characteristics and bargaining context, and Paper A documents varied, context-dependent plaintiff motivations and uses of specific performance that diverge from standard economic or rights-based assumptions.

shared_topics.topic: strategic and signaling uses of remedies and negotiated/delegated outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Both papers consider remedies as strategic instruments rather than mere compensation mechanisms: Paper A shows parties use specific performance instrumentally (as bargaining chips) and that remedy choice can signal merits to courts, while Paper B frames damages as a priced termination option that parties may strategically select or contract over.

shared_topics.topic: role of attorneys and courts in shaping remedy selection and enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Both studies examine non-ideal actors and institutions affecting remedies: Paper A documents attorneys' biases toward money judgments and courts' inferences from remedy choices, and Paper B analyzes how courts enforce or limit contracted-for damages and the implications of judicially imposed default rules for parties' contracting autonomy.

shared_topics.topic: gap between economic theory assumptions and real-world enforceability/implementation of remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both papers critique the empirical validity of standard law-and-economics assumptions: Paper B questions assumptions (full information, contractibility) that justify expectation damages as optimal, and Paper A provides empirical evidence that enforcement difficulties, lack of clear performance standards, and social dynamics undermine theoretical predictions about specific performance.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2001wislrev681!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:COMMENTARY BREACH AND PENALTY AS CONTRACTUAL NORM AND CONTRACTUAL ANOMIE
compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:COMMENTARY BREACH AND PENALTY AS CONTRACTUAL NORM AND CONTRACTUAL ANOMIE

shared_topics.topic: use of penalties versus expectation damages as the appropriate remedy for breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically studies the high reliance on and judicial tolerance for penalty clauses in Russian contracts, while Paper B critiques the conventional assumption that expectation damages are the universally optimal remedy and highlights that parties may prefer heterogeneous measures (including penalties) depending on context.

shared_topics.topic: the explanatory power of the efficient-breach theory for real-world contracting behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A tests whether reliance on penalties signals hostility to efficient breach and finds little linkage, and Paper B interrogates the efficient-breach rationale for defaulting to expectation damages, arguing the model's assumptions often fail and its predictions are incomplete.

shared_topics.topic: how courts' default rules and judicial intervention shape or contradict parties' contractual choices about remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents judicial tolerance of punitive penalty clauses in Russia and links that tolerance to legal activism, whereas Paper B shows how courts in established systems often enforce a one-size default (expectation damages) or strike down contractual deviations, raising questions about damages exceptionalism.

shared_topics.topic: the role of bargaining power/market power in determining remedial provisions in contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically investigates whether plaintiffs with market power impose penalty clauses on weaker parties and finds little support for that common wisdom, while Paper B emphasizes that variation in parties' characteristics and bargaining positions should lead to diverse negotiated damages provisions rather than a single optimal measure.

shared_topics.topic: empirical evidence challenging law-and-economics theoretical assumptions about default remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A provides empirical survey data from post-communist Russia that contradicts some Western theoretical predictions about penalties and contracting, and Paper B draws on critiques and empirical puzzles to argue that law-and-economics models (favoring expectation damages) oversimplify party heterogeneity and contractual practices.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 116columlrev2005!!ARTICLE: ECONOMIC ANALYSIS OF CONTRACT LAW FROM THE INTERNAL POINT OF VIEW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ECONOMIC ANALYSIS OF CONTRACT LAW FROM THE INTERNAL POINT OF VIEW

shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the law-and-economics claim that expectation damages are the single optimal default across contexts, showing theoretical complications and heterogeneity that undermine the efficient-breach story; Paper B interrogates the perform-or-pay (expectation) norm from the perspective of internalizers versus externalizers, showing that assuming everyone responds to expectation damages as simple incentives can mis-specify optimal doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: party heterogeneity and its implications for damages design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that parties differ (risk, liquidity, industry volatility, bargaining power) and therefore would rationally choose different damages terms rather than a one-size-fits-all default; Paper B models a population split between 'internalizers' and 'externalizers' and shows how that heterogeneity changes the welfare-optimal shape and interpretation of damages and related rules.

shared_topics.topic: contractibility of damages provisions and judicial limits on bargaining
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents and criticizes how courts often strike down or limit contracted-for supra‑compensatory damages, arguing this damages exceptionalism prevents parties from trading toward their preferred risk/price outcomes; Paper B analyzes stipulated-damages clauses and the penalty doctrine, and explores how enforceability and interpretation of such clauses affect parties' perceived duties and behavior.

shared_topics.topic: how damages rules influence parties' behavior beyond simple price incentives (investment, performance decisions, crowding out)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses incentive effects of expectation damages — including risks of overinvestment or misaligned incentives — that complicate the efficient-breach rationale; Paper B develops how legal norms (perform-or-pay vs duty-to-perform) can crowd out moral motivations or alter investment/performance choices among internalizers and externalizers, changing the doctrinal desirability of rules.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal responses to supra‑compensatory liability (penalty, willful breach, supercompensation) and their justification
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the tension between courts' resistance to supra‑compensatory damages and the theoretical debate over whether expectation damages are under- or over‑compensatory; Paper B examines doctrines like the penalty rule and willful breach (supercompensatory liability), offering explanations for them that depend on the internalizer/externalizer distinction and their differing responses to liability regimes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 84nclrev1927!!ARTICLE: A BRIDGE, A TAX REVOLT, AND THE STRUGGLE TO INDUSTRIALIZE: A COMMENT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A BRIDGE, A TAX REVOLT, AND THE STRUGGLE TO INDUSTRIALIZE: A COMMENT

shared_topics.topic: measurement of damages for breach (expectation vs alternative measures)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether expectation damages are the optimal default and surveys economic critiques and heterogeneity in contracted damage terms, while Paper B analyzes how a court in the Luten Bridge case selected a restrictive measure of damages and the doctrinal implications of that choice.

shared_topics.topic: anticipatory breach and the duty to mitigate damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how the prospect of breach and the design of damages affect parties' incentives (the efficient-breach literature and its complications), and Paper B centers on an anticipatory breach dispute (Luten Bridge), focusing on mitigation and the appropriate damages calculus when a promisor elects not to perform.

shared_topics.topic: judicial role versus party autonomy in setting remedy rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes 'damages exceptionalism' where courts limit parties' ability to contract around default damages rules, and Paper B emphasizes that common law judges, through case decisions like Luten Bridge, actively shape and sometimes depart from prior rules—illustrating courts' central role in defining contractual remedies.

shared_topics.topic: viewing breach as a priced option (obligation to perform versus obligation to pay damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the contract-as-option framing (pricing termination options and heterogeneity of option prices) as an alternative lens on damages, and Paper B engages the same conceptual divide by questioning whether contracts impose an absolute duty to perform or merely a duty to perform or pay damages when promissory breach occurs.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 93califlrev975!!ARTICLE: Actual and Virtual Specific Performance, the Theory of Efficient Breach, and the Indifference Principle in Contract Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Actual and Virtual Specific Performance, the Theory of Efficient Breach, and the Indifference Principle in Contract Law

shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions the textbook claim that expectation damages are universally optimal and highlights heterogeneity across parties and transactions; Paper B analyzes how expectation damages systematically fall short of making promisees indifferent between performance and remedy and challenges their adequacy as a remedial default.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the law-and-economics defense of expectation damages to the efficient-breach argument and presents critiques showing its assumptions can fail; Paper B critically examines the theory of efficient breach, arguing it neither necessarily promotes efficiency nor should dictate limiting specific performance.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses incentive problems such as overinvestment and misaligned risk-taking that can arise when parties expect expectation damages, producing under- or over-compensation; Paper B examines how damages and specific performance affect inducements to perform, mitigation duties, opportunism, and the promisee's ability to obtain virtual specific performance.

shared_topics.topic: the judicial role in shaping default remedies and the enforceability of contractually chosen remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents and criticizes courts' tendency to override or restrict contracted-for damages provisions and the resulting 'damages exceptionalism'; Paper B develops principles for when courts should award actual specific performance versus cover (virtual performance) and thus prescribes judicial standards for choosing among remedial options.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:Intentional Interference with Contract and the Doctrineof Efficient Breach: Fine Tuning the Notion of the ContractBreacher as Wrongdoer

shared_topics.topic: how remedies (expectation damages vs specific performance) affect incentives and whether damages adequately deter or compensate breaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that some breaches are 'wrongful' because damages (or specific performance) are inadequate to deter or remedy them, and uses that distinction to limit tort liability for inducing breaches; Paper B analyzes circumstances where expectation damages under- or over-compensate, altering investment and performance incentives and undermining the claim that expectation damages are universally optimal.
