shared_topics.justification: Paper B documents and criticizes courts' tendency to override or limit privately negotiated damages provisions and questions the presumption that one default (expectation damages) is universally preferred by parties; Paper A similarly critiques judicial doctrine that imposes tort liability in ways that conflict with contracting parties' ex ante choice framework and calls for doctrinal calibration that respects contract-law incentives.

shared_topics.topic: conceptualizing breach as an 'option' (the exit/termination price) and how its pricing or inducement by third parties affects social welfare
shared_topics.justification: Paper B frames damages as the price of the contractual termination option and argues heterogeneity in optimal pricing across parties and contexts; Paper A treats breach as an exercised option (the choice to breach and pay damages) and analyzes when third-party inducement of that option should be actionable based on whether the resulting exercise is socially desirable or wrongful.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 63fordhamlrev665!!ARTICLE: CONSEQUENTIAL DAMAGES FOR COMMERCIAL LOSS: AN ALTERNATIVE TO HADLEY v. BAXENDALE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONSEQUENTIAL DAMAGES FOR COMMERCIAL LOSS: AN ALTERNATIVE TO HADLEY v. BAXENDALE

shared_topics.topic: whether a single, uniform default rule for contractual damages is appropriate
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that applying one inflexible standard (the Hadley rule) across all commercial contexts is fundamentally flawed and proposes a trifurcated standard; Paper B contests the assumption that a single optimal measure (expectation damages) exists and shows why damages should vary with context and contracting parties.

shared_topics.topic: how damages rules should allocate incentives and internalize the costs of breach (law-and-economics concerns)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B engages deeply with the law-and-economics literature (efficient breach, internalization, under/over‑compensation, investment distortions) to question expectation damages; Paper A evaluates the relevant policy considerations underlying consequential damages, which includes the incentive effects of different liability scopes.

shared_topics.topic: reforming or replacing traditional doctrinal defaults (Hadley v. Baxendale and expectation damages) with context‑sensitive alternatives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly critiques Hadley v. Baxendale and proposes an alternative trifurcated liability framework for commercial loss; Paper B critiques the orthodox preference for expectation damages and argues against treating that doctrine as the universal default.

shared_topics.justification: Paper B documents how parties often fail to specify remedies, how courts second‑guess or strike down supra‑compensatory agreed damages, and questions damages exceptionalism; Paper A’s argument for varying liability by contractual situation implicates the degree to which defaults (or judicial doctrines) should defer to the parties' arrangements and the particular contract context.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 24jlegalstud139!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT REMEDIES AND OPTIONS PRICING
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT REMEDIES AND OPTIONS PRICING

shared_topics.topic: damages as a priced termination option (the 'option' framing of remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops an option-pricing framework that treats money damages as giving the promisor an option to buy back performance, and Paper B cites and echoes the literature (Scott & Triantis; Goldberg) that conceptualizes damages as a priced termination option and emphasizes heterogeneity in option prices.

shared_topics.topic: default rule versus bargained-for damages (whether courts should impose expectation damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues parties can and would adjust contract price to reflect which remedy will apply and analyzes distributional effects of default remedies, while Paper B criticizes the assumption of a single optimal default (expectation damages) and highlights that sophisticated parties would choose heterogeneous damages terms.

shared_topics.topic: transaction costs and the theory of efficient breach in shaping remedy choice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reviews the transaction-costs account of why courts choose money damages or specific performance and studies how different transaction costs affect breach/performance incentives, and Paper B engages with efficient-breach theory and its reliance on simplifying assumptions, showing how transaction-costs and related frictions complicate the optimality of expectation damages.

shared_topics.topic: risk allocation and parties' risk preferences affecting preferred remedies/damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how risk aversion and variability under money damages versus specific performance change parties' preferences, and Paper B emphasizes that firms' volatility, liquidity, and risk characteristics should lead to different negotiated damages provisions rather than a single default.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 116columlrev2005!!ARTICLE: ECONOMIC ANALYSIS OF CONTRACT LAW FROM THE INTERNAL POINT OF VIEW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ECONOMIC ANALYSIS OF CONTRACT LAW FROM THE INTERNAL POINT OF VIEW

shared_topics.topic: the optimality of expectation damages as the default rule

shared_topics.topic: how damages rules shape incentives to perform or breach (including efficiency tradeoffs)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how different doctrinal forms (expectation, stipulated damages, willful-breach penalties) alter internalizers' and externalizers' perform-or-breach choices and can produce crowding-out or misaligned incentives, while Paper B surveys economic critiques showing expectation damages can produce over- or under-investment and other incentive failures.

shared_topics.topic: heterogeneity of contracting parties and the limits of a one-size-fits-all damages rule
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models a mixed population of internalizers and externalizers and shows that a single damages regime may be optimal for one group but harmful for the other, and Paper B emphasizes heterogeneity (risk, liquidity, bargaining power) to argue that different parties will rationally choose different damages arrangements so a single optimal measure is implausible.

shared_topics.topic: contracted-for (stipulated) damages, courts' reluctance to honor supra‑compensatory terms, and the penalty doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how internalizers interpret stipulated-damages clauses and how the penalty doctrine affects their duty to perform, and Paper B documents and criticizes judicial practice that limits parties' ability to contract for supra‑compensatory remedies, arguing damages terms are treated as unusually hard to opt out of.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: FAULT AT THE CONTRACT-TORT INTERFACE

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the modernization of contract rhetorically embraced a strict-liability posture and thereby reshaped the default rules that govern contractual responsibility, while Paper B directly debates what the appropriate default damages rule should be (expectation vs alternatives) and whether a single default measure is justified.

shared_topics.topic: tension between private ordering (party autonomy) and judicial/public regulation in shaping remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that nineteenth‑century conceptualizations drew the contract–tort border along a private‑ordering vs public‑regulation line that still distorts thinking, and Paper B documents and critiques courts' willingness to override or constrain parties' contracted damages terms, highlighting the same autonomy vs judicial intervention conflict.

shared_topics.topic: how theoretical and historical narratives shape contemporary doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces historical shifts in the meaning of fault and how that intellectual history structured modern private law, while Paper B traces the influence of law‑and‑economics (theory of efficient breach) and subsequent critiques on contemporary thinking about damages.

shared_topics.topic: the contract–tort boundary as it pertains to remedies for harm (warranty/products liability vs breach damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally studies the contract–tort interface in the context of products liability and warranty problems, showing how conceptual choices affect who gets compensated and how, and Paper B engages the remedial side of private law—how breach is compensated and whether compensation rules properly allocate losses—thereby addressing overlapping questions about which regime (contract or tort) and which remedial logic should govern particular harms.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines law-and-economics arguments (efficient breach, under/over‑compensation, investment incentives) underlying the choice of damages measure, and Paper B argues that limiting damages to foreseeable losses promoted industrial and commercial growth and similarly shapes economic behavior.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques 'damages exceptionalism' and argues courts often override bargained‑for damages provisions, while Paper B notes statutory and common‑law defaults (Hadley and codifications) govern damages unless parties agree otherwise, raising the same tension between defaults and private ordering.

shared_topics.topic: how liability/damages regimes affect firm decisions and market organization
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses firm characteristics (risk, capital, volatility) to explain why parties would negotiate heterogeneous damages pricing, and Paper B explicitly considers how liability‑limiting doctrines influence multinational firm location and the development of commerce (including e‑commerce).

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Modification: The Self-Help Specific Performance Remedy.

shared_topics.topic: adequacy and optimality of expectation damages versus alternative remedies (including specific performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions whether expectation damages are the universally optimal default and surveys critiques that expectation damages can be under- or over-compensatory; Paper B analyzes when damages are legally inadequate and argues that reliance on substitutionary damages creates pressures that make specific performance or other remedies salient and sometimes necessary.

shared_topics.topic: remedial rules create strategic incentives and opportunistic behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how the expectation-damages regime can distort parties' investment and performance incentives (e.g., causing overinvestment or misaligned breach decisions); Paper B shows how undercompensatory damages and current modification doctrine create promisee opportunism (the 'self-help specific performance' problem) and strategic modification behavior.

shared_topics.topic: treating remedial entitlements (damages/specific performance) as priced contract terms or termination options that affect bargaining and contract design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames damages as part of the contract's pricing scheme and as the price of a termination option that sophisticated parties would negotiate; Paper B examines how modification and the availability (or absence) of particular remedies change the effective value of performance and breach, and thus alter parties' bargaining incentives and the structure of agreements.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: Intentions, Guilt and Social Interactions

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how a responder's aversion to insincerity and beliefs about a proposer's intentions determine whether she accepts offers and social interactions; Paper B examines how parties' expectations about counterpart behavior (and the incentives set by damages) shape whether contracts are performed or breached and what remedy parties would prefer.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A models social interaction as a dynamic psychological game with incomplete information where beliefs about social type produce equilibria with sincere or insincere offers; Paper B critiques the efficient-breach model's full-information assumptions and emphasizes how private information and parties' expectations affect the desirability of default damage rules.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that responders care about proposers' social types (prosocial vs not) and that differing types produce different interaction outcomes; Paper B argues that firms and contracting parties differ (risk, liquidity, volatility) and therefore a single, one-size-fits-all damages rule is unlikely to be optimal across heterogeneous transactions.

shared_topics.topic: limits of standard economic models and the need to incorporate psychological or institutional constraints
shared_topics.justification: Paper A challenges the standard game-theoretic assumption that only actions matter by incorporating psychological game theory and belief-dependent preferences; Paper B questions the standard law-and-economics defense of expectation damages based on simplified efficient-breach models, arguing empirical and incentive complexities require richer modeling and institutional attention.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 46sandiegolrev705!!Article: The Collateral Source Rule in Contract Cases
compared_to.partner_title: Article: The Collateral Source Rule in Contract Cases

shared_topics.topic: whether a single default damages rule should govern contract disputes versus allowing heterogeneity or party-specific remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes whether contract recoveries should be uniformly reduced by collateral-source payments or vary with the nature of the collateral and contractual context, while Paper B critiques the assumption that expectation damages are the single optimal default and argues for variation and parties' ability to choose different damages regimes.

shared_topics.topic: judicial intervention versus party autonomy in setting or enforcing damages remedies (including courts' treatment of contracted-for remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how courts have treated the collateral source rule in contract cases—sometimes categorically excluding it—and the doctrinal confusion that results, and Paper B shows how courts frequently second-guess or invalidate bespoke damages provisions, enforcing an 'off-the-rack' default instead of parties' negotiated terms.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on whether third‑party payments and subrogation should reduce a defendant's liability—affecting who ultimately bears loss—while Paper B examines how expectation damages and alternative measures influence breach decisions, under- or over-investment, and the pricing of the option to terminate a contract.

shared_topics.topic: policy foundations for damages rules in contract law (efficiency, compensation, and fairness considerations)
