papers.node_id: 100yalelj369!!ARTICLE: The Myth that Promisees Prefer Supracompensatory Remedies: An Analysis of Contracting for Damage Measures.
papers.title: ARTICLE: The Myth that Promisees Prefer Supracompensatory Remedies: An Analysis of Contracting for Damage Measures.
papers.abstract:
Courts will not enforce liquidated damage clauses when a stipulated sum exceeds (i) the harm that the promisee could reasonably expect to suffer from breach or (ii) the actual harm that breach turned out to cause.Courts traditionally have not awarded punitive damages "for a breach of contract unless the conduct constituting the breach is also a tort for which punitive damages are recoverable."Courts also will not grant specific performance "if damages would be adequate to protect the expectation interest of the injured party," nor will courts enforce contracts that accord promisees a right to specific relief.
These three rules share the goal of limiting a promisee's recovery to his lost expectation.  The liquidated damage rule prevents the promisee from contracting for a supracompensatory remedy, and the punitive damage rule prevents courts from awarding such a remedy.  The specific performance rule achieves the law's goal indirectly.  A promisee who has a right to specific performance can compel the promisor to perform even when the promisor's loss from performance would exceed the promisee's gain.  A promisor can purchase her freedom, but sophisticated promisees sometimes will demand more than their expectation as the price.  Permitting specific performance only when damages could not protect the expectation interest limits the ability of promisees to obtain supracompensatory payments by threatening to seek specific relief.  The ban on "specific performance clauses" prevents a promisee from obtaining by contract the power that the general specific performance rule aims to abolish.
These three rules rest on a normative premise and on a positive premise.  The normative premise holds that supracompensatory remedies are undesirable.  The positive premise holds that promisees prefer supracompensatory remedies, and so must be prevented from getting them.  The normative premise is true but the positive premise is false.  It is shown below that promisees do not want contractual damage measures that would grant more than their lost expectation.  Several legal implications follow from this showing.
, the initial, or "ex ante," branch of the liquidated damage rule is unnecessary.  Courts do not have to prevent promisees from obtaining penalty clauses if promisees do not want penalty clauses.  The ex ante rule is not merely unnecessary: judicial review produces mischief.  Courts sometimes mistake compensatory damage measures for penalties, and so have found that particular liquidated damage clauses would inevitably overcompensate promisees when those clauses only protected the expectation.  Thus, the ex ante branch of the liquidated damage rule should be abandoned.
The "ex post" branch of the liquidated damage rule, which bans clauses that overcompensate in fact, seems justifiable at first glance.  An ex ante reasonable estimate of the damages that the promisee will later incur may exceed the promisee's actual loss.  The normative premise that supracompensatory remedies are undesirable then apparently justifies the ex post branch of the rule, because it implies that courts should not enforce liquidated damage clauses that exceed actual damages.  This view is unpersuasive: party estimates may err, but courts generally do not review contracts to ensure that performance under a contract's terms yields the consequences that the parties expected it to have.  The general absence of judicial review follows from two premises: even with the benefit of hindsight, courts seldom could do better for the parties than the parties can do for themselves; and the willingness of courts to attempt to rescue parties from bad deals reduces the parties' incentive to write good contracts originally.  These premises support foregoing judicial review of the liquidated damage term just as they support foregoing review of other contract terms.  Thus the ex post branch of the liquidated damage rule should be repealed as well.
Some courts have relaxed the traditional prohibition against awarding punitive damages in ordinary contract actions.  The traditional rule should be restored.  A state-supplied right to sue for punitive damages is similar to a contract-supplied right to sue for a penalty; in both cases, a disappointed promisee would sue on the rightifit existed.  Showing that promisees prefer the right not to exist implies both that a promisee would reject a contract that contained a penalty clause and would vote against a punitive damages regime if he could.  This promisee preference should control.
Finally, parties should be permitted to contract for specific relief.  The current ban on such contracts can be justified on grounds similar to those that underlie the liquidated damage rule.  The ex ante aspect of this justification holds that a right to specific performance functions similarly to a right to sue on a penalty clause: both rights permit promisees to compel inefficient performances.  If promisees want this power, then they should be prevented from contracting for specific relief, just as they are prevented from contracting for penalties.  But promisees do not want this power.  Rather, promisees prefer specific performance primarily when their expectation cannot be monetized; in this circumstance, a promisee neither could prove damages nor create a liquidated damage clause.  Because specific relief is efficient relative to no relief, courts should enforce specific performance contracts.  If courts were to do this, then arguably they should police these contracts specially, just as they police liquidated damage clauses specially.  Again, the ex post justification for judicial review holds that the parties' initial belief that specific performance was necessary may turn out to be mistaken, but the promisee might then use his contract right to specific relief to extort a supracompensatory payment from the promisor.  As is shown below, promisees do not use the specific performance remedy to exploit today, and would be unlikely to use the remedy for exploitation were they able to contract freely for it.  Hence, courts should not police specific performance contracts specially.If specific relief clauses become enforceable, the current specific performance rule would not be the best default (what would be is a difficult question).
Part I shows that promisees prefer compensatory remedies.  Part II explores the normative implications of this preference.  Part III defends the use of certain assumptions that underlie the argument.  Part IV considers one important and sometimes unrealistic assumption in detail.  This assumption holds that promisees always sue to protect their expectation interest; in particular, promisees always detect breaches and never are deterred from suing by high legal costs.  The former aspect of the assumption often is plausible because breach usually is easy to detect; the latter aspect is more questionable because legal costs do seem to deter some suits.  Part IV makes two claims.  First, promisees prefer not to solve the "collection cost problem" with penalty clauses.  Second, the state should not respond to the inefficiencies that sometimes follow from underenforcement of the law with punitive damage awards.  Rather, the state should encourage promisees to sue by reducing collection costs.  Part V considers the recent trend to award punitive damages for contractbreaches which disadvantage individuals.  This trend is particularly manifest in two contexts, the wrongful denial of insurance benefits to individual insuredsand dismissals from employment.Awarding punitive damages in the former case is undesirable; awarding them in the latter case may be wise only when an unregulated right to dismiss would create an externality, such as reducing a firm's incentive to obey the law.

questions.question: Do promisees (the non-breaching parties) prefer supracompensatory remedies that can yield more than their expected loss, or do they prefer remedies that simply compensate their expectation loss?

Should courts or the state intervene to prevent parties from contracting for supracompensatory remedies (penalty-like or punitive contractual terms), or is such judicial policing unnecessary or harmful given promisee preferences?

Do parties prefer-and should they be permitted to contract for-inelike (specific, non-monetary) relief instead of monetary compensation, particularly when expectation losses are difficult or impossible to monetize?

matched_themes: Should courts allow punitive or other extracompensatory damages for willful or abusive contract breaches, and what are the efficiency and fairness trade-offs?
When should courts permit plaintiffs to pursue tort claims alongside or instead of contract claims to obtain broader remedies, and how does allowing tort claims change damages outcomes?
How should courts treat pre-agreed breach payments and liquidated damages clauses (enforce, reform, apportion, or void)?
How do remedial rules for potentially illegal contracts affect parties' incentives to enter socially harmful or beneficial agreements?

What moral and legal limits should constrain the commodification of promises-i.e., which promises ought not be treated as market commodities and how should the law reflect anti-commodification concerns?
What counterfactual baseline should courts use to measure plaintiffs' losses for compensation purposes?
Does giving the promisee a unilateral right to demand performance or elect a damages measure that captures promisor's forgone gains vindicate moral intuitions while preserving ex post efficiency?
How should default liability rules interact with parties' freedom to allocate risks by contract and duties of disclosure to achieve efficient and fair risk allocation?
Do courts actually prefer monetary damages over specific (in-kind) remedies, or do they grant specific relief except when independent reasons exist to deny it?
When should courts order specific performance (in-kind relief) versus awarding monetary damages?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?

Do contracting parties prefer in-kind remedies or monetary damages, and how do risk preferences, transaction costs, and contracting experience (laypersons versus businesspeople) shape that preference?
What standards and procedural safeguards should govern awards of punitive and other nonpecuniary damages in contract disputes to balance compensation and protection against abuse?
Should the promisor or the promisee have the default right to choose between performance and payment to achieve allocative efficiency?
Should parties be presumptively permitted to contractually specify nonstandard damage remedies, or should courts retain authority to impose defaults?
Does making in-kind performance the legal default (rather than monetary compensation) change parties' enforcement choices, moral judgments, and economic efficiency?
When should courts prefer or enforce in-kind (specific) performance rather than monetary damages for breach of contract?
How should courts treat and enforce stipulated remedies (liquidated damages clauses) versus substituting judicial remedies?
How do transaction costs, enforcement frictions, and institutional realities alter the theoretical efficiency of breach-plus-compensation?

Can party-designed enforcement mechanisms (pre-agreed penalties, arbitration, bonding, reputational systems) reliably produce efficient breach outcomes without judicial intervention, and when do they fail?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
Should courts limit recoverable consequential damages that are grossly disproportionate to the contract price, and would such limits promote economic efficiency?
Should courts police and limit supracompensatory contractual remedies (penalty-like clauses), or does allowing parties to contract for such terms respect autonomy and promote efficient contracting?
How should remedial and enforcement rules be structured to achieve efficient behavior when populations include both internalizers and externalizers?
Can courts reliably determine ex post whether a breach would increase social welfare so that remedy choice can be used to promote efficiency?
To what extent does empirical uncertainty about measuring gains and losses limit courts' ability to design remedies that reflect non-welfare ethical preferences without sacrificing efficiency?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
Do parties and courts actually choose heterogeneous, context-tailored damage provisions in contracting, and under what conditions would such customization be voluntarily chosen or socially desirable?
When and under what standards should courts award disgorgement or remedies that strip gains from breaching parties?

Should contractual clauses that impose predetermined monetary payments for breach be treated as punitive (unenforceable) or as enforceable measures of compensation, and what factors predict courts' enforcement decisions?

Do repeat players, contract drafting strategies, secrecy about dispute outcomes, and presentation techniques enable stronger parties to extract one-sided terms and undermine the protective aims of contract law?
To what extent should moral blameworthiness and non-economic considerations influence the design and application of contract remedies?
When is an indirect remedy (one that induces self-compliance) preferable to a direct remedy that delivers the outcome?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 59ohiostlj339!!ARTICLE: Disproportionality and the Law of Consequential Damages: Default Theory and Cognitive Reality
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Disproportionality and the Law of Consequential Damages: Default Theory and Cognitive Reality

shared_topics.topic: limits on contractual remedies that produce supracompensatory outcomes (penalty clauses, punitive damages, liquidated damages, specific performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the doctrinal rules that bar or police penalty clauses, punitive awards, and specific-performance clauses and argues courts should relax ex ante/ex post policing because promisees do not prefer supracompensatory remedies; Paper B examines the doctrinally similar disproportionality limitation on consequential damages and assesses when courts should deny recovery to avoid disproportionate compensation.

shared_topics.topic: the justification of judicial policing vs leaving remedial terms as defaults (efficiency and default-rule analysis)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A weighs normative and positive premises and questions the need for judicial review of liquidated-damage and specific-performance clauses on efficiency and default-rule grounds; Paper B applies classic default-rule theory to disproportionality and then modifies that analysis using behavioral findings to determine when a legal default limiting damages is efficient.

shared_topics.topic: ex ante versus ex post assessment of damages clauses and parties' estimates of risk and loss
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes ex ante and ex post branches of the liquidated-damages rule and critiques courts' post-hoc reassessment of parties' estimates of harm; Paper B similarly contrasts foreseeability/prior allocation of risk with later assessment of disproportionality, focusing on how parties' ex ante pricing of risk may be inadequate.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of parties' bounded rationality or mistaken beliefs about risk on optimal remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A challenges the positive assumption that promisees will seek supracompensatory remedies and discusses how error (e.g., misestimates or collection costs) should affect judicial intervention; Paper B brings cognitive psychology and experimental economics to show parties systematically misestimate remote risks and argues the law should account for those biases when deciding whether to apply a disproportionality constraint.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of remote, low-probability/high-magnitude risks and when the law should limit recovery for such risks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses situations where party estimates of future harm may err and whether courts should prevent parties from contracting for remedies that would exploit such errors; Paper B focuses on the class of remote, infrequent, and non-salient risks that parties tend to undervalue and argues disproportionality should be available to limit liability in those contexts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 118wvalrev369!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT REMEDIES IN ACTION: SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT REMEDIES IN ACTION: SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE

shared_topics.topic: promisees' choice between specific performance and expectation (money) damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A challenges the assumption that promisees prefer supracompensatory remedies and argues promisees generally prefer compensatory monetary remedies; Paper B empirically documents that many plaintiffs opt out of specific performance in favor of money damages and analyzes the reasons for that choice (enforcement difficulty, lawyer bias, signaling, etc.).

shared_topics.topic: practical enforceability and implementation problems of specific performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers whether courts should permit parties to contract for specific relief and questions judicial policing given enforcement realities, while Paper B provides qualitative evidence that specific performance is often hard to implement—especially for unique goods—due to lack of quality standards, bad faith, and execution obstacles.

shared_topics.topic: judicial review and contractual policing of remedial clauses (liquidated damages, penalties, specific performance clauses)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues against judicial policing of ex ante and ex post liquidated-damage clauses and for allowing specific-performance clauses, whereas Paper B questions current doctrinal limits (e.g., restricting specific performance to unique goods), highlighting how legal defaults and enforcement rules affect parties' behavior and outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: instrumental uses of remedies (leverage, signaling, and attorney influence) and implications for theory
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions the positive premise that promisees seek supracompensatory remedies to exploit promisors and discusses how remedial rules interact with parties' incentives, while Paper B documents that parties and lawyers often use specific performance instrumentally—as bargaining leverage, a signal to courts, or shaped by attorney preferences—challenging core assumptions in both economic and rights-based contract theories.

shared_topics.topic: policy and normative implications for remedy design in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A derives normative prescriptions (e.g., restore punitive-damages bar, allow contracting for specific relief, repeal liquidated-damage review), and Paper B draws policy conclusions from empirical findings (e.g., rethinking the uniqueness rule, attending to enforcement mechanisms, and factoring attorney incentives), with both engaging the question of how remedial doctrine should be reformed given parties' actual behavior and enforcement realities.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83lawcontempprob151!!ARTICLE: BLACK MARKETS AND THE EXCHANGE STRUCTURE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BLACK MARKETS AND THE EXCHANGE STRUCTURE

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules shape and constrain private bargains/exchanges
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how judicial doctrines (liquidated damages, punitive damages, and specific performance rules) constrain the terms parties can lawfully contract for, while Paper B shows how statute and legal recognition (disabilities, price rules, eligibility rules) create or foreclose particular exchanges and thereby shape markets.

shared_topics.topic: the justification for prohibiting or disallowing particular transactions or contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the normative and positive rationales for banning penalty clauses, punitive awards, and certain specific-performance clauses, arguing the positive premise is false; Paper B surveys the rationales for criminalizing or otherwise prohibiting consensual exchanges (efficiency, fairness, system survival) and evaluates when prohibition is warranted to preserve an exchange structure.

shared_topics.topic: timing of legal intervention — ex ante disabilities versus ex post sanctions/enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes ex ante and ex post branches of the liquidated-damages rule and questions the need for ex ante policing of clauses, while Paper B emphasizes that law first disables exchanges (pre-transaction limits) and only secondarily applies sanctions, analyzing differences between early restraints and later punishments.

shared_topics.topic: the use of supracompensatory sanctions (punitive 'kickers') versus non‑penal regulatory devices to control transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts compensatory remedies with punitive damages and bans on penalty clauses, arguing for limiting supracompensatory relief and preferring compensatory mechanisms; Paper B contrasts 'kickers' (supracompensatory penalties) with disabilities (hands‑tying, unenforceability) as alternate tools for preventing transgressive exchanges and preserving norms.

shared_topics.topic: deference to private party preferences versus state paternalism in contract and exchange regulation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes promisee preferences and argues courts should respect contracting choices rather than paternalistically invalidating penalty or specific‑performance clauses, while Paper B explores the extent to which authorities should impose exchange rules (including criminalization or disabilities) rather than leave parties free to make consensual transactions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 33connlrev181!!ARTICLE: The Boundaries of Extracompensatory Relief for Abusive Breach of Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Boundaries of Extracompensatory Relief for Abusive Breach of Contract

shared_topics.topic: permissibility of punitive/extracompensatory damages for breach of contract
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when extracompensatory (punitive) damages can be viable in contract law, arguing they must be limited to severable subcategories; Paper B critiques recent relaxation of the punitive-damages bar and argues the traditional prohibition should be restored because promisees do not in fact prefer supracompensatory remedies.

shared_topics.topic: limits on promisees contracting for or obtaining supracompensatory remedies (liquidated damages and specific performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B centrally examines the doctrines that prevent promisees from obtaining penalties or contractual rights to specific performance and argues many of those judicial restraints are unnecessary; Paper A engages the related question of why contract doctrine generally confines recovery to expectation damages and evaluates doctrinal experiments that sought to expand remedies.

shared_topics.topic: insurance bad-faith/wrongful denial as a special category permitting extracompensatory relief
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats the insurance bad-faith cases as the paradigmatic exception to the no-punitive-damages rule and uses them to develop a severability-based theory; Paper B explicitly discusses the trend toward awarding punitive damages for wrongful denial of insurance benefits and evaluates whether that context justifies departure from the traditional rule.

shared_topics.topic: tension between predictability/cost-of-contracting and deterrence/punishment for abusive breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the core problem as protecting the predictability of the cost of breach while responding to abusive conduct and proposes severability as the solution; Paper B similarly grounds its critique in efficiency and the goal of limiting rewards to expectation, arguing that supracompensatory remedies undermine the predictability and efficiency of contracting.

shared_topics.topic: institutional choice (judicial policing versus legislative or contractual solutions) for setting remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that the viability of extracompensatory responses often depends on implementation mode and argues some remedies are better imposed by statute than common law; Paper B evaluates judicial review of liquidated-damage and specific-performance clauses and urges changing default judicial policing (or reducing it) in favor of allowing parties or different institutional responses to determine remedial rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 39umiamilrev723!!ARTICLE: Economic Theory and the Present Value of Future Lost Earnings: An Integration, Unification, and Simplification of Court Adopted Methodologies
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Economic Theory and the Present Value of Future Lost Earnings: An Integration, Unification, and Simplification of Court Adopted Methodologies

shared_topics.topic: judicial policing of damage-measure rules (whether courts should mandate, supervise, or defer to particular methods)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes courts for adopting or mandating particular present-value methodologies for lost-earnings awards and urges a single, economically grounded approach (the offset method); Paper B criticizes judicial review of contractual damage terms (liquidated damages, specific-performance clauses) and argues courts often should not police parties' chosen remedial measures.

shared_topics.topic: using economic theory to evaluate and reform legal doctrines on damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses economic relationships (nominal vs. real rates, growth rates, mathematical equivalence of present-value models) to demonstrate which legal methods are valid and unbiased; Paper B deploys incentive and preference-based economic reasoning to argue that promisees prefer compensatory remedies and to recommend reforming liquidated-damages, punitive-damages, and specific-performance rules.

shared_topics.topic: concern with biased, supracompensatory, or inequitable damage awards and how to prevent them
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents that existing present-value methods can be grossly biased in favor of plaintiffs or defendants and seeks a method minimizing bias; Paper B interrogates the premise that promisees want supracompensatory remedies, defends limiting such remedies, and argues against contracting or judicial awards that produce overcompensation.

shared_topics.topic: the role of ex ante versus ex post assessment, forecasting, and predictability in damage measurement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A insists that despite forecasting difficulties, stable economic relationships make lost-earnings awards more predictable and reduce the need for speculative forecasts; Paper B analyzes the ex ante and ex post branches of the liquidated-damage rule, arguing that ex ante/ ex post judicial second-guessing of parties' forecasts and estimates is often unwarranted and harms contractual autonomy.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 108michlrev633!!ARTICLE: DO LIQUIDATED DAMAGES ENCOURAGE BREACH? A PSYCHOLOGICAL EXPERIMENT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DO LIQUIDATED DAMAGES ENCOURAGE BREACH? A PSYCHOLOGICAL EXPERIMENT

shared_topics.topic: behavioral effect of liquidated‑damage / penalty clauses on breach decisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A presents experimental evidence that stipulating damages in the contract (liquidated‑damages or penalty clauses) makes promissors more willing to breach when profitable, while Paper B analyzes the strategic role of such clauses in contracting and whether parties would actually want penalty‑style remedies, so both engage with how liquidated/penalty terms change parties' incentives to perform or breach.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal treatment and judicial review of liquidated‑damage clauses (ex ante and ex post rules)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B provides a doctrinal critique arguing the ex ante and ex post branches of the liquidated‑damages rule are unnecessary or should be repealed, and Paper A considers policy implications of making remedies explicit (and how formal clauses alter behavior), so both address whether and how courts should police stipulated damages.

shared_topics.topic: comparative evaluation of remedies for breach (expectation damages vs stipulated damages, punitive damages, and specific performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts expectation damages with liquidated damages as background law versus contract term explanations for efficient breach, and Paper B systematically compares expectation damages, punitive damages, and specific performance rules and their enforceability, with both discussing tradeoffs across remedies.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between moral/social norms, reputation, and formalized contractual sanctions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A experimentally documents that formalizing sanctions (liquidated damages) attenuates moral aversion to breach and alters beliefs about others' expectations and reputational costs, while Paper B engages the positive and normative question of whether promisees would use contractual remedies (or courts) opportunistically, so both examine how legal rules interact with moral norms and reputational incentives.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 89bulrev1397!!ARTICLE: A THEORY OF SELF-HELP REMEDIES IN CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A THEORY OF SELF-HELP REMEDIES IN CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: adequacy of damages as a remedy and the law's allowance of self-help (withholding/refusal/specific performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when parties may withhold or refuse performance (or complete performance) because damages would not adequately compensate them, and how the law allocates the loss; Paper B interrogates courts' limits on supracompensatory remedies and defends limiting promisees to expectation damages while evaluating when specific performance is appropriate.

shared_topics.topic: regulation of contractual arrangements that alter remedial entitlements (penalty/liquidated damages clauses and specific-performance clauses)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines doctrinal rules (e.g., accord and satisfaction, voluntary payment, U.C.C. §1-308) governing parties' bargains and settlements that effectively change who bears loss, while Paper B focuses on the enforceability of liquidated-damage clauses, bans on contracting for punitive remedies, and the pros/cons of permitting contracts for specific relief.

shared_topics.topic: how parties' bargaining and nonjudicial strategies (threats, settlements, reserve-of-rights) interact with remedy doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies the 'nonperformance option' — threats to withhold performance, tender-with-reservation-of-rights, and duress/settlement dynamics — and how the law prods settlement or performance depending on harm; Paper B treats the strategic role of remedial rights (penalties, specific performance) as bargaining leverage and analyzes whether promisees would actually demand supracompensatory rights.

shared_topics.topic: the normative tension between efficiency (economic) justifications and autonomy/party-preference in shaping remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques prevailing economic accounts (e.g., efficient breach) and argues remedial simplicity and autonomy explain many doctrines allowing waste to avoid short-changing rights; Paper B directly tests the economic assumption that promisees want supracompensatory remedies and draws implications for default rules and judicial policing of contracts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1551!!ARTICLE: COULD BREACH OF CONTRACT BE IMMORAL?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: COULD BREACH OF CONTRACT BE IMMORAL?

shared_topics.topic: whether punitive or supracompensatory remedies (penalties/punitive damages) should be available for breach of contract
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions the traditional judicial bar on punitive damages and argues that some gratuitous breaches are morally punishable beyond expectation compensation, directly challenging the rationale for forbidding supracompensatory remedies; Paper B addresses the same set of doctrines (liquidated-damage/penalty rules and punitive damages), arguing promisees do not want penalty-style remedies and defending limits on supracompensatory awards while tracing the implications for enforcement rules.

shared_topics.topic: the efficiency (efficient-breach) rationale for limiting remedies and whether law should encourage breach for economic reasons
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly criticizes the efficient-breach justification for barring punitive remedies as morally problematic because it legitimates and encourages immoral breaches; Paper B engages the efficiency argument in justifying and critiquing doctrines (e.g., limiting specific performance to avoid inefficient compelled performance and the ex ante/ex post branches of penalty review), treating efficiency as central to when courts should police contractual remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between legal remedies and the moral content of promises (whether legal damages exhaust promissory duties)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that available legal remedies do not necessarily exhaust the moral duty created by promising and that some breaches remain morally wrongful despite compensatory damages; Paper B engages the normative premise about what remedies are desirable (that compensatory expectation protection suffices) and examines when extra-legal or extra-compensatory relief (punitive damages, specific performance) is normatively justified.

shared_topics.topic: the role and enforceability of specific performance (performance as such) versus expectation damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores the moral importance of performance as such to promising and whether promisees have claims to performance beyond damages; Paper B analyzes the doctrinal rule limiting contractual rights to specific performance, arguing promisees generally prefer compensatory remedies and proposing when courts should enforce specific-relief clauses and when they should be policed.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 97valrev1939!!ARTICLE: THE MYTH OF EFFICIENT BREACH: NEW DEFENSES OF THE EXPECTATION INTEREST
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE MYTH OF EFFICIENT BREACH: NEW DEFENSES OF THE EXPECTATION INTEREST

shared_topics.topic: whether the expectation interest should be protected by damages (liability rule) or by specific performance (property rule)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B centrally debates liability-versus-property rule protection of the expectation, defending damages (liability rules) against critics who favor specific performance or restitution; Paper A likewise engages the damages-vs-specific-performance question, arguing promisees generally prefer compensatory (monetary) remedies while also defending enforcement of contractual specific-performance clauses in the narrow cases where expectation cannot be monetized.

shared_topics.topic: whether promisees actually prefer supracompensatory remedies (penalty clauses, liquidated penalties, or rights that enable extortionate leverage)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly challenges the positive premise that promisees want supracompensatory remedies, arguing courts' prophylactic bans are unnecessary and counterproductive; Paper B likewise interrogates assumptions about party preferences over remedies (showing under its model promisees are not worse off under liability rules and examining how price and bargaining shape remedy choice).

shared_topics.topic: the scope and justification for judicial policing of contractual remedial terms (ex ante and ex post review of liquidated damages and enforceability of specific-relief clauses)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes and criticizes both the ex ante and ex post branches of the liquidated-damage rule and the ban on specific-performance clauses, arguing judicial review often misclassifies compensatory terms as penalties; Paper B engages the role courts play in interpreting and enforcing remedial defaults, and how judicial capacity to assess values interacts with the choice of default (liability vs property) and parties' incentives to contract.

shared_topics.topic: the status of alternative remedial measures (disgorgement/gain-based damages and punitive damages) relative to expectation damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper B examines restitutionary (disgorgement) and gain-based damages as proposed alternatives to expectation damages and notes the doctrinal shifts toward those measures; Paper A addresses the rising use of punitive and gain-based awards in contract contexts, arguing against routine punitive damages and situating those trends relative to the expectation-protection regime.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 93califlrev975!!ARTICLE: Actual and Virtual Specific Performance, the Theory of Efficient Breach, and the Indifference Principle in Contract Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Actual and Virtual Specific Performance, the Theory of Efficient Breach, and the Indifference Principle in Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: adequacy of expectation damages and the indifference principle
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze whether expectation damages actually make promisees indifferent between performance and legal relief: Paper B develops the 'indifference principle' and argues expectation damages systematically fall short, while Paper A shows promisees prefer compensatory (expectation) remedies and questions whether additional remedies are necessary to achieve indifference.

shared_topics.topic: the proper role and availability of specific performance
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage substantively with when courts should grant or enforce specific performance — Paper B weighs the costs and benefits of routine actual specific performance versus market-based 'virtual' specific performance, and Paper A argues parties should be able to contract for specific relief and that promisees primarily want specific performance only when expectation is not monetizable.

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of contractual remedial clauses (liquidated damages, penalties, and specific-performance clauses)
shared_topics.justification: Both articles consider whether parties should be permitted to contract for supracompensatory remedies: Paper A critiques the ex ante and ex post policing of liquidated-damage and penalty clauses and defends allowing specific-performance clauses, while Paper B addresses how remedial rules and contract terms interact with incentives for performance and cover.

shared_topics.topic: relation between the theory of efficient breach and remedial doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Both papers confront the efficient-breach idea and its implications for remedy rules: Paper B directly critiques the efficiency case for encouraging breach and examines its impact on specific performance frequency, while Paper A discusses how rules (liquidated damages, punitive damages, specific performance) aim to prevent promisees from extracting supracompensatory payments and how that interacts with incentives to breach or perform.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2013michstlrev167!!ARTICLE: A NIHILISTIC VIEW OF THE EFFICIENT BREACH
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A NIHILISTIC VIEW OF THE EFFICIENT BREACH

shared_topics.topic: the role of expectancy (expectation) damages in promoting or discouraging the 'efficient breach'
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers the expectation interest as the normative baseline for remedies, arguing promisees prefer compensatory (expectation-protecting) damages and that doctrine should reflect that; Paper B is devoted to whether the expectancy measure encourages efficient breach and concludes that the link between expectancy and efficiency is indeterminate and contested.

shared_topics.topic: the comparative merits of damages versus specific performance as default remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how specific performance interacts with the expectation interest and argues parties should be allowed to contract for specific relief because promisees mainly want it when expectation cannot be monetized; Paper B analyzes specific performance alongside expectancy, arguing specific performance is economically flawed and that no single remedy can reliably be favored to induce efficient outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the permissibility and policing of contract terms that can produce supracompensatory outcomes (penalties, liquidated damages, punitive damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly critiques the liquidated-damage/penalty and punitive-damages rules and the courts' policing (ex ante/ex post) of clauses that might overcompensate promisees, arguing much of that policing is unnecessary; Paper B engages the problem indirectly by questioning whether remedies (including damage rules) correctly induce internalization of breach costs and noting errors (false positives/negatives) in identifying efficient breaches that arise from how courts and scholars treat remedial rules.

shared_topics.topic: the normative foundations of remedial rules—efficiency versus other values (promissory morality, behavioral limits on rationality)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts a normative premise (supracompensatory remedies undesirable) with an empirical claim about promisee preferences and argues doctrine should follow promisees' revealed preferences; Paper B juxtaposes economic-efficiency accounts with deontological critiques and behavioral/happiness evidence to show that efficiency as a normative justification for remedy choice is indeterminate.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 103marqlrev1!!ARTICLE: DISGORGING EMOLUMENTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DISGORGING EMOLUMENTS

shared_topics.topic: whether courts should permit or limit non‑compensatory remedies (punitive/penalty awards, disgorgement, or specific performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contests the doctrinal bans on penalty clauses and punitive damages and argues promisees do not want supracompensatory remedies while also urging greater freedom to contract for specific performance; Paper B advocates restitutionary disgorgement as a non‑compensatory remedy for unlawful emoluments and evaluates its doctrinal and constitutional fit against alternatives like punitive or mere compensatory relief.

shared_topics.topic: compensatory vs restitutionary remedies as the appropriate tool to accomplish legal goals (expectation protection vs unjust enrichment/anti‑corruption)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds its analysis in the expectation interest and recommends limiting remedies to compensatory measures (except where specific relief is necessary), whereas Paper B situates disgorgement within restitution law and argues restitutionary remedies better serve anti‑corruption and unjust enrichment objectives.

shared_topics.topic: the institutional question of who should create, police, or expand remedies (courts policing contractual/constitutional terms vs legislative or private ordering solutions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes judicial policing of liquidated damage clauses and specific performance terms and urges less ex ante/ex post review so parties can order their affairs; Paper B similarly weighs judicial/common‑law routes against a statutory solution for disgorgement, considering which institutional path best secures enforcement and legitimacy.

shared_topics.topic: remedy design as a means of deterrence, accountability, and dealing with enforcement/collection costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how remedies (or lack thereof) affect parties' incentives to sue, collection costs, and the desirability of punitive awards as deterrence in limited contexts; Paper B emphasizes that an effective remedy (disgorgement) is necessary to deter self‑dealing by officials and to give emoluments provisions real bite, and it addresses obstacles to achieving that enforcement.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 42villlrev65!!ARTICLE: REVIVING JACOB AND YOUNGS, INC. v. KENT: MATERIAL BREACH DOCTRINE RECONSIDERED
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: REVIVING JACOB AND YOUNGS, INC. v. KENT: MATERIAL BREACH DOCTRINE RECONSIDERED

shared_topics.topic: judicial policing of contractual freedom and party autonomy
shared_topics.justification: Both papers critique existing judicial intervention that constrains contracting—Paper A argues courts unnecessarily police liquidated‑damage and specific‑performance clauses (advocating greater deference to parties), while Paper B criticizes courts' muddled application of material breach/condition doctrine and urges a clearer, principled framework (Cardozo's approach) to guide judicial decisionmaking.

shared_topics.topic: choice of remedies—when to award damages, specific performance, termination, or punitive relief
shared_topics.justification: Both engage substantively with which remedies the law should permit or limit: Paper A analyzes compensatory versus supracompensatory remedies (liquidated damages, punitive damages, specific performance), and Paper B focuses on doctrinal rules that determine when a nonbreaching party may suspend performance or terminate (as opposed to seeking damages).

shared_topics.topic: standards for assessing breach severity and ex ante vs ex post evaluation
shared_topics.justification: Both examine how courts should evaluate the seriousness of contractual deviation and the timing of review—Paper A distinguishes and critiques the ex ante and ex post branches of the liquidated‑damages rule, while Paper B interrogates the indeterminate multi‑factor material breach test and urges a more focused, context‑sensitive assessment (à la Jacob & Youngs).

shared_topics.topic: opportunism, incentives, and the prevention of extortionate outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Both are concerned with parties using doctrinal rules to extract inefficient gains: Paper A worries promisees will use specific performance or penalty clauses to obtain supracompensatory payments (arguing empirically they do not), and Paper B addresses how material breach doctrine can either enable or deter opportunistic suspension/termination and proposes rules to promote good‑faith, efficient performance.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2012utahlrev861!!ARTICLE: Taking Outcomes Seriously
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Taking Outcomes Seriously

shared_topics.topic: whether damages and remedies should be measured solely by pecuniary expectation loss versus a broader conception of outcome
shared_topics.justification: Paper A experimentally argues that people value non-pecuniary aspects of outcomes (intentionality, voluntariness, identity of actor) so welfare assessments should go beyond monetary end results; Paper B engages the same question in the contract-remedies context by defending the norm that promisees' recovery should be limited to expectation loss and critiquing doctrines that permit supracompensatory awards.

shared_topics.topic: empirical and normative implications of promisee/recipient preferences for legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A provides experimental evidence about how laypersons and businesspeople evaluate outcomes and uses that to recommend changes to damage rules, while Paper B analyzes (and purports to demonstrate) promisees' preferences over compensatory versus penalty-like remedies and derives doctrinal implications for liquidated damages, punitive damages, and specific performance.

shared_topics.topic: the legal treatment of compelled or nonvoluntary transfers (compelled giving / specific performance) and its welfare effects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that unwilling or coerced transfers reduce recipients' valuation and recommends accounting for 'compelled giving' in damages, whereas Paper B examines the role of specific performance and the ban on contracts for specific relief—addressing whether courts should allow coercive remedies and how promisees use the power to compel performance.

shared_topics.topic: how courts should police or refrain from policing contractual terms (liquidated damages, penalties, and specific-performance clauses) in light of welfare and behavioral considerations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that narrow economic measures may misprice harms and supports doctrinal changes (e.g., compensating for unwilling transfers, reconsidering punitive/emotional damages), and Paper B argues courts currently overcorrect by invalidating or policing clauses (ex ante/ex post liquidated damages review, bans on specific-performance clauses and punitive contractual remedies) and should relax or rethink those policing rules based on promisee preferences and efficiency.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 103marqlrev1!!ARTICLE: DISGORGING EMOLUMENTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DISGORGING EMOLUMENTS

shared_topics.topic: whether remedies should be compensatory (expectation/restitution) or supracompensatory/punitive
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes contract doctrine limiting supracompensatory remedies (penalty clauses, punitive damages, specific performance) and argues promisees prefer compensatory expectation protection; Paper B debates whether unconstitutional or improper emoluments should be addressed by punitive sanctions or by restitutionary disgorgement, advocating restitution over other remedial forms.

shared_topics.topic: the role of restitutionary/disgorgement relief versus expectation damages in preventing unjust enrichment
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes restricting recoveries to lost expectation to avoid promisees obtaining supracompetatory gains, while Paper B situates disgorgement within restitution law as the appropriate tool to strip officials of unlawful gains and prevent unjust enrichment.

shared_topics.topic: who (courts, parties, or legislatures) should determine and police remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques judicial policing of liquidated-damage and specific-performance clauses and argues for relaxing ex ante/ex post review and permitting contractual remediation choices; Paper B examines the absence of textual remedies for constitutional emoluments and proposes statutory and common-law paths for courts and legislatures to operationalize disgorgement relief.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial design affects deterrence, accountability, and social costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A assesses when punitive or specific remedies produce inefficient extortion or perverse incentives and argues remedies should be tailored to promote efficient contracting and enforcement (including reducing collection costs), while Paper B argues disgorgement both deters corruption/self-dealing and enhances governmental accountability by removing incentives to profit from office.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 117yaleljpocketpart14!!ARTICLE: What Efficiency Demands: The Efficient Performance Hypothesis Defended
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: What Efficiency Demands: The Efficient Performance Hypothesis Defended

shared_topics.topic: comparative efficiency and function of specific performance versus expectation damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how specific performance and expectation damages operate to protect the promisee's expectation, argues promisees generally prefer compensatory remedies and that specific-performance clauses should be enforceable when expectation cannot be monetized; Paper B analyzes how specific performance, expectation damages, and disgorgement serve distinct economic functions under different entitlement regimes and defends the view that either remedy can be made consistent with allocative efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: desirability and enforceability of supracompensatory remedies (penalties, punitive damages, liquidated damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly interrogates whether promisees want penalty clauses or punitive remedies and argues courts should relax policing of liquidated-damage clauses because promisees do not prefer supracompensatory awards; Paper B treats the design and choice of remedies (including transfers like disgorgement and liquidated terms) as central to efficiency and shows that assignment and enforcement of remedial rules materially affect incentives, allocation, and whether courts should permit contractual selection of remedies.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of legal entitlements/decision rights between promisor and promisee and its effect on efficient outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the implications of giving promisees the power to obtain specific performance (and critiques rules that prevent promisees from contracting for such power), while Paper B explicitly contrasts the Holmesian promisor-option (efficient breach) with the efficient performance hypothesis (promisee entitlement) and analyzes how whose right it is to choose performance or pay damages changes economic incentives and allocations.

shared_topics.topic: role of courts, default rules, and judicial policing (transaction costs and judicial determination costs) in remedy design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques both ex ante and ex post judicial policing of liquidated-damage clauses and the ban on specific-performance clauses, arguing courts often do more harm than good; Paper B emphasizes judicial determination and litigation costs, transaction-cost indeterminacy among remedies, and the empirical contingency of which default rule promotes efficiency, thereby engaging the same question of how aggressively courts should police or defer to contracting parties on remedial rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2012utahlrev861!!ARTICLE: Taking Outcomes Seriously
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Taking Outcomes Seriously

shared_topics.topic: enforceability and role of liquidated-damage clauses
shared_topics.justification: Both papers directly address liquidated damages: Paper A analyzes the doctrinal justifications for the ex ante and ex post prohibitions on penalty clauses and argues courts should relax review and enforce party-chosen damage measures, while Paper B questions whether standard wealth-based damages capture people’s valuations and argues experimental evidence supports greater enforcement or adjustment of liquidated measures to reflect non-pecuniary valuation effects.

shared_topics.topic: whether punitive or supracompensatory remedies should be available in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the issue of supracompensatory remedies — Paper A evaluates the normative and positive grounds for banning punitive damages and penalties (arguing promisees do not want supracompensatory rights), whereas Paper B’s experiments suggest people value intentionality and motive and therefore provides empirical reasons to reconsider when punitive or emotional-disturbance awards might improve welfare.

shared_topics.topic: specific performance versus monetary compensation (property/relief rule choice)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers examine the choice between coercive specific performance and money damages: Paper A defends allowing contracting for specific relief and argues promisees typically do not seek it to extort supracompensation, while Paper B shows that ‘compelled giving’ or legal coercion changes recipients’ valuations and thus bears on whether property rules (specific performance) or liability rules (damages) maximize welfare.

shared_topics.topic: role of non-pecuniary factors (intentionality, willingness/cooperation, identity) in valuing outcomes and designing remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both works treat more than dollar losses as relevant to remedy design — Paper B provides experimental evidence that intentionality, unwilling giving, and actor identity alter outcome valuation and urges incorporating these into damages, and Paper A discusses promisee preferences and exploitation concerns (e.g., using specific performance or penalty clauses) that hinge on behavioral responses to coercion and bargaining incentives.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 20hofstralrev941!!SYMPOSIUM: THE FUTURE OF LAW AND ECONOMICS: THE NEGLIGENCE-OPPORTUNISM TRADEOFF IN CONTRACT LAW.
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE FUTURE OF LAW AND ECONOMICS: THE NEGLIGENCE-OPPORTUNISM TRADEOFF IN CONTRACT LAW.

shared_topics.topic: deterrence targets in contract law (negligence versus opportunism/exploitation)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze which kinds of conduct legal rules should deter: Paper A formulates a negligence–opportunism tradeoff and argues for prioritizing deterrence of opportunistic (exploitative) breaches, while Paper B evaluates remedies (penalty clauses, punitive damages, specific performance) as instruments to deter or permit exploitation and asks whether courts should block promisees from obtaining supracompensatory relief to prevent opportunistic extortion.

shared_topics.topic: efficiency-based reform of contract doctrine and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both use law-and-economics reasoning to recommend doctrinal change: Paper A proposes restructuring contract law around fault and parties' reasons for breach to maximize efficient contracting, and Paper B applies efficiency logic to argue for abolishing certain judicial controls on liquidated damages and for restoring/reshaping rules on punitive damages and specific performance.

shared_topics.topic: the relevance of parties' incentives and preferences for designing default rules
shared_topics.justification: Both papers insist that rules should account for how parties actually behave and what they prefer: Paper A focuses on parties' reasons for making and breaking contracts as the proper basis for doctrine, and Paper B empirically/analytically claims promisees prefer compensatory (not supracompensatory) remedies and that those preferences should inform whether courts restrict contractual terms.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate scope of judicial review or policing of contractual terms and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the question of how actively courts should intervene in private contracts: Paper A critiques traditional litigator-centered doctrines and calls for doctrinal design that better targets undesirable behavior, affecting enforcement priorities, while Paper B explicitly argues against special judicial policing of liquidated-damage and specific-performance clauses and defends limiting state intervention in remedy design.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2001wislrev681!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:COMMENTARY BREACH AND PENALTY AS CONTRACTUAL NORM AND CONTRACTUAL ANOMIE
compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:COMMENTARY BREACH AND PENALTY AS CONTRACTUAL NORM AND CONTRACTUAL ANOMIE

shared_topics.topic: judicial enforcement and tolerance of supracompensatory remedies (penalty clauses, liquidated damages, punitive damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically documents a high reliance on penalty clauses and an unusually high judicial tolerance for penalties in post‑communist Russia; Paper B doctrinally analyzes the rules that limit enforcement of liquidated damages and punitive contractual remedies and argues which branches of those rules are justified or should be abandoned.

shared_topics.topic: relationship between parties' market/bargaining power and the use or imposition of penalty clauses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A tests whether firms with market power force less powerful counterparties to accept penalty clauses and finds little support for that hypothesis in Russia; Paper B interrogates whether sophisticated or powerful promisees seek supracompensatory remedies (or extract specific‑performance rights) and how bargaining power shapes the threats and prices of performance.

shared_topics.topic: role of litigation propensity, legal activism, and enforcement/collection costs in shaping contracting behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A finds a strong link between plaintiffs' legal activism (versus nonlegal cooperation) and propensity to use penalties, emphasizing how legal culture affects contracting; Paper B models promisees' incentives to sue, the deterrent effects of collection costs, and recommends reducing enforcement costs rather than supplying punitive remedies.

shared_topics.topic: effects of penalties and specific‑performance rights on efficient breach and contractual efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines whether use of penalties correlates with antipathy to the notion of efficient breach and finds no clear linkage; Paper B centers its normative analysis on how supracompensatory remedies and specific performance can prevent efficient breach and evaluates when courts should restrict or allow such remedies to promote efficiency.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 76marqlrev519!!ARTICLE: Divorce Law: Exclusions and Disproportionate Divisions of Marital Estate
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Divorce Law: Exclusions and Disproportionate Divisions of Marital Estate

shared_topics.topic: judicial policing of private entitlements and limits on party autonomy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how statute and courts exclude gifted and inherited assets from the divisible marital estate—thereby limiting spouses' ability to treat those assets as marital property—while Paper B critiques courts' policing of contracting (liquidated-damage clauses, punitive damages, and specific-performance clauses) that restrict what parties may agree to, so both assess when and how courts should restrict private arrangements.

shared_topics.topic: preventing disproportionate or supracompensatory allocations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses the problem of disproportionate divisions of the marital estate when certain property is excluded or treated specially, and Paper B analyzes doctrinal rules (and their justification) that prevent promisees from obtaining supracompensatory recoveries, so both engage with legal mechanisms designed to curb excessive or unfair transfers.

shared_topics.topic: how legal characterization determines entitlements and relief
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on characterizing assets (gifted/inherited versus marital) to determine property-division entitlements on divorce, while Paper B focuses on classifying contractual remedies (penalty vs legitimate liquidated damages; monetary damages vs specific performance) to determine what relief is available—each shows how classification rules shape substantive outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: policy and normative evaluation of statutory or doctrinal rules governing distributions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates the statutory framework (Section 767.255) and its consequences for fair divisions of marital property, and Paper B explicitly weighs normative and positive premises underlying rules that limit remedies, so both engage in policy-based critique of legal rules that allocate resources or remedies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 50mdlrev253!!ARTICLE: LAW AND EQUITY IN CONTRACT ENFORCEMENT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: LAW AND EQUITY IN CONTRACT ENFORCEMENT

shared_topics.topic: when specific performance is appropriate versus monetary damages as an adequate remedy
shared_topics.justification: Both papers center the question of when courts should grant specific performance instead of awarding expectation damages: Paper A argues promisees generally prefer compensatory monetary remedies and contends courts should permit contracting for specific relief when expectations cannot be monetized, while Paper B analyzes the doctrinal rule that specific performance is available only when damages are inadequate and interrogates the coherence and application of that rule.

shared_topics.topic: the justification for a distinct 'fairness' or equitable defense that can deny specific performance
shared_topics.justification: Both articles examine the moral or fairness-based reasons courts invoke to withhold equitable relief: Paper B critiques the indeterminate fairness defense that bars specific performance despite permitting damages, and Paper A challenges the normative premise behind denying supracompensatory remedies (including equitable powers) by testing whether promisees actually want such rights.

shared_topics.topic: whether and how courts should police contractual remedial clauses (judicial review of liquidated damages and specific-performance clauses)
shared_topics.justification: Both works engage the question of judicial review of parties' remedial choices: Paper A argues against the ex ante and ex post policing of liquidated-damage clauses and for enforcing parties' agreements on specific relief, while Paper B investigates why courts exercise discretion to deny equitable enforcement and whether that discretion functions as special policing of contractual outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the centrality of the expectation interest and efficiency/distributional tradeoffs in remedy design
shared_topics.justification: Both papers anchor their analyses in the expectation-interest concept and consider efficiency and distributional consequences: Paper A frames the rules (liquidated damages, punitive damages, specific performance) as mechanisms to constrain recoveries to expectation and evaluates their efficiency effects, and Paper B weighs how specific performance versus damages impacts resource allocation, third-party interests, and the balance between contractual stability and ad hoc fairness.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 120harvlrev708!!ARTICLE: THE DIVERGENCE OF CONTRACT AND PROMISE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE DIVERGENCE OF CONTRACT AND PROMISE

shared_topics.topic: whether punitive damages should be available for breach of contract
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage the prohibition on punitive damages in contract law: Paper A defends restoring the traditional ban (arguing punitive awards resemble contract-supplied penalties and promisees do not want them), while Paper B highlights the prohibition as a salient way contract law diverges from moral reactions to intentional promissory breach and questions whether that divergence is normatively appropriate.

shared_topics.topic: the proper scope of compensatory (expectation) remedies versus supracompensatory/penalty remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both articles analyze the law's effort to confine promisees to their expectation interest—Paper A directly disputes the positive justification for rules limiting liquidated damages and specific performance as guarding against supracompensatory outcomes, and Paper B contrasts contract law's compensatory focus with moral norms about promises and the moral significance of breach.

shared_topics.topic: whether legal contract doctrine should track, accommodate, or diverge from the moral norms governing promises (the law's normative justification and its acceptability to moral agents)
shared_topics.justification: Both works probe the normative foundations of contract doctrines: Paper B develops an ‘accommodationist’ framework arguing contract law should be compatible with moral agency and some features of interpersonal promising, while Paper A tests and rejects a positive normative premise (that promisees prefer supracompensatory remedies) and draws implications about which remedial rules courts should retain or abandon to better reflect norms about promising.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate degree and form of judicial scrutiny of contractual damage measures
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues normatively that judicial policing of penalty clauses and specific-performance clauses does more harm than good and should be scaled back or eliminated, while Paper B engages descriptively and analytically with how courts do (and should) review stipulated-damages provisions under statutes and the Restatement, exploring the standards and case law that constitute such judicial scrutiny.

shared_topics.topic: how to measure 'actual harm' for purposes of deeming a stipulated sum punitive or compensatory (inclusion/exclusion of avoidable, unforeseeable, and uncertain losses)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B directly analyzes which categories of losses (reasonably avoidable, unforeseeable, uncertain) should count as 'actual harm' under modern statutory and Restatement tests; Paper A engages the same issue at the doctrinal level when criticizing the ex post branch that invalidates clauses based on after-the-fact comparisons to actual loss and questions the legitimacy and effects of courts remeasuring parties' agreed allocations.
