papers.node_id: 80califlrev563!!ARTICLE: The Principle of Hadley v. Baxendale.
papers.title: ARTICLE: The Principle of Hadley v. Baxendale.
papers.abstract:
In 1854 the Court of Exchequer Chamber decided the now-famous case ofHadley v. Baxendale.The basic facts are well-known.  Briefly, the plaintiffs owned a flour mill that went down because of a break in the crankshaft that worked the mill.  As a result, the plaintiffs wanted to transport the broken shaft to the original manufacturer, Joyce & Co. of Greenwich, to serve as a pattern for the manufacture of a new shaft.  They therefore sent an employee to the local office of the defendants, who were large-scale public carriers trading under the name Pickford & Co.  The employee told Pickford's clerk that the mill was stopped and that the shaft must be sent immediately.  The clerk answered that if the shaftwas sent up by twelve o'clock any day, it would be delivered at Greenwich on the following day.
The shaft was placed in Pickford's hands the next day before twelve o'clock, and Hadley paid £ 2 4d. for its shipment.  Pickford's clerk was told that a special entry, if required, should be made to hasten delivery.  In the event, delivery was delayed for five days "by some neglect":Pickford routed the shipment through London and instead of immediately forwarding the shaft from London to Greenwich by rail, kept the shaft in London for several days and then sent it to Greenwich by canal together with an unrelated shipment of iron goods that Pickford was transporting to Joyce.Completion of the new shaft by Joyce was correspondingly delayed, and the mill was down five extra days.  The plaintiffs claimed that
they thereby were unable to supply many of their customers with flour, sharps, and bran during that period, and were obliged to buy flour to supply some of their other customers, and lost the means and opportunity of selling flour, sharps, and bran, and were deprived of gains and profits which otherwise would have accrued to them, and were unable to employ their workmen, to whom they were compelled to pay wages during that period. . . .
On the basis of these claims, the plaintiffs asked for damages of £ 300.  Pickford argued that the damages claimed were "too remote."The plaintiffs responded that these damages were "not too remote, for they are . . . the natural and necessary consequence of the defendants' default."The trial court "left the case generally to the jury,"which awarded the plaintiffs damages of £ 25 above and beyond £ 25 that Pickford had already paid into court.  The Exchequer Chamber reversed, but not on the theory of remoteness.  Instead, it said that a party injured by a breach of contract can recover only those damages that either should "reasonably be considered . . . [as] arising naturally, i.e., according to the usual course of things" from the breach, or might "reasonably be supposed to have been in the contemplation of both parties, at the time they made the contract, as the probable result of the breach of it."The court concluded that the plaintiffs had failed to satisfy either test.The two branches of the court's holding have come to be known as the first and second rules ofHadley v. Baxendale.
Most contracts can be characterized as sales of commodities (using that term broadly to include goods, land, and services) for a money price.  The two rules ofHadley v. Baxendaleare normally applied only to cases involving a breach by the seller of a commodity, because usually a buyer's major obligation is to pay money, and the nonpayment of a money price rarely implicates those two rules.  For convenience, in the balance of this Article I shall therefore refer to the party in breach of a contract as the seller and to the party injured by a breach as the buyer.
On the basis of the two rules ofHadley v. Baxendale,contract law has conventionally distinguished between general or direct damages on the one hand and special or consequential damages on the other.  General or direct damages are the damages that flow from a given type of breach without regard to the buyer's particular circumstances.  General damages are never barred by the principle ofHadley v. Baxendalebecause by their very definition such damages should "reasonably be considered . . . [as] arising naturally, i.e., according to the usual course of things from the breach."For example, if a seller breaches a contract for the sale of goods, it follows naturally that the buyer suffers damages equal to the difference between the contract price and the market or cover price.  This difference can normally be recovered as general damages.
Special or consequential damages are the damages above and beyond general damages that flow from a breach as a result of the buyer's particular circumstances.  Typically, consequential damagesconsist of lost profits (although other kinds of consequential damages may occur).  In particular, consequential damages typically consist of the difference between the profits the buyer actually made in transactions with third persons and the profits he would have made if the seller had performed.  For example, suppose a seller breaches a contract for the sale of a factor of production, such as a die press, that the buyer plans to use rather than resell.  The buyer's consequential damages are the difference between the profits he earned on his actual postbreach output and the profits he would have earned if the die press had been furnished as promised.
The second rule ofHadley v. Baxendalehas traditionally been conceptualizedto mean that consequential damages can be recovered only if, at the time the contract was made, the seller had reason to foresee that the consequential damages were the probable result of the breach.Under this conceptualization of the second rule, the first rule is simply a special case of the second: if a given type of damage arises "naturally, i.e., according to the usual course of things" from the breach of a given contract (the first rule), then a seller will always have reason to foresee that the given type of damages are the probable result of the breach (the second rule).  Therefore, in the balance of this Article I will refer to this conceptualization of the second rule as the principle ofHadley v. Baxendale.
Two important characteristics of the principle ofHadley v. Baxendaleshould be briefly stated at the outset.  First, the principle is a default rule.Essentially, the principle serves as a device to limit sellers' liability.  If the principle were dropped from the law, sellers could still limit liability by contractual provisions that preclude consequential damages, set a dollar or formula limit on liability, offer varying liability limits in exchange for higher or lower prices, or substitute for dollar liability some other obligation, such as replacement or repair.Second, although the principle is often characterized as a "foreseeability doctrine,"the principle as traditionally formulated and applied cuts off most foreseeable damages.
This second characteristic of the principle ofHadley v. Baxendalecan best be understood by distinguishing among three levels of foreseeability.
The first level is foreseeability in the ordinary sense of that term, that is, in the sense that an event -- here, damage of a certain type --couldhave been foreseen.  In that sense of the term, almost any damage that actually occurs was likely to have been foreseeable.
A second level of foreseeability requires not only that a certain type of damage could have been foreseen, but that the prospect that this damage would occur was more than marginal, or not insignificant.  I will usethe termreasonably foreseeableto refer to damages that are foreseeable at this second level.
A third and most demanding level of foreseeability requires not only that the damage could have been foreseen, and that the prospect it would occur was more than marginal, or not insignificant, but that viewed ex ante it wasprobableor highly probable that the damage would result.
The principle ofHadley v. Baxendale,as traditionally formulated and applied, ratchets up the requirement of foreseeability to the third, exceptionally demanding level,and thereby cuts off both damages that could have been foreseen and damages that are reasonably foreseeable.  Accordingly, it is inaccurate, or at least oversimplified, to treat theHadleyprinciple simply as a foreseeability doctrine.  On the one hand, the principle cuts off most foreseeable damages.  On the other, a foreseeability limitation would apply in contract law even if the principle ofHadley v. Baxendalewere dropped.
The thesis of this Article is as follows: In most areas of law, liability requires a showing only of proximate cause.  That principle, like the principle ofHadley v. Baxendale,normally turns or should turn on some standard of foreseeability.  Therefore, the choice between a regime based onHadley v. Baxendaleand a regime based on proximate cause is not a choice between liability for foreseeable losses and liability for all losses caused in fact.  Rather, it is a choice between competing standards of foreseeability, and between competing times for applying the standard -- the time when the contract is made or the time when the contract is breached.
As traditionally formulated and applied,Hadley v. Baxendalereflects three basic choices on these axes: (1) An extremely strict standard of foreseeability, which requires that the damage not be merely foreseeable or reasonably foreseeable, but probable or even highly probable.  (2) A uniform standard of foreseeability, regardless of the nature of the interest invaded and the nature of the breach.  (3) An application of the foreseeability standard at the time the contract is made rather than at the time the contract is breached.
These choices defeat reasonable expectations and fall short in terms of efficiency.  Accordingly, the principle ofHadley v. Baxendaleshouldbe dropped from contract law in favor of a regime of proximate cause -- or more accurately, a regime of proximate cause, contractual allocations of loss, and fair disclosure.  The precise standard of foreseeability under this regime should depend not on whether the action is labeled contract or tort, but on the nature of the interest invaded and the wrong involved -- on whether, for example, the injury involves harm to the person, physical injury to property, lost profits, out-of-pocket costs, or opportunity costs, and on whether the breach was inadvertent or opportunistic.  When lost profits or forgone opportunities are involved, the baseline standard should be what I call reasonable foreseeability -- that is, whether the prospect that the damage would occur was more than marginal, or not insignificant.  Furthermore, reasonable foreseeability should be determined as of the time of the breach, so that in deciding whether to breach the seller must sweep into his calculus all the costs that he should reasonably foresee will be incurred by the buyer as a result of breach.
Part I of this Article will examine the close connections between the principle ofHadley v. Baxendaleand classical contract law.  Part II will compare the principle ofHadley v. Baxendalewith the general principle of expectation damages and the principles of damages outside contract law.  Part III will examine the modern arguments for the principle ofHadley v. Baxendale.Part IV will develop the preferable regime of proximate cause, contractual allocations of loss, and fair disclosure.  Part V will show that modern contract law and practice are now moving toward that regime.

questions.question: Should recovery for losses caused by a breach of contract be limited to losses that were highly probable at the time the contract was made, or should liability instead be assessed at the time of breach using a foreseeability standard that allows recovery of losses that were reasonably foreseeable?

Should the standard for imposing liability for breach-related losses vary according to the type of harm (for example, lost profits, physical damage, out-of-pocket costs, or opportunity costs) and according to the nature of the breach (for example, inadvertent versus opportunistic)?
How should default liability rules interact with parties' ability to allocate losses by contract and with duties of disclosure to achieve efficient and fair risk allocation?

matched_themes: Should parties and courts adopt fault-based remedial regimes that distinguish among breaches by reason when allocating remedies?
What counterfactual baseline should courts use to measure plaintiffs' losses for compensation purposes?
How should default liability rules interact with parties' freedom to allocate risks by contract and duties of disclosure to achieve efficient and fair risk allocation?
Should parties be presumptively permitted to contractually specify nonstandard damage remedies, or should courts retain authority to impose defaults?
Does the promisor's motive for breaching (loss-avoiding vs gain-seeking) affect how much compensation promisees need to accept nonperformance?
How should courts treat and enforce stipulated remedies (liquidated damages clauses) versus substituting judicial remedies?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
Should courts limit recoverable consequential damages that are grossly disproportionate to the contract price, and would such limits promote economic efficiency?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
Do parties and courts actually choose heterogeneous, context-tailored damage provisions in contracting, and under what conditions would such customization be voluntarily chosen or socially desirable?
Do limits on recoverable damages (foreseeability, certainty, avoidability) substantially reduce awards below full compensation, and should courts liberalize those limits?
Do courts consider the breaching party's blameworthiness or opportunistic behavior when selecting among compensatory remedies?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 10jempiricallegalstud512!!ARTICLE: Reference Points and Contractual Choices: An Experimental Examination
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Reference Points and Contractual Choices: An Experimental Examination

shared_topics.topic: the role of parties' expectations at formation in determining liability and damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the Hadley v. Baxendale rule fixes foreseeability at the time the contract is made (versus at breach) to limit recoverable consequential damages; Paper B shows experimentally that framing and reference points at formation change parties' perceived payoffs and thus their expectations about obligations and outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: contractual allocation of risk and the interaction of default rules with explicit terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats Hadley as a default rule that limits sellers' liability and argues parties can and should use contractual provisions to allocate losses, while Paper B studies how contract design (e.g., bonus vs. penalty frames) and framing-induced biases change the effective allocation of incentives and thus highlights the importance of explicit terms.

shared_topics.topic: ambiguity and uncertainty in contractual obligations and how interpretation affects outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights problems arising from imposing rigid foreseeability rules given parties' differing information and expectations and calls for fair disclosure and clearer allocations, whereas Paper B experimentally investigates how legal ambiguity gives parties room to adopt self‑serving interpretations—especially under loss frames—altering performance and payoffs.

shared_topics.topic: how rules and framing shape performance incentives and breach decisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the timing and stringency of foreseeability rules affect the breacher's calculus and hence incentives to perform or breach, and Paper B demonstrates that gain/loss framing of contract payoffs materially changes effort levels and interpretive choices that determine performance.

shared_topics.topic: normative policy implications for contract law focused on efficiency and behaviorally informed rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advances a normative proposal to replace Hadley with a proximate‑cause regime plus contractual allocation and disclosure to improve efficiency, while Paper B draws practical and doctrinal implications from behavioral evidence (loss aversion, framing) for how contract law and contracting practice should be designed to promote better outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 56sclrev93!!ARTICLE:The Shadow Code
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:The Shadow Code

shared_topics.topic: the role and standard of foreseeability/remoteness in contract damages
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze Hadley v. Baxendale's remoteness/foreseeability limitation — Paper A critiques Hadley for imposing an excessively strict (probability-level) foreseeability standard and argues for a proximate-cause/reasonable-foreseeability approach (applied at breach), while Paper B incorporates a foreseeability limit into SC 4 and discusses how damages should be confined to losses that are reasonably foreseeable when computing surplus.

shared_topics.topic: how expectation damages (lost profits) should be calculated (surplus/expectation framework)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the computation of expectation-type awards for lost profits: Paper A discusses direct versus consequential lost profits and argues for a foreseeability standard tied to types of interests (lost profits among them), while Paper B offers a unified, surplus-based formula (anticipated minus actual surplus) that yields expectation-equivalent awards including lost profits across buyer/seller and partial-performance contexts.

shared_topics.topic: the distinction and recovery rules for general/direct versus special/consequential/incidental losses
shared_topics.justification: Both papers treat the legal split between general (direct) and special (consequential or incidental) damages: Paper A traces that split to Hadley and critiques its operation; Paper B criticizes fragmented U.C.C./Restatement definitions (and confused uses of 'consequential' and 'incidental') and replaces them with a single surplus framework that subsumes those categories.

shared_topics.topic: recognized limitations on recovery (certainty, mitigation, mitigation duties and non-speculative proof)

shared_topics.topic: normative reform toward a unified or alternative damages regime
shared_topics.justification: Both are reform-minded: Paper A advocates abandoning Hadley in favor of a regime based on proximate cause combined with contractual allocation and fair disclosure, while Paper B proposes the Shadow Code as a single, surplus-based section to unify and clarify the U.C.C./Restatement damage rules.

shared_topics.topic: the Hadley foreseeability limitation on consequential damages

shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops the classic split between general/direct damages (market/cover price) and special/consequential damages (lost profits from the buyer's particular circumstances), and Paper B discusses how these limits (and related requirements of certainty and mitigation) produce systematic undercompensation of contract plaintiffs, particularly with respect to lost profits and similar economic losses.

shared_topics.topic: when the foreseeability/foreknowledge inquiry should be applied (time of contract formation versus time of breach)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the relevant foreseeability standard should be applied at the time of breach rather than at contract formation, whereas Paper B explains the prevailing doctrine that measures assumed risks by reference to what the parties knew or should have known at formation and highlights the effects of that timing on plaintiffs' recoveries.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between contract remedial rules and tort doctrines (proximate cause, punitive and nonpecuniary awards)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advocates replacing the Hadley regime with a proximate cause framework (bringing contract damages closer to tort principles) and tailoring foreseeability standards to the interest invaded, while Paper B surveys and critiques the movement to import tort‑style remedies into contract actions—especially punitive and nonpecuniary damages—and considers how tort remedies affect the goal of full compensation.

shared_topics.topic: default rules, contractual allocation of risk, and the extent to which parties can limit or shift liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats Hadley as a default rule that sellers can contract around (liability caps, exclusions, substitutes for money liability), and Paper B similarly documents how doctrines (attorney fee rules, limitations on interest, and foreseeability) and contractual choices allocate the risk of error and often leave plaintiffs undercompensated, discussing the role of contractual and doctrinal mechanisms in distributing losses.

shared_topics.topic: recoverability of consequential damages (lost profits) and foreseeability/remoteness limits
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how damage rules should allow recovery of lost profit and the costs necessary to earn it across varied fact patterns, while Paper B centers on Hadley v. shared_topics.topic: how damage rules create incentives and affect efficiency (efficient breach and breach calculus)

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes separating profit from value and recovering lost surplus plus costs incurred to earn that profit (including reliance-type costs), while Paper B interrogates when lost profits and other post-breach losses should be compensated under traditional doctrine versus a proximate-cause/expectation regime.

shared_topics.topic: predictability and stability of damage awards and doctrinal reform to reduce variability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that Hadley’s bright‑line foreseeability rule disrupts reasonable expectations and efficiency and recommends doctrinal reform (proximate cause, contractual allocation, disclosure) to make outcomes more predictable; Paper B documents historical volatility and then shows an empirically stable differential discount rate that could serve as a benchmark to reduce inequitable variation in awards.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate timing and perspective for measuring losses (ex ante vs ex post valuation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes whether foreseeability should be assessed at contract formation or at breach and argues damages should reflect what a breaching party could reasonably foresee at breach; Paper B necessarily confronts temporal valuation in calculating present value of future lost earnings—forecasting future earnings and returns over the loss period and choosing discounting assumptions that reflect expected conditions over time.

shared_topics.topic: use of economic and empirical analysis to inform legal rules for quantifying damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A deploys law-and-economics reasoning (efficiency, incentive effects) to critique Hadley and to prescribe a damages regime sensitive to the nature of the interest invaded; Paper B performs an empirical economic study (after‑tax rates, occupational stability) to recommend a defensible, economically grounded benchmark for discounting future lost earnings.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:AN ALTERNATIVE PARADIGM FOR VALUING BREACH OF REGISTRATION RIGHTS AND LOSS OF LIQUIDITY

shared_topics.topic: recoverability and valuation of consequential damages for loss of opportunity or liquidity
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grapples with how to value harms that arise from being deprived of the ability to sell (loss of liquidity and lost opportunities to reallocate capital), including mitigation concerns; Paper B analyzes when consequential damages (notably lost profits and foregone opportunities) are recoverable under Hadley and urges a different foreseeability standard that would affect recoverability of such consequential losses.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that the duration of the loss of registration/liquidity is central and proposes damages equal to price decline over the suspension plus hypothetical interest computed over that period, while Paper B focuses on whether foreseeability should be assessed at contract formation or at the time of breach and argues timing affects which losses are foreseeable and thus recoverable.

shared_topics.topic: the incorporation of economic/financial analysis and efficiency considerations into legal damages rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates financial models (Black–Scholes, short-sale costs, synthetic replication) to derive a market-consistent measure of liquidity loss, and Paper B foregrounds efficiency analysis in critiquing Hadley, advocating a proximate-cause regime that aligns liability rules and contractual allocations with economic significance of different harms (lost profits, opportunity costs, etc.).

papers.title: ARTICLE: THE RIGHT TO REQUIRE PERFORMANCE IN INTERNATIONAL SALES: TOWARDS AN INTERNATIONAL INTERPRETATION OF THE VIENNA CONVENTION.
papers.abstract:
The United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods("Sales Convention" or "Convention") is now law.The Convention was drafted by the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law ("UNCITRAL"), a representative body with delegates from thirty-six states, representing all of the regions of the world.UNCITRAL began its work on a Sales Convention in 1968.The full Commission met once a year for two to four weeks until a draft of the Convention was approved by the Commission in 1978.A diplomatic conference of sixty-two statesmeeting in Vienna in 1980 reviewed this draft, made a number of changes, and gave unanimous approval to the Sales Convention.The United States ratified the Convention on December 11, 1986,and the Convention came into force January 1, 1988.
As law, the Sales Convention is unusual in the relative purity of its origins.Throughout the drafting process, the UNCITRAL delegates struggled to overcome the conceptual barriers of their various national legal backgrounds and to discover common solutions to typical problems.  Professor John Honnold, who served as Chief of the United Nations International Trade Law Branch ("Secretariat") and Secretary to the Commission,has described this method of drafting:
The Secretariat studies and proposals laid before the legislative bodydid not lead off in difficult areas with proposed legislative drafts.Instead, the delegates were confronted with what the puzzled civil law delegates called the "common-law case method" -- concrete hypothetical cases calling for decisions as toresultrather than legislativewords. . . .

questions.question: Whether parties to international sales contracts have an enforceable right to require contractual performance (in-kind remedies) rather than only monetary compensation, and how that right should be interpreted uniformly across jurisdictions.

How an international instrument governing cross-border sales should be interpreted to reconcile divergent national legal traditions and produce a common, transnational approach to remedies for breach.

matched_themes: How have historical, geographic, institutional, and transnational influences shaped the evolution and transplantation of contract doctrines and remedies?
How should international instruments reconcile divergent national traditions to create transnational rules on remedies for cross-border sales?

papers.title: ARTICLE: THE ROLE OF FAULT IN CONTRACT LAW: UNCONSCIONABILITY, UNEXPECTED CIRCUMSTANCES, INTERPRETATION, MISTAKE, AND NONPERFORMANCE
papers.abstract:
The Second Restatement of Contracts states: "Contract liability is strict liability. It is an accepted maxim that pacta sunt servanda, contracts are to be kept. The obligor is therefore liable in damages for breach of contract even if he is without fault … ."Similarly, Farnsworth's treatise states that "contract law is, in its essential design, a law of strict liability, and theaccompanying system of remedies operates without regard to fault."These statements, and many others like them, are incorrect.
As a normative matter, fault should be a building block of contract law. One part of the human condition is that we hold many moral values concerning right and wrong. Contract law cannot escape this condition. Accordingly, the basic principle that tells us how to make the best possible rules of contract law - or any law, for that matter - must accommodate not only policy and empirical propositions, but also moral values, including values concerning various types of fault. This principle is as follows:
First. If, but only if, appropriate conditions are satisfied, and subject to appropriate constraints, the law should effectuate the objectives of parties to promissory transactions.
. The rules that determine the conditions to, and the constraints on, the legal effectuation of the objectives of parties to promissory transactions, and the way in which those objectives are to be ascertained, should consist of those rules that best take into account all relevant moral, policy, and empirical propositions.
Based on this principle, it should not be surprising that fault is a pervasive element in contract law. Some areas of contract law, such as unconscionability, are almost entirely fault based. Other areas, including interpretation, include sectors that are fault based in significant part. Still other areas, such as liability for nonperformance, might superficially appear to be based on strict liability, but can best be understood as resting in significant part on fault.
In this Article, I will discuss some important areas of contract law in which fault should and does figure very heavily. The point is not to exhaust the areas in which fault should and does play an important role, but to illustrate how contract law is fault based to a significant extent, and to examine the different ways in which fault figures in contract law.
Fault comes in different flavors and degrees. For contract-law purposes, fault can be divided into the violation of strong moral norms, such as the norm against lying, and the violation of somewhat weaker moral norms - in particular, the norm that an actor should give due regard to the legitimate interests of others. The major type of contract-law fault in the latter category is negligence, or lack of due care. In this Article I will discuss the role of different kinds of fault in five important areas of contract law: unconscionability, unexpected circumstances, interpretation, mistake, and liability for nonperformance.

shared_topics.topic: fault as a factor in choosing remedies and measuring damages (expectation, reliance, restitution, mitigation)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how different damage measures and remedial doctrines should vary with the reason for breach: Paper A explains why courts use expectation, reliance, and restitution differently depending on the type of breach and doctrines (mitigation, foreseeability) that reduce awards, and Paper B treats liability for nonperformance and related remedial choices as significantly informed by different kinds of fault.

shared_topics.topic: use of fault to create incentives and promote efficient contracting behavior
shared_topics.justification: Both works frame rules about fault as incentive tools: Paper A develops an economic account showing how fault-based damage rules induce desirable promisor and promisee behavior, and Paper B connects fault (including negligence and moral fault) to policymaking in contract law, implying that fault-sensitive rules better align conduct with social and moral objectives.

shared_topics.topic: distinguishing types/grades of fault (negligence, opportunism, accidental mistake) and tailoring doctrinal responses
shared_topics.justification: Both papers subdivide breaches or faults and argue for different legal responses: Paper A categorizes breaches that should not have been made, should not be performed, or should not be breached and recommends different measures accordingly, while Paper B distinguishes moral fault and negligence and examines fault's role in specific doctrines (unconscionability, mistake, interpretation, unexpected circumstances, nonperformance).

shared_topics.topic: the proper scope of remedies for breach — compensation versus supra‑compensatory punishment and the role of deterrence

papers.node_id: 43yalejintll143!!ARTICLE: The Role of the State in Contract Law: The Common-Civil Law Divide
papers.title: ARTICLE: The Role of the State in Contract Law: The Common-Civil Law Divide
papers.abstract:
How do the laws of contract differ across jurisdictions? This question has attracted a tremendous amount of interest over time. In fact, for most of the history of comparative law as a discipline, contract law wasthemain area of focus of comparative legal study.This is understandable: internationalcommerce has always triggered significant interest in foreign laws, and contracts are a central tool for economic activity. Perhaps unsurprisingly, contract law has also been an area where harmonization and unification efforts have proliferated, though with varying degrees of success.
The vast majority of existing works on comparative contract law are doctrinal in nature, reporting differences and similarities between the legal rules of various countries.Some studies also go beyond mere description to undertake normative analyses, specifically addressing whether the legal regime of a given jurisdiction is superior, inferior, or equally desirable to those prevailing elsewhere, in view of different histories, cultures, and preferences. However, even the best "functional" analyses, exemplified by the seminal work of Konrad Zweigert and Hein Kotz, operate primarily at the level of legal doctrine, with comparatively little focus on the economic and political environment.
The result is that, even if we have learned a great deal abouthowcontract law differs across jurisdictions, we still know comparatively little aboutwhyandso what. The observed differences in the various dimensions of contract law are generally treated as isolated, unrelated, and arbitrary--mostly the product of serendipitous developments in legal history.Still lacking are broader accounts of how the existing distinctions relate to one another, as well as to other aspects of the legal, economic, and political systems.Interestingly,this gap in comparative contract law stands in sharp contrast to the state of the art in other areas of comparative study--such as comparative corporate governance and comparative constitutional law--where the various rules and doctrines are increasingly examined jointly and in functional terms, in view of the underlying economic and political structures.
This Article undertakes to examine in a coordinated manner some of the central--and persisting--doctrinal distinctions in the laws of contract of common and civil law jurisdictions. The classification of legal systems into the legal families of common law and civil law has long played a central role in comparative law scholarship and, more recently, also in the economic literature, which has posited a strong connection between legal traditions and various economic outcomes.While the importance and continued vitality of legal family categorizations have come under attack, they continue to play a useful descriptive and didactic role in broadly mapping the legal regimes of multiple jurisdictions.
The analysis here will simultaneously examine the distinctions between the common and civil law of contracts that have received the lion's share of attention in both scholarly and practical commentary.These are:(i) The stronger duty of good faith in the civil law;(ii) The greater number of mandatory contract rules in the civil law;(iii) The greater intervention in the interpretation and revision of contract terms in the civil law;(iv) The greater enforcement of penalty clauses in the civil law;(v) The greater availability of specific performance in the civil law; and(vi) The greater availability of contract discharge through a "fresh start" in bankruptcy in the common law.At first sight, it is hard to make sense of these distinctions. The presence of (i) a broader duty of good faith, (ii) more mandatory rules, and (iii) the greater judicial rewriting of contract terms in civil law jurisdictions may lead one to conclude that common law systems provide a stronger role for freedom of contract than do civil law systems--which is indeed a common stereotype in business practice.Yet this view is not without difficulties. If the common law is truly devoted to sanctity of contract, why does it (iv) deny enforcement to penalty clauses freely agreed by the parties, (v) refuse to grant specific performance as a matter of right (even if the parties specifically choose this remedy), and (vi) more easily discharge contracts in bankruptcy proceedings?
(i) The stronger duty of good faith in the civil law;(ii) The greater number of mandatory contract rules in the civil law;(iii) The greater intervention in the interpretation and revision of contract terms in the civil law;(iv) The greater enforcement of penalty clauses in the civil law;(v) The greater availability of specific performance in the civil law; and(vi) The greater availability of contract discharge through a "fresh start" in bankruptcy in the common law.
This Article suggests that these differences can be explained by the distinct roles of the State in shaping contract law in common and civil law systems. In civil law systems, the State tends to play a stronger part in all respects.On the one hand, the State, through legislatures and courts, goes further in providing and policing the substantive terms of the agreement to ensure compliance with broader social values and objectives. On the other hand, once the contract passes muster under this test, the State is also willing to sanction breaches with more severe consequences: namely, by permitting the enforcement of penalty clauses, granting specific performance, and making it more difficult to discharge contractual obligations in bankruptcy proceedings.
Common law systems, by contrast, embrace the opposite approach: legislatures and courts are less willing both to meddle with the terms of the contract and to offer relief to the aggrieved party if voluntary performance is not forthcoming. Under Ian Macneil's conceptualization of the two dimensionsof freedom of contract, the common law favors only a narrow version of it, in the sense of "freedom from restraint" in "making or receiving promises."It is the civil law that embraces a stronger version of the other side of freedom of contract, the "power of contract," which consists in the ability to secure legal sanctions for non-performance.
So how does this overarching pattern relate to prevailing conceptions about common and civil law systems more generally? The character of contract law appears to map the findings of the burgeoning literature on the role of the State across legal traditions, with common law systems boasting moreliberal, and civil law systems moreinterventionist, arrangements of contract law and enforcement.It is, however, partly in tension with the prevailing notion that the common law necessarily places greater value on--and provides stronger enforcement to-private contracting schemes.
Indeed, once the more modest remedies for breach of contract are taken into account, State support to private contracts in common law jurisdictions looks far more fragile. In other words, the common law's apparent intervention to restrict the remedies available for breach of contract effectively results in a more limited use of the State's coercive powers in contract enforcement.To put it differently, the common law is not so much supportive of private contracts as it is conducive to private ordering, including with respect to mechanisms for the enforcement of contractual obligations.
At a high level of generality, the different roles of the State in (i) policing the terms of the contract and (ii) calibrating the remedies for non-performance can be viewed as alternative mechanisms to mitigate the effects of harsh contractual commitments. These different approaches are unlikely to guarantee identical results. Yet the analysis offered here highlights how substantive control of contract terms and discharge in bankruptcy can serve as alternative mechanisms for allocating contract risk and mitigating the effects of harsh bargains--a crucial relationship that has been largely overlooked by the existing literature. In this context, the ultimate outcomes in both systems are closer than one would anticipate by focusing on individual rules or styles of State intervention in isolation.
Ascertaining the practical import of these doctrinal differences requires further investigation, including a greater focus on "the law in action." This would be a fruitful area for future research. Although contract institutions play a central role in institutional economics, the existing studies on the subject say very little about legal rules and doctrines--the stuff one learns in law school. In contrast to early works on "law and finance," which examined the effects ofparticular legal rules of corporate and bankruptcy law,studies on contract institutions rely exclusively on measures of procedure (i.e., the time, cost, and number of procedures necessary to enforce a contract).The result is that the existing literature on institutional economics does not have much to say about the comparative contours and economic impact of contract law rules and doctrines; in other words, it is largely "institution free."Given the existence of formal variation in the substance of contract laws, however, it seems premature to dismiss their relevance without proper inquiry.
The exposition that follows proceeds in four parts. Part I surveys the core doctrinal differences between civil and common law traditions in the area of contract law and enforcement, as well as the form of State involvement that they implicate. Part II explores the extent to which the diverse approaches of the State to private agreements across legal traditions entail real discrepancies or imply functional substitution. Part III then outlines the general distinctions between common law and civil law jurisdictions as they pertain to the role of the State, and examines how the existing literature on institutional economics has neglected the study of contract law. This Article concludes by reflecting on the future of comparative contract law.

questions.question: Whether variation in the degree and form of State involvement in shaping and policing private contracts across legal systems explains systematic cross-jurisdictional differences in contract rules and remedies.

Whether greater State control over contract substance combined with stronger judicial remedies in some legal systems functionally substitutes for weaker State control combined with greater private ordering in others, yielding similar allocations of contractual risk.
Whether the doctrinal differences in contract law across legal traditions produce measurable differences in contracting behavior and economic outcomes in practice (the 'law in action').

matched_themes: Should courts allow punitive or other extracompensatory damages for willful or abusive contract breaches, and what are the efficiency and fairness trade-offs?
How should courts treat pre-agreed breach payments and liquidated damages clauses (enforce, reform, apportion, or void)?
To what extent does variation in state involvement across legal systems explain cross-jurisdictional differences in contract rules and remedies?
How should default liability rules interact with parties' freedom to allocate risks by contract and duties of disclosure to achieve efficient and fair risk allocation?
Do courts actually prefer monetary damages over specific (in-kind) remedies, or do they grant specific relief except when independent reasons exist to deny it?
Are civil-law systems less receptive than common-law systems to permitting breaches that increase overall welfare when compensation is possible?
When should courts order specific performance (in-kind relief) versus awarding monetary damages?
Should the promisor or the promisee have the default right to choose between performance and payment to achieve allocative efficiency?
Should parties be presumptively permitted to contractually specify nonstandard damage remedies, or should courts retain authority to impose defaults?
How should courts treat and enforce stipulated remedies (liquidated damages clauses) versus substituting judicial remedies?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
Should courts police and limit supracompensatory contractual remedies (penalty-like clauses), or does allowing parties to contract for such terms respect autonomy and promote efficient contracting?

Should contractual clauses that impose predetermined monetary payments for breach be treated as punitive (unenforceable) or as enforceable measures of compensation, and what factors predict courts' enforcement decisions?
When is an indirect remedy (one that induces self-compliance) preferable to a direct remedy that delivers the outcome?
Should courts more readily grant equitable relief to compel performance when monetary damages undercompensate and public interests are implicated?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 93valrev59!!ARTICLE: THE MISSING INTEREST: RESTORATION OF THE CONTRACTUAL EQUIVALENCE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE MISSING INTEREST: RESTORATION OF THE CONTRACTUAL EQUIVALENCE

shared_topics.topic: the role and calibration of remedies in contract law (which remedies are available and how they are shaped by legal systems)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how common and civil law systems differ in calibrating remedies (e.g., enforcement of penalty clauses, specific performance, discharge in bankruptcy) as part of the State's approach to contract law; Paper B closely examines the doctrinal space of remedies by identifying a previously overlooked remedial goal (the restoration interest) and argues for expanding the set of remedies courts should routinely award.

shared_topics.topic: specific performance and monetary reliefs (coherence and availability of equitable and monetary awards)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts the greater availability of specific performance and enforcement of penalty clauses in civil law with the common law's more limited relief; Paper B interrogates cases where courts award specific performance together with monetary adjustments (interest, price reductions) and explains these through the restoration-of-equivalence concept.

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations and theories justifying remedial rules (will theory, efficiency, corrective/distributive justice, and the State's role)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates differences in remedial doctrines within broader accounts of the State's role and policy orientations across legal families (liberal vs interventionist) and touches on functional consequences; Paper B evaluates the restoration interest under multiple normative theories (will theory, economic efficiency, corrective and distributive justice) to justify expanding remedial doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: remedies as mechanisms for allocating contract risk and mitigating harsh bargains
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that substantive control of contract terms and the calibration of remedies (including bankruptcy discharge) are alternative mechanisms to mitigate harsh contractual commitments across systems; Paper B contends that restoration remedies reallocate losses and incentives in cases of partial, defective, or delayed performance, thereby mitigating harsh outcomes and sometimes doing so more efficiently.

shared_topics.topic: limits of existing conceptual frameworks in contract scholarship and the need to incorporate doctrinal realities
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques institutional economics and comparative literature for being 'institution free' and neglecting substantive doctrinal variation in contract law; Paper B criticizes the dominance of Fuller and Perdue's tripartite remedy taxonomy as incomplete and introduces the restoration interest to better account for observed remedial practice.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: What Efficiency Demands: The Efficient Performance Hypothesis Defended

shared_topics.topic: the economic role of specific performance as a contract remedy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes specific performance as an economic instrument that proxies party valuations under competing entitlement regimes (efficient breach vs efficient performance) and as one of several remedies (alongside expectation damages and disgorgement) that can be calibrated to produce efficient allocations; Paper B highlights that civil law jurisdictions more readily grant specific performance and treats its availability as a key doctrinal distinction that interacts with the State's role in shaping contractual outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: how assignment of legal entitlements or powers to perform/breach affects allocation and incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the contrast between giving the promisor the legal right to choose nonperformance (efficient breach) versus giving the promisee that power (efficient performance) and shows how this assignment changes who makes the allocative decision; Paper B frames a related distinction as the civil-law 'power of contract' versus the common-law 'freedom from restraint,' describing how differences in who can secure sanctions or performance shape enforcement and bargaining outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between remedies/rules and broader institutional/state structures in mitigating harsh bargains
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that remedies (expectation damages, disgorgement, specific performance) operate economically to encourage efficient allocations but leaves the final choice empirically contingent and sensitive to litigation, bargaining, and transaction costs; Paper B argues that common vs civil law differences in mandatory rules, penalty enforcement, specific performance, and bankruptcy discharge reflect alternative ways the State calibrates rules and remedies to mitigate harsh contractual commitments and allocate contract risk.

shared_topics.topic: the need for empirical or 'law in action' analysis to resolve theoretical indeterminacy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A repeatedly stresses that analytical equivalence between efficient breach and efficient performance leaves the tie-breaker to empirical facts (transaction costs, market structure, judicial costs) and expresses skepticism about resolving it purely analytically; Paper B likewise calls for greater focus on the law in action and empirical investigation to ascertain the practical import of doctrinal differences across legal families.

shared_topics.topic: judicial intervention in contract terms and its economic consequences for private ordering
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses courts' decision rules and the costs of judicial determination as factors that shape which remedial regime promotes allocative efficiency and gives examples of court-imposed procedures to achieve efficient allocation; Paper B documents that civil-law judges intervene more in interpreting and revising contract terms and analyzes how that judicial intervention functions as an alternative to other institutional mechanisms for addressing harsh or inefficient bargains.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83lawcontempprob151!!ARTICLE: BLACK MARKETS AND THE EXCHANGE STRUCTURE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BLACK MARKETS AND THE EXCHANGE STRUCTURE

shared_topics.topic: the role of the state in structuring and policing private exchanges
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how civil and common law systems differ in the degree and manners in which legislatures and courts police contract terms and enforce bargains, while Paper B argues that law (through officials and legal rules) is the formative force that creates, delimits, and preserves (or disables) exchange relationships and black markets.

shared_topics.topic: legal disabilities versus remedial sanctions as instruments of regulation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares substantive doctrinal choices (mandatory rules, judicial revision, enforcement of penalty clauses, specific performance, bankruptcy discharge) as ways the State calibrates remedies and constraints on contracts, and Paper B emphasizes that legal 'disabilities' (voiding, unenforceability) are primary tools to prevent transgressive exchanges while penalties ('kickers') are secondary deterrents.

shared_topics.topic: the balance between private ordering and state intervention in market transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that common law favors private ordering and limited State meddling while civil law affords stronger State support and intervention for enforcing bargains, and Paper B examines how many exchanges occur without law, how private ordering often governs exchange, and how/state intervention (when used) reshapes or restrains those private orders.

shared_topics.topic: how law preserves or reshapes established exchange norms/transaction structures
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames doctrinal differences as alternative mechanisms (policing terms vs remedial calibration) to mitigate harsh bargains and allocate contract risk, and Paper B develops the idea that criminalization, disabilities, civil penalties, and private law are deployed to preserve an established transaction structure and prevent conversions of exchange norms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 38sandiegolrev137!!SYMPOSIUM: "W(H)ITHER THE RELIANCE INTEREST?"+:Finding Fault with Wonnell's "Two Contractual Wrongs"
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: "W(H)ITHER THE RELIANCE INTEREST?"+:Finding Fault with Wonnell's "Two Contractual Wrongs"

shared_topics.topic: how the choice of remedy (expectation vs reliance vs specific performance/penalties) implements policy goals like deterrence and reliance protection
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes expectation and reliance damages in moral and economic terms—expectation as deterrence of breach vs reliance as deterrence of wrongful contracting—while Paper B compares how civil and common law systems employ remedies (specific performance, penalty clauses, limited damages) to achieve social and contractual policy objectives.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts and the State in calibrating contractual remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that courts can and should make fault-based distinctions when selecting remedies for breach, whereas Paper B locates such calibration within broader institutional differences, showing how legislatures and courts in civil and common law systems vary in policing terms and enforcing remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the idea that remedies and substantive control of contract terms are alternative or complementary mechanisms for mitigating harsh bargains and allocating contract risk
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats reliance remedies as a response to wrongful contracting conduct (affecting how contracts are enforced), and Paper B explicitly argues that substantive policing of terms and tougher remedies in civil law can functionally substitute for looser substantive rules and milder remedies in common law.

shared_topics.topic: whether contract law should adopt a single, unitary remedial theory or a pluralistic, fault-sensitive regime
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the prevailing yearning for a unitary remedial interest and advocates embracing a fault-based (reason-for-breach) remedial regime; Paper B documents divergent doctrinal systems and implicitly supports pluralized institutional approaches by showing how different traditions distribute regulation between terms and remedies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 12jempiricallegalstud29!!ARTICLE: Damages Versus Specific Performance: Lessons from Commercial Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Damages Versus Specific Performance: Lessons from Commercial Contracts

shared_topics.topic: availability and use of specific performance as a contract remedy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A identifies greater judicial willingness to award specific performance in civil-law systems versus the common-law preference for damages, while Paper B empirically analyzes how sophisticated parties actually include (or omit) clauses seeking specific performance in commercial contracts.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules and judicial enforcement shape private contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A attributes cross‑jurisdictional doctrinal differences to distinct roles of the State in policing terms and calibrating remedies, and Paper B examines the black‑letter rule (courts' preference for damages) and how that background enforcement regime influences parties' ex ante contract choices.

shared_topics.topic: parties' ability to contract around default remedial rules and the tension with mandatory law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how civil law's mandatory rules limit private ordering while common law allows more freedom (but with weaker remedies), and Paper B studies explicit contractual attempts to opt into specific performance (i.e., to alter the default remedial regime) and the prevalence of such opt‑outs across contract types.

shared_topics.topic: the value of empirical, 'law in action' study of contract doctrines and terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A calls for more empirical research to assess the practical import of doctrinal differences, and Paper B supplies such empirical evidence by analyzing thousands of real commercial contracts to reveal how remedy rules operate in practice.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 76marqlrev519!!ARTICLE: Divorce Law: Exclusions and Disproportionate Divisions of Marital Estate
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Divorce Law: Exclusions and Disproportionate Divisions of Marital Estate

shared_topics.topic: the role of the State in regulating private ordering and economic entitlements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how Wisconsin statutory law and courts determine which assets (e.g., gifts and inheritances) are excluded from the marital estate and how courts may order disproportionate divisions, while Paper B theorizes how legislatures and courts in common and civil law systems shape contract terms, policing, and remedies—both interrogating how state institutions allocate and enforce private rights.

shared_topics.topic: mandatory rules versus private autonomy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines statutory exclusions and limits on how spouses can privately allocate or retain property at divorce, and Paper B compares the greater prevalence of mandatory contract rules in civil law with the common law's different approach—both papers engage with when the law imposes nonwaivable rules that constrain private arrangements.

shared_topics.topic: judicial intervention to revise economic allocations or obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers judicial authority to order disproportionate divisions of the marital estate (departing from equal division) under the statute, and Paper B analyzes judicial intervention in interpreting, revising, or enforcing contract terms (including rewriting provisions and calibrating remedies), so both address courts' power to adjust private bargains for perceived fairness or policy reasons.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal classifications produce distributive/economic effects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the doctrinal label of assets (gift, inheritance, marital property) and how that classification affects division on divorce, while Paper B shows how doctrinal distinctions in contract law (e.g., enforceability of penalty clauses, availability of specific performance, discharge rules) change parties' economic risks and outcomes—both trace how legal categories shape material distributions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 64hastingslj679!!Article: Consenting Under Stress
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Consenting Under Stress

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal mechanisms for responding to impaired consent and unequal bargaining power
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how doctrines like duress, unconscionability, and undue influence fail or could be retooled to address consent impaired by severe stress, while Paper B examines doctrinal differences (mandatory rules, good faith, judicial revision) as mechanisms civil and common law systems use to curb harsh bargains and address asymmetric power in contracting.

shared_topics.topic: the proper role of the state and courts in policing contracts versus preserving freedom of contract
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for greater judicial attention and potential relief when stress undermines consent, challenging laissez-faire enforcement, and Paper B explains how common and civil law traditions embody different state intervention levels—both engage the question of when and how courts/state should intervene to restrain or enforce private bargains.

shared_topics.topic: incorporating non-legal social science and empirical inquiry into contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws on biology, neuroscience, psychology, and sociology to ground legal assessments of stressed consent, while Paper B urges incorporation of economic, political, and empirical 'law in action' analysis to understand how contract rules function in practice; both advocate interdisciplinary evidence to inform doctrine and policy.

shared_topics.topic: diagnosing doctrinal gaps and proposing reforms or tools for adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes a four‑element analytical framework and practical guidance for judges to assess stress-based consent claims, and Paper B calls for coordinated comparative analysis and further empirical work to rethink doctrinal distinctions and suggest functional substitutes—each paper therefore identifies shortcomings in current doctrine and urges concrete reform and better judicial tools.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2004wislrev507!!SYMPOSIUM: PROMISSORY FRAUD WITHOUT BREACH
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: PROMISSORY FRAUD WITHOUT BREACH

shared_topics.topic: how the State's choice of remedies and sanctions determines the practical force of promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares how civil and common law systems allocate remedies (specific performance, enforcement of penalty clauses, ease of discharge in bankruptcy) and shows that these choices shape how strongly the State enforces private contracts; Paper B analyzes promissory fraud as a route to compensatory, punitive, and even criminal sanctions for insincere promises, showing how non-contractual remedies can strengthen deterrence against false promises.

shared_topics.topic: the promisor's mental state at formation (good faith vs insincere promise) as a doctrinal pivot
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights differences in the duty of good faith across legal families and how courts police contractual intent and fairness, while Paper B centers on promissory misrepresentations—false statements about present intent—and develops doctrine for when an asserted intent can be treated as a lie.

shared_topics.topic: when absence of contract enforcement should be supplemented by tort or fraud doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores how states can choose between policing substantive terms and calibrating remedies (including tolerating greater private ordering), raising the question of other legal backstops for abusive bargains; Paper B argues promissory fraud can and should provide liability in many situations where contract remedies are unavailable or deliberately suspended.

shared_topics.topic: the idea that different legal rules or doctrines can functionally substitute to mitigate harsh bargains or allocate contract risk
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that substantive control of contract terms, remedial regimes, and bankruptcy discharge are alternative mechanisms for addressing oppressive commitments across legal traditions; Paper B shows promissory fraud operates as a functional substitute to contract enforcement—permitting freedom from contract while still deterring and remedying the worst instances of insincere promising.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 33connlrev181!!ARTICLE: The Boundaries of Extracompensatory Relief for Abusive Breach of Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Boundaries of Extracompensatory Relief for Abusive Breach of Contract

shared_topics.topic: how institutional form (legislation vs common law) shapes remedies for breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the viability of extracompensatory responses to abusive breach often depends on the process of implementation—legislative solutions can better achieve severability than ad hoc common-law development—while Paper B centrally analyzes how the differing roles of legislatures and courts in civil and common law systems produce divergent remedial regimes for contract breaches.

shared_topics.topic: calibration and limits of remedies for breach (punitive/extracompensatory versus traditional remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates when and why courts might (or should not) award extracompensatory/punitive damages for certain breaches, and Paper B compares how civil and common law systems formally permit or restrict remedial options (e.g., enforcement of penalty clauses, specific performance, discharge in bankruptcy), both engaging with where and why the law draws remedial boundaries.

shared_topics.topic: differential treatment of contract categories to confine heightened sanctions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a severability principle holding that extracompensatory punishments are viable only when keyed to particular transaction types (e.g., insurance), and Paper B shows that legal systems systematically treat classes of contracts differently (through mandatory rules, good faith duties, and remedial availability), both addressing targeted, category-based responses to contractual problems.

shared_topics.topic: the trade-off between predictability/facilitating exchange and sanctioning abusive conduct
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the central tension between stabilizing the ‘exit price’ of contracts to encourage trade and imposing disincentives for abusive breach, while Paper B assesses how varying degrees of State intervention (and different remedial regimes) reflect alternative mechanisms to mitigate harsh bargains without undermining contractual freedom and market ordering.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 55amulrev87!!ARTICLE:CO-INVEST AT YOUR OWN RISK: AN EXPLORATION OF POTENTIAL REMEDIAL THEORIES FOR BREACHES OF RIGHTS OF FIRST REFUSAL IN THE VENTURE CAPITAL CONTEXT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:CO-INVEST AT YOUR OWN RISK: AN EXPLORATION OF POTENTIAL REMEDIAL THEORIES FOR BREACHES OF RIGHTS OF FIRST REFUSAL IN THE VENTURE CAPITAL CONTEXT

shared_topics.topic: availability and enforcement of specific contractual remedies (specific performance, penalties/liquidated damages, expectation damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares how common‑law and civil‑law systems differ in granting specific performance and enforcing penalty clauses, while Paper B analyzes which remedies (conversion, specific performance, expectation damages) fit breaches of rights of first refusal in venture capital and advocates standardized liquidated damages clauses.

shared_topics.topic: use of remedies and contract design to allocate risk and mitigate harsh bargains
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that differences in policing contract terms and calibrating remedies function as alternative mechanisms to mitigate harsh contractual commitments, and Paper B develops a remedial framework (including liquidated damages) that allocates monitoring costs and investment risk between co‑investors and managers.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between private ordering (reputation, market norms) and legal enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts common‑law tendencies toward private ordering with civil‑law state intervention in enforcing contracts, while Paper B examines the role of reputation as an industry enforcement mechanism in venture capital and how formal legal remedies should interact with that private enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: economic/agency‑based explanations for why contract rules and remedies are chosen
shared_topics.justification: Paper A calls for comparative contract doctrine to be explained in light of economic and political structures rather than doctrinal isolation, and Paper B applies agency theory of monitoring costs to justify particular remedial outcomes for breaches of co‑investment agreements.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 105michlrev559!!ARTICLE: THE DISGORGEMENT INTEREST IN CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE DISGORGEMENT INTEREST IN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: design and normative justification of remedies for breach (expectation, restitution, disgorgement, specific performance, penalties)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that contract law should recognize the disgorgement interest alongside expectation and reliance remedies and critiques doctrinal and normative bases for its exclusion, while Paper B systematically compares which remedies (including specific performance and enforceable penalties) are available across common and civil law systems and explains how these doctrinal choices reflect different regulatory philosophies.

shared_topics.topic: how remedies shape incentives and allocate contract risk (including the efficient-breach/indifference critique)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how perfect disgorgement would make a promisor indifferent between performance and breach and critiques the efficient-breach rationale for denying disgorgement; Paper B examines how different remedy regimes (availability of specific performance, penalty enforcement, and bankruptcy discharge) functionally allocate risk and mitigate harsh bargains across legal traditions.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts, restatements, and the State in creating and enforcing contract doctrines and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces how the Restatement, case law, and doctrinal choices affected the omission of disgorgement and considers judicial decisions that do recognize promisor-gain remedies, whereas Paper B locates major doctrinal differences in contract law within broader patterns of state and judicial intervention across common and civil law systems.

shared_topics.topic: availability and limits of non-compensatory or gain-based relief (disgorgement, penalty clauses, and specific performance as alternative sanctions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on disgorgement as a gain-based remedy and discusses when promisor gains should be apportioned or disgorged, and Paper B engages substantively with other non-compensatory remedies—penalty clauses and specific performance—comparing their enforcement and limits across legal families.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 36jlegalstud379!!ARTICLE: Sanctions by Social Norms and the Law: Substitutes or Complements?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Sanctions by Social Norms and the Law: Substitutes or Complements?

shared_topics.topic: whether formal law and informal social norms act as substitutes or complements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A builds a formal model showing conditions (e.g., high social connectedness vs low) under which social norms and law either substitute for or complement one another; Paper B frames civil- vs common-law choices as alternative or complementary modes of state involvement that can substitute for or reinforce private ordering in contract law.

shared_topics.topic: how state design of enforcement and remedial rules shapes private ordering and contracting outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models the government as a principal that designs costly formal rules which interact with community-imposed norms to influence agents' behavior; Paper B analyzes how legislatures and courts (through mandatory rules, good-faith duties, remedies, and bankruptcy discharge) shape the extent and form of private contracting and enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: welfare trade-offs of relying on social norms versus legal intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly compares social-welfare outcomes under reliance on internal/external social sanctions versus costly legal sanctions and shows when law increases welfare; Paper B discusses how state policing of terms and calibrating remedies serve to mitigate harsh bargains and allocate contract risk, with implications for welfare and the desirability of intervention.

shared_topics.topic: monitoring, observability, and sanctioning mechanisms for compliance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes social connectedness and observability as enabling external social sanctions and internalized guilt, affecting norm compliance; Paper B treats state monitoring and judicial enforcement (policing contract terms and applying remedies) as an alternative monitoring-sanctioning infrastructure that affects contractual compliance.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1551!!ARTICLE: COULD BREACH OF CONTRACT BE IMMORAL?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: COULD BREACH OF CONTRACT BE IMMORAL?

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate remedies for breach of contract (expectation, punitive, specific performance, penalty clauses)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether contract law's remedies—especially the bar on punitive damages versus expectation damages—correctly track moral blameworthiness for breach; Paper B systematically compares how common and civil law traditions allocate remedies (enforcement of penalty clauses, availability of specific performance) and how those choices reflect different state roles.

shared_topics.topic: interpretation of incomplete contracts and the role of background law/gap‑filling in creating duties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on Shavell's claim that in incomplete contracts background gap‑filling law shows what parties would have agreed and thus whether a promissory breach is immoral; Paper B examines judicial intervention in interpretation and revision of contract terms across legal families, i.e., how courts and law fill gaps and police terms.

shared_topics.topic: normative justifications for contract doctrines—morality versus policy (state objectives, social values, economic efficiency)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A challenges the efficiency‑breach rationale on moral grounds, arguing law should not embody justifications that encourage immoral conduct; Paper B investigates how civil and common law systems reflect distinct normative choices about state intervention, social values, and economic policy in shaping contract rules and enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: tension between private ordering/freedom of contract and state enforcement/intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises concerns about whether legal rules (like barring punitive damages) improperly permit or encourage behavior that conflicts with promissory morality and private expectations; Paper B analyzes how common law favors private ordering and limited state coercion while civil law provides stronger state policing and enforcement, highlighting alternative mechanisms for managing harsh bargains.
