compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: Intentions, Guilt and Social Interactions

shared_topics.topic: the role of intentions (good faith/sincerity) in determining outcomes and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the doctrinal duty of good faith in civil law and how parties' states of mind shape judges' willingness to police contracts, while Paper B models how perceived sincerity or guilt (intentions) alters receivers' payoffs and their acceptance of offers in social and legal contexts.

shared_topics.topic: how enforcement mechanisms and sanction structures affect willingness to perform or accept exchanges
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares remedies (penalty clauses, specific performance, bankruptcy discharge) and shows how different sanctioning regimes allocate contract risk, and Paper B shows how expectations about consequences of insincere behavior (guilt, reputational loss) influence whether mutually beneficial trades occur.

shared_topics.topic: state intervention versus private ordering as alternative ways to secure cooperation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts stronger state policing of contract terms in civil law with common-law reliance on private ordering, and Paper B examines when informal norms (sincerity, beliefs) support or undermine voluntary social cooperation absent formal enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: the need to integrate belief-dependent preferences and doctrinal/legal detail into economic models of exchange
shared_topics.justification: Paper A calls for institutional economics to incorporate substantive contract doctrines rather than procedure-only measures, and Paper B employs psychological game theory and interdependent-type preferences to formally capture how beliefs about others' motives affect strategic interaction.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 78mdlrev147!!ARTICLE: THE ERROR THEORY OF CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE ERROR THEORY OF CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: availability and role of specific performance versus damages as the default remedy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A presents empirical evidence about lay beliefs regarding whether specific performance or damages is the typical remedy and analyzes how mistaken beliefs about remedies affect consent-based justifications; Paper B directly compares common- and civil-law systems on the greater availability of specific performance in civil law and the common-law reluctance to grant it, treating remedial regimes as a central doctrinal distinction.

shared_topics.topic: the State's role in policing substantive contract terms and the regulation of boilerplate/standardized terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that background legal rules and implicit terms (and the regulation of boilerplate content) matter to whether parties actually consent, urging regulatory responses to unfair standardized terms; Paper B analyzes how civil-law and common-law systems differ in legislative and judicial policing of contract substance (mandatory rules, judicial revision, enforcement of penalty clauses), framing these as contrasting modes of State involvement.

shared_topics.topic: the need for empirical 'law in action' study of contract doctrines and their practical effects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A builds and reports empirical studies about lay beliefs of contract formation and remedies to ground doctrinal and normative claims; Paper B calls for more empirical investigation of how doctrinal differences operate in practice and criticizes comparative work for neglecting the economic and social consequences of substantive contract rules.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy of autonomy/consent-based justifications versus alternative normative foundations for contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly challenges promise/consent-based (autonomy) theories of contract in light of widespread legal ignorance and argues for turning to second-best or alternative normative accounts (e.g., consequentialist or regulatory approaches); Paper B situates doctrinal differences in terms of differing conceptions of freedom of contract and the State's role, engaging with whether private ordering or State intervention better justifies particular contract regimes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45umemlrev59!!Article: Justice and Harsh Results: Beyond Individualism and Collectivism in Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Justice and Harsh Results: Beyond Individualism and Collectivism in Contracts

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts and the State in policing and enforcing contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes systemic differences between civil and common law in how legislatures and courts police substantive contract terms and enforce performance, while Paper B debates whether courts should intervene to mitigate harsh contractual results or strictly enforce agreed terms in individual cases like Jacob & Youngs.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between party autonomy (freedom of contract) and substantive fairness/social values
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames common law as privileging a narrower freedom-from-restraint and civil law as enabling state-backed power to secure performance, and Paper B explicitly contrasts individualist (autonomy) and collectivist (social values) approaches—advocating a Thomist balance that vindicates both promise-keeping and substantive fairness.

shared_topics.topic: judicial interpretation, revision, or mitigation of contract terms to avoid harsh outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A identifies greater judicial rewriting and intervention in contract terms in civil law systems as a doctrinal distinction, while Paper B centers on whether judges should reinterpret or soften application of contract terms (as in Cardozo's Jacob & Youngs opinion) to avert disproportionate results.

shared_topics.topic: which remedies or sanctions for breach are appropriate and enforceable
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares doctrines such as enforcement of penalty clauses, availability of specific performance, and bankruptcy discharge across legal families, and Paper B interrogates the justice of withholding payment or enforcing performance in response to trivial breaches, using Jacob & Youngs to assess appropriate remedies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 17geomasonlrev483!!ARTICLE: HARM, AMBIGUITY, AND THE REGULATION OF ILLEGAL CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: HARM, AMBIGUITY, AND THE REGULATION OF ILLEGAL CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: how remedies function as instruments of deterrence and incentive alignment
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how remedies (non-enforcement, restitution, etc.) affect ex ante contracting incentives and the social costs of over- and under-deterrence, and Paper B treats remedies (and their availability) as alternative state mechanisms to mitigate harsh bargains and allocate contractual risk across legal families.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between freedom of contract/private ordering and mandatory legal constraints
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that illegal-contract doctrines create an immutable default that parties cannot opt out of and can chill beneficial contracting, whereas Paper B contrasts common-law private-ordering approaches with civil-law mandatory rules and judicial intervention, exploring tradeoffs between laissez-faire contracting and state-imposed limits.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal design and legal uncertainty affect parties' ex ante contracting decisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds ambiguity about whether a contract is illegal and how that uncertainty amplifies overdeterrence, and Paper B emphasizes the need to study the 'law in action'—how different substantive doctrines and institutional designs across jurisdictions actually influence contracting behavior and outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 117michlrev885!!ARTICLE: Moral Diversity and Efficient Breach
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Moral Diversity and Efficient Breach

shared_topics.topic: comparative availability and role of remedies (specific performance, expectation damages, penalty/liquidated damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A systematically contrasts common- and civil-law regimes' approaches to remedies—noting differences in enforcement of penalty clauses, availability of specific performance, and bankruptcy discharge—while Paper B analyzes how remedies (expectation damages, liquidated-damage clauses, and the prospect of specific performance) affect parties' incentives to perform or efficiently breach and evaluates these remedies as policy tools.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules and state intervention shape contracting behavior and outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that differing degrees of State involvement (policing contract terms vs calibrating remedies) explain doctrinal contrasts across legal families, and Paper B shows how the existing legal framework and contract language (and proposed mandated clauses) alter parties' moral perceptions and choices, influencing aggregate economic outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: mandatory contract terms versus freedom of contract
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that civil-law systems feature more mandatory contract rules and judicial revision whereas common-law systems favor private ordering, and Paper B proposes a regulatory intervention—a mandatory exit clause—to change the substantive terms of contracts so as to align moral beliefs and induce efficient breaches.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between contract doctrine and economic efficiency/distributional consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A calls for study of how doctrinal differences in contract law affect economic outcomes and institutional economics, and Paper B empirically and normatively examines how current doctrines produce Pareto-inefficient behavior and distributional harms between moralist individuals and Holmesian firms, proposing doctrinal/regulatory fixes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 55amulrev87!!ARTICLE:CO-INVEST AT YOUR OWN RISK: AN EXPLORATION OF POTENTIAL REMEDIAL THEORIES FOR BREACHES OF RIGHTS OF FIRST REFUSAL IN THE VENTURE CAPITAL CONTEXT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:CO-INVEST AT YOUR OWN RISK: AN EXPLORATION OF POTENTIAL REMEDIAL THEORIES FOR BREACHES OF RIGHTS OF FIRST REFUSAL IN THE VENTURE CAPITAL CONTEXT

papers.title: ARTICLE: THE STRUCTURE OF JUDICIAL ADMINISTRATION AND THE DEVELOPMENT OF CONTRACT LAW IN SEVENTEENTH-CENTURY ENGLAND Copyright © 1983 by Clinton W. Francis.
papers.abstract:
The aim of this Article is to demonstrate the importance of considerations of judicial administration in the development of the common law of contract in preindustrial seventeenth-century England.  These administrative problems arose from an attempt to accommodate the rapidly increasing amounts of contract litigation within the existing common law court structure, a structure held constant by those who had vested financial and professional interests in ensuring that the two benches -- the Common Pleas and King's Bench -- retained the lion's share of important litigation within the realm.
Most treatises on the early common law of contract can be described as "internal" historiographies.They are almost universally concerned with doctrinal legal history and primarily offer a "description" rather than a "thesis." They either ignore or openly avoid analysis of causation in legal development,or they attempt to explain contract law as a symptom of the "retarded intellectual growth" of the common law system.Those rare departures from the doctrinal legal history mold have constructed rather vague economic paradigms that depict the development of contract law as an evolutionary process paralleling the movement of English society from a feudal to a market-based economy.It is hoped that the present work, in attempting to link law to the dynamics of common law administration, will make some contribution toward unravelling the complex causal questions underlying the development of the early common law of contract.
The seventeenth-century common law system faced conflicting pressures.  The caseload capacity of the system was limited by the existing court structure.  The incumbent officeholders and the legal profession both had vested interests in maintaining the structure; "institutional" reform was impossible.  With the income and prestige of the system dependent on the volume oflitigation that it handled, however, there were strong incentives to maximize caseload capacity.  Judges tried to accommodate as many cases as possible within the existing court structure.  To do so, they developed an administrative structure that both conserved judicial energy through delegation of function, and facilitated tight judicial control over the delegated task.  This "controlled-delegation" strategy strongly influenced the development of both procedural and substantive common law, especially contract law.  With contract actions making up as much as eighty to ninety percent of seventeenth-century common law litigation, the courts were acutely sensitive to the need for tailoring contract law to facilitate judicial administration.
This work will demonstrate how the controlled-delegation strategy influenced the development of seventeenth-century contract law.  To make the task more manageable, the present inquiry is limited to an investigation of how the common law handled the issue of plaintiff breach in contract actions.  In contract litigation a defendant often defaults in response to or in conjunction with some corresponding breach by the plaintiff.  A case of this kind can be one of the most demanding confronting a legal system.  The modern approach to the issue of plaintiff breach involves close scrutiny of the terms of the contract and the broader facts of the case, with the judge or jury determining, for example, whether the plaintiff had substantially performed, and assessing damages in light of the cross allegations of breach.  In contrast, the seventeenth-century common law adopted a strict law of conditions to decide the issue of plaintiff breach in contract actions.  If the defendant raised plaintiff breach in defense, the seventeenth-century common law courts used an all-or-nothing approach.  They simply determined whether the plaintiff's performance was a condition precedent or whether the reciprocal obligations were independent.  There was no notion of substantial performance, and the courts refused to allow competing damages claims to be adjusted in the same action.  If the plaintiff's performance was held to be a condition precedent, the court insisted on his entire performance.  If on the other hand the mutual obligations were held to be independent, the defendant was forced to recover his damages in a separate cross action.
The common law courts also facilitated the use of contract bonds, which could impose unlimited penalties on the breaching party.  Accordingly, had they wished, the parties to an agreement could, at the time of agreement, have secured performance of their reciprocal covenants by entering into mutual bonds defeasible on performance.  This would allow the plaintiff to recover the full amount of the bond without the need for a jury assessment of damages.
The thesis unfolds in four parts.  Parts I and II explore how and why the common law courts implemented the controlled-delegation strategy and how the resulting administrative structure influenced the development of the commonlaw of contract.  Part I focuses on the courts sitting in banc at Westminster.  It examines how they delegated fact finding to the jury and shielded themselves from the burdensome task of reviewing lengthy special verdicts.  It also examines how the central courts set up a system of jury control by utilizing the energies of the litigants in pleading to narrow the issue put to the jury, and how the courts developed a structure of procedural and substantive rules -- of which the law of conditions was an integral part -- to regulate the form and content of the issue put to the jury.  Part II explores how the courts, having committed themselves to the jury as an administrative expedient, found its use plagued by problems that they attempted to counter by limiting both its use and the scope of the issues referred to it, and by exercising tight control over the jury function.  In particular, Part II focuses on four strategies that common law courts used successfully to handle issues of plaintiff breach in contract actions: the confinement of trial proceedings through pleading rules; the restriction on the availability of a damages remedy in favor of recovery of an entire "sum certain"; the facilitation of the use of bonds that provided formal proof and liquidated the amount of recovery; and, in those cases in which a damages remedy was available, the limitation of trial proceedings to the single issue reached in pleading.  Part III examines how the common law administrative structure broke down as the procedural and substantive law rules used to implement the controlled-delegation strategy developed into a technical science that threatened miscarriage for error of form.  It also examines how, during the course of the seventeenth century, reaction to this growing atrophy brought about changes both in the administrative structure and in the law of contract.  Part IV examines the issue of the relationship of external power, and in particular the developing seventeenth-century commercialism, to the common law of contract.  It attempts to show that a prima facie charge of class bias cannot be leveled against the substantive contract law of the period, and that, in fact, when commercial expectations clashed with the judges' vested interests in the common law institutions, the latter prevailed, even at the cost of frustrating the former.  It concludes, following the work of Max Weber, with a suggested link between the formalism engendered by the common law's administrative structure and the development of the market economy in England.

questions.question: Did the administrative capacity and case-management practices of central courts influence the substantive development of contract rules governing breach and remedies?

Did procedural devices designed to limit trials and delegate fact-finding (such as tightened pleading, formalized instruments, and narrow jury issues) produce rigid, all-or-nothing outcomes in contract litigation?
Did the institutional and financial interests of courts and legal officeholders cause contract law to prioritize administrative convenience and institutional stability over evolving commercial needs?

matched_themes: Should courts allow punitive or other extracompensatory damages for willful or abusive contract breaches, and what are the efficiency and fairness trade-offs?
What standard should courts apply to determine whether a party's deviation from contractual obligations is significant enough to excuse the other party's performance?
How should courts treat pre-agreed breach payments and liquidated damages clauses (enforce, reform, apportion, or void)?
Should courts allow apportionment of contractual damages when the non-breaching party's reliance or failure to cooperate contributed to the loss?
How do institutional features-court capacity, procedural devices, and evidentiary rules-affect the substantive development and practical application of contract remedies?
Should parties be presumptively permitted to contractually specify nonstandard damage remedies, or should courts retain authority to impose defaults?
How should courts treat and enforce stipulated remedies (liquidated damages clauses) versus substituting judicial remedies?
How do transaction costs, enforcement frictions, and institutional realities alter the theoretical efficiency of breach-plus-compensation?

Can party-designed enforcement mechanisms (pre-agreed penalties, arbitration, bonding, reputational systems) reliably produce efficient breach outcomes without judicial intervention, and when do they fail?
Should courts police and limit supracompensatory contractual remedies (penalty-like clauses), or does allowing parties to contract for such terms respect autonomy and promote efficient contracting?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?

Should contractual clauses that impose predetermined monetary payments for breach be treated as punitive (unenforceable) or as enforceable measures of compensation, and what factors predict courts' enforcement decisions?

Do repeat players, contract drafting strategies, secrecy about dispute outcomes, and presentation techniques enable stronger parties to extract one-sided terms and undermine the protective aims of contract law?
When is an indirect remedy (one that induces self-compliance) preferable to a direct remedy that delivers the outcome?

papers.node_id: 60lalrev233!!ARTICLE: The Wasted Sacrifice of Lessors' Lost Profit Claims in Bankruptcy
papers.title: ARTICLE: The Wasted Sacrifice of Lessors' Lost Profit Claims in Bankruptcy
papers.abstract:
sets the maximum allowable amount of a real property lessor's claim for damages arising from breach of lease.To the extent that a lessor's damages claim under nonbankruptcy law exceeds the maximum amount, it is disallowed in the tenant's bankruptcy case. The implicit premise for such disallowance is that real property lessors' damages claims are less worthy of respect in bankruptcy than other claims for damages against the debtor.Real property leases are legally distinct from other contractual relationships that allocate property rights.But, it does not obviously follow from the distinction that adamages claim for breach of a real property lease is inferior to other claims. Because it discriminates against real property lessors' lost profit claims, Section 502(b)(6) contravenes the bankruptcy slogan that like-situated creditors ought to be treated alike, or that "equality is equity."
This article considers Section 502(b)(6) in light of the political, economic, and legal forces that shaped it. Part II explains how Section 502(b)(6) applies to a lessors' claim. Part III explores the history of real property lessors' claims for damages in bankruptcy cases from the beginning of the twentieth century. Part IV considers the stated justifications for disallowance of lessor's claims under Section 502(b)(6) and concludes that they are unconvincing. Disallowance of part of lessors' damages claims under Section 502(b)(6) reflects and perpetuates irrational bias against such claims. Moreover, such disallowance contradicts both contractual theory and modern bankruptcy policy.

questions.question: Whether bankruptcy rules that cap or disallow landlords' lost-profit damages for breach of lease are legally and economically justified compared with treating those claims like other unsecured claims.
Whether applying a cap to landlords' damages constitutes unjustified discrimination against landlords relative to other creditors, contradicting principles of equal treatment in bankruptcy.
How political, economic, and legal history explains the development and persistence of special limits on landlords' damages in bankruptcy proceedings.

matched_themes: How should default liability rules interact with parties' freedom to allocate risks by contract and duties of disclosure to achieve efficient and fair risk allocation?
Should parties be presumptively permitted to contractually specify nonstandard damage remedies, or should courts retain authority to impose defaults?
Should courts limit recoverable consequential damages that are grossly disproportionate to the contract price, and would such limits promote economic efficiency?
Should courts police and limit supracompensatory contractual remedies (penalty-like clauses), or does allowing parties to contract for such terms respect autonomy and promote efficient contracting?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
Are caps on landlords' contractual damages in bankruptcy legally and economically justified compared with treatment of other unsecured claims?

papers.node_id: 14jempiricallegalstud527!!ARTICLE: Unbundling Efficient Breach: An Experiment
papers.title: ARTICLE: Unbundling Efficient Breach: An Experiment
papers.authors: Maria Bigoni; Stefania Bortolotti; Francesco Parisi; Ariel Porat
papers.abstract:
On the question of efficient breach, there exists a subtle tension between the economic and the moral viewpoints. Both perspectives consider the failure to keep a promiseexcusable in at least some subset of cases when the net social benefit of breach is sufficiently large (Warkol 1998:321). Yet they do not always agree on the boundary conditions when such breaches may be permitted. Assuming Kaldor-Hicks wealth maximization, the standard economic analysis contends that if the promisor gains more than the promisee loses from a breach, then a damages rule (allowing nonperformance with compensation) will be efficient. Moreover, to the extent that expectation damages are perfectly compensatory, and the promisee is thereby fully compensated, such a breach would be Pareto efficient, leaving neither party in a worse position than if the promisor had in fact performed. In contrast, deontological philosophers of contract law take the moral duty to keep one's promises as a foundational principle of contracts that cannot be brushed aside by cost-benefit analyses (Sidhu 2006; Mather 1999; Fried 1981; Shiffrin 2009, 2012).
Judicial and lay intuitions seem ambivalent with respect to the notion of efficient breach (Warkol 1998; Baron & Wilkinson-Ryan 2009; Zamir & Medina 2010). In general, the intuitions of laymen seem to track consequentialist (economic) reasoning in cases of loss-avoiding breach, while being deontological (moralist) in cases of gain-seeking breach. Consider, for instance, two firms renting a restaurant for their annual event. In the first case, the restaurant's owners try to cancel the reservation due to the sudden demise of the chef and ask the firm to breach the contract, offering some compensation, as replacing the chef in haste would be too costly. In the second case, the restaurant's owners want to breach the contract because they received a better offer from another group willing to rent the space on the same date. We believe that one might well be more inclined to forego performance and ask for a lower compensation in the first (loss-avoiding breach) rather than in the second example (gain-seeking breach). This thought experiment suggests that the distinction between loss-avoiding and gain-seeking breach may be analytically important.
In line with our intuition, survey-based studies (Baron & Wilkinson-Ryan, 2009) suggest that lay intuitions about the excusableness of nonperformance are surprisingly nuanced. Survey participants were tolerant of breach in cases where the promisor sought to pay damages in lieu of performance to mitigate unanticipated costs (loss-avoiding breach). Yet they were unwilling to excuse performance when the promisor breached to pursue a better deal (gain-seeking breach).
Existing empirical evidence on these issues relies exclusively on anecdotal evidence from court cases, and from nonincentivized surveys. Unfortunately, data about actually occurring breaches are scarce. Moreover, comparing real-world loss-avoiding and gain-seeking breaches is difficult, as many important variables--interested parties, amount of surplus generated by the contract, available information, and so forth--may vary from one case to the other, hence making it difficult to draw any inference. Economic reasons, such as allocative efficiency, productive efficiency, restrained incentives, information-forcing effects, and competitive effects could also drive any observed difference (see Bigoni et al. 2016). In this article, we adopt a novel approach to the problem, and test whether the motives behind a breach are behaviorally relevant by means of a controlled laboratory experiment. We utilize an incentivized economic experiment granting tight control over the relevant parameters and allowing to exogenouslymanipulate the variables of interest. We understand incentivized experiments as a new and important source of evidence that can complement real-world and survey data.
We introduce a novel Contract-Breach Game, where buyers and sellers sign a binding contract and, afterward, a shock might occur. We exogenously vary the shock to simulate loss-avoiding and gain-seeking breaches. As specific performance remedies apply to the contract, the promisee can force the promisor to perform the act(s) stated in the contract, unless both parties agree on the compensation and cancel the contract. This study is the first to investigate these issues in a nonhypothetical, strategic environment, where subjects make decisions with real pecuniary consequences, both for themselves and for other participants of the experiment. Our results confirm that, broadly speaking, lay intuition finds empirical support: the promisees require higher compensation to consent to gain-seeking than to loss-avoiding breaches. Interestingly enough, we can provide a behavioral explanation for the observed difference. Our results are in line with behavioral arguments suggesting that people dislike highly unequal distributions of wealth (Fehr & Schmidt 1999; Bolton & Ockenfels 2000). More specifically, inequality-averse subjects in our experiment are more willing to accept a low offer in cases of loss-avoiding breaches than in gain-seeking breaches. These findings are consistent with the results of a recent experiment by Mittlaender Leme de Souza (2016), who investigates how the perception of the moral value of a breach depends on the breach's consequences, and shows that breaches aimed at avoiding unanticipated unequal outcomes are generally considered moral.
The article is structured as follows. In Section II, we review the moral and economic arguments for efficient breach in the prior literature. In Section III, we present the Contract-Breach Game and describe the experimental design. In Section IV, we present the results of our experiment, which show that people's reactions differ with respect to gain-seeking and loss-avoiding breaches, while remaining undistinguishable across seller breaches and buyer breaches--consistent with our intuition. In Section V, we conclude with a summary of our results and possible policy implications. We also explain the limits of our conclusions given the design and nature of our experiment.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Markets as a Moral Foundation for Contract Law

papers.node_id: 73califlrev1!!ARTICLE: Unity in Tort, Contract, and Property: The Model of Precaution.
papers.title: ARTICLE: Unity in Tort, Contract, and Property: The Model of Precaution.
papers.abstract:
Much of the common law is concerned with allocating the costs of harm, such as the harm caused by accidents, nuisances, breaches of contract, or governmental takings of private property.  There are at least two distinct goals for adopting allocative cost rules: theequitygoal of compensating victims and theefficiencygoal of minimizing costs to society as a whole.These goals in turn can be formulated as two principles: the compensation principle and the marginal principle.  The compensation principle states that victims should be compensated for harm caused by others.  The marginal principle states that social costs should be minimized by equating the incremental benefit of each precautionary activity to its incremental cost.
Is the common law primarily concerned with the justice of compensation or the efficiency of cost minimization?  Presented this way, the two principles appear to be rival theories of law.This Article, however, poses a different question: How does the common law combine the goal of compensation with the goal of minimizing social costs?  The two principles now appear as complementary, rather than rival, explanations.  As a result, this Article assumes that there are circumstances in which compensation is required for reasons of justice and examines mechanismsthat attempt to provide compensation, without undermining incentives for efficient behavior.
In addition to direct costs, there are many indirect social costs of harm, such as the cost of precautions against harm, the cost of bearing the risk of harm, the cost of obtaining information about risk, and the cost of settling disputes.Analyzing all of these costs thoroughly, however, is impossible in an article of modest length.  Consequently, this Article selects two types of cost for detailed analysis, the direct cost of harm and the cost of precautions against it.  The "model of precaution" is my label for an account of the relationship between these two types of costs.
There is justification in terms of economic theory for developing the model of precaution before considering other types of indirect costs.  An economic model is built up by mathematical deduction from axioms describing the behavior of individuals and organizations.This axiomatic structure contains an accepted order of simplification, which is dictated by the internal structure of economic reasoning.Following this order, the simplest level of analysis assumes away the costs of risk aversion, the costs of obtaining information about risk, and the transaction costs of dispute resolution.  Thus, the model of precaution is basic in terms of the internal structure of economic reasoning.  Furthermore, this Article shows that the model of precaution is similar in structure for torts, contracts, and property.  Thus the theme of the Article is the unity of the common law at the simplest level of economic analysis.
Part I of this Article describes the simple model as applied to torts, contracts, and property.  This Part describes three common-law mechanisms for compensating victims that also create incentives for efficient behavior.  Part II then provides several examples of the model's explanatory power by applying it to several legal rules and practices.  Finally, Part III contains a brief discussion of the consequences of relaxing some of the simplifying assumptions.  The use of graphs or algebra is kept to a minimum, although a mathematical appendix is included following the Article for the benefit of those who find quantitative analysis helpful.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a 'model of precaution' that explicitly frames legal rules in terms of the compensation principle (making victims whole) and the marginal principle (equating incremental precaution benefits and costs) to show how compensation and efficiency can be combined; Paper B examines how contractual damage regimes (e.g., higher liability for willful breaches) reflect parties' tradeoffs between compensation and incentives not to breach or to take precautions.

shared_topics.topic: the role of fault/intentionality versus strict liability in determining damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes negligence- and liability-based rules as mechanisms that tie liability to parties' precautionary behavior (i.e., fault influences incentives); Paper B empirically documents that sophisticated M&A contracts commonly distinguish 'willful breach' and increase damages when fault/intentionality is present, contradicting the doctrinal ideal of no-fault contract damages.

shared_topics.topic: design of damages and contractual/tort rules as mechanisms to allocate costs and shape behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A describes specific common-law mechanisms across tort, contract, and property that both compensate victims and create efficient incentives, focusing on how damages and liability rules allocate direct and precaution costs; Paper B studies the concrete design choices in M&A contracts—clauses that scale liability by culpability—showing how parties engineer damage rules to allocate costs and influence behavior.

shared_topics.topic: tension between economic/legal theory (efficient breach/strict liability) and real-world practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops an economic model to explain and justify legal rules but also discusses limits and when compensatory justice requires departures from pure efficiency models; Paper B demonstrates empirically that actual contracting practice (especially among sophisticated parties) often departs from the textbook efficient‑breach/strict‑liability model by incorporating fault-sensitive provisions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83columlrev35!!ARTICLE: THE STRUCTURE OF JUDICIAL ADMINISTRATION AND THE DEVELOPMENT OF CONTRACT LAW IN SEVENTEENTH-CENTURY ENGLAND Copyright © 1983 by Clinton W. Francis.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE STRUCTURE OF JUDICIAL ADMINISTRATION AND THE DEVELOPMENT OF CONTRACT LAW IN SEVENTEENTH-CENTURY ENGLAND Copyright © 1983 by Clinton W. Francis.

shared_topics.topic: how procedural and administrative constraints shape substantive contract doctrines and incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows in detail how the seventeenth‑century courts' need to manage caseloads and delegate functions produced pleading rules and a strict law of conditions that structured parties' behavior; Paper B analyzes, at a more abstract level, how legal rules (in tort, contract, and property) create incentives and can be evaluated by their effect on agents' precautionary and performance choices.

shared_topics.topic: the role of remedies (liquidated sums, bonds, and damages) in allocating risk and motivating behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the courts' facilitation of contract bonds and the choice between recovery of a sum certain versus jury‑assessed damages, while Paper B studies how compensation rules and the form of remedies influence incentives for precaution and the allocation of social costs.

shared_topics.topic: tension between efficiency (minimizing social costs) and other institutional goals (justice, formality, or vested interests)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B explicitly frames legal rules as balancing a compensation goal and an efficiency (marginal) goal; Paper A documents historical instances where judicial institutional interests and formal proceduralism trumped commercial efficiency, revealing the same kind of tradeoff between institutional/formal goals and efficient market expectations.

shared_topics.topic: the significance of litigation and dispute‑resolution costs for legal rule design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A demonstrates how the administrative burden of trials, jury control, and pleading rules drove doctrinal developments in contract law, and Paper B includes the cost of settling disputes among the indirect social costs that legal rules must account for when designing mechanisms that compensate victims without undermining incentives.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: An Examination of Judicial Reasoning - When a Penalty Is Not a Penalty

shared_topics.topic: tension between compensatory rules and efficiency/deterrence incentives
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze whether legal rules should prioritize compensating victims or promoting efficient behavior: Paper A presents the compensation principle versus the marginal (efficiency) principle across tort, contract, and property, while Paper B debates whether contract damages should remain purely compensatory (invalidating penalties) or allow supracompensatory clauses that may serve other incentives.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules allocate costs/risk and thereby shape parties' precautions and incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a 'model of precaution' linking direct harm and precaution costs across domains, and Paper B examines how enforceability of liquidated-damages/penalty clauses allocates contractual risk and affects parties' incentives to perform or take precautions.

shared_topics.topic: whether rigid per se doctrines should give way to flexible, economically-informed standards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies mechanisms that both compensate and preserve efficient incentives, implicitly questioning rigid rules, while Paper B criticizes the centuries-old per se penalty rule and argues for reform toward a more flexible, predictable, and economically sensible approach.

shared_topics.topic: the role of economic reasoning in interpreting and reforming common-law doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with economic arguments about rules: Paper A formalizes legal doctrines with economic modeling to show unity across domains, and Paper B invokes economic concepts (efficiency, freedom of contract, predictability) to evaluate and propose changes to the common-law penalty doctrine.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 4wmmarybuslrev493!!ARTICLE: CLASHING POLICIES OR CONFUSING PRECEDENTS: THE "GROSS NEGLIGENCE" EXCEPTION TO CONSEQUENTIAL DAMAGES DISCLAIMERS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CLASHING POLICIES OR CONFUSING PRECEDENTS: THE "GROSS NEGLIGENCE" EXCEPTION TO CONSEQUENTIAL DAMAGES DISCLAIMERS

shared_topics.topic: how contractual limitations of liability affect parties' incentives to take precautions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how upholding or invalidating consequential-damages disclaimers in commercial contracts changes parties' risk allocations and thus their incentives (arguing for enforcing agreed limits to preserve freedom of contract), while Paper B develops an economic "model of precaution" showing how liability rules across tort, contract, and property create incentives for efficient precaution-taking.

shared_topics.topic: whether public-policy or fault-based exceptions should override negotiated risk allocations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the judicial use of public-policy doctrines (unconscionability, gross negligence, willful misconduct) to negate contractually agreed liability limits in commercial settings, and Paper B addresses when compensation (for justice) should be required despite possible efficiency costs — i.e., when legal rules should impose liability rather than respect private allocations.

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal and functional role of fault standards (gross negligence, recklessness, intent) in assigning liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on courts' inconsistent use of terms like gross negligence, recklessness, and intentional misconduct to justify voiding liability limits, while Paper B's precaution model relies on how fault/standards of care allocate losses and drive precaution decisions across torts, contracts, and property.

shared_topics.topic: the use and limits of monetary damages (direct vs consequential) as instruments for compensation and cost-minimization
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the enforceability and limits of consequential-damages disclaimers under the UCC and the consequences of invalidating those disclaimers, whereas Paper B analyzes monetary compensation (direct harms) and its relationship to the marginal cost of precautions as part of a unified framework for minimizing social costs while providing compensation.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Sanctions by Social Norms and the Law: Substitutes or Complements?

shared_topics.topic: balancing compensation and incentives for precaution/compliance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how compensation (the compensation principle) can be combined with incentives to minimize social costs (the marginal principle) so victims are made whole without undermining precaution, and Paper B studies how legal sanctions and social norms can be designed or combined so that deterrence of undesirable acts is achieved without crowding out intrinsic motivation.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between formal legal rules and informal social mechanisms (substitutes vs complements)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats tort, contract, and property rules as distinct common-law mechanisms that can be arranged to provide compensation and incentives, while Paper B explicitly models when social norms and formal law operate as substitutes or complements and how their joint use affects outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: use of simplified economic models to derive legal-policy implications and social-welfare conditions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a 'model of precaution' (a simplified economic framework) to draw implications across tort, contract, and property, and Paper B uses a simple/common-agency economic model to determine when law should supplement or replace social norms to maximize welfare.

shared_topics.topic: importance of information, observability, enforcement and transaction costs in rule design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights (and sometimes abstracts from) costs such as information acquisition, dispute-settlement, and precaution that shape legal incentives, and Paper B centers on observability/social connectedness and the comparative costs of informal versus formal enforcement in explaining when law improves outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 59ohiostlj339!!ARTICLE: Disproportionality and the Law of Consequential Damages: Default Theory and Cognitive Reality
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Disproportionality and the Law of Consequential Damages: Default Theory and Cognitive Reality

shared_topics.topic: balancing compensation of victims with incentives for efficient precautions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A formulates the compensation principle versus the marginal (efficiency) principle and analyzes legal mechanisms that both compensate victims and preserve incentives to take precautions; Paper B analyzes how limits on consequential damages (disproportionality) affect the allocation of losses and incentives under contract law and whether such limits can sensibly reduce over- or under-compensation without distorting behavior.

shared_topics.topic: use of economic/default-rule analysis to evaluate liability doctrines across doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops an economic 'model of precaution' and applies it uniformly to tort, contract, and property rules to explain doctrinal choices, while Paper B evaluates the disproportionality constraint using default-rule theory from law-and-economics to assess whether that constraint makes sense as a legal default.

shared_topics.topic: the role of risk, foreseeability, and information in allocating liability and damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A isolates direct harms and the cost of precautions (and initially abstracts from information and risk-aversion) to show how liability rules affect precaution choices, and Paper B centers on foreseeability (Hadley) and the mismatch between contract price and consequential damages—especially for low-probability/high-loss events—highlighting how information about risk conditions liability outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: limits of standard rational-actor assumptions (information costs and cognitive biases) and their implications for rule design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A acknowledges that relaxing simplifying assumptions about risk aversion and information costs changes the model's predictions and discusses consequences, while Paper B brings empirical cognitive-psychology evidence that parties systematically underestimate remote risks and argues that such departures from rationality justify doctrinal adjustments like a disproportionality test.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:Intentional Interference with Contract and the Doctrineof Efficient Breach: Fine Tuning the Notion of the ContractBreacher as Wrongdoer

shared_topics.topic: how to balance compensation and efficiency when imposing tort liability for contractual breaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly confronts the tension between compensating injured promisees and preserving the incentives for efficient breach, arguing that interference liability should be limited to cases that cause 'wrongful' (undesirable) breaches; Paper B formalizes the same tradeoff more broadly, modeling how compensation (the compensation principle) can be combined with incentives for cost-minimizing behavior (the marginal principle) across torts, contracts, and property.

shared_topics.topic: application of law-and-economics models to reconcile tort and contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses law-and-economics reasoning (the doctrine of efficient breach) to propose a reframing of intentional interference doctrine, while Paper B develops a general economic 'model of precaution' to unify and explain rules in tort, contract, and property, i.e., both papers deploy economic modeling to reinterpret and harmonize common-law doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: when contract remedies are inadequate and tort rules should supplement them
shared_topics.justification: Paper A identifies classes of breaches that contract remedies fail to deter or compensate (e.g., where damages/specifc performance are inadequate) and argues tort interference should address those gaps; Paper B similarly examines mechanisms by which the common law compensates victims without destroying efficient incentives, implicitly addressing when supplemental rules (beyond contract remedies) are justified.

shared_topics.topic: criteria for labeling breaches or inducements as 'wrongful' or 'improper'
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops the notion of 'wrongful breach' to determine when mere inducement should be tortious, tying improperness to the nature of the resulting breach; Paper B engages the related question at a structural level by asking when harms merit compensation under its model of precaution and thus when legal rules should treat an act as warranting liability.

shared_topics.topic: reconciling compensation and incentives in damage rules

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules measure and define 'harm' for allocating loss
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers its analysis on the relationship between direct harm and precaution costs as the basic inputs for liability rules in tort, contract, and property, while Paper B probes the doctrinal meaning of 'actual harm' versus 'anticipated harm' for liquidated-damages enforcement and which components of loss should be included.

shared_topics.topic: the role of foreseeability, avoidability/mitigation, and certainty limits in awarding damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A identifies precaution, information, and risk-bearing costs (which relate to foreseeability and precaution incentives) as important indirect costs affecting legal allocation, and Paper B directly examines whether and how avoidability, foreseeability, and certainty limitations should exclude or include particular losses in the 'actual harm' calculation.

shared_topics.topic: using economic reasoning to evaluate and shape common-law doctrines of remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly constructs an economic model to explain unity across tort, contract, and property doctrines under efficiency and compensation principles, and Paper B employs expectation-damages concepts and economic-functional reasoning to recommend how courts should interpret statutory and Restatement provisions governing stipulated damages.

shared_topics.topic: economic/deterrence account of appropriate remedies (punish vs price)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage substantive economic models to explain why the law assigns monetary damages versus punitive sanctions: Paper A uses economic reasoning about precaution and marginal cost/benefit to justify liability rules that induce efficient care, and Paper B applies the deterrence/efficiency rationale (the idea that 'criminal law punishes while tort law prices') to explain the civil treatment of tort and contract breaches versus crimes.

shared_topics.topic: comparative analysis of torts, contracts, and property when harms are equivalent
shared_topics.justification: Both papers compare how the common law treats similar or identical harms arising in tort, contract, and property settings: Paper A argues for a unified precaution model that applies across those categories, and Paper B constructs isomorphic scenarios (same monetary loss via theft, negligence, or breach) to probe why only some breaches are criminalized.

shared_topics.topic: interaction of moral/blameworthiness (intent/voluntariness) with legal allocation of sanctions
shared_topics.justification: Both consider non‑purely‑economic factors—moral responsibility, intent, and voluntariness—in explaining liability and remedies: Paper A frames compensation as sometimes required for justice alongside efficiency concerns, and Paper B scrutinizes moral models (blameworthiness, intentionality) and refines them by distinguishing voluntary versus non‑voluntary obligations to explain why contract breaches are typically left in the civil sphere.

shared_topics.topic: economic/incentive modeling of private-law rules to guide doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Both works employ economic-style incentive reasoning to evaluate and propose doctrinal rules: Paper A uses incentive analysis to recommend a structured remedy framework for arguably illegal contracts, and Paper B builds a formal precaution model to unify tort, contract, and property rules around efficiency and compensation goals.

shared_topics.topic: role of uncertainty, information costs, and ambiguity in parties' ex ante decision‑making

papers.node_id: 117yaleljpocketpart14!!ARTICLE: What Efficiency Demands: The Efficient Performance Hypothesis Defended
papers.title: ARTICLE: What Efficiency Demands: The Efficient Performance Hypothesis Defended
papers.abstract:
I appreciate the comments and thoughtful engagement by Professors Coleman,Kraus,and Posneron my essay "The Efficient Performance Hypothesis."A few words of clarification may be helpful with regard to these comments, as well as the original essay. Let me begin with Professor Kraus's comment -- the most critical of the three in both tone and substance. Regrettably, Professor Kraus' comment misses the point of the essay and his tangents contain a number of mistakes. I will attempt to clarify.
My essay did not advance a particular moral view of contract. It demonstrates, instead, that allocative efficiency can be made consistent with different moral views of contract. The competing views I employed to make this point were: (1) the promisor has the legal entitlement to choose nonperformance and payment of damages (i.e., the so-called Holmesian option) and (2) the promisee instead has the legal entitlement to choose nonperformance and payment of damages. Professor Kraus claims that these two views necessarily reduce to the promisee not having or having the right to specific performance. This reductionist claim is wrong, as I will demonstrate below, but even if it was correct it would not undermine the point of my essay,which again is simply to show that different and competing moral views can be made consistent with efficiency.
Professor Kraus obscures my thesis by focusing on specific performance. He says, "Brooks concludes that morality requires specific performance, and not expectation damages because '[b]reach of a legal contract without excuse iswrongconduct.'"In fact, I draw no such conclusion about specific performance and expectation damages. Clearly, either remedy could be consistent with viewing breach as wrong, and nothing I say in the essay denies this basic point. So why does Professor Kraus believe that I am invoking a moral argument in favor of the legal right to specific performance?
Because he conflates the economics of remedies with the morality of remedies. Here is his argument: he begins by rightly noting that promisees have options under the standard breach rule -- that is, the option to get expectation damages or nothing at all. This option, he says, is not so different from the option they have under my proposal. Therefore, the standard rule and my proposal may be expressed as follows:
(i) Standard Rule: given promisor non-performance, promisee can elect damages or nothing; and
(ii) Proposed Rule: given promisor non-performance, promisee can elect damages or specific performance.
Since the only difference he can see between (i) and (ii), is "nothing" and "specific performance," he argues that "Brooks' moral thesis reduces to the claim that remedies that entitle the promisee to specific performance avoid the moral objection to expectation damages." But, of course, there is another difference between (i) and (ii), which lies in the antecedent condition of the promisor's non-performance. Under the efficient breach hypothesis, as structured in the essay, the promisor has the legal right to determine nonperformance, while under the efficient performance hypothesis that right belongs to the promisee. This is the key moral distinction between the two regimes, not the remedies. This is emphasized in the essay. Nothing for me here turns on the morality of the remedies (expectation damages, disgorgement or specific performance), which is not to say that there aren't sound ethical reasons to prefer one remedy to another, but that was not the point of my analysis.
More generally, Professor Kraus fails to recognize that specific performance serves a distinct economic (as opposed to moral) function under the two regimes. Under efficient breach, specific performance is simply an economic instrument that allows the promisor to compare the cost of performance against the value of performance (measured by expectation damages), whileunder efficient performance, specific performance allows the promisee to compare the value of performance against the cost of performance (measured by disgorgement). Specific performance is no more morally required under one regime than the other. Specific performance, expectation damages and disgorgement serve economic functions here, encouraging the party with the option (in terms of rights or powers) to make an efficient allocation. And just as the efficient breach hypothesis works with right or power so does the efficient performance argument. Imagine that the two competing moral visions of contract enforcement were (1) the promisor has the right to perform or pay and (2) the promisor does not have the right to perform or pay. Note that the promisee does not necessarily have a right to performance under either vision, but assume that she is able nonetheless to secure performance through force, guile, or some fortunate circumstance. The promisee has the power to get performance, but she would only secure performance, if that meant giving up her claim to expectation damages, when performance is efficient.
Specific performance serves only as a proxy for the promisee's value (with disgorgement proxing the promisor's cost) under efficient performance, just as specific performance serves as a proxy for the promisor's cost (with expectation proxing the promisee's value) under efficient breach. To really make clear that the right to specific performance is not required consider the following: let's say that the rule is that the promisee gets to choose between disgorgement and expectation damages. Now disgorgement proxies the promisor's cost while expectation proxies the promisee's value (specific performance is absent here: the promisee has no right to enjoy performance and will end up with money damages in any event). To get efficient allocation the court imposes the following decision rule: if the promisee chooses disgorgement there will be not performance and she will simply get the cash transfer. However, if the promisee chooses expectation damages then performance will be ordered and immediately liquidated for the promisee's benefit (which is to say, performance will be sold on the market and the market price received will be handed over to the promisee). In this case, the decision rule (with the promisee effectively making the allocative choice) leads to efficiency, but the promisee never gets performance; nor does she have a right to it.This illustration is not offered asa practical alternative, it is merely offered to highlight the distinction between the economics of remedies and the morality of remedies, a distinction that Professor Kraus comment does not fully appreciate.
have no quarrel with his general comments about the moral arguments for and against specific performance. They are beside the point, as I was neither explicitly nor implicitly asserting any moral distinction to specific performance. But if one must insist, despite the hazards of doing so, that the moral distinction uniquely present in the efficient performance hypothesis is the promisee's right to specific performance then so be it. That insistence still preserves the thesis of the essay, namely that efficiency can be made consistent with competing moral views of contract enforcement.
Professor Kraus finally makes a number of challenges regarding the efficiency claims in my essay. These arguments too are somewhat unfocused, some concern specific performance as an efficient remedy and others are more focused on the efficient performance hypothesis. None are particularly compelling.I agree, of course, that the relative efficiency of a contractualregime depends on a host of empirical variables, including relevant market structures, judicial determination costs, litigation costs, search and negotiation costs, ex ante and ex post. The efficiency indeterminacy I describe is empirically contingent, and while Professor Kraus' armchair empiricism doesn't resolve the matter for me, I cannot say that his intuition is any worse than mine.
Another point of clarification concerns Professor Coleman's claim that I mistakenly conflate the Holmesian notion of the promisor right (option) to breach with the efficient breach hypothesis. He urges instead that "efficient breach" entails a breach of a duty (not the exercise of a right or privilege).This a reasonable interpretation of "efficient breach," but by no means the only reasonable one. There have certainly been plausible efficient breach arguments based on a right to breach (what Professor Schiffin called the strong version of the efficient breach argument in her recent article),not just the mere power or capacity to breach (the weak version of the argument). For instance, Professors Shavell advances an incomplete contracts framework to suggest that nonperformance and payment of expectation damages when performance is not cost justified (i.e., efficient breaching) may be considered default term in incomplete contracts because that is what the parties would have negotiated.While it is not clear to me that the parties would have negotiated necessarily for expectation damages, his argument of an implied term to efficiently breach suggests a form of efficient breach consistent with the Holmesian option to breach. Similarly, Judge Posner inPatton v. Mid-Contintent Systems, Inc.,described "certain fundamentals of contractual liability" by claiming that "[t]he promisor promises in effect either to perform or compensate the promisee for the cost of non-performance."So while Professor Coleman is correct to say that it would be a mistake to equate the right to breach necessarily with efficient breach (which I did not do), he is mistaken to argue that the right to breach is necessarily disjoin from efficient breach.
But this is really a trivial point of contention. I couldn't agree more with Professor Coleman's basic point. His prior work with Professor Kraus, calling for greater attention to the normative content of existing categories of legal entitlement is surely right and greatly under-appreciated in the literature. My essay, as Professor Coleman observes, is less ambitious than what they call for, but it is nonetheless sympathetic. That larger ambition was simply not the principal the objective of my essay, which was to show that efficiency embraces a much broader range of legal rights than is traditionally suggested by efficiency advocates.
My essay is also sympathetic to the prior work of Professor Posner and his comment. He is right to suggest that the demands of efficiency may become quite exclusive, ex post, once relevant facts are known. Professor Posner made a similar point several years ago,and Professor Craswell made a similar point before him,and Professor Rogerson before him,and Professor Shavell before him,and Professor Coase before them.Each identified key indeterminacies regarding efficiency claims about contract remedies. Professor Coase, for example, argued that if ex post bargaining costs are zero then all remedies lead to allocative efficiency.Without some assumptions of differing bargaining costs associated with one remedy or another, efficiency won't tell you which remedy to pick. Of course, even with zero transaction costs the remedies create different distributive effects, which will have indirect consequences for resource allocation and investment efficiency. Hence the well-known argument that competing efficiency concerns (such as investment, search, precaution and bargaining) leave matters indeterminate until we know how the remedies specifically respond to these various concerns and contribute to overall welfare.
My point is that the indeterminacy is more profound: even along the sole dimension of allocative efficiency we are not in a position to say, analytically, which remedy is the most efficient. Efficient breach and efficient performance can be made analytically equivalent in terms of allocation of resources and distribution of wealth. Any tie-breaker must be an empirical one. I am deeplyskeptical of our capacity and willingness to search out that empirical answer. And in any event, resolving fundamental economic indeterminacies won't end the debate. It will merely signal a clean start of the debate over efficiency and morality in contracts: when we really know what efficiency demands. One can only hope, though I am equally skeptical here, that when that day comes we will also know what morality demands.
