papers.node_id: 56sclrev93!!ARTICLE:The Shadow Code
papers.title: ARTICLE:The Shadow Code
papers.abstract:
Lying in the shadow of contract law are unifying principles for calculating damages. These principles integrate the purposes motivating rules formalized in Article 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code(U.C.C.) and the Restatement (Second) of Contracts(Restatement) and their computational methods. Neither the U.C.C. nor the Restatement rules reflect these principles in any way that is apparent on their face. On the contrary, for each type of contract breach, the damage rules in Article 2 of the U.C.C. offer apparently distinct formulas, the applications of which depend on whether the non-breaching party was a buyer or seller, obtained partial performance, or arranged a substitute performance. The Restatement offers different formulas depending on the unhelpful and ultimately irrelevant distinction between the expectation and reliance interests. The Shadow Code offers an approach to contract damage calculations that explicitly reflects the well-recognized compensatory goal.
The Shadow Code restates the law of damages in a single section applicable to all breaches of contract. That section is based on the notion that people contract in order to improve their well-being. Each party ordinarily hopes for some improvement, or "surplus" of benefits over costs, as a result of contracting. The principle that a party injured by another's breach is entitled to be put in the position he or she would have occupied had the other performed as promised is not novel, but lies at the heart of the U.C.C. and the Restatement.The surplus-based approach to damages recognizes an injured party's entitlement to the difference between the surplus he or she would have realized had the other performed as promised and the actual surplus obtained. Section 1 of The Shadow Code articulates this central principle that applies to all types of parties - whetherconsumers or merchants, buyers or sellers - who are injured in all types of partial and total contract breaches.
The surplus-based approach requires no inventive types of information. While reflecting a consideration of costs and benefits, the surplus-based approach alters neither the philosophic orientation of damages rules nor the bottom line amount of damages awarded. The Shadow Code yields damages awards mathematically equivalent to both U.C.C. Article 2 and the Restatement.
The Shadow Code reveals goals of legal remedies for breach of contract that have long been buried in the details of the U.C.C. and the Restatement and for that reason, reveals the intuition behind both of them. The key to the surplus-based approach is distinguishing between "anticipated surplus," the improvement in well-being (potentially negative for a losing contract) the injured party would have realized had the other performed as promised, and "actual surplus," the improvement in well-being (often negative) resulting from the breach. The Shadow Code follows its basic principle of Section 1 ["SC 1"] with only two explanatory sections, Sections 2 ["SC 2"] and 3 ["SC 3"], defining, respectively, anticipated and actual surplus. The principle of lost surplus relies on a comparison of the benefits and costs of contracting and recognizes as broad a definition of benefits as the Restatement of Restitution, which states that "[a] person confers a benefit upon another if he … in any way adds to the other's security or advantage."Costs may similarly be defined as subtracting from the other's security or advantage. The comments and illustrations to SC 2 and SC 3 of The Shadow Code display the broad range of costs and benefits relevant to calculating lost surplus. With its general principle in SC 1 and explanations in SC 2 and SC 3, The Shadow Code draws together hugely disparate rules. The Shadow Code spares future generations of law students, lawyers, and judges the difficulty of applying different rules for cases involving sales of goods and for other exchanges, and within the realm of sales of goods, different rules for buyers and sellers in a multiplicity of factual contexts.
The Shadow Code may also be used in conjunction with existing codes to resolve difficult cases and to check the application of any of the myriad of rules arising from the U.C.C. and Restatement. Our position is that any computation arising from application of one of the rules in the U.C.C. or Restatement giving a damage award that is not equal to the difference between anticipated and actual surplus must be the result of an incorrect understanding of the U.C.C. or Restatement, or an understanding inconsistent with the U.C.C.'s or Restatement'sunderlying goals.The surplus-based approach is mathematically equivalent to an interpretation of those rules consistent with their acknowledged purposes.
Section 4 of The Shadow Code codifies generally recognized limitations on contract damages. Section 4 ["SC 4"] recognizes that claimed losses must not be too speculative in either their existence or amount, that injured parties must take reasonable steps to mitigate their losses, and that damages are limited to those thatare reasonably foreseeable. These limitations are well established in contract law.The purpose of SC 4 is to clarify ambiguities in the rules governing limitations on recovery and describe how damages calculated using the surplus-based approach account for these limitations.
In a companion article, we give detailed justifications for offering such an alternative code.Aside from its ability to reveal what lies beneath the established approaches and to provide a check on the accurate application of the established rules, The Shadow Code has three types of advantages over current contract damages rules that might be summarized as: (1) changing the jurisprudential and methodological orientation of damages remedies to align goals with rules, (2) refining terminology to eliminate confusion, and (3) facilitating analysis of the incentives created by remedies.
At the most fundamental level, The Shadow Code alters the jurisprudential perspective of the Restatement and methodology of the U.C.C. The Restatement distinguishes between cases in which an injured party seeks only to recover out-of-pocket expenses (the "reliance" interest) and those in which an injured party also seeks to recover its improvement in well-being (the "expectation" interest).The only case in which a party would choose the former, given that anticipated losses are deducted when calculating reliance damages,is where the existence or extent of any anticipated improvement cannot be proved with sufficient certainty. Well-recognized evidentiary rules (embodied in SC 4 and demonstrated by the comments and illustrations therein) requiring proof of loss with reasonable certainty address both cases without need for recognizing the "interest-based" approach. The U.C.C. approach is to offer a different rule for each type of circumstance in which a breach occurs. There are different rules for buyers and sellers;different rules for buyers who reject goods, who accept defective goods, or who arrange substitute transactions when the seller breaches;different rules for sellers who resell and those who do not; and different rules for those who cannot collect the purchase price.The welter of rules creates ambiguities in interpretation, wastingthe time of courts.This observation is hardly new to the literature on contract damages. Professor Peters observed that "the interrelationship between the various remedies is often left unnecessarily obscure in Article 2; a remedy which is permitted by one section appears to be interdicted by another; conduct apparently harmless when viewed from the vantage of one provision is fraught with danger when considered by another section."By clearly relating the goal of its provisions to the language of the rules, The Shadow Code is designed to eliminate ambiguity.
In addition to a variety of different rules for different circumstances, U.C.C. 2-714 allows damages to be "determined in any manner which is reasonable." The Shadow Code offers a single rule covering all types of breach. It defines what is reasonable. Because The Shadow Code produces an equivalent computational result, the U.C.C. formulas may be used when availability of evidence recommends them. The U.C.C. approach, however, conceals, while the surplus-based approach reveals, the fundamental principle on which each rule is based: the principle that an injured party is entitled to its lost surplus. The Shadow Code eliminates the unnecessary multiplicity of specialized rules while preserving their availability.
Of particularly practical import, The Shadow Code eliminates conflicting definitions of terms used in the U.C.C. and the Restatement. Perhaps most significant is the substitution of the term "surplus" for "profit." Courts sometimes use the word "profit" to refer to the extent to which contracting would improve a party's well-being. Courts are often conflicted, however, in their terminology, with great variation in use of the terms "profit," "gross profit," "net profit," and "clearprofit.""Surplus" refers to the excess of benefits over costseither anticipated, in the sense that the injured party would have realized them had the other party performed, or actual, as a measure of the state of affairs given the other party's breach.This excess is a measure of any improvement in well-being resulting from the contract in question, including a negative improvement. In the case of a contract for which the anticipated surplus was positive, the party would have been able to use the surplus to, for instance, take a vacation, pay for overhead expenses that were not incurred as a result of this contract, or invest in other ventures. Also standing in the way of a uniform rule for contract damages is the fact that consumers do not contract in order to derive a "profit" in the customary sense at all. Rather, consumers, like businesses, contract in order to improve their well-being, which the concept of "surplus" captures.
Also of practical significance is The Shadow Code's avoidance of the terms "consequential" and "incidental" costs. The U.C.C. and Restatement differ on the definition of "consequential losses," with the former including lost profitsand the latter referring to personal injury and property damage.In the contract remedies literature, beginning with an influential article by Lon Fuller and William Perdue, incidental costs are costs incurred by a party, not because he or she was obliged by contract to incur them, but because incurring them enhances the surplus hoped for from the other's performance.It is analytically helpful to distinguish the costs of performance ("performance costs" in The Shadow Code) from "surplus enhancingcosts" (in The Shadow Code). Modern scholars have adopted Fuller and Perdue's terminology.However, the usage bears no relationship to the Restatement's or the U.C.C.'s meaning of "incidental costs," which refers to the costs a party incurs in order to minimize the losses resulting from another's failure to perform.In the comments and illustrations to The Shadow Code, costs incurred only from the other party's breach are called "breach-related costs." The black letter of The Shadow Code avoids distinguishing among types of costs incurred as a result of contracting because all losses are recoverable, subject to well recognized limitations described in SC 4. This terminology is useful in explaining (as shown in the comments and illustrations) the variety of expenditures that might reduce anticipated or actual surplus.
Finally, the analytical structure of the surplus-based approach to contract damages facilitates theoretical analysis of contract damages rules. For several decades, scholars have attempted to derive models of legal remedies for breach of contract in order to evaluate incentives. Over time, these models have evolved from a very general mathematical form that was useful for analysis of incentives to make and break promises, to rely on promises, and to mitigate losses.They were not particularly subtle and failed to capture the variety of circumstances in which contracts are breached. Unlike The Shadow Code, they were not designed to be universally applicable tools for calculating damages. Subsequent models based the foundation of their approaches on total benefitsrather than on surplus, as The Shadow Code does, or, if they focused on surplus, presented a series of formulas, in the manner of the U.C.C., applicable to breaches of different types.The universality of a complex model based on lost surplusprovided the foundation for The Shadow Code. While it captured the variety of circumstances in which contracts might be breached, it was cumbersome and unwieldy in application. The Shadow Code presents a straightforward version of that model.
Analytically, the surplus-based approach requires only a comparison of the anticipated and actual surplus:
Damage Award =Anticipated SurplusminusActual Surplus Because each surplus is affected by anticipated and actual benefits and costs, and because all types of costs fall under one of the headings of performance, surplus-enhancing or breach-related, the surplus-based damages rule may be applied in various ways. The structure of the surplus-based rule invites one to compare the injured party's position after the breach (actual surplus) with the position that party would have occupied following performance (anticipated surplus):
Damage Award =(Anticipated Benefits - Anticipated Performance Costs - Anticipated Surplus-Enhancing Costs)minus(Actual Benefits - Actual Performance Costs - Actual Surplus-Enhancing Costs - Breach-Related Costs) There are many variations on this formula. One of the most useful is one that compares anticipated and actual revenues on one hand and anticipated and actual costs on the other:
Damage Award =(Anticipated - Actual Benefits)minus(Anticipated - Actual Costs). For instance, the surplus-based rule provides that an injured party who incurred no costs and derived no benefit from the breaching party is entitled to her lost surplus (anticipated benefits less anticipated costs). More complicated cases involving partial performance (some actual benefit), cover or resale (some actual benefit and actual cost), and breaches of warranty may similarly be analyzed without recognizing any distinction between buyers and sellers in the basic structure of the rule. The comments and illustrations to The Shadow Code provide computations for every category of circumstances in which contracts are breached.

questions.question: Whether a single surplus-based damages formula-measuring the difference between anticipated surplus and actual surplus-can uniformly calculate compensatory damages for all types of contract breaches.

Whether a surplus-based framework is mathematically equivalent to the various existing, disparate damages rules and can reproduce their monetary awards while simplifying terminology and reducing doctrinal ambiguity.

Whether framing contract remedies around anticipated versus actual surplus better aligns damages with the compensatory goal, clarifies limitations (such as certainty, mitigation, and foreseeability), and facilitates analysis of the incentives created by remedies.

matched_themes: What counterfactual baseline should courts use to measure plaintiffs' losses for compensation purposes?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?
Is a surplus-based damages rule practically equivalent to existing formulas and does it reduce ambiguity in application?
Should contract damages be measured as lost surplus (net benefit) rather than expectancy or market value as a general rule?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
Would a surplus-based (lost-surplus or net-benefit) formula for contract damages simplify and improve compensation and incentives compared with existing measures?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 80califlrev563!!ARTICLE: The Principle of Hadley v. Baxendale.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Principle of Hadley v. Baxendale.

shared_topics.topic: the role and standard of foreseeability/remoteness in contract damages
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze Hadley v. Baxendale's remoteness/foreseeability limitation — Paper A critiques Hadley for imposing an excessively strict (probability-level) foreseeability standard and argues for a proximate-cause/reasonable-foreseeability approach (applied at breach), while Paper B incorporates a foreseeability limit into SC 4 and discusses how damages should be confined to losses that are reasonably foreseeable when computing surplus.

shared_topics.topic: how expectation damages (lost profits) should be calculated (surplus/expectation framework)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the computation of expectation-type awards for lost profits: Paper A discusses direct versus consequential lost profits and argues for a foreseeability standard tied to types of interests (lost profits among them), while Paper B offers a unified, surplus-based formula (anticipated minus actual surplus) that yields expectation-equivalent awards including lost profits across buyer/seller and partial-performance contexts.

shared_topics.topic: the distinction and recovery rules for general/direct versus special/consequential/incidental losses
shared_topics.justification: Both papers treat the legal split between general (direct) and special (consequential or incidental) damages: Paper A traces that split to Hadley and critiques its operation; Paper B criticizes fragmented U.C.C./Restatement definitions (and confused uses of 'consequential' and 'incidental') and replaces them with a single surplus framework that subsumes those categories.

shared_topics.topic: recognized limitations on recovery (certainty, mitigation, mitigation duties and non-speculative proof)
shared_topics.justification: Both works explicitly address the classical limits on contract remedies — Paper A situates remoteness among limiting doctrines and discusses evidence and policy; Paper B codifies these limits in SC 4 (certainty, mitigation, foreseeability) and explains how the surplus calculation accommodates them.

shared_topics.topic: normative reform toward a unified or alternative damages regime
shared_topics.justification: Both are reform-minded: Paper A advocates abandoning Hadley in favor of a regime based on proximate cause combined with contractual allocation and fair disclosure, while Paper B proposes the Shadow Code as a single, surplus-based section to unify and clarify the U.C.C./Restatement damage rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 104marqlrev141!!ARTICLE: THE MYTH OF OPTIMAL EXPECTATION DAMAGES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE MYTH OF OPTIMAL EXPECTATION DAMAGES

shared_topics.topic: whether expectation damages (a single uniform measure) are the optimal default rule for breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly critiques the canonical law-and-economics justification for a single optimal expectation-damages rule (the efficient-breach argument) and argues that a single default is implausible across heterogeneous parties; Paper B engages the same question by restating the compensatory goal in surplus terms and proposing a single surplus-based formula that it argues is normatively equivalent to expectation-based doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: how to compute damages in practice (formulas and components: anticipated v. actual benefits and costs, cover/resale, partial performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses what expectation damages should include (e.g., replacement costs and transaction costs) and highlights how different fact patterns can alter proper measurement; Paper B offers an explicit surplus-based computational formula (anticipated minus actual surplus) and maps that formula onto the various UCC/Restatement computations for cover, resale, partial performance and warranty cases.

shared_topics.topic: the role and treatment of various cost categories and limits (transaction costs, performance costs, breach‑related costs, consequential/incidental losses, mitigation and foreseeability)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises concerns about transaction costs and how expectation damages may over- or under-compensate when those costs or incentives are present; Paper B systematically classifies costs (performance, surplus‑enhancing, breach‑related) and codifies limitations such as mitigation, reasonable certainty, and foreseeability within its surplus framework.

shared_topics.topic: whether damages rules should be uniformly applied by courts or reflect parties' contractual choices and heterogeneity
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that sophisticated parties negotiate a variety of damages/termination prices and that courts’ resistance to contracting-out of damages is problematic; Paper B addresses the desirability of a unified, general principle (the Shadow Code) that applies across buyers, sellers, consumers and merchants, while situating that principle alongside existing contract terms and evidentiary choices.

shared_topics.topic: use of law-and-economics and incentive analysis to justify and critique damages doctrines (efficient breach, incentives to invest/rely/mitigate)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages the law-and-economics literature (efficient breach, incentive effects, over‑investment and reliance problems) to challenge the simple economic case for expectation damages; Paper B deploys an economic surplus model to reveal incentives and to show how a single surplus-based rule clarifies the incentive effects of remedies and aligns with UCC/Restatement goals.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 39umiamilrev723!!ARTICLE: Economic Theory and the Present Value of Future Lost Earnings: An Integration, Unification, and Simplification of Court Adopted Methodologies
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Economic Theory and the Present Value of Future Lost Earnings: An Integration, Unification, and Simplification of Court Adopted Methodologies

shared_topics.topic: unifying and simplifying disparate damages rules into a single principled methodology
shared_topics.justification: Both papers criticize the multiplicity and ambiguity of court-adopted rules for calculating damages and propose a single, overarching rule (The Shadow Code's surplus rule in Paper A; a preferred, conceptually valid present-value/offset methodology in Paper B) that consolidates existing formulas while preserving their legitimate results.

shared_topics.topic: need for precise economic and legal definitions/terminology to avoid bias and error
shared_topics.justification: Both works argue that inconsistent or incorrect definitions (Paper A: profit vs surplus, consequential/incidental costs; Paper B: nominal vs real/below-market interest rates and related parameters) produce inconsistent and biased awards, and that careful definitional clarity is necessary for fair computation.

shared_topics.topic: mathematical equivalence of alternative formulations when parameters are correctly specified
shared_topics.justification: Each paper shows that apparently different judicial formulas are mathematically equivalent to the proposed unified approach if the underlying quantities are correctly defined and estimated, and uses that equivalence to justify preferring a clearer, single framework.

shared_topics.topic: managing evidentiary limits and preventing speculative or inequitable awards
shared_topics.justification: Both discuss legal limits on recoverable damages—concern about overly speculative awards and the need for proof with reasonable certainty, mitigation, and foreseeability (SC 4 in Paper A; the Supreme Court's and circuits' concerns about speculation and acceptable methodologies in Paper B)—and propose frameworks that incorporate those limitations.

shared_topics.topic: applying economic theory to evaluate incentives created by damages rules and to guide legal methodology

shared_topics.topic: normative grounding of contractual obligations — moral obligation, voluntariness, and the expectation vs reliance distinction

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal unification and clarity in remedies for breach (reconciling UCC/Restatement/common‑law rules)

compared_to.partner_node_id: 27iowajcorpl505!!SYMPOSIUM IN MEMORY OF DAVID H. VERNON:Contract Lore
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM IN MEMORY OF DAVID H. VERNON:Contract Lore

shared_topics.justification: Both works argue that surface rules or rhetoric (whether folk beliefs about contracts or the multiplicity of U.C.C. and Restatement formulas) obscure a single compensatory aim: Paper A exposes widely repeated but misleading doctrinal statements as 'lore' that conceal how courts actually operate, and Paper B offers the 'Shadow Code' to reveal and restate the unifying surplus-based principle behind disparate statutory and Restatement provisions.

shared_topics.topic: limitations on recoverable damages (certainty, mitigation, foreseeability)

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Recovery of Damages for Lost Profits: The Historical Development

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: When Lightning Strikes: Hadley v. Baxendale's Probability Standard Applied to Long-Shot Contracts

shared_topics.topic: limits on recovery for speculative or low-probability gains (foreseeability/probability)

papers.node_id: 2001wislrev681!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:COMMENTARY BREACH AND PENALTY AS CONTRACTUAL NORM AND CONTRACTUAL ANOMIE
papers.title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:COMMENTARY BREACH AND PENALTY AS CONTRACTUAL NORM AND CONTRACTUAL ANOMIE
papers.abstract:
In the paper on which I have been privileged to be asked to comment,Kathryn Hendley, Peter Murrell, and Randi Ryterman report some of the results of an outstanding piece of empirical research. They have examined the contracting behavior of enterprises in the most important post-communist, aspirant capitalist economy, Russia, and have tried to assess how far those enterprises are able to adopt capitalist commercial practices. In a number of other recent papers written independently or jointly by the authors (and Barry Ickes) and in Hendley's book on Russian labor law, the extent of the adoption of a range of these practices has been examined. The paper on which I have been asked to comment concentrates on the use of penalties in contract disputes.
The authors show that in Russia there is, by comparison to the situation in the established capitalist economies, a remarkably high reliance on penalties, and a similarly high judicial tolerance of these. Three variables (the first two themselves disaggregated into further variables) are used to explain the propensity to use penalties: the extent of the plaintiff's market power; the extent of the plaintiff's legal activism (as opposed to reliance on non-legal remedies including cooperation based on longstanding relationships); and the extent to which efficient breach is regarded as legitimate. In the established capitalist economies, the first two variables would be expected to be strongly positively correlated with a propensity to use penalties. But Russia very decidedly does not have such an economy and a very important purpose of the research is to "inquire whether the outcomes that would be predicted by Western theorizing on contract law have come to pass." The authors' conclusion is that:
We found little support for the common wisdom that enterprises with market power are taking advantage of the less powerful by forcing them to include penalty clauses and then insisting that those penalties be paid if payment is overdue. The survey results also indicate that the availability and use of punitive damages for contractual breach do not translate into an unwillingness to pursue advantageous business opportunities. Put more simply, the use of penalties is not linked to an antipathy for efficient breaches. On the other hand, there is an undeniable link between legal activism and the propensity to use penalties, suggesting that an overall familiarity with legalistic tactics spills over into the realm of remedies. The support for our hypothesis that the use of penalties will decreasewhen trading partners have a longstanding relationship was tepid at best.
The authors show that in important respects the behavior of Russian enterprises differs from what we would expect in capitalist economies, but they do not put forward an overall explanation of this. I tentatively wish to do so.
also wish to make explicit a point about legal and economic policy formulation that the authors leave implicit until the conclusion of Penalties. The authors' research has been difficult, but it is vital that such research be carried out. Not only are there the problems of conducting empirical research in a foreign country and language, but the Russian economy in general and commercial legal system in particular are currently in a state of disorganization that compounds these problems. Furthermore, from what one can gather, such is the extent of gangsterism in Russia that research of this sort can be attended by personal danger. Though it would be trivially easy to point to failings in the methodology of the research if one assesses it by the standards of what one might have done were that research conducted in, say, the United States, it is to the enormous credit of the authors that they have managed to achieve what they have achieved under the circumstances. And this work is, as I say, vital. It is a most commendable attempt to conduct empirical research into the restructuring of the Russian economy, and to offer recommendations for reform. This is a welcome change, for it is a crucial feature of the Russian restructuring that it has been guided by advice formulated on merely theoretical grounds. This research is further evidence that this advice has therefore been in important respects shamefully suspect.

questions.question: To what extent do firms in post-communist Russia include and have courts enforce contractual penalty clauses as a common remedy for breach?
Is a firm's propensity to use contractual penalties related to its market power, its tendency to rely on formal legal tactics (legal activism), or the duration/quality of its trading relationships?
Does the availability and use of contractual penalties discourage firms from engaging in efficient breaches or pursuing otherwise advantageous business opportunities?

matched_themes: Should courts allow punitive or other extracompensatory damages for willful or abusive contract breaches, and what are the efficiency and fairness trade-offs?
Do pre-agreed breach-payment clauses (liquidated damages) change parties' beliefs about norms and moral aversion to breach, and do such clauses increase or decrease the willingness to breach?
Should parties be presumptively permitted to contractually specify nonstandard damage remedies, or should courts retain authority to impose defaults?
How should courts treat and enforce stipulated remedies (liquidated damages clauses) versus substituting judicial remedies?
How do transaction costs, enforcement frictions, and institutional realities alter the theoretical efficiency of breach-plus-compensation?

Can party-designed enforcement mechanisms (pre-agreed penalties, arbitration, bonding, reputational systems) reliably produce efficient breach outcomes without judicial intervention, and when do they fail?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
Do enforceable contractual damage remedies substitute for or complement informal relational governance in franchise and other repeated relationships?
Do doctrinal differences across legal traditions produce measurable differences in contracting behavior and economic outcomes in practice?

Should contractual clauses that impose predetermined monetary payments for breach be treated as punitive (unenforceable) or as enforceable measures of compensation, and what factors predict courts' enforcement decisions?

Do repeat players, contract drafting strategies, secrecy about dispute outcomes, and presentation techniques enable stronger parties to extract one-sided terms and undermine the protective aims of contract law?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 84nclrev1927!!ARTICLE: A BRIDGE, A TAX REVOLT, AND THE STRUGGLE TO INDUSTRIALIZE: A COMMENT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A BRIDGE, A TAX REVOLT, AND THE STRUGGLE TO INDUSTRIALIZE: A COMMENT

shared_topics.topic: measurement and form of remedies for breach (mitigation, restrictive measures, and penalties)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the Luten Bridge decision's choice of a restrictive measure of damages and the duty to mitigate after anticipatory breach; Paper B empirically examines widespread use of contractual penalties and punitive remedies in Russia and how courts tolerate those remedies.

shared_topics.topic: legitimacy and consequences of efficient breach as a contractual norm
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames anticipatory breach versus an obligation to perform as a jurisprudential question about whether promissors must perform or may breach and pay damages; Paper B explicitly investigates whether Russian firms regard efficient breach as legitimate and whether penalty clauses signal antipathy to efficient breach.

shared_topics.topic: role of judges, courts, and legal enforcement in shaping contract norms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how common-law judges and reported decisions develop and migrate contractual doctrines (e.g., mitigation, anticipatory breach) over time; Paper B studies judicial tolerance of penalties and links firms' legal activism and court behavior to the enforcement of contractual norms.

shared_topics.topic: influence of wider economic and political context on contract performance and breach decisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates Rockingham County's breach in the economic and political clash between agrarianism and New South development, showing context drove the refusal to perform; Paper B situates contracting behavior and reliance on penalties within post-communist Russia's institutional disorganization, market structure, and informal threats.

shared_topics.topic: value of grounded empirical or case-based inquiry for understanding and reforming contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends the pedagogic and analytic value of detailed case studies (adding local facts to doctrinal rules) for understanding legal reasoning and doctrine; Paper B praises and relies on empirical field research to reveal how contract remedies operate in practice and to inform policy recommendations for legal reform.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 77ucinlrev991!!LAW AND LITERATURE SYMPOSIUM: "SOME SORT OF CHRONICLER I AM": NARRATION AND THE POETRY OF LAWRENCE JOSEPH: ARTICLE: RESTITUTIONARY DISGORGEMENT AS A MORAL COMPASS FOR BREACH OF CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: LAW AND LITERATURE SYMPOSIUM: "SOME SORT OF CHRONICLER I AM": NARRATION AND THE POETRY OF LAWRENCE JOSEPH: ARTICLE: RESTITUTIONARY DISGORGEMENT AS A MORAL COMPASS FOR BREACH OF CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: monetary remedies beyond expectation damages (disgorgement, penalties, punitive damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the Restatement's authorization of restitutionary disgorgement for opportunistic breaches as an alternative to expectation damages, while Paper B empirically examines the widespread contractual use and judicial tolerance of penalty clauses and punitive damages in Russia; both engage substantively with when and why courts and parties employ non‑expectation monetary remedies.

shared_topics.topic: deterrence and punishment as goals of contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds disgorgement's novel incorporation of condemnation, deterrence, and punishment into contract remedies, challenging the traditional choice/efficient breach model, and Paper B investigates whether penalty regimes function as deterrents in practice and how their availability influences parties' behavior.

shared_topics.topic: the legitimacy of efficient breach and normative models of contract behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts the efficient‑breach/utilitarian framework with virtue‑ethics and corrective‑justice rationales underpinning disgorgement, and Paper B explicitly studies whether efficient breach is regarded as legitimate in Russian commercial practice and how that perception correlates with penalty use.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts, legal doctrine, and legal culture in shaping remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how the Restatement black‑letter rule and judges' proper application could reshape contractual doctrine (mitigation, foreseeability, expectancy), while Paper B documents judicial tolerance and legal activism in Russia as decisive factors in the adoption and enforcement of penalty clauses, linking doctrinal application to on‑the‑ground outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: how remedy design affects contracting practices and renegotiation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues disgorgement may incentivize renegotiation and alter parties' promise‑keeping behavior, and Paper B examines whether the presence of penalty clauses (and longstanding relational practices) changes enterprises' reliance on legal versus cooperative nonlegal remedies when contracts are breached.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 104marqlrev141!!ARTICLE: THE MYTH OF OPTIMAL EXPECTATION DAMAGES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE MYTH OF OPTIMAL EXPECTATION DAMAGES

shared_topics.topic: use of penalties versus expectation damages as the appropriate remedy for breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically studies the high reliance on and judicial tolerance for penalty clauses in Russian contracts, while Paper B critiques the conventional assumption that expectation damages are the universally optimal remedy and highlights that parties may prefer heterogeneous measures (including penalties) depending on context.

shared_topics.topic: the explanatory power of the efficient-breach theory for real-world contracting behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A tests whether reliance on penalties signals hostility to efficient breach and finds little linkage, and Paper B interrogates the efficient-breach rationale for defaulting to expectation damages, arguing the model's assumptions often fail and its predictions are incomplete.

shared_topics.topic: how courts' default rules and judicial intervention shape or contradict parties' contractual choices about remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents judicial tolerance of punitive penalty clauses in Russia and links that tolerance to legal activism, whereas Paper B shows how courts in established systems often enforce a one-size default (expectation damages) or strike down contractual deviations, raising questions about damages exceptionalism.

shared_topics.topic: the role of bargaining power/market power in determining remedial provisions in contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically investigates whether plaintiffs with market power impose penalty clauses on weaker parties and finds little support for that common wisdom, while Paper B emphasizes that variation in parties' characteristics and bargaining positions should lead to diverse negotiated damages provisions rather than a single optimal measure.

shared_topics.topic: empirical evidence challenging law-and-economics theoretical assumptions about default remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A provides empirical survey data from post-communist Russia that contradicts some Western theoretical predictions about penalties and contracting, and Paper B draws on critiques and empirical puzzles to argue that law-and-economics models (favoring expectation damages) oversimplify party heterogeneity and contractual practices.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1517!!ARTICLE: WILLFULNESS VERSUS EXPECTATION: A PROMISOR-BASED DEFENSE OF WILLFUL BREACH DOCTRINE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: WILLFULNESS VERSUS EXPECTATION: A PROMISOR-BASED DEFENSE OF WILLFUL BREACH DOCTRINE

shared_topics.topic: remedies exceeding expectation (penalties, disgorgement, and punitive clauses)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes judicial doctrines that award promisees more than expectation (disgorgement of promisor gains) when breaches are "willful," while Paper B empirically examines the widespread use and judicial tolerance of contractual penalty clauses and punitive remedies in Russian commercial practice.

shared_topics.topic: how remedy design shapes ex ante contracting incentives and credible commitments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that enhanced remedies for willful breach function to allow promisors to credibly commit ex ante not to take low-cost breaches, altering prices and bargaining; Paper B investigates whether the availability and use of penalties influence firms' willingness to pursue or avoid breaches and how that affects contracting strategies.

shared_topics.topic: the normative status of efficient breach versus punitive/deterrent approaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends limiting "efficient breach" leeway by treating some breaches as out-of-bounds and justifying stronger remedies to deter them, while Paper B explores whether efficient breach is regarded as legitimate in practice and whether penalties reflect antipathy to or acceptance of efficient breach.

shared_topics.topic: role of courts, enforcement practices, and legal culture in shaping contract outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on doctrinal rules courts use to identify and sanction willful breaches and how those doctrines operate, while Paper B provides empirical evidence on judicial tolerance, legal activism, and how local enforcement practices in Russia affect use of penalties and contracting behavior.

shared_topics.topic: deterrence of opportunistic, low-cost-to-avoid breaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers its concept of "willful breach" on opportunistic breaches that could have been avoided at little or no joint cost and endorses denying promisor gains to deter them; Paper B considers whether penalties are used to deter opportunistic misconduct in contracts and whether market power or relationships mediate that deterrence.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 116columlrev2005!!ARTICLE: ECONOMIC ANALYSIS OF CONTRACT LAW FROM THE INTERNAL POINT OF VIEW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ECONOMIC ANALYSIS OF CONTRACT LAW FROM THE INTERNAL POINT OF VIEW

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how stipulated-damages and penalty clauses affect behavior of 'internalizers' versus 'externalizers'—including whether such clauses change perceived primary duties and crowd out moral motivation—while Paper B empirically documents the widespread use and judicial tolerance of penalty clauses in Russian contracting and investigates how their presence correlates with contracting behavior.

shared_topics.topic: the legitimacy and role of 'efficient breach' in shaping contractual remedies and practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A theorizes how perform-or-pay regimes and doctrines like willful breach interact with notions of efficient breach (and how internalizers respond to them), whereas Paper B empirically asks whether efficient breach is regarded as legitimate in Russian commerce and tests whether penalties are used to punish or deter efficient breaches.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules and norms (versus sanctions) influence contracting behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops the internalizer/externalizer distinction to show that legal norms can directly guide action and sometimes crowd out moral motivations, and Paper B shows that familiarity with legalistic tactics and the broader legal environment (including acceptance of penalties) shapes enterprise contracting strategies in Russia.

shared_topics.topic: the role of judicial enforcement, tolerance, and institutional context in the functioning of contractual remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how doctrines (penalty doctrine, willful breach, duress, enforcement standards) alter incentives and information for different types of actors, while Paper B documents the Russian judiciary's tolerance of penalties and argues that institutional disorganization and enforcement patterns materially affect how penalties are used and perceived.

shared_topics.topic: using empirical evidence to evaluate and reform contract law doctrine and policy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws on empirical literature to motivate modeling of internalizers and to argue that assumptions about legal subjects should inform optimal doctrine, and Paper B provides original empirical research on Russian contracting to challenge theoretical prescriptions and to inform legal and economic policy recommendations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 14jempiricallegalstud527!!ARTICLE: Unbundling Efficient Breach: An Experiment
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Unbundling Efficient Breach: An Experiment

shared_topics.justification: Both works examine how non-economic factors affect breach-related behavior: Paper A links firms' legal activism and familiarity with legal tactics to propensity to use penalties, and Paper B documents how moral intuitions and inequality aversion (normative attitudes) shape acceptance of different types of breaches.

shared_topics.topic: empirical investigation of contracting norms using non-doctrinal methods
shared_topics.justification: Each paper contributes empirical evidence on contracting practices beyond doctrinal argument: Paper A reports survey-based field evidence from Russian firms on penalty use, whereas Paper B provides controlled, incentivized laboratory evidence on how breach motives and compensation affect behavior.

shared_topics.topic: use of contractual penalties and stipulated remedies (liquidated damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically documents the high prevalence and judicial tolerance of penalty clauses in Russian commercial contracts and analyzes factors predicting their use; Paper B treats stipulated remedies (including liquidated damages) as party-designed enforcement devices and evaluates their efficiency relative to damages and specific performance.

shared_topics.topic: the concept and legitimacy of efficient breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates whether Russian firms view efficient breach as legitimate and whether penalty use deters opportunistic refusal to perform, while Paper B centers on the efficient-breach framework and asks which remedies (damages, specific performance, or stipulated remedies) best promote Pareto-superior breaches.

shared_topics.topic: the role of nonlegal market mechanisms (reputation, long‑term relationships, self‑help) in achieving enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares legal activism to reliance on nonlegal remedies such as cooperation based on longstanding trading relationships and finds limited evidence that relationships reduce penalties; Paper B analyzes how market forces (reputation), bonding, arbitration, and other self-help arrangements can substitute for or complement judicial remedies to induce efficient performance.

shared_topics.topic: how institutional and judicial context shapes contracting behavior and remedy choice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links Russian institutional features — legal disorganization, judicial tolerance of penalties, and modes of legal activism — to distinctive contracting practices that depart from Western predictions; Paper B examines how courts' remedy rules (e.g., routine specific performance versus monetary damages) affect ex ante contract formation, ex post renegotiation costs, and the set of exchanges parties are willing to enter.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Dependent Promises in the History of Leases and Other Contracts

shared_topics.topic: when breach of one party justifies withholding performance or triggers other remedies (dependency of obligations vs penalties)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the doctrinal question of whether one party's breach justifies the other's non‑performance (i.e., whether promises are dependent or independent), using historical examples like sale and lease covenants; Paper B empirically examines how Russian firms use contractual penalties and whether such remedies substitute for or discourage 'efficient breach' and refusal to perform.

shared_topics.topic: comparative and historical development of contract doctrines across jurisdictions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reevaluates the asserted historical trajectory (England and France) from independent to dependent promises and asks why doctrines changed or persisted; Paper B compares Russian contracting outcomes to those predicted by Western contract theory and seeks explanations for divergence from established capitalist practices.

shared_topics.topic: the role of judges and judicial norms in shaping contract enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how judges (e.g., Lord Mansfield and other justices) influenced whether promises were treated as dependent or independent; Paper B documents judicial tolerance of penalty clauses in Russia and links judicial behavior (legal activism/tolerance) to patterns of contractual enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between formal legal rules and commercial practices/relationships (including the legitimacy of efficient breach)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links doctrinal choices about dependence/independence to commercial reasons and property/contract practice (e.g., leases, expectations of parties), while Paper B studies how market power, longstanding trading relationships, and attitudes toward efficient breach affect use of penalties and real‑world contracting behavior.

shared_topics.topic: tension between extracompensatory penalties and the goal of efficient breach / predictability of breach costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates whether the availability of penalties discourages opportunistic or efficient breaches (finding little linkage), while Paper B develops the theoretical tension between disincentives (punitive relief) and the contract-law aim of predictable exit prices and efficient exchanges.

shared_topics.topic: role of legal institutions, judicial behavior, and legal culture (legal activism) in shaping contracting norms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links firms' propensity to use penalties to their legal activism and highlights the impact of a disordered judicial/legal environment in post‑communist Russia; Paper B examines how the choice of institutional forum (courts/common law versus legislation) and judicial application affects whether extracompensatory remedies can be viably imposed.

shared_topics.topic: limits and contextualization of extracompensatory relief (severability, transaction‑specific rules, and relational constraints)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A tests contextual factors such as longstanding relationships and market power as limits on penalty use (with mixed support), whereas Paper B argues that extracompensatory damages are viable only when limited to conceptually severable subcategories (e.g., certain transaction types) and discusses how scope and implementation determine collateral effects on the broader pool of transactions.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how the availability and use of penalties link to broader policy and legal reform in a transitioning economy, and Paper B systematically identifies and evaluates the policy concerns that should determine the scope of liability for commercial loss.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents high judicial tolerance for penalties in Russia and considers its implications for market behavior and reform, while Paper B critiques the prevailing judicial application of Hadley v. shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys pending lawsuits, critiques their pleading of remedies, and proposes statutory and common-law paths to achieve disgorgement; Paper B links firms' legal activism to propensity to invoke penalties and offers empirical-grounded recommendations for legal and economic reform of contractual enforcement.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A reports unusually high judicial tolerance for penalty enforcement in the Russian context and discusses institutional factors affecting enforcement, while Paper B surveys case law demonstrating that courts sometimes enforce or fashion disgorgement and other deterrent remedies despite doctrinal prejudices against punishment in contract law.

shared_topics.topic: implications for law and policy reform based on judicial practice and doctrinal interpretation

papers.node_id: 2001wislrev639!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:COMMENTARY PUNITIVE DAMAGES FOR CONTRACTUAL BREACHES IN COMPARATIVE PERSPECTIVE: THE USE OF PENALTIES BY RUSSIAN ENTERPRISES
papers.title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:COMMENTARY PUNITIVE DAMAGES FOR CONTRACTUAL BREACHES IN COMPARATIVE PERSPECTIVE: THE USE OF PENALTIES BY RUSSIAN ENTERPRISES
papers.authors: Kathryn Hendley; Peter Murrell; Randi Ryterman
papers.abstract: The remedies available for breach of contract vary among legal systems. In most European countries, breaching parties may be required to pay punitive damages in addition to compensating those left in the lurch for actual losses.In the United States, by contrast, those wronged are generally limited to compensatory damages.Underlying this discord is a fundamental difference in assumptions about how economic actors will respond to the availability of punitive damages for contractual breaches. Comparative analysis provides a means of testing these assumptions when such tests are impossible using information from the United States alone. In this paper, we take advantage of the transition from state socialism to market capitalism in Russia to examine the impact of the introduction of penalties as a possible remedy for non-payment of contractual obligations. Drawing on evidence from a 1997 enterprise survey as well as research into doctrinal development, we investigate how Russian courts and industrial enterprises have responded to this new option, and inquire whether the outcomes that would be predicted by Western theorizing on contract law have come to pass.

questions.question: Does the introduction of punitive contractual penalties reduce non-payment and increase compliance with contract obligations by enterprises?
How do courts and firms actually use the newly available penalty remedy after its introduction (e.g., how frequently and in what circumstances are penalties sought or awarded)?
Do the empirical outcomes following the introduction of penalties align with the predictions of Western economic/theoretical models about how punitive remedies affect contracting behavior?

matched_themes: Should courts allow punitive or other extracompensatory damages for willful or abusive contract breaches, and what are the efficiency and fairness trade-offs?
How should courts treat pre-agreed breach payments and liquidated damages clauses (enforce, reform, apportion, or void)?
How have historical, geographic, institutional, and transnational influences shaped the evolution and transplantation of contract doctrines and remedies?
Do courts actually prefer monetary damages over specific (in-kind) remedies, or do they grant specific relief except when independent reasons exist to deny it?
Are civil-law systems less receptive than common-law systems to permitting breaches that increase overall welfare when compensation is possible?
Should parties be presumptively permitted to contractually specify nonstandard damage remedies, or should courts retain authority to impose defaults?
How should courts treat and enforce stipulated remedies (liquidated damages clauses) versus substituting judicial remedies?
How do transaction costs, enforcement frictions, and institutional realities alter the theoretical efficiency of breach-plus-compensation?

Can party-designed enforcement mechanisms (pre-agreed penalties, arbitration, bonding, reputational systems) reliably produce efficient breach outcomes without judicial intervention, and when do they fail?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
Should courts award disgorgement or force surrender of breacher gains in addition to compensation to deter opportunistic breaches?
Should courts police and limit supracompensatory contractual remedies (penalty-like clauses), or does allowing parties to contract for such terms respect autonomy and promote efficient contracting?
Do enforceable contractual damage remedies substitute for or complement informal relational governance in franchise and other repeated relationships?
How should remedial and enforcement rules be structured to achieve efficient behavior when populations include both internalizers and externalizers?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
Do parties and courts actually choose heterogeneous, context-tailored damage provisions in contracting, and under what conditions would such customization be voluntarily chosen or socially desirable?
Do doctrinal differences across legal traditions produce measurable differences in contracting behavior and economic outcomes in practice?
When and under what standards should courts award disgorgement or remedies that strip gains from breaching parties?

Should contractual clauses that impose predetermined monetary payments for breach be treated as punitive (unenforceable) or as enforceable measures of compensation, and what factors predict courts' enforcement decisions?
When is an indirect remedy (one that induces self-compliance) preferable to a direct remedy that delivers the outcome?

papers.node_id: 77ucinlrev991!!LAW AND LITERATURE SYMPOSIUM: "SOME SORT OF CHRONICLER I AM": NARRATION AND THE POETRY OF LAWRENCE JOSEPH: ARTICLE: RESTITUTIONARY DISGORGEMENT AS A MORAL COMPASS FOR BREACH OF CONTRACT
papers.title: LAW AND LITERATURE SYMPOSIUM: "SOME SORT OF CHRONICLER I AM": NARRATION AND THE POETRY OF LAWRENCE JOSEPH: ARTICLE: RESTITUTIONARY DISGORGEMENT AS A MORAL COMPASS FOR BREACH OF CONTRACT
papers.abstract:
There is a quiet revolution underway. Section 39 of the pending Restatement (Third) of Restitution and Unjust Enrichment sanctions a restitutionary remedy of disgorgement where one profits from an "opportunistic breach."While couched in the language of limitation, this section is breathtaking in its potential transformation of the traditional contractual landscape from a choice model of contract law to a perspective that values keeping promises and condemns certain breaches. Condemnation may support the aims of deterrenceand punishment,conventional goals for criminaland tort lawbut foreign to contract law.The choice model emphasizes individual freedom to choose behavior, including contract breach, without fear of punishment.An actor is free to enter a contract and choose to breach as long as she is prepared to pay for the consequences of breach.In general, contract law does not morally judge the breaching party.Section 39 injectsblameworthiness into the remedy calculation for breach of contract by authorizing restitutionary disgorgement for certain breaches--opportunistic ones.
The title of this new section is "Profit Derived from Opportunistic Breach."The section provides a restitutionary disgorgement remedy for opportunistic breaches of contract. If the contract breach is "both material and opportunistic," the aggrieved party may seek to disgorge "the profit realized by the defaulting promisor as a result of breach."For such breaches, the defendant unjustly sits with a benefit. Disgorgement corrects the imbalance by yielding the profits to the injured party where the breacher derived profits from an opportunistic breach.
But what is an opportunistic breach? No consensus definition exists. It has a pejorative connotation unless one views as an "ultimate virtue" taking selfish advantage of opportunities.At minimum, common conceptions might include exploitive, selfish, and advantageous behavior. Opportunistic may further mean "exploiting opportunities and situations in general, especially in a devious, unscrupulous, or unprincipled way."The Restatement employs "conscious advantage-taking" and "taking without asking."Section 39 limits "opportunism" in the black-letter by requiring the breach to be "deliberate" and "profitable" and dictating further that a damage remedy must be "inadequate."Regardless of the precise definition, section 39 requires an assessment of the breaching party's mens rea and seeks to deter, if not punish, breach. In other words, section 39 creates an incentive for parties to keep their word.
In an article predating the pending Restatement, Professor Andrew Kull, the reporter, poses the question: "Is there a disgorgement remedy for breach of contract?"As the drafter of the Restatement, he now definitively answers the question in the affirmative by providing section 39 towards achieving that end. Section 39 will operationalize the restitutionary disgorgement remedy for a subset of contract breaches. According to Professor Kull, this provision is an "essentially new" rule, although case support already exists.
In Professor Kull's earlier article, published in 2001, he concludes, "Disgorgement awarding the plaintiff more than he lost is justified in a narrow class of cases in which the defendant's election to breach imposes harms that a potential liability for provable damages will not adequately deter."In narrowing the category of applicability, he then offers a "hypothesis, that the necessary breach of contract be both profitable and opportunistic."Section 39 now encapsulates this hypothesis. Professor Kull carefully delimits the precise meters of application of this essentially new rule. His stewardship and thethorough revision process for the Restatement of Restitution evidence the expanse of knowledge and thoughtful consideration that he and the American Law Institute members bring to the project.
With the benefit of hindsight regarding the original version of the Restatement of Restitutionand an ounce of trepidation regarding how the revisions might be misapplied, Professor Kull uses surgical precision to carve the exact contours of any potentially new territory covered by section 39. Will his direction for narrow application be appreciated and understood by students, scholars, lawyers, and judges? Assuming judges "get it right," is it possible that the principles underlying section 39 will strike a chord and have broader implications nonetheless? If so, should we fear this potentially larger significance or embrace it cautiously?
This Article explores the moral underpinnings and potentially broad consequences of restitutionary disgorgement as proposed in the pending Restatement (Third) of Restitution.According to Professor Mark Gergen, the "most important," or perhaps, "best part" of the pending Restatement is the provision for "disgorgement for knowing wrongs in the case of opportunistic breach of contract."Yet, the Reporter unveils the draft Restatement with serious words of demarcation and limitation. Perhaps Professor Kull wisely includes limiting language in order to direct proper applications.
Despite this narrowing context, there may be effects--potentially unintended--that will stem from the underlying moral foundation of the disgorgement remedy. The consequences may be far-reaching for a host of traditional contract doctrines including mitigation, foreseeability, and expectancy. Such effects may include altering the traditional Holmesian choice model of contracts to a conception grounded in moral obligation and judgment.Restitutionary disgorgement for breach of contract warrants support because it broadens the alternatives for remedying contract breach. Embracing the remedy's formalization in the Restatement also necessarily brings a moral stance that encourages keeping promises and deters conscious advantage-taking without asking.
Restitutionary disgorgement lures plaintiffs with its result--stripping defendants' profits from breach. The threat of disgorgement ideally would encourage a potential breaching party to renegotiate with the other party.The remedy offers a wealth-distribution preference for the aggrieved party over the conscious breacher. What is the philosophical rationale for this new preference? The remedy reflects Kantian notions by seeking to treat the non-breaching party as an end rather than a means to an end. Its restitutionary roots are Aristotelian in that the remedy seeks to correct the unjust enrichment. Through the lens of virtue ethics, which focuses on the actor's moral character, does section 39 emphasize the development of moral character? Section 39's focus on the character and motives of the breaching agent appears to comport with a basic conception of virtue ethics.
This moral position poses tension with the utilitarian model of consequentialism that underlies economic influences in American contract law. A utilitarian position includes the translation of all items into money damages and the maximization of well-being that flows as a consequence of the encouraged action. For example, efficient breach theory encourages breach when one party will be economically "better off" and the other party not "worse off" because the breaching party is willing to pay the consequences of breach, such as expectancy damages.
In contrast, the restitutionary disgorgement remedy appears to be inspired by virtue ethics because it requires that one consider the effects of opportunistic breach on the character of the defendant and the plaintiff who might become discouraged or vengeful in the face of insufficient redress for breach. It encourages behavior deemed to be more virtuous--keeping promises or at least treating the vulnerable party better by asking before consciously taking. The monetary remedy--disgorging profits gained through breach--will serve to deter opportunistic breaches, but will not measure plaintiff's harm. It is difficult to understand why plaintiff should receive the wealth preference unless we acknowledge that the remedy seeks to commodifyintangible harms.Accordingly, restitutionary disgorgement for breach of contract favors certain notions of justice over the economic influences of traditional contract law.
This Article will examine the philosophical and practical challenges restitutionary disgorgement poses and concludes that the values Section 39 fosters will move contract law in a desirable direction. Part II of this Article sets forth the new restitutionary disgorgement provision, the pending black-letter restatement of the law. Part III includes an exploration of Professor Kull's rationale supporting disgorgement for opportunistic breach in limited circumstances. This Part will also analyze the language of limitation that purports to limit the new provision's scope. Part IV will suggest the significance of the disgorgement provision despite the prescribed narrow boundaries of its intended application. Part IV will also explore whether this provision sounds the death knell for the efficient breach model.This Article will conclude that the restitutionary disgorgement remedy for opportunistic breach of contract will have significantly broader reach, at least theoretically, than intended, but that we should welcome the conceptual movement because it would import a corrective justice baseline into the field of contract law.

questions.question: Will authorizing disgorgement of profits for opportunistic breaches of contract shift contract law away from a choice-based, economic model (which tolerates breaches if damages are paid) toward a framework that enforces moral obligation and deters opportunistic conduct?

Is a disgorgement remedy for opportunistic contract breaches normatively justified on moral and philosophical grounds (for example, corrective justice, Kantian or virtue-ethics reasons) as compared with traditional monetary damages?

Would adopting a disgorgement remedy for certain breaches produce broader doctrinal and practical effects on remedies, parties' incentives, and established principles governing the consequences of breach?

matched_themes: Should courts allow punitive or other extracompensatory damages for willful or abusive contract breaches, and what are the efficiency and fairness trade-offs?
Should parties and courts adopt fault-based remedial regimes that distinguish among breaches by reason when allocating remedies?
Does giving the promisee a unilateral right to demand performance or elect a damages measure that captures promisor's forgone gains vindicate moral intuitions while preserving ex post efficiency?
Do monetary expectation damages make promisees indifferent between actual performance and monetary compensation?
What standards and procedural safeguards should govern awards of punitive and other nonpecuniary damages in contract disputes to balance compensation and protection against abuse?
Should the promisor or the promisee have the default right to choose between performance and payment to achieve allocative efficiency?
Does the promisor's motive for breaching (loss-avoiding vs gain-seeking) affect how much compensation promisees need to accept nonperformance?

Should remedies and contract law be structured to preserve conditions necessary for moral agency and promissory responsibility, rather than treating promises solely as instruments of economic cooperation?
Does allowing a promisor to breach and pay damages (breach-plus-damages) improve economic efficiency relative to enforcing performance?
Should courts award disgorgement or force surrender of breacher gains in addition to compensation to deter opportunistic breaches?
Should courts police and limit supracompensatory contractual remedies (penalty-like clauses), or does allowing parties to contract for such terms respect autonomy and promote efficient contracting?
How should remedial and enforcement rules be structured to achieve efficient behavior when populations include both internalizers and externalizers?
Should courts strip breachers of gains (disgorgement) in opportunistic or deliberate breaches, and what are the doctrinal and incentive effects of allowing disgorgement remedies in contract law?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
Do courts consider the breaching party's blameworthiness or opportunistic behavior when selecting among compensatory remedies?
Can reflective remedies or penalty-adjustment devices that 'reflect' excess conduct across uncertain legal caps produce better ex-ante incentives when legal standards are uncertain?
When and under what standards should courts award disgorgement or remedies that strip gains from breaching parties?
To what extent should moral blameworthiness and non-economic considerations influence the design and application of contract remedies?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 63washlrev607!!ARTICLE: THE RIGHT TO REQUIRE PERFORMANCE IN INTERNATIONAL SALES: TOWARDS AN INTERNATIONAL INTERPRETATION OF THE VIENNA CONVENTION.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE RIGHT TO REQUIRE PERFORMANCE IN INTERNATIONAL SALES: TOWARDS AN INTERNATIONAL INTERPRETATION OF THE VIENNA CONVENTION.

shared_topics.topic: remedies for breach of contract (disgorgement versus specific performance/right to require performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes a restitutionary disgorgement remedy (Section 39 of the Restatement (Third)) that strips profits from opportunistic breachers, while Paper B examines the scope and international interpretation of the buyer's right to require performance under the Vienna Convention, so both centrally engage with what remedies the law should furnish for breach of contract and when those remedies are appropriate.

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations of contract law — moral obligation versus economic efficiency (the efficient-breach debate)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly contrasts virtue-ethical/Kantian reasons for enforcing promise-keeping with the utilitarian efficient-breach model dominant in American contract theory, and Paper B implicates parallel normative choices by confronting civil-law and common-law philosophies (performance-oriented vs damages-oriented solutions) in the drafting and interpretation of the CISG.

shared_topics.topic: the role of authoritative instruments in shaping contract doctrine and interpretation (Restatements and Conventions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how a Restatement (Third) provision will operationalize and potentially reshape domestic contract doctrine via black-letter rules and moral framing, while Paper B treats the Vienna Convention as a supranational instrument whose text and interpretive approach will guide international and domestic application of sales-contract rules.

shared_topics.topic: reconciling divergent legal traditions and doctrinal concepts in drafting and application
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights tension between the traditional American 'choice' model and a new moralized remedy that may import other legal values, and Paper B describes how UNCITRAL delegates from varied national systems negotiated conceptual differences (civil-law vs common-law) to produce a Convention and seeks an international interpretive approach.

shared_topics.topic: definitional scope and doctrinal uncertainty about key concepts (e.g., 'opportunistic breach' and the 'right to require performance')
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the lack of consensus over what counts as an 'opportunistic breach' and the mens rea required for disgorgement, and Paper B focuses on interpreting the parameters and application of the buyer's right to require performance under the CISG, so both probe the boundaries and meanings of central remedial concepts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 9minnjlscitech861!!SYMPOSIUM: Intentions, Guilt and Social Interactions
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: Intentions, Guilt and Social Interactions

shared_topics.topic: the relevance of actors' intentions or motives to outcomes

shared_topics.topic: how beliefs about sincerity affect whether parties transact or renegotiate
shared_topics.justification: Paper A suggests disgorgement will incentivize renegotiation and keeping promises by altering parties' expectations about breach consequences, and Paper B shows formally that responders accept or reject offers depending on beliefs about the proposer's sincerity, determining whether mutually beneficial exchanges occur.

shared_topics.topic: tension between moral/judgmental norms and standard consequentialist/efficiency models
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts virtue-ethical and Kantian impulses behind disgorgement with the traditional economic 'efficient breach' model, while Paper B challenges standard game-theoretic outcome-only preferences by incorporating guilt/insincerity that make intentions payoff-relevant.

shared_topics.topic: use of sanctions or corrective mechanisms (legal remedies vs social reactions) to enforce norms and trust
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats restitutionary disgorgement as a legal sanction aimed at deterrence, condemnation, and corrective justice for opportunistic breaches, whereas Paper B analyzes social sanctions—rejection, loss of trust, reputational effects and guilt—that alter incentives and sustain prosocial behavior.

shared_topics.topic: inference about unobservable types or mental states (signaling, belief-dependent preferences)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A requires courts to infer the breacher's deliberate, profitable motive to apply Section 39, implicating judgments about character and intent, and Paper B formally models interdependent types and belief-dependent preferences (psychological games) whereby players infer social type/sincerity from behavior.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Attaching Tort Claims to Contract Actions: An Economic Analysis of Contort

shared_topics.topic: injecting deterrence, punishment, or moral judgment into contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that suing in tort can yield punitive or deterrent remedies unavailable in contract, and Paper B argues that disgorgement under §39 expressly introduces blameworthiness and condemnatory incentives into contract law to deter opportunistic breaches.

shared_topics.topic: blurring the doctrinal boundaries between contract, tort, and restitution (the 'contort' phenomenon)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly studies the merger of contract and tort doctrines and tests for attaching tort claims to contract actions, and Paper B treats restitutionary disgorgement as a doctrinal development that shifts contract law toward restitutionary and tort-like principles.

shared_topics.topic: tension between economic/efficiency models and moral or corrective-justice approaches to remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates contract damages goals using an economic model and why traditional limits exist, whereas Paper B contrasts the utilitarian efficient-breach paradigm with virtue-ethics and corrective-justice rationales motivating disgorgement.

shared_topics.topic: potential ripple effects on traditional contract doctrines (foreseeability, mitigation, expectancy, and damages limits)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the rationale for limiting contract damages and the doctrinal tests for attaching tort claims, and Paper B predicts that disgorgement could alter doctrines like mitigation, foreseeability, and expectancy by changing remedial priorities and wealth-transfer incentives.
