shared_topics.justification: Both pieces examine when contract law remedies are insufficient or unavailable and whether tort doctrines should step in: Paper A asks whether promissory fraud liability can exist when contractual enforcement is barred, and Paper B evaluates how the proposed UCC revisions affect the availability and scope of noncontractual remedies in sales law.

shared_topics.topic: policy tradeoffs between freedom of contract and policing egregious deception in commercial transactions

shared_topics.topic: the evidentiary and normative role of an actor's present intent in regulating exchanges
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the promisor's present intent (and its misrepresentation) as a factual basis for fraud liability, distinguishing not intending to perform from intending not to perform; Paper B treats actors' intent (e.g., purposeful evasion of exchange rules or planning to pay fines) as key to whether transactions are criminalized or met with stronger legal responses.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: MODERN MARINE INSURANCE: COVERAGES, CURRENT ISSUES, AND CONNECTIONS:Reform of the Insurance Law of England and Wales - Separate Laws for the Different Needs of Businesses and Consumers

papers.node_id: 11texwesleyanlrev505!!SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:FORESEEABILITY AND DAMAGES:HADLEY V. BAXENDALE: CONTRACT DOCTRINE OR COMPENSATION RULE?
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:FORESEEABILITY AND DAMAGES:HADLEY V. BAXENDALE: CONTRACT DOCTRINE OR COMPENSATION RULE?
papers.abstract:
If you do me a wrong, the ripple effects of that wrong may well - as any philosopher or insurance analyst will tell you - extend almost as far as you like. Some 180 years before the events at Hadley's Mill, commemorated in this conference, lawyers in England had to deal with the question of whether legal liability was equally susceptible to this outgrowth of chaos theory. Take a case of 1674, so briefly reported that we can reproduce it in full:
The plaintiff declares, that the defendant in consideration of £ 10 promised to let him enjoy certain iron mills for six months; and it appeared that the iron mills were worth but £ 20 per annum, and yet damages were given to £ 500 by reason of the loss of stock laid in; and per curiam the Jury may well find such damages, for they are not bound to give only the £ 10 but also all the special damages.
This result, obvious to us, clearly surprised at least someone then, or it would not have been reported (or for that matter appealed). But it is cases such as these - £ 500 damages for deprivation of a benefit worth a mere £ 10 - that set the scene for arguments about remoteness. Unless liability for long-tail consequential losses is to be entirely open-ended, some ad hoc way to limit them has to be found. There are, of course, a number of possible means at hand. In the years before 1854,the courts experimented with several of them (though one would be hard put to it to extract any clear results from this experimentation).Thus, the courts sometimes took refuge in fairly vague doctrines such as causation (did the wrong really cause the damage?).On other occasions, the courts regarded the matter as turning on the content of the duty itself.Sometimes they simply relied on a more vague or impressionistic test that made it clear that some remote losses could not be claimed; however, this test was decidedly non-committal as to the precise grounds of non-liability.But a test of foreseeability of some sort eventually prevailed,and - as everyone knows - was finally cemented in Hadley v. Baxendale.
Now, Hadley v. Baxendale is of course a breach of contract case, and is today invariably taught as part of the contracts course. For a student to mention it in, say, a torts essay is regarded by most as a serious mistake - an error demonstrated, as any law professor will confirm, by high authority on both sides of the Atlantic.But at this point a conundrum arises: why should this be? Why should Hadley v. Baxendale be confined to contract, given that it aims to solve the problem of over-extended liability for consequential losses, and that this problem arises in tort just as much as in contract?
In looking for an answer to this problem, one thing is clear: we have to look at events substantially after 1854. Prior to Hadley, there waslittle, if any, sign that anyone regarded the doctrine of remoteness as applying differently in contract and tort. If anything, the reverse was the case: remoteness was regarded as a unitary doctrine affecting remedies as a whole. Thus, there were clear mid-nineteenth-century suggestions that tort damages were constrained by a foreseeability test fairly similar to that in Hadley. Take the 1850 English decision in Rigby v. Hewitt,a completely ordinary traffic accident case, save that the events leading to the plaintiff's injury were somewhat tortuous.There, Pollock CB clearly inclined to the view that tort liability extended only to "consequences that may reasonably be expected to result,"an opinion he repeated elsewhere.And, in case this discussion is thought too Anglocentric, views of this sort were amply paralleled in a number of early U.S. tort decisions.
Now, it is true that Hadley v. Baxendale itself was argued purely as a contract case. It is also noteworthy that at least one of the authorities the court cited - Art. 1150 of the French Civil Code- referred specifically to contractual rather than delictual liability. Nevertheless, this is probably not a fact to be taken too seriously. Even after Hadley v. Baxendale was decided, a respectable line of authority in England continued to reason in a similar, general way, that all consequential claims were subject to a single remoteness rule, whatever their basis. Matthews v. Discount Corp.in 1869, for example, involved damages for trover.The defendant, who held receipts for jute for a lenderwho had taken them as security, wrongfully parted with them to the by-then insolvent borrower.The lender successfully recovered his loss on what thereby had become an unsecured loan to a judgment-proof debtor.The result is hardly surprising; however, what is interesting is that the Matthews decision was specifically grounded on the basis that the loss was within the Hadley criteria. Again, in Sharp v. Powell,the defendant caused a nuisance by washing down a cart in a public street on a freezing day.The street iced over and a passing horse broke a leg as a result.Bovill CJ denied recovery on remoteness grounds.Although Bovill did not cite Hadley, his reasoning clearly reflected the principle contained in Hadley.Further, if a more uncompromising statement is needed, one can find it in The Notting Hill.Following a marine collision, owners of cargo on the innocent ship suffered a loss of profit when, as a result, their cargo was delivered late on a falling market.They failed on remoteness grounds to recover this from the other vessel, Brett MR saying simply that "the rule with regard to remoteness of damage is precisely the same whether the damages are claimed in actions of contract or of tort, and it has been laid down many times both in Hadley v. Baxendale and other cases."A series of similar judicial statements persisted into the early twentieth century.Nor was this a peculiarlyEnglish phenomenon, a line of transatlantic authorities did much the same thing at the same time.
How then, did the present orthodoxy - that a different, and more generous, rule of remoteness applies in tort - come to be accepted? It is true that the identification of contract and tort was never beyond question, and that occasional early authorities did accept that Hadley was inapplicable to tort.But, the impetus for the systematic separation of tortious and contractual liability, it is suggested, arose from two factors in particular. Both arose from certain features of the then burgeoning tort of negligence. The first of these was the establishment of the rule that the defendant was liable for injuring a plaintiff - in modern terms, owed her a duty of care - if it was even remotely foreseeable that she might suffer damage as a result of his actions. The second was the "thin skull" rule, whose corollary was that the defendant was liable for the full extent of damage suffered by an unusually vulnerable plaintiff. From the 1870s, both of these were perceived to cause difficulties for courts pressed to apply Hadley in the tort context.
Take first the duty of care. The degree of foreseeability required to establish a duty of care has always in practice been much less than that required under Hadley. But, if that degree of foreseeability is established, it then hardly makes sense to take away with the left hand what has just been given by the right by saying that the loss is too remote and therefore the plaintiff cannot recover after all. An 1871 federal decision from California, rejecting the application of Hadley v. Baxendale in tort, demonstrated the point nicely.Bowas v. Pioneer Tow Line, was a classic river collision case, in which a barge under tow carelessly rammed a stern-wheeler from behind.As luck wouldhave it, an engineer was then working on (or rather in) the wheel, and was badly injured.Not surprisingly, the court said the engineer could sue, even though it was hardly foreseeable within Hadley v. Baxendale that he would be there at the time.Further the court chose to allow the action on the simple basis that a different rule applied in tort.
In regard to the "thin skull" rule, the potential for mismatch was equally clear. A defendant took the vulnerable plaintiff as he found her, even if her vulnerability was entirely unforeseeable to him. To that extent, his liability clearly extended beyond the Hadley criteria to damage he could never have contemplated at all. It was an English case that seems first to have invoked this point as a reason to confine Hadley to contract. Phillips v. London & South Western Railway Co.,in 1879 was an ordinary railroad negligence suit, the only complication being that the plaintiff who had been wrongfully disabled was an extraordinarily (and unforeseeably) well-paid physician.The Court of Appeals had no difficulty in saying that the unforeseeable size of the income was out of account.The defendants had to take the plaintiff as they found him.
Cases, such as those referred to above, started the movement. From then onwards we can trace the growth of the idea that remoteness in tort is analytically different from that in contract. In England, a unitary jurisdiction, picking up the trail is not too difficult. The case that effectively cemented the issue was The Argentinoin 1888. The point was simple (and commercially vital). Could the owners of a ship disabled in a maritime collision recover lost charter profits from the owners of the vessel in fault? In the Court of Appeals, one judge held they could not, on the basis that these earnings would not have been in the defendants' contemplation under Hadley's case. But the majority held that, this being a tort suit, Hadley had no application,and allowed the claim.After The Argentino was decided, asteady stream of English casesaccepted that the Hadley limitationsdid not apply in tort; a development paralleled once again in theU.S.
For a time, indeed, the breach appeared absolute, because the accepted view came to be that a tort defendant's liability for consequential loss was not only outside the Hadley v. Baxendale remoteness rule, but was unaffected by any foreseeability criterion at all.When in 1961, the English courts decided that consequential damages in tort were after all subject to a foreseeability limitation,it might have been expected that this would presage a return to the application of Hadley v. Baxendale in tort cases as with contract ones. But doubts were expressed as to this some six years later,and in 1969, Lord Reid in the House of Lords regarded it as clear that the degrees of foreseeability required were different, with a much laxer test applying in tort.Equally, it is hard today to find much support in the U.S. for the application of Hadley in tort.

papers.node_id: 11texwesleyanlrev481!!SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:FORESEEABILITY AND DAMAGES:THE COMMON-LAW HISTORY OF NON-ECONOMIC DAMAGES IN BREACH OF CONTRACT ACTIONS VERSUS WILLFUL BREACH OF CONTRACT ACTIONS
papers.abstract:
If one word could be used to describe the historical common-law philosophy of awarding damages before the mid-nineteenth century, it would be "discretion." If one word could be used to describe the common-law philosophy of awarding damages after the mid-nineteenth century, it would be "limitation." In an era in which courts are creating many limitations on the recoverability of damages in general, one particularly interesting area of law is the recoverability of non-economic damages in breach of contract actions. For purposes of this Article, non-economic compensatory damages primarily include an award for mental or emotional distress, but can also include any other type of damages awarded to make a party whole, absent some pecuniary or economic loss, such as humiliation, embarrassment, or loss of ability to enjoy life. The limiting rules and so-called guidelines adopted by modern American courts regarding the recoverability of non-economic damages in breach of contract actions are disorganized and contradictory at best. How did the law governing this concept become so entangled?
This Article traces the common-law history of the general damages laws of the Anglo-Saxon peoples from 600 A.D. to the more limiting laws regarding recoverability of non-economic damages in breach of contract actions in the United States today. It also explores the progression of courts' control over juries, and the courts' attempt to provide meaningful guidance to juries charged with assessing damages. A common thread running throughout the centuries is how to best control verdicts with awards of excessive or inadequate damages in breach of contract actions. While the common law has certainly progressed from the early days of criminally punishing jurors who "incorrectly" assessed damages, it has created a modern maze of legal tangles and confusion for scholars and practitioners alike.
In order to properly understand how the American courts established the myriad of rules governing the assessment of non-economic damages in breach of contract actions, it is important to first explore the more general history of awarding damages under the common law.

questions.question: How has the common-law approach to awarding non-economic damages in breach of contract cases evolved from early Anglo-Saxon practice to modern American law?

How and why have courts developed limits, guidelines, and mechanisms (including control over juries) for assessing non-economic damages in contract disputes, producing the current fragmented and contradictory rules?

shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces modern shifts in modification doctrine away from formalistic consideration-based theories toward approaches addressing opportunism, and Paper B offers a long-run history of damages law from early common law to modern limitations—both engage with how remedial doctrines have developed over time.

papers.node_id: 11texwesleyanlrev225!!SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:FOREWORD: HADLEY V. BAXENDALE AND THE SEAMLESS WEB OF LAW
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:FOREWORD: HADLEY V. BAXENDALE AND THE SEAMLESS WEB OF LAW
papers.abstract:
Through a happy serendipity Frank Snyder, of Texas Wesleyan University School of Law, happened to be doing some research on the web when he ran across documents suggesting that an urban renewal project was rebuilding a flour mill in Gloucester, England. After some additional research, he concluded that this building, long known as "Priday's Mill," was, in fact, Joseph and Jonah Hadley's old City Flour Mills. By coincidence this happened to be on the eve of the 150th anniversary of the case in which that mill figured prominently, Hadley v. Baxendale.Though the case is likely known by name to most lawyers (as in "the rule of ..."), Gloucester officials, and even local historians were oblivious to the connection between their mill and this monument of contract law - until, that is, the fertile and creative Frank raised with them the possibility of co-sponsoring the sparkling conference on Hadley, "The Common Law of Contracts as a World Force in Two Ages of Revolution," that Frank organized in Gloucester in the summer of 2004.
If I tried to discuss all the papers, I would give them only a superficial reference; there are too many to cover with any depth. I did, however, want to discuss some fine examples of the conference and then consider the broader issues that they raise about Hadley as an artifact of the common law, both the common law of the mid-nineteenth century and the common law of the early twenty-first. As the title of the conference suggests, Hadley illustrates how wide-ranging and intertwined the common law is, both in geographic and cultural terms and in terms of its flexibility as the world around us changes.
. Hadley - and the Influence of Context (Herein of Richard Danzig, Pryor & Hoshauer, Joseph Perillo and Joseph Pothier)
At the risk of stating the obvious for many readers, please allow me to review Hadley briefly. On May 12, 1853, Joseph and Jonah Hadley, trading as the City Flour Mills, discovered that the crank shaft on their mill had broken, and the next day gave it to Pickford & Co., "the well-known carriers," to transport it across England to Greenwich "as a pattern for a new one."Pickfords misconsigned the shaft and delayed its replacement by five days, causing the Hadleys a considerable loss of profits. The Hadleys sued Pickfords's managing director, Joseph Baxendale, claiming damages of £ 300. Witnesses testified to a £ 120 loss, the jury gave damages of £ 50, and the Court of Exchequer, on a rule nisi (essentially a motion for new trial), gave a rule absolute, and remanded the case for a new trial, directing the trial judge to instruct the jury that "they ought not to take the loss of profits into consideration at all in estimating the damages."
To justify this instruction the court put forth the famous rule of Hadley v. Baxendale:
The [Hadleys'] loss of profits … cannot reasonably be considered such a consequence of the breach of contract as could have been fairly and reasonably contemplated by both the parties when they made this contract. For such loss would neither have flowed naturally from the breach of this contract in the great multitude of cases occurring under ordinary circumstances, nor were the special circumstances, which perhaps would have made it a reasonable and natural consequence of such breach of contract, communicated to or known by the defendants.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Loss Aversion and the Law

shared_topics.topic: the role of parties' expectations or reference points in assigning liability and shaping remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that recoverable losses turn on what was communicated and reasonably contemplated by the contracting parties (their shared expectations), and Paper B develops the idea that legal baselines and reference points (and loss aversion) determine whether harms are perceived as losses warranting redress, arguing the law both mirrors and shapes those baselines.

shared_topics.topic: historical and evolutionary explanations for why legal doctrines take their particular form
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats Hadley as an artifact of the common law that evolved across historical and cultural contexts and asks why the rule assumed its shape in two ages of revolution, while Paper B offers evolutionary and plaintiff-driven explanations for the centrality of loss aversion in law and uses historical-developmental reasoning to account for asymmetries across legal fields.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:Intentional Interference with Contract and the Doctrineof Efficient Breach: Fine Tuning the Notion of the ContractBreacher as Wrongdoer

shared_topics.topic: limits and adequacy of contract remedies (damages vs specific performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on when contract remedies (damages) fail to deter or make whole — identifying breaches for which damages are inadequate and specific performance unavailable — and argues tort interference should be assessed by whether the induced breach is one that contract law would (or would not) deter. Paper B analyzes Hadley v. Baxendale, a foundational rule defining which losses are recoverable in contract (thus delimitating the practical scope and adequacy of damages), illustrating how the common law draws boundaries on contractual remedies.

shared_topics.topic: how contract doctrine evolves to balance economic efficiency and normative notions of wrongdoing

Paper B situates Hadley historically and thematically to show how the common law of contract adapts across eras and contexts, reflecting shifting policy priorities (including notions of fairness, foreseeability, and economical allocation of risk).

BAXENDALE:RULES, PRINCIPLES, OR JUST WORDS?:THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS: ARE BROAD RINCIPLES BETTER THAN DETAILED RULES? AN EMPIRICAL INVESTIGATION 1 This Article is substantially based on research conducted with the support of the Australian Research Council (Linkage Program) and the Law and Justice Foundation of New South Wales. A full report is soon to be published as M.P. Ellinghaus and E.W. Wright (with M. Karras), Models of Contract Law: An Empirical Evaluation of Their Utility, L. & Just. Found. of N.S.W. (forthcoming).
papers.authors: M. P. Ellinghaus; E. W. Wright
papers.abstract:
The common law of contracts consists of precepts of varying levels of determinacy stated in non-canonical formin judgments given in the course of deciding real life disputes. It includes, at one end of aspectrum, rules that apply when relatively few facts are established. At the other end of the spectrum there are broad principles, the application of which requires wider-ranging investigation of the facts.
The appropriate level of determinacy of common law rules is the subject of a long-standing jurisprudential debate about the relative utility of "rules" and "principles." The debate includes controversy about the meaning of these two terms. We have adopted the rough-and-ready dichotomy of "broad principles" and "detailed rules" in the hope of transcending the established theoretical discourse of principles, standards, and rules, and their many derivatives and embellish-ments.
The greater level of indeterminacy that is a necessary feature of broad principles typically arouses concern among common lawyers, whose natural tendency is to mediate their application by elaborating ancillary and more detailed rules which, it is hoped, will deprive broad principles of open-ended operation and reduce the scope of forensic inquiry. This is particularly true in the law of contracts.
The debate about the relative utility of broad principles and detailed rules underlies a number of recurrent controversies of particular relevance to the enforcement of contract law. One example of these recurrent controversies is the ambit of broad standards of conduct such as good faith and unconscionability. The adoption of such standards is often characterised as pursuing pragmatism instead of principle, or abandoning general justice in favour of individualised dispute resolution.
This debate is also at the core of the current controversy in Australia and the UK over discretionary remedialism, that is, the view that courts should have discretion to award any remedy appropriate in an individual case, rather than being limited to specified remedies. Opponents of remedial discretion base their argument on the view that to discard specification in favour of discretion is to descend into an intuitive and unpredictable form of justice that ultimately involves abandonment of the rule of law. Proponents of discretionary remedialism, on the other hand, regard it as "a valid and valuable part of legal decision-making."
The case against the use of broad principles is that broad principles replace the finely tuned logic and specificity of detailed rules with generalized discretions, leading to unpredictable outcomes.It is said thatdetailed rules lead to more predictable and more just outcomes, with attendant gains in accessibility and efficiency. This view has dominated the development of the common law for at least two centuries. Most readers will be familiar at least in outline with this jurisprudential debate and will know their own position on it.
In this Article we are not endeavouring to engage in the debate at the level of theory. Rather, we are responding to the absence of any empirical verification of the assumptions on which the theory proceeds. Whether broad principles or detailed rules produce more just or more predictable outcomes is a question that has largely been left to the realm of speculative analysis. Additionally, no empirical studies have been conducted despite commentators' occasional requests for them.
In this Article we report the results of three experiments involving the participation of 1800 subjects (law students and non-law students) in the resolution of disputes and the evaluation of judgments, using three different law models: (1) the common law of contracts (Case Law); (2) UNIDROIT Principles of International Commercial Contracts, a model code published by the International Institute for the Unification of Private Law in 1994 (UPICC); (3) the Australian Contract Code, a model code, written by us, and published by the Law Reform Commission of Victoria in 1992 (ACC). The research on which this Article is based was prompted by our interest in the codification of Australian contract law. In order to demonstrate its relevance to the jurisprudential debate, it is necessary to give some description of each of these three models.

questions.question: Whether broad, indeterminate legal principles or detailed, determinate rules produce more predictable outcomes when people resolve contract disputes.
Whether broad principles or detailed rules lead to outcomes that decision-makers and observers perceive as more just or fair in contract disputes.

Whether different legal models (case-based precedent, a principles-based code, and a rules-based code) systematically alter the resolution of disputes and the evaluation of judgments (in terms of predictability and perceived justice).

matched_themes: Should parties and courts adopt fault-based remedial regimes that distinguish among breaches by reason when allocating remedies?
Should parties be presumptively permitted to contractually specify nonstandard damage remedies, or should courts retain authority to impose defaults?
How should courts treat and enforce stipulated remedies (liquidated damages clauses) versus substituting judicial remedies?
Do doctrinal differences across legal traditions produce measurable differences in contracting behavior and economic outcomes in practice?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83lawcontempprob151!!ARTICLE: BLACK MARKETS AND THE EXCHANGE STRUCTURE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BLACK MARKETS AND THE EXCHANGE STRUCTURE

shared_topics.topic: the relative merits of detailed rules versus broad principles in governing private transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts discrete legal disabilities and penalties with broader normative structures that channel exchanges (invoking property rules vs liability rules), while Paper B empirically tests the long‑running jurisprudential debate over whether detailed rules or broad principles produce more predictable and just outcomes in contract law.

shared_topics.topic: how law shapes which exchanges are permissible (and thereby creates black markets or governs contractual scope)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that legal disabilities and prescribed exchange terms fundamentally create 'black markets' by delimiting permissible exchanges, and Paper B examines how different legal models (common law rules versus model codes) define and enforce the permissible content and scope of contractual transactions.

shared_topics.topic: the trade‑off between predictability/determinacy and flexibility/evolution in transactional law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that exchange structures must be able to bend and evolve—cautioning against rigid criminal enforcement that would freeze norms—while Paper B directly probes whether detailed rules (predictable) or broad principles (flexible) better serve dispute resolution and adaptive justice in contract law.

shared_topics.topic: the role of remedies and enforcement instruments (criminal, civil, or discretionary remedies) in preserving exchange norms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes a spectrum of responses—legal disabilities, civil and criminal 'kickers,' and nonlegal sanctions—used to deter or disable transgressive exchanges, whereas Paper B focuses on the remedialism debate over whether courts should have discretionary remedies versus specified remedies and the effects of those choices on enforcement of contracts.

shared_topics.topic: normative bases for regulating or criminalizing exchanges (efficiency, fairness, and system survival)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques efficiency‑only accounts for criminalization and emphasizes fairness and the need to preserve an exchange structure (system survival) as justificatory grounds, and Paper B engages the normative implications of choosing rules or principles—weighing concerns about predictability, justice, and the rule of law in transactional regulation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1381!!ARTICLE: IN (PARTIAL) DEFENSE OF STRICT LIABILITY IN CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: IN (PARTIAL) DEFENSE OF STRICT LIABILITY IN CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: the suitability of detailed rules versus broad principles for contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically tests whether broad principles or detailed rules produce more predictable and just outcomes by comparing common-law case models to model codes; Paper B engages the same dichotomy by defending a rule-like strict-liability core of contract doctrine against more fault-based, principle-driven approaches.

shared_topics.topic: whether contract law should be fault-based or a no-fault/strict-liability regime
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses the rise of broad standards (e.g., good faith, unconscionability) that introduce fault-like inquiry into contract disputes; Paper B argues descriptively and normatively that contract law retains a no-fault or strict-liability core and explains why courts resist importing comparative-fault reasoning into core breach liability.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal design affects predictability, efficiency, and transaction costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats predictability and efficiency as central metrics in the rules-versus-principles debate and measures participants' evaluations empirically; Paper B argues that a strict-liability rule-set reduces contracting costs and better facilitates informal/relational contracting, advancing similar efficiency and predictability concerns.

shared_topics.topic: the scope and form of remedies and courts' remedial discretion (mitigation, damages, discretionary remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly examines the controversy over discretionary remedialism versus specified remedies as part of the rules/principles debate; Paper B analyzes remedial doctrines (e.g., mitigation, willful-breach adjustments) and documents courts' reluctance to use them to allocate fault or deter inefficient behavior, engaging the same remedial-policy questions.

shared_topics.topic: empirical or descriptive evaluation of how courts actually apply contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reports experimental empirical work comparing case-law outcomes to model codes to test jurisprudential assumptions; Paper B marshals case-sample evidence showing that courts apply a strict-liability core in practice and uses that descriptive account to support normative claims.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 116columlrev2005!!ARTICLE: ECONOMIC ANALYSIS OF CONTRACT LAW FROM THE INTERNAL POINT OF VIEW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ECONOMIC ANALYSIS OF CONTRACT LAW FROM THE INTERNAL POINT OF VIEW

shared_topics.topic: level of determinacy in contract law (detailed rules vs broad principles/standards)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how choice between bright-line rules and open-ended standards (e.g., UCC-style standards) shapes internalizers' and externalizers' interpretation and compliance, while Paper B empirically investigates whether broad principles or detailed rules produce more predictable and just outcomes in contract disputes.

shared_topics.topic: behavioral effects of rule form, including crowding out of moral motivations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops the theory that legal norms can ‘crowd out’ internalized moral motivations (changing performance vs breach choices), and Paper B examines, via experiments, whether indeterminate principles versus rules lead to different behavioral and adjudicative responses that affect parties' conduct and expectations.

shared_topics.topic: remedies and remedial discretion (expectation damages, stipulated damages, discretionary remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates how different remedial doctrines — expectation damages, stipulated damages, willful-breach penalties, and doctrines governing enforceability of modifications — influence internalizers' duty perceptions and behavior; Paper B directly addresses the controversy over discretionary remedialism versus specified remedies and tests how different remedial regimes perform in practice.

shared_topics.topic: empirical evaluation of legal models and the realism of behavioral assumptions about legal subjects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A appeals to theoretical considerations and empirical literature to argue that models assuming only self-interested 'externalizers' are unrealistic, while Paper B conducts large-scale empirical experiments comparing case law and model codes to test competing assumptions about how legal formulations work in practice.

shared_topics.topic: normative objectives of contract law (efficiency/social-welfare vs promissory morality/individualized justice)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts social-welfare-maximizing designs of contract law with approaches that vindicate promissory morality and examines how subject-conceptions affect optimal design, and Paper B frames the rules-vs-principles debate in normative terms (predictability, rule of law, individualized justice) and empirically assesses which approaches better realize those values.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 71vandlrev61!!ARTICLE: Contract as Commodified Promise
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contract as Commodified Promise

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations for shaping contract doctrine (rules/principles versus market/commercial justifications)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically probes the long‑standing jurisprudential debate over whether broad principles or detailed rules better promote justice and predictability in contract law; Paper B develops and defends a market‑based normative justification (commodification of promises) as the appropriate lens for structuring contract doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: criteria for enforceability of promises (which promises courts should enforce)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages with doctrines and standards (e.g. good faith, unconscionability, discretionary remedialism) that determine when courts will enforce agreements, while Paper B offers a theory—commercial promises as commodified promises—that specifies which promises deserve enforcement and proposes presumptions to that effect.

shared_topics.topic: design and limits of contractual remedies (discretionary remedialism versus specified remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses the controversy over allowing courts broad remedial discretion versus limiting remedies to specified categories and the predictability/justice tradeoffs; Paper B analyzes how treating promises as marketable goods bears on appropriate remedies and how remedial design can exacerbate or mitigate over‑commodification.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate doctrinal form (rules, standards, presumptions) and its effects on predictability and justice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically tests the practical consequences of applied doctrinal form—detailed rules versus broad principles—on decision‑making and outcomes; Paper B recommends doctrinal reforms (e.g., demoting consideration to a presumption, presumptive enforceability) and thereby engages the same question of whether doctrines should be rigid rules, standards, or presumptions.

shared_topics.topic: moral and societal limits on enforcement (illegality, anti‑commodification, unconscionability)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats doctrines like unconscionability and good faith as mechanisms that limit enforcement and reflect non‑market values, and debates whether broad principles improperly individualize justice; Paper B explicitly develops anti‑commodification norms to justify limits such as illegality and to explain why some promises (gifts, certain markets) should not be fully commodified or enforced.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1583!!ARTICLE: THE FAULT PRINCIPLE AS THE CHAMELEON OF CONTRACT LAW: A MARKET FUNCTION APPROACH
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE FAULT PRINCIPLE AS THE CHAMELEON OF CONTRACT LAW: A MARKET FUNCTION APPROACH

shared_topics.topic: the role of model codes and transnational instruments (UNIDROIT, CISG, PECL) in shaping domestic contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly uses the UNIDROIT Principles and a draft Australian Contract Code as comparator models in experiments about contract adjudication, while Paper B traces the historical and doctrinal influence of instruments like the CISG, UNIDROIT Principles and the Principles of European Contract Law on liability regimes and on harmonization between legal systems.

shared_topics.topic: the tradeoff between broad principles/standards and detailed rules in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically tests the jurisprudential debate over whether broad principles or detailed rules yield more predictable and just outcomes, and Paper B addresses an analogous tension by analyzing how doctrinal choices (strict liability vs fault and related doctrinal devices) instantiate more rule-like or principle-like approaches and why a nuanced mix is used.

shared_topics.topic: comparative/codification perspectives and the convergence of civil and common law approaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is motivated by questions about codification of Australian contract law and compares case law with model codes, while Paper B adopts a comparative law lens to show how civil and common‑law traditions have converged into nuanced mixtures (and into European/UNIDROIT instruments) rather than starkly different regimes.

shared_topics.topic: design and limits of remedies and sanctions for breach (remedial discretion vs specified sanctions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the controversy over discretionary remedialism versus specified remedies in contract adjudication, and Paper B examines remedial design such as Nachfrist/second‑chance doctrines and limits on sanctions under different liability regimes.

shared_topics.topic: grounding doctrinal choice in practical criteria (empirics, market expectations, or function)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A seeks empirical verification of theoretical claims about rules versus principles by running experiments, while Paper B argues for a 'market function' criterion to guide the balance between strict and fault liability—both privileging practical/functional guidance over purely abstract theorizing.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 82columlrev1365!!ARTICLE: In Defense of Money Damages for Breach of Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: In Defense of Money Damages for Breach of Contract

shared_topics.topic: whether courts should have remedial discretion versus specified remedies in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames and empirically investigates the contemporary jurisprudential debate over discretionary remedialism versus specified remedies (noting the UK/Australia controversy), while Paper B directly argues against making a single remedy (specific performance) the routine rule and defends preserving tailored money-damages rules and case-by-case flexibility.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate level of determinacy (rules versus broad principles) for contract doctrines and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is an empirical study explicitly comparing the utility of broad principles against detailed rules in contract law, and Paper B engages the same issue in substance by criticizing a universal rule of specific performance and urging selective, rule-based adjustments to money-damages doctrine rather than adopting an open-ended remedial principle.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs among efficiency, predictability, and fairness when selecting contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates claims that detailed rules produce greater predictability, efficiency, and justice compared with broad principles, and Paper B analyzes economic-efficiency and fairness arguments for and against making specific performance the normal remedy versus retaining or reforming money damages.

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations for contract relief (moral obligation, good faith, unconscionability) and their implications for remedy choice
shared_topics.justification: Paper B appeals to the moral obligation of promise as a justificatory strand for remedy design (and examines how different remedies reflect or strengthen promise ethics), while Paper A discusses substantive standards such as good faith and unconscionability and how adopting principled standards versus rules affects the pursuit of moral or pragmatic aims in remedies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 80brooklynlrev173!!ARTICLE: The Compensation Myth and U.C.C. Section 2-713
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Compensation Myth and U.C.C. Section 2-713

shared_topics.topic: remedial discretion versus specified remedies in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically interrogates the jurisprudential debate over whether courts should have broad remedial discretion or be constrained by specified rules, and Paper B examines the practical and normative consequences of a particular statutory remedy (U.C.C. §2-713) and whether courts should reinterpret rather than repeal or rigidly apply it.

shared_topics.topic: assumptions about damages (compensation, market-price formulas) and predictability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses claims that detailed rules produce more predictable and just outcomes in remedies, while Paper B directly challenges the foundational assumption that market-price/contract-price damages under §2-713 reliably yield compensation, exposing a shared concern with whether doctrinal devices actually produce predictable, compensatory results.

shared_topics.topic: codification versus common-law models and their normative implications
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares the common law of contracts with model codes (UNIDROIT Principles and an Australian Contract Code) to assess how codification affects determinacy and outcomes, and Paper B focuses on a key provision of a major codification (the U.C.C.) to explore how a statutory rule should be interpreted and integrated with broader contract doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: the role of judicial interpretation in shaping contract doctrine and avoiding doctrinal disruption
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how judges attempt to mediate broad principles by elaborating ancillary rules and how remedial discretion may impact the rule of law, while Paper B advocates interpretive strategies for §2-713 (rather than repeal) to avoid disruptive consequences and to guide courts toward pragmatic outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 17geomasonlrev483!!ARTICLE: HARM, AMBIGUITY, AND THE REGULATION OF ILLEGAL CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: HARM, AMBIGUITY, AND THE REGULATION OF ILLEGAL CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: judicial remedial discretion versus specified remedial rules in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically investigates the jurisprudential debate over discretionary remedialism versus specified remedies in contract disputes, while Paper B critiques the presumptive non-enforcement remedy (and the Restatement's fact‑driven exceptions) and proposes a more structured, harm‑sensitive remedial rule set.

shared_topics.topic: how legal ambiguity or indeterminacy affects ex ante contracting and deterrence
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies (by experiment) how varying levels of determinacy in rules versus principles affect predictability and decision‑making, and Paper B analyzes how uncertainty about whether a contract is illegal amplifies overdeterrence or underdeterrence and alters parties' willingness to innovate or transact.

shared_topics.topic: the tradeoff between broad principles and detailed rules (predictability versus flexibility/equity)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly tests the comparative utility of broad principles against detailed rules in producing predictable and just outcomes, and Paper B addresses a parallel tradeoff by arguing that the current broad, discretionary approach to illegal‑contract remedies can misalign incentives and that remedy design should better calibrate flexibility to harm.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of different legal frameworks (case law, codes, Restatement/statutes) on contracting incentives and market behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares three models — common law case law, the UPICC, and a model Australian Contract Code — to see how each shapes dispute resolution and predictability, while Paper B critiques statutory/regulatory vagueness and the Restatement's approach for their real‑world effects on markets (e.g., deterring innovative transactions like asset‑purchase financing).

compared_to.partner_node_id: 55amjcompl721!!ARTICLE: Why No "Efficient Breach" in the Civil Law?: A Comparative Assessment of the Doctrine of Efficient Breach of Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Why No "Efficient Breach" in the Civil Law?: A Comparative Assessment of the Doctrine of Efficient Breach of Contract

shared_topics.topic: the role of good faith and broad standards (e.g., unconscionability) in contract law and their tension with efficiency-based doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the civil‑law emphasis on good faith and the moral duty to perform undermines acceptance of the law‑and‑economics notion of efficient breach, while Paper B treats good faith and unconscionability as examples of broad principles whose adoption raises debate about predictability and utility in contract adjudication.

shared_topics.topic: how remedies (expectation damages versus specific performance and remedial discretion) shape incentives to perform or breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that the availability of monetary damages (and the expectation‑damages framework) in common law makes efficient breach feasible, whereas civil systems that favor specific performance impede it; Paper B empirically interrogates the costs and benefits of remedial specificity versus judicial remedial discretion in contract law.

shared_topics.topic: comparative analysis of common law versus codified/civil‑law or model code approaches to contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares the Anglo‑American common law origins of the efficient‑breach doctrine with civil‑law traditions (France, Germany) to explain doctrinal and cultural resistance, while Paper B directly compares common‑law case law with model codes (UNIDROIT, Australian Contract Code) to assess differences arising from codification and legal models.

shared_topics.topic: the tradeoff between determinacy (detailed rules) and flexibility (broad principles) and its effects on predictability and economic outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper B explicitly tests whether detailed rules or broad principles produce more predictable or just outcomes, and Paper A discusses how structural (doctrinal) and cultural elements of a legal system—such as rule‑like remedies or principle‑based duties—affect whether efficiency‑oriented doctrines like efficient breach can operate.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 17geomasonlrev483!!ARTICLE: HARM, AMBIGUITY, AND THE REGULATION OF ILLEGAL CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: HARM, AMBIGUITY, AND THE REGULATION OF ILLEGAL CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: design and scope of remedial rules (discretionary remedies versus specified remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates the long-standing debate over whether courts should have broad remedial discretion or be constrained to specified remedies as a central instance of the rules-vs-principles question in contract law; Paper B focuses on the remedial regime for illegal contracts (non-enforcement, restitution, etc.), arguing that the current default remedial rules are poorly aligned with the harms they are supposed to deter and should be restructured accordingly.

shared_topics.topic: legal indeterminacy (broad principles vs detailed rules) and its practical consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically interrogates the normative debate over broad principles versus detailed rules, emphasizing how indeterminacy affects predictability and judicial inquiry; Paper B shows how statutory and doctrinal ambiguity about when a contract is illegal amplifies overdeterrence and underdeterrence, linking legal vagueness to real-world contracting outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: incentive and deterrence effects of doctrinal choices on contracting behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the rules-versus-principles debate in part around whether different doctrinal forms produce more predictable, efficient, or just outcomes for parties (and tests this empirically); Paper B analyzes how specific remedies (and uncertainty about legality) shape parties' ex ante incentives to form or structure bargains and argues remedies should be chosen with their deterrent effects in mind.

shared_topics.topic: the role and costs of default rules / codification versus case-by-case adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates model codes (UNIDROIT, Australian Contract Code) versus common-law case law as competing doctrinal architectures and whether codification (more detailed rules) improves outcomes; Paper B highlights the social cost of immutable default remedial rules for illegal contracts—which parties cannot contract around—and calls for a more structured default regime that better accounts for harm and uncertainty.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 93valrev59!!ARTICLE: THE MISSING INTEREST: RESTORATION OF THE CONTRACTUAL EQUIVALENCE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE MISSING INTEREST: RESTORATION OF THE CONTRACTUAL EQUIVALENCE

shared_topics.topic: classification of contract remedies / interests (beyond expectation, reliance, restitution)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly challenges the dominant Fuller & Perdue tripartite schema by identifying a distinct 'restoration of contractual equivalence' interest; Paper B engages the same kind of conceptual question by empirically comparing different doctrinal models (common law case law vs model codes) that embody alternative ways of categorizing and applying remedial rules and principles.

shared_topics.topic: remedial discretion versus specified rules (predictability versus flexibility in relief)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for broader availability and combination of restoration remedies and discusses parties' election among remedies, while Paper B empirically studies the jurisprudential debate over broad principles versus detailed rules — including the controversy over discretionary remedialism — and its effects on predictability and justice.

shared_topics.topic: role of codes and legislative provisions versus judicial common law in shaping remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how statutory and treaty provisions (e.g., CISG Article 50) and judicial doctrines instantiate or obscure restorative remedies, and Paper B empirically compares the outcomes under common law case law, the UNIDROIT Principles, and a proposed Australian Contract Code to assess how different legal forms affect contract enforcement and remedies.

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations for choosing and evaluating remedies (rule‑of‑law, efficiency, justice, and party autonomy)

papers.abstract:
In 1854, the English Exchequer Court delivered the landmark case of Hadley v. Baxendale.That case provided, for the first time in the common law, a defined rule regarding the limitations on recovery of damages for breach of contract. It has been widely celebrated as a landmark in the law of contracts, and more widely as a triumph of the common law system. A little over a decade after it was decided, it had already become highly regarded, for Chief Baron Pollock stated in1866: "'[A] more extensive and accurate knowledge of decisions in our law books, and a more accurate power of analyzing and discussing them, and … a larger acquaintance with the exigencies of commerce and the business of life, never combined to assist at the formation of any decision.'"White and Summers state that knowledge of the case "'has become a sine qua non to second-year standing in law school.'"Richard Danzig notes the "pedagogical centrality" of the case and its characterization as a "judicial invention."Corbin has claimed that Hadley is "'more often cited as authority than any other case in the law of damages.'"A German scholar, Florian Faust, notes that Hadley's "fame is based on the fact that the case formally introduced the rule of foreseeability into the common law of contract … ."Perhaps most famously of all, Grant Gilmore stated that "Hadley v. Baxendale is still, and presumably always will be, a fixed star in the jurisprudential firmament."
Is this recognition deserved? To some extent, inarguably it is. But is the judicial "inventiveness" ascribed to the Hadley court fully warranted? Was it created out of whole-cloth by ingenious practitioners of the common law? This Article seeks to answer that question, though the title perhaps eliminates any attempt at suspense, for the civil law was most assuredly referenced for the Hadley rule. After this initial introduction, Part II of this Article will discuss the facts and holding of the Hadley case, and describe fully the civilian sources for the rules announced by the Hadley court. Part III will discuss generally the concept of legal transplants, and the interrelation between the development of a particular legal rule and the context of the society in which it is promulgated. Part IV will present, by way of illustration and example only, a handful of other instances in which Anglo-American courts have borrowed from the civil law for purposes of "creating" new common law doctrine. Part V will offer some concluding remarks.

questions.question: Was a prominent common-law contractual limitation on damages an original judicial invention within the common-law tradition, or was it derived from preexisting civil-law sources?
To what extent and by what methods do common-law courts borrow concepts from civil-law systems when creating or shaping new doctrines?
How do social, economic, and institutional contexts affect whether and how legal rules are transplanted from civil-law traditions into the common law?

papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:THE BOUNDARIES OF CONTRACT IN A GLOBAL ECONOMY:HADLEY'S LIABILITY-LIMITING AND COMMERCE-ENHANCING PRINCIPLES APPLIED IN THE BRITISH COMMONWEALTH AND THE U.S.A
papers.abstract:
The venerable decision, of which we here celebrate the sesquicentennial, can be broadly read as necessary to aid nascent industry trying to prosper in the middle years of the Industrial Revolution. Professor Grant Gilmore's prediction of the impending death of contracts including consequential damageswas premature in Anglo-American jurisprudence. Just as Sir Henry Maine noted the movement in the ancient regime from status (slave, freeman, seignior, serf) to contract, as inferior types like married women and the baseborn acquired, at a glacial pace, the right to contract independently;thecentury marked movement from contract to codification of legal and equitable principles. Witness as codification the British Sale of Goods Act 1893, as subsequently expanded, and the U.S. Uniform Commercial Code. Once a contract for the sale of goods exists, unless the parties have agreed otherwise, statutes step in to codify the rules of Hadley v. Baxendale,which sets limits on "consequential" or "special" damages.
Assuming that the ratio decidendi (American rationale) of the revered British case of Hadley v. Baxendale is to limit business liability, it is worth considering, first, the impact of a particular legal regime's liability-limiting rules on a multinational company's decision of where to locate a particular firm. Does the firm go where the costs of litigation are relatively smaller and, if so, what relationship exists between lowered costs of litigation and liability-limiting rules such as Hadley v. Baxendale? Second, it is worth considering whether a particular regime's view on data privacy is based upon intent to limit business' liability, or whether the regime values personal privacy more than business' right to collect and disseminate data that might be considered property of the human data subject? Because the rationale of Hadley v. Baxendale may apply to both the business-location decision and a legal regime's view on data privacy in E-commerce, this paper examines a possible nexus between Hadley v. Baxendale itself and: (a) the business-location decision; and (b) the protection or disregard of data privacy.
The conceit of this piece is that society stands roughly at the same place regarding international commerce, including, particularly, E-commerce and related data-privacy issues, in the year 2004, as the common-law world stood regarding burgeoning industry in the Industrial Revolution when the British court rendered the fateful decision in Hadley v. Baxendale. The point is that Hadley v. Baxendale's limitation of damages to foreseeable damages allowed the rapid growth of commerce in the middle years of the industrial revolution, while the emergence of an international data privacy commitment will allow for the growth of E-commerce in the digital age, at least in the long term, by ultimately fostering buyer confidence in the integrity of internet sales of goods and services. Likewise, the mercantile concern with limitation of litigation costs in a global market will ensure the continued relevance and applicability of the rationale of Hadley v. Baxendale.

questions.question: Whether limits on business liability and predictable liability rules affect multinational firms' choices about where to locate operations (i.e., do firms prefer jurisdictions with lower litigation costs or narrower exposure to damages).

Whether a legal regime's orientation toward limiting business liability is associated with weaker legal protection for personal data (i.e., do liability-focused regimes favor business data-collection and dissemination over individual privacy).
Whether imposing limits on recoverable damages and creating predictable liability rules promotes the growth of commerce and e-commerce by increasing buyer confidence in online transactions.

Do doctrinal differences across legal traditions produce measurable differences in contracting behavior and economic outcomes in practice?

papers.node_id: 20hofstralrev757!!SYMPOSIUM: THE FUTURE OF LAW AND ECONOMICS: POST-REVOLUTIONARY LAW AND ECONOMICS: A FOREWORD TO THE SYMPOSIUM *© 1992 Anthony D'Amato..
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: THE FUTURE OF LAW AND ECONOMICS: POST-REVOLUTIONARY LAW AND ECONOMICS: A FOREWORD TO THE SYMPOSIUM *© 1992 Anthony D'Amato..
papers.abstract:
The Lanec (short for Law and Economics) movement of the 1970s hit the legal landscape like a nuclear device and permanently irradiated it.  A couple of decades later, as we sift through the fallout, we are entitled to ask whether anything fundamental has changed.  Every contributor to this Symposium seems to answer yes.  Maybe they're like the book reviewer who believes deep in her heart that the book is worthless, but if she reveals it the editor will conclude that there is no point in printing her review.  Contributor Leonard Jaffee is infuriated and outraged by the vision that Lanec provides,Judge Richard Posner patiently defends it,George Cohen is troubled by awarp in the vision,and Linz Audainand Linda Schwartzsteindoggedly search for ways of linking Lanec to other recent jurisprudential movements in order to prove it guiltless by association.  All of these writers seem to feel that Lanec makes a difference.
Let me put my own biases on the table, if they're not apparent already.In general I applaud the greater precision that has come to legal studies through economics as well as through the other social sciences.  Since many judicial decisions are proclaimed to be based on policy considerations, at minimum we owe judges sound empirical research and statistical clarity regarding social policies.  Although I reserve judgment on whether, in any given case, a party's fate ought to be decided on the basis of general social policy (are judges in the social transfer-payment business?), or evenwhetherbroad policies can constrain judicial decision-making,at least one cannot seriously dispute the proposition thatifpolicy considerations are to be assumed to be relevant to judicial decisions, they ought to be grounded upon hard data accurately presented.
But has Lanec changed the nature of the law?  I'm not sure that it has lived up to the hopes or hypes of its original enthusiasts.  The initial hope -- one that I once shared -- is to take the subjectivity out of judicial decision-making.Lanec says this can be accomplished by asimple compared quantification: comparing the values of the parties by counting dollars.  If the defendant values the decision more than the plaintiff, that is a good Lanec-reason to award the decision to the defendant.  On the other hand, if the defendant in a tort action, for example, was the cheapest accident avoider, that is a good Lanecreason to award the decision to the plaintiff.If in a child-custody case the father is willing to spend more dollars on the child than the mother is willing to spend, award custody to the father.  The invisible hand of the marketplace, with some help from its Lanec practitioners, thus controls the decisions in the courtroom, and not idiosyncratic judges.  What Lanec promises us is predictability and a thriving economy.

questions.question: Whether the law-and-economics movement has materially changed judicial decision-making and the fundamental character of the law.

Whether reducing disputes to monetary comparisons of parties' valuations (a dollar-counting approach) removes subjectivity from judicial decision-making and produces more predictable and economically efficient outcomes.
Whether judicial decisions that rest on policy considerations should be-and are-grounded in sound empirical and statistical social-science research.

matched_themes: Should parties and courts adopt fault-based remedial regimes that distinguish among breaches by reason when allocating remedies?

Should remedies and contract law be structured to preserve conditions necessary for moral agency and promissory responsibility, rather than treating promises solely as instruments of economic cooperation?
Should a uniform, single damages measure apply across contract types, or should damages be heterogeneous (multi-tiered or tailored) depending on parties, transactions, and contexts?
What are the conceptual and methodological limits of the law-and-economics approach, and has the movement materially changed judicial decision-making?

papers.node_id: 20hofstralrev941!!SYMPOSIUM: THE FUTURE OF LAW AND ECONOMICS: THE NEGLIGENCE-OPPORTUNISM TRADEOFF IN CONTRACT LAW.
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: THE FUTURE OF LAW AND ECONOMICS: THE NEGLIGENCE-OPPORTUNISM TRADEOFF IN CONTRACT LAW.
papers.abstract:
Over the past two decades, Law and Economics scholars have developed two different analytical approaches to contract law without examining the relationship between them.  The first approach, based on the idea of the "least-cost-avoider" developed in tort law, aims to deter "negligent" contracting behavior by punishing a contracting party who fails to take cost-justified precautions.  The second approach aims to deter "opportunistic" contracting behavior by punishing a contracting party who affirmatively acts contrary to some contractual expectation or social norm.Typically, scholars focus on one approach or the other in their work.  Rarely do scholars combine thetwo approaches.Never have scholars combined them in any systematic way.
This paper will develop a general fault-based economic theory of contract law that combines the least-cost-avoider and opportunism approaches.  In many cases, these approaches point toward the same outcome, but often they conflict and present what I call the negligence-opportunism tradeoff: the legal rule must favor the deterrence of one type of behavior over the other.  The negligence-opportunism tradeoff captures to a large degree the fundamental tension in contract law largely ignored by economists but traditionally recognized by lawyers: the tension between individual freedom of contract and social regulation of the marketplace.In resolving this tradeoff, I argue on efficiency grounds that the law should place a presumptive priority on deterring potentially opportunistic behavior over deterring potentially negligent behavior.  To give priority to deterring negligence over deterring opportunism -- which many economists often implicitly advocate -- perversely rewards deceitful sleaziness while often punishing hapless incompetence, and cracks the foundation of trust necessary forefficient contracting behavior to occur.
My broader thesis is that focusing on this tradeoff leads to a revision of traditional thinking about contract law.  Traditional contract law is organized from a litigator's perspective: Was a valid contract formed?; Was it breached?; Is there any excuse?; What remedies are available?  Doctrines have been carved out based on this schema: offer and acceptance, consideration, conditions, mistake, impossibility, and damages.  But the traditional approach often blinds us to the underlying economic relationships and doctrinal similarities.  An economic approach to contract can illuminate these relationships and similarities.  Courts and scholars should shift attention away from their obsession with what kinds of promises the law should enforce.  Instead, the economic approach I advocate suggests that what matters more are the parties' reasons for making and breaking their contracts.  Formulating contract doctrine along these lines will lead us to create and enforce contract law that is more efficient -- and more just.

questions.question: Whether placing presumptive priority on deterring opportunistic contracting behavior (over deterring negligent contracting behavior) produces greater economic efficiency and preserves the trust needed for efficient contracting.

Whether organizing contract law around parties' reasons for making and breaking agreements (a fault-based, economic approach) yields more efficient and just outcomes than organizing it around formal questions of promise formation and remedies.

matched_themes: Should courts allow punitive or other extracompensatory damages for willful or abusive contract breaches, and what are the efficiency and fairness trade-offs?
Should parties and courts adopt fault-based remedial regimes that distinguish among breaches by reason when allocating remedies?

Does the promisor's motive for breaching (loss-avoiding vs gain-seeking) affect how much compensation promisees need to accept nonperformance?
Should the availability of legal remedies or contractual incompleteness change the moral assessment of a party who breaches under unanticipated circumstances?

Should remedies and contract law be structured to preserve conditions necessary for moral agency and promissory responsibility, rather than treating promises solely as instruments of economic cooperation?
How should remedial and enforcement rules be structured to achieve efficient behavior when populations include both internalizers and externalizers?
Do courts consider the breaching party's blameworthiness or opportunistic behavior when selecting among compensatory remedies?
To what extent should moral blameworthiness and non-economic considerations influence the design and application of contract remedies?

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Myth that Promisees Prefer Supracompensatory Remedies: An Analysis of Contracting for Damage Measures.

shared_topics.topic: deterrence targets in contract law (negligence versus opportunism/exploitation)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze which kinds of conduct legal rules should deter: Paper A formulates a negligence–opportunism tradeoff and argues for prioritizing deterrence of opportunistic (exploitative) breaches, while Paper B evaluates remedies (penalty clauses, punitive damages, specific performance) as instruments to deter or permit exploitation and asks whether courts should block promisees from obtaining supracompensatory relief to prevent opportunistic extortion.

shared_topics.topic: efficiency-based reform of contract doctrine and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both use law-and-economics reasoning to recommend doctrinal change: Paper A proposes restructuring contract law around fault and parties' reasons for breach to maximize efficient contracting, and Paper B applies efficiency logic to argue for abolishing certain judicial controls on liquidated damages and for restoring/reshaping rules on punitive damages and specific performance.

shared_topics.topic: the relevance of parties' incentives and preferences for designing default rules
shared_topics.justification: Both papers insist that rules should account for how parties actually behave and what they prefer: Paper A focuses on parties' reasons for making and breaking contracts as the proper basis for doctrine, and Paper B empirically/analytically claims promisees prefer compensatory (not supracompensatory) remedies and that those preferences should inform whether courts restrict contractual terms.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate scope of judicial review or policing of contractual terms and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the question of how actively courts should intervene in private contracts: Paper A critiques traditional litigator-centered doctrines and calls for doctrinal design that better targets undesirable behavior, affecting enforcement priorities, while Paper B explicitly argues against special judicial policing of liquidated-damage and specific-performance clauses and defends limiting state intervention in remedy design.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 35loyuchilj555!!ARTICLE:Against Supercompensation: A Proposed Limitation on the Land Buyer's Right To Elect Between Damages and Specific Performance as a Remedy for Breach of Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:Against Supercompensation: A Proposed Limitation on the Land Buyer's Right To Elect Between Damages and Specific Performance as a Remedy for Breach of Contract

shared_topics.topic: deterring opportunistic behavior by contract parties through remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how plaintiffs can opportunistically time an election between specific performance and damages to capture post‑breach market gains, producing supercompensation; Paper B develops a general negligence–opportunism framework and argues contract law should be structured to prioritize deterrence of opportunistic breaches.

shared_topics.topic: the efficiency of the choice between expectation damages and specific performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically and doctrinally analyzes how the plaintiff's ability to elect damages or specific performance in land sales produces inefficient overcompensation, while Paper B critiques traditional remedial schemas and urges that remedy design be judged by economic efficiency (focusing on the parties' reasons for breach and the incentives created by different remedies).

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal reform of contract law grounded in law-and-economics
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes a concrete limitation on the election between remedies to eliminate supercompensation, and Paper B argues for reorienting contract doctrines (formation, breach, excuses, remedies) around an economic fault-based account that better aligns incentives and prevents opportunism.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and incentives in contract disputes (who bears market and performance risk)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how remedy election lets plaintiffs shift market risk away from themselves (capturing upside, avoiding downside), creating perverse incentives; Paper B addresses how rules (assigning liability to least‑cost avoiders or deterring opportunists) determine who bears precaution and breach risks and thereby shape contracting behavior.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 97valrev1939!!ARTICLE: THE MYTH OF EFFICIENT BREACH: NEW DEFENSES OF THE EXPECTATION INTEREST
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE MYTH OF EFFICIENT BREACH: NEW DEFENSES OF THE EXPECTATION INTEREST

shared_topics.topic: remedy design (damages v. specific performance) as the mechanism for allocating breach gains and deterring nonperformance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly debates liability-rule (expectation damages) versus property-rule (specific performance) and restitutionary alternatives, defending damages as the appropriate default; Paper B addresses how contract rules and remedies should punish and deter opportunistic breaches versus negligent conduct, which has direct implications for whether courts favor monetary damages, injunctions, or other sanctions to shape behavior.

shared_topics.topic: efficiency-based economic justification of contract doctrine (efficient breach, least-cost-avoider, and transactional incentives)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes and critiques the economic theory of 'efficient breach' and uses Coasean reasoning to justify liability-rule defaults; Paper B brings in the least-cost-avoider/tort-style analysis and frames a negligence–opportunism tradeoff, using efficiency arguments to recommend prioritizing deterrence of opportunism in designing rules.

shared_topics.topic: the role of transaction costs, renegotiation, and investments in choosing default contractual rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how transaction costs, the possibility of renegotiation, and party investments undermine the naive Coase assumptions and thereby justify liability-rule defaults; Paper B's negligence–opportunism framework likewise depends on bargaining and enforcement costs (and who can avoid costs) to determine whether rules should focus on deterring negligence or opportunism.

shared_topics.topic: deterring opportunism, promissory morality, and the preservation of commercial trust
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages with moral critiques that liability rules permit 'efficient breach' and argues that damages are consistent with promissory norms in commercial settings; Paper B centers the prevention of opportunistic, trust‑undermining behavior as a primary goal of contract law and argues rules should prioritize deterrence of such behavior to sustain efficient market relationships.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107michlrev1445!!ARTICLE: THE FAULT THAT LIES WITHIN OUR CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE FAULT THAT LIES WITHIN OUR CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: whether contract law is properly characterized as strict liability or inherently fault-based

shared_topics.topic: how parties' intent, fault, and reasons for breach should figure into doctrinal design and liability rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques simplistic treatments of contractual intent and the relationship between intent and fault, and Paper B argues contract doctrine should focus on parties' reasons for making and breaking promises (deterring opportunism vs negligence) rather than formalistic categories like offer/acceptance.

shared_topics.topic: the normative and efficiency tradeoffs in using fault to deter different types of wrongful conduct in contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the normative importance of fault and warns against efforts to 'exorcize' fault from contract law, while Paper B analyzes the negligence–opportunism tradeoff and argues for prioritizing deterrence of opportunistic behavior on efficiency and trust grounds.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 52tullrev659!!ARTICLE: Dependent Promises in the History of Leases and Other Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Dependent Promises in the History of Leases and Other Contracts

shared_topics.topic: whether a breach by one party justifies the other's refusal to perform (dependent vs. independent promises / conditions precedent)
